I have personally made multiple calls and reports to my local FAA person Tom Fecks. He guided me to http://faa-aae.my.site.com/s/hotline to make my concerns official. I have not once heard anything back about my allegations. These drones are a major safety concern to rail safety. Rail yards are incredibly soft targets for terrorism and with managers constantly flying drones over our heads, we will become desensitized to their presence. There’s plenty of videos online now showing how effective drones are in combat scenarios and we don’t need anything like that happening in America. Another thing is rail worker safety. Managers crash these drones occasionally and it’s only a matter of time before a worker gets hit with one. Another safety concern is if workers are always scanning the skies for the drones, that takes their attention off of what the should be focused on which is moving rail cars. This more than likely has already caused injury somewhere in the country. We must keep our railroads and our country safe WITHOUT flying drones around active rail facilities.
Drone operation in the rail industry is a distraction in an already dangerous environment.  When crew are being monitored or followed by drones, the drone becomes the focus and not the task at hand.

My main concerns with this regulation are:

1. Drones are already highly regulated

Each year, more regulations are proposed that would restrict legitimate unmanned aircraft usage further. The reason behind the regulations is apparent—people are constantly violating existing regulations. However, why will people decide to honor new regulations surrounding “critical” infrastructure?

Every time new regulations are introduced, it only hurts the people who are legally operating an unmanned aircraft under 14 CFR Part 107 regulations or USC 44809 recreational exception.

2. This regulation will hurt businesses

My first point with this regulation is the impact it will have on legitimate businesses that use drones for business functions. On a daily basis, a business might need to operate a drone to gather photos. An inspection company might need to photograph the roof of a home for insurance claims. With this regulation, if there’s a “critical” power grid two houses down, that business would be unable to perform their duties from the sound of this regulation.

3. The inconsistency between manned and unmanned aircraft restrictions

I was recently traveling through the Rocky Mountains. As expected, Grand Teton National Park is off limits to drone operations. Ironically, amidst this National Parks is an KJAC airport with commercial jets landing and taking off frequently, disturbing the environment. Yet, drones which are significantly quieter, smaller, and less dangerous are prohibited.

My point here is this: If “critical” infrastructure is to be off limits to drones, it should also be off limits to manned aircraft. In reality, a regulation is not going to stop someone with malicious intent from flying a drone or aircraft into an area. A criminal is not going to stop committing a crime because a law exists. “Critical” infrastructure should be off limits to manned aircraft as well.

A manned aircraft has the capacity to do immense damage to critical infrastructure like a dam or power grid. A drone wouldn’t be able to do comparable damage unless it was equipped with weaponry (which violates other FAA regulations).

4. Requests through FAA drone zone to fly in controlled airspace already takes 90+ days for approval
When LAANC approval is unavailable in controlled airspace, authorization had to be done through the FAA drone zone website. FAA drone zone takes well over 90 days to be approved or rejected. If it is required to give 90+ days of notice to operate within “critical” infrastructure, that becomes unreasonable. Waiting a quarter of the year to conduct compliant and legal aerial imagery for business purposes is ridiculous.

As I understand it, the proposed regulations would be a notification-based system rather than approval-based. This helps partially with this problem, but there are two remaining questions I see:
1. If I launch a drone and a “critical” infrastructure is added to the airspace in my flight path in the middle of an operation, would I be in violation of this new regulation?
2. How much notice must Part 107 operators provide to facilities? Even a small delay can directly impact businesses. It seems appropriate that it be allowable to submit a notice anytime prior to the start of the operation.

5. If someone is intent on damaging “critical” infrastructure, this regulation won’t stop them

Currently there are two categories of drone operators (outside of cases where the FAA makes exceptions). You either fly under the standard 14 CFR Part 107 regulations or USC 44809 recreational exception. Anyone operating a drone outside of those two cases is already violating the law.

If a rule is added to restrict the airspace near “critical” infrastructure, who do you think is going to follow that rule? Those who are already legally operating drones under 14 CFR Part 107 regulations or USC 44809 do not have the intention to damage “critical” infrastructure. The people who would fly near and potentially damage that infrastructure are those who are already breaking the existing laws. Since they’re already breaking the law, why would they honor a new law that protects “critical” infrastructure?

The proposed regulations would only hurt those who respect and operate in compliance with existing regulations.

comments.commenter: Comment from Virginia Department of Aviation
comments.comment_text:
Commonwealth of Virginia Department of Aviation
Memorandum of Agreement - June 18, 2026

RE: Federal Aviation Administration: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Designation - Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility

To Whom It May Concern:

The Virginia Department of Aviation has reviewed the Federal Aviation Administration: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility. Following our review, the Department have the following comments.

1. The text proposes the applicant for a UAFR be the facility operator or proprietor be the applicant and the FAA would ultimately determine whether or not to issue the UAFR. The Department proposes a review process similar to that involving a 7460 Airspace Evaluation application, where the FAA receives the application from the applicant but circulates to the states and other stakeholders for comment. This seems consistent with an existing FAA process and would allow entities more familiar with site to weigh in on factors that may not be included in the application.

2. There should be additional consideration for the states themselves to be the applicant for a UAFR that is expedited in the event of a state of emergency. Although consideration is given to first responder operations, a more widespread UAFR may be a necessity during a regional or statewide emergency event such as a hurricane.

3. FAA has indicated they are seeking input and relative data on Remote ID. Additionally, the NPRM indicates that the information on UAFRs will be posted on a website. Several states are standing up UAS Flight Information Exchanges (FIX's). These states include: Virginia, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Ohio, and Oklahoma. While others are looking into these data sharing websites that depict drone operations within a specific area. We suggest in addition to merely posting the UAFRs on a website that they share the data with the State FIX's to provide an accurate operational picture for the operators in order to reduce potential incursions while the FAA would be receiving data from the FIX's sensors on the accuracy and range of Remote ID transmitters.

4. The NPRM limits the UAFR boundaries to the property lines of the site. While this does cause the least impact to the NAS, the Department suggests a tiered approach. While the property boundaries may be sufficient for event venues and places of gathering, it may not be sufficient for critical or defense facilities. An example is a UAS operating above the street just outside the Huntington Ingalls Shipyard in Newport News where there have been known espionage attempts. With the limits being bound by the property lines, a UAS can operate just above and beyond the security fence and be operating within the law. A tiered boundary based on the infrastructure itself versus the property boundary may be more in line with the intent of the UAFR.

5. The NPRM states the applicant should provide the information to ensure compliance with NEPA. The Department suggests, similarly to our response in Comment #1, that the application be shared with the appropriate state agencies to ensure compliance.

6. The NPRM references the 500 commercial service airports but do not make any reference to the general aviation airports. The Department suggests the air traffic pattern and the approach and departure corridors up to a predetermined altitude be included as eligible permanent UAFR areas. The approach and departure corridors can coincide with the approach and departure paths of existing or planned instrument approach and departure procedures.

Sincerely,
S. Scott Denny
Advanced Air Mobility Program Manager
Virginia Department of Aviation

comments.commenter: Comment from Gerrittsen Beach Fire Department / Volunteer Firemen’s Association of the City of New York
comments.comment_text:
To the Federal Aviation Administration:

I am submitting this supplemental comment today, June 22, 2026, to add to the comment I previously submitted on May 7, 2026.

I support the FAA's goal. Sensitive facilities need protection from careless, unsafe, or malicious drone activity. Nobody should use a drone to interfere with emergency operations, harass people, fly recklessly, deliver contraband, or create a safety issue near critical infrastructure or public safety locations.

Since my original comment, New York has enacted a drone law that appears to address some of the same facility protection concerns as this UAFR rulemaking (NYS ARTICLE 280
Offenses Relating to Unlawful Use of a Drone). That law creates a new prohibited space concept above and within 500 feet around certain locations, including fire department stations, police stations, dispatch stations, large gatherings, critical infrastructure, and schools.

I understand the purpose behind that law. My concern is that a 500 foot buffer around broad categories of locations could function like a state created no fly area, even though FAA is proposing a federal UAFR process for facility based UAS restrictions. That could unintentionally box out legitimate public safety drone operations.

The Gerrittsen Beach Fire Department operates a public safety drone program under Part 107. We use drones for brush fires, search and rescue, water rescue support, fireground and hazmat overwatch, storm checks, damage assessment, training, and mutual aid. These are public safety flights used to protect life and property.

In New York City, everything is close together. Firehouses, police facilities, schools, utilities, bridges, waterways, critical infrastructure, large gatherings, residential neighborhoods, and emergency response areas can all overlap. If federal UAFRs, state prohibited space rules, and local concerns overlap, public safety drone operators may not know which rule controls, who can approve the flight, whether FAA approval is enough, or whether an FAA compliant operation still creates a state issue.

During an emergency, that confusion can slow down operations meant to protect the public. Public safety departments should not have to guess during a brush fire, search and rescue call, water rescue, storm event, or hazmat incident whether they are about to violate a state airspace rule while operating under FAA rules and incident command.

That is why the FAA's UAFR process matters. Facility based drone restrictions should be handled through one clear FAA managed process. States and local governments should still be able to enforce laws against reckless, criminal, harassing, contraband related, or emergency interfering drone use. But creating airspace restrictions around facilities is different and should be coordinated through FAA.

I am especially concerned about recognized volunteer fire departments and similar emergency response organizations. Volunteer fire departments may not fit neatly into language written for government or law enforcement agencies, but we are still part of the emergency response system. When operating under incident command or supporting a local emergency response, the rules need to give us a practical way to operate.

I respectfully ask FAA to make the final rule clear that:

1. Public safety Part 107 operations should be allowed within standard UAFRs when connected to emergency response, incident assessment, training, preparedness, mapping, equipment checks, or safe launch and recovery.

2. Standard UAFRs should remain notice based, not permission based, for legitimate public safety operations.

3. During emergencies, public safety operators should be allowed to notify the facility as soon as reasonably possible when advance notice is not practical.

4. Recognized volunteer fire departments and emergency response organizations operating under incident command should be treated the same as other public safety operators for notification purposes.

5. FAA should explain how UAFRs interact with state and local drone laws so public safety operators are not caught between conflicting rules.

6. State and local governments may enforce laws against reckless, criminal, harassing, contraband related, or emergency interfering drone use, but facility based airspace restrictions should be handled through FAA.

7. UAFR applicants should consider impacts on public safety launch sites, recovery areas, training areas, mutual aid operations, and emergency response corridors.

The bottom line is simple. I support protecting sensitive facilities and stopping reckless or malicious drone use. But the final FAA rule should make sure public safety drone programs are not accidentally boxed out by overlapping federal, state, and local restrictions.

Respectfully submitted,

Daniel Cavanagh
Chief of Department
Gerrittsen Beach Fire Department
President
Volunteer Firemen's Association of the City of New York

As a railroad switchman with over 20 years of service, I have serious concerns regarding the use of drones by railroad management for operational testing and employee observation.

Railroad work requires constant situational awareness and focus. Employees must continuously monitor moving equipment, track conditions, radio communications, vehicle traffic, weather conditions, and the actions of fellow crew members. Any unnecessary distraction can reduce an employee’s ability to safely perform these duties.

The presence of drones overhead creates a significant distraction. Rather than allowing employees to focus entirely on the safe execution of switching operations, workers become aware that they are being continuously monitored from above. This can shift attention away from the task at hand and toward the drone itself, reducing concentration on actual hazards present in the work environment.

Additionally, drones are often perceived not as tools for evaluating overall operational safety, but as tools used to identify minor technical violations or “gotcha” situations. This can encourage employees to focus excessively on avoiding small procedural errors rather than maintaining broad situational awareness and safe work practices.

For example, it is similar to issuing a speeding citation for driving 25.5 mph in a 25 mph zone while ignoring the overall context of safe driving behavior. When employees believe they are being scrutinized primarily for minor infractions, their attention can become divided between performing the work and anticipating how their actions appear from a drone’s perspective.

Human factors research has consistently shown that distractions and divided attention increase risk in safety-sensitive occupations. The railroad industry should carefully consider whether drone-based observation may unintentionally create new hazards by diverting employees’ attention from the operational environment.

My concern is that increased focus on drone surveillance, rather than on the safe performance of railroad duties, could ultimately contribute to an accident or injury. Any safety program should prioritize improving situational awareness and hazard recognition, not introduce additional distractions into an already high-risk work environment.

comments.commenter: Comment from HUNTRAK Defense Systems, Inc.
comments.comment_text:
Re: Docket FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03; FR Doc. 2026-08943, "Designation - Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility"; implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016.

HUNTRAK Defense Systems, Inc. respectfully submits these comments on the FAA's NPRM implementing Section 2209. HUNTRAK is an early-stage, U.S.-based developer of passive, receive-only, multi-sensor systems for small uncrewed-aircraft-system (UAS) detection and airspace awareness. Its work is limited to detection and situational awareness; it does not transmit, jam, decrypt, disable, interdict, or otherwise affect any aircraft or signal.

HUNTRAK supports a transparent, consistent process for eligible fixed-site facilities to request Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) while preserving the FAA's authority over the National Airspace System. We support the proposed Section 74.56 requirement that eligible facilities be able, directly or through a contracted service, to receive broadcast Remote Identification messages.

We respectfully recommend that the final rule:

1. Expressly recognize lawful passive detection. Clarify that new Part 74 does not prohibit fixed-site operators from deploying lawful, passive, receive-only detection technologies for situational awareness, compliance monitoring, and incident documentation, and that passive detection confers no airspace-control or enforcement authority.

2. Treat the passive-RF Remote ID minimum as a floor, not a ceiling. Because Remote ID reception alone cannot detect non-cooperative aircraft (drones not broadcasting Remote ID, or autonomous or RF-silent drones), confirm that more advanced lawful passive approaches (acoustic, electro-optical, infrared, and multi-sensor fusion) are acceptable means of meeting and exceeding the requirement.

3. Maintain a clear distinction between detection and mitigation. Passive detection receives information without transmitting toward, interfering with, controlling, or disabling an aircraft or signal. Mitigation raises materially different legal, safety, and spectrum considerations. The rule should address the two separately and make clear that authorizing a UAFR does not authorize mitigation.

4. Provide an accessible, workable application process usable by smaller facilities as well as large operators. Consistent with Section 74.56(4), the FAA should permit reliance on qualified contracted monitoring services while keeping responsibility for the UAFR with the eligible operator or proprietor.

5. Address Remote Identification data retention proportionately. If retention is required, set a reasonable, clearly-defined period with privacy, cybersecurity, and access-control safeguards; hosted platforms can support compliant, auditable retention. Any requirement should be proportionate to the cost burden on smaller facilities.

6. Use technology-neutral, standards-based requirements rather than favoring a single sensor type, protocol, or vendor; emphasize measurable functions, interoperability, cybersecurity, and data governance.

HUNTRAK appreciates the FAA's work to implement Section 2209. Clear recognition of lawful passive detection (distinct from mitigation, and able to extend beyond the passive-RF Remote ID minimum) will help operators understand their responsibilities and adopt appropriate awareness tools.

Respectfully submitted,
HUNTRAK Defense Systems, Inc.
Office of the Chief Executive Officer

comments.commenter: Comment from Northern Plains UAS Test Site
comments.comment_text:
June 1st, 2026
Submitted electronically via Federal eRulemaking Portal: www.regulations.gov
Docket Operations, M-30
United States Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Room W12-140, West Building Ground Floor
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Northern Plains UAS Test Site Comments on the Federal Aviation Administration,
Department of Transportation Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, “Designation of Unmanned
Aircraft Flight Restrictions [Docket No. FAA-2026-4558]
To Whom It May Concern:
The following comments are respectfully submitted in response to the Federal Aviation
Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking related to proposed Part 74. These
comments are intended to support regulatory clarity, operational scalability, and efficient
implementation of unmanned aircraft system (UAS) operations within restricted airspace
environments. The recommendations below are focused on improving consistency,
streamlining operational approval processes, and ensuring the final rule remains practical
for both operators and regulators.
Respectfully Submitted,
Trevor Woods
Executive Director, Northern Plains UAS Test Site

1. Introduction
The comments below identify areas where specific revisions, additional criteria, and
operational processes would strengthen the effectiveness and implementation of proposed
Part 74. These recommendations are organized by regulatory section and provide
suggested revisions intended to improve usability, transparency, and scalability.
2. Recommendations
2.1. Evaluation (§74.100)
Comment
We recommend the FAA define "good cause" as circumstances in which immediate action is
necessary to address a demonstrated safety, security, or national defense concern and
where the delay associated with notice-and-comment procedures would materially increase
operational risk. Proposed §74.6 would permit the FAA to forgo notice-and-comment
procedures when good cause exists but does not define the circumstances under which that
authority would be exercised. Because the use of the good-cause exception directly affects
public participation and operator awareness, we recommend the FAA adopt objective
criteria for its application. Specifically, good cause should be limited to circumstances
involving a demonstrated national security, homeland security, or immediate public safety
threat where delay associated with notice-and-comment procedures would materially
increase risk. Establishing these criteria would improve transparency and consistency while
preserving the FAA's ability to respond rapidly to urgent situations.
Resolution
Define "good cause" as circumstances in which immediate action is necessary to address a
demonstrated national security, homeland security, or public safety threat and where delay
associated with notice-and-comment procedures would materially increase risk. The FAA
should document the basis for any good-cause determination and limit use of the exception
to situations where the restriction is narrowly tailored to the identified threat.
Rationale and Data
Clear and objective evaluation standards will improve regulatory predictability, reduce
inconsistent interpretation, and provide operators with greater confidence in the approval
process.
2.2. Term (§74.200)
Comment
Proposed §74.6 would establish a five-year duration for Special UAFRs. We recommend the FAA
establish a recurring review or revalidation process at least once every three years to confirm
the continued necessity and appropriateness of approved restrictions or operational authorities.

This would align with existing FAA internal practices that generally reevaluate orders and
regulations on a 3-year basis and would ensure approvals remain current with evolving
operational, technological, and safety considerations. The review should confirm that the
operational need for the restriction continues to exist, that the facility remains eligible under
Part 74, and that no significant changes have occurred to the facility, surrounding airspace, or
operational environment that would materially affect the original approval.
Resolution
Require an administrative review every three years to confirm continued operational need,
facility eligibility, and that no material changes have occurred to the facility, surrounding
airspace, or operational environment.
Rationale and Data
Periodic review aligns with existing FAA practices that routinely reevaluate orders and
regulations and ensures authorizations remain current, justified, and operationally relevant.
2.3 Allowed Operations (§74.250) – “Sustained Operations”
Comment
Proposed §74.250(a)(2) requires that an unmanned aircraft operating within a UAFR
"transition the UAFR in the shortest amount of time practicable." While this requirement
may be appropriate for operators merely transiting through a restricted area, it appears to
preclude sustained operations conducted within a UAFR except through discretionary
authorization by the Administrator. We recommend the FAA establish a formal sustained-
operations approval process within Part 74 rather than requiring operators to seek
individual approvals or exemptions for recurring activities. As written, the proposal does
not provide a clear pathway for long-duration or recurring operations that must remain
within the restricted area to accomplish the intended mission. A standardized approval
framework would provide greater regulatory certainty while maintaining appropriate
oversight and safety controls.
Resolution
Establish a sustained-operations approval process allowing operators to conduct recurring
or long-duration activities within a UAFR under a single authorization when the operation
remains within an approved scope, geographic area, and set of operating procedures.
Rationale and Data
Providing consistent expectations for sustained operations would improve predictability for
operators while reducing administrative burden for both industry and the FAA.

2.4. Access Procedures (§74.251)- “Re-Occurring Operations”
Comment
Proposed §74.251 establishes a mechanism for operators to access/transit UAFRs but does
not clearly identify how recurring or long-term operations will be managed once initial
approval is granted. As written, operators may be required to repeatedly seek authorization
for substantially identical operations. We recommend the FAA develop a streamlined,
automated access and authorization system similar in concept to the Low Altitude
Authorization and Notification Capability (LAANC) framework. Such a system would
improve operational efficiency by enabling faster approval processing while maintaining
appropriate oversight and safety controls.
Additionally, we recommend:
•Streamlining approval processes for Part 146 operational areas through the use of
multi-year approvals where appropriate.
•Providing additional clarification, potentially through an Advisory Circular or other
means, regarding what constitutes a “form and manner acceptable to the
Administrator.”
•Ensuring all submission processes and authorization systems are designed to be
practical, accessible, and user-friendly for the typical operator.
Resolution
Develop a streamlined, automated approval system similar to LAANC to enable rapid
authorization processing. The system should allow operators to submit requests
electronically, track application status, obtain recurring authorizations for approved
operations, and receive automated approvals for predefined low-risk activities that meet
established criteria. Additionally, provide clarification regarding the required “form and
manner acceptable” through an Advisory Circular and ensure the process remains practical
and accessible for typical operators. Multi-year approvals for Part 146 operational areas
should also be considered where appropriate.
Rationale and Data
A scalable and automated approval process would improve operational efficiency, reduce
delays, and better support routine UAS operations while maintaining FAA oversight.

2.5. Altitude Ceiling (§74.60)
Comment
Proposed §74.60 generally limits UAFRs to 400 feet AGL but permits the altitude ceiling to
extend above 400 feet when the tallest component of the protected facility exceeds 300 feet
AGL. Under §74.60(c), the restricted airspace may extend from the surface to the height of
the tallest structure plus 100 feet, rounded up to the next 50-foot increment. While the
proposed restriction would therefore extend into airspace that may be routinely utilized by
manned aircraft operating in accordance with applicable regulations, the associated
operational restrictions would continue to apply exclusively to unmanned aircraft.
We recommend the FAA provide a clear risk-based justification for extending UAFRs above
400 feet AGL while limiting the resulting restrictions solely to unmanned aircraft
operations. If the FAA has determined that unmanned aircraft present unique safety,
security, or operational concerns at these higher altitudes that are not similarly presented
by manned aircraft, that rationale should be explicitly documented in the final rule.
Providing this explanation would improve stakeholder understanding, enhance regulatory
consistency, and help demonstrate that the vertical scope of the proposed restrictions is
appropriately tailored to the risks the rule is intended to address.
Resolution
Proposed §74.60(c) permits UAFRs to extend above 400 feet AGL when the protected
facility contains structures exceeding 300 feet AGL. We recommend the FAA provide a
detailed explanation of the safety, security, or operational basis for applying restrictions
exclusively to unmanned aircraft within these higher-altitude portions of a UAFR, where
manned aircraft may also routinely operate.
Rationale and Data
The NPRM generally aligns UAFRs with the operational environment of unmanned aircraft
by limiting the altitude ceiling to 400 feet AGL. However, §74.60(c) allows restrictions to
extend above 400 feet AGL based on the height of structures located within the facility
boundary. At these altitudes, the restricted airspace may overlap with airspace routinely
occupied by manned aircraft operating under existing regulations. Despite this overlap, the
proposed restrictions would continue to apply only to unmanned aircraft operations. While
there may be valid reasons for this distinction, the NPRM does not clearly explain why
operations above 400 feet AGL warrant restrictions on one class of aircraft but not another.
Additional explanation would improve transparency, support regulatory consistency, and
help ensure the scope of the restriction remains proportional to the risks being addressed.
3. Conclusion

We appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed Part 74 rulemaking.
These recommendations are intended to support the FAA’s efforts to establish a clear,
efficient, and scalable regulatory framework for UAS operations while maintaining safety
and operational effectiveness within the National Airspace System.

To Whom It May Concern,
I am a Part 107 Remote Pilot and commercial drone operator. While I support reasonable protections for truly sensitive facilities, I believe the proposed Section 2209 rule is overly broad and could create significant unintended consequences for both commercial and recreational drone operators.
The proposal would allow a wide range of facilities to seek Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (UAFR) status, potentially creating a patchwork of low-altitude restricted airspace that limits lawful drone operations. This would have a substantial impact on commercial operators who provide infrastructure inspections, construction documentation, surveying, emergency response support, filmmaking, and other valuable services. Restricting access to these areas could make many routine operations more difficult, costly, and time-consuming.
As the owner of a commercial drone company serving the film, television, and advertising industries, I frequently operate in urban environments where electrical infrastructure, telecommunications facilities, rail corridors, and other potentially eligible sites are common. Requiring separate approvals from facility owners could delay projects and increase costs without providing a meaningful security benefit.
The proposal also places unnecessary restrictions on recreational pilots. Many facilities that may qualify for UAFR designation are located near parks, open spaces, and long-established flying locations. Recreational pilots who comply with FAA rules, maintain visual line of sight, fly below 400 feet, and broadcast Remote ID should not automatically lose access to these areas.
I am also concerned about over-designation. Not every infrastructure asset presents a national security risk. The FAA should require applicants to demonstrate a specific security vulnerability and show why existing laws and regulations are insufficient before granting a UAFR. Any restricted area should be limited to the minimum size necessary to address the identified concern.
The drone industry has invested heavily in compliance, training, certification, and safety. Expanding restricted airspace without a clear, efficient authorization process could undermine innovation and economic growth while having little effect on individuals who intend to ignore the rules.
I respectfully request that the FAA:
Apply strict criteria for UAFR designation.
Ensure restricted areas are narrowly tailored.
Create a simple authorization process similar to LAANC.
Preserve access for legitimate commercial operations.
Allow reasonable recreational operations where appropriate.
Prevent unnecessary expansion of restricted airspace.
The FAA should protect critical infrastructure while preserving the ability of responsible drone operators to safely and legally use the National Airspace System.
Respectfully,
Hrant G.

Reduced staffing, fewer tools, and unrealistic expectations all contribute to fatigue — and fatigue is one of the most dangerous conditions in railroad operations. When workers are exhausted and still pressured to meet impossible standards, introducing drone surveillance only amplifies the stress.

Subject: Comments on NPRM – Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) – Docket FAA-2026-4558.

I am a professional Part 107 remote pilot and operator with 4 years of experience providing commercial drone services across the United States. I support the FAA’s effort to address legitimate safety and security concerns at critical infrastructure sites through a clear, standardized process. However, I urge the FAA to finalize a rule that is minimally burdensome on lawful commercial operators and maintains the highest possible bar for approving flight restrictions.

Key Recommendations:
1. Preserve routine overflight access. Professional drone pilots routinely need to transit or operate near critical infrastructure for essential commercial and public-benefit work (e.g., infrastructure inspections, utility corridor mapping, construction monitoring, emergency response support, and precision agriculture). Blanket or easily granted restrictions would unnecessarily disrupt these operations and harm the commercial UAS industry.

2. Set a very high bar for restricted airspace approval. UAFR requests should only be granted when the applicant provides clear, documented, site-specific evidence of credible threats that cannot be adequately mitigated through existing tools (Remote ID, LAANC, airspace coordination, or security protocols). National security or homeland security justifications must meet a rigorous standard and include input from relevant federal security agencies, not merely local preference.

3. Minimize bureaucracy and keep processes simple. Any approved UAFR must include clear, publicly available boundaries, straightforward waiver/transit procedures, and advance notification requirements that do not exceed what is operationally necessary. Excessive paperwork, repeated renewals, or vague approval criteria would create undue regulatory burden on small business operators. Ideally, approvals for overflight would be online, automated and similar to the current LAANC approval system for airspace management - even include this category in the current LAANC approval system

4. Protect legitimate commercial activity, like flights by Part 107 drone operators. The final rule should explicitly recognize that safe, compliant Part 107 operations (including visual line-of-sight transits and data-collection flights) are generally compatible with critical infrastructure protection when Remote ID is broadcast and basic coordination occurs.

A balanced rule that protects genuine high-risk sites without creating a patchwork of overly restrictive zones will best serve both national security and the continued safe integration of commercial drones.Thank you for considering these comments.Respectfully submitted,
Daniel Snyder
One Ring Drones - EIN# 87-3385928
Naples FL
oneringdrones@gmail.com
Professional Remote Pilot – Part 107 - 4620670

I submit this comment in strong support of the proposed rule establishing Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) around critical infrastructure under Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016.

The Security Imperative:

I write as a former U.S. Marine Corps Signals Intelligence and Electronic Warfare Officer, with professional experience in wireless communications, satellite systems, and defense technology consulting. The threat this rule addresses is not theoretical from my vantage point.

UAS platforms are no longer limited to commercial imaging or recreation. Their use for reconnaissance, site mapping, and payload delivery against fixed infrastructure has been documented in active conflict environments and cited as an emerging domestic threat by federal intelligence and law enforcement agencies. A malicious actor can conduct pre-attack surveillance without trespassing, identify hazardous material locations, and in a weaponized configuration execute an attack with no current regulatory mechanism to clearly prohibit it. The UAFR framework fills a critical and long-overdue gap.

The vulnerability surface is broader than commonly discussed. Chemical facilities, water treatment plants, energy nodes, and transportation hubs represent the obvious tier. But the FAA should also weigh the threat profile of high-density venues including stadiums, amusement parks, and large commercial entertainment districts. These are significant economic centers of gravity with concentrated civilian populations. A drone-delivered payload or weaponized swarm at such a venue carries mass casualty and economic disruption potential rivaling traditional infrastructure targets. Designation criteria should be interpreted broadly enough to include high-density venues meeting the threshold for regional or national debilitating impact.

Buffer zone boundaries should be defined narrowly and facility-specifically rather than as broad circular designations. A standardized fast-track authorization pathway for vetted Part 107 operators, analogous to LAANC, should be embedded in the final rule.

Design the Rule to Evolve:

The FAA should resist structural rigidity here. Counter-UAS detection and mitigation technology is advancing rapidly. Standoff distances necessary today may be reducible as detection matures and automated response solutions allow humans to move from being "in the loop" to "on the loop" with machine-assisted mitigation.

Today, maximum standoff is warranted because detection and response capabilities are not yet mature or universally deployed. A facility lacking certified counter-UAS detection, integrated law enforcement protocols, and Remote ID enforcement capability needs more airspace buffer because human response timelines remain substantial. As capabilities mature, the FAA should have built-in mechanisms to adjust UAFR parameters downward for facilities demonstrating adequate detection and response capability. The final rule should include a structured review process and mandatory renewal provisions to prevent designations becoming permanent by default.

A Note on the Comment Record:

The FAA should evaluate a significant portion of this docket with clear-eyed context. A majority of comments originate from railroad workers directed to comment by SMART-TD, a major rail labor union, through a coordinated campaign documented on their national website. The core grievance is railroad management using drones to conduct Operations Testing, which is workplace surveillance on company property. The union separately petitioned the FAA under Docket No. 2025-1908 to prohibit this. A UAFR restricts external operators. It cannot restrict a facility owner operating drones on their own property. This is a labor-management dispute belonging in arbitration or OSHA proceedings, not FAA airspace regulation.

To be fair, comments addressing the inability to distinguish a management drone from a hostile actor over hazardous rail cars raise a concern genuinely within scope. That security ambiguity deserves serious weight. But comments centered on employer surveillance anxiety are not substantive airspace security arguments. The FAA's obligation under the APA is to weigh arguments on their merits. This comment volume reflects union organizing capacity, not the strength of the underlying security case.

Finalize this rule to serve its actual purpose: protecting critical infrastructure and high-density civilian venues from a credible and evolving drone threat, with built-in flexibility to adapt as counter-UAS technology and legal response frameworks mature.

Respectfully submitted,

A former USMC SIGINT/EW Officer & Defense and Security Consultant

Require coordination between individual UAFRs and jurisdiction-wide airspace management programs.

The proposed rule is facility-centric. Individual facilities apply for individual UAFRs, and the airspace designations are published through FAA Order JO 7400.12. What the rule does not address is the coordination layer between a UAFR designation and the broader jurisdiction in which it sits.
In our assessment work, we consistently find that effective airspace management depends on jurisdictional awareness: the ability of a county sheriff's office, a municipal public safety department, or a regional coordination body to understand what is happening in the airspace above their jurisdiction and to integrate that picture into operational response. A UAFR designation changes the legal status of airspace in a jurisdiction. If the jurisdiction has no awareness of the designation, no integration with the detection and notification systems that serve the designated facility, and no coordination protocols with the facility's site manager, the UAFR creates a legal restriction without creating a governance layer to manage it.

The final rule should require UAFR applicants to document how the designation will be communicated to and coordinated with the relevant state or local law enforcement and emergency management agencies. It should also require that UAFR boundary data be published in machine-readable formats integrated with existing UAS flight planning infrastructure on the day any designation takes effect. Operators should never discover a UAFR through violation.

Mandate a fast-track authorization pathway for commercial operators.

The proposed rule creates restrictions with no corresponding authorization system. The practical consequence is that Part 107 commercial operators performing facility-invited work (infrastructure inspections, utility surveys, maintenance documentation) will have no reliable pathway to access UAFR airspace even when the facility has authorized them. The LAANC program demonstrated that the private sector can build and operate fast, reliable airspace authorization infrastructure under FAA authorization. A UAFR authorization platform requires more facility-level customization than LAANC's geographic zone model, but the architecture is achievable and the market will build it if the FAA requires it. The final rule should mandate that any active UAFR include a defined, FAA-authorized authorization pathway for compliant commercial operators and emergency services personnel. That pathway should provide near-real-time field verification, allow facilities to pre-register authorized operators by Remote ID, and produce a logged record of all authorized operations within the UAFR. Without this requirement, the rule effectively grounds the commercial operators that the facilities themselves depend on for maintenance and inspection.

Explicitly recognize passive, non-cooperative detection as meeting the detection capability requirement under proposed § 74.56.

Proposed § 74.56 requires UAFR applicants to demonstrate capability to receive and log Remote ID broadcasts from unmanned aircraft operating within or near the UAFR. This is a necessary but insufficient requirement. A malicious operator will not broadcast Remote ID. Remote ID-dependent detection provides no protection against the threat scenarios that most justify UAFR designations: deliberate surveillance of facility operations, payload delivery, and coordinated incursions.

Passive, non-cooperative detection systems that receive ambient signals without emitting, jamming, or interfering with any aircraft or communication system are the most practically deployable detection layer available to private-sector facility operators. These systems do not require FCC coordination, do not implicate jamming prohibition statutes, and can be deployed immediately without federal authorization.

The final rule should explicitly state that passive, non-cooperative detection capability meets and supplements the Remote ID reception requirement under § 74.56, and should clarify that operating such systems does not constitute "interference" under existing law. Without that clarification, facilities will remain uncertain whether deploying the most effective available detection layer is legally permissible, and many will forgo it. That uncertainty directly undermines the layered security standard the rule intends to require.

comments.commenter: Comment from Office of the Attorney General of the State of New York
comments.comment_text: The Office of the Attorney General of the State of New York respectfully requests that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) provide a 30-day extension for public comments on the notice of proposed rulemaking titled "Designation: Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility" for the reasons stated in the attached letter. We respectfully request that any notice by the FAA concerning this request be published in the Federal Register no later than July 3, 2026.

I am currently a passenger locomotive engineer who's career began at Union Pacific in 2008, and spans 5 western states. I have several concerns about unmanned aircraft operations near railroad facilities.

First, a drone flying near switching operations is very distracting to a crew performing work that is extremely safety sensitive. A distraction at the wrong moment can cost a worker life or limb in a split second. I've witnessed first hand on several occasions where Union Pacific officials flying drones to "observe" switching operations have caused workers to pay more attention to the drone than the work they are doing, causing an unnecessarily dangerous high risk situation.

Second, I have valid concerns about terrorism. Freight rail hauls poisonous and toxic hazardous materials in very high volumes through population centers throughout the country. A drone attack on a tank car loaded with a toxic inhalation hazardous material in an urban area could kill or injure an entire city's population. There is no way to tell if a drone flying near a train car loaded with hazardous material is friend or foe from the ground, so no drone should be allowed anywhere near freight rail operations.

Lastly, something that I frequently experience as a passenger train engineer is rail fans using drones to film our trains as we operate them. They are small, fast, and very distracting. Operating a train with 200 passengers at high speed requires my full attention to do so safely. My passengers deserve my full attention and focus on getting them to their destination safely. A drone distracting me as I operate creates unnecessary danger to me, and my passengers.

The right thing to do for both the public and rail workers is to pass a rule banning drone operations near rail facilities and operations.

Thank you,
Jeremy Hansen
SLC, Utah

This section includes these statements: “Consistent with requirements under 14 CFR Part
89, unless other authorized by the Administrator, UA operations within a UAFR will be
required to broadcast Remote ID. This underpins the FSF’s requirements to have
technology to sense Remote ID broadcast signals and will allow them to match the allowed
UA operations Remote ID serial number with the notification the FAF received via the UAFR
module notifying them of the allowed operations with requisite Remote ID serial number.
This is a crucial aspect for addressing security concerns over these sensitive facilities.”
FPVFC comments on 2209 NPRM.docx 8

FPV Freedom Coalition comments on FAA 2209 NPRM
FPVFC Comment:
As this is characterized as a “crucial aspect” for addressing security concerns, this section
needs to be formally added to the NPRM via a new window of comments. This content
rises to that of a new rule and if it remains in the Advisory Circular, it will result in a violation
of statute by the FAA of rulemaking outside the notice and comment process.
Next, this requirement for the FSF to match notified Remote ID serial numbers with
broadcast Remote ID serial numbers is nearly impossible and opens the FSF to litigation.
Both will result in widespread non-compliance. This AC-based rule is nearly impossible
because for transit of a Standard UAFR, the UAV operator must only notify the FSF. If this
notification is close to the time of transit, how could a FSF be responsible for matching
Remote ID serial numbers. In the case of Specialized UAFR, this becomes difficult, costly
and risky as any mistake could result in a criminal penalty of a UAV operator. Mistakes
would result in litigation of the FSF. This is a risk few FSF proprietors should take.
The FPVFC requests the FAA to scrap this section.
FPVFC comments on 2209 NPRM.docx 9

I work in the transportation industry for Union Pacific, I was working a local and was being tested at my home terminal and when I was being briefed by the manager at that terminal he told me to watch out for drone testing at my future pick ups in my route for the local job I was on that day.  Every time I went to a different industry my focus was blurred because of the drone testing.  The drone only has a top view and the testing can be easily miss judged by the distance between equipment and other hazards the employee is avoiding but the drone might not see it, I bring this up because after the test is performed (we) the employees don't find out about the test until days later and it's hard to fight your case at that point.

Please don’t add more restrictions for hard
Working professional drone operators. The DJI ban was bad enough. More restrictions will be horrible for this most beneficial industry.
Thank you.

This rulemaking is particularly significant given the documented increase in unauthorized drone activity across critical infrastructure sectors, including energy facilities. The absence of a clear, consistent framework has limited the ability of owners and operators to proactively mitigate these risks through airspace protections. DTM views the proposed UAFR construct as a foundational control that enhances deterrence, improves situational awareness, and establishes a regulatory mechanism for protecting facilities. At the same time, we recognize the FAA’s responsibility to balance security needs with the continued integration and safe operation of UAS within the National Airspace System (NAS), and we support this balanced approach.

As the FAA advances toward a final rule, it is essential that the framework remains practical, risk-informed, and operationally implementable for industry stakeholders. This includes ensuring clarity in eligibility criteria, timely processing of applications, and alignment with existing security and compliance obligations. DTM emphasizes that UAFRs should be viewed as an initial step, not a complete solution. While they provide an important deterrent and regulatory safeguard, additional clarity and progress on scalable, lawful counter-UAS capabilities will be necessary to fully address the evolving threat landscape facing critical infrastructure owners and operators.

Drone usage for operations testing should have never been implemented in the first place. I voiced my concerns to management and much like every other valid concern it was downplayed. I have been tested around 150 times in the last calendar year. Drones are the biggest distraction I have ever encountered, 22 year employee btw. Even when drones aren’t out we are consistently watching out for them creating distractions. Bnsf also does not stop you from moving when they see a serious rules violation. They let you keep working until you are finished with the industry, work or current moves being made. I have questioned them about this and the response was “we like to observe”. “Sometime we can’t observe because of a serious rules violation at the start of testing”. I for one feel harassed since drone testing has been implemented. 150 times in a year is excessive considering my peers are around 10-15 a year.

Comments Submitted re: Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity
to a Fixed Site Facility - FAA-2026-4558-0001. Submitted June 29, 2026.
My name is Ed Ruttledge, and I reside at the following address:
295 Church Street, SE #404
Salem, Oregon 97301
I am a semi-professional photographer. Retired, I provide photographic and video content
as an unpaid volunteer to government entities and non-profit organizations which have
included the following:
• Cascade Volcano Observatory (USGS)
• State of Oregon
• Tillamook Public Utility District
• The Tierra Del Mar Neighborhood Association
• The Vashon Island Nature Center
• Intercity Transit – Olympia, Washington
• The Civita Institute
I am a Certified Remote Pilot (#4234594) and presently have three small camera drones
registered with the FAA.
The primary purpose of my involvement with UAS devices has been to extend my
photographic capabilities. As technology advanced, it became possible to capture whole
new perspectives, especially in landscape and architectural photography by using small
UAS devices such as the Skydio 2+ and DJI Air3 I presently own. My considerable
photographic experience was in still photography. But my work with UAS devices
platforms has developed my interest in doing video work as well. While I have become a
skilled pilot of these UAV devices, flying a UAV is secondary to its function as a camera
platform.
There a myriad of issues raised by this proposed rule. I will focus on three topics in my
comments. I reserve my privilege to submit additional commentary within the comment
period. My comments regarding the proposed rules include the following:
• There needs to be a clear statement of Federal pre-emption - declaring UAS
airspace regulation to be an exclusive FAA function. This would preempt any state,
tribal, territorial, local or private entity rule that restricts UAS operations based on
proximity to critical infrastructure. Without such Federal pre-emption, we can
realistically expect to have a patchwork of regulations from a myriad of jurisdictions
or other entities impacting the operation of UAS devices within the NAS. Further,
notice to UAS pilots would become fragmented as would any waiver or
authorization procedures.

• Transit through a Standard UAFR should not be prohibited, especially if the device
broadcasts Remote ID, and moves through the Standard UFAR in the shortest
practicable time.
• Measurable care should be taken in determining what constitutes “critical
infrastructure.” Definitions need to be unambiguous. For example, what if
electrical substations and cell towers are included as “critical infrastructure?”
They are everywhere. Is the T-Mobile Gateway sitting on my windowsill, which
sends and receives 5G voice and data transmissions, a cell tower? What about the
series of undersea landing nodes that populate the California and Oregon
coastlines [and, which are usually underground and often purposefully obscured]?
Transit corridors crisscross every neighborhood. Even the definition of what is a
“railroad” could be debated. For example, is the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system in
Eugene, Oregon a “railroad?” Would the Rail Riders attraction in Tillamook County,
Oregon be a “railroad” or, perhaps, a linear “amusement park?”
Thank you for your consideration of the above in drafting the rule.

Drone photography has become one of the most important tools for making the very often hidden world of industrial animal agriculture visible to the public which people should have the basic right to look up and learn about. I sincerely hope the FAA will carefully consider the crucial public value of aerial photojournalism as it evaluates this proposal.
