comments.commenter: Comment from American Association of Port Authorities
comments.comment_text:
July 3, 2026
Docket Operations
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue, S.E., Room W58-213
Washington, D.C. 20590-0001
Desk Officer for Federal Aviation Administration
Office of Management and Budget
Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
New Executive Office Building
725 17th Street, N.W.,
Room 10202
Washington, D.C. 20053
Re: Comments on Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03 – Designation – Restrict
the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
Dear Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Office of Rulemaking,
The American Association of Port Authorities (AAPA) appreciates the opportunity to comment
on the FAA’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) concerning the designation of unmanned
aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs) around eligible fixed site facilities. AAPA represents public
port authorities throughout the United States, including many of the nation’s largest strategic
seaports and critical infrastructure hubs.
AAPA applauds the FAA’s efforts to implement Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and
Security Act of 2016. Establishing a process for eligible facilities to seek drone flight restrictions
is a meaningful step toward addressing the growing threat posed by unauthorized unmanned
aircraft systems (UAS) operating over critical infrastructure.
America's ports increasingly face drone-related vulnerabilities and operational disruptions. Ports
routinely handle hazardous materials, military cargo, cruise passengers, energy products,
chemical shipments, and essential consumer goods that are vital to national economic and
homeland security. Unauthorized drone activity in the vicinity of any of these facilities raises
safety, surveillance, and operational concerns. Moreover, the threat posed by attack drones is
particularly acute in the cruise sector, where a single vessel may carry several thousand
passengers and crew. A successful attack against a large passenger vessel could result in
catastrophic loss of life on a scale rivaling the casualties inflicted during previous terrorist
attacks, underscoring the urgent need for stronger protections for America’s seaports and
maritime gateways.
Strategic seaports are increasingly recognized as high value targets for foreign intelligence
collection, cyber-enabled surveillance, and disruptive activities involving UAS. Operational
disruptions at major ports can rapidly cascade throughout national and regional supply chains,
1

affecting fuel distribution, agricultural exports, manufacturing inputs, military readiness, and
consumer goods availability. Many ports also support Department of War and Department of
Transportation strategic sealift and military outload operations, further elevating their importance
to national security.
Because of these unique operational and national security responsibilities, ports warrant special
consideration within the FAA's implementation of Section 2209. The consequences of
unauthorized drone activity at a port may extend far beyond the immediate facility and impact
broader economic resilience, defense readiness, and homeland security objectives.
Given the sensitivity of their operations and proximity to large population centers, ports
represent some of the most mature and security-conscious critical infrastructure operators in the
nation. Accordingly, many port facilities are regulated under the Maritime Transportation
Security Act of 2002 (MTSA), maintain approved Facility Security Plans (FSPs), comply with
Maritime Security (MARSEC) requirements, and coordinate closely with the U.S. Coast Guard
(USCG) and federal law enforcement agencies.
AAPA strongly supports FAA’s recognition that fixed site facilities regulated under MTSA
explicitly qualify for UAFRs. We also appreciate the FAA’s acknowledgment that unmanned
aircraft may pose risks associated with surveillance, cyber intrusion, operational disruption, and
physical attacks against critical infrastructure.
AAPA respectfully offers the following recommendations and concerns regarding the proposed
rule:
Streamline Eligibility for Maritime Transportation Facilities: AAPA strongly encourages
FAA to establish an expedited or presumptive approval pathway for maritime facilities already
regulated under MTSA and operating under an active USCG-approved FSP or Alternate Security
Plan.
The NPRM appropriately recognizes that maritime transportation facilities regulated under
MTSA are eligible to request a UAFR. These facilities already undergo extensive federal security
oversight and maintain layered physical and cybersecurity protections. Ports should not be
required to duplicate extensive security demonstrations already validated through USCG
processes. Further, MTSA-regulated facilities already satisfy many of the security and
vulnerability assessment requirements contemplated by the NPRM. FSPs, Facility Security
Assessments, Alternate Security Programs, Area Maritime Security Committee participation, and
ongoing USCG oversight provide a robust security framework that FAA should leverage
wherever possible. Aligning UAFR eligibility with existing MTSA requirements would reduce
administrative burden, eliminate duplicative federal review, and advance broader interagency
efficiency objectives.
Accordingly, AAPA recommends that:
• MTSA-regulated facilities with approved FSPs automatically qualify to apply for a
UAFR;
2

• The FAA establish a streamlined review process for strategic seaports and maritime
critical infrastructure; and
• Existing USCG security documentation be accepted in lieu of duplicative FAA-specific
submissions where practicable.
Recognize Port Authorities as Governing Critical Infrastructure Operators: The NPRM
currently places substantial emphasis on individual site operators and property interests.
However, many public port authorities are governmental entities with statutory authority over
complex multi-tenant critical infrastructure environments.
Ports frequently contain multiple energy, cargo, and cruise terminals, chemical facilities, rail
operations, and federally regulated maritime facilities operating within a unified security
environment. Requiring each tenant individually to apply for separate UAFRs would create
inefficiency, inconsistency, and unnecessary administrative burdens.
AAPA recommends that FAA:
• Explicitly recognize port authorities as eligible applicants to apply for UAFRs covering
multiple facilities within port jurisdictional boundaries;
• Allow port authorities to coordinate UAFRs on behalf of tenants and operators; and
• Clarify that tenant objections or lack of participation should not prevent a port authority
from applying for a UAFR covering publicly governed port property.
As governmental entities responsible for the safety and security of maritime infrastructure, port
authorities should retain the ability to coordinate drone security measures across their jurisdiction
if they choose.
Allow Flexibility Beyond Strict Property-Line Boundaries: AAPA is concerned that the
proposed limitation restricting UAFR lateral boundaries strictly to property lines may create
significant operational and security gaps for ports and industrial waterfront facilities. Maritime
facilities are fundamentally different from many land-based critical infrastructure sites. Ports by
definition include waterside operational areas, including ship berths, mooring dolphins, vessel
loading zones, and navigation channels. These maritime assets operate as interconnected
facilities with rail corridors and public roadways in a unified security environment. As a result,
many ports contain noncontiguous parcels, with public roadways bisecting secure facilities,
shared intermodal corridors, or waterside operational areas. Connected energy and chemical
infrastructure can also be separated by easements or transportation corridors. Limiting UAFRs to
upland property boundaries may leave many of the assets most in need of protection uncovered.
For MTSA-regulated facilities, FAA should consider allowing applicants to define UAFR
boundaries consistent with the USCG-recognized security footprint reflected in approved FSPs
and related security documentation. Such an approach would better reflect the operational
realities of maritime facilities and ensure protection of waterside assets, vessel berths, and
adjacent security zones that are integral to port operations.
3

In addition, modern UAS platforms equipped with advanced optical zoom, thermal imaging, and
other surveillance capabilities may collect sensitive information while operating outside a
facility's strict property lines. FAA should provide applicants flexibility to justify reasonable
security buffer areas to address demonstrated surveillance vulnerabilities and operational risks.
AAPA encourages FAA to:
• Allow reasonable flexibility to extend UAFR boundaries beyond strict property lines
when justified by operational security considerations;
• Permit interconnected maritime and industrial facilities to be treated as a unified security
site where appropriate;
• Consider operational realities unique to ports and waterfront infrastructure such as flight
restrictions over critical navigation channels; and
• Accept USCG-recognized security footprints reflected in approved FSPs.
Address Vertical Boundary Limitations and Aerial Surveillance Risks: AAPA encourages
FAA to further evaluate whether the proposed vertical limitations adequately account for the
unique characteristics of maritime facilities, existing FAA operational authorities, and the
capabilities of modern UAS.
The NPRM generally limits UAFRs to 400 feet above ground level unless a facility contains
structures exceeding 300 feet in height. While AAPA appreciates FAA's effort to align UAFR
ceilings with existing small UAS operating limitations, this approach may not fully address the
security risks facing maritime facilities.
Many port facilities contain ship-to-shore cranes, container handling equipment, refinery
structures, loading arms, communications infrastructure, and other industrial assets that routinely
exceed 150 to 250 feet in height. Under 14 CFR § 107.51(b), small UAS may operate up to 400
feet above a structure's immediate uppermost limit. As a result, a drone operating near a 250-foot
ship-to-shore crane could potentially fly as high as 650 feet above ground level while remaining
compliant with existing FAA regulations.
AAPA appreciates the exception proposed in 14 § 74.60(c), which would allow the FAA to raise
a UAFR's altitude ceiling when a facility contains a structure exceeding 300 feet in height.
However, many maritime facilities contain critical infrastructure below that threshold.
Consequently, a port facility with a 250-foot ship-to-shore crane could face a circumstance where
drones are authorized to operate substantially above the proposed UAFR ceiling while still
maintaining the ability to observe terminal operations and other sensitive activities.
This issue is particularly significant because modern UAS platforms are increasingly capable of
conducting detailed surveillance from substantial distances and altitudes. High-resolution
cameras, advanced optical zoom capabilities, thermal imaging systems, wireless signal collection
technologies, and other commercially available tools may allow operators to observe cargo
operations, military vessel movements, security procedures, access control points, hazardous
material handling activities, and other sensitive operational information without physically
entering a facility's immediate perimeter.
4

Beyond traditional visual surveillance, UAS may also be capable of collecting information
regarding security personnel assignments and patrol patterns, operational movements, facility
vulnerabilities, and other indicators of security posture. Certain UAS platforms may also
facilitate cyber-enabled reconnaissance activities, including the collection of wireless network
information, signal interception, packet capture, or communications disruption attempts. In
addition, thermal imaging capabilities may reveal heat signatures associated with critical
infrastructure, refrigerated cargo, electrical substations, machinery, vessels, vehicles, or
personnel activity, potentially allowing UAS operators to identify active versus dormant
facilities, equipment, or operational areas. These concerns are particularly acute at Strategic
Seaports and other facilities supporting military deployments, defense logistics, energy
transportation, and critical supply chain operations, where collected information could have
significant homeland security or national defense implications.
From a security perspective, the risk is not solely the drone's physical presence over a facility,
but also its ability to collect intelligence regarding critical infrastructure operations. A drone
operating above or adjacent to a facility may be capable of observing many of the same activities
that would otherwise be protected by physical barriers, fencing, waterside security measures, and
restricted access controls. In many cases, the intelligence collection value of a drone may persist
even when the aircraft remains outside the proposed lateral or vertical boundaries of a UAFR.
Accordingly, AAPA recommends that FAA:
• Consider additional flexibility for facilities containing exceptionally tall industrial
structures, including ship-to-shore cranes, refinery infrastructure, and other maritime
assets;
• Allow applicants to demonstrate a need for expanded vertical protections based on
facility-specific security risks and infrastructure characteristics;
• Evaluate whether existing altitude exceptions could create unintended surveillance
opportunities that undermine the effectiveness of UAFRs; and
• Consider amending the altitude restriction proposed in 14 § 74.60 to be 400 feet above
the tallest structure on the facility.
Improve Coordination and Processing Capacity: The NPRM acknowledges that FAA expects
significant application volume and potential delays. AAPA shares concerns regarding whether
FAA possesses sufficient staffing and resources to review potentially thousands of applications in
a timely manner.
AAPA encourages FAA to:
• Expand interagency coordination with Sector Risk Management Agencies (SRMAs),
including USCG and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS);
• Increase reviewer staffing and technical expertise;
• Consider phased or prioritized implementation for nationally significant critical
infrastructure sectors, such as for those already maintaining FSPs;
• Develop proposed website-based notice mechanisms to streamline processing while
preserving meaningful public comment opportunities; and
5

• Prioritize review and approval of applications submitted by Strategic Seaports and other
nationally significant facilities supporting military deployments, defense logistics, and
strategic sealift operations.
Address Authorized Operations and Operational Flexibility: Ports routinely utilize drones
for infrastructure inspections, environmental monitoring, emergency response, waterside
surveillance, construction management, hazard assessments, and other legitimate operational
purposes. AAPA requests clarification that UAFRs will not unintentionally impede authorized
and beneficial port-related UAS operations.
AAPA supports FAA’s exploration of “whitelisting” Remote ID serial numbers and encourages
the development of scalable systems that allow approved operators to conduct legitimate
operations within UAFRs efficiently and securely. However, AAPA cautions that serial number-
based whitelisting alone may not provide sufficient operational flexibility for large port
complexes. At major ports, authorized drone flights may number in the hundreds or thousands
annually, and the inventory of approved aircraft may change frequently as drones are added,
replaced, retired, or assigned to different operational functions.
To preserve FAA’s ultimate authority over the National Airspace System while ensuring timely,
risk-based decision making, AAPA recommends that FAA develop localized or streamlined
mechanisms for approving authorized UAS operations within UAFRs at complex critical
infrastructure environments such as public port authorities. Such mechanisms could include
FAA-approved port UAS management plans, streamlined authorization procedures for trusted
operators, recurring authorization frameworks, or other scalable processes that recognize port
authorities as distinct from individual fixed-site operators.
Many port authorities already maintain mature drone airspace management practices, operational
experience, security coordination protocols, and technology-enabled situational awareness
capabilities. FAA should consider leveraging these capabilities by allowing port authorities to
coordinate authorized UAS operations across multiple facilities within a port-wide UAFR,
subject to FAA-approved parameters and appropriate reporting requirements. Quarterly reporting
on authorized flight activity, combined with timely notification of unauthorized incursions or
mitigation-related incidents, would provide FAA with continued oversight while avoiding
unnecessary administrative delays for routine, beneficial port operations.
AAPA also encourages FAA to provide flexibility for port authorities and maritime facilities to
satisfy any Remote ID monitoring, notification, or situational awareness requirements through
shared or port-wide capabilities. Many ports operate as multi-tenant environments with
numerous terminals and operators located within a common security framework. Requiring
duplicative systems for each facility could create unnecessary expense while reducing
operational efficiency. FAA should allow port authorities or other coordinating entities to
provide shared capabilities on behalf of multiple facilities where appropriate.
Protect Sensitive Security Information and Security Documentation: Maritime facility
applications for UAFRs may require submission of information already protected under federal
6

security programs, including FSPs, Facility Security Assessments, vulnerability analyses,
security system configurations, and related operational information.
AAPA requests that FAA clearly state in the final rule that Sensitive Security Information and
other protected security materials submitted in support of UAFR applications will receive
appropriate protection from public disclosure and will not be incorporated into public notices or
comment processes in a manner that could compromise facility security.
Continue Advancing Detection and Mitigation Authorities: While AAPA supports the
establishment of UAFRs, the NPRM itself acknowledges an important limitation: the proposal does not
independently authorize any additional drone detection or mitigation authorities.
While UAFRs represent an important step forward, they are most effective when paired with sufficient
detection and mitigation capabilities. Establishing restricted airspace without providing operators and law
enforcement adequate means to identify and respond to unauthorized incursions limits the practical
effectiveness of the program.
UAFRs are an important legal and airspace management tool, but they alone will not deter malicious
actors intentionally disregarding federal law. Ports continue to face real-world drone threats, including
surveillance concerns and operational vulnerabilities.
Accordingly, AAPA urges continued federal efforts to:
• Expand authorized counter-UAS detection and mitigation capabilities for critical
infrastructure;
• Accelerate the promulgation of approved drone mitigation technologies by federal
authorities, including as contemplated under the Safer Skies Act, so that ports and other
critical infrastructure operators have adequate lead time to research, test, procure, and
deploy mitigation systems appropriate for their individualized operating environments;
• Increase federal training capacity and available seats for authorized counter-UAS
operators;
• Strengthen interagency coordination among FAA, DHS, the Department of Justice, the
Transportation Security Administration (TSA), and USCG in countering UAS threats;
• Ensure strategic seaports are appropriately prioritized in future counter-UAS initiatives;
and
• Evaluate funding mechanisms and support programs for local law enforcement agencies
and public port authorities responsible for responding to drone threats affecting critical
infrastructure and strategic sealift operations.
America’s ports are foundational to national defense, supply chain resilience, energy security,
and economic stability. As drone technology evolves, maritime infrastructure operators require
practical, scalable, and coordinated tools to address emerging threats while preserving the
efficiency of the National Airspace System.
AAPA appreciates the FAA’s engagement with stakeholders and its efforts to establish a long-
overdue framework for protecting critical infrastructure from unauthorized UAS activity. We
look forward to continued collaboration with FAA, DHS, TSA, and USCG to ensure maritime
7

transportation facilities can effectively utilize this framework while recognizing the unique
operational realities of the port environment.
Thank you for considering these comments.
Sincerely,
Sang Yi
President & CEO
American Association of Port Authorities
8

CAFOs (Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations) should not be included in the restrictions of operating unmanned aircrafts. While CAFOs are fixed facility sites, it is in the public's interest to be able to see how large in scale CAFOs are as on-the-ground imaging cannot capture their scale accurately. In addition, CAFOs are typically well-hidden, out of the public's view - the public deserves to know just how vast CAFOs are so they can better understand the impact of land use, water use, and animal welfare concerns. Unmanned aircrafts allow for a non-invasive way to document CAFOs and to serve public interests.

I support a restriction on the operations of unmanned (Part 107) or manned aircraft (Part 103) in close proximity to a fixed site facility.   There needs to be a definitive, objective criteria to keep these types of vehicles a safe distance from fixed site facilities, such as power stations, wind turbine farms, transmission lines, bridges, AToN facilitates, ports, etc.   But, also, since Part 103 aircraft have very vague restrictions, and because there has been a monumental proliferation in Part 103 aircraft since Part 103 was instituted, particularly with powered paragliding activist, it would be nonsensical to restrict unmanned aircraft from these sites without also including manned aircraft that utilize Part 103 for their operations from these sites as well, because it is virtually the same problem except with a different category of aircraft.  Unmanned Aircraft (UAS) contemplated here only weight up to 55 lbs, yet unregistered Part 107 aircraft are operated unlicensed aviators in aircraft that can weigh upwards of 254 lbs (empty) -plus- the weight of fuel and persons on board, making these vehicles even more hazardous to the infrastructure and bystanders than any UAS contemplated here.   So, if the FAA adopts restrictions for UAS, it should seriously consider adopting the same rules for Part 103 operations.
Drone usage over agriculture facilities should not be restricted.

comments.commenter: Comment from International Association of Venue Managers
comments.comment_text:
June 30, 2026
Michelle Ferritto, Office of Rulemaking, Federal Aviation Administration
Docket Operations;
U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT)
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Room W58-213, West Building 5th Floor,
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility, Docket FAA-2026-4558
Dear Ms. Ferritto,
Thank you for this opportunity to provide comments regarding the FAA’s proposed rule to
establish criteria for unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFR) to “critical infrastructure
facilities.”
Background:
The International Association of Venue Managers (IAVM) represents public assembly
venues, including auditoriums, arenas, convention centers, exhibit halls, stadiums,
performing arts centers, university complexes, and amphitheaters. Member venues attract
millions of patrons to an astonishing variety of events including sporting events, concerts,
conventions, conferences, and performance art.
The Threat:
While IAVM venue managers meticulously plan every detail of the events they host to
ensure the safety of our guests, a new threat has emerged that we cannot control - the use

of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs or drones) in the airspace above outdoor events.
Venues rely on the assistance of law enforcement to police airspace above events, and
current law only allows law enforcement to take actions to detect, take control of, destroy,
or otherwise interfere with an unmanned aircraft in certain limited circumstances.
Commercial Facilities:
We appreciate the focus of the proposed rule on critical infrastructure. The commercial
facilities sector includes a wide range of sites that draw large crowds of people for
shopping, business, entertainment, or lodging. Venues where IAVM members work are part
of the “public assembly” subsector, for example, arenas and convention centers.
The proposed rule includes several criteria that venues must meet in order to obtain UAV
flight restrictions for their facilities. While we appreciate the risk to theme and
entertainment parks from UAVs, the proposed rule’s focus on that sector disregards the
many other types of commercial facilities and creates critical security gaps across the
sector. We urge the FAA to revise the rule’s threshold criteria as outlined below in order to
protect the entire sector.
Temporary v. Permanent:
The rule proposes that facilities must not be “a stadium or venue where the events may be
covered by temporary flight restrictions (TFRs).” First, we urge the agency to expand the
TFRs. Current temporary restrictions protect stadiums that host NFL, NCAA Division I
football, MLB, and major motor speedway events and seat over 30,000 people, and the FAA
now has authority to grant TFRs to other venues, but the 30,000-seat threshold remains.
The vast majority of IAVM members work at event venues that seat under 30,000 and don’t
qualify for TFRs. This highlights serious gaps in protections for event attendees that should
be addressed.
For the proposed rule, we understand this criteria is an attempt to focus the rule on
permanent, ongoing facilities and events like large theme parks. We also appreciate the
FAA’s position that TFRs are often more appropriate for events that have a defined start and
stop time, like concerts. However, we ask the FAA to consider the threat venues face and
allow for more flexibility and options for venues.
Venue operators face a dizzying and often conflicting array of federal, state, and local laws
and regulations regarding UAVs above their facilities. Different criteria across agencies,
unclear authorities, conflicting rules, and competing jurisdictions combine to create a
regulatory minefield. Under the current system, venue operators are forced to spend
limited time and resources applying, and re-applying, for various temporary restrictions.
Venues should have the option to apply for a permanent UAFR in order to provide

continuous protection to their visitors and staff and not spend time and money constantly
applying and reapplying for temporary restrictions. This would provide certainty, as
opposed to the ad hoc system of TFRs in place now, and it would increase visitor and staff
safety. We urge the FAA to remove this criteria from the final rule.
Annual Attendance:
The proposed rule sets a minimum annual attendance of 2.5 million in the previous year.
This is an extremely high threshold that only the most visited amusement parks in the
country will meet. The threshold immediately excludes a large portion of the sector from
even attempting to obtain a UAFR to protect their visitors and employees from airborne
threats.
For example, the famed outdoor concert venue Red Rocks Amphitheatre located near
Denver, CO had an annual attendance in 2025 of 1.75 million, making it the second most

in 2025 Sporting KC, a Major League Soccer team located in Kansas City, KS drew an
average of just under 17,000 fans over 17 home games, for a total annual attendance of
around 282,000. Fans attending Sporting KC soccer games, concerts at Red Rocks, and
events at other outdoor venues across the country that host hundreds of thousands of
visitors a year deserve to be protected. We urge the FAA to lower the minimum annual

Public Comment on Docket No. FAA-2026-4558

Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
Notice No. 26-03 / 26-03A | RIN 2120-AL33

Submitted via regulations.gov, Docket FAA-2026-4558
Comment period

I am submitting this comment to urge the FAA to decline to establish food and agriculture sector eligibility criteria for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) under proposed 14 CFR Part 74 — or, at minimum, to draft any such criteria narrowly enough that they cannot be used to shield animal agriculture operations from public observation and documentation.

1. The statutory purpose does not support broad agricultural eligibility

Section 2209 and proposed § 74.56 require applicants to demonstrate that a restriction is necessary for aviation safety, protection of people or property on the ground, national security, or homeland security. The other 14 sectors named in NSM-22 — nuclear facilities, dams, chemical plants, defense sites — present concrete, well-documented physical or security vulnerabilities where an unmanned aircraft incident could cause catastrophic harm. A typical concentrated animal feeding operation (CAFO) or slaughter facility does not present a comparable profile. The FAA's own UAFR framework conditions eligibility on a "documented safety or security need," including evidence of existing drone activity near the facility and the consequences of an exploited vulnerability — not on a facility's preference for privacy or favorable public perception.

2. The rule should not become a vehicle for shielding facilities from transparency

Routine drone photography of animal agriculture sites overwhelmingly serves a different purpose than the threats this rule is designed to address: it documents animal welfare conditions, environmental discharges (such as manure lagoon runoff into waterways), and food safety practices that are otherwise extremely difficult for journalists, researchers, and the public to observe, since these facilities are typically located on private land with no public access points. If the FAA permits agricultural facilities to obtain UAFRs without requiring a genuine, documented security threat distinct from "unwanted observation," the rule will function as a no-fly zone for accountability journalism and animal welfare investigation rather than as a tool for aviation safety.

3. Recommended criteria, if the FAA proceeds

If the FAA does establish food and agriculture eligibility criteria, I urge it to require, at minimum:

A documented incident-based threshold. Applicants should be required to show specific instances of drones interfering with aviation safety (e.g., conflicts with agricultural aircraft under Part 137) or creating a demonstrable safety/security hazard — not simply that drone photography has occurred near the facility.
An explicit exclusion for newsgathering and investigative documentation. The rule should make clear that a UAFR may not be granted or enforced in a manner that restricts drone operations conducted for journalistic, research, or public-interest documentation purposes, consistent with the trusted-operator carve-outs already contemplated for Parts 91, 107, 108, 135, and 137.
A high evidentiary bar matched to the other 15 sectors. Eligibility criteria for food and agriculture facilities should require a showing of risk comparable in severity to that required of chemical plants or energy facilities, not a lower threshold justified by operational convenience or reputational concerns.

4. Conclusion

The FAA's mandate under Section 2209 is aviation safety and security — not the management of public perception of an industry. I respectfully ask the FAA to either omit food and agriculture eligibility criteria from the final rule, or adopt criteria narrow enough to prevent UAFRs from being used to suppress legitimate transparency into animal welfare, environmental compliance, and food production practices that are otherwise inaccessible to the public.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 — Designation: Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
I’m a licensed Part 107 drone pilot writing to urge the FAA to exclude factory farms and other industrial animal agriculture facilities from the “Food and Agriculture” critical infrastructure sector eligible for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) — or, at minimum, to set a strict, evidence-based bar for any facility seeking one.
Section 2209 exists to protect sites where a drone poses a real safety or security threat: power plants, refineries, prisons, dams. A barn complex or manure lagoon doesn’t fit that category, and Congress removed the open-ended “other locations” catch-all in 2024 specifically to keep this rule narrow. The NPRM lists Food and Agriculture as an eligible sector but leaves its criteria blank — this comment urges the FAA to either drop the sector or write criteria that demand a documented threat, not just a desire to avoid scrutiny.
Licensed drone pilots are one of the only independent checks left on this industry. Ag-gag laws in many states already criminalize undercover ground investigation, even on public land. Legal drone flight in public airspace has become one of the few remaining lawful ways to document conditions invisible from the road: lagoon overflows, overcrowding, ventilation failures, and waste mismanagement.
This matters directly to consumers. Labels like “humane” and “free-range” are loosely regulated and rarely verified independently. Aerial documentation is often the only real check between marketing claims and reality — restricting it widens the information gap between producers and the people buying their products.
It matters for public health too. Outside documentation has repeatedly driven faster scrutiny of biosecurity failures during avian flu and other livestock disease events than industry self-reporting alone. If “biosecurity” becomes the default justification for airspace restriction, it should require actual evidence of a drone-related transmission or disruption risk — not just an assertion.
It matters for the environment. CAFOs are a major source of water pollution, and enforcement leans heavily on self-reporting and under-resourced inspections. Aerial observation has repeatedly caught lagoon breaches and unpermitted waste application invisible from ground level. Restricting drone access removes one of the few independent environmental checks this industry has.
And it matters for the animals raised in these facilities, whose treatment is visible to the public — when it’s visible at all — largely because of legal aerial documentation.
I ask the FAA to:
1.Exclude CAFOs and similar facilities from Food and Agriculture sector UAFR eligibility, absent documented drone-specific safety risk.
2.If the sector is retained, require rigorous criteria: documented vulnerability, exhausted self-help measures, and no reliance on unsupported biosecurity claims.
3.Protect Part 107 commercial transit rights within any granted UAFR, so notification requirements can’t be used to anticipate and block documentation flights.
4.Require enhanced public notice for agricultural UAFR applications, reaching regulators, journalists, and the public.
5.State explicitly that UAFR designation does not shield facilities from lawful environmental, public health, or animal welfare documentation.
The FAA’s job under Section 2209 is narrow: protect genuinely high-risk sites from real drone threats. Industrial animal agriculture doesn’t naturally belong in that category, and this rule shouldn’t become a tool for shielding it from the scrutiny a functioning food system depends on.
Respectfully submitted,
Jam Allison
Portland, OR​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

AirView Consulting appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, "Designation: Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility" (Docket FAA-2026-4558).

AirView supports the FAA's objective of establishing a structured, transparent process for protecting facilities that present legitimate national security, public safety, and critical infrastructure concerns. A standardized framework provides greater consistency for facility operators while improving regulatory certainty for legitimate unmanned aircraft operators.

Based on our experience supporting public safety organizations, emergency management, Medical Reserve Corps operations, FAA regulatory compliance, unmanned aircraft integration, and multi-agency coordination, we respectfully offer the following recommendations:

1. Preserve Emergency Response Capability

The final rule should clearly recognize that authorized public safety operations—including law enforcement, fire service, emergency medical services, emergency management agencies, Medical Reserve Corps organizations, and other authorized disaster-response missions—may require timely access within or near designated restricted areas during emergencies. The final rule should provide a practical and predictable mechanism for rapid operational coordination when emergency response requires access.

2. Provide a Clear Process for Authorized Operators

The rule should establish transparent procedures allowing properly authorized operators to request and receive approval for legitimate operations near designated facilities. Predictable approval criteria will improve compliance while supporting lawful governmental, commercial, and public safety operations.

3. Maintain Narrow, Risk-Based Restrictions

Restrictions should remain limited to those reasonably necessary to address demonstrated security or safety risks. Narrowly tailored restrictions will better protect critical facilities while minimizing unnecessary impacts on legitimate unmanned aircraft operations.

4. Encourage Coordinated Situational Awareness

As unmanned aircraft become increasingly integrated into emergency response operations, coordinated situational awareness becomes increasingly important. Technologies and operational procedures that improve coordination among authorized responders—including shared operating picture capabilities such as Team Awareness Kit (TAK)—can improve safety, reduce confusion, and enhance operational effectiveness while supporting compliance with FAA requirements.

AirView Consulting supports the FAA's effort to establish a consistent national framework for protecting qualifying fixed-site facilities while continuing the safe integration of unmanned aircraft into the National Airspace System.

To Whom It May Concern:
The Bank Policy Institute1 and American Bankers Association2 appreciate the opportunity to
comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's proposed rule to restrict drone operations over
certain critical infrastructure sites. As the proposal notes, unmanned aircraft systems pose unique and
evolving threats to the critical physical infrastructure operated by financial institutions.3
The financial industry supports the FAA's proposed implementation of section 2209 because it
establishes a lawful, measured, and necessary process for restricting unmanned aircraft operations near
qualifying critical infrastructure sites. Congress directed the FAA to create a process under which
operators or proprietors of certain fixed-site facilities may request an unmanned aircraft flight
restriction.4 The proposal would do so through a new part 74 framework requiring applicants to show a
site-specific need grounded in aviation safety, protection of people and property on the ground,
national security, or homeland security.
Our members operate thousands of facilities that support the continuity, resilience, and security
of the financial services sector. Unauthorized unmanned aircraft activity near those sites can create
obvious and legitimate risks including: surveillance, hostile reconnaissance, operational disruption,
interference with emergency response, and threats to executives, employees, customers, and critical
business functions. This is also an area where cyber and physical security converge. Unauthorized
1 The Bank Policy Institute is a nonpartisan public policy, research, and advocacy group that represents universal
banks, regional banks, and the major foreign banks doing business in the United States. The Institute produces
academic research and analysis on regulatory and monetary policy topics, analyzes and comments on proposed
regulations, and represents the financial services industry with respect to cybersecurity, fraud, and other
information security issues. Business, Innovation, Technology and Security (“BITS”), BPI’s technology policy
division, provides an executive-level forum to discuss and promote current and emerging technology, foster
innovation, reduce fraud, and improve cybersecurity and risk management practices for the financial sector.
2 The American Bankers Association is the voice of the nation’s $26.1 trillion banking industry, which is composed
of small, regional and large banks that together employ over 2 million people, safeguard $20.5 trillion in deposits
and extend $13.7 trillion in loans.
3 Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility, 91 Fed. Reg.
24650, 24669 (proposed May 6, 2026).
4 Id. at 24650.
1

drone activity can enhance threat actor reconnaissance efforts for planning cyber intrusions, fraud,
extortion, and ransomware attacks.
The proposed rule addresses those risks in a sensible way. It does not impose a blanket
prohibition on drone operations. Instead, it creates a petition-based framework with facility-specific
justification, defined boundaries, FAA review, and limited exceptions for certain operations within a
designated unmanned aircraft flight restriction.
That balance matters. A designated restriction gives compliant operators clear notice of where
they cannot fly. It also helps corporate security teams and law enforcement distinguish authorized
activities from those that are suspicious or unlawful—strengthening preventive security before an
incident occurs. Similarly, we appreciate that the proposal provides other critical infrastructure sectors
we depend upon (e.g. energy, water, and telecommunications) with the same pathway to petition the
FAA for an unmanned aircraft flight restriction when circumstances warrant.
Financial sector criteria
The proposed criteria for the financial sector5 appropriately identify the facilities most
susceptible to unmanned aircraft risk. The NPRM would limit eligibility to fixed-site facilities that meet
the statutory definition of critical infrastructure and fall within identified sectors, a structure that helps
focus relief on facilities whose disruption could have a debilitating effect on security or national
economic security.
That approach fits the financial sector. Not every office or branch warrants a flight restriction.
But certain financial services facilities perform functions whose disruption could impair payment flows,
liquidity management, cash operations, data security, crisis response, or other core business functions.
A rule that ties eligibility to fixed-site critical infrastructure, rather than to an entire industry in the
abstract, gives the FAA an administrable standard and gives applicants a clear burden to meet.
Under the proposed rule, applicants would be required to submit information on existing
unmanned aircraft activity over a facility, the nature of the facility’s assets and associated vulnerabilities,
and risks due to unmanned aircraft. While this is not an unreasonable request, the sensitivity of this
information would require the FAA to implement robust data security measures to prevent improper
disclosure directly damaging to applicants.
Moreover, applicants should not have to wait until a critical unmanned aircraft incident has
already occurred at specific site to be granted an UAFR. It is also not clear whether the FAA would apply
some threshold to what it considered appropriate or inappropriate levels of activity given that not all
potential drone threats are equal. Instead, the FAA should permit applicants to use both site-specific
activity as well as evidence of actual or potential risks at similarly situated critical infrastructure facilities
to justify the placement of an UAFR at a financial institution-related site.
5 Id. at 24669.
2

Requested clarification
The FAA should clarify that a designation under proposed part 74 would not prohibit a financial
institution from using drones for its own lawful physical security purposes at an eligible financial services
facility, provided the institution complies with otherwise applicable FAA requirements. The preamble
already states that a UAFR would not itself authorize a geo-fence or other electromagnetic barrier6 and
that certain operations under parts 91, 107, 108, 135, and 137 may operate within a UAFR subject to
specified conditions, including Remote ID and notice requirements.7
A short clarification in proposed section 74.250 would avoid confusion. Financial institutions
may use drones for perimeter inspection, incident assessment, emergency response support, or other
security-related functions at covered facilities. The final rule should make clear that the UAFR
framework aims to deter unauthorized operations, not to disable lawful security operations conducted
by or for the protected facility itself. That clarification would reinforce the rule's security purpose and
reduce the risk that institutions decline useful and lawful protective measures because of regulatory
uncertainty.
Conclusion
We support the proposed rule and encourage the FAA to finalize it. The proposal implements
section 2209 through a clear and disciplined process that respects both security needs on the ground
and the FAA's responsibility to preserve safe and efficient use of the airspace. With the clarification
above, the rule will better protect financial services facilities and the broader critical infrastructure
ecosystem on which the banking system depends.
Sincerely,

American Bankers Association

As the InfraGard Dams Sector Chief for Region 8, I submit this comment to emphasize the
critical importance of protecting Dams Sector assets from unauthorized unmanned aircraft
systems (UAS) operations. The Dams Sector is one of the 16 critical infrastructure sectors and
includes dams, navigation locks, and levees. These assets provide essential services supporting
water supply, flood control, navigation, agriculture, energy generation, and protection of other
critical infrastructure.
1. Overview Section – Inclusion of Levees
The overview section appropriately highlights the importance of dams and locks but does not
adequately address the vital role of levees in our nation’s infrastructure. I recommend adding the
following language (or similar) to provide a more complete description of the Dams Sector:
Levees are essential man-made embankments designed to protect approximately 23 million
people and more than $2 trillion in infrastructure by containing rising river levels and blocking
coastal storm surges (National Levee Database, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers). By confining
water to specific channels, levees prevent the inundation of floodplains, enabling the
development of major urban centers and the cultivation of high-yield agricultural regions.
Beyond local protection, these structures safeguard vital national transportation and energy
networks in low-lying areas. For example, the Lafourche Basin Levee System in Louisiana helps
protect a nuclear power plant from inundation that could result in a catastrophic failure of the
reactor cooling system.
2. Eligibility Criteria – Dams
The proposed eligibility criteria for dams are unnecessarily stringent and may leave many critical
assets vulnerable to UAS incursions. High or significant hazard potential dams, as classified in
the National Inventory of Dams, along with all dams that have hydroelectric generation or
pumped hydro storage capability, should be eligible to apply for an Unmanned Aircraft Flight
Restriction (UAFR).
The significant costs associated with repairing damage to dams or their appurtenances —
whether from intentional or accidental UAS activity — strongly support broader eligibility. Even
lower-hazard dams can have substantial regional or national consequences if compromised.
3. Eligibility Criteria – Locks and Levees
The eligibility criteria for navigation locks are also too narrow. Any lock serving a navigation
function should be eligible for a UAFR, given their importance to commercial transportation and
supply chains.
Levees should be explicitly included in the acceptance criteria. Many levees directly protect
populations, agricultural lands, and assets belonging to multiple other critical infrastructure
sectors (e.g., energy, transportation systems, water and wastewater systems). Levees that provide
such protection should qualify for UAFR designation.
Dams, locks, and levees are integral to community water systems and collectively support
national resilience across sectors. Broadening eligibility for these assets would better align the
rule with the full scope and risk profile of the Dams Sector.
Thank you,
Kris Schartau
InfraGard Dams Sector Chief for Region 8

in the Hampton Roads, Virginia region — including at least one facility that meets the
NPRM’s eligible critical infrastructure criteria — in planning real-world UAFR
operational deployments.
LONGBOW strongly supports the proposed Part 74 framework. Establishing defined,
chartable, verifiable, and legally enforceable airspace protection around critical
infrastructure is a necessary step in maturing the National Airspace System for scalable
UAS integration. The NPRM creates the correct structural foundation. These comments
identify specific areas where the final rule’s implementation framework — particularly
its data architecture, operator access workflow, and notification requirements — would
benefit from additional FAA guidance and minimum standards.
LONGBOW submits seven technical positions below, organized by the sections of the
NPRM to which they most directly apply.
II. POSITIONS
Position 1: Require Machine-Readable UAFR Data Publication
Regulatory context: The NPRM proposes that designated UAFRs be published in
FAA Order JO 7400.12 (incorporated by reference under §74.30) and noticed through
the Federal Register. The rule does not specify a structured data format, schema, or
machine-readable publication mechanism for UAFR boundaries.
LONGBOW’s position: The FAA should require that UAFR boundaries, vertical
limits, site identifiers, effective dates, expiration dates, designation status, and UAFR
type (standard vs. Special) be published in a machine-readable, structured format
accessible to UAS Service Suppliers (USS), UTM providers, and operational systems
such as PEGASUS GUARDIAN in near real time.
Rationale: Manual charting and NOTAM-based publication alone are insufficient for
real-time airspace enforcement in high-tempo BVLOS operations. A UAFR that is not
machine-readable in a structured format cannot be programmatically ingested into the
monitoring, deconfliction, and corridor authorization systems that the FAA
contemplates under the Part 108 framework. As the proposed rule itself acknowledges, a
UAFR has defined horizontal and vertical limits and may carry multiple operational
terms. These parameters must be available as structured data — not only graphical
depictions — for the operational infrastructure serving UAFR sites to function correctly.
EUROCAE ED-269 CHG 1:2025 (Minimum Operational Performance Standard for
UAS Geographical Zones) defines how geographic restriction zones must be structured
and published in machine-readable form, including required fields for zone type,
altitude limits, time windows, responsible authority, and applicable operator categories.
The companion standard EUROCAE ED-318:2024 (Technical Specification for
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 | Page 2 of 9

Geographical Zones and U-Space Data Provision and Exchange) defines the machine-
readable data format and exchange protocol for publishing those zones to UTM service
providers — the more directly applicable specification for the data publication
architecture Position 1 recommends. Together, ED-269 CHG 1:2025 and ED-318:2024
have been adopted across European UTM implementations and demonstrate that a
standardized, machine-readable geographic restriction zone schema is both technically
feasible and operationally proven at scale. LONGBOW recommends the FAA use this
standards pair as the template for UAFR data publication rather than developing a novel
schema from scratch.
The FAA Data Exchange (LAANC infrastructure) already delivers structured airspace
authorization data to USS providers under interfaces conforming to ASTM F3548-21
(UAS Traffic Management USS Interoperability). LONGBOW recommends the FAA
extend the F3548-21 data model explicitly to include UAFR boundaries, leveraging the
existing USS ecosystem to propagate UAFR status to operators pre-flight. A UAFR data
layer structured as an extension of F3548-21 — rather than a parallel and potentially
conflicting specification — would enable immediate integration by the USS providers
already certified under LAANC.
As an FAA-designated LAANC USS since 2023, LONGBOW has direct operational
experience with the LAANC facility map and grid architecture. UAFR boundaries should
be published as a structured overlay that aligns with — and does not contradict — the
existing LAANC facility grid. Where a UAFR is established over or adjacent to a LAANC-
covered facility, the UAFR boundary geometry, vertical limits, and authorization status
must be expressed in the same coordinate and grid reference system as the surrounding
LAANC authorization surfaces. Misaligned or overlapping representations between
LAANC-authorized airspace and UAFR-restricted airspace will create operator
confusion, USS deconfliction failures, and legal ambiguity about which authorization
state governs a specific location and altitude. The LAANC model provides the correct
template: facility-anchored, grid-aligned, machine-readable, and propagated to
operators through USS providers in near real time. UAFR publication should be an
extension of that model, not a separate layer.
Minimum recommended specification: UAFR GeoJSON (RFC 7946) or ED-269-
aligned geometry with: site_id, uafr_type (standard/special), facility sector, horizontal
boundary, AGL floor and ceiling, effective_date, status (active/suspended/expired),
last_modified timestamp, LAANC facility_id cross-reference where applicable, and a
public-access API endpoint conforming to OpenAPI Specification 3.x.
Position 2: Establish a Standardized Digital Notification Interface for Facility
Operators
Regulatory context: The NPRM requires that operators seeking access to a standard
UAFR provide advance notification to the facility operator/proprietor. The proposed
rule does not define a standard data format, notification channel, response workflow, or
minimum acknowledgment timeline for this notification.
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 | Page 3 of 9

LONGBOW’s position: This is the most operationally critical gap in the proposed
rule. The FAA should establish minimum standards — or mandate a standardized API —
for the facility notification workflow. Without a standard interface, each UAFR site will
develop an ad-hoc process, creating a fragmented, unscalable notification ecosystem
that fails operators conducting cross-facility or corridor operations.
Rationale: Under the proposed Part 108 framework, a single drone delivery route may
transit multiple UAFR sites. A national UAS logistics operator cannot manually contact
each facility by phone or email before each flight. The operational reality of scalable
BVLOS operations requires a notification mechanism that is:
1. Digital and structured — notification data (operator identity, aircraft
registration, Remote ID serials, certificate type, mission time window, approved
area) submitted and received in machine-readable form
2. Near real-time — time-sensitive operations cannot tolerate multi-hour or
same-business-day response windows
3. Auditable — the notification and any facility acknowledgment must be
timestamped and cryptographically durable for evidence and compliance
purposes
4. Revocable — the facility must be able to withdraw acknowledgment for a
specific mission window and have that state propagated to monitoring
infrastructure
LONGBOW recommends the FAA require UAFR sites above a threshold complexity
(e.g., facilities where BVLOS corridor operations are anticipated) to accept notifications
via a FAA-defined structured API, with a reference implementation made available
through the existing USS/UTM ecosystem. Smaller sites or lower-complexity UAFRs
could satisfy notification requirements through a web-based portal that generates a
machine-readable confirmation artifact.
Without this standard, the two most important UAFR compliance
functions — knowing who is supposed to be there and notifying the
facility when someone arrives — cannot be reliably automated,
correlated, or enforced.
Position 3: Define Minimum Performance Standards for Fixed-Site Remote ID
Monitoring Infrastructure
Regulatory context: The NPRM makes Remote ID operationally central to UAFR
compliance. Fixed-site applicants are expected to have the capability to receive Remote
ID broadcasts, either directly or through contracted services. The proposed rule does not
specify minimum coverage, receiver density, timestamping, retention, or health-
monitoring requirements for Remote ID sensing infrastructure at UAFR sites.
LONGBOW’s position: The FAA should establish minimum performance
characteristics for fixed-site Remote ID monitoring deployed to support UAFR
operations, including:
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 | Page 4 of 9

• Coverage validation — a documented methodology for demonstrating that the
deployed receiver network achieves adequate ground-level and low-altitude
coverage within the designated UAFR boundary
• Timestamping precision — Remote ID messages used in compliance and
evidence workflows must carry traceable UTC timestamps to a defined precision
(LONGBOW recommends 100ms or better); fixed-site receivers should
synchronize to UTC using IEEE 1588-2019 Precision Time Protocol (PTP) (as
amended by IEEE 1588a/d/c/e through 2024) or equivalent, consistent with
evidence admissibility standards
• Retention duration — logged Remote ID messages should be retained for a
minimum period sufficient to support FAA annual reporting requirements and
law enforcement investigations (LONGBOW recommends 365 days minimum)
• Receiver health monitoring — UAFR sites should be able to demonstrate that
their Remote ID receiver network was operational and recording during any
period for which they assert compliance monitoring
ASTM F3411-22a (Standard Specification for Remote ID and Tracking), the technical
standard underlying FAA Part 89, defines the Remote ID broadcast message format and
minimum transmission intervals for UAS. It does not, however, address fixed-site
receiver requirements: coverage methodology, receiver density, timestamping precision,
retention duration, or health monitoring are outside the scope of F3411-22a. This gap is
intentional in the context of the existing rule — but it creates a critical deficiency for
UAFR compliance, where a fixed-site operator must be able to affirmatively
demonstrate what was observed, when, and with what fidelity. A UAFR compliance
record is only as valid as the completeness and integrity of the underlying sensing
record. Without minimum standards, UAFR sites may deploy insufficient sensing
infrastructure, creating gaps that undermine the evidentiary chain when violations
occur. For Special UAFRs where criminal penalties may attach, the sensing record must
meet a higher evidentiary bar.
LONGBOW’s PEGASUS GUARDIAN architecture already implements these
capabilities; we recommend the FAA adopt minimum standards that make them floor
requirements for all UAFR operational monitoring.
Position 4: Establish a Secure, Auditable Authorized-Operator Whitelist Model
Regulatory context: The NPRM envisions a process by which certain operators
establish their authorization status to operate within a specific UAFR. The proposed rule
does not specify how an operator’s authorization is recorded, maintained, updated, or
communicated to the UAFR site’s monitoring infrastructure.
LONGBOW’s position: The FAA should establish a secure, revocable, auditable
whitelist model that links operator identity, aircraft registration, Remote ID serials, and
certificate/permit type into a structured authorization record associated with a specific
UAFR site and mission scope.
Key design requirements:
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 | Page 5 of 9

1. One-time credential submission — an operator should be able to submit
certificate credentials and Remote ID serial numbers once and reference a
credential record for subsequent missions, rather than resubmitting on each
notification
2. Revocability — the facility operator or FAA should be able to revoke a whitelist
entry with immediate effect, and that revocation should propagate to monitoring
infrastructure
3. API-based updates — whitelist records should be queryable and updateable via
a structured API to support real-time correlation against observed Remote ID
broadcasts
4. Trust scoring — the FAA should consider whether to allow UAFR sites to
maintain tiered trust levels based on operator history (e.g., repeated successful
prior missions vs. first contact)
5. Privacy protection — operator identity and certificate data held in whitelists
should be handled under appropriate privacy controls, with access limited to the
specific facility and authorized law enforcement
Rationale: The authorization problem is the core unsolved operational challenge in the
NPRM. The rule creates a clear legal distinction between authorized and unauthorized
operations, but does not define how that distinction is made machine-readable and
verifiable in real time. A monitoring system that cannot programmatically distinguish a
known whitelisted operator from an unknown intruder cannot serve the facility
notification, risk scoring, or evidence documentation functions the NPRM envisions.
Position 5: Define a Standard Evidence Package Schema
Regulatory context: The NPRM envisions that UAFR sites will be able to document
violations and provide information to law enforcement. The proposed rule does not
specify the content, format, or integrity requirements for UAFR incident
documentation.
LONGBOW’s position: The FAA should define a standard evidence package schema
for UAFR incidents that includes at minimum:
• Track history with timestamped position data and altitude AGL
• Sensor sources contributing to the track (Remote ID, radar, RF, EO/IR, acoustic,
ADS-B)
• Observed Remote ID serial (or null/missing/mismatch notation)
• Authorization and notification state at time of incursion
(notified/whitelisted/unknown/denied)
• Behavior flags (hovering, loitering, route deviation, RID-missing, RID-mismatch)
• Risk score and rule triggers
• Chain-of-custody metadata including hash of logged sensor records, record
creation timestamp, and custodian identity
• Export format compatible with law enforcement and FAA reporting requirements
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 | Page 6 of 9

Rationale: Without a standard schema, incident documentation will vary widely across
UAFR sites, making cross-site pattern analysis, multi-agency coordination, and FAA
compliance auditing impractical. LONGBOW has developed a canonical UAFR Event
Object as part of its PEGASUS GUARDIAN product architecture; we recommend the
FAA align the final rule’s evidence requirements with a published minimum data
standard.
For Special UAFRs where criminal penalties may apply, chain-of-custody integrity is
essential. Established federal standards provide the applicable framework. NIST SP
800-86 (Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response) defines the
principles for acquiring, preserving, and presenting digital evidence in a manner
admissible in legal proceedings — UAFR evidence packages should conform to its chain-
of-custody requirements. Cryptographic timestamps on UAFR event records should
conform to RFC 3161 (Internet X.509 PKI Time-Stamp Protocol) as updated by RFC
5816 (which added SHA-2 algorithm support), providing a legally recognized
mechanism for proving that a record existed at a specific time and has not been altered
since. For prosecutable Special UAFR violations, evidence handling should additionally
conform to ISO/IEC 27037 (Guidelines for identification, collection, acquisition and
preservation of digital evidence), the international standard for digital evidence that
underpins cross-agency and cross-jurisdictional case transfer. The FAA should specify
these standards by reference in the final rule rather than defining a novel evidence
handling framework.
Position 6: Preserve Lawful Airspace Access for Critical Operations
Regulatory context: The NPRM proposes that certain vetted operator categories —
Part 91, 107, 108, 135, 137 — retain access rights within standard UAFRs subject to
notification. This is the correct design.
LONGBOW’s position: LONGBOW strongly supports the FAA’s intent to preserve
lawful access for vetted operators and urges the FAA to ensure the final rule’s
notification and authorization requirements do not inadvertently create access burdens
that prevent operationally critical UAS missions.
Specific applications that must be preserved:
• Public safety and emergency response — law enforcement, fire, search and
rescue, and emergency management UAS operations under jurisdictional
authority must not be delayed or impeded by notification workflows that cannot
accommodate exigent circumstances
• Medical logistics — Level I trauma centers with helipads are specifically
identified as eligible UAFR facilities; the final rule must ensure that medical
drone operations (organ transport, blood delivery, emergency supply) operating
to or through UAFRs can satisfy notification requirements without endangering
patient outcomes
• Infrastructure inspection — utility operators inspecting their own
infrastructure within a UAFR they petition for should not be required to notify
themselves
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 | Page 7 of 9

• Disaster response and utility restoration — emergency UAS operations
during and after natural disasters must have a defined expedited access process
that does not require full pre-flight notification when the UAFR site itself is the
subject of the response
Rationale: UAFRs should make critical infrastructure more secure, not less
operationally capable. The access framework should be designed with the assumption
that high-frequency legitimate operations will be the norm at most UAFR sites, and that
the notification and whitelist system exists to facilitate — not impede — that access
while documenting the record.
Position 7: Establish a Controlled Information Model for Special UAFR Site Data
Regulatory context: The NPRM creates Special UAFRs for high-security federal,
defense, intelligence, and homeland security sites. The locations and boundaries of
some Special UAFR sites may themselves be sensitive.
LONGBOW’s position: The FAA should establish a controlled information handling
model for Special UAFR site data that allows the rule’s technical requirements —
machine-readable boundaries, notification APIs, monitoring standards — to be
implemented without requiring that sensitive site details be publicly disclosed.
Recommended framework:
1. Public layer — Special UAFRs are designated and charted at a sufficient level to
prevent accidental airspace incursion, with enough geographic specificity that an
operator in preflight planning can identify the UAFR and comply with
notification requirements
2. Controlled layer — detailed site geometry, sensor architecture, monitoring
coverage, and operational terms are accessible only to the UAFR petitioner,
designated monitoring providers, and authorized using-agency personnel,
protected under applicable information-security frameworks
3. Segmented notification — using-agency approval workflows for Special UAFR
access are conducted through secure channels that do not require sensitive site
data to transit public networks or be logged in shared USS infrastructure
Rationale: The value of the Special UAFR framework depends on whether high-
security federal and defense sites actually petition for designation. If the designation
process or the resulting machine-readable data publication exposes sensitive
operational details, security-conscious facilities will decline to petition. A tiered
information model preserves the security value of the designation for those sites while
maintaining the operational benefits of structured UAFR data for standard-site
operations.
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 | Page 8 of 9

III. CONCLUSION
LONGBOW supports the proposed Part 74 rulemaking. Establishing persistent, legally
enforceable, machine-readable airspace protection around critical infrastructure is the
correct regulatory architecture for low-altitude UAS integration at scale. The NPRM
provides the correct structural foundation.
The seven positions above identify implementation-layer gaps — particularly in operator
notification standards and authorized-operator verification — where additional FAA
specificity in the final rule will determine whether UAFR operational compliance is
achievable at scale or collapses into a patchwork of site-specific, non-interoperable
processes.
LONGBOW is prepared to engage directly with FAA staff on any of the technical
positions above, to share PEGASUS GUARDIAN architecture documentation relevant to
the rulemaking record, or to participate in any advisory or industry working group the
FAA convenes in connection with Part 74 implementation.

Dear Administrator:
On behalf of the Boston Red Sox, we are providing comments on the FAA’s Proposed Rule on
unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (“UAFRs”) with respect to fixed site facilities. We applaud
the Administration for proposing this rule and we support the goals, approach and specific
procedures as proposed. We offer the following comments for your consideration.
We agree wholeheartedly with the Administration’s recognition that sports and entertainment
venues should be included in the types of critical commercial facilities that merit protection from
unauthorized unmanned aircraft flights. The language in the proposed rule (§ 74.82) aptly
captures the serious consequences that could stem from a UAV security intrusion at a venue such
as Fenway Park: “The cascading effects of a UAV incident occurring at a facility serving this
large of a community would extend beyond the target facility and negatively affect supply
chains, tourism, and the nation's economy.” We invest significant resources, time and focus to
safeguard our ballparks – both Fenway Park in Boston and our spring training facility, JetBlue
Park in Ft. Myers, Florida – because any type of security breach would not only endanger our
large numbers of fans, employees and players, but would also create major actual and symbolic
damage to the entire outdoor sports and live entertainment industry. Last year, the Department
of Homeland Security recognized Fenway Park for SAFETY Act designation, and our
collaborative efforts with federal, state and local law enforcement underscore the stakes when it
comes to protecting against all types of physical security threats.
With respect to eligibility for limitations on unmanned aircraft flights, we urge the
Administration to modify several proposed criteria in § 74.82 in order to provide for more
flexibility to consider all of the circumstances when adopting UAFRs. Specifically:
• Outdoor sports and live entertainment venues should be eligible to seek permanent
special UAFRs regardless of whether they are able to obtain temporary flight

restrictions as well. Fenway Park, like most other large venues, hosts a wide range of
events and activities in addition to its core offering, Major League baseball games.
Those events include movie nights and amateur high school and college sports events
attended by anywhere from a few thousand people to tens of thousands, as well as
private events in the ballpark for schools, charitable and civic organizations, private
companies and other clients. Temporary flight restrictions would not be available for
this array of smaller events, but a potential UAV incident involving those types of
events could threaten serious direct physical and economic damage (including the
dangers of bodily injury or death), and any breach at any time at Fenway Park would
have serious consequences to our business and the entire industry.
• The criterion for a venue being “primarily outdoors and not enclosed” is vague and not
necessary. Many large sports and entertainment venues include significant spaces that
are covered and/or enclosed areas, and those entire venues merit protection.
• The minimum total attendance requirement of 2.5 million visitors or more in the prior
year is unnecessarily restrictive. Although Fenway Park surpasses this threshold each
year, some Major League Baseball facilities might not, and our organization urges
protection for every venue at which our team participates. In addition, our spring
training facility hosts approximately a full month of Major League spring training
games featuring all of our top players and thousands of fans. JetBlue Park and all other
spring training venues should be eligible for UAFRs even though they do not host 2.5
million fans a year.
• The requirement that a venue be “open to the public” for at least 120 days a year is
likewise unnecessarily restrictive. Does “open to the public” include activities and
events that a venue hosts for charitable organizations and corporate or individual
clients? Does it include smaller events and tours? In any case, Fenway Park typically
has approximately 120 large public entertainment and other events each year, but if in a
given year it was “open to the public” only for 81 or 90 or 100 dates, it would still be a
major economic engine for the city and region. As emphasized above, any security
breach involving Fenway Park could have widespread, long-lasting repercussions, and
an inflexible minimum number of events would artificially limit the effectiveness of the
Administration’s proposed regulatory regime.
In short, we urge the Administration to remove these limiting criteria for eligibility and instead to
allow any outdoor sports and live entertainment venue with seating capacity of at least 5,000
persons to apply for UAFR protections, without including unnecessary limiting requirements.
With respect to the geographic extent of restrictions, we strongly support a program that would
include not only the specific venue property itself within property lines, but also a lateral zone
with a radius of at least 1,000 feet. When venues like Fenway Park host large events with
thousands of people, the large crowds entering and exiting the venue could be vulnerable to
incidents involving UAVs, and an incident outside of the venue could cause as much human,
economic and psychological damage as an event inside the venue.
2

In the same spirit of encouraging flexibility, we urge the Administration not to require formal
security assessments for all venues seeking restrictions. There may be some instances in which a
formal assessment is warranted. There will surely be many cases, however, such as large
professional sports venues, where no formal assessment is needed and it is intuitively obvious
that permanent UAFR protections are appropriate.
As we understand the proposed rule, a venue would be able to request a special UAFR
designation that would still allow for drone flights in its airspace if specifically authorized by the
venue operator and the FAA. We encourage the FAA to make clear in its final rule and
accompanying materials that certain authorized unmanned aircraft flights may be allowed. On
limited occasions, sports and entertainment venues may wish to grant access to drones operated
by reputable, licensed entities to capture video footage or for other safe, valid entertainment
purposes. The UAFR process should accommodate such authorized, safe uses of drone
technology.
As the FAA continues the rulemaking process, we would be glad to speak with your staff to
provide further feedback and guidance based on our extensive experience operating one of
America’s iconic entertainment venues and providing a safe experience to millions of fans and
visitors each year.
We appreciate the opportunity to provide this feedback and again applaud the Administration for
moving forward with these important measures.
Sincerely,
David S. Friedman
Executive Vice President, Legal & Government Affairs

Security & Ballpark Operations
