Dear Administrator Bedford:
The Texas Department of Transportation is pleased to provide comments to the
proposed rule posted by the Federal Aviation Administration on May 6, 2026:
Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility. TxDOT offers the following comments on the proposed rule:
FAA proposes that operators or proprietors within the Transportation
sector may apply for a UAFR if the facility meets one of the following
criteria:
Highway bridges or tunnels that serve 50,000 or more vehicles daily and have a
structure length of at least a half mile.
• Comment: TxDOT agrees with the inclusion of highway bridges and tunnels
in the Transportation Systems Sector as eligible critical infrastructure.
However, the setting thresholds (50,000+ Average Daily Traffic AND a half-
mile length) are insufficient. Many structurally critical or economically vital
bridges may fall just short of the half-mile mark or see seasonal traffic
variations, yet their destruction or disruption would still have a debilitating
regional impact.
• Recommendation: Revise the eligibility threshold to allow State DOTs to
designate critical bridges based on structural criticality (e.g., fracture-critical
bridges), lack of viable detour routes, or overall economic impact to the
region, rather than relying solely on vehicle counts and length metrics.
The facility must have designated security personnel... [and] security
monitoring must include the capability, either directly or through a
contracted service, to receive broadcast Remote Identification messages
from unmanned aircraft.
• Comment: TxDOT supports the rule’s inclusion of security measures to
ensure Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) are actively monitored.
However, the rule does not fully reflect the physical and financial realities of
transportation infrastructure. Highway bridges and tunnels rarely have
dedicated, on-site "designated security personnel". Furthermore, outfitting

multiple bridges with Remote ID (RID) radio-frequency receivers (costing an

City of Mesa Comments on FAA Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Critical Facility
General Comments
The City of Mesa appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).
Mesa supports the FAA's efforts to protect critical infrastructure from unauthorized or malicious unmanned aircraft activity while maintaining public access to the National Airspace System.
As Arizona's third-largest city and a provider of critical municipal services, Mesa owns and operates infrastructure supporting public health, safety, economic security, transportation, emergency response, communications, and regional water and energy reliability. The City encourages the FAA to adopt a risk-based framework recognizing the role local governments play in providing and protecting critical infrastructure.
Municipal Critical Infrastructure Should Be Eligible
The City recommends that the FAA establish eligibility criteria allowing municipal critical infrastructure to qualify for UAFRs when disruption, surveillance, interference, or attack could adversely affect public health and safety, homeland security, economic security, continuity of government operations, or community resilience.
Eligibility criteria should focus on the criticality of a facility and the consequences of disruption rather than whether a facility is publicly or privately owned.
Eligible facilities should include infrastructure within the following sectors:
• Emergency services, including emergency communications centers, emergency operations centers, and critical public safety facilities;
• Communications and information technology facilities, including public safety communications infrastructure, municipal data centers, and operational control systems;
• Water and wastewater systems, including treatment plants, reclamation facilities, pump stations, reservoirs, recharge facilities, utility operations centers, and SCADA systems;
• Energy systems, including electric generation, transmission and distribution facilities, natural gas infrastructure, utility operations centers, and SCADA systems;
• Transportation systems, including airport operational facilities, transportation management centers, transit operations facilities, and transportation communications infrastructure; and
• Government facilities necessary to maintain continuity of essential public services.
Authorized Government and Utility Operations
The City recommends that the FAA expressly allow authorized unmanned aircraft operations conducted by or on behalf of the owner or operator of a protected facility. Municipalities and public utilities rely on drones for infrastructure inspections, utility operations, emergency response, damage assessment, and public safety missions. The City further recommends that the FAA establish a standing authorization or expedited approval process for these operations so that essential governmental and utility functions can continue while supporting the security objectives of the UAFR program.
Recommended Eligibility Criteria
The City recommends that the FAA evaluate eligibility based on objective risk and consequence factors, including:
Population Served
Facilities should receive consideration based on the number of residents and businesses dependent upon their operation.
Critical Customer Impacts
The FAA should consider whether a facility supports:
• Emergency response agencies;
• Hospitals and healthcare facilities;
• Critical utility and infrastructure facilities;
• Essential government operations;
• Airports;
• Defense and aerospace facilities;
• Semiconductor manufacturing and advanced technology facilities; and
• Major employers.
Consequence of Failure
Eligibility should consider whether a drone-related incident could result in:
• Disruption of emergency response or communications capabilities;
• Significant public health and safety impacts;
• Loss or disruption of water, wastewater, reclaimed water, electric, or natural gas services;
• Compromise of drinking water quality or treatment processes resulting from interference, contamination, or disruption of water treatment operations;
• Interruption of transportation operations;
• Loss of operational control systems; or
• Significant economic disruption.
Security and Operational Vulnerability
The FAA should evaluate:
• Documented unauthorized drone activity;
• Exposure of critical infrastructure components;
• Vulnerabilities identifiable through aerial surveillance;
• Cybersecurity risks associated with access to sensitive facilities; and
• Potential disruption of essential public services.

July 1, 2026

The Honorable Bryan Bedford
Administrator
Federal Aviation Administration
U.S. Department of Transportation
800 Independence Avenue SW
Washington, DC 20591

SUBJECT: COMMENTS ON THE FAA NOTICE OF PROPOSED RULEMAKING ON UNMANNED AIRCRAFT FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS (DOCKET NO. FAA-2026-4558)

Dear Administrator Bedford:

On behalf of the undersigned California ports, we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) establishing a process for fixed-site facilities to request an Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (UAFR). California's ports play a critical role in the national supply chain, international trade, and economic security, and therefore have a strong interest in ensuring that unmanned aircraft system (UAS) protections adequately address the unique risks present in complex maritime environments.

The comments below identify key areas where the proposed rule, as written, does not fully reflect the operational realities of major seaports, particularly those with extensive waterfront infrastructure. We respectfully offer recommendations to ensure the final rule aligns with both aviation-safety priorities and long-established maritime security frameworks administered by the U.S. Coast Guard.

1. Need for UAFR Coverage Over Waterside Areas Adjacent to Critical Waterfront Assets

Under the proposed rule, a Standard UAFR may only encompass the airspace directly above a fixed-site facility owned by an applicant. While this may function adequately for inland fixed-site facilities, it creates significant gaps for seaport facilities, where critical infrastructure often sits on waterfronts, adjacent to open waterways.

Many high-risk waterfront assets, such as passenger terminals, refined-product berths, liquid bulk facilities, container wharves, and security-sensitive utility corridors, are located along water channels, turning basins, slips, and other navigable waterways extending throughout port complexes. These same waterways frequently serve as the operational backbone of maritime commerce and as primary approach paths for vessels, public-safety agencies, and daily industrial marine operations.

Because public port authorities generally own the land but not the adjacent navigable waters, the proposed rule's strict property-line limitation prevents UAFRs from covering waterside approaches. This leaves substantial unprotected airspace in areas where drone incursions often occur, particularly offshore or over open water, where operators may exploit unobstructed approach paths to sensitive facilities.

To ensure meaningful protection of waterfront infrastructure, we respectfully request that the FAA revise the rule to allow UAFRs to extend over:

Water channels, basins, and slips that are controlled, managed, or operationally relied upon by a Port or other fixed-site facility;
Waterside approach zones essential to the security of waterfront critical infrastructure; and
Adjacent harbor or outer-harbor areas where drone threats routinely originate or transit.

Recognizing these waterfront areas within potential UAFR boundaries is essential to aligning the rule with the operational profiles of major seaports and with federal recognition that maritime critical infrastructure encompasses both land-side and water-side elements under the Maritime Transportation Security Act (MTSA).

2. Need for a Single Consolidated UAFR for the Entire Port Complex

Large seaports frequently operate under a landlord model in which a public port authority owns the property while multiple private tenants operate terminal and industrial facilities. Under the proposed rule, it is unclear whether each tenant would need to file separate UAFR applications.

A tenant-by-tenant approach would result in a fragmented patchwork of small, inconsistent, and potentially overlapping UAFR boundaries, despite the fact that seaports function as unified operational systems. Such fragmentation would create enforcement challenges, reduce situational awareness for airspace users, and undermine the clarity the UAFR framework is intended to provide.

We recommend that the FAA allow a single, consolidated UAFR application submitted by a public port authority or comparable facility operator on behalf of all tenants and operators within a port complex. A consolidated UAFR would:

Establish a coherent, clearly defined protected airspace;
Enhance enforceability and situational awareness for aviation and maritime stakeholders; and
Align with existing MTSA frameworks, in which port authorities, not individual tenants, are responsible for comprehensive, area-wide security planning.

3. Recognition of Existing Federally Mandated Maritime Security Assessments as Sufficient for Special UAFR Eligibility

The proposed rule proposes that Special UAFRs require a verified security assessment demonstrating credible threats. Ports already conduct rigorous federally mandated assessments under the MTSA framework, including:

Facility Security Assessments (FSAs) for regulated facilities; and
Area Maritime Security Assessments (AMSAs) overseen by the U.S. Coast Guard's Captain of the Port.

These assessments are detailed, comprehensive, and designed specifically to evaluate risks associated with waterfront critical infrastructure, including aerial-approach vulnerabilities over water and from the maritime domain.

Requiring ports to produce duplicative FAA-specific assessments would increase administrative burden without improving security outcomes. We strongly urge FAA to formally recognize MTSA FSAs and AMSAs as acceptable and sufficient documentation for Special UAFR qualification. This will maintain interagency consistency, reduce redundant work, and ensure that drone-airspace determinations remain aligned with the vetted security posture already established by federal maritime authorities.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important rulemaking. California's ports stand ready to collaborate with the FAA to ensure that drone-related airspace protections are harmonized with existing maritime security practices and remain responsive to the operational needs of the nation's most critical gateways.

We look forward to ongoing coordination as the FAA refines and implements the UAFR framework.

Sincerely,

EUGENE D. SEROKA
Executive Director
Port of Los Angeles

DR. NOEL HACEGABA
Chief Executive Officer
Port of Long Beach

KRISTI MCKENNEY
Executive Director
Port of Oakland

COMMENTS OF THE ALLIANCE FOR TELECOMMUNICATIONS INDUSTRY
SOLUTIONS
The Alliance for Telecommunications Industry Solutions (ATIS) respectfully submits these
comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking (NPRM) on the designation of Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) near
fixed site facilities.
I. Introduction
ATIS is a leading global standards development and technical planning organization that
advances technical and operational standards for the information and communications
technologies (ICT) sector. Its diverse membership spans key ICT stakeholders, including
wireless, wireline, and VoIP service providers, equipment manufacturers, broadband providers,
software developers, consumer electronics firms, public safety agencies, and internet service
providers. As a founding partner and the North American Organizational Partner of the Third
Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), ATIS plays a pivotal role in shaping global wireless
specifications, including 4G LTE, 5G NR, and now 6G.
ATIS' Next G Alliance (NGA) is the preeminent North American authority on 6G technology,
charged with advancing United States leadership in next-generation wireless networks.1 The
NGA’s membership spans the full ecosystem required to deploy advanced network capabilities at
national scale: carriers, vendors, universities, research institutions, and government partners.
ATIS also convenes the ATIS Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAV) Initiative, a dedicated program
developing technical standards and policy frameworks for unmanned aircraft integration using
mobile network infrastructure.2
1 More information on ATIS’ Next G Alliance can be found at https://nextgalliance.org/.
2 More information on ATIS’ Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAV) Initiative can be found at
https://atis.org/initiatives/uncrewed-aerial-vehicles-uavs/.

ATIS supports the FAA's objective of protecting critical infrastructure from the safety and
security risks posed by unauthorized Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) operations and
commends the agency for its balanced approach to preserving airspace access for legitimate UAS
operators. These comments identify two active ATIS workstreams with direct relevance to the
questions the FAA has raised in this proceeding. ATIS stands ready to serve as an ongoing
resource to the agency as the outcome of this rulemaking is implemented.
II. The Enforcement Challenge and the Role of the Mobile Network
The NPRM is candid about a fundamental limitation of the proposed framework: the UAFR is a
legal designation, not a physical barrier. Law abiding UAS operators will comply with the
restriction; the safety and security risk will flow from those who do not. The FAA explicitly
acknowledges this and solicits comment on what technological or procedural requirements
should govern UAS access within UAFRs, including how UAS operators should establish their
credibility and whether requirements beyond Remote ID are appropriate.
ATIS submits that the mobile network is uniquely positioned to serve as a technology substrate
for UAFR access management and enforcement support. Mobile Network Operator (MNO)
infrastructure already covers virtually every fixed site facility likely to seek a UAFR in the
United States. It offers network-authenticated identity, two-way communication, and persistent
tracking capabilities that complement and, in key respects, improve upon broadcast-based
identification systems. Remote ID is necessary but not sufficient for the UAFR access-control
problem. As a broadcast protocol dependent on UAS operator compliance and local receiver
infrastructure, it provides no network-authenticated identity verification and no real-time
communication capability between a UAS operator and a facility.
Two ATIS workstreams are developing the standards and technical frameworks to realize the
mobile network's potential in this context. Both are in the initial but meaningful stages, and ATIS
submits them here to inform the FAA's awareness of this emerging work rather than to propose
specific regulatory requirements at this time.
III. Universal Secure Electronic Conspicuity via Mobile Networks
ATIS’ UAV Initiative has begun work on a framework for Universal Secure Electronic
Conspicuity (USEC) using mobile networks. USEC is a dual-mode architecture in which MNO-
based cellular connectivity serves as the primary layer for UAS identification, authorization, and
tracking, with PC5/A2X direct sidelink communication providing a complementary channel
where network connectivity may be limited. This work is aligned with the U.S. Department of
Transportation’s (DOT) Mobile Network Aviation Assessment Program (MNAAP), an effort
assessing cellular technologies as the foundation for next-generation airspace conspicuity and
deconfliction.
USEC is directly relevant to the questions the FAA has raised in this proceeding. The NPRM
asks what information a UAS operator should provide to establish credibility and demonstrate

they are not a security threat, and whether there are additional technological requirements
beyond Remote ID that should govern access through a UAFR. Network-authenticated identity,
confirmed through the UAS operator's MNO, offers a meaningfully higher assurance signal than
broadcast Remote ID alone, with the added benefit of leveraging infrastructure already in place
at or near virtually every eligible facility in the country.
ATIS filed comments in the FCC's related "Unleashing American Drone Dominance" proceeding
(GN Docket 26-74) introducing the USEC framework and will continue to advance it through
standards development and government engagement. The work is promising but still maturing,
and ATIS does not propose specific USEC-related regulatory requirements at this stage. We raise
it here to ensure the FAA is aware of this development as it shapes the UAFR access framework
and companion Advisory Circular guidance, and to signal ATIS' availability as a technical
resource as the standards develop.
IV. ISAC-Enabled Sensing and Airspace Awareness
Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) is a foundational capability of 6G networks that
combines radar-like spatial sensing with wireless communications within a unified system.
Rather than requiring separate sensing infrastructure, an ISAC-enabled network uses its existing
radio access equipment to simultaneously communicate with connected devices and sense the
surrounding environment -- detecting the presence, movement, and characteristics of objects
within its coverage area, whether those objects are network-connected or not.
This capability is directly relevant to the UAFR enforcement challenge. USEC addresses
cooperative UAS whose operators are flying in compliance with network-layer conspicuity
requirements. ISAC addresses the broader airspace picture, including non-cooperative UAS that
broadcast no identity signal or are operating without authorization. A non-cooperative drone is,
by definition, the highest-risk scenario a UAFR is designed to address, and ISAC offers the
prospect of persistent airspace awareness within and around a UAFR boundary without requiring
facility-specific detection hardware.
The Next G Alliance launched the ISAC Data Initiative (ISAC–DI) in June 2026 to address one
of the central practical challenges in realizing ISAC's value: how sensing data generated by 6G-
enabled networks is synthesized, packaged, and delivered to operational decision-making
systems in standardized, usable forms.3 Drone detection and tracking is a key use case for ISAC
and the ISAC-DI will help ensure that the information obtained from MNO ISAC systems can be
delivered effectively to agencies such as the FAA, the Department of Homeland Security, and the
Department of War, who also have requirements for these capabilities.
As with USEC, ATIS raises the ISAC-DI here to inform the FAA's awareness of this work, not to
propose specific regulatory requirements. The initiative has launched, and the standards for data
3 More information on the Next G Alliance ISAC Data Initiative (ISAC-DI) can be found at
https://nextgalliance.org/initiative/isac-data-initiative/.

packaging, delivery interfaces, and interoperability are in development. ATIS anticipates that this
work will become increasingly relevant to the UAFR framework as it progresses, and we
welcome the opportunity to keep the FAA informed.
V. Conclusion and Request for Engagement
ATIS supports the UAFR rulemaking's core objectives and the FAA's balanced approach to
protecting critical infrastructure while preserving legitimate airspace access. The mobile network
represents a significant and underutilized resource for making UAFRs operationally effective.
ATIS is actively working on projects that will make network-based conspicuity and airspace
sensing interoperable and deployable at scale.
Both workstreams are at early stages, and ATIS is not in a position to propose specific regulatory
requirements at this time. We respectfully request two acknowledgements of the FAA:
1. That the FAA take note of the USEC and ISAC-DI workstreams as they develop the
companion Advisory Circular and implementation guidance for the UAFR
framework, recognizing that network-based solutions are likely to become relevant to
both access management and enforcement support as the technology matures; and
2. That the FAA engage with ATIS through the ATIS UAV Initiative and the Next G
Alliance ISAC-DI so that agency staff can remain informed of progress and so that
ATIS can ensure that its work is responsive to FAA's operational and regulatory
requirements.
ATIS stands ready to brief FAA staff on these workstreams and serve as a technical resource as
these standards are developed and mature.
Respectfully submitted,
David Young
Vice President, Technology Policy and Government Relations
Alliance for Telecommunications Industry Solutions
1200 G Street, NW
Suite 500
Washington, D.C. 20005
(202) 628-6380
July 6, 2026

Agricultural transparency is vital in a democratic society. There should be no regulations restricting legally operated drones from accessing footage needed to educate the public. Accountability is also paramount in a democracy and limiting access to how our food supply is being managed is nefarious.

As a certified Part 107 commercial drone photographer specializing in real estate, I am deeply concerned about the proposed Section 2209 flight restrictions.While I respect the need to secure critical infrastructure, this rule creates severe operational and economic challenges for small businesses like mine:Unpredictable No-Fly Zones: Restricting airspace around everyday structures will ground real estate marketing for hundreds of nearby residential homes, hurting homeowners and local economies.Mapping and Visibility Issues: If these restricted zones are not instantly integrated into standard LAANC and B4UFLY apps, safe pilots risk accidentally drifting into restricted areas.No Fast-Track Access: Commercial pilots need a rapid, automated waiver process to safely photograph properties that happen to border these sensitive sites.I urge the FAA to mandate real-time digital mapping for all Section 2209 restrictions and create a fast-tracked access system for certified Part 107 operators before finalizing this rule.

Comments on NPRM: Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (Section 2209)

As an FAA Part 107 certified remote pilot who operates drones strictly for commercial enterprise, I am writing to oppose the "advanced notice" transit requirement in the proposed Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs). Piling administrative hurdles onto vetted professionals is an ineffective security strategy that penalizes those already following the rules while doing nothing to deter bad actors or uncertified hobbyists.

The security concerns driving this NPRM are not caused by Part 107 pilots. Commercial operators invest significant time and money to study airspace, pass federal examinations, and undergo TSA background checks to ensure safe and responsible operations. Our drones are tools for business, not toys for social media fame. The root of the security risk stems from uncertified flyers who can easily purchase highly capable, enterprise-grade hardware without any verification of licensing, training, or intent.

Instead of creating an ambiguous, burdensome pre-flight notification system that disrupts time-sensitive commercial workflows, the FAA should leverage the technology it has already mandated: Remote ID.

Rather than treating every drone silhouette as an anonymous threat, the FAA should implement an extra data transfer protocol within the Remote ID broadcast framework. This protocol would allow a certified pilot’s Remote ID signal to transmit a secure, verified token indicating "Part 107 Certified Status."

When transiting a standard UFR, a facility's security team would instantly see that a vetted, background-checked professional is in the airspace. This solves the facility's security concern through automated data tracking without forcing a business owner to file redundant paperwork for every transit.

I urge the FAA to reject the manual notification model for Part 107 pilots. Instead, the final rule should grant a complete transit exemption to Part 107 operators, utilizing an updated Remote ID protocol to broadcast our verified professional status to ground security in real-time.

I am writing as a recreational drone hobbyist to strongly oppose several provisions in the proposed framework for Section 2209 Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs). While facility security is important, the current proposal creates unsafe, unworkable, and highly discriminatory restrictions on the hobbyist community.Furthermore, the rule is highly ambiguous and open to subjective interpretation by facility managers, creating a fragmented regulatory environment that makes compliance nearly impossible for the average flyer. Discriminatory Airspace RestrictionsThe proposal unfairly targets unmanned aircraft under the guise of security. If a facility represents a legitimate "airspace vulnerability" severe enough to warrant a flight ban, then that risk applies to all aircraft. Singling out drones while allowing manned aircraft to operate freely over the same low-altitude airspace undermines the logic of the security threat. If the airspace is genuinely unsafe or vulnerable, it should be restricted via the existing Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) framework for all operators, rather than creating a dual-standard system that penalizes drone hobbyists.3. Unacceptable Private Access to Pilot DataI vehemently oppose any mechanism that allows private business entities or facility operators to access FAA databases to retrieve pilot registration or personal data. Granting private corporations access to sensitive federal databases poses severe privacy and security risks for pilots. Hobbyists should not be subjected to tracking, profiling, or harassment by private security personnel simply for operating in public airspace. The FAA must maintain strict data privacy and ensure that pilot information is only accessible to law enforcement agencies under established legal protocols.For these reasons, I urge the FAA to reject the current notification mandates, eliminate private data sharing, and utilize existing, uniform airspace restriction mechanisms that apply fairly to all aviators.

§ 74.250 (a)(2) of the proposed rule, proposes that operations within a UAFR must transit a UAFR in the shortest amount of time practicable.  While there is some comment on the type of operations that would be permitted, it would be important to outline specific operations that would be permitted.  For example, a Part 107 pilot frequently needs to capture images or video of a property or facility, not only from directly above that property, but also at an angle from the property.  This requires that the UAS must hover over an adjacent property, or repeatedly transit the adjacent property in order to do mapping tasks in a grid-like pattern.  If specific operations such as this were included in the rule as acceptable in § 74.250 (a)(2) that would eliminate confusion and stress with the pilot and the facility's security personnel.  A better solution might also be to allow the pilot to specify the type of operations that will be need over the boundaries of the UAFR as part of the notification so that the pilot and the security personnel of the fixed site facility can both be clear about what is taking place.

Drone photography is in the public's interest. It exposes what doors conceal. By limiting drone photography, it emboldens and individuals and especially corporations to carry out cruelty without witnesses or consequence.

I URGE YOU STRENUOUSLY:

Do NOT restrict drone activity for legal certified drone operators, in PARTICULAR as regards to farms of any kind, including animal farms, factory farms, or any other area in which animals are enclosed for commercial profit.

WE THE PEOPLE demand FULL TRANSPARENCY as to where our food comes from - and we are NOT willing to just take a company's word for it. There needs to be unrestricted airways that allow us, the AMERICAN PEOPLE to see what is happening on and around and inside: factory farms, wild public lands, BLM controlled lands where wild horses roam, rodeos and commercial dog breeding facilities.

Re: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558

I am a certificated remote pilot and small-business UAS operator. I support protecting critical infrastructure, but those measures must be balanced against lawful access to the National Airspace System by responsible operators.

I generally agree with the concerns and recommendations expressed by Greg Reverdiau of Pilot Institute. Established and identifiable operators should retain a practical way to operate within or transit a Standard UAFR when otherwise lawful. A pilot using a registered aircraft, broadcasting Remote ID, and providing advance notification should not be treated as an unidentified threat. Recreational operators under 49 U.S.C. § 44809 also should not be categorically excluded if they meet appropriate identification and safety requirements.

I recommend that the final rule include:

1. A trusted-operator and trusted-aircraft whitelist.

The FAA should create a voluntary whitelist allowing operators to verify credentials, aircraft registration, Remote ID serial number, contact information, and applicable waivers or authority. Once verified, an operator should not have to repeatedly provide the same information to each facility. The whitelist would not grant unrestricted access, but would confirm that an aircraft is identifiable and tied to a known operator.

2. An integrated electronic notification system.

UAFR notification should be built into FAA-recognized flight-planning applications in a manner similar to LAANC. When a planned flight intersects a UAFR, the application should identify the restriction, accept the location, date, time, aircraft, and purpose, notify the facility and FAA, and generate a timestamped confirmation.

Pilots should not have to locate a facility manager, call a security desk, leave a voicemail, or send an email without knowing whether it was received. Electronic notification and documented receipt would protect both parties.

Notification must remain notification, not a request for private permission. A facility should not be able to block an otherwise lawful operation by refusing to respond or creating its own approval process.

3. Facility funding for the notification system.

Facilities receiving special protection over portions of the National Airspace System receive the primary benefit and should fund the system through application fees, renewal fees, or another appropriate mechanism. These costs should not be shifted to pilots or small UAS businesses, and pilots should not be charged for each required notification.

4. A clear prohibition on unauthorized interference.

A UAFR must not provide or imply authority for a facility owner, employee, contractor, or private security officer to jam or spoof signals, take control of an aircraft, force it to land, capture or seize it, shoot at it, damage or destroy it, direct another person to interfere with it, or attempt any of those actions.

Such interference can cause a crash into people, vehicles, buildings, roads, power infrastructure, or other property, creating a greater hazard than the flight itself. Every UAFR applicant should acknowledge in writing that the restriction grants no counter-UAS or aircraft-interference authority, and security personnel should be trained accordingly.

5. Meaningful consequences for intentional interference.

The FAA should coordinate with the Department of Justice and Congress, where necessary, to ensure clear criminal penalties for anyone who knowingly and intentionally jams, seizes, forces down, damages, or destroys a lawful unmanned aircraft without specific statutory counter-UAS authority.

Consequences should include FAA civil penalties, criminal referral, restitution for the aircraft, payload, lost data, property damage, and direct losses, possible suspension or cancellation of the facility’s UAFR, preservation of relevant records, and a formal reporting process.

A facility receiving protected-airspace benefits should not be permitted to intentionally endanger an aircraft, its operator, people on the ground, or surrounding property.

6. Narrow, visible, and reviewable restrictions.

Each UAFR should use the smallest reasonable horizontal and vertical dimensions necessary to address a documented threat. Boundaries, altitudes, effective dates, contact procedures, and notification requirements should be published electronically and integrated into commonly used flight-planning applications.

Restrictions should have expiration dates and require periodic review and renewal. They should not unnecessarily prevent lawful work on adjacent properties or create large private exclusion zones over public airspace.

Responsible and identifiable pilots should be treated as partners in aviation safety, not presumed threats. A verified whitelist, automated notification, documented receipts, narrowly tailored restrictions, and strong penalties for unauthorized interference would improve security while preserving lawful aviation access.

As a certified remote pilot, I am concerned that a multi-layer patchwork of regulations is emerging here. The FAA has the authority via the Interstate Commerce Clause and airspace authorities to implement a single standard.

Instead of having 50 different state laws on CIKR plus new federal rules, it would make sense for pilots operating under the federal procedure to be exempt from state laws that may apply to a facility.

If FAA cannot accomplish this, it really makes no sense to add another layer of confusion atop poorly-designed state and local rules.

This proposed rule does not go far enough by exempting private citizens from its protections.  Businesses deemed "critical infrastructure" should have access to UAFR protection because of the physical and information-gathering threats UAS systems pose to them and - hence - the threat they pose to our national industry as whole.  Makes sense.  However, private citizens have just as much at stake. To whom it may concern:
The California Cattlemen’s Association (CCA) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments
responsive to the Federal Aviation Administration’s notice of proposed rulemaking to establish a
process for fixed site facilities to request and maintain unmanned aircraft flight restrictions in the
airspace above their operations. CCA is a statewide trade association representing more than 1,700
cattle ranchers and beef producers throughout the state of California. CCA’s purpose is “Nourishing

CCA strongly supports FAA’s establishment of a process by which fixed site facilities may request

threats that unmanned aircraft such as drones pose to ranching operations and provide brief
responses to FAA’s questions regarding criteria applicable to the food and agriculture sector.
Risks of Unmanned Aircraft to Livestock Operations
Unmanned aircraft, such as drones, present a wide range of risks for livestock operations. Drones
directly and indirectly harm animals, can enhance risk of car strikes, can introduce biosecurity
threats, and pose enhanced wildfire risk in remote agricultural areas.
Direct and indirect harm to livestock animals: Collisions with obstacles such as trees, power
lines, or telecommunications poles can damage drones, causing them to fall to the earth.1 When
drones are operated over areas where livestock are heavily concentrated – such as a sale yard or a
confined animal feeding operation – such uncontrolled descent risks direct harm to livestock below.
Additionally, drones are “likely to cause negative stress effects” in livestock.2 Livestock which are
exposed to birds of prey in their natural environment exhibit “a greater unease” when exposed to

erratically may also stress livestock.4 Stress from improperly operated drones could cause livestock to
flee, increasing the risk that animals will injure themselves on rough terrain or even by driving
themselves through infrastructure such as fences. Additionally, increased stress in livestock has been
associated with loss of pregnancies, lower weigh gain, and lower body condition scores.
Indirect risk to humans: As discussed above, a drone pilot inexperienced in animal husbandry may
stress livestock with swift or erratic movements. External stressors often cause livestock to flee, and
animals have been observed knocking down fencing to escape perceived threats. Livestock escaping
a ranch may stray onto adjacent roads and highways, increasing the risk of vehicle strikes which
could catastrophically harm motorists.
More perniciously, drones could be used to intentionally herd animals away from ranches, feedyards,
livestock markets, or slaughter facilities. In recent years, radical animal rights groups have
increasingly used drones as a propaganda tool to cause reputational harm to confined animal feeding
operations.5 These groups have also engaged in the theft of livestock from ranch operations,
euphemistically termed “open rescue.”6 It is foreseeable that these groups could marry these efforts
in the future, using drones to drive livestock through fencelines in a misguided effort to “rescue”
them. Such actions would not only harm ranchers’ operations, they could also pose substantial risks
to motorists on highways adjoining rural ranches. Likewise, it is foreseeable that criminals, terrorists,
or other bad actors wishing to inflict damage upon the populace could use such tactics to create
mayhem, destruction, injuries, and even deaths.
Biosecurity risks: Drones flown above private agricultural operations typically take off from public
land. While farmers and ranchers often institute biosecurity controls for on-the-ground visitors to
the operation, they cannot impose biosecurity controls above their land. As a result, drones flown
above or landing upon private agricultural ground risk biological contamination, such as the
introduction of invasive weeds or pests to the agricultural operation. Drones which move between
multiple ranches also risk disease transmission from one herd to another. At a time when the
USDA, state agricultural agencies, and ranchers nationwide are actively working to combat the
threats of Avian Influenza and New World Screwworm, the FAA should seek to implement
regulations which enable ranchers to better protect the biosecurity of their operations.
Fire and wildfire risk: Most drones are powered by lithium-ion or lithium-polymer batteries. The
FAA recognizes that lithium batteries pose a fire hazard, noting that “Ignition of lithium metal
batteries can be caused when a battery short circuits, is overcharged, is heated to extreme
temperatures, is mishandled, or is otherwise defective.”7 Lithium batteries in drones operated above
rangelands could conceivably combust for a wide variety of reasons. For example, a lithium battery
could become overheated while operating in direct sunlight, or could become damaged after an
3 Id.
4 PURDUE UNIVERSITY EXTENSION, LIVESTOCK REACTION TO UAV FLIGHT,
https://extension.purdue.edu/uav/animal-agriculture/livestock-reaction-to-uav-flight-example.html.
5 Emily K. Upchurch, Comment, Drone on the Farm: The Benefits and Controversies Surrounding the Future of
Unmanned Aircraft Systems in Agriculture, 20 DRAKE J. OF AGRIC. L. 309, 323 (2015).
6 See, e.g., Robert Rodriguez, Animal Rights Activists Charged Criminally for Taking Goats from Kings County Dairy, THE

uncontrolled fall to the ground caused by impact with infrastructure or birds. Rangelands are
comprised of grasses and other forage which are highly-combustible, are often situated in or near
forested environments, and may not be closely and actively monitored at all times. As a result, the
risks to “people and property on the ground” of a lithium battery fire originating on rangelands is
significant. The potential of such fires developing into large conflagrations may foreseeably implicate
national and homeland security, as well.
Response to Solicitations within the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking poses three questions to aid the FAA in developing criteria for
which “fixed site facilities” within the food and agriculture sector may request an unmanned aircraft
flight restriction. We address each question in brief below, but in short, we believe the potential risks
to agricultural infrastructure and the food supply chain are severe enough that FAA ought to permit
a wide range of food and agricultural sites to apply for unmanned aircraft flight restrictions.
1. What types of facilities within this sector should be considered for a UAFR? Specifically,
those that could have debilitating regional or national-level consequences.
CCA urges the FAA to consider most agricultural operations eligible to apply for UAFRs. While
operations where animals are confined – dairies, feedyards, auction yards, slaughter facilities, etc. –
are more likely to be targeted by bad actors and perhaps carry the greatest risks to the nation’s food
supply chain and food security, improper or nefarious use of unmanned aircraft above any
agricultural operations could pose regional or national threats. Drone-sparked wildfires could quickly
become serious regional emergencies necessitating state and national response, and biosecurity
threats to any ranch could quickly cascade into challenges for the regional and national food supply.
As such, FAA should consider allowing all farms, ranches, dairies, feed yards, auction yards,
slaughter facilities, and other agricultural operations to apply for UAFRs.
2. What characteristics should be considered in the development of gating criteria for those
facilities?
CCA urges the FAA not to impose arbitrary gating criteria to the food and agricultural sector.
Regardless of the size or economic footprint of a farm or ranch, harms from negligent or ill-
intended drone use could quickly spread to regional or national crises.
3. Should the population served or regional or national economic impact be considered in
the development of gating criteria, and if so, what are appropriate thresholds?
No, CCA does not believe that population or economic thresholds should be applied in determining
which fixed site facilities may apply for UAFR.
Conclusion
CCA appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the FAA’s proposal to establish a process
for fixed site facilities to request and maintain unmanned aircraft flight restrictions in the airspace
above their operations. Unmanned aircraft pose a multitude of threats to livestock operations, from
relatively localized impacts to individual livestock to regional and national concerns relating to
wildfire risk and biosecurity. Because these risks exist for virtually all agricultural operations with

potentially-significant impacts on regional and national infrastructure – including the broader food
supply chain – we urge FAA to make UAFR available to all agricultural operators.
Sincerely,
Kirk Wilbur
Vice President of Government Affairs

RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03 – Designation—
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity
to a Fixed Site Facility
To whom it may concern:
Farm security is national security.
America’s food supply is not merely an economic asset—it is a strategic
national asset. The ability of the United States to feed itself, sustain global markets,
and maintain resilient domestic supply chains is inseparable from our national
security.
As Commissioner of Agriculture for the Commonwealth of Kentucky, I
appreciate the Federal Aviation Administration’s efforts to implement Section 2209
of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 in a manner that balances
innovation in unmanned aircraft systems with legitimate security and safety
concerns. The proposed rule appropriately recognizes that eligibility for Unmanned
Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) should be limited to facilities whose disruption
would have a demonstrable impact on public safety, national economic security, or
the resilience of critical infrastructure.
For too long, though, agriculture has been viewed solely through the lens of
production and commerce. In reality, agriculture is critical infrastructure every bit
as essential as energy, transportation, telecommunications, and water systems. A
nation that cannot secure its food supply cannot secure its future.
The United States Department of Homeland Security formally recognizes food
and agriculture as one of the Nation’s sixteen critical infrastructure sectors because
disruptions to agricultural production, processing, or distribution can undermine
economic stability, public confidence, and national resilience. America’s adversaries
understand this reality. Foreign animal diseases, cyberattacks against agricultural
supply chains, industrial espionage, intentional contamination, and the exploitation
of emerging technologies—including unmanned aircraft systems—represent evolving
threats to our food system.

Corporate Drive Complex 502-573-0450
Frankfort, KY 40601 www.kyagr.com
Unlike many other critical infrastructure sectors, agriculture encompasses
geographically dispersed production systems that ultimately depend upon a network
of fixed facilities responsible for animal health, food processing, storage,
transportation, chemical manufacturing, and supply chain continuity. A disruption
at a major processing facility, grain terminal, fertilizer depot, veterinary diagnostic
laboratory, or food distribution hub would not simply affect one company or one
community. Such an event could ripple across multiple states, increase food prices,
disrupt exports, threaten animal health, and weaken America’s ability to respond to
emergencies.
Our geopolitical competitors increasingly recognize that strategic advantage is
achieved not only through military strength, but through the ability to disrupt
essential supply chains. Protecting America’s food system must therefore be
understood as a core component of homeland security. Accordingly, the FAA should
ensure that the eligibility criteria for the food and agriculture sector adequately
reflect the modern realities of agricultural production and supply chains.
To that end, I strongly recommend that the FAA partner with USDA to develop
measurable eligibility thresholds for regionally and nationally significant
agricultural facilities and include them in a table similar to the Chemical Sector
portion of the proposed rulemaking. This type of collaborative regulation would
ensure measurable thresholds and would improve consistency, reduce administrative
burden, and limit requests for applicability determinations. Additionally, USDA
involvement would ensure the significance of the national security interest in the
recommended sites below and would eliminate the potential that thresholds set by
the FAA are too high and therefore inapplicable to smaller states or states with
differing agricultural strengths.
I recommend that the FAA adopt the following eligibility criteria for fixed-site
facilities within the food and agricultural sector.
First, eligibility should extend to facilities that represent significant
aggregation points or chokepoints within regional or national food supply chains.
Such facilities should include:
• Grain elevators, inland terminals, export terminals, and feed mills with
annual throughput exceeding a threshold established by the FAA in
consultation with the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
• Livestock transfer points, auctions, and markets, including transportation and
exchange points which may or may not be fixed site locations.
• Livestock breeding and reproduction facilities.

Corporate Drive Complex 502-573-0450
Frankfort, KY 40601 www.kyagr.com
• Meat processing, poultry processing, dairy processing, and food manufacturing
facilities that meet size, production volume, or workforce thresholds indicative
of regional or national significance.
• Cold storage and food distribution centers that serve multi-state supply chains
or support emergency food distribution networks.
Second, eligibility should include fixed facilities whose disruption could
materially affect animal health, plant health, or biosecurity, including:
• State and federal veterinary diagnostic laboratories.
• High-containment animal disease research facilities.
• Livestock quarantine facilities or other sites that are synonymous with animal
disease control.
• Seed repositories, germplasm centers, and facilities maintaining critical
genetic resources.
• Major livestock markets and animal concentration points with established
disease surveillance responsibilities, including sites that serve significant
regional or national agriculture, transportation, or supply-chain functions.
• Facilities supporting foreign animal disease response operations.
Third, eligibility should extend to facilities that manufacture, store, or
distribute essential agricultural inputs where a disruption could impair food
production capacity, including:
• Fertilizer manufacturing facilities and major distribution terminals.
• Crop protection product manufacturing and formulation facilities.
• Large-scale agricultural chemical storage sites.
• Animal feed ingredient processing facilities.
• Fuel terminals dedicated to agricultural operations.
Fourth, eligibility should include any farming operation with a defined
procurement relationship with an institutional purchaser, like a hospital, school or
university, and military installation.
Fifth, eligibility should include irrigation, water and wastewater management,
and agricultural energy infrastructure where the facility serves a substantial
agricultural production area and already satisfies applicable critical infrastructure
definitions.
Relative to all the above recommendations, eligibility should not be limited
solely to facilities under direct federal ownership or operation. Privately owned
facilities that satisfy objective, risk-based criteria should be afforded equal

Corporate Drive Complex 502-573-0450
Frankfort, KY 40601 www.kyagr.com
consideration. Additionally, eligibility should not be tethered to a size requirement.
Rather, the focus should be on the specific purpose of the fixed site facility, regardless
of its size.
The FAA has appropriately chosen a risk-based framework rather than a
blanket approach. By adopting generous but objective eligibility criteria for the food
and agriculture sector, the agency can protect genuinely critical facilities without
unnecessarily restricting legitimate unmanned aircraft operations or innovation in
precision agriculture.
At the same time, I strongly encourage the FAA to maintain clear guardrails
to ensure consistency with the intent of Section 2209. First, eligibility should apply
primarily to fixed-site facilities with clearly defined boundaries. However, in some
instances, targeted exceptions for specific non-fixed operations may be necessary for
full protection of the sector. Also, any boundary should be reasonably limited to
preserve drone instruction and education services that are necessary for ensuring
operators are properly trained for on-farm applications, whether commercially or
personally. Second, restrictions should preserve exemptions for authorized
agricultural aviation activities, emergency response operations, governmental
inspections, and FAA-approved commercial unmanned aircraft operations. Third,
applicants should demonstrate that disruption, sabotage, espionage, contamination,
or interference at the facility would create measurable consequences for food security,
public safety, animal health, or supply chain resilience. And finally, UAFRs should
remain geographically limited to the minimum area necessary to address the
identified risk.
As the FAA finalizes this rulemaking, it should recognize that safeguarding
agricultural infrastructure is not solely about protecting private property—it is about
protecting the American people. When farmers lose access to fertilizer, feed,
processing capacity, or animal health resources, consumers face higher prices and
greater uncertainty. When critical agricultural facilities are disrupted, rural
economies suffer, exports decline, and America’s strategic resilience is diminished.
Food security is homeland security.
I appreciate the opportunity to provide comments and encourage the FAA to
work closely with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, state departments of
agriculture, and industry stakeholders to finalize practical eligibility standards that
recognize agriculture’s indispensable role in securing our nation’s future.

RE: Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility [Docket No. FAA-2026-4558]
Dear Administrator Bedford:
On behalf of the Commercial Space Federation (CSF), the leading trade association
representing the American space industry, thank you for the opportunity to comment on the
Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Proposed Rule on Designation-Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility [Docket No. FAA-2026-4558].
As the FAA considers updating unmanned aircraft flight restriction (UAFR) eligibility, CSF
strongly encourages the FAA to extend UAFR eligibility to FAA-licensed spaceports, permitted
private space facilities, remote space infrastructure, and related space operations sites.
The space industry is a critical contributor to national security, economic development,
and scientific advancement, and ensuring the operational security of spaceports, space launch
and reentry facilities, and public/privately-owned space infrastructure is in the national interest.
Commercial space activity is expanding rapidly, operational cadence is increasing, and
significant investments are being made into both launch and non-launch ground infrastructure to
support critical national security priorities, such as the National Security Space Launch Program,
Golden Dome for America, and NASA's Artemis Program. These investments deserve
extraordinary protection.
This infrastructure includes not only launch sites but also vehicle manufacturing
facilities, rocket engine test stands, propellant production and storage facilities, spacecraft
integration centers, and research and development complexes—many of which are intentionally
located in remote areas due to safety, security, and operational requirements.
However, unlike similar facilities such as airports and certain military installations,
commercial space infrastructure—whether located at active spaceports or at standalone remote
sites—is only able to utilize temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) during active operations to
secure the airspace. Treating spaceports and private space infrastructure as a regulatory
afterthought to airports, rather than peer categories deserving the same protection, leaves an
increasingly important segment of national security infrastructure exposed to threats posed by
unauthorized unmanned aircraft system (UAS) activity.
Commercial Space Federation | 1301 Connecticut Avenue NW, Suite 250, Washington D.C.

The risk profile of spaceports, launch and reentry infrastructure, and remote private space
facilities makes them attractive, low-friction targets for unauthorized UAS activity. Many of
these facilities sit on remote or sparsely monitored land, hold high-value hardware and
proprietary technology in the open for extended periods, host hazardous materials including
cryogenic propellants and hypergolic fuels, and conduct sensitive testing operations.
Additionally, these sites draw recreational drone operators and photographers seeking close-up
footage of facilities, vehicles, and proprietary systems.
As noted in the Proposed Rule, "…commercial spaceports are susceptible to UAS
operations due to the high impact of drone incidents near these sites." This vulnerability extends
equally to private space infrastructure facilities that may be located hundreds of miles from
traditional spaceports but contain equally sensitive technology, hazardous operations, and
national security-relevant capabilities.
Securing space launch and reentry infrastructure, as well as associated manufacturing,
testing, and integration facilities, from unauthorized drone activity is critical to protecting U.S.
national security priorities while maintaining public safety and the protection of intellectual
property rights. Therefore, CSF respectfully recommends that the FAA designate FAA-licensed
commercial, private, and government spaceports, as well as private space infrastructure facilities
regardless of geographic location, as protected facilities for purposes of Section 2209 eligibility
and related counter-UAS authority.
Thank you for your consideration of this request to provide Section 2209 UAFR
eligibility to commercial space launch and reentry facilities, remote private space infrastructure,
and related operations sites. CSF looks forward to working with the FAA to ensure continued
American superiority in space.
Sincerely,

Re: Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility, Docket no. Docket No. FAA-2026-4558.
Dear Ms. Locke,
Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments in response to the Federal Aviation
Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) concerning the Designation-Restrict
the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility. The growing use of
unmanned aircraft, or drones, presents significant opportunities for the business community, and we
appreciate the FAA’s diligent efforts to ensure their safe integration into the national airspace
system. In these comments we, the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC), will
highlight issues relevant to the construction industry, who use drones every day.
AGC is the nation’s leading construction trade association. It dates to 1918 and today represents
more than 28,000 member firms including construction contractor firms both union and open-shop,
suppliers, and service providers. Through a nationwide network of 87 chapters in all 50 states, D.C.,
and Puerto Rico, AGC contractors are engaged in the construction of the nation’s highways,
bridges, utilities, airports, transit systems, public and private buildings, water works facilities and
multi-family housing units, among other projects critical to the economy.
Our members don’t typically operate the kind of fixed site facilities that are empowered by the
proposed rule, but they do work on those facilities, and their drone operations could be impacted by
the proposed rule. AGC supports the concept of unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFR) for
sensitive facilities, but we would urge FAA to ensure that the proposal does not disrupt legitimate
construction activity within or near those facilities and that the authorization process is predictable
and efficient.
I. UAFRs Must Accommodate Ongoing Construction Operations
The proposed rule contemplates restricting unmanned aircraft operations within designated areas
unless authorized by the FAA and the using agency. As described, operators may be required to
obtain both agency permission and FAA approval “in a form and manner acceptable to the
Administrator.”
2111 Wilson Blvd., Suite 1000, Arlington, VA 22201 | 703.548.3118 | AGC.org

2
While we understand the need for layered authorizations, this framework risks capturing routine
construction operations, particularly where the project is occurring inside or immediately adjacent to
the fixed site facility.
Contractors rely on drones every day to perform tasks such as topographic mapping, equipment
tracking, land surveying, site security, structural assessments, and safety inspections. These activities
can be completed in a fraction of the time while reducing the need to place personnel in potentially
hazardous situations. The facilities captured by the proposed rule, most of which are government or
military facilities, benefit greatly from the efficiency gains drones bring to the jobsite.
To ensure that this valuable tool is not taken away, FAA should do more to ensure that legitimate
construction operations are allowed under proposed § 74.250. The proposed rule asked for
comment on “whether the language in (a)(2) is broad enough to enable both legitimate transitory
and non-transitory operations within a UAFR, with the appropriate notification to the fixed site
facility, while still preserving the integrity of the airspace restriction.” We don’t think that it is.
As proposed, § 74.250(2) would require a drone to transition the UAFR in the shortest amount of
time practicable. Not only does this not recognize the legitimacy of certain non-transitory drone
operations, it forbids them. Drones that stay within the bounds of a UAFR, such as those in use on
a construction project within or adjacent to the facility, cannot be said to transition the space at all,
much less in the shortest time practicable.
There is no language in proposed § 74.250 that recognizes the legitimacy of certain non-transitory
drone use within a UAFR. We recommend that in the final rule, § 74.250(2) is amended to read
“The unmanned aircraft transitions or operates within the UAFR in the shortest amount of time
practicable.”
FAA should also clarify that non-transitory operations conducted within a UAFR may be authorized
where coordinated with the using agency, that contractors operating under a valid construction
contract within the facility are eligible for such authorization, and that using agencies can rely on an
FAA “whitelist” for operators associated with active projects and pre-approved by FAA.
Lastly, we believe using agencies should be required to provide points of contact for each UAFR
that are either publicly posted or can be reached through FAA. Our members have found that while
working with FAA is very easy to coordinate, other agencies can be less so.
II. Authorization and Notice Requirements Must Be Efficient and Workable
The main impact of the proposed rule on our members is the authorization and notice requirements
in proposed § 74.255. When contractors accept a project in or adjacent to a UAFR, they will need to
provide notice to the fixed site facility in a form and manner acceptable to the Administrator.
AGC supports a coordinated approval process but asks for more clarity regarding timelines for
approvals and whether approvals can be granted on a project-wide or recurring basis.
2111 Wilson Blvd., Suite 300, Arlington, VA 22201 | 703.548.3118 | AGC.org

3
Timelines are critical to any construction job. Without predictable timelines, contractors cannot
sequence work, price risk, or ensure compliance, particularly on federally funded projects with strict
delivery schedules.
Project-based authorizations would allow a single authorization to cover all drone operations for the
duration of a construction process. For example, on large infrastructure projects within secured
facilities, drones are routinely used for daily progress monitoring and safety inspections. Requiring
repeated authorization or prohibiting non-transitory operations would create delays and increase
reliance on more dangerous inspection techniques.
We also want to be sure that contractors are aware of any existing UAFR and the consequent notice
requirements during the contracting process. To that end, the Administrator should consider
requiring that operators of a fixed site facility holding a UAFR to disclose that to any contractors
who are engaged on site.
III. Conclusion
Thank you again for the opportunity to comment. AGC is very supportive of FAA’s efforts to safely
integrate drones into the national airspace system. Please consider our minor recommended
amendment, which would ensure that non-transitory construction operations are authorized by the
proposed rule. Without these changes, the proposed rule risks restricting routine construction
operations and introducing unnecessary delays into critical infrastructure projects. With targeted
revisions, FAA can protect sensitive facilities while preserving the operational benefits of UAS
technology.
Very Respectfully,
Spencer Phillips Deniz Mustafa
Counsel, Regulatory and Litigation Advocacy Senior Director, Construction Advocacy
2111 Wilson Blvd., Suite 300, Arlington, VA 22201 | 703.548.3118 | AGC.org

Re: Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility; Docket number FAA-2026-4558
To Whom It May Concern:
The Monterey Bay Aquarium (Aquarium) supports the intent of the proposed Federal
Aviation Administration Unmanned Aerial Systems Flight Restriction (UAFR) over
critical infrastructure and public venues. The support is based on the recognized
threats that drones represent to life safety. The proposed restrictions will reduce the
probability of unauthorized drone activity over facilities with high density public
spaces and sensitive biological collections. Additionally, the UAFR restrictions will
provide tools for law enforcement to regulate unauthorized drone flights.
The Aquarium is a world class tourist destination, with over two million visitors
annually, and a facility entrusted with the care of marine wildlife, including species
protected under federal law. And we encourage you to take facilities such as ours into
account as you finalize definitions and criteria for applications. Unauthorized drone
operations near the Aquarium present several safety and security concerns, including
the risk of injury to guests or staff from loss of control, mechanical failure, intentional
misuse, or collisions with structures. Drones may also interfere with emergency
operations, crowd management, law enforcement response, and incident command
during a public safety event.
In addition to life safety concerns, unauthorized drone activity may adversely affect
sensitive and endangered species housed at the Aquarium. Low altitude overflight can
create unnecessary stress to animals. Facilities that care for protected wildlife require
an added level of operational stability, particularly where species recovery,
rehabilitation and public education intersect.
The Aquarium also supports narrowly tailored exceptions within the UAFR for public
safety, emergency response, and authorized scientific research. Public safety agencies
should retain the ability to operate drones when justified by life safety needs,
emergency management, law enforcement, fire response, search and rescue,

hazardous conditions, or other urgent operational requirements. Similarly, scientific
research flights should be permitted when authorized by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife
Service or other appropriate regulatory authority and when such activity supports
protected species research, conservation, recovery, or animal welfare objectives.
These exceptions are essential to ensure that the restriction does not unintentionally
limit lifesaving operations or legitimate federally permitted conservation science.
The Aquarium further encourages the FAA to consider Remote ID, geofencing,
detection capabilities, operator notification tools, and other available technologies as
protective measures. These tools can help identify compliant operators, deter
unauthorized flights, support timely response to unsafe activity, and reduce
unnecessary enforcement burdens. Technology-based protective measures, when
paired with clear flight restrictions and appropriate exceptions, provide a balanced
approach that improves safety without creating unnecessary disruption to lawful UAS
operations.
In summary, the Aquarium supports drone flight restrictions over critical
infrastructure and public venues where unauthorized UAS activity presents
foreseeable risks to life safety, emergency response, and endangered species. We
respectfully urge the FAA to adopt a balanced approach that protects the public and
sensitive wildlife, preserves public safety and scientific research exceptions, avoids
unnecessary impacts to commercial drone operators, and incorporates Remote ID and
other technologies to support effective implementation.
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Jeff Field
Director of Security, Safety, Emergency Management
886 Cannery Row Monterey, California 93940 831.648.4800 MontereyBayAquarium.org

Background:
 
Cleveland Metroparks is a separate political subdivision of the State of Ohio, formed under 
Chapter 1545 of the Ohio Revised Code. Cleveland Metroparks is responsible for the ownership, 
operation, and management of an extensive regional park system serving the greater Cleveland 
area. Cleveland Metroparks' mission is to conserve natural resources while providing safe, high 
quality recreational and educational opportunities to the public. 
Cleveland Metroparks manages more than 25,000 acres of parkland and a wide range of sites that 
attract significant annual visitation. These include high-use recreational areas such as Edgewater 
Park, which receives over 1.5 million visitors annually, and Cleveland Metroparks Zoo, which 
also welcomes more than 1.3 million guests each year. Cleveland Metroparks Zoo also includes 
dozens of outdoor exhibits, animal habitats, and attractions including elevated and open-air 
features like ziplines. 
In addition to recreational assets, Cleveland Metroparks is responsible for the management and 
maintenance of infrastructure such as dams, government-operated facilities, and other built 
resources (such as break walls) that support both public use and operational functions. These 
sites are often situated within open environments that are directly exposed to low-altitude 
airspace and are frequently occupied by large numbers of visitors, staff, and protected wildlife. 
As part of its core responsibilities, Cleveland Metroparks prioritizes public safety, the protection 
of wildlife and zoological assets, and the preservation of infrastructure necessary to park 
operations and regional economic activity. The presence of high visitor volumes, sensitive 
natural and zoological resources, and critical infrastructure creates environments in which UAS 
incidents may have significant safety, operational, and economic consequences. 
Cleveland Metroparks recognizes the importance of the FAA's efforts to establish a framework 
for restricting unmanned aircraft operations in close proximity to sensitive facilities. As a

This would ensure that facilities sensitive to UAS risk are not excluded solely because they

Proposed Rule Change: The proposed rule allows certain dams to qualify for a UAFR if they 
are assigned a high or significant hazard potential classification and meet at least one of three 
additional thresholds tied to particular outputs or economic function. Specifically, qualifying 
dams must satisfy one of the following: (1) hydroelectric dams with a combined nameplate

(2) serve as the primary drinking water source for a population exceeding 500,000; or (3) 
facilities with annual total water deliveries exceeding $100 million or 800,000 acre-feet.

appropriately focuses on the consequences of failure, the additional thresholds exclude a 
substantial category of smaller dams that present comparable risks to downstream populations. 
These additional criteria favor large-scale infrastructure based on output and capacity, rather than 
focusing on the potential consequences to human life and likelihood of dam failure. 
For example, the Hinckley Lake Dam, operated by Cleveland Metroparks, is classified as a high 
hazard potential dam, meaning that failure could result in significant loss of life. More than 100 
residents and businesses are downstream of the dam and would be directly impacted by a dam 
failure, potentially resulting in significant loss of life. Despite the high hazard potential, 
Hinckley Lake Dam would not qualify for a UAFR under the proposed rule because it does not

satisfy any of the additional thresholds related to power generation, drinking water supply, or 
water delivery volume. 
The proposed criteria exclude dams where the consequences of failure may be severe or likely 
because the dam does not meet the large-scale operational or economic benchmarks. The risk 
posed by UAS operations in the vicinity of a dam is not contingent only on whether the facility 
generates a certain level of power or serves a population above a specific threshold. Rather, the 
relevant consideration is whether an interference, disruption, or incident near the dam could 
contribute to conditions that increase the likelihood or consequences of failure. By conditioning 
eligibility on substantial output-based metrics, the proposed rule fails to capture high-hazard 
dams where safety risks are driven by potential loss of life rather than size or economic output. 
Alternative Approach: Cleveland Metroparks recommends that the FAA revise the eligibility 
criteria for dams to instead focus on the likelihood and consequences associated with dam 
failure. At a minimum, the FAA should allow any dam designated as having a high hazard 
potential in the National Inventory of Dams to qualify for a UAFR, regardless of whether it 
meets any additional output-based thresholds. This is an appropriate baseline because a high 
hazard classification already reflects a determination that failure of the dam would likely cause 
the loss of human life. In addition, the FAA should consider allowing poor or unsatisfactory 
dams to qualify for an UAFR. Dams in these conditions are more vulnerable to failure from 
UAS-related incidents and elevate the overall risks profile of the facility. 
To the extent that the FAA retains economic or output-based thresholds, those factors should 
serve only as alternative pathways to eligibility rather than prerequisites. Conditioning eligibility 
on such economic or output-based criteria risks excluding facilities that present significant safety 
concerns solely because they do not meet arbitrary scale or economic benchmarks. 
By incorporating both hazard classification and indicators of structural condition into UAFR 
eligibility criteria, the FAA would ensure that facilities presented with the most significant and 
pressing safety risk are not excluded from consideration. This approach would better align with 
the proposal's stated objective of safeguarding lives in the event of dam failure by focusing on 
where failure is most consequential and likely to occur.

Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility — 91 FR 24650 (Government Services and Facilities)

and Facilities Sector ("GSFS") to high risk, high security facilities with a national or homeland
