in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,” 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (May 6, 2026). As described
comprehensively in the recent academic article presented at the American Institute of
Aeronautics and Astronautics, An Overview of Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) Public Good
Applications: Patient Transport and Organ Transport, a notable gap exists for cold ischemic or
normothermic perfusion transport using unmanned aircraft that can transport payloads in excess
of 50 pounds for distances of more than 150 miles. The concept of operations on which Atlas
Response is focused will close this gap by using aircraft capable of safely engaging in such
transport. The public benefits of this capability are paramount to the company and will have
significantly positive effects on patients whose lives are saved as a result of such transport.
The notice of proposed rulemaking, based on section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety
and Security Act of 2016, would affect Atlas Response’s potential operations to the extent that
the company travels from or to hospitals or medical facilities. The proposed rule would also
affect Atlas Response’s operations to the extent that the company conducts operations on behalf

of or in relation to medical facilities located at sites governed by the United States military or
other federal entities. Given the unique nature of the company’s potential operations, Atlas
Response welcomes the opportunity to submit this comment and join the public discourse
concerning security concerns at certain fixed site facilities.
I. Notification Process and Issuance of Approvals
Consistent with views from several stakeholders in the unmanned aircraft systems (UAS)
industry, Atlas Response urges the FAA to consider carefully the mechanism for designating
fixed sites, notifying the public of the existence of such sites and receiving requisite notice from
any remote pilot or operator prior to their entry into airspace that is designated as a Standard
UAFR. As with the FAA’s Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability system
(LAANC), the FAA is able to receive and disseminate information concerning an intended
operation in an automated manner, provided the area subject to the Standard UAFR is accurately
depicted and remains up to date via the system the FAA might implement.
Similarly, Atlas Response urges the FAA to permit using agencies that oversee Special
UAFRs to implement their own forms of automated reviews and approvals, contemporaneous
with advising the FAA at the time of each approval. Under proposed section 74.251, a person
may access a special UAFR only pursuant to fulfilling two requirements: the unmanned aircraft
must have approval of the using agency and unless the using agency itself is operating the
unmanned aircraft, the operation must have the FAA's approval. Atlas Response recommends the
FAA alter this language to ensure FAA “approval” is not required; rather, the using agency may
approve and advise the FAA of its choice in issuing such approval. This streamlined approach
will increase the efficiency of operations, which will be necessary in circumstances such as Atlas
2

Response's operations, which would involve delivery of organs, blood, medical supplies, or
necessary equipment as expeditiously as possible.
More broadly, Atlas Response recommends that the final rule establish a standing access
agreement mechanism for Standard UAFRs applicable to the Healthcare and Public Health
Sector. Under this mechanism, a fixed site healthcare facility that obtains a Standard UAFR
designation would be authorized to identify, by name, one or more medical cargo operators that
are authorized to conduct operations under 14 CFR part 135 as standing authorized operators
within that UAFR. Once a standing authorization is on file with the FAA, the designated
operator’s individual missions would require only mission-specific notification under § 74.255
— not affirmative per-mission approval. This mechanism eliminates per-flight administrative
latency that is structurally incompatible with organ and biologic transport timelines, while
maintaining full FAA visibility into all operations through the required notification process. The
FAA could implement this mechanism through the UAFR Module portal mentioned in the
preamble of the proposed rule and described in its draft Advisory Circular that accompanies the
rule.
II. Temporary Transit
A. Risk-Based Model
Atlas Response supports the exception for temporary transit as contemplated in proposed
section 74.250 but suggests amendments that will enable the FAA to enact a scalable solution
based on the level of risk. Under proposed section 74.250, UAS operations are eligible for
temporary transit over designated Standard UAFRs but such transit is available only for
operations that occur in accordance with 14 CFR parts 91, 107, 108, 135 or 137. Atlas Response
urges the FAA to consider amending the language concerning temporary transit in a manner that
3

addresses the level of risk each intended operation might present. Such a scalable model is
consistent with the FAA’s longstanding safety continuum approach. Although the safety
continuum framework generally applies to aircraft certification models, the framework is
appropriate with security concerns regarding fixed site facilities because not all operational
frameworks present the same level of security risk. Such an approach is directly consistent with
Executive Order 14307, Unleashing American Drone Dominance (June 6, 2025), and with the
FAA’s statutory responsibilities under 49 U.S.C. § 40103(a)(2), which require the FAA to
balance the public’s right of transit in the airspace with the national security risks that might exist
over certain sites.
Adopting a risk-based model for operations would preserve the appropriate balance
between the public interest in transiting the airspace and the level of risk that could exist. An
operator that holds an air carrier certificate under 14 CFR parts 119 and 135, for example, must
be a U.S. citizen and has already undergone a significant level of scrutiny throughout the process
of obtaining the certificate. Similarly, operations that may occur under proposed 14 CFR part
108 will only be conducted by personnel who have undergone security screening by the
Transportation Security Administration (TSA). While various sites all present varying levels of
security risk, disclosure of the level of risk in and of itself might prompt security concerns. As a
result, the FAA and its security partners might consider a streamlined approach based simply on
the type of operation, of which the FAA would be apprised, given the need for unequivocal
applicability of operating rules with which each operator must comply.
B. Categorical Authorization
Atlas Response further recommends that the FAA recognize part 135 air carrier
certification as a categorical clearance for purposes of Special UAFR transit access. An operator
4

that holds an air carrier certificate under 14 CFR parts 119 and 135 has already satisfied the core
security concerns the UAFR framework is designed to address. Part 135 certification requires,
among other things, TSA security threat assessments of all relevant personnel, drug and alcohol
testing programs equivalent to those required of commercial airlines, FAA-approved
maintenance programs and safety management systems, and demonstrated compliance with
operating specifications issued by the FAA. These requirements are not merely procedural, but
involve intense review under well-developed standards. Moreover, operators that hold a
certificate under 14 CFR part 135 are subject to ongoing oversight from a principal inspector that
remains familiar with the certificate holder and its management personnel, as described in 14
CFR part 119. Overall, air carrier certification can and should function as an efficient means for
granting categorical clearance to transit UAFR facility sites as appropriate for the certificate
holder’s operation.
The FAA’s own proposed rule acknowledges this distinction, noting that permitted
operations include those “conducted under Parts 91, 107, 108, 135, and 137, which have met
rigorous FAA safety requirements and [TSA] security threat assessments where applicable.” 91
Fed. Reg. at 24653. An air carrier authorized to conduct operations under part 135 is, by
regulatory definition, not the threat to a facility that a UAFR is designed to prevent. Accordingly,
Atlas Response urges the FAA to confirm in the final rule that operators authorized to conduct
operations under part 135 are presumptively authorized for UAFR transit access and need not
receive affirmative, per-mission approval, but are subject only to the notification requirements of
proposed § 74.255. This approach is consistent with the FAA’s risk-based framework, directly
advances the Administration’s policy objectives under Executive Order 14307, and eliminates
5

the risk that life-critical organ transport missions will be delayed by administrative review
processes that will be incompatible with transplant viability windows.
III. Legal Framework
Atlas Response further suggests the FAA reconsider the proposed rule’s expansive
statement concerning preemption over state authorities, in the interest of clarity and efficiency.
While Atlas Response acknowledges and does not question the FAA’s statements in its State and
Local Regulation of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Fact Sheet (July 14, 2023) concerning
the agency’s preemption of authority over state or local laws aimed at regulating aviation safety
or airspace efficiency, Atlas Response is concerned that the proposed language of part 74
generally does not observe state and local government entities’ standards or policies that apply to
UAS operations. The potential inconsistency between state restrictions or requirements and the
proposed provisions of part 74 could lead to circumstances in which the FAA permits an
operation, yet the state prohibits it, and vice versa.
In Florida, for example, the Legislature has defined broadly “critical infrastructure” for
purposes of UAS operational restrictions; in general, a person may operate a UAS over critical
infrastructure only after first receiving authorization from the proprietor or owner of the
infrastructure site. § 330.41, Fla. Stat. (2026). The FAA’s proposed rule would result in
duplicative notification over sites such as seaports, airports or spaceports; mining facilities; or
power generation or transmission facilities, because Florida would require the UAS operator to
obtain authorization from the proprietor or owner while the FAA would require the UAS
operator to submit notification or request affirmative authorization from the same proprietor or
owner.
6

The FAA’s proposed rule does not address duplicative reporting or potential
inconsistencies; rather, it focuses on scope of authorities of both the FAA and state and local
governments. Atlas Response concurs with the FAA’s general assessment that state and local
government entities are fully authorized to enact restrictions concerning privacy, land use or
facility access issues, while the FAA maintains broad authority over airspace safety and
efficiency. In implementation, however, the two scopes of authority will converge when both
authorities can permissibly coexist. Given the likelihood of duplicative applicability of both such
provisions, duplicative reporting requirements that are legally defensible are likely to exist. In
the interest of increasing the efficiency with which urgent, time-sensitive potential operations
must occur, Atlas Response asks the FAA to address the practicality of dual requirements for
notification or interaction with critical infrastructure site owners or proprietors. In this regard, the
FAA should clarify that the proposed rule must operate alongside state and local provisions that
are defensible, rather than preempt them. Atlas Response urges the FAA to use automation tools
and its authority to enter into unique agreements to address how duplicative reports or
notifications may be filed simultaneously in a manner consistent with the proposed rule. For
example, the FAA may enter into memoranda of understanding with state or local governments
under its authority codified at 49 U.S.C. § 106, to agree with a mechanism that will facilitate a
UAS operator’s submission of only one notification that can fulfill two consistent requirements.
IV. Healthcare and Public Health Sector: Access for Designated Medical Cargo
Operators
Atlas Response specifically supports the inclusion of the Healthcare and Public Health
Sector under proposed § 74.92 and urges the FAA to establish a standing access framework for
7

that sector. Such a framework should reflect the unique operational requirements of time-critical
medical cargo missions.
Hospitals, transplant centers, organ procurement organizations, and blood banking
facilities represent precisely the category of fixed site facility from which, using a clearly defined
access framework, a UAFR designation would most benefit. A transplantable organ, such as a
kidney, heart, liver, or lung, carries a cold ischemia window measured in hours, not days. An
OrganOx metra normothermic perfusion console, which sustains a donor heart or liver during
transport, weighs approximately 165 pounds and requires continuous power and temperature
management throughout the mission. For a Part 135 medical cargo operator transporting such a
payload to a hospital helipad, any per-flight administrative delay, whether at the hospital UAFR
or at an intermediate waypoint, could directly threaten patient survival.
Atlas Response urges the FAA to establish, in the final rule or in accompanying guidance
under the Healthcare and Public Health Sector provisions of § 74.92, that a service agreement
between such a fixed site healthcare facility and a medical cargo operator authorized to conduct
operations under part 135 constitutes a standing access authorization for all missions conducted
under that agreement. Under this framework, the hospital’s designation of a medical cargo
carrier as an authorized operator would satisfy the access requirements of proposed § 74.250 and
§ 74.255 for all covered missions. The Standard UAFR facility would receive mission-specific
notification provided at the time of dispatch. Similarly, the standing access authorization would
constitute automatic permission to enter Special UAFR airspace, rather than requiring per-
mission FAA approval to spend time in the area as needed for loading or delivery of the medical
cargo at issue. This standing access model is consistent with how the FAA manages UAS
operations in other contexts, is proportionate to the regulatory authorizations that an air carrier
8

certificated under part 135 has received and is essential to ensuring that the UAFR framework
does not create a regulatory barrier to the delivery of life-saving medical cargo.
Atlas Response further urges the FAA to take the opportunity in this rulemaking to
clarify that part 135 cargo operations that occur beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS), when
operating with active Remote Identification broadcast in accordance with 14 CFR part 89, are
expressly included within the allowed operations described in proposed § 74.250. The proposed
rule’s reference to allowed operations under Part 135 should be read to include BVLOS
configurations authorized under the operator's FAA-issued operations specifications, without
requiring additional per-flight authorization beyond the notification process of § 74.255.
V. Government Policy
Enabling efficient operation of UAS that can occur in a manner consistent with national
security is a notable and challenging requirement. Consistent with President Trump’s Executive
Order 14305, Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty (June 6, 2025) and Executive Order
14307, Unleashing American Drone Dominance (June 6, 2025), accelerating the safe
commercialization of drone technologies and fully integrating UAS into the National Airspace
System is critical for the current moment in history, provided such operations can occur safely
and do not present threats to U.S. critical infrastructure or others in the airspace.
Atlas Response seeks to join the FAA and its security partners in ensuring that such
operations can not only occur but can do so in an efficient manner that does not stymie the
growth of the UAS industry. Indeed, the Government has emphasized that efficiency in
approvals and rescission of unnecessary processes is a priority; for Atlas Response, increasing
efficiency by eradicating bureaucracy or unnecessary steps can have lifesaving effects. Fulfilling
the goal of ensuring the United States dominates with regard to UAS technology, innovative
9

ideas, simultaneously with resolution of national security concerns will not be possible if owners
or proprietors of critical infrastructure, as well as UAS operators, encounter layers of delay.
Accordingly, Atlas Response recommends the FAA amend its regulations and policies to the
greatest extent possible to reduce duplicative notification, permit notifications to occur in an
efficient manner, and clarify the availability of temporary transit. Further, if statutory
amendments are necessary, Atlas Response recommends the FAA work with its federal partners
as necessary to petition to Congress to create flexibility for the FAA to procure and implement
efficient mechanisms to use a streamlined, efficient notification and review process or take other
measures to ensure the FAA can fulfill the Administration’s goal of unleashing American drone
dominance.
Atlas Response would welcome the opportunity for further discussion of these and other
considerations with the FAA or other federal agencies that are responsible for evaluating the
policies for the proposed rule. The company appreciates the occasion to provide suggestions and
trusts that you will consider these suggestions fully.
Respectfully submitted,

Designation of Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (14 CFR Part 74)
To the Docket:
Zing Drone Solutions (Zing Drone Delivery Inc.) submits the following comments on the Federal Aviation
Administration's notice of proposed rulemaking establishing 14 CFR Part 74, Designation of Unmanned
Aircraft Flight Restrictions, published in the Federal Register on May 6, 2026 (Vol. 91, No. 87).
I. Interest of the Commenter
Zing Drone Solutions designs and manufactures Remote Identification broadcast equipment (Z-RID, Z-RID
Lite) and unmanned aircraft detection systems (Z-Scan, Z-Scan Mini) for corrections, public safety, and
critical infrastructure operators. Zing's detection systems are fielded at correctional facilities and critical
infrastructure sites and rely on passive reception of Remote ID broadcasts, consistent with 14 CFR part 89,
to build a real time picture of unmanned aircraft activity around a protected facility. Zing's products and
deployment experience are directly relevant to the security monitoring and detection requirements the
FAA proposes to establish in Subpart B of Part 74, and Zing offers the following comments to support a
workable, cost effective, and technology neutral final rule.
II. Zing supports the Remote ID based security monitoring requirement in Section 74.56(d), and
recommends FAA adopt a defined means of compliance.
Proposed Section 74.56(d) would require an eligible facility's protective security to include the capability
to receive broadcast Remote Identification messages from unmanned aircraft operating within or near a
requested UAFR, using equipment compatible with part 89. Zing strongly supports this requirement.
Remote ID reception is the lowest cost and most broadly deployable means available today for a fixed site
facility to establish situational awareness of unmanned aircraft activity, and it does not require the facility
to hold any FCC license or spectrum authorization to receive it.
The proposed text does not, however, specify what “equipment that is compatible with the requirements
of part 89” means in practice, and there is no test standard or means of compliance to help facilities and

equipment vendors demonstrate compliance. This ambiguity risks inconsistent implementation and
disputes during the evaluation process under Section 74.100. Zing recommends the final rule direct FAA to
publish an advisory circular or technical standard order defining minimum performance requirements for
Remote ID reception equipment, addressing at minimum: (1) supported broadcast methods (Bluetooth
4/5 and Wi-Fi, as specified in part 89 subpart D); (2) minimum detection range and message decode
reliability; and (3) data retention and reporting format sufficient to support the update obligation in
Section 74.20. A defined means of compliance would let facilities and vendors build to a known bar and
would give FAA a consistent basis for evaluating protective security under Sections 74.66 and 74.100.
Remote ID reception equipment capable of satisfying Section 74.56(d) is commercially available today
from multiple manufacturers, including Zing's own Z-Scan and Z-Scan Mini product lines, and does not
depend on new technology development. Zing recommends the same advisory circular also include
installation guidance, addressing sensor siting and spacing relative to the facility's lateral boundary and
local terrain, the minimum number of sensors needed for full perimeter coverage, and integration with an
existing security operations center or guard force. Installation guidance of this kind would give facilities
and their security contractors a consistent basis for designing a compliant system, and would shorten the
time between an FAA conditional approval and a facility's demonstration that its protective security is
actually in place.
Zing further recommends the final rule confirm that a passive, receive only Remote ID monitoring system,
one that does not transmit, interrogate, or otherwise interact with an aircraft or its control link, fully
satisfies Section 74.56(d) and does not implicate the existing proviso in that section that “nothing in this
paragraph authorizes electronic interference or interception of aircraft or navigation signals.” Passive
Remote ID reception involves no interference with or interception of navigation signals; it is materially
different from active counter-UAS methods such as radar or radio frequency direction finding of a control
link, and the final rule should make that distinction explicit so facilities and their security contractors are
not deterred from deploying passive Remote ID monitoring out of an abundance of caution.
III. The 24 month demonstration of need in Section 74.66(a) should include a phased pathway for
facilities that have never operated detection equipment.
Section 74.66(a) requires an applicant to describe existing unmanned aircraft traffic patterns over the fixed
site facility during the last 24 months. Many eligible facilities, particularly those newly captured by the
sector criteria in Subpart C, such as correctional facilities meeting the 500 inmate threshold in Section
74.87(b) or mid-size energy, dams, and water facilities meeting the thresholds in Sections 74.85 and 74.88,
have never deployed detection equipment and therefore have no historical data to report. This creates a
practical barrier: a facility cannot demonstrate 24 months of traffic history without first deploying a
detection system, but many facilities will reasonably wait for UAFR designation, and the cost certainty a
UAFR provides, before making that investment.
Zing recommends the final rule allow an applicant lacking historical data to satisfy Section 74.66(a) with a
shorter baseline period, for example 90 days, of data collected from a newly deployed Remote ID
monitoring system during the application process, supplemented by a qualitative narrative addressing
known or anticipated traffic patterns based on the facility's location, sector, and comparable facilities. This
approach preserves the demonstration of need requirement while removing a barrier that would
otherwise fall hardest on smaller and newly captured facilities, the same population the rule is intended to
help.

IV. FAA should clarify that shared or regionally operated detection infrastructure can satisfy
Section 74.56(d) for multiple co-located facilities.
Section 74.56(d) already contemplates that a facility may satisfy the Remote ID reception requirement
“directly or through a contracted service.” Zing has observed in the field that many eligible facilities under
Subpart C cluster geographically, for example dams, associated substations, and water conveyance
infrastructure along a shared river corridor, or multiple energy and communications facilities along a
transportation corridor. A single, regionally deployed network of passive Remote ID sensors can provide
overlapping coverage of several qualifying facilities in such a cluster at a materially lower per facility cost
than a standalone system at each site.
Zing recommends the final rule or accompanying guidance confirm that a shared regional detection
network, whether operated by one of the participating facilities, a regional authority, or a contracted third
party service, satisfies Section 74.56(d) for each participating facility, provided each facility receives its
own reporting and retains the ability to meet its update obligations under Section 74.20. This clarification
would materially reduce the cost of compliance for smaller Subpart C facilities without weakening the
security monitoring requirement, and would encourage the kind of distributed detection coverage that
gives FAA and facility operators a more complete operating picture of unmanned aircraft activity near
critical infrastructure.
V. FAA should clarify how facility security personnel are expected to receive and act on Remote ID
detections, and should publish clear, pilot facing guidance on the penalties for violating a UAFR.
Proposed Part 74 establishes a detection and reporting obligation for the facility (Sections 74.20 and
74.56(d)) and an enforcement authority for FAA (Section 74.260), but it does not describe the operational
link between the two: what a facility's security personnel should do when their Remote ID monitoring
system detects an unmanned aircraft operating in apparent violation of a UAFR. Zing recommends the
final rule, or the advisory circular recommended in Section II above, address the following: (1) a defined
channel and format for a facility to report a suspected UAFR violation to FAA closer to real time, distinct
from the annual reporting obligation in Section 74.20(b), so that time-sensitive violations can support
enforcement action under Section 74.260; (2) the information a facility should capture and retain to
support that report, for example the Remote ID serial number, time, and estimated location of the
detected aircraft, consistent with the data elements already described for allowed operations in Section
74.255(b); and (3) when a facility should contact local law enforcement in addition to, or instead of, FAA,
for a detection that appears to present an active security threat rather than an inadvertent incursion.
Relatedly, Section 74.260 states that a knowing or willful violation of a UAFR issued for a national security
or homeland security purpose may be subject to criminal penalties under 49 U.S.C. 46307, and that any
UAFR violation may also be subject to civil penalty or certificate action. Zing recommends FAA state these
penalties in plain terms in a form suitable for pilot facing publications, for example UAS Facility Maps,
B4UFLY, and comparable industry electronic flight bag products, so operators understand the specific
consequences of operating in a designated UAFR before those consequences arise. Clear, consistently
published penalty language should improve compliance and reduce the number of inadvertent incursions
that a facility's Remote ID monitoring system, and ultimately FAA, must otherwise sort out after the fact.
VI. FAA should clarify whether and when the equipment required by Section 74.56(d) must be
installed and operating relative to application submission and UAFR approval.

Section 74.54(d) requires an applicant to demonstrate protective security, including the Remote ID
reception capability in Section 74.56(d), as a condition of eligibility, but the proposed rule does not state
whether that capability must be installed and operating at the time the application is submitted, at the
time of FAA's conditional approval under Section 74.100(c), or by the effective date of a final designation.
This is a practical question for facilities budgeting and procuring equipment. A facility should not need to
have fully installed and operating detection equipment months before it knows whether FAA will approve
its application, but a facility also should not receive a UAFR before it can demonstrate the required
protective security is actually in place.
Zing recommends the final rule specify that an applicant must demonstrate that protective security under
Section 74.56, including a Remote ID reception capability, is installed and operational no later than the
date FAA issues a conditional approval under Section 74.100(c), and that FAA confirm the capability
remains operational before publishing the final designation. This would let facilities defer capital
investment in detection equipment until they have reasonable assurance FAA intends to approve their
application, while still ensuring the required security capability is in place before a UAFR takes effect. Zing
further recommends FAA state a minimum lead time, for example 60 days, between installation and final
designation, sufficient to allow a facility to build the baseline detection history recommended in Section III
above.
VII. FAA should complete the reserved Food and Agriculture and Water and Wastewater sector
criteria before the final rule.
Sections 74.90 and 74.96 are reserved. Zing recognizes that sector specific criteria for these two sectors
may still be under development. Leaving them reserved in the final rule, however, would mean that
otherwise eligible facilities in these two sectors, which are designated critical infrastructure sectors under
the same NSM-22 framework that Section 74.1 relies on for the rest of Subpart C, have no path to apply for
a UAFR while comparable facilities in other sectors do. Zing recommends that FAA complete criteria for
these two sectors prior to publishing the final rule, or, if that is not feasible, commit to a specific timeline
for a follow on rulemaking so that affected facilities are not left without a pathway for an indefinite period.
VIII. Conclusion
Zing supports FAA's overall approach in proposed Part 74 and the security monitoring requirement in
Section 74.56(d) in particular. Establishing a defined means of compliance and installation guidance for
Remote ID based detection, confirming that this equipment is commercially available today, allowing a
phased demonstration of need for facilities without detection history, recognizing shared regional
detection infrastructure, clarifying how facilities report detections and what penalties apply to violators,
clarifying the timing for installing required equipment relative to application and approval, and completing
the reserved sector criteria would together make the rule more workable while preserving its security
purpose. Zing appreciates the opportunity to comment and would welcome the opportunity to provide
additional technical information to FAA as it finalizes this rule.

Respectfully submitted,
Ian Annase
Founder & CEO, Zing Drone Solutions (Zing Drone Delivery Inc.)
ian@zingdrones.com | 619-813-6563
4529 NW A Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801

I oppose the inclusion of the Food and Agriculture sector (§ 74.90) amongst the critical infrastructure facilities that could obtain Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).

Ag gag laws like these serve only to hide abuses from public scrutiny and make it easier for farms to take advantage of their staff and harm animals.

I oppose including the Food and Agriculture sector (§ 74.90) among facilities eligible for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).
There is no evidence that drones pose a safety or security threat to agricultural facilities. Instead, drones have exposed animal abuse, illegal housing conditions, and environmental violations at factory farms that would otherwise remain hidden from public view.
Rather than creating safety risks, drones promote transparency and accountability by documenting unlawful and unethical practices. I urge you to exclude the Food and Agriculture sector from receiving UAFRs and preserve the public's ability to expose wrongdoing.

I strongly oppose this proposal.  I value transparency and public access to information, and the animal agriculture community should not be unfairly protected and hidden.   If they have nothing to hide, they should have no problems with exposing themselves to their actions which is in the best interest of the public.

SONOMA COUNTY FARM BUREAU

Affiliated with California Farm Bureau and American Farm Bureau Federation

Submitted via www.regulations. gov

July 31, 2026

Bryan Bedford

Administrator

Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue
Washington, DC 20591

Re: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03 — Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility

Dear Administrator Bedford:

The Sonoma County Farm Bureau appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Federal Aviation
Administration's proposed designation to restrict the operation of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in
close proximity to designated fixed-site facilities.

For more than one hundred years, the Sonoma County Farm Bureau has represented the farmers, ranchers,
dairy producers, processors, and agricultural businesses that comprise one of California's most diverse
agricultural economies. Our members produce milk, poultry, eggs, livestock, winegrapes, specialty crops,
and numerous other agricultural commodities that are essential components of California's and the
Nation's food supply.

The Farm Bureau supports the FAA's efforts to evaluate whether additional protections are warranted for
facilities whose disruption could adversely affect public safety, economic security, or other national
interests. We respectfully submit that agricultural production and food processing facilities merit serious
consideration within that framework because they perform essential functions that extend well beyond
private commercial activity.

Congress has vested the FAA with broad authority under 49 U.S.C. § 40103 to regulate the use of the
National Airspace System to ensure its safe and efficient use. The Agency likewise possesses authority to
establish restrictions on unmanned aircraft operations when necessary to protect safety, security, and
other governmental interests. This rulemaking presents an appropriate opportunity to exercise that
authority in a manner that recognizes agriculture's unique role in sustaining the Nation's food system.

The federal government has long recognized the Food and Agriculture Sector as one of the Nation's sixteen
critical infrastructure sectors. Under Presidential Policy Directive 21 (Critical Infrastructure Security and

Resilience) and the National Infrastructure Protection Plan, the Food and Agriculture Sector is identified as
essential to national security, economic vitality, and public health. This designation reflects the reality that
disruptions affecting agricultural production, food processing, storage, transportation, and distribution can

3589 Westwind Blvd., Santa Rosa, CA 95403 * Phone (707) 544-5575 * Fax (707) 544-7452 * www.sonomatb.org

have cascading consequences throughout the national economy and the food supply. Protecting
agricultural infrastructure from unnecessary operational risks is therefore not merely a local concern, but a
matter of national importance.

This federal recognition is reinforced locally. The Sonoma County Board of Supervisors has formally
declared agriculture to be critical infrastructure, recognizing its indispensable role in food production,
economic resilience, environmental stewardship, emergency preparedness, and the overall welfare of
Sonoma County residents. The resolution also acknowledges that intentional interference with agricultural
operations can inflict substantial financial harm on producers, processors, employees, and the communities
that depend upon them. By recognizing agriculture as critical infrastructure, Sonoma County established an
important policy framework that supports meaningful consequences for unlawful actions that disrupt or
threaten essential agricultural operations. While the County's declaration does not establish federal policy,
it demonstrates the growing recognition among state and local governments that agriculture deserves the
same thoughtful consideration afforded to other sectors of critical infrastructure.

Sonoma County's agricultural economy encompasses commercial dairies, poultry farms, livestock ranches,
vineyards, specialty crop operations, feed suppliers, food processors, cold storage facilities, and distribution
networks. Together, these operations form an integrated food production system upon which consumers
rely every day. Disruption at any point within this system has the potential to affect food production,
processing capacity, transportation logistics, employee safety, animal welfare, and market stability well
beyond county boundaries.

Unfortunately, these concerns are not hypothetical. Sonoma County poultry farms, dairies, and agricultural
processing facilities have experienced repeated unauthorized drone activity by individuals seeking to
capture aerial footage without the knowledge or consent of property owners. The resulting footage has
often been edited, selectively presented, and disseminated to advance advocacy campaigns rather than
provide an objective representation of modern agricultural practices. Whatever the motivation behind
these flights, unauthorized UAS operations over active agricultural facilities create legitimate concerns
regarding aviation safety, operational security, employee privacy, livestock management, and biosecurity.

For livestock and poultry operations in particular, unauthorized low-altitude drone flights can disturb
animals, interfere with routine husbandry practices, distract employees operating equipment, and
undermine carefully maintained biosecurity protocols. At a time when producers continue to respond to
highly pathogenic avian influenza and prepare for other foreign animal disease threats, reducing
unnecessary intrusion into food production facilities is an important component of protecting animal
health, employee safety, and the resilience of the Nation's food supply.

At the same time, the Sonoma County Farm Bureau strongly supports the responsible use of unmanned
aircraft systems in agriculture. Farmers and ranchers throughout California increasingly rely upon UAS
technology for precision agriculture, irrigation management, livestock observation, infrastructure
inspection, wildfire assessment, environmental monitoring, conservation planning, and regulatory
compliance. These technologies improve productivity, worker safety, environmental stewardship, and the
efficient management of agricultural operations.

Accordingly, we encourage the FAA to adopt a balanced regulatory framework that distinguishes between
unauthorized operations posing security and operational risks and legitimate agricultural uses conducted
by property owners, employees, contractors, researchers, and other authorized operators. Restrictions
should deter activities intended to surveil, harass, disrupt, or interfere with protected agricultural facilities

3589 Westwind Blvd., Santa Rosa, CA 95403 ¢ Phone (707) 544-5575 * Fax (707) 544-7452 * www.sonomafb.org

while preserving the ability of agricultural producers to continue utilizing UAS technology in support of safe,
efficient, and sustainable farming and ranching practices.

As the FAA evaluates which facilities warrant additional protection under this proposal, we respectfully
encourage the Agency to recognize that agricultural production and food processing facilities already
occupy a unique position within federal critical infrastructure policy. Extending appropriate operational
protections to these facilities would be consistent with the FAA's statutory responsibility to ensure the safe
and efficient use of the National Airspace System, existing federal critical infrastructure policy, and the
compelling public interest in maintaining a secure, resilient, and reliable domestic food supply.

The Sonoma County Farm Bureau appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and thanks the
FAA for considering the unique operational needs of American agriculture as it develops a balanced
regulatory framework for unmanned aircraft systems.

Introduction
Unmanned aircraft have become an increasingly serious threat to U.S. critical infrastructure.
Small, commercially available drones can bypass traditional perimeter defenses to conduct
surveillance, collect sensitive facility data, or deliver conductive materials, incendiary devices,
and explosives. Recent incidents involving electrical substations, military installations, and other
sensitive facilities demonstrate that this threat is no longer abstract, while advances in autonomy
and payload capacity will only make these systems more difficult to detect and defeat.
The Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA’s) proposed process for establishing unmanned
aircraft flight restrictions could help address this threat by reducing unauthorized overflights and
distinguishing legitimate operators from potentially malicious actors. However, the current
proposal places an unnecessarily high and poorly defined burden of proof on critical
infrastructure owners and operators seeking protection to demonstrate vulnerabilities that are
already broadly recognized by Congress, the administration, and federal security agencies. It also
risks limiting the national security value of Section 2209 by requiring applicants to disclose
existing security measures.
The FAA should revise its proposed framework to provide critical infrastructure with more
proactive and predictable protection. Specifically, the agency should ease and clarify the
application requirements for standard flight restrictions, strengthen consequences for deliberate
violations involving national security risks, and reserve special restrictions for defense-specific
critical infrastructure.
Unmanned Aircraft Pose a Critical National Security Risk
Unmanned aircraft pose a distinct threat to fixed U.S. critical infrastructure sites because they
combine surveillance, access, and payload delivery in a small and relatively inexpensive
platform that can bypass fences, gates, and other ground-based defenses. The Cybersecurity and
Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recognizes unmanned aircraft as both a cyber and
physical threat to critical infrastructure and warns that drones can be converted into or used to
carry improvised explosive devices capable of harming people and infrastructure.1 A
commercially available drone can rapidly map a generation facility or a transmission substation,
identify transformers, control buildings, security posts, and operating patterns, providing the
drone operator with information that would be difficult to collect from the ground.2 Malicious
actors can also modify the same platform to carry conductive materials, incendiary devices, or
explosives, introducing greater sabotage risks from both criminals and nation-state actors.
Recent cases demonstrate how easily drones can be used to collect information about sensitive
facilities. In November 2024, federal authorities arrested a man for allegedly flying an

Identification Poster and Postcard,” accessed July 24, 2026. (https://www.cisa.gov/resources-
tools/resources/suspicious-uas-identification-poster-and-postcard)
2 Jack Burnham, Craig Singleton, and RADM (Ret.) Mark Montgomery, “Section 232 National Security
Investigation of Imports of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) and Their Parts and Components,” Foundation for
Defense of Democracies, August 6, 2025. (https://www.fdd.org/analysis/2025/08/06/section-232-national-security-
investigation-of-imports-of-unmanned-aircraft-systems-uas-and-their-parts-and-components)

unregistered drone over Vandenberg Space Force Base and photographing the installation.3
Systems at the base detected the drone approximately one mile above the base on the same day
that SpaceX launched rockets carrying payloads for the National Reconnaissance Office.4 In a
separate case, federal prosecutors charged a Canadian citizen with using a drone on three
occasions in January 2025 to photograph launch complexes, a payload-processing facility, a
submarine wharf, and munitions bunkers at Cape Canaveral Space Force Base.5 Although these
incidents involved defense installations, they illustrate a surveillance capability that is equally
relevant to energy infrastructure: drones can provide users with detailed information about
facilities, critical assets, security perimeters, and operating patterns. The Nuclear Regulatory
Commission has also received numerous reports of drones operating over nuclear power plants
and, in 2024, began requiring operators to report such sightings to federal authorities and local
law enforcement.6
More concerningly, other domestic incidents highlight the risk of another dangerous yet
increasingly plausible scenario: a strike which destroys equipment whose loss would cause
cascading effects across the U.S. economy.
In July 2020, authorities recovered a modified drone near a Pennsylvania electrical substation.
Luckily the drone had crashed prior to reaching its target because authorities discovered a copper
wire suspended beneath the drone, likely to create a short circuit.7 Four years later, federal
authorities disrupted a plot to attack a Nashville electrical substation. Before his arrest, the
defendant researched attacks on substations, conducted reconnaissance of the intended target,
and prepared to attach an armed explosive device to a drone.8
While these strikes would have likely caused similar outages to those caused by major weather
events, a more deliberate assault could isolate and destroy targets or components that are difficult
to replace or transport and remain essential to generating and transmitting large amounts of
electricity. The Department of Energy (DOE) estimates that more than 90 percent of electricity
consumed in the United States passes through high-voltage or large power transformers at some

point.9 Large power transformers are expensive, difficult to transport, typically custom-made,
and often not interchangeable.10 The destruction of even a limited number of carefully selected
components could therefore create restoration challenges far more severe than utilities ordinarily
face after storm damage. DOE has historically estimated procurement periods of at least one
year, although the department stated in 2026 that lead times for large transformers had increased
to between three and four years.11
Recent attacks in Ukraine illustrate how drones can target the electrical grid’s most consequential
components. Russian forces have used small drones controlled through fiber-optic cables, which
make them impossible to jam, to penetrate barriers around high-voltage substations and strike
autotransformers. These large pieces of equipment change voltage so that electricity can move
between different parts of the transmission grid. Destroying an autotransformer can disable an
entire transformer unit, eliminating a major pathway for moving electricity into or through a
region and isolating a region from a national grid.12 Although the United States does not face the
same wartime conditions as Ukraine, these attacks demonstrate the threat vector available to a
knowledgeable adversary: inexpensive drones can bypass perimeter security, exploit gaps in
fixed defenses, and destroy individual components to create widespread geographic impact.
American utilities attempt to manage the risk of equipment failure by maintaining strategically
located spares, participating in mutual-assistance arrangements, and designing systems to reroute
electricity when individual components fail. Yet these measures do not eliminate the danger
posed by a coordinated attack on scarce or non-interchangeable equipment. Industry
representatives identified a compound event — such as severe weather occurring alongside a
physical, cyber, or drone-enabled attack — as particularly concerning because repair crews,
replacement equipment, communications systems, and alternative transmission routes could
already be under strain. These risks will likely only grow more pressing as advances in autonomy
render commercial drones capable of independently evading defensive systems.13
Surveillance and sabotage risks intersect with another critical dimension: the ubiquity of
Chinese-produced unmanned aircraft in the United States. While the Federal Communications
Commission and Congress have banned new drones and related equipment produced by Chinese
firms such as DJI and Autel Robotics, many of their older systems remain present within the
domestic market.14 These systems pose a range of national security threats, with the CISA, the

Reconsideration of Action in Rulemaking Proceeding Application for Review of Action in Rulemaking Proceeding,”

FBI, Commerce Department, and Department of Defense (DOD) all warning of DJI’s ties to the
Chinese military and its insufficient cybersecurity practices.15
The presence of Chinese-produced drones presents a new set of dangers to U.S. critical
infrastructure. Rather than assist a radicalized “lone wolf” actor or criminal element to conduct
an operation against U.S. critical infrastructure, Chinese-produced drones may pass information
directly back to Beijing, complementing its current efforts to conduct operational preparation of
the battlefield by targeting critical infrastructure in cyberspace. Both the FBI and Department of
Homeland Security (DHS) have warned explicitly that Chinese-produced drones pose a threat to
critical infrastructure and may expose collected information — such as detailed imagery,
geolocation information, facility layouts, and operational data — to Chinese authorities.16 Such
information may allow China to map privately-owned and -operated nodes across the American
economy essential for maintaining military mobility — providing targeting information for
Beijing’s ongoing cyber and potential future kinetic operation against U.S. critical
infrastructure.17
The FAA Should Enhance Its Role in Safeguarding Critical Infrastructure
In response to this threat, the FAA should use flight restrictions to give critical infrastructure
owners and operators clearer airspaces, allowing them to readily identify possible threats from
malicious actors. The agency can enhance national security by preventing legitimate actors from
incidentally conducting dangerous overflights.
However, the proposed rule extends an unclear and potentially onerous burden of proof for
owner-operators seeking protection and its requirements exceed the FAA’s statutory authority
under relevant Congressional legislation and run counter to the Trump administration’s executive
order.
The agency’s proposal attempts to balance public access with protecting critical infrastructure by
requiring owner operators to extensively document their risk profile rather than assuming that
such assets are inherently vulnerable and require protection. To file for an Unmanned Aircraft
Flight Restriction (UAFR), an applicant must also already have protective security measures
commensurate with its “criticality” and file a report on the amount of drone traffic currently
within the vicinity of their facility. These rules are even more stringent for “high-risk” sites, as
the FAA would require this subset of applicants to have preexisting layered defenses against
drones and other possible threats.
However, the FAA has declined to outline a clear standard of proof that would be sufficient for a
successful application — specific security measures such as the presence of Remote ID sensing,
the consistency of overflights that would trigger protective measures, or how these overflights

reconsideration-of-action-in-rulemaking-proceeding-application-for-review-of-action-in-rulemaking-proceeding)
15 Ibid.
16 Ibid.
17 Ibid; Mike Minihan and RADM (Ret.) Mark Montgomery, “America’s Military Plans Depend on Infrastructure It
Doesn’t Secure,” Foundation for Defense of Democracies, July 13, 2026.
(https://www.fdd.org/analysis/2026/07/13/americas-military-plans-depend-on-infrastructure-it-doesnt-secure)
Foundation for Defense of Democracies www.fdd.org
4

must be documented across different sites and operators. Along with inherently placing the
burden of proof on owner-operators, these gaps add regulatory uncertainty that may deter certain
operators from initially applying for protection regardless of the severity of the threat.
Moreover, there is limited evidence to suggest that these requirements are supported by
congressional statute or administrative intent. While the FAA’s proposal operationalizes Section
2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act (FESSA) of 2016, its structure implies
safeguards not named in the statute, overly limiting its national security impacts. Under Section
2209, Congress required the FAA to consider aviation safety, protection of property and
individuals, and national security in determining restrictions on drones flying over fixed
facilities.18 Pointedly, this section was intended as a specific carveout from the FAA’s statutory
focus on protecting the public’s right-of-transit under 49 U.S.C. § 40103.19 While the agency’s
default authority from Congress is to protect Americans’ right to access airspace, Section 2209
mandates that the FAA focus specifically on critical infrastructure protection, even if may
intercede on the public’s right to transit or access certain locations. To that end, the relevant
statute requires the FAA to solely focus on each specific criterion, either together or separately, in
reaching a determination to grant a UAFR, not to develop multi-part tests that fall outside of its
bounds. Moreover, since FESSA’s passage, Congress has largely sought to heighten drone
security measures by dispensing authorization to intercept unmanned aircraft towards state, local,
and tribal governments under the Safer Skies Act, which was passed as part of the FY2026
National Defense Authorization Act.20
The Trump administration has also clearly outlined the necessity of securing the airspace over
critical infrastructure in Executive Order 14305. While the FAA cites this order as its impetus for
its proposal, the order explicitly prioritizes safeguarding critical infrastructure, stating that such
installations are “subject to frequent — and often unidentified — UAS incursions” and that
“immediate action is needed to ensure […] that its airspace remains safe and secure.”21 The
executive order requires DOD, DHS, Department of Justice (DOJ), and Department of
Transportation (DOT) to recommend whether the White House should designate critical
infrastructure as “covered facilities” or “covered assets” under 6 U.S.C. 124n and 10 U.S.C.
130i — statutes which authorize the destruction of unmanned aircraft that approach such
facilities.22 Moreover, the order also requires DHS, FAA, and sector risk management agencies
to publish guidance that aids critical infrastructure owners and operators in better deploying
security technologies to counter intrusions by unmanned aircraft — a process disrupted by the
FAA’s insistence that applicants highlight their current security protocols to receive a restriction
order.23
The FAA’s approach to managing flight restriction orders cuts against recent interagency and
state actions to counter drones, particularly those produced by foreign adversaries. Along with

codified at 49 U.S.C. § 40101 note.
19 Sovereignty and use of airspace, 49 U.S.C. §40103. (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/40103)
20 National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Pub. L. No. 119-60, div. H, tit. LXXXVI, §§ 8601-8607,
139 Stat. 718, 1938-45 (2025).
21 Executive Order 14305, 90 Fed. Reg. 24719, “Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty,” June 11, 2025.
22 Ibid.
23 Ibid.

the FBI and DHS warning that Chinese-produced drones pose a direct threat to critical
infrastructure, Congress and DOJ have banned federal funds from being used to purchase DJI
products, particularly by law enforcement, recognizing their risk to security operations. States
such as Arizona, Arkansas, and Louisiana have also passed laws that preemptively restrict
unauthorized flights over critical infrastructure sites, such as power plants, without the need for
owners and operators to petition for protection.
Recommendations
Both the Trump administration and Congress have rightly noted the national security risks posed
by the unsafe operation of drones around sensitive sites. The FAA can contribute to its national
security mission by preventing lawful operators from conducting overflights of critical
infrastructure. Drones that continue to operate in restricted areas will, by definition, be violating
the law.
To clarify the operating picture so that law enforcement can prosecute criminal or nation-state
actors, the FAA should focus on easing the burden of proof on owners and operators, enhancing
penalties for unlawful access of restricted airspace, and adding additional safeguards for defense-
specific critical infrastructure.
 The FAA should ease the burden of proof for applicants seeking a UAFR and
proactively provide greater protection to critical infrastructure. The risk posed by
small drones to U.S. critical infrastructure is well documented by multiple national
security agencies, the Trump administration, Congress, and a range of state, local, and
tribal governments. As such, the FAA should not require standard UAFR applicants to
provide overflight statistics or detail how drones pose a risk to their facilities. Instead, the
FAA should explicitly place the burden on other airspace users to demonstrate why a
given restriction will unduly hinder their public-access rights. The agency should also
allow a standard UAFR to apply for a longer period of time, with renewal periods tied to
either major changes in site design or five-year increments.
 The FAA should consider applying criminal penalties for violations of standard
UAFRs in certain national security-related circumstances. While drone operators
should likely receive civil penalties in the case of accidental violations, the United States
has already experienced a pattern of UAS intrusions that suggest ties to either criminal
organizations, terrorism, or an adversarial nation-state actor. As such, the FAA should
consider applying criminal penalties under 49 U.S.C. 40103(b)(3) and 46307 for
violations of standard UAFRs when those violations relate to national security.
 The FAA should limit the application of a Special UAFR to defense-specific critical
infrastructure. The agency’s proposed delineation between “critical infrastructure” and
facilities that support “defense production, intelligence operations, continuity of
government functions, or other activities where disruption could create significant
national security risks” is unnecessarily broad and generates regulatory uncertainty due to
overlapping statutory definitions. Rather, the FAA should limit the application for a
special UAFR to defense-specific critical infrastructure owner-operators, such as those
Foundation for Defense of Democracies www.fdd.org
6

outlined in 16 U.S.C. § 824o-1 and DoDD 3020.45, along with the recommendation of a
designated national security agency (DHS, DOD, DOE, and DOJ).
Conclusion
The FAA cannot eliminate the threat posed by malicious drones, but it can make it easier to
identify potentially dangerous activity by reducing legitimate and accidental overflights of
sensitive facilities. The agency should revise its proposal to place fewer burdens on critical

facilities essential to U.S. national security, economic resilience, and public health and safety.
Thank you for considering our comments. We look forward to seeing how our input is
incorporated into the FAA’s final rule.

Re: Comments of BrightAI Corporation on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, “Designation—
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,” Docket
No. FAA-2026-4558; RIN 2120-AL33; 91 FR 24650 (May 6, 2026)
To the Federal Aviation Administration:
BrightAI Corporation (“BrightAI”) respectfully submits these comments in response to the Federal
Aviation Administration’s (“FAA”) notice of proposed rulemaking implementing Section 2209 of the
FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016 through a new 14 CFR Part 74.
I. Interest of BrightAI
BrightAI is a Delaware corporation headquartered at 1001 Page Mill Road, Building 3, Palo Alto,
California, and an enterprise provider of AI-enabled industrial monitoring. BrightAI operates small
unmanned aircraft to inspect and build high-resolution digital twins of critical-infrastructure sites—
including electric generation and delivery, oil and gas, and water and wastewater facilities—for the
facility owners and operators who would be eligible to petition for an unmanned aircraft flight restriction
(“UAFR”) under proposed Part 74. BrightAI conducts these operations under 14 CFR Part 107, including
beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations under FAA waiver 107W-2026-00907. BrightAI therefore has a
direct interest in this proceeding from both perspectives the rule implicates: as the commercial operator
conducting authorized flights over these facilities, and as a technology partner to the critical-infrastructure
owners the rule is designed to protect.
II. Summary of BrightAI’s Position
BrightAI supports the FAA’s implementation of Section 2209 and the objective of protecting critical
infrastructure from unauthorized unmanned aircraft. We write only to ensure that the final rule
distinguishes the operator a facility has engaged to inspect its own assets from the unauthorized activity
the rule targets, and that it does not inadvertently impede the authorized inspection flights on which those
facilities increasingly rely for safety, maintenance, and resilience. BrightAI offers five recommendations,
each of which responds to a question on which the FAA expressly sought comment:
1. Confirm that § 74.250(a)(2) permits non-transitory operations conducted by or for the facility
owner, and adopt rule text to that effect;
2. Adopt an operator-level, standing “whitelist” for access notification under § 74.255;
3. Protect operators’ Remote ID and flight-path data from retention and disclosure beyond what
security requires;
4. Cap the UAFR lateral boundary at the applicant’s property line; and

5. Confirm that standard Part 89 Remote ID is sufficient, and keep Special UAFR designations
narrow.
III. BrightAI supports the rule’s security objective.
Protecting critical infrastructure from hostile or careless unmanned aircraft aligns with the interests of
BrightAI’s customers and with BrightAI’s own. BrightAI does not ask the FAA to weaken the restriction.
Our recommendations are directed solely at cleanly separating the operator a facility has hired to inspect
it from the unauthorized activity Section 2209 is meant to address.
IV. Section 74.250(a)(2) should expressly accommodate non-transitory operations conducted by or
for the facility owner.
Proposed § 74.250(a)(2) would require operations to transit a UAFR “in the shortest amount of time
practicable.” 91 FR 24676. That standard is appropriate for aircraft merely passing through restricted
airspace, but it does not fit the authorized inspection operations that critical-infrastructure owners depend
on. Infrastructure inspection is inherently non-transitory: an initial site survey requires a lengthy,
meandering flight across the entire facility to capture the imagery needed to build a complete digital twin,
and subsequent flights loiter and orbit over specific assets identified as needing closer inspection. The
FAA recognized this tension, asking whether the language of (a)(2) is “broad enough to enable both
legitimate transitory and non-transitory operations within a UAFR,” and citing “business applications of
the fixed site facility (e.g., infrastructure inspection)” as an example. 91 FR 24676. The FAA further
sought comment on “specific categories of operations that limitations should or should not apply to, and
any additional language FAA should consider” to strike that balance. Id. BrightAI recommends that the
FAA answer that question in the rule text by expressly providing that operations conducted by, or under
contract with, the operator or proprietor of the fixed site facility, over that facility, are not subject to the
shortest-practicable-transit limitation. Such operations already qualify as allowed operations under §
74.250(a)(3) and (c) when conducted under Part 107; what they require is an exception to (a)(2). BrightAI
proposes the following language: “(2) The unmanned aircraft transitions the UAFR in the shortest amount
of time practicable, except that this paragraph does not apply to an operation conducted by, or under
contract with, the operator or proprietor of the fixed site facility, over that fixed site facility, where notice
has been provided in accordance with § 74.255.” Where the facility owner has itself engaged the operator,
the security rationale for minimizing dwell time is absent, and the Remote ID and notification conditions
of § 74.250 already give the facility visibility into the operation. To the extent the FAA prefers to address
this as a discrete category rather than an exception, the recommendation is equally responsive to its
related request for comment on adding “other categories of allowed operations.” 91 FR 24677.
V. The Section 74.255 access-notification process should be an operator-level, standing whitelist.
Proposed § 74.255 would require an operator to notify the fixed site facility before operating in a UAFR.
For the recurring, programmatic inspection work that critical-infrastructure owners contract for, per-flight
notification does not scale. BrightAI supports the alternative the FAA describes—a one-time submission
of airman certificate and Remote ID serial numbers that populates a “whitelist” made available to fixed
site facilities—and asks the FAA to adopt it as the standard mechanism. 91 FR 24678. To be workable at
scale, the whitelist should be operator-level and recognized across standard UAFRs rather than requiring
separate registration at each facility, and it should support automated, machine-to-machine submission.
BrightAI further asks the FAA to ensure that, wherever access requires agency-specific authorization
rather than mere notification—most notably for Special UAFRs, which require the approval of both the

using agency and, where the operator is not the using agency, the Administrator (§ 74.251(a))—the
pathway for a facility’s own contracted operator is prompt and capable of being pre-established, including
through a standing approval under § 74.251(a)(2). A facility that petitions for a UAFR should not, as a
practical consequence, be unable to authorize the very operator it has engaged to inspect the site because
that operator faces a lengthy approval queue.
VI. The final rule should protect operators’ Remote ID and flight-path data.
Proposed §§ 74.56 and 74.255 will cause fixed site facilities—and, as the FAA notes, third-party security-
monitoring vendors that facilities may engage, since § 74.56 permits the required Remote ID sensing
capability to be met “either directly or through a contracted service”—to collect Remote ID and related
data on operations transiting a UAFR. For a commercial operator, that data reveals competitively
sensitive information: which facilities it serves, how often it flies, its routes, and its inspection
methodology. The FAA has asked whether it should impose a retention requirement for this data and, if
so, of what duration. 91 FR 24662. BrightAI recommends that the FAA (i) limit any retention to the
minimum necessary for the security purpose; (ii) prohibit the sale, licensing, or onward disclosure of
operator data collected under Part 74, except as necessary for a law-enforcement or security response; and
(iii) recognize an operator’s flight-path and operational-pattern data as confidential commercial
information. The FAA has already built this protection into Part 74 on the applicant side: it developed a
system through which UAFR applicants may submit “confidential business information and sensitive,
classified, or proprietary information” with appropriate protections. 91 FR 24661. BrightAI asks only that
an operator’s commercially sensitive data receive equivalent treatment. Absent such limits, a security-
motivated data-collection regime could become a channel through which competitors obtain and replicate
an operator’s proprietary flight paths.
VII. The UAFR lateral boundary should not extend beyond the applicant’s property line.
Proposed § 74.58(b) would require that a requested UAFR boundary not exceed the operator or
proprietor’s property boundary, and the FAA has asked whether the property line should be the maximum
perimeter of a UAFR in all cases or whether the boundary should be permitted to extend beyond it. 91 FR
24662–63. BrightAI urges the FAA to retain the property line as the outer limit. A UAFR confined to the
petitioner’s own property restricts the airspace over the asset the petitioner controls, which is the interest
Section 2209 protects. Extending a restriction beyond the property line would create buffer zones over
land the petitioner does not own and would foreclose lawful operations that never overfly the protected
facility. That consequence is especially acute for linear-corridor inspections—for example, imaging along
a right-of-way of utility poles or pipeline—where an operator flying the corridor may pass near, but not
over, a facility that has obtained a UAFR. The FAA has already stated that, in applying § 74.58(b), it
“will, where feasible, preserve low-risk flight corridors between adjacent facilities to support commercial
UAS routes and other NAS users.” 91 FR 24662. Capping the boundary at the property line preserves the
FAA’s security objective while avoiding an unnecessary and compounding restriction on operations over
adjacent parcels.
VIII. Standard Part 89 Remote ID is sufficient, and Special UAFR eligibility should remain
narrow.
Two further points concern proportionality. First, proposed § 74.250(a)(1) appropriately relies on Remote
ID broadcast under 14 CFR Part 89 to make operators conspicuous, and the FAA asks whether “more

stringent Remote ID broadcast requirements should be imposed on UAS operating within a UAFR
beyond the standard broadcast requirements outlined in 14 CFR part 89.” 91 FR 24662. BrightAI
recommends against a heightened standard. Modern commercial unmanned aircraft already broadcast
standard Remote ID by default under FAA-accepted Declarations of Compliance, and standard broadcast
Remote ID is sufficient to allow a facility to distinguish compliant from non-compliant operations. A
UAFR-specific broadcast mandate would impose equipage costs and could strand compliant fleets
without a commensurate security benefit. Second, the distinction between Standard and Special UAFRs
matters: because Special UAFRs bar operations absent affirmative permission (§§ 74.6, 74.251), and
because § 74.250(a)(4) limits the allowed-operations pathway to standard UAFRs only, a Special
designation does not merely add a permission step—it removes the allowed-operations pathway
altogether. A broad application of that category would sweep ordinary critical-infrastructure facilities into
a permission-gated regime and burden the routine authorized inspection those facilities need. BrightAI
asks the FAA to keep Special UAFR eligibility narrow and evidence-based—reserved for sites with a
demonstrated national-security or safety threat—and to require any such facility to maintain a workable
access pathway for its own authorized operators. 91 FR 24677.
IX. Conclusion
BrightAI appreciates the opportunity to comment and reiterates its support for the FAA’s implementation
of Section 2209 and the protection of critical infrastructure from unauthorized unmanned aircraft. The
recommendations above are intended to ensure that the final rule achieves that security objective while
preserving the authorized inspection operations that critical-infrastructure owners rely on. BrightAI would
welcome the opportunity to provide additional operational data or to assist the FAA—including through
the FAA’s UAS Innovation Zone and related initiatives—in developing a workable authorized-operator
access and whitelist model. Please contact the undersigned with any questions.
Respectfully submitted,
/Paul Leblond/

Vice President, Legal Counsel

July 31, 2026

Michelle Ferritto

RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558: Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to
a Fixed Site Facility
Dear Ms. Ferritto,
Rose Acre Farms, Inc., the second largest egg producer in the United States, appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) "Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility" published in the Federal Register on May 6, 2026, by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Rose
Acre Farms supports the NRPM which establishes a process for operators and proprietors of certain facilities to request and
maintain an unmanned aircraft flight restriction. Further, we believe that the NRPM represents an important step toward
protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening biosecurity, and safeguarding the nation's food supply while allowing for the
continued responsible use of unmanned aircraft systems.
Drones have become valuable tools for agriculture. Producers routinely use unmanned aircraft to monitor crops, inspect
infrastructure, assess livestock, and improve operational efficiency. However, like many emerging technologies, drones can
also be misused. As drone technology has become more affordable and accessible, animal rights activist organizations and
other groups have increasingly incorporated drones into campaigns targeting farms and food production facilities. These
operations often involve capturing aerial footage for so-called investigations, documentaries, media campaigns, or
coordinated activist efforts designed to generate public attention rather than provide complete context.
The concern extends well beyond privacy. Low-altitude drone activity around poultry operations can cause unnecessary
stress for animals, disrupt normal farm operations, and raise legitimate biosecurity concerns, just to name a few. Aircraft
moving between multiple agricultural sites have the potential to contribute to disease transmission risks if not operated
responsibly. During a time when the United States continues to face animal disease threats including Highly Pathogenic
Avian Influenza (HPAI), we believe that strengthening agricultural biosecurity and reducing unnecessary aerial activity
around sensitive livestock, poultry, and food facilities is a reasonable precaution.
Disruptions caused by unauthorized surveillance, repeated drone activity, or security incidents can have consequences that
extend beyond individual farms or food producing facilities and may negatively impact consumer confidence, supply
chains, and the resiliency and safety of the U.S. food system.
Further, the unauthorized use of unmanned aircraft could be used to unlawfully gain proprietary information on new
agricultural innovations or even target the safety of the food supply, from either domestic or foreign perpetrators. Providing
operators of eligible facilities with a clear process to request unmanned aircraft flight restrictions is a practical way to help
reduce these risks while preserving legitimate commercial, governmental, and authorized drone operations.
We have observed a growing use of drones alongside other activities such as surveillance, coordinated campaigns, and, in
1

some cases, trespassing. While the vast majority of drone operators act responsibly and lawfully, the increasing use of
drones by groups targeting agricultural operations underscores the need for a clear regulatory framework that enables
vulnerable facilities to request additional protections when justified.
For these reasons, Rose Acre Farms support the FAA's NPRM and encourage the Agency to expedite finalization.
Strengthening protections around eligible facilities will improve agricultural security, support biosecurity preparedness,
protect critical food production infrastructure, and reinforce the resilience of the nation's food system while maintaining
responsible access to the benefits of drone technology.
Thank you in advance for your consideration, and we are available to provide additional information if it would be helpful
to the Agency's efforts.
Respectfully submitted,
Joseph A. Miller
General Counsel
