comments.commenter: Comment from Academy of Model Aeronautics  (AMA)
comments.comment_text:
Public Comment on NPRM: Designation of Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (Part 74)
[Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03] RIN 2120-AL33
On behalf of the Academy of Model Aeronautics (AMA), representing 150,000 members and
approximately 2,400 chartered flying sites across the United States, we appreciate the
opportunity to provide comments on the Federal Aviation Administration’s Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding the designation of Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions
(UAFRs) under Part 74.
AMA recognizes and supports the importance of protecting sensitive facilities and critical
infrastructure from legitimate security threats. For decades, our organization has promoted safe,
responsible, and community based model aviation, with a strong emphasis on education, safety,
and compliance with federal requirements. Our members operate within visual line of sight and
often at established flying sites. These locations have a long history of safe and responsible
operations.
While we understand the statutory direction provided by Congress in 2016 under Section 2209,
we are concerned that, as currently proposed, this rule could have unintended consequences for
recreational and educational model aviation without a corresponding and clearly demonstrated
security benefit.
Scope and Definition of Critical Infrastructure
The proposed rule adopts an extremely broad definition of “critical infrastructure,”
encompassing 16 sectors that include a wide range of facilities with varying levels of risk. As
written, this approach could allow a substantial number of low-risk or widely distributed
facilities to qualify for airspace restrictions.
AMA recommends that the FAA adopt a more narrowly tailored, risk-based framework that
limits eligibility to facilities with clearly demonstrated, high-consequence security concerns. At a
minimum, the FAA should establish tiered criteria to differentiate between nationally significant
assets and lower-risk facilities.
Proliferation and Cumulative Impact of Restricted Airspace

The NPRM does not establish limits on the number, density, or cumulative impact of UAFRs.
While individual restrictions may appear reasonable in isolation, the aggregate effect could result
in a patchwork of overlapping restricted areas that significantly reduces available airspace,
particularly in urban and infrastructure-dense regions.
We urge the FAA to evaluate cumulative and regional impacts as part of the approval process
and to ensure that the national airspace system remains usable for lawful recreational and
educational activities.
Size, Altitude, and Duration of Restrictions
The proposal does not define clear limits on lateral boundaries or altitude ceilings, nor does it
sufficiently constrain the use of continuous, year-round restrictions. This creates the potential for
overly broad and permanent limitations that extend well beyond what is necessary to address
specific risks.
AMA recommends that the FAA require all restrictions to be narrowly tailored in size and
altitude, based on objective risk criteria, and that continuous restrictions be limited to the
highest-risk scenarios and subject to mandatory periodic review and sunset provisions.
Demonstration of Need
The proposed “demonstration of need” standard lacks specificity and does not require applicants
to provide evidence of a credible or documented unmanned aircraft threat. Without a clearly
defined threshold, there is a risk that approvals could become routine rather than exceptional.
We recommend that the FAA require applicants to demonstrate a specific, credible threat and to
show that existing legal authorities and security measures are insufficient to address that threat.
Impact on Existing Recreational Flying Sites
The NPRM does not address the impact of UAFRs on existing, established recreational flying
sites, including AMA chartered clubs that have operated safely for decades. The absence of any
grandfathering provision or required impact assessment raises significant concerns that
longstanding community-based sites could be displaced without consideration.
AMA strongly urges the FAA to include protections for existing flying sites, including required
consultation with affected stakeholders, impact analysis, and mechanisms to preserve access
where safe operations can continue.
Access and Operational Flexibility
While the rule references “allowed operations” within restricted areas, it does not provide a clear,
practical pathway for recreational or educational users to obtain authorization. Without a defined
and accessible process, these provisions may offer little meaningful relief.

We recommend that the FAA establish clear, streamlined procedures for access, including the
ability to grant standing authorizations for recognized community-based organizations such as
AMA clubs. Additionally, consideration should be given to allowing facility representatives to
coordinate access for known, low-risk users where appropriate.
Transparency and Awareness
To ensure compliance, it is critical that all UAFRs be easily discoverable and integrated into
existing FAA tools and platforms. Without real-time, accessible information, even well-
intentioned operators may inadvertently violate restricted airspace.
AMA recommends that all restrictions be published in a centralized, publicly accessible, and
machine-readable format, with integration into widely used applications such as LAANC and
B4UFLY.
Consistency with Congressional Intent
Congress, through Section 2209, directed the FAA to create a process for evaluating and
approving restrictions on a case-by-case basis. Importantly, Congress has not mandated blanket
restrictions for any category of facilities, including correctional institutions, despite ongoing
security concerns.
The proposed rule should remain consistent with this intent by ensuring that restrictions are
targeted, justified, and limited, rather than broadly applied in a manner that unnecessarily
impacts lawful users of the national airspace system.
Conclusion
AMA respectfully requests that the FAA revise the proposed rule to incorporate stronger
safeguards, clearer standards, and meaningful protections for recreational and educational model
aviation. Our community has a long history of safe operation and serves as an important pipeline
for aviation education, innovation, and workforce development.
We stand ready to work collaboratively with the FAA to ensure that security objectives are met
without unnecessarily restricting access to the national airspace system for responsible users.
Thank you for your consideration.
Respectfully,
Tyler Dobbs
Executive Director
Academy of Model Aeronautics

comments.comment_text:
Comments of the Outdoor Amusement Business Association
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close
Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
The Outdoor Amusement Business Association (OABA) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments
regarding the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) establishing a
process for the designation of Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) around eligible fixed site
facilities.
The OABA is the national trade association representing the owners and operators of traveling carnivals,
mobile amusement providers, games, concessions, and related businesses that operate at thousands of
county fairs, state fairs, festivals, and community celebrations across the United States. Every year, OABA
members safely entertain tens of millions of Americans while partnering with fairgrounds, municipalities,
agricultural societies, and community organizations.
Protecting Fairgrounds and the Public
The OABA strongly supports the FAA's efforts to provide operators of critical facilities with an avenue to
request restrictions on unauthorized drone operations when necessary to protect people and property.
We encourage the FAA to recognize that fairgrounds hosting large public events present many of the
same safety concerns that justify additional protections.
Modern fairs routinely attract crowds numbering in the tens of thousands of people. Within a relatively
compact footprint, these venues include:
• Large amusement rides with significant vertical structures;
• Temporary electrical distribution systems;
• Fuel storage and generators;
• Livestock exhibits;
• Food preparation areas;
• Outdoor concerts and grandstand entertainment;
• Fireworks displays and other special events; and
• Densely populated pedestrian areas.
An unauthorized drone operating over these activities presents obvious safety risks. Even a small
unmanned aircraft can become a dangerous projectile if it collides with a ride, loses power over a crowd,
interferes with emergency operations, or is intentionally used to disrupt an event.
Many fairs serve as the largest annual gathering within their communities. Some state fairs attract
attendance comparable to major professional sporting events. Unlike permanent stadiums, however, fairs

frequently operate in open environments with numerous temporary structures and extensive public
access, creating unique vulnerabilities to unlawful drone activity.
Fairgrounds Should Be Eligible Facilities
The OABA encourages the FAA to clarify that fairgrounds hosting large public events may qualify for UAFR
consideration when operators can demonstrate the necessary statutory criteria.
While fairgrounds may not operate continuously throughout the year, many serve as permanent facilities
that regularly host events involving substantial public attendance. During fair operations, these locations
present elevated risks to public safety that warrant consideration alongside other eligible facilities.
We recommend that FAA provide guidance recognizing that temporary or seasonal events held at
established fairgrounds may justify time-limited UAFRs when supported by documented public safety
concerns.
Flexibility for Temporary Events
Because fairs and festivals operate on scheduled dates throughout the year, the OABA encourages the
FAA to ensure that the application process allows for temporary or event-specific flight restrictions rather
than requiring year-round designations.
A flexible process would allow operators to seek protection only during periods when large public
gatherings are occurring, minimizing unnecessary impacts on legitimate unmanned aircraft operations
while maximizing public safety.
Authorized Operations
The OABA also supports the FAA's proposal to allow appropriate authorized operations within designated
UAFRs, including emergency response, law enforcement, and other approved governmental activities.
Many fairs work closely with local police, fire departments, emergency management agencies, and public
safety officials. These agencies increasingly rely on drones for emergency response, search and rescue,
crowd management, and incident assessment. The final rule should continue to preserve these important
public safety missions.
Balancing Innovation and Safety
OABA recognizes the tremendous economic and technological benefits provided by the commercial
unmanned aircraft industry. Responsible drone operations play an important role in infrastructure
inspection, photography, agriculture, emergency response, and numerous commercial applications.

Accordingly, OABA supports an approach that carefully balances these legitimate uses with the need to
protect large public gatherings from unauthorized or reckless operations. We believe the proposed UAFR
process provides an appropriate framework for achieving that balance, provided that event venues such
as fairgrounds have a meaningful opportunity to seek protection when warranted.
Conclusion
The Outdoor Amusement Business Association appreciates the FAA's work implementing Section 2209 of
the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act.
As the FAA moves toward a final rule, OABA respectfully requests that the Agency:
1. Recognize that fairgrounds hosting large public events present significant public safety concerns
deserving consideration under the UAFR process.
2. Clarify that permanent fairgrounds conducting seasonal events may qualify for event-specific
UAFRs when statutory criteria are met.
3. Establish a flexible application process that accommodates temporary events rather than
requiring year-round restrictions.
4. Preserve appropriate exemptions for emergency responders, law enforcement, and other
authorized governmental operations.
5. Continue balancing the interests of responsible commercial UAS operators with the paramount
need to protect large public gatherings.
America's fairs are cherished community institutions that safely welcome millions of visitors each year.
Providing fair operators with an effective mechanism to address unlawful drone activity will strengthen
public safety.
We appreciate the opportunity to comment and looks forward to continuing to work with the FAA as this
rulemaking progresses.
Sincerely,
Greg Chiecko, President
Outdoor Amusement Business Associa`on
1305 Memorial Avenue
West Springfield MA 01089-3578

comments.commenter: Comment from American Public Transportation Association
comments.comment_text:
August 3, 2026
The Honorable Bryan Bedford
Administrator
Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue SW
Washington, DC 20591
Docket Operations
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Room W58–213, West Building 5th Floor
Washington, DC 20590–0001
Re: FAA NPRM (Docket No. 2026-4558) Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close
Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
Dear Administrator Bedford:
The American Public Transportation Association (APTA) represents the $102 billion public transportation industry
that directly employs more than 450,000 people and supports millions of private-sector jobs. APTA supports the
Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) commitment to establishing a process for operators and proprietors of
certain fixed site facilities to request and maintain an unmanned aircraft flight restriction (UAFR). APTA and public
transportation agencies have a long history of successful partnership and collaboration with the U.S. Department of
Transportation, and we look forward to continuing this important work together.
Safety is the public transportation industry’s highest priority, including for bus and passenger rail operators. The
employees who manage and operate public transportation systems are committed to strengthening the safety of their
systems, passengers, colleagues, and the public. On behalf of our members, APTA appreciates the opportunity to
respond to the FAA’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, “Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft
in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,” published in the Federal Register at 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 on May 6, 2026
(UAFR NPRM). APTA is pleased to offer the following comments on the UAFR NPRM.
Definition of Qualifying Hub
APTA believes that the definition of intermodal passenger transportation hubs is too restrictive as the definition of a
hub is a facility that serves multiple modes (i.e., ferries, commuter rail, heavy rail transit, Amtrak, intracity buses,
and intercity buses). APTA also suggests adding passenger ridership as a category to allow hubs that meet a specific
volume threshold to qualify regardless of the number of services it provides.

DOT Docket Operations
August 3, 2026
Page 2
As the FAA notes in the UAFR NPRM, the mass transit and passenger rail subsector systems include buses, heavy
rail (subways), light rail, commuter rail, and monorail systems. These systems manage billions of passenger trips
annually and are considered vulnerable due to high passenger volume and open access environments. Facilities
serving multiple transportation modes (such as bus, rail, and ferry connections) are considered high-value sites.
These surface transportation hubs qualify for targeted airspace restrictions due to their importance and risk exposure.
Additional Considerations for Special Events, Accidents, and Incidents
Rail infrastructure is extensive and critical to national coordination and defense. While the FAA rejected broad
airspace restrictions along entire rail corridors to avoid disrupting transit access and efficiency, APTA strongly
encourages FAA to consider restricting the operation of unmanned aircraft during special events with high transit
usage, accidents, and incidents.
Twenty-six public transit agencies in 11 U.S. host cities have expanded service, strengthened safety and security,
upgraded infrastructure, and coordinated operations to move millions of fans, workers, and visitors during the 2026
Federation International Football Association (FIFA) World Cup. While APTA understands that FAA must balance
the need to protect transportation infrastructure with maintaining the efficient movement of people, events like the
FIFA World Cup, and future mega-events like the Olympics in Los Angeles and in Salt Lake City are about more
than just moving people – they also include the need to secure critical infrastructure. The December 2025 Federal
Communications Commission (FCC) National Security Determination explicitly identifies World Cup and Olympic
venues as potential targets for Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) enabled surveillance. Security measures like
perimeter fences, magnetometers, and bag checks are rendered irrelevant by an airborne threat, and the rapid
proliferation and technological maturation of UAS has fundamentally transformed the threat landscape for public
safety and event security. Accordingly, FAA must ensure that public transportation agencies have the ability to
request a UAFR for these events.
Moreover, for accidents, the potential for impacts on life safety activities alone should serve as justification for
clearing airspace during an accident. A UAS hovering over an accident scene could interfere with operational
activities and distract and endanger first responders. Furthermore, for threat incidents, the concern of UAS-enabled
attack scenarios and UAS-enabled surveillance is a safety and security concern. Protecting sensitive critical
infrastructure locations from UAS incursion is crucial for national security and public safety. The threats to mass
transit from a UAS that could deliver explosive payloads to crowded stations, disperse chemical or biological
agents, conduct a cyber-attack, perform physical sabotage of critical rail infrastructure, and/or coordinated
GPS/communication jamming, suggest focus should be extended to owners and operators that convey a safety or
security risks when applying for an UAFR.
Expanded Criteria
APTA recommends that FAA consider revising the criteria allowing transportation operators to apply for a UAFR.
FAA’s proposed regulations would require the applicant to identify the lateral boundaries for the requested UAFR,
and that the requested UAFR boundary not exceed the operator or proprietor’s property boundary.1 However, there
1 See 91 Fed. Reg. 24622, 24685 (May 6, 2026).

DOT Docket Operations
August 3, 2026
Page 3
are certain circumstances when the FAA should expand the lateral boundaries beyond the property line. There may
be conditions where expanding airspace restrictions beyond physical property boundaries is critical to mitigating
risks to a facility. Transit agencies would need to demonstrate the need that a facility is specifically vulnerable to
UAS exploitation.
Large open-air intercity, commuter, and mass transit railyards should be eligible for consideration for UAFR
because UAS malfunctions or intentional sabotage could damage critical rail infrastructure. Such damage could
significantly disrupt transit operations. A malfunctioning UAS over catenary-powered mass transit tracks could also
create major service disruptions, especially along the Northeast Corridor. The FAA should also consider areas
around tunnel entrances that serve intercity, commuter, or mass transit train traffic, where UAS-related damage to
critical rail infrastructure at or inside an entrance could severely disrupt service.
Conclusion
APTA supports the expansion of the certification requirements and criteria applicable to the mass transit and
passenger rail subsector for restricting the operation of unmanned aircraft. Public transportation owners and
operators should have the ability to apply for a UAFR based on credible safety or security threats or conditions.
APTA encourages the FAA to provide a practical process for requesting both permanent and temporary UAFRs,
reflect on the unique safety and security concerns and threats associated with the mass transit and passenger rail
subsector and permit reasonable restrictions established by risk assessments, available intelligence, operational
requirements, and facility footprint.
APTA appreciates the opportunity to comment on this UAFR NPRM. If finalized, these UAFR procedures will
greatly assist the public transportation sector’s ability to address the increase in UAS operators, and the concomitant
threat posed by the proliferation of unregulated UAS. APTA looks forward to assisting FAA in decisions on any
proposed changes protecting critical infrastructure. If you have questions regarding topics discussed in this letter,
please contact Polly Hanson, Senior Director of Security, Risk and Emergency Management at (703) 505-2523) or
phanson@apta.com, or contact Taria Barron, General Counsel, at (202) 496-4808 or tbarron@apta.com. Thank you
for your consideration. We look forward to continuing to work with FAA to improve transportation safety and
security.
Sincerely,
Paul P. Skoutelas
President and CEO

I am a certificated remote pilot, and this proposed rule is a betrayal of everything Part 107 was built to do. It does not "restrict operations near fixed sites." It guts the one thing that made lawful commercial drone flight possible in this country: a single, national, knowable rulebook. Withdraw it.

**Part 107's entire purpose was to kill the patchwork. This rule resurrects it.** Before 107, flying commercially meant chasing exemptions and guessing at a map no one could see. Part 107 ended that chaos with one federal standard: meet the rules, and the airspace is open to you, with LAANC and the UAS Facility Maps telling you in advance where you stand. This proposal takes a sledgehammer to that. It hands the operators of "fixed site facilities" — across **sixteen** critical-infrastructure sectors — a mechanism to carve their own private no-fly bubbles out of the National Airspace System, one filing at a time, forever. That is not a rule. It is a machine for manufacturing an endless, decentralized patchwork drawn by whoever files paperwork, not by anyone with aviation-safety expertise. It is the pre-107 world in a new suit.

**You cannot comply with a map that never stops changing.** The most basic duty of any airspace rule is that a pilot can know, before takeoff, whether a flight is legal. This proposal makes that impossible. UAFRs are petition-driven and rolling, so a route that is legal today is a violation next week because a facility owner filed a request. Sixteen sectors — energy, water, comms, transportation, data centers, corrections, chemical, finance — is not a narrow carve-out. It is most of the built environment, woven through every city and corridor in America. And where is the operator supposed to look? Unless every UAFR is instantly and freely pushed into LAANC and the Facility Maps, this rule turns routine flight planning into a legal minefield and dumps the burden of an incomplete dataset onto the pilot. A rule you cannot look up is not a regulation. It is a trap.

**The transit ban is the tell, and it is indefensible.** Buried in the FAA's own request for data is the real payload: operators may not even be allowed to *transit* these zones. This is not about hovering over a site or photographing it. It is whether a lawful pilot flying Point A to Point B may pass *through* the airspace above at all. If transit is banned, every UAFR stops being a bubble and becomes a wall. Stack enough walls across a metro area and the airspace is sliced into disconnected islands no commercial operator can legally cross. Delivery, inspection, agriculture, mapping, public-safety, real estate — the entire lawful Part 107 economy depends on being able to *get somewhere*. A no-transit regime doesn't regulate that economy. It strangles it. That the FAA is only now asking what this costs operators is a stunning admission it proposed the rule without understanding what it does to the people who fly under it.

**"Security" is not a blank check.** Genuine threats already have tools: Part 99, TFRs, Section 2209's own statutory limits, and existing national-security authorities. The rot here is breadth and delegation. When the triggers are as vast as "aviation safety, protection of people and property, national security, or homeland security," and you hand that trigger to private facility owners across sixteen sectors, the exception devours the rule. Every owner thinks their site is critical. Let each act on that belief, one filing at a time, and you don't get a security framework — you get the sky closed by attrition.

**What the FAA must do:**

1. **Protect transit.** Lawful through-flight over a UAFR must be the default. A no-transit regime is disqualifying — strike it.
2. **One real-time source of truth.** Every UAFR must be published, machine-readable, and live in LAANC and the Facility Maps *before* it takes effect, with zero legal exposure for operators relying on those tools in good faith.
3. **Real limits on eligibility.** Owners must prove specific, credible risk existing authorities don't already cover — not recite one of four sweeping justifications.
4. **Cap the geometry and total footprint.** Bound each zone's size and analyze the *cumulative* effect of overlapping UAFRs on ordinary operations — not each request in a vacuum.
5. **Finish the economics first.** You concede you lack transit-cost data. This rule cannot be finalized until that record exists and is open for comment.

Part 107 was a promise: play by one clear set of rules and the sky is open to you. This proposal breaks it — trading a knowable national standard for a private-actor patchwork no honest operator can navigate, and flirting with a transit ban that would sever the airspace itself. This is not a refinement of Part 107. It is its unraveling. Reject it.
-

Comments of the International Association of Fairs and Expositions, Inc.
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close
Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
The International Association of Fairs and Expositions, Inc (IAFE) appreciates the opportunity to submit
comments regarding the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)
establishing a process for the designation of Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) around
eligible fixed site facilities.
The IAFE is the international trade association representing the agricultural fair industry, In addition to
the more than 2500 county and state fairs in the US, we also represent the traveling carnivals, mobile
amusement providers, games, concessions, and related businesses that make fairs part of the fabric of
America. Every year, IAFE members safely entertain tens of millions of Americans year-round.
Protecting Fairgrounds and the Public
The IAFE strongly supports the FAA's efforts to provide operators of critical facilities with an avenue to
request restrictions on unauthorized drone operations when necessary to protect people and property.
We encourage the FAA to recognize that fairgrounds hosting large public events present many of the
same safety concerns that justify additional protections.
Modern fairs routinely attract crowds ranging from a few thousand to hudreds of thousands of people
daily. Within a relatively compact footprint, these venues include:
• Large amusement rides with significant vertical structures;
• Temporary electrical distribution systems;
• Fuel storage and generators;
• Livestock exhibits;
• Food preparation areas;
• Outdoor concerts and grandstand entertainment;
• Fireworks displays and other special events; and
• Densely populated pedestrian areas.
An unauthorized drone operating over these activities presents obvious safety risks. Even a small,
unmanned aircraft can become a dangerous projectile if it collides with a ride, loses power over a crowd,
interferes with emergency operations, or is intentionally used to disrupt an event.

Many fairs serve as the largest annual gathering within their communities. Some state fairs attract
attendance that exceed that of major professional sporting events. Unlike permanent stadiums,
however, fairs frequently operate in open environments with numerous temporary structures and
extensive public access, creating unique vulnerabilities to unlawful drone activity.
Fairgrounds Should Be Eligible Facilities
The IAFE encourages the FAA to clarify that fairgrounds hosting large public events may qualify for UAFR
consideration when operators can demonstrate the necessary statutory criteria.
A recent study showed that 68% of the US population attends an event at a fairground during the year.
While some fairgrounds may not operate continuously throughout the year, many serve as permanent
facilities that regularly host events involving substantial public attendance. During fair operations, these
locations present elevated risks to public safety that warrant consideration alongside other eligible
facilities.
We recommend that FAA provide guidance recognizing that temporary or seasonal events held at
established fairgrounds may justify time-limited UAFRs when supported by documented public safety
concerns.
Flexibility for Temporary Events
Because fairs and festivals operate on scheduled dates throughout the year, the IAFE encourages the
FAA to ensure that the application process allows for temporary or event-specific flight restrictions
rather than requiring year-round designations.
A flexible process would allow operators to seek protection only during periods when large public
gatherings are occurring, minimizing unnecessary impacts on legitimate unmanned aircraft operations
while maximizing public safety.
Authorized Operations
The IAFE also supports the FAA's proposal to allow appropriate authorized operations within designated
UAFRs, including emergency response, law enforcement, and other approved governmental activities.
Fairs work closely with local police, fire departments, emergency management agencies, and public
safety officials. These agencies increasingly rely on drones for emergency response, search and rescue,
crowd management, and incident assessment. The final rule should continue to preserve these
important public safety missions.

Balancing Innovation and Safety
IAFE recognizes the tremendous economic and technological benefits provided by the commercial
unmanned aircraft industry. Responsible drone operations play an important role in infrastructure
inspection, photography, agriculture, emergency response, and numerous commercial applications.
Accordingly, IAFE supports an approach that carefully balances these legitimate uses with the need to
protect large public gatherings from unauthorized or reckless operations. We believe the proposed
UAFR process provides an appropriate framework for achieving that balance, if event venues such as
fairgrounds have a meaningful opportunity to seek protection when warranted.
Conclusion
The International Association of Fairs and Expositions, Inc. appreciates the FAA's work implementing
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act.
As the FAA moves toward a final rule, IAFE respectfully requests that the Agency:
1. Recognize that fairgrounds hosting large public events present significant public safety concerns
deserving consideration under the UAFR process.
2. Clarify that permanent fairgrounds conducting seasonal events may qualify for event-specific
UAFRs when statutory criteria are met.
3. Establish a flexible application process that accommodates temporary events rather than
requiring year-round restrictions.
4. Preserve appropriate exemptions for emergency responders, law enforcement, and other
authorized governmental operations.
5. Continue balancing the interests of responsible commercial UAS operators with the paramount
need to protect large public gatherings.
America's fairs are cherished community institutions that safely welcome millions of visitors each year.
Providing fair operators with an effective mechanism to address unlawful drone activity will strengthen
public safety.
We appreciate the opportunity to comment and look forward to continuing to work with the FAA as this
rulemaking progresses.
David Grindle
President/CEO

August 2, 2026
Submitted via www.regulations.gov
U.S. Department of Transportation
Docket Operations
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Room W58-213, West Building, 5th Floor
Washington, DC 20590
Re: Comments in Response to FAA Section 2209 NPRM: Designation - Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility [Docket

To whom it may concern:
GPA Midstream Association1 (GPA Midstream or the Association) appreciates the opportunity to
comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking implementing
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016.2
GPA Midstream members operate critical energy infrastructure that supports the regional, national,
and global movement of natural gas, propane, butane, ethane, and other natural gas liquids. The
infrastructure operated by our members is essential to U.S. energy security, economic growth, and
manufacturing competitiveness. Unauthorized unmanned aircraft system (UAS) operations near
critical infrastructure can create safety, security, operational, and emergency response concerns in
the complex industrial environments where our members operate. It is critical to prevent
unauthorized UAS activity, but not all UAS activity should be prohibited. Where GPA Midstream
members use UAS for safe and effective operational purposes, those activities should remain
permissible.
GPA Midstream especially requests FAA revisit the criteria for the natural gas subsector within
the energy sector. We respectfully recommend that FAA revise that eligibility criteria to allow
1 GPA Midstream has served the U.S. energy industry since 1921 and represents approximately 45 domestic corporate
members that directly employ 57,000 employees engaged in the gathering, transporting, processing, treating, storage,
and marketing of natural gas, natural gas liquids, crude oil and refined products, commonly referred to as “midstream
activities.” The work of our members indirectly creates or impacts an additional 470,000 jobs across the U.S. economy.
In 2024, GPA Midstream members had an economic impact of $191 billion through operating 502,900 miles of gas
gathering pipelines, gathering more than 91 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas, and operating more than 342
natural gas processing facilities that delivered pipeline quality gas into markets across a majority of the U.S. interstate

consideration of facility-specific risk factors, rather than relying solely on a fixed threshold. There
may be a need for a facility that processes less than 500 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d) of
natural gas to be granted a Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (UAFR). FAA could look to other
government agencies for guidance on what is a critical facility. For instance, the Transportation
Security Administration (TSA) has criteria to determine critical facilities. Lower-throughput
facilities may still be critical—for example, because of location, interconnectivity, product
handled, proximity to populated areas, or role in regional energy reliability.
GPA Midstream also urges FAA to provide clear protections for any facility-specific information
submitted as part of the UAFR application or review process. While FAA may need certain
information, such information may include sensitive operational or commercial details. FAA
should ensure that any submitted information is appropriately protected.
We strongly support the FAA's efforts to implement Section 2209 and establish a practical
framework for protecting qualifying fixed-site critical infrastructure from unsafe or unauthorized
UAS operations. A well-designed UAFR program will improve awareness among UAS operators
and provide greater clarity regarding protected airspace. The FAA has an important opportunity to
implement Section 2209 in a manner that strengthens protection of critical infrastructure while
preserving safe and lawful UAS operations within the National Airspace System. The final rule
should strike an appropriate balance among security, aviation safety, operational practicality, and
continued innovation.
GPA Midstream also supports and commends the comments submitted by the American Fuel &
Petrochemical Manufacturers (AFPM) and respectfully encourages the FAA to carefully consider
the recommendations and perspectives outlined in their filing.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments.
Sincerely,
Stuart Saulters

Tulsa, Oklahoma 74135

To: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), submitted through the Federal
Register
From: LTC Robert Thompson, Program Manager, sUAS Detection Program
(Operation Desert Guardian), Arizona National Guard, Arizona Department of
Emergency and Military Affairs
Subject: Public Comment on the FAA Proposed Rule: Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility (FAA Docket No.
FAA–2026–4558)
Introduction
My name is LTC Robert Thompson, and I serve as the Program Manager for the Arizona
National Guard's sUAS Detection Program, operating under the Arizona Governor’s
Operation Desert Guardian (ODG) Task Force. Our program provides specialized counter-
UAS (C-UAS) support to state and local law enforcement (LEA) partners to counter the use
of drones by Transnational Criminal Organizations (TCOs). As a practitioner responsible for
implementing airspace security measures "on the ground," I submit these comments to
highlight the operational impacts and unintended security risks created by the FAA's
proposed rules restricting UAS operations near critical infrastructure.
Background: The Problem the Regulation Fails to Address
The FAA's proposed rules aims to create Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs)
over critical infrastructure. While we support this goal, the rule is built on two flawed
assumptions: (1) that malicious actors will comply with flight restrictions, and (2) that the
burden of enforcement should fall solely on the facility owner. Our operational experience
shows that TCOs and other adversaries routinely use modified, custom-built "dark drones"
that ignore geofencing and do not broadcast the required Remote ID signals. This
regulation, as written, creates a "paper shield" that stops compliant hobbyists but does
nothing to deter criminal actors.
Analysis of Negative Impacts & Recommendations
Based on our analysis, we have identified three major flaws in the proposed rule that will
negatively impact public safety and national security. We offer concrete recommendations
to remedy these issues.
• Impact 1: The Enforcement Gap (A Paper Rule Needs Sensors)
• Analysis: The proposed rule correctly notes that a UAFR’s primary benefit is
that “compliant operators would avoid the designated airspace” (Page
24651, para. B). However, it fails to create a viable enforcement mechanism

for non-compliant operators. While facilities are required to install Remote ID
sensors (§ 74.56), there is no mechanism to share that data with law
enforcement for real-time interdiction. This directly conflicts with the intent
of Arizona state law ARS 13-3729, which makes it a felony to loiter over a
critical facility in the furtherance of a criminal offense but requires law
enforcement to have the situational awareness to act.
• Recommendation: The FAA must require or strongly encourage facilities
granted a UAFR to integrate their sensor data feeds into state or regional law
enforcement Common Operating Pictures (COPs). This would create a
network of sensors that provides actionable intelligence to officers on the
ground, turning the UAFR from a passive boundary into an active,
electronically monitored tripwire.
• Impact 2: The National Security & OPSEC Threat of Foreign Geofencing
• Analysis: The proposed rule creates two significant security vulnerabilities for
law enforcement. First, as noted by the Arizona Department of Homeland
Security, the application process itself requires facilities to submit highly
sensitive vulnerability assessments, which could then become public record
(Page 24652, para. D). This appears to directly conflict with the principles of
the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII) Program, which is
designed to prevent the public exposure of voluntarily shared security data.
Second, by forcing LEAs that use foreign-made drones to request geofence
unlocks from the manufacturer, the rule would compel the transfer of
tactical law enforcement flight plans and critical infrastructure locations to
foreign corporate servers, creating an unacceptable counter-intelligence
risk.
• Recommendation: To resolve both the flight restrictions and the
administrative burdens, the FAA must mandate a "State-Managed, Federally
Mandated" public safety registry. Under this model:
Physical Flight Bypass: The FAA must require all drone manufacturers
o
to support a standardized digital "bypass key" to override geofencing
software. Crucially, the authority to issue and administer these keys
must be delegated directly to a designated state-level entity, such as
the State's Homeland Security or Emergency Management agency.

Tactical Whitelisting: Public safety agencies will pre-register their
o
drones' Remote ID signatures into this state-managed registry. When
a whitelisted agency drone enters a UAFR during an emergency, the
system will automatically recognize it as a friendly asset, bypassing all
notification requirements and allowing for seamless, real-time
tactical transit without compromising operational security to federal
or foreign databases.
• Impact 3: The "Unknown/Dark Drone" Threat
• Analysis: The rule heavily relies on the assumption that operators will
broadcast Remote ID. TCOs and malicious actors routinely disable Remote
ID, rendering them invisible to the systems mandated by this rule.
• Recommendation: The FAA must explicitly clarify that facilities granted
UAFRs are legally permitted to deploy advanced detection systems beyond
simple Remote ID receivers. This includes, but is not limited to, passive RF
detection systems and active radar systems necessary to detect non-
compliant, "dark drones," provided the operation of such systems is
coordinated with appropriate state and federal authorities.
Conclusion
Arizona is on the front lines of combating sophisticated criminal actors, foreign, and

enforcement officers tasked with securing our communities.

comments.commenter: Comment from City of Chesapeake Public Utilities
comments.comment_text:
To Whom It May Concern:

The City of Chesapeake (the “City”) submits these comments in strong support of the Federal Aviation Administration’s (“FAA”) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking titled “Designation – Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,” published on May 6, 2026. This action would, in part, implement Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016, by establishing a process for operators and proprietors of certain fixed site facilities to request and maintain an unmanned aircraft flight restriction. This rule is necessary and important.
The proposed rule specifically seeks comments on the following topics to inform the development of the criteria for the water and wastewater systems sector, and accordingly, the City offers the following comments:

1.What types of drinking water and wastewater systems should be considered in development of gating criteria?
The City proposes that public-serving systems permitted through the health department, or similar state-level authorities, should be considered in the development of gating criteria. Although it is unclear how narrowly the FAA intends to define “drinking water and wastewater systems,” the size of the facility is certainly relevant. The category should certainly include water treatment plants, wastewater treatment plants, and raw water impoundments that are sources for water treatment plants within a specified distance of certain intake structures. Larger point targets/facilities should also be considered for inclusion in this category, such as water storage tanks (both elevated and ground storage).

2.What are the characteristics of drinking water and wastewater systems that should be considered in development of gating criteria?
Public-serving systems, specifically ones that serve: (1) critical infrastructure facilities (serving power plants or other critical infrastructure per the national definition); (2) national defense essential facilities (military bases, etc.); (3) continuity of government facilities (legislative buildings, key government buildings, etc.); and (4) key public health facilities, should be included in the definition of “drinking water and wastewater systems” as contemplated in the rule.
3.Should population served by a drinking water or wastewater system be considered in development of gating criteria, and if so, what are appropriate population thresholds?
Regardless of population size, a water treatment plant is life-essential to the community it serves and should be treated as such in the development of gating criteria.

4.Should critical customers served by a drinking water or wastewater system be considered in development of gating criteria?
Yes, referencing the characteristics emphasized in response to #2 above.

5.Should a history of unauthorized drone flight over a drinking water or wastewater system be considered in development of gating criteria?

No, the history of unauthorized drone flight over a drinking water or wastewater system should not be considered in the development of gating criteria. The threat of unauthorized drone flight is evolving so quickly that history is not a reliable indicator of future incidents. Instead, past unauthorized drone flights should be used as a template for potential future incursions in other locations.

Thank you for this opportunity to provide comments on this important rulemaking.

Respectfully submitted,

Michael Stites
Director of Public Utilities
City of Chesapeake, Virginia

comments.commenter: Comment from City of Houston, Houston Airport System
comments.comment_text: Comments of the Houston Airport System

The intention of the proposed rule makes sense, but the execution favors the applicant greatly over other UAS operators. Without rebalancing the concerns of facilities against the legitimate commercial drone operators, and the worker safety benefits provided by drones, this will create a real economic hardship and expose US workers to hazards needlessly.
My concerns stem from the experience I have had with existing flight restrictions. I have had my commercial operation held up by multiple long duration and large area TFRs. I use drones to get photographs of billboard ads, and inspect billboard structures. Drones allow me to do this from the safety of the ground. One June 17 of this year there were so many 3+ square mile, and 30+ day TFRs that my ability to do this was severely impacted. This was made worse because the TFRs were clustered in the busier parts of metro Nashville, TN where I needed to work. When I did reach out to gain access to work in the TFRs, I was informed that I had to pick each location, date, and time in advance. As a drone operator, that makes it very difficult to react to weather, new customer opportunities, or an issue on the billboard quickly.
It is with this background that I express the following concerns about this ruling greatly favoring the applicant, and not the rest of the UAS operators.
1.The 16 critical infrastructure sectors cover nearly every facility imaginable: chemical; commercial facilities; communications; critical manufacturing; dams; defense industrial base; emergency services; energy; financial services; food and agriculture; government services and facilities; healthcare and public health; information technology; nuclear reactors, materials, and waste; transportation systems; and water and wastewater. While there is a second requirement of being critical infrastructure, that definition is also very broad. Critical Infrastructure is defined as “systems and assets, whether physical or virtual, so vital to the United States that the incapacity or destruction of such systems and assets would have a debilitating effect on security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or any combination of those matters.”
2.The 30-day comment public comment period requires many busy people to be constantly monitoring proposed UAFRs in their area in order to voice their concern about a UAFR before it is ruled on.
3.There is an appeal process for if an application is rejected, but there is no appeal process for UAS operators to appeal an application that was granted.
4.The 2 leading cause of DEATH in the workplace in the USA was falls, slips, and trips in 2024. Section G discusses the cost of this proposal being an anticipated $21 million to $31 million. The authors of the proposal have not considered the level of safety drone operations provide to workers. I don’t see any references to OSHA, NATE, or ANSI, standards or input.
Recent drone attacks against Wildberries, a major online retailer commonly described as Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, demonstrate how commercial warehouses can become drone targets and be characterized as economically or strategically important. Under the proposal’s qualitative standards, an Amazon fulfillment center could plausibly argue that it is part of a nationally important logistics system, is vulnerable to UAS attack, and that its disruption would affect regional commerce or downstream customers. Whether that argument succeeds would depend substantially on FAA discretion rather than a clear quantitative threshold.
Based on the proposed ruling, it is possible an Amazon warehouse could get a UAFR for their entire property where a billboard is also located. If I, the impacted UAS operator, did not monitor proposed UAFR publication list in the 30 days before the UAFR was issued, I would have no ability to request that application be reviewed. If that billboard then needed to be inspected, I would not be able to conduct this inspection using a drone in that location. Instead, I would need to physically climb onto the structure, where this is a real danger from falling.
I request that the following additions to this regulation be considered:
1.Establish objective and quantitative eligibility criteria.
2.Provide geographic and automated notice of proposed UAFRs.
3.Create an administrative review process for substantially affected UAS operators.
4.Permit recurring or standing access for verified commercial operations.
5.Consider the occupational-safety consequences of displacing drone inspections with work at height.
6.Include commercial UAS costs and lost opportunities in its economic analysis.
7.Require applicants and FAA to consider less restrictive alternatives before restricting lawful operations.

utilities the ability to request appropriate UAS flight restrictions represents a proactive
and necessary enhancement to the security and resilience of the nation's critical
infrastructure.
The City of Henderson respectfully provides the following responses to the FAA’s
questions regarding the Water Sector.
Water Sector – Question 1
What types of drinking water and wastewater systems should be considered in
development of gating criteria?
The FAA should prioritize facilities whose disruption would have the greatest impact
on public health, environmental protection, and continuity of essential services.
Recommended priority includes:
1. Wastewater Treatment Plants
2. Drinking Water Reservoirs
3. Water and Wastewater Pump Stations
4. Water Booster Stations
5. Wastewater Lift Stations
These facilities perform critical operational functions and, in many cases, represent
key nodes whose disruption could affect large portions of the community.
Water Sector – Question 2
What are the characteristics of drinking water and wastewater systems that
should be considered in development of gating criteria?
Eligibility should be based on operational risk rather than facility size alone. Important
considerations include:
• Presence of single points of failure that could significantly disrupt water or
wastewater operations.
• Storage or use of hazardous chemicals, including treatment chemicals that
could pose risks if intentionally targeted.
• Potential consequences of service interruption, including impacts to drinking
water quality, wastewater treatment, environmental compliance, and public
health.
• Geographic service area and the number of interconnected facilities
dependent upon the asset.
• Importance of the facility to overall system resilience and emergency response
capability.
2

Facilities possessing one or more of these characteristics warrant additional
protection from unauthorized UAS operations.
Water Sector – Question 3
Should population served by a drinking water or wastewater system be
considered in development of gating criteria, and if so, what are appropriate
population thresholds?
Yes. Population served should be a significant factor in determining eligibility; however, it
should not be the sole determining criterion.
The City of Henderson serves a population of more than 350,000 residents, and that number
continues to grow. While larger populations naturally increase the consequences of service
disruptions, the FAA should avoid relying exclusively on fixed numerical thresholds. Instead,
consideration should be given to the percentage of a community's population served,
recognizing that infrastructure serving a smaller jurisdiction may be equally vital to that
community.
The FAA should also consider the unique geographic realities of the Desert Southwest. Water
infrastructure in arid regions represents a true community lifeline because there are few, if
any, practical alternatives when service is interrupted. Extended disruptions can rapidly affect
public health, firefighting capability, healthcare operations, sanitation, economic activity, and
overall community resilience. Unlike regions with abundant natural water resources,
communities in Southern Nevada rely almost entirely on engineered water treatment,
storage, and distribution systems to sustain daily life.
Population criteria should therefore be evaluated alongside the presence of critical
customers and community demographics, including:
• Hospitals and healthcare facilities
• Emergency medical services
• Fire and law enforcement agencies
• Emergency Operations Centers
• Schools and educational facilities
• Other Critical Infrastructure and Key Resources (CIKR)
• Communities with limited system redundancy or alternative water supplies
A comprehensive, risk-based methodology that evaluates both the number of people
affected and the consequences of service interruption will provide a more effective and
equitable framework for determining eligibility for UAS flight restrictions.
3

Water Sector – Question 4
Should critical customers served by a drinking water or wastewater system be
considered in development of gating criteria?
Yes.
Protection of facilities serving critical customers should be a primary consideration.
Systems supporting National Critical Functions and community lifeline sectors should
receive priority consideration.
Examples include:
• Healthcare facilities
• Emergency response agencies
• Public safety communications
• Government continuity facilities
• Military installations
• Energy infrastructure
• Transportation infrastructure
• Public health agencies
Interruptions affecting these customers have cascading impacts that extend well
beyond the utility itself.
Water Sector – Question 5
Should a history of unauthorized drone flight over a drinking water or
wastewater system be considered in development of gating criteria?
Yes.
Documented unauthorized drone activity should be recognized as an indicator of
elevated risk and vulnerability. Repeated or suspicious UAS operations may
demonstrate surveillance, reconnaissance, or attempts to identify vulnerabilities for
future malicious activity.
While the absence of documented incidents should not preclude a facility from
eligibility, a documented history of unauthorized UAS activity should strengthen the
justification for approving a flight restriction request.
4

Conclusion
The City of Henderson Department of Utility Services and Department of Emergency
Management support the FAA’s efforts to establish a process that allows water and
wastewater utilities to request unmanned aircraft flight restrictions over critical
infrastructure. We encourage the FAA to adopt flexible, risk-based gating criteria that
consider operational criticality, public health impacts, hazardous materials,
infrastructure interdependencies, critical customers, and documented threat activity
rather than relying solely on facility size or population served.
Protecting essential water and wastewater infrastructure from unauthorized UAS
activity strengthens community resilience, safeguards public health, and supports
national critical infrastructure security objectives.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments and for considering the
perspectives of municipal water and wastewater utilities as the FAA develops this
important program.
Respectfully,
Priscilla Howell, Director
City of Henderson
Department of Utility Services
Ryan Turner, Director
City of Henderson
Department of Emergency Management
5

3 August 2026
