Re: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking – Designation to Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed-Site Facility
Dear Sir or Madam:
Asylon Incorporated ("Asylon") appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments in
response to the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
(NPRM), Designation to Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to
a Fixed-Site Facility (Docket No. FAA-2026-4558).
Asylon commends the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for developing a thoughtful
proposal that recognizes the need to protect critical infrastructure while continuing to
enable legitimate commercial unmanned aircraft system (UAS) operations. Compared to
previous UAS rulemakings, this proposal reflects a practical and balanced approach that
acknowledges both the evolving security environment and the growing role of
professional commercial UAS operators in supporting critical infrastructure, public safety,
and national security.
Asylon supports the FAA's overall objective of establishing a framework that protects
sensitive facilities from unauthorized drone activity while preserving access for trusted,
authorized operators performing legitimate operational missions. Asylon's comments are
directed primarily toward implementation of Standard Unmanned Aircraft Flight
Restrictions (UAFRs), which we expect will accommodate the majority of recurring
commercial security operations conducted on behalf of facility owners and operators. As
implementation proceeds, however, we believe several targeted clarifications would
improve the rule's effectiveness while avoiding unintended impacts on these recurring
commercial security operations.
Redefining the standard for Automated Physical Security through the use of Humans, Robots, and AI. www.AsylonRobotics.com

About Asylon
Founded in 2015, Asylon is a U.S.-based robotics and automated physical operations
company providing, among other services, persistent aerial and ground security solutions
for commercial, industrial, and government customers. Asylon integrates automated
unmanned aircraft systems, robotic ground platforms, and remote operations capabilities
to provide recurring security patrols, incident response, perimeter protection, and
infrastructure monitoring.
Unlike many commercial drone operations that involve one-time inspections or point-to-
point flights, Asylon's operational model is centered on recurring, facility-authorized
automated operations conducted on behalf of infrastructure owners and operators.
These include scheduled security patrols, launch-on-alarm response missions, incident
verification, and persistent overwatch of critical infrastructure facilities. To date, Asylon
has conducted more than 400,000 aerial- and ground-based missions in support of our
commercial and government clients across the United States. Similarly, Asylon has
extensive experience collaborating with the FAA in the UAS Integration Pilot Program
(IPP) and BEYOND program and holds nine Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) waivers
for a variety of complex operations.
Because of this operational experience, Asylon believes it is uniquely positioned to
provide practical recommendations regarding implementation of Section 2209 as it
applies to trusted commercial operators conducting recurring security missions.
Overall, Asylon supports the proposed rule and believes it represents an important step
toward protecting critical infrastructure while enabling responsible commercial UAS
operations. The recommendations below are intended to improve implementation of the
rule for recurring authorized operations without changing their underlying objectives.
General Support
Asylon supports the FAA's recognition that protecting critical infrastructure requires a
balanced approach that deters unauthorized operations while continuing to
accommodate legitimate commercial activities performed on behalf of facility owners and
operators.
In particular, Asylon supports the proposal's emphasis on:
 Protecting designated critical infrastructure facilities from unauthorized UAS
operations;
 Recognizing the importance of authorized commercial operations supporting
facility owners;
 Encouraging layered security concepts;
 Incorporating Remote ID as an operational tool; and
 Establishing a national framework rather than relying on inconsistent local
approaches.
Asylon believes these concepts provide an appropriate foundation for future
implementation and can improve both aviation safety and infrastructure security.
Redefining the standard for Automated Physical Security through the use of Humans, Robots, and AI. www.AsylonRobotics.com

However, successful implementation will depend on ensuring that recurring commercial
security operations are accommodated through practical authorization processes that
recognize the unique nature of persistent automated operations.
Recommendation 1 – Explicitly Accommodate Persistent, Facility-Authorized Security
Operations
Asylon respectfully recommends that the FAA clarify how recurring, facility-authorized
security operations are intended to be accommodated within Standard UAFRs.
The NPRM appropriately recognizes that certain UAS operations may be authorized
within designated UAFRs. However, portions of the proposed regulatory text appear
written primarily with transient operations in mind - such as inspections, overflights, or
one-time missions that enter and exit a restricted area in the "shortest amount of time
practicable."
While this approach may be appropriate for many commercial operations, it does not fully
reflect the operational characteristics of persistent automated security missions.
Asylon's operations routinely include scheduled perimeter patrols, launch-on-alarm
response missions, incident verification, recurring dock-based deployments, and
temporary loitering over areas of interest at the direction of the facility owner or operator.
These missions are intentionally designed to maintain an ongoing presence within the
protected facility rather than simply transit through it.
Accordingly, Asylon recommends that the FAA clarify in the final rule or associated
implementation guidance that recurring, facility-authorized security operations, including
persistent automated patrols, are fully consistent with the intent of Section 2209 when
conducted with the approval of the affected facility.
Asylon recommends that the FAA expressly recognize facility-authorized recurring
security operations as a category of authorized recurring operations within Standard
UAFRs. Such operations should include recurring perimeter patrols, dock-based
automated security operations, launch-on-alarm response, incident verification, and
temporary loitering or overwatch conducted in support of facility security.
Providing this clarification in either the regulatory text or accompanying implementation
guidance would eliminate uncertainty for operators whose missions are intentionally
designed to remain within the protected area rather than simply transit through it.
The Advisory Circular should also clarify that these recurring operations are not subject
to the expectation that authorized aircraft merely transit a UAFR in the "shortest amount
of time practicable," as persistent security operations are intentionally designed to
remain within the protected area while performing the facility owner's authorized mission.
These clarifications would provide certainty for both facility owners and trusted
commercial operators while preserving the FAA's broader security objectives.
Redefining the standard for Automated Physical Security through the use of Humans, Robots, and AI. www.AsylonRobotics.com

Recommendation 2 – Allow Standing Authorizations for Recurring Commercial
Operations
Asylon recommends that the FAA expressly allow standing operational authorizations for
recurring commercial UAS operations conducted on behalf of facility owners.
Many automated security operations occur on predictable schedules or under long-term
service agreements. Requiring repetitive notifications or recurring operational approvals
for each individual flight would create unnecessary administrative burdens without
providing a corresponding safety or security benefit.
For example, an automated security provider conducting scheduled perimeter patrols
multiple times each day at the same facility should not be required to repeatedly
coordinate identical operations when those operations have already been approved by
the facility owner.
The final rule should therefore provide sufficient flexibility for facility operators to
authorize recurring commercial UAS activities through standing approvals or other long-
term authorization mechanisms, while maintaining appropriate oversight and
accountability.
This approach would improve operational efficiency, reduce unnecessary administrative
burden, and better support scalable commercial security operations.
Recommendation 3 – Support Digital Authorization and Automated Recognition of
Trusted Operators
Asylon supports the FAA's emphasis on Remote ID as an important component of
infrastructure protection and airspace awareness.
As implementation moves forward, Asylon encourages the FAA to consider mechanisms
that enable facility operators to efficiently distinguish trusted, authorized commercial
operators from unauthorized aircraft. This capability should reduce operational friction
for authorized operators while allowing facility personnel and security operators to focus
attention on unidentified or unauthorized aircraft.
Future implementation should support digital authorization methods that allow recurring
operators approved by a facility owner to be recognized efficiently through standardized,
machine-readable processes rather than relying solely on manual coordination or case-
by-case verification.
Such an approach would improve operational efficiency while supporting the FAA's
broader objectives of enhancing security, improving situational awareness, and
facilitating compliance.
Importantly, these mechanisms should remain flexible enough to evolve alongside future
UAS Traffic Management (UTM) capabilities, Remote ID technologies, and other digital
aviation services.
Redefining the standard for Automated Physical Security through the use of Humans, Robots, and AI. www.AsylonRobotics.com

Recommendation 4 – Maintain Compatibility with Future Scalable BVLOS Operations
Although this rulemaking appropriately focuses on Section 2209 implementation, Asylon
encourages the FAA to ensure that the final rule remains compatible with future
regulatory frameworks supporting scalable BVLOS operations.
Persistent automated security operations increasingly rely on remote operations centers,
dock-based aircraft, recurring patrol missions, and other operational concepts that are
expected to become more common as BVLOS regulations continue to evolve.
Accordingly, implementation of Section 2209 should avoid unintentionally creating
procedural barriers that could limit future deployment of trusted commercial automated
systems operating under subsequent FAA regulatory frameworks.
Maintaining compatibility between Section 2209 implementation and future BVLOS
regulations will help ensure that infrastructure operators can continue adopting advanced
automation technologies while maintaining appropriate levels of safety, security, and
regulatory oversight.
Recommendation 5 – Develop Clear Implementation Guidance
Asylon encourages the FAA to publish comprehensive implementation guidance
concurrent with, or as soon as practicable following, publication of the final rule.
While the proposed regulation appropriately establishes the legal framework for UAFRs,
additional implementation guidance will be essential to promote consistent application
across facility owners, commercial operators, and FAA personnel.
Asylon recommends that the guidance address topics including:
 Recurring facility-authorized operations;
 Standing operational authorizations;
 Notification expectations for recurring commercial activities;
 Digital authorization processes and operator recognition;
 Remote ID monitoring considerations;
 Application of the "shortest amount of time practicable" standard for authorized
operations conducted entirely within a UAFR;
 Timely publication of UAFRs through FAA-approved flight planning, situational
awareness, and other digital aeronautical information services used by
commercial UAS operators; and
 Recommended operational best practices for facility owners and authorized UAS
operators.
Providing clear implementation guidance will promote consistent national application of
the rule, reduce unnecessary administrative burden, and improve both infrastructure
security and operational compliance.
Redefining the standard for Automated Physical Security through the use of Humans, Robots, and AI. www.AsylonRobotics.com

Conclusion
Asylon appreciates the FAA's efforts to implement Section 2209 in a manner that
enhances protection of critical infrastructure while recognizing the continued growth and
maturation of the commercial UAS industry.
The proposed rule represents an important step toward establishing a national framework
that addresses unauthorized drone activity while preserving the ability of trusted
commercial operators to safely and effectively perform legitimate missions on behalf of
facility owners and operators.
Asylon believes the recommendations outlined in these comments would further
strengthen the final rule by providing additional clarity for recurring automated security
operations, improving administrative efficiency for both operators and facility owners,
and supporting the continued evolution of scalable commercial UAS operations.
Asylon respectfully encourages the FAA to ensure that implementation of the final rule
remains flexible enough to accommodate emerging operational concepts, future BVLOS
regulatory frameworks, and evolving digital authorization capabilities. As automated
systems become increasingly integrated into critical infrastructure protection, regulatory
clarity and operational consistency will be essential to achieving the objectives of Section
2209.
Finally, Asylon encourages the FAA to continue engaging industry stakeholders
throughout implementation of the final rule and development of associated guidance.
Collaboration between government and experienced commercial operators will help
ensure the regulation achieves its intended security objectives while supporting
innovation and the safe integration of advanced UAS operations into the National
Airspace System. Asylon stands ready to support the FAA as it develops implementation
guidance and operational best practices for trusted commercial operators conducting
recurring security missions within designated UAFRs.
Asylon appreciates the opportunity to comment on this important rulemaking and looks
forward to continued collaboration with the FAA.
Respectfully submitted,
Brent McLaughlin
Co-Founder and COO
Asylon Incorporated
Redefining the standard for Automated Physical Security through the use of Humans, Robots, and AI. www.AsylonRobotics.com

The FAA lacks a legal justification for allowing facilities in the food and agriculture sector to obtain flight restrictions. There are no known cases of drones injuring people or property in this sector, while drone footage supports public accountability by documenting pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, and animal-treatment concerns, which are all very important things for the general public to be able to find information about.
I am writing to urge the FAA to allow drones to fly over agricultural property.  Transparency in agriculture is important.   I care very much about this.

Why hold the shade closed when so much pain is going on the other side? Let us be able to continue to show the public the cruelty going on behind closed doors.

Speak for those who cannot.

I oppose allowing the food and agriculture sector to obtain flight restrictions that could hide pollution affecting soil and other public concerns. The FAA has identified no national-security, economic, public-health, or safety justification, and no known cases of drones injuring people or property in this sector.

I strongly oppose pressure to allow the food and agriculture sector to obtain UAFRs. The FAA has not shown a safety or security justification, making this unnecessary and there is a significant cost. Drone footage supports accountability for pollution, biohazards, and animal-treatment concerns and gives government agencies the ability to enforce the laws and regulations voters support.

Historical evidence does not show drone risks in the food and agriculture sector. Drone footage supports public accountability by documenting pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, and animal-treatment concerns. The FAA should not grant flight restrictions to this sector.

Public engagement requires transparency, not new flight restrictions for the food and agriculture sector. The FAA has not shown a national-security, economic, public-health, or safety justification for UAFRs. Drone footage can document pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims, strengthening public accountability.

I oppose allowing the food and agriculture sector to harvest Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions without a demonstrated safety, security, economic, or public-health justification. Drone footage supports accountability by documenting pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, and animal-treatment concerns, and this measure is a blatant attempt to reduce corporate accountability.

The court should reject UAFRs for the food and agriculture sector. The FAA has shown no safety or security justification, while drone footage documents pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, and animal-treatment concerns.

The importance of drone footage for public accountability weighs against flight restrictions in the food and agriculture sector. The FAA has identified no demonstrated safety, security, health, or economic justification for limiting this documentation.

The FAA should keep the food and agriculture sector open to public accountability and reject UAFRs. There is no demonstrated safety or security risk, while drone footage can expose pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, and animal-treatment concerns.

There is no documented national-security, economic, public-health, or safety justification for allowing the food and agriculture sector to obtain unmanned aircraft flight restrictions. Drone footage supports public accountability by documenting pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims. The FAA should not grant these restrictions.

The FAA should disclose any demonstrated safety, security, economic, or public-health justification before allowing the food and agriculture sector to seek UAFRs. Drone footage supports accountability by documenting pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims.

I urge you not to adopt this proposed restriction. Restrictions on unmanned aircraft could limit transparency, accountability, and the ability of the public, journalists, researchers, and advocates to document matters of legitimate public concern. Drones are an important tool for capturing evidence of environmental issues, unsafe conditions, and potential animal welfare violations that may otherwise go unseen.

Restrictions should not prevent responsible individuals from using technology to document and bring attention to issues that impact the public interest. Maintaining the ability to conduct lawful aerial documentation is essential for accountability and ensuring that wrongdoing does not remain hidden.

Additionally, restrictions on unmanned aircraft can unintentionally affect hobbyists, photographers, surveyors, search-and-rescue volunteers, and small businesses that use drones responsibly and in compliance with existing FAA regulations.

I encourage policymakers to focus on targeted enforcement against misuse rather than creating broad restrictions that impact responsible operators.

As a citizen, I oppose allowing the food and agriculture sector to obtain unmanned aircraft flight restrictions. The FAA has shown no safety, security, economic, or public-health justification or sector-specific drone risk. Drone footage supports accountability by documenting pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims.
What are these fixed site facilities so concerned about the public seeing?

The public deserves accountability in the food and agriculture sector, not expanded flight restrictions that shield facilities from scrutiny. The FAA has identified no national-security, economic, public-health, or safety justification for these restrictions. Drone footage can document pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims.

I oppose the inclusion of the Food and Agriculture sector (§ 74.90) amongst the critical infrastructure facilities that could obtain Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).

The proposal highlights safety concerns (e.g. “protection of people and property on the ground”) as the key factor in considering requests for UAFRs. However, there is no documented evidence of drones at agricultural facilities threatening the safety or security of animals, workers, or farm equipment. To the contrary, recent drone footage at factory farms has revealed workers abusing animals (e.g. calves being kicked at Agresti Calf Ranch), illegal calf hutches with inadequate space (e.g. at Grimmius Cattle Company, in violation of California Penal Code 597t), and dead piles that violate environmental law and present a hazard to public health (e.g. at Vera Goat Dairy). Drones do not present safety concerns at these facilities; they expose them.

It is only because of drones that the public can see the reality of these factory farms, which can otherwise operate out of sight and free from accountability when they violate the law. I urge you not to shield these facilities from public scrutiny – please exclude the Food and Agriculture sector from receiving UAFRs.

comments.comment_text:
August 3, 2026
Submitted electronically at Regulations.gov

Michelle Ferritto

Office of Rule Making

Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue, SW
Washington, DC 30591

RE: Designation: Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility

Dear Ms. Ferritto:

The Pacific Egg & Poultry Association (PEPA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) notice of proposed rulemaking “Designation —
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”
published in the Federal Register on May 6", 2026.

PEPA supports the FAA’s proposal to establish a process for operators and proprietors of
certain fixed site facilities to request an unmanned aircraft flight restriction (UAFR). We
also support the proposed criteria requiring applicants to demonstrate that a UAFR is
necessary for aviation safety, protection of people and property on the ground, national
security or homeland security, while allowing authorized operation within the restricted
area.

For more than 100 years PEPA has represented poultry farmers throughout the western
United States. Our members operate both production and processing facilities, which play
a vital role in the nation’s domestic food supply. Protecting these facilities from disease
introduction is one of our industry’s highest priorities.

The poultry industry has experienced several devastating disease outbreaks over the years
including exotic Newcastle Disease, and most recently Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza.
These events have resulted in significant economic losses, disruptions to food production,
and increased costs for producers and consumers alike. In response, the industry has
worked closely with local, state, and federal partners to develop and implement rigorous
biosecurity measures to prevent, detect, control and eradicate poultry diseases.

Despite these efforts, the increasing use of drones presents an emerging challenge to
agriculture biosecurity. Unauthorized drone activity over poultry facilities can compromise
farm security, disrupt operations, and create concerns regarding the inadvertent or
intentional introduction of disease agents. In addition, drones equipped with sophisticated
imaging technology can identify and map production facilities, increasing the vulnerability
of critical agricultural infrastructure.

America’s poultry farms are an essential component of the nation’s food security. The
ability to protect these facilities from unnecessary risks is critical to maintaining a stable,
secure domestic egg and poultry supply. Providing facility owners with a practical
mechanism to request flight restrictions where justified would be an important step in
reducing unnecessary risks while balancing the legitimate uses of unmanned aircraft.

PEPA respectfully encourages the FAA to ensure that commercial poultry production and
processing facilities are eligible to seek UAFRs when they can demonstrate that restrictions
are necessary to protect public safety, critical food infrastructure, and agricultural
biosecurity. We also encourage the FAA to coordinate with the U.S. Department of
Agriculture and state animal health officials when evaluating requests involving livestock
and poultry facilities to ensure that biosecurity consideration receive appropriate weight.

We appreciate the FAA’s consideration of these comments and its efforts to protect critical
infrastructure. We look forward to continuing to work with the FAA and our federal and
state partners to strengthen the security and resilience of the nation’s poultry industry.

Sincerely,

ON

Debra J. dock

Executive Director
Pacific Egg & Poultry Association

COMMENTS OF AX ENTERPRIZE, LLC
Docket No. FAA-2025-1908
Designation of UAS Facility Restrictions Under Section 2209
Comments on Volume II of the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
Executive Summary
AX Enterprize appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) implementing Section 2209 through the establishment
of UAS Facility Restrictions (UAFRs).
AX supports the proposed rule. The NPRM establishes a balanced framework for protecting
eligible fixed-site facilities while preserving the FAA's responsibility to ensure the safety and
efficiency of the National Airspace System (NAS).
These comments focus on implementation. In most cases, AX recommends clarification through
the preamble or Draft Advisory Circular rather than changes to the proposed regulatory text. This
approach preserves regulatory flexibility while improving consistency and long-term
administration of the program.
General Comments
AX Enterprize appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on this Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking.
AX develops and integrates technologies supporting air domain awareness, unmanned traffic
management, and Remote ID implementation. AX also operates the New York UAS Test Site on
behalf of Oneida County, one of the FAA-designated UAS Test Sites. These comments are
informed by operational experience supporting integration of unmanned aircraft into the National
Airspace System.
AX supports implementation of Section 2209 and agrees that qualifying facilities should have
access to a structured process for requesting protection from unauthorized UAS operations. AX
also agrees with the FAA's approach of balancing facility protection with the Agency's broader
statutory responsibilities, including aviation safety, efficient use of the National Airspace
System, and the public right of transit.

Accordingly, AX limits its comments to areas where clarification would improve implementation
or long-term administration of the program. These comments are organized in the same sequence
as Volume II of the NPRM to facilitate review.
PART 74 – PROPOSED REGULATORY
TEXT
Comment R-1 – §74.205 Eligibility
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation
Clarify in the preamble that eligibility to submit a petition does not create an expectation that a
UAFR will be approved.
Rationale
The proposed eligibility criteria appropriately identify who may petition under Section 2209.
Clarifying that eligibility and approval are separate determinations reinforces that each petition
will be evaluated on its individual merits using the criteria established in the final rule.
Recommended FAA Action
Clarify in the Preamble.
Comment R-2 – §74.210 Petition Requirements
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation
Encourage petitioners to demonstrate why the requested lateral and vertical dimensions represent
the minimum practical airspace necessary to achieve the intended security objective.
Rationale
A proportionality statement will improve petition quality and promote nationally consistent
evaluations while preserving FAA discretion. Because implementation practices may evolve, this
recommendation is better addressed through guidance than through additional regulatory text.
Recommended FAA Action

Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment R-3 – §74.215 FAA Evaluation
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation
Provide representative examples illustrating application of the petition evaluation criteria.
Rationale
Representative examples will improve consistency among reviewers and applicants while
preserving the flexibility necessary to evaluate each petition based on its individual
circumstances.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment R-4 – §74.220 FAA Determination
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation
No changes recommended.
Rationale
The proposed determination process appropriately preserves FAA discretion while providing a
structured framework for approving, modifying, or denying petitions.
Recommended FAA Action
Retain as proposed.
Comment R-5 – §74.225 Renewal, Amendment, and
Revocation
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation

Clarify that renewal requests should demonstrate that the operational need continues to exist and
that the approved UAFR remains appropriately tailored.
Rationale
Periodic reassessment helps ensure that restrictions remain proportional as facilities, surrounding
operations, and security considerations evolve.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment R-6 – §74.230 Publication of UAFRs
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation
Publish approved UAFRs in standardized, machine-readable digital formats in addition to
existing aeronautical publications.
Rationale
Standardized digital publication improves interoperability with flight planning tools, UTM
services, and other aviation systems while reducing implementation costs and transcription
errors.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment R-7 – §74.250 Authorized Operations
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation
Provide implementation guidance describing representative authorization processes for recurring
governmental and public safety operations.
Rationale
Illustrative guidance will promote nationally consistent implementation while preserving
flexibility for differing operational environments.

Recommended FAA Action
Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment R-8 – §74.255 Emergency Operations
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation
No regulatory changes recommended.
Rationale
The proposed approach appropriately preserves operational flexibility for emergency response
activities. Representative coordination examples would assist implementation without limiting
FAA discretion.
Recommended FAA Action
Retain as proposed. Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment R-9 – §74.260 Modification or Termination
AX Position: Support.
Recommendation
No regulatory changes recommended.
Rationale
The proposed authority to modify or terminate UAFRs provides the flexibility necessary to
respond to changing operational conditions while preserving efficient use of the National
Airspace System.
Recommended FAA Action
Retain as proposed.
Comments on Specific FAA Requests for
Comment

Comment RFC-1
Eligible Sectors
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests comment on its proposal to limit UAFRs to eligible fixed-site facilities within the
sixteen critical infrastructure sectors and requests information on additional sectors, eligibility
criteria, vulnerabilities, and the potential number of eligible facilities.
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Retain the proposed approach of limiting eligibility to facilities within the sixteen nationally
recognized critical infrastructure sectors.
Rationale
The proposed approach appropriately aligns Section 2209 with the nationally established critical
infrastructure framework while preserving consistency across Federal agencies. Expanding
eligibility beyond the identified sectors at this stage would substantially increase administrative
complexity, increase the number of petitions, and create greater impacts on the National
Airspace System (NAS). If additional sectors are considered in the future, the FAA should
establish objective, nationally applicable eligibility criteria through subsequent rulemaking rather
than case-by-case interpretation.
Recommended FAA Action
Retain as proposed.
Comment RFC-2
Sector Eligibility Criteria
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests comment regarding the minimum criteria that should apply within eligible sectors
and the basis for those criteria.
AX Position
Support.

Recommendation
Retain a performance-based eligibility framework centered on demonstrated operational risk
rather than facility category alone.
Rationale
Eligibility should continue to depend upon the applicant's ability to demonstrate that unmanned
aircraft present a credible aviation safety, public safety, national security, or homeland security
concern. Facility ownership or industry classification alone should not establish eligibility. A
performance-based approach provides the FAA flexibility to evaluate differing operational
environments while maintaining nationally consistent standards.
Recommended FAA Action
Retain as proposed.
Comment RFC-3
Facility Vulnerability Assessment
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests information describing facility-specific vulnerabilities, the consequences if those
vulnerabilities were exploited, and how a UAFR would reduce those risks.
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Encourage applicants to submit risk-based analyses that clearly connect identified vulnerabilities
to the requested UAFR dimensions.
Rationale
The effectiveness of a UAFR depends on demonstrating a logical relationship between the
identified threat, the protected asset, and the requested airspace restriction. Documentation
should emphasize operational consequences rather than speculative threats and should explain
why the requested dimensions are the minimum practical airspace necessary to achieve the
intended security objective.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand the Advisory Circular.

Comment RFC-4
Number of Eligible Facilities
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests information concerning the number of facilities that may satisfy the proposed
eligibility criteria.
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Continue evaluating program scalability using the number of facilities reasonably expected to
satisfy both the statutory eligibility requirements and the proposed performance-based criteria.
Rationale
The number of facilities within a critical infrastructure sector does not necessarily represent the
number of likely applicants. The FAA's workload should be estimated using facilities that both
satisfy the eligibility criteria and can demonstrate the operational need required under Part 74.
Recommended FAA Action
Clarify in the PRIA.
Comment RFC-5
Additional Allowed Operations
AX Position
Support – Clarification Requested.
Recommendation
Expand the categories of allowed operations to include additional FAA-authorized commercial
operations that demonstrate an equivalent level of safety, security, and operational
accountability.
Rationale

As new operational rules such as Part 108 are implemented, additional trusted commercial
operators will routinely perform missions supporting critical infrastructure, emergency
management, public safety, and commercial logistics. Eligibility should be based on
demonstrated safety oversight and operational accountability rather than solely on the applicable
operating rule.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-6
Establishing Operator Trust
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Adopt a performance-based trust model that relies upon existing FAA certification, Remote ID
compliance, and applicable security vetting rather than creating new approval processes
whenever possible.
Rationale
Existing FAA certification frameworks already provide significant operational accountability.
Building upon those systems reduces administrative burden while supporting consistent
implementation across government and commercial operators.
Recommended FAA Action
Clarify in the Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-7
Technological Requirements
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation

Maintain technology-neutral performance requirements.
Rationale
The regulation should define the operational outcome rather than prescribe specific technologies.
This approach encourages innovation while allowing Remote ID, future network-based
identification services, and other emerging capabilities to satisfy equivalent performance
objectives.
Recommended FAA Action
Retain performance-based implementation.
Comment RFC-8
Economic Effects
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Evaluate cumulative operational impacts on commercial UAS operators where multiple UAFRs
exist within a metropolitan area or transportation corridor.
Rationale
Individual UAFRs may have limited operational impact; however, multiple adjacent restrictions
could significantly affect infrastructure inspection, utility operations, emergency response,
surveying, and future BVLOS services. Evaluating cumulative impacts will produce a more
representative assessment of long-term economic effects.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand the PRIA.
Comment RFC-9
Remote ID Sensing Capability (§74.56)
FAA Request for Comment

FAA requests comment on whether requiring Remote ID sensing capability is sufficient, whether
additional minimum performance standards are necessary, and whether additional Remote ID
sensing requirements should be established.
AX Position
Support with clarification.
Recommendation
Retain the requirement for Remote ID sensing while adopting performance-based sensing
requirements rather than prescribing specific hardware or sensing architectures.
Discussion
AX strongly supports requiring facilities requesting a UAFR to maintain the capability to receive
FAA-compliant Remote ID broadcasts. This establishes a minimum level of airspace awareness
while remaining achievable for a broad range of critical infrastructure operators.
However, the regulation should avoid specifying particular receiver technologies, sensor types,
communications architectures, or deployment models.
Instead, FAA should establish measurable performance objectives, including:
• Reliable detection of compliant Part 89 broadcasts throughout the protected area.
• Time synchronization sufficient for operational awareness.
• Integration capability with enterprise security systems.
• Logging sufficient for operational review.
• Ability to distinguish compliant and non-compliant aircraft.
This allows future innovation while avoiding premature technology lock-in.
Recommended FAA Action
Clarify in Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-10
More Stringent Remote ID Requirements
FAA Request for Comment
FAA asks whether additional Remote ID broadcast requirements should be imposed for
operations inside a UAFR and requests empirical information regarding current Remote ID
performance.

AX Position
Support with significant modification.
Recommendation
FAA should avoid requiring additional broadcast messages that reveal more information than
already required under Part 89.
Instead, FAA should improve authentication while preserving operator privacy.
Discussion
Current Remote ID successfully establishes aircraft conspicuity.
The primary remaining challenge is not visibility—it is trust.
Additional broadcast information that exposes operator identity, aircraft ownership, mission
purpose, or persistent identifiers increases operational security risks while providing limited
additional value to facility operators.
Instead, FAA should encourage:
• cryptographic authentication,
• message integrity,
• trusted identity verification,
• privacy-preserving identifiers,
• authenticated authorization services.
This approach aligns with future standards under ASTM and DRIP while protecting legitimate
commercial operators.
Recommended FAA Action
Modify proposal.
Comment RFC-11
Single Session Remote ID
AX Recommendation
FAA should specifically permit authenticated Single Session Remote IDs for trusted operations.
Discussion

AX recommends that FAA recognize authenticated Single Session IDs as an acceptable means of
satisfying identification requirements.
Single Session IDs provide:
• operational accountability;
• law enforcement attribution;
• protection against long-term operator tracking;
• protection of operator location;
• reduced stalking risk;
• reduced commercial intelligence gathering;
• preservation of mission confidentiality.
Identity resolution should occur only through authorized government services rather than public
broadcasts.
This preserves the balance between public safety and operational security.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-12
Data Retention Requirements
FAA Request for Comment
FAA seeks comment regarding whether Remote ID sensing data should be retained and, if so, for
what duration.
AX Position
Support limited retention.
Recommendation
FAA should establish a flexible, risk-based retention period rather than a universal requirement.
Discussion
Mandatory long-term retention creates:
• cybersecurity risk,
• storage expense,

• privacy concerns,
• unnecessary administrative burden.
Routine compliant operations generally provide little continuing investigative value.
Instead:
• normal operations should be retained for a limited period;
• incidents may be retained longer;
• operators should remain free to retain records voluntarily if operationally necessary.
FAA should avoid creating a nationwide repository of routine aircraft movement information.
Recommended FAA Action
Modify proposal.
Comment RFC-13
Notification Requirements
FAA Request for Comment
FAA seeks comment regarding notification requirements before operating within a UAFR.
AX Position
Support modernization.
Recommendation
FAA should minimize manual notification through automated digital authorization.
Discussion
Routine notification by telephone, e-mail, or manual coordination will not scale.
Instead, FAA should encourage:
• automated authorization;
• digital approvals;
• machine-readable permissions;
• enterprise interfaces;

• USS integration;
• standardized APIs.
Notification should become an automated exchange of authorization data rather than a manual
administrative process.
This supports future BVLOS operations while reducing workload for both operators and facility
managers.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-14
Whitelisting of Trusted Operators
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests comment regarding Remote ID whitelists and automated identification of trusted
operators.
AX Position
Strong Support.
Recommendation
FAA should pursue a trusted authorization architecture rather than static whitelists.
Discussion
Static whitelists quickly become difficult to maintain as operations scale.
A better approach is dynamic authorization in which:
• operator credentials,
• aircraft authorization,
• mission approval,
• current permissions,
are validated in real time.
This model better supports:

• changing aircraft,
• temporary approvals,
• emergency operations,
• public safety missions,
• commercial BVLOS,
• future automation.
Dynamic authorization also improves cybersecurity by reducing stale credential lists.
Recommended FAA Action
Clarify in Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-15
Technology Solutions Supporting UAFRs
FAA Request for Comment
FAA seeks comment regarding technological solutions that balance security needs with future
UAS scalability.
AX Position
Strong Support.
Recommendation
FAA should encourage interoperable, standards-based enterprise architectures.
Discussion
Future UAFR implementation should leverage:
• ASTM Remote ID;
• USS interoperability;
• digital authorization;
• authenticated identity services;
• enterprise air domain awareness;
• sensor fusion;
• federated information exchange.
These capabilities allow facilities to verify legitimate operations without creating proprietary
ecosystems.

Technology should remain:
• vendor neutral,
• standards based,
• interoperable,
• scalable,
• cyber resilient.
This approach preserves innovation while avoiding vendor lock-in.
Recommended FAA Action
Retain performance-based implementation.
Comment RFC-16
Future Scalability of the UAFR Program
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests comment on implementation approaches that will support long-term
administration of the UAFR program.
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Design implementation processes that scale through standardized digital workflows rather than
increasing administrative review.
Rationale
The number of UAFR petitions, amendments, and renewals is expected to grow over time.
Standardized digital submissions, structured data, and automated workflow management will
improve consistency while reducing administrative burden for both applicants and the FAA.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand the Advisory Circular and evaluate administrative efficiencies in the PRIA.
Comment RFC-17
Integration with Future FAA Services

FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests comment regarding future operational integration.
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Implementation guidance should anticipate integration with future FAA digital services without
prescribing specific technologies.
Rationale
The UAFR program should remain compatible with future FAA modernization initiatives,
including digital aeronautical information services, UTM capabilities, and evolving authorization
systems. Technology-neutral implementation will preserve flexibility while reducing future
implementation costs.
Recommended FAA Action
Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-18
Enterprise Airspace Awareness
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests comment regarding operational awareness within UAFRs.
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Recognize that facility operators may employ multiple complementary surveillance sources in
addition to Remote ID.
Rationale
Remote ID provides identification of compliant UAS but is not intended to serve as the sole

compliant Remote ID with other lawful surveillance capabilities appropriate to their operational

environment. The regulation should remain technology-neutral while recognizing that layered air

Clarify in the Preamble and expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-19
Cybersecurity
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests comment on implementation considerations.
AX Position
Support.
Recommendation
Encourage cybersecurity best practices for systems supporting UAFR administration without

Rationale
Digital authorization, Remote ID sensing, and operational data management introduce

Expand the Advisory Circular.
Comment RFC-20
Interoperability
FAA Request for Comment
FAA requests comment regarding implementation approaches.
AX Position

Support.

Encourage implementation using open, consensus-based standards wherever practical.
Rationale
Interoperability promotes competition, reduces long-term costs, and simplifies integration among

Expand the Advisory Circular.

3 August 2026
To:
UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558, Notice No. 26-03, Designation—Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
From:
LifeFlight of Maine
189 Odlin Road, Building 600
Bangor, ME 04401
LifeFlight of Maine respectfully submits the following comments in response to the Federal
Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking entitled Designation—Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility (Docket No. FAA-2026-
4558; Notice No. 26-03).
LifeFlight of Maine is a non-profit provider of critical care ground ambulance, helicopter, and
fixed wing air ambulance services throughout Maine and under mutual aid provisions throughout
northern New England. LifeFlight holds Part 135 Air Carrier Certificate 5L0A257Q. LifeFlight
supports over fifty hospitals in Maine and northern New England with helicopter air ambulance
services.
We support the FAA’s objective of protecting critical infrastructure, sensitive facilities, and the
public from unsafe or unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations. We appreciate Congress’
directive that the FAA establish a process through which certain fixed-site facilities may request
unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs). LifeFlight is also a member of Vertical Flight
International (VAI) and broadly supports the comments they have posted to this NPRM, and we
have included specific comments from VAI appliable to our concern for critical healthcare
facilities.
Our comments focus specifically on the proposed eligibility criteria and workability of the NPRM
for healthcare and public health facilities seeking Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).
We are very concerned that the proposed framework does not adequately balance
security objectives, operational practicality, and the continued safe integration of
unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) into the National Airspace System (NAS) proximate to
hospitals with active helipads conducting emergency unscheduled operations.

Further, we are concerned as to the undue burden placed on healthcare facilities with existing
aviation infrastructure. For facilities already publicly registered in the FAA Aviation Data and
Information Portal (ADIP) the requirements to additionally seek UAFR’s to protect aviation
operations proximate to the hospital helipad are extensive and unbalanced between workload
burden/management, risks, and benefits.
I. As proposed, the NPRM definition of healthcare facilities as critical infrastructure
eligible for a UAFR is too narrow and negatively impacting aviation safety.
The FAA requests comments on its determination to limit UAFRs to those fixed site facilities
within the sixteen sectors discussed above. Are there additional facility types in this sector that
should be considered?
Criteria. FAA proposes that operators or proprietors within the healthcare and public health
sector may apply for a UAFR if the facility is a Level I trauma center with helipad(s) or pediatric
level I trauma center with helipad(s).
Drones pose a threat to facilities in this sector because they could collide or interfere with
helicopters transporting patients, medical professionals, biologics, and urgent medical
equipment and supplies. Drones could also interfere with power supplies and communication
systems leading to operational disruptions and potential harm to patients.”
LifeFlight supports the FAA's recognition that healthcare facilities constitute critical
infrastructure, but we note the proposed eligibility criteria does not begin to meet the risks
across the low altitude critical emergency healthcare infrastructure in the United States. This
limitation is not consistent with the emergency air ambulance operating sector in the US. As
written, Level I Trauma designation by the American College of Surgeons includes 230 hospital
facilities, representing four percent (4%) of the over five thousand acute care hospitals with
emergency facilities conducting on-site medical helicopter operations. Additionally, as
proposed, the critical medical facility definition does not include free standing emergency
departments, rural clinics, or community co-located EMS stations and medical helicopter base
sites.
Virtually every acute care emergency hospital in the country, regardless of size, ranging from
Rural Emergency and Critical Access Hospitals to our major tertiary receiving centers actively
engage in medical helicopter transport as referring, receiving, or both sides of helicopter air
ambulance transport. All these facilities are vital critical emergency community infrastructure
requiring protection of their helipads and air space tied to required approach and departure
procedures under FAA regulations. Our particular concern is hospitals with helipads.
It is important to note that rather than the media pictured trauma medevac from emergency
scenes to trauma centers, the majority of all air ambulance transports are between healthcare
facilities emergently moving patients to higher levels of care. The proposed criteria rely primarily
upon narrow administrative trauma designations rather than actual healthcare criticality,
patient acuity, transportation dependency, and consequences to public health.

We believe the FAA should expand eligibility for enhanced operational protections beyond Level I
trauma centers. The safety concerns associated with unanticipated UAS activity near all acute
care emergency hospitals are often comparable to those associated with designated Level I
trauma centers.
As an example, In Maine there are thirty-four hospitals with emergency departments, three free
standing hospital associated emergency facilities, and several rural clinics, including on islands,
supporting 24/365 emergency care. These only include a single Level I Trauma Center and single
Level II Trauma Center. The distinction between Level I and Level II is primarily academic. The
facility with the most flight activity is a Level II Trauma Center. The remaining 34/39 emergency
facilities range from community hospitals, critical access hospitals, free standing hospitals
associated with emergency departments, and a VA hospital. Thirty-three of the thirty-seven
(33/37) emergency facilities have helipads with regular unscheduled emergency use.
The FAA should consider expanding healthcare and public health sector beyond Level 1 trauma
centers to include all medical facilities with a helipad and demonstrated manned aviation
operations with an ADIP location identifier. If FAA's rationale in including Level 1 trauma centers
is to address the distinct threat UAS poses to facilities in this sector due to a high collision or
interference potential, why would this not be expanded to include other such medical facilities
with similar operations and risk profiles?
Recommendation: Accordingly, the FAA should expand healthcare eligibility criteria to include
a broader risk- based framework that better reflects the statutory definition of critical
infrastructure to include all publicly identified and licensed emergency medical receiving
facilities with an onsite helipad and a FAA locator identifier in the ADIP database.
II. The administrative burden placed on healthcare facilities is significant and
unbalanced with benefit.
The NPRM proposes facilities seeking a standard UAFR submit extensive information regarding
facility operations, security considerations, and justification for the requested restriction. This
information is intended to support FAA's evaluation and would become part of the public
regulatory process. As proposed, the process to seek UFAR’s is a tremendous burden to small
hospitals and healthcare facilities with aviation infrastructure already included in the FAA’s
regulatory process and ADIP.
As an example, under: Externalities (§ 74.68) In addition to evaluating the effect a UAFR would
have on the applicant's facility, FAA would also evaluate what effect, if any, the UAFR would have
on adjacent landowners and airspace users. Proposed § 74.68 would require the applicant to
describe in a form and manner acceptable to the Administrator: (1) the costs, disruptions, or
other negative effects to users of the airspace, including known traffic circumnavigating the
facility; and (2) any efforts the operator or proprietor of the fixed site facility has taken or would
take to reduce or limit those costs, disruptions, or other negative effects.

As proposed the burdens noted above are not reasonable for small healthcare facilities. They do
not possess the proposed required information about airspace use and do not have control or
the ability to include adjoining non-hospital owned property in the UFAR required paperwork. As
the airspace necessary for 8:1 approach within the 400’ AGL of the highest obstacle required
approach and departure paths can extend 3,000-5000 ft. beyond the helipad/ hospital
boundaries with the required paperwork extreme and unmanageable even for large centers.
As VAI has noted, the draft proposal imposes substantial burdens on facility operators while
providing limited practical security or safety benefits particularly where broad categories of
operations are permitted access through a notification-based process to allow unmanned
aircraft activity in proximity to their helipads with 24/365 emergent unscheduled helicopter air
ambulance operations. At the same time, the proposal allows numerous categories of UAS
operations to access Standard UAFRs upon providing notice to the facility operator who has no
means to deconflict potential multi-users in the airspace over top of a hospital helipad. The FAA
expressly states that operators meeting the applicable requirements may access a UAFR after
providing notification and that facility operators have no authority to approve or deny access.
Consequently, the practical effect of a Standard UAFR may be limited to providing situational
awareness rather than restricting operations.
LifeFlight agrees with VAI and questions whether many facilities will perceive sufficient benefit to
justify the administrative burden, public disclosure obligations, and potential security risks
associated with obtaining a Standard UAFR. The FAA should further evaluate whether the
proposed framework delivers meaningful protections commensurate with the effort
required of applicants.
The FAA should therefore consider whether medical facilities with locator criteria documented
in the FAA Aviation Data and Information Portal (ADIP) demonstrating routine helicopter
operations should be eligible for Special UAFR consideration regardless of trauma center
designation. This could include automated granting of a Special UAFR for existing low altitude
aviation facilities with ADIO location identifiers. Such an approach would better account for
facilities where aviation activity is not incidental but rather constitutes a core operational
function.
Recommendation: The FAA should issue a Special UFAR to include required airspace under
Title 14 CFR 77.9. for all publicly identified and licensed emergency medical receiving facilities
with an onsite helipad and an FAA identifier in the ADIP database.
III. The proposed NPRM relies on notification procedures rather than coordination
and management of low altitude airspace. Notification does not equal
coordination.
As noted by VAI, the NPRM appears to assume that all eligible facilities have similar operational
needs. However, many critical healthcare infrastructure facilities routinely host emergency
aviation operations that are themselves integral to safety, security, inspection, maintenance, or
emergency response functions.

For these healthcare facilities, a simple notification-based access model may not adequately
address operational conflicts created by unanticipated UAS activity concurrent with emergency
unscheduled operations. Throughout this NPRM, FAA relies heavily on notification as a means
of mitigating security and operational risks. However, notification alone does not ensure
operational coordination, deconfliction, or meaningful security protection.
As medical helicopters operate emergent, unscheduled operations 24/365, a notification of
unmanned operations is not coordination of airspace, or an equivalent level of safety, especially
for beyond line-of-sight operations, with the added risks of low visibility at night or ongoing
instrument approach and departure procedures from hospital helipads.
The recently published Air Ambulance Quality and Patient Safety Advisory Committee Report to
Congress emphasized the importance of improving aviation infrastructure awareness,
operational safety, and data integrity associated with air medical transportation. The increasing
integration of UAS, advanced air mobility aircraft, and traditional helicopter air ambulance
operations will require accurate infrastructure inventories and enhanced protection of
healthcare transportation corridors.
LifeFlight agrees with VAI and believes the final rule should place greater emphasis on
coordination, situational awareness, and risk management rather than relying primarily on
notice-based mechanisms.
Recommendation: The FAA should ensure that implementation of Section 2209 strengthens—
not inadvertently weakens—the safety of emergency medical aviation operations. The final Rule
should establish secure and protected flight corridors and routes for all manned and unmanned
operations into and out of licensed emergency facilities with a FAA locator in the ADIP to assure
the safety of low altitude operations.
IV. Additional Protections Must Be Afforded for Facilities with Existing Aviation
Operations. LifeFlight supports automated continuous UFAR’s for all 24/365
emergency healthcare facilities with onsite helipads
The NPRM correctly identifies the risk that unmanned aircraft may interfere with helicopters
transporting patients, medical personnel, biologics, and urgent medical supplies. However, the
FAA's proposed framework does not adequately account for the unique characteristics of
heliport operations. Helicopter Air Ambulance operations are conducted 24/365 on an
emergent and unscheduled basis.
The NPRM goal is to limit the size of UFAR’s to optimize availability of the NAS for unmanned
operations. As proposed, a UAFR would include airspace with clearly defined horizontal and
vertical limits within which unmanned aircraft would be restricted from operating.

The FAA solicits comments on whether the property line of a facility applying for a UAFR should
be the maximum perimeter of a UAFR in all cases or whether there are certain circumstances
FAA should expand the lateral boundaries beyond the property line.
Lateral Boundary (§ 74.58)
Proposed § 74.58(a) would require the applicant to identify the lateral boundaries for the
requested UAFR. Paragraph (b) would require that the requested UAFR boundary not exceeds
the operator or proprietor's property boundary. The purpose of these limitations is to make sure
that the requested UAFR is limited to property over which the applicant has a legal right or
interest. For example, in the case of an application with a single operator or proprietor, the
applicant would have legal control of the facility and all property below the requested UAFR. In
the case where the requested UAFR would extend over a fixed site facility and encompass
additional property within the legal control of a third-party other than the operator or proprietor
of the facility, the third-party would be considered an operator or proprietor for purposes of
proposed part 74 and must be included in the application.
The FAA solicits comments on whether the property line of a facility applying for a UAFR should
be the maximum perimeter of a UAFR in all cases or whether there are certain circumstances
FAA should expand the lateral boundaries beyond the property line.
As noted above, the potential inclusion of third party non-owned property is not manageable for
hospitals with existing emergency unscheduled operations and is inconsistent with safe
operations into and out of hospital helipads.
In addition to the risk of unscheduled general flight operations, there is substantial risk to beyond
line-of-sight unmanned operations during low visibility as over forty percent of HAA operations
occur during night hours as noted in the most recent FAA compilation of HAA operating data. 1
We note that in addition to low visibility night operations, LifeFlight operates using IFR flight rules
and virtually every hospital facility in Maine, along with multiple predetermined emergency
landing areas throughout the state have instrument flight approach and departure procedures.
This requires additional safety measures for BLOS unmanned operations.
Further, increasing numbers of hospitals are implementing instrument flight approach and
departure procedures to enhance the safety and reliability of inter-hospital transfer, the largest
number of low altitude operations. By nature, these operations occur with limited visibility in
tight quarters with high workload for pilots. Unlike airports, the FAA Airport Master Record does
not contain comprehensive approach and departure path information for heliports.
Consequently, unmanned aircraft operators frequently lack sufficient information to identify and
avoid helicopter operating areas. Further, the pilot in command may modify approach and
departures to account for wind direction, strength, and flow.
1 FAA Aviation Safety: Helicopter Air Ambulance (HAA) Operations Data Calendar Year 2024

The FAA acknowledges in the NPRM that the Healthcare and Public Health Sector protect all
sectors of the economy from hazards such as terrorism, infectious disease outbreaks, natural
disasters, and other emergencies. Healthcare facilities supported by helicopter air ambulance
operations represent a unique subset of critical infrastructure because their operational
continuity directly affects patient survival outcomes measured in minutes rather than hours.
Unlike many critical infrastructure sectors, disruptions to medical aviation operations can
immediately impact life-saving transportation of patients, organs, blood products,
pharmaceuticals, medical personnel, and specialized equipment.
This deficiency creates elevated risk during low-altitude arrival and departure operations where
helicopter traffic routinely operates below 500 feet above ground level. As proposed, the UFAR
process and limitations are not consistent with improving hospital heliport aviation safety. As
noted earlier, the required airspace to safely conduct approach and departures extend out from
the helipad, generally beyond hospital owned property. Based on current regulations and criteria
outlined in FAA Advisory Circular AC 150/5390-2D, Heliport Design, the optimum boundary for a
heliport would equate to a radius of 5,000 feet from the heliport obstructions as classified in
Title 14 CFR 77.9. A UAS operation flying at 400 feet AGL over terrain equal in height to the
heliport would begin to penetrate the heliports 8:1 approach surface at a distance of 3,200
feet. If the terrain the UAS was over was higher than the heliport by 100’ this penetration would
also occur at the start of the airspace at 4,000 feet.
As such, LifeFlight supports continuous Special UFAR’s for all 24/365 emergency healthcare
facilities with onsite helipads with sufficient lateral boundaries to assure protection of airspace
necessary to safely conduct emergency unscheduled helicopter operations. In these cases, it is
not unreasonable for unmanned operations to be assigned flight paths around rather than
through approach and departure paths and procedures.
Recommendation: The FAA should automatically designate all publicly identified and licensed
emergency medical receiving facilities with an onsite helipad with an FAA identifier in the ADIP
database as full time UFAR’s with adequate air space and deconfliction protection from other
aviation operations to assure safe approach and departure paths/procedures for medical
helicopter operations. The UFAR’s may require extensions beyond the facility property
boundaries consistent with FAA issued Heliport Design Standards.
V. The Proposed Standard UAFR Structure Does Not Provide Meaningful Security
Benefits
LifeFlight supports the following from the VAI: “the NPRM does not adequately demonstrate the
proposed Standard UAFR framework will meaningfully reduce the risks posed by malicious or
unauthorized UAS activity. In addition to low level medical helicopter operations, most medical
centers have specific air intakes to separate outside air from operating rooms and sterile
materials handling. These intakes represent a significant risk for malicious UAS use. The NPRM
appears to assume that unauthorized operators will self-identify by failing to comply with the
notification requirements. However, individuals intending to conduct malicious activity may

simply ignore both the notification process and the underlying UAFR restrictions, limiting the
proposal's effectiveness as a security measure.
The proposed rule places substantial obligations on fixed-site facility operators seeking
protection, including preparation of detailed applications, submission of potentially sensitive
information, and ongoing administrative responsibilities. At the same time, numerous categories
of UAS operations may access Standard UAFRs through a notification-based process that does
not require facility approval.
As a result, the NPRM raises a fundamental policy question: what security benefit is actually
achieved by a Standard UAFR relative to existing authorities and operational practices?
The FAA repeatedly notes that the proposal would help distinguish authorized operators from
unauthorized operators. However, VAI is concerned that the proposal primarily affects
compliant operators while providing limited deterrence against genuinely malicious actors.
A bad actor intending to conduct surveillance, disruption, criminal activity, or an intentional
attack is unlikely to be deterred by a requirement to avoid a designated UAFR or provide advance
notification before entering one. By contrast, legitimate commercial operators, infrastructure
inspectors, surveyors, photographers, utility operators, public safety agencies, and recreational
users are likely to comply with the rule's requirements.
Consequently, the proposal appears to impose the greatest burden on those operators already
inclined to comply with applicable regulations while offering uncertain benefits against the very
actors whose activities prompted Congress to enact Section 2209.”
Recommendation: The FAA should provide additional analysis demonstrating how the
proposed framework materially reduces risk and should explain why the anticipated benefits
justify the burdens imposed on facility operators, UAS operators, and the broader aviation
community.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed Rule. We hope our comments
improve the Final Rule balancing safety, risks, optimal use of the NAS, and administrative
burdens for all users and operations in the NAS. In summary our recommendations:

licensed emergency medical receiving facilities with an onsite helipad and a FAA locator

Recommendation: Assure implementation of Section 2209 strengthens—not inadvertently

flight corridors and routes for all manned and unmanned operations into and out of licensed
emergency facilities with a FAA locator in the ADIP to assure the safety of low altitude
operations.

designate all publicly identified and licensed emergency medical receiving facilities with an

space and deconfliction protection from other aviation operations. Extend UFAR’s beyond the
