I submit this comment in my personal capacity as an FAA-certificated Remote Pilot under 14 CFR
Part 107 and as a professional UAS operator with substantial field experience in Colorado’s
mountain, public-land, infrastructure-adjacent, and mixed-use airspace environments. These
comments are my own and do not represent any other organization.
I support the FAA’s effort to create a federal process for protecting genuinely sensitive fixed-site
facilities from unsafe or unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations. A clear federal process is
preferable to a growing patchwork of state and local restrictions that can create confusion for
remote pilots, facility operators, public agencies, recreational users, and law enforcement.
At the same time, the final rule should be narrowly tailored. A UAFR should not be granted merely
because a facility is important, visible, sensitive-looking, controversial, located on public land, or part
of a larger infrastructure network. The applicant should be required to demonstrate a specific UAS-
related vulnerability, a credible consequence if that vulnerability is exploited, why existing physical
security and non-airspace measures are insufficient, and why the requested restriction is
appropriately tailored. The applicant should also explain why less burdensome boundaries,
procedures, or access conditions would not adequately address the documented risk. Eligibility to
apply should not become entitlement to restricted airspace.
The FAA should preserve the fixed-site character of the rule. Nothing in the final rule should create,
imply, or invite a general no-fly rule over pipelines, utility corridors, railroad corridors, transmission
rights-of-way, or other linear infrastructure merely because those features cross public land or serve
critical functions. The rule should remain focused on discrete fixed-site assets, such as qualifying
pump stations, compressor stations, substations, control rooms, refineries, chemical facilities, and
other defined facilities that meet the rule’s criteria. Corridor-wide restrictions would be difficult to
administer, difficult to display accurately to pilots, and inconsistent with a practical, scalable UAS
operating environment. Stated another way, the presence of a railroad track, pipeline, buried utility,
easement, or right-of-way on public land should not by itself support a UAFR; the restriction should
attach only to a qualifying fixed-site facility with a documented UAS-related risk.
UAFRs should be limited laterally and vertically to the smallest practicable airspace volume needed
to address the documented risk. The lateral boundary should not become a mechanism for
converting easements, rights-of-way, rail alignments, pipelines, or large infrastructure networks into
broad low-altitude exclusion zones. FAA should reject requests that would effectively restrict
airspace over long corridors rather than over a qualifying fixed-site facility.
Where a proposed UAFR would overlap public lands, burden public access, or materially affect
Tribal interests, historic or cultural resources, recreation lands, wilderness, Wild and Scenic Rivers,
wildlife habitat, or other federally or state-recognized protected public resources, FAA should
document coordination with the appropriate land-management agency and, where applicable,
affected Tribal governments before approval. That coordination should inform FAA’s review, but it
should not become a separate non-federal airspace approval process. Adjacency to public land, a
utility easement, or a right-of-way should not justify expanding a UAFR beyond the applicant’s
documented fixed-site need.
The Standard UAFR process should be usable in the real world. FAA should build notification and
approval into existing FAA-recognized UAS data and authorization pathways rather than creating a

separate facility-by-facility permission maze. For Standard UAFRs, a LAANC-like or DroneZone-
integrated notify-and-fly system would be far more likely to produce compliance than an opaque
manual process. The system should be available through official FAA UAS data services and
approved UAS service suppliers, provide timely confirmation where appropriate, including
automated confirmation where feasible, display UAFRs in machine-readable formats, and give
operators clear instructions before flight.
The final rule should also clarify that approved or properly notified access to a Standard UAFR may
involve more than direct transit. Many legitimate UAS operations require hovering, orbiting, lateral
repositioning, repeated passes, photography, mapping, thermal inspection, damage assessment,
public-safety coordination, environmental documentation, historic-resource documentation, or
public-interest media work. FAA should distinguish between unauthorized loitering and approved
mission profiles that require more than simply crossing the area in the shortest practicable time.
FAA should consider whether a limited pathway is appropriate for compliant recreational operations
under 49 U.S.C. § 44809 within certain lower-risk Standard UAFRs. I am not suggesting recreational
access to Special UAFRs or truly high-risk fixed sites. However, a categorical omission of § 44809
operations may be overbroad for lower-risk Standard UAFRs, especially where the protected facility
is small, common, adjacent to parks or public spaces, and where FAA determines the security risk is
low enough and the operation is brief, visual-line-of-sight, Remote ID-compliant, and conducted
under recognized safety guidelines.
Part 74 should remain an airspace restriction process only. A UAFR should not authorize, imply,
encourage, or normalize private or state/local counter-UAS detection, jamming, spoofing, kinetic
interdiction, command-link interference, seizure of control, or other mitigation activities absent
separate federal authority. The final rule should state clearly in regulatory text that UAFR
designation does not provide counter-UAS authority.
FAA should clarify the relationship between Part 74 and state, local, territorial, or Tribal critical-
infrastructure restrictions so that operators are not left with overlapping or conflicting airspace rules.
Unmanned aircraft airspace restrictions based on proximity to critical infrastructure or fixed-site
facilities should be treated as part of FAA’s federal airspace framework unless independently
authorized by federal law. That clarification should address state, local, territorial, or Tribal rules that
restrict, prohibit, condition, or penalize UAS flight operations in the National Airspace System based
on proximity to critical infrastructure, while preserving traditional authority over privacy, trespass,
nuisance, reckless endangerment, land use, law-enforcement operations, and control of launch or
landing from property where those laws do not regulate airspace efficiency or aviation safety.
Finally, UAFRs should not become permanent by inertia. FAA should require periodic validation,
public renewal notice for Standard UAFRs, updated evidence of continuing need, and a meaningful
process for affected operators, local governments, land managers, or the public to request
modification or cancellation where a UAFR becomes overbroad, obsolete, inaccurate, or
unnecessarily disruptive to lawful UAS operations.
In short, FAA should adopt Part 74 as a narrowly tailored federal process for documented fixed-site
risks, not as a broad corridor-restriction tool or as another layer on top of inconsistent state and
local airspace rules. The final rule should protect genuinely sensitive facilities while preserving lawful

Part 107 operations, future BVLOS scalability, appropriate recreational access, public-interest
documentation, and the public’s right of transit through the National Airspace System.

To Whom It May Concern:
I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and U.S.
Department of Transportation (DOT) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) titled “Designation—
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,” implementing
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016.1 I submit these comments in my
individual capacity. The views expressed here are my own and do not necessarily represent the positions
of any organization with which I am affiliated.
I. Background
I have spent more than 36 years working at the intersection of aerospace engineering, unmanned systems,
and public policy. I am an aerospace engineer by training, and I have served in engineering and leadership
roles spanning defense, industry, academia, and government. I served as a member of the FAA’s UAS
Detection and Mitigation Aviation Rulemaking Committee (ARC), which examined precisely the problem

Committee, the FAA’s Advanced Aviation Advisory Committee, and other federal and state advisory
bodies, and I lead the electronic conspicuity working group within the FAA’s BEYOND program. I currently
serve on the board of directors of the Commercial Drone Alliance (CDA), and I have testified before
Congress on aviation innovation. I have also spent much of my career designing, building, and operating
the safety infrastructure—radar networks, sensing systems, and command-and-control architectures—
that enables large-scale UAS operations in rural airspace. My comments below draw on that operational
and engineering experience.2

II. Support for the Comments of the Commercial Drone Alliance
I have reviewed the comments submitted by the CDA in response to this rulemaking, and I fully support
them. The CDA’s first principles are correct: airspace awareness around critical infrastructure requires a
multi-layered approach; it is possible to enable beneficial operations while preventing harmful ones;
dynamic airspace management is essential to achieving American drone dominance; and a uniform
federal framework is needed to prevent a fragmented patchwork of airspace restrictions. I likewise
support the CDA’s specific recommendations, including automated notification, whitelist-based access,
safeguarding of security-sensitive application information, service-based detection models under the
proposed Part 146 framework, and clarification of the performance-based transit requirements. Rather
than repeat those arguments, I write separately to offer several observations drawn from my own
engineering and rulemaking-committee experience.
III. Individual Observations and Recommendations
A. Restrictions Without Detection Create the Appearance of Security, Not Security
The central lesson of my service on the UAS Detection and Mitigation ARC is that an airspace restriction
is a legal instrument, not a physical capability. A published Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (UAFR)
will shape the behavior of lawful, informed operators—and will be invisible in practice to the careless and
irrelevant to the criminal. If the final rule allows facilities to obtain restrictions without meaningful
detection capability, it risks creating a false sense of security: facilities may believe they are protected
because a line exists on a chart, while their actual awareness of what is flying above them remains
unchanged. I therefore urge the FAA to adopt the CDA’s recommendations to require, or at minimum
strongly encourage and favorably weight, real detection capability—capable of observing both
cooperative and non-cooperative aircraft, and extending beyond the immediate UAFR boundary—as a
condition of designation.3 To be clear, this recommendation is risk-based and technology-neutral: the
objective is improved situational awareness proportionate to a facility’s demonstrated risk, not a mandate
for any particular sensing modality. Extending detection awareness beyond the UAFR boundary serves
solely to improve warning time and situational awareness; it implies no expansion of the restricted
airspace itself, which remains fixed by the legal boundary of the designation. The final rule could also
reasonably distinguish between baseline detection expectations—such as Remote ID monitoring—
applicable to all UAFR facilities, and enhanced non-cooperative detection capabilities appropriate for
higher-risk facilities. Detection is not an accessory to this rule; it is the mechanism by which the rule’s
security purpose is actually achieved.
B. Discrimination Between Compliant and Non-Compliant Aircraft Is the Core Technical Problem
The security value of a UAFR does not come from keeping compliant drones out; it comes from making
non-compliant drones conspicuous. Today, a facility observing an unknown aircraft overhead has no
practical way to know whether it is an authorized operation, a careless hobbyist, or a genuine threat—
and that uncertainty, not the presence of the aircraft, is the security problem. The Part 74 framework is

valuable because it can shrink that uncertainty: when compliant operators broadcast Remote
Identification,4 provide automated notification, and appear on whitelists, operations that cannot readily
be correlated with authorized activity become appropriate candidates for additional assessment. This is
why I urge the FAA to treat the CDA’s recommendations on automated notification, network Remote ID,
and whitelist databases not as operator conveniences but as security measures. Every step that makes
compliance easier and more machine-readable sharpens the contrast between the lawful and the
unlawful, which is the entire game in counter-UAS security.
C. Electronic Conspicuity Lessons Apply Directly to This Rule
My work leading the electronic conspicuity working group in the FAA’s BEYOND program has reinforced a
simple principle: identification and awareness technologies deliver their value only when they are
interoperable, standards-based, and near-universally adopted. A patchwork of proprietary, facility-
specific notification systems would replicate at low altitude the fragmentation problems the aviation
community has spent decades solving at higher altitudes. The final rule should therefore be technology-
neutral and performance-based, should accommodate network Remote ID and future conspicuity
technologies alongside broadcast Remote ID, and should encourage standardized, machine-readable
interfaces—so that a single compliant equipage and notification approach works at every UAFR in the
country, rather than requiring operators to integrate separately with thousands of facilities.
D. Guard Against Over-Designation
Restrictions are subject to a form of inflation: each individual designation may seem reasonable, but the
cumulative effect of thousands of designations is an airspace that is fragmented for lawful operators and
unchanged for unlawful ones. The FAA should hold the line on rigorous, evidence-based demonstration
of need, grounded in verifiable detection data rather than anecdote, as the CDA recommends. Rigorous
standards serve a dual purpose: they protect the security objectives of the rule, and they protect the long-
term public acceptance and legitimacy of the UAFR framework itself—a framework perceived as handing
out restrictions freely will invite challenge and non-compliance in a way that a disciplined, evidence-based
framework will not. The integrity of the Part 74 framework over the long term will depend less on how
the first hundred UAFRs are designated than on the discipline applied to the next ten thousand
applications.
E. The Economics of Detection Will Determine Whether This Rule Works Outside Major
Metropolitan Areas
Having built and operated detection and sensing infrastructure in rural airspace, I can attest that the
engineering is achievable—but the economics are unforgiving. A stand-alone detection capability sized
for a single facility is beyond the practical reach of most rural hospitals, utilities, cooperatives, and
municipalities, even though the infrastructure those facilities represent is often irreplaceable within their
regions. If the final rule implicitly assumes facility-owned detection, its protections will concentrate where
capital concentrates: in major metropolitan areas. The service-based model the CDA recommends—
certified detection- and surveillance-as-a-service providers, authorized through an extensible framework
such as the proposed Part 146—changes that calculus fundamentally, because a single networked sensing

infrastructure can serve many facilities across a wide region at a fraction of the individual cost.5 I urge the
FAA to expressly enable such service models in the final rule, and to view them as the primary path by
which the rule’s protections will reach rural America. Like the detection recommendations above, these
service models should remain technology-neutral and performance-based, and detection expectations
should be scaled to demonstrated risk so that they do not become de facto barriers to participation for
smaller facilities. The same reasoning applies to transit: automated, machine-to-machine notification is
what makes long-distance rural UAS missions—agricultural operations, infrastructure inspection, medical
logistics—economically viable in an airspace with many UAFRs.
IV. Conclusion
Finally, I encourage the FAA to implement Part 74 not as a stand-alone program but as one element of an
integrated low-altitude airspace ecosystem. Part 74’s restrictions, Part 108’s operating framework, Part
146’s certified data services, and the FAA’s broader UAS Traffic Management capabilities each depend on
the others: the notification and detection architectures this rule requires are the same architectures Part
108 operations will generate and Part 146 providers will certify. Implemented as a coherent whole rather
than as independent regulatory silos, they can constitute the dynamic, data-driven airspace system that
both security and scalability require.
The NPRM is a constructive and overdue step toward a low-altitude airspace system that protects
sensitive facilities while enabling the beneficial UAS operations that increasingly serve the American
public. Its success will turn on implementation choices: pairing restrictions with real detection, making
compliance automated and machine-readable, holding designations to an evidence-based standard, and
ensuring the economics work outside major metropolitan areas. I support the comments of the
Commercial Drone Alliance, and I appreciate the FAA’s consideration of these individual observations. I
would be glad to serve as a resource to the agency as this rulemaking progresses.

I oppose flight restrictions for the food and agriculture sector because enforcement and public accountability depend on drone documentation of pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims. The FAA has shown no demonstrated drone risk.

To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to any proposal that would allow industrial animal agriculture facilities to be designated as "critical infrastructure" eligible for flight restrictions under Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act.

Drones operated by journalists, photojournalists, investigators, and concerned citizens serve a vital oversight role in documenting animal welfare, labor conditions, and environmental compliance at concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) and industrial agricultural sites. Restricting airspace above these facilities shields private operations from public transparency and severely undermines First Amendment protections and freedom of the press. Freedom of information relies on the ability to monitor high-impact industries independently, especially given that traditional ground-level access is often prohibited by facility operators.

Furthermore, the Federal Aviation Administration already maintains a robust regulatory framework under 14 CFR Part 107 governing small unmanned aircraft systems. Existing federal regulations—including prohibitions against operating over people, beyond visual line of sight, or in a reckless manner—are fully sufficient to preserve airspace safety and protect low-altitude flight operations. Establishing blanket airspace restrictions over agricultural sites is an unnecessary misuse of safety mandates to insulate private entities from public scrutiny.

I urge the FAA to reject the inclusion of food and industrial agricultural facilities under Section 2209 designations and to keep public airspace open for press freedom, transparency, and accountability.

I strongly oppose allowing the food and agriculture sector to obtain flight restrictions that prevent the public from using drones to observe pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, and animal-treatment concerns. The FAA has shown no safety or security justification for preventing the public from accessing this information.

The Iowa Cattlemen’s Association (ICA) is a grassroots organization representing nearly 8,000
independent cattle producers and stakeholders affiliated with the beef cattle industry. We
appreciate the opportunity to submit the following comments on the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking by the Federal Aviation Administration Office of Rulemaking for the proposed
changes to restrictions of the operation of unmanned aircrafts in close proximity to fixed site
facilities.
Iowa’s beef cattle industry is vital to the economy of our state and our producers' livelihoods.
With more than 3.45 million head of cattle and calves, our industry generates more than $9.45
billion of economic activity. As the voice of Iowa’s beef business, it is important that ICA bring
forward the concerns and ideals of Iowa’s cattle producers to this topic.
Background
ICA supports the Federal Aviation Administration's efforts to strengthen protections for facilities
where unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations could pose risks to public safety, national
security, or critical infrastructure. As the FAA considers expanding the categories of fixed-site
facilities eligible for UAS flight restrictions, ICA urges the agency to explicitly recognize
livestock production facilities as critical components of the nation's food and agricultural
infrastructure and make them eligible for these protections.
Modern livestock production facilities are essential to maintaining a safe, secure, and resilient
domestic food supply. Beef cattle operations represent significant investments in livestock, feed
infrastructure, water systems, animal health, and employee safety. Unauthorized drone activity
over these facilities can disrupt livestock behavior, interfere with routine management practices,
distract employees operating equipment or handling animals, and expose sensitive operational

information. These impacts present legitimate operational and safety concerns for producers.
The cattle industry has also made substantial investments in biosecurity and foreign animal
disease preparedness. Producers work diligently to prevent the introduction and spread of
diseases that could have catastrophic consequences for the U.S. livestock industry and national
food supply. Unauthorized aerial access to livestock facilities creates additional biosecurity
concerns by enabling surveillance of facility layouts, animal concentrations, and operational
practices without the knowledge or consent of the producer. As threats to critical infrastructure
continue to evolve, protecting the security of livestock production facilities should be viewed as
an important component of safeguarding the nation's food system.
Congress has already recognized the need to protect agricultural operations from unauthorized
unmanned aircraft activity. Likewise, Iowa law prohibits the use of unmanned aircraft systems to
conduct surveillance of agricultural operations without the property owner's consent,
acknowledging the unique privacy, operational, and biosecurity interests associated with farming
and livestock production. Federal UAS policy should complement these protections by ensuring
that producers have appropriate safeguards against unauthorized drone operations that could
threaten their operations or the broader food supply.
Recommendations
CA respectfully recommends that the FAA include livestock production facilities among the
categories of fixed-site facilities eligible to request UAS operating restrictions where justified by
security, operational, or biosecurity concerns. The agency should establish clear criteria that
recognize factors such as livestock density, the presence of animal health infrastructure, feed and
water systems, disease response capabilities, and the facility's importance within the agricultural
supply chain. Providing a pathway for qualifying livestock facilities to obtain appropriate
protections would better align FAA policy with the realities of modern agriculture while
preserving the beneficial uses of UAS technology when operated lawfully and with landowner
permission.
The United States depends upon a safe, secure, and resilient food production system. Livestock
production facilities are a foundational part of the nation's critical agricultural infrastructure, and
their protection contributes directly to homeland security, food security, and animal health
preparedness. ICA appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and encourages the
FAA to ensure that livestock production facilities are eligible for UAS protections under the final
rule.

I oppose the inclusion of the Food and Agriculture sector (§ 74.90) amongst the critical infrastructure facilities that could obtain Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).

The proposal highlights safety concerns (e.g. “protection of people and property on the ground”) as the key factor in considering requests for UAFRs. However, there is no documented evidence of drones at agricultural facilities threatening the safety or security of animals, workers, or farm equipment. To the contrary, recent drone footage at factory farms has revealed workers abusing animals (e.g. calves being kicked at Agresti Calf Ranch), illegal calf hutches with inadequate space (e.g. at Grimmius Cattle Company, in violation of California Penal Code 597t), and dead piles that violate environmental law and present a hazard to public health (e.g. at Vera Goat Dairy). Drones do not present safety concerns at these facilities; they expose them.

It is only because of drones that the public can see the reality of these factory farms, which can otherwise operate out of sight and free from accountability when they violate the law. I urge you not to shield these facilities from public scrutiny – please exclude the Food and Agriculture sector from receiving UAFRs.

To Whom It May Concern,

I am registering my strong opposition to any proposal allowing industrial animal agriculture facilities to be designated as "critical infrastructure" eligible for flight restrictions under Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act.

Drones operated by journalists, photojournalists, investigators, and concerned citizens play an absolutely vital role in documenting animal welfare, labor conditions, and environmental compliance at concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) and industrial agricultural sites. Restricting airspace above these facilities shields private operations from public transparency and severely undermines First Amendment protections and freedom of the press. Freedom of information relies on the ability to monitor high-impact industries independently, especially given that traditional ground-level access is usually prohibited by facility operators.

The Federal Aviation Administration currently maintains a robust regulatory framework under 14 CFR Part 107 governing small unmanned aircraft systems. Existing federal regulations—including prohibitions against operating over people, beyond visual line of sight, or in a reckless manner—are fully sufficient to preserve airspace safety and protect low-altitude flight operations. Establishing blanket airspace restrictions over agricultural sites is an unnecessary misuse of safety mandates to insulate private entities from public scrutiny. The FAA must reject the inclusion of food and industrial agricultural facilities under Section 2209 designations and to keep public airspace open for press freedom, transparency, and accountability.

I oppose allowing food and agriculture facilities to obtain Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs). Drone photojournalism is one of the only tools the public has to see inside factory farms and hold them accountable.

There is no documented evidence of drones threatening safety or security at these facilities, but there is a documented history of drone footage exposing false marketing claims, environmental violations, and animal welfare abuses.

This rule could let the largest, most powerful operations shield themselves from scrutiny — the opposite of what the public interest requires. I urge the FAA not to develop gating criteria for this sector and not to grant UAFRs to food and agriculture facilities.

comments.commenter: Comment from International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers
comments.comment_text:
COMMENTS OF THE
INTERNATIONAL BROTHERHOOD OF ELECTRICAL WORKERS
ON THE FAA’S PROPOSED UNMANNED AIRCRAFT
FLIGHT RESTRICTION RULE
RIN 2120-AL33
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (“IBEW”) appreciates the
opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration’s (“FAA”) notice of
proposed rulemaking on creating an unmanned aircraft flight restriction (“UAFR”)
application process. 91 Fed. Reg. 24,650 (May 6, 2026). The IBEW supports UAFRs
and urges the FAA to expand the availability of UAFRs to protect the safety of the
IBEW’s members.
The IBEW is a labor organization that represents approximately 901,000
active and retired members in the broadcasting, telecommunications, construction,
manufacturing, railroad, and public utility industries, as well as public sector
workers who work for government agencies. Construction and utility workers
represented by the IBEW perform regular maintenance and emergency repairs of
electrical infrastructure across the country. That includes the construction and
repair of hundreds of thousands of miles of transmission lines.
From the start, one of the IBEW’s core purposes has been to promote safety
and reduce injuries for electrical workers. Work on and around electricity
infrastructure, including transmission lines and substations, is complex, time-
sensitive, and hazardous. Indeed, the founder of the IBEW, Henry Miller, was killed
while working on power lines to restore service after a storm. Unmanned aircrafts
(“UAs”) operating near transmission lines and substations increase the risk of injury

or death for electrical workers.
The proposed rule correctly recognizes that electricity infrastructure is critical.
However, the scope of electricity infrastructure covered by the proposed rule is
underinclusive. The FAA should revise the proposed rule to make high-voltage
transmission lines eligible for a UAFR and to lower the threshold for coverage of
electrical substations to 115 kilovolts. And because construction and utility crews
need priority access to electricity infrastructure and other critical infrastructure
during construction and repairs to maintain or restore electrical service, the FAA
should revise the proposed rule to require thirty days’ advanced notice of UA
operation in an area with a UAFR and to allow project owners to deny permission for
UA operation.
I. Electrical Workers Perform Hazardous Work on and Around
Transmission Lines and Substations.
The U.S. electrical grid is connected by over 600,000 miles of transmission lines
and over 79,000 transmission substations. See U.S. Dep’t of Energy, Grid
Modernization and the Smart Grid;1 Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Sec. Agency,
Sector Spotlight: Electricity Substation Physical Security.2 Transmission
infrastructure moves power from generating facilities (e.g., coal, nuclear, natural gas,
and renewable energy plants) to local regions, where it is then distributed at a lower
1 https://www.energy.gov/oe/grid-modernization-and-smart-grid (last visited
Aug. 5, 2026).
2 https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2023-02/Sector%20Spotlight%20
Electricity%20Substation%20Physical%20Security_508.pdf (last visited Aug. 5,
2026).
2

voltage to homes, businesses, schools, hospitals, and others.
The electrical grid is vulnerable to disruption by weather, earthquakes, vehicle
crashes, and other factors. See Off. of Elec. Delivery & Energy Reliability, DOE/OE-
0017, United States Electricity Industry Primer 31 (July 2015).3 Outages, downed
live wires, and other disruptions require rapid response to protect public safety and
restore or ensure continued service. Utilities prepare year-round to improve their
ability to respond to disruptions, including by increasing the durability and reliability
of transmission infrastructure and by inspecting and maintaining transmission
infrastructure. Id. at 33-35.
IBEW members work on electrical infrastructure across the United States and
Canada. They construct, maintain, inspect, and repair transmission lines and
substations, including in response to emergencies. Some of this work is done using
helicopters, which IBEW members use to string cables, replace conductors, restore
power after an emergency, and perform other critical utility activities. These
helicopter operations are conducted in close proximity to energized lines and to other
personnel.
Work on and around electrical infrastructure is hazardous, and reports of
fatalities associated with power line work are sadly common.4 Workers risk
3 https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2015/12/f28/united-states-electricity-
industry-primer.pdf
4 E.g., Mich. Fatality Assessment & Control Evaluation Project, MIFACE
Investigation Rep. #08MI037, Lineman Electrocuted When He Contacted 7,200-Volt
Power Line (July 31, 2009), https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/165284; Iowa Dep’t of Pub.
Health, FACE No. 93-IA-015, Lineman Electrocuted After Contacting 7,200 Volt
3

electrocution, falls, and other hazards. OSHA, Electric Power Generation,
Transmission, and Distribution Industry.5 Nearly half of all electrical fatalities
reported to OSHA are caused by contact with overhead power lines. Elec. Safety
Found. Int’l, Workplace Injury & Fatality Statistics (Mar. 5, 2026).6 And about one-
third of all electrical fatalities are caused by unexpected contact with energized
equipment or contact with nearby energized equipment. Id. Tree trimmers and other
workers not directly dealing with overhead power lines are also at risk of injury from
accidental contacts.7
Workers on or coordinating with helicopters around transmission lines are at
particular risk of injury or death. In one case, a helicopter with an attached cable
hovered near an energized transmission line while workers built additional support
Transmission Line While Installing New Pole (Oct. 19, 1993),
https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/166851; NIOSH, FACE 92-02, Lineman Electrocuted
After Contacting Energized Conductor While Working from the Bucket of an Aerial
Lift Truck in Virginia (Jan. 1, 1992), https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/167298; N.J.
Fatality Assessment & Control Evaluation Project, N.J. Case Rep. 91NJ003, Power
Substation Worker Falls 12 Feet to His Death After Contacting a 26,000 Volt Power
Line (July 23, 1991), https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/170128.
5 https://www.osha.gov/power-generation/industry-hazards (last visited Aug. 5,
2026).
6 https://www.esfi.org/workplace-safety/workplace-injury-fatality-statistics/
7 E.g., Ky. Injury Prevention & Rsch. Ctr., Rep. No. 16KY013, Tree Trimmer
Electrocuted and Dies While Trimming Tree Away from Power Lines (May 24, 2017),
https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/164985; Mich. Fatality Assessment & Control
Evaluation Project, MIFACE Investigation #02MI208, Laborer Electrocuted When
Antenna on Top of Steel Pole Building Contacts 14400-Volt Energized Line (Dec. 6,
2003), https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/169167; N.J. Fatality Assessment & Control
Evaluation Project, N.J. Case Rep. 93NJ026, One Firefighter Electrocuted and One
Seriously Injured When an Aluminum Extension Ladder Contacts a 7,600 Volt
Overhead Power Line (June 24, 1993), https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/170096.
4

towers and repaired the foundations of existing towers. A gust of wind blew the cable
carried by the helicopter, causing it to make contact with the transmission line. A
worker touching or standing close to the cable when it made contact with the
transmission line was killed. See Alaska Occupational Injury Prevention Program,
FACE 99-AK-011, Laborer/Rigger Electrocuted During an Aerial Lift of Equipment
(Jan. 24, 2000).8
UAs flown by any kind of operator around transmission lines and substations
threaten the ability to promptly install and maintain transmission infrastructure,
while endangering the workers who perform that work. UAs can accidentally contact
transmission lines or substations, which can result in power disruptions, injury, or
death. Their mere presence in the area can also disrupt carefully planned
construction operations.
II. High-Voltage Transmission Lines and 115-Kilovolt Substations Should
Be Eligible for a UAFR.
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L.
No. 114-190, 130 Stat. 615, 634-35, as amended, makes the FAA responsible for
establishing a process for applying for UAFRs. That process must allow operators or
proprietors of “critical infrastructure” to apply for a UAFR, which should be granted
based on considerations of, among other things, the protection of persons and
property. Id. Executive Order 14305 directed the FAA to promptly engage in
rulemaking and promulgate a final rule under Section 2209.
8 https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/169095
5

Executive Order 14305 interpreted the term “critical infrastructure” to “ha[ve]
the meaning given in 42 U.S.C. 5195c(e).” 90 Fed. Reg. 24,719, 24,719 (June 11,
2025). 42 U.S.C. § 5195c(e) defines “critical infrastructure” to mean “systems and
assets . . . so vital to the United States that the incapacity or destruction of such
systems and assets would have a debilitating impact on security, national economic
security, national public health or safety, or any combination of those matters.” The
proposed rule designates the following electricity industry facilities as critical
infrastructure: power generation facilities with a combined nameplate capacity of 500
megawatts or greater, electrical substations with a capacity of 500 kilovolts or
greater, and electrical substations with a capacity of 345 kilovolts or greater in the
Electric Reliability Council of Texas. 14 C.F.R. § 74.88(a) (proposed).
High-voltage transmission lines and substations with a capacity of 115
kilovolts or more are also critical infrastructure and should be eligible for UAFRs.
They are “so vital” that their incapacity has “a debilitating impact on security,
national economic security, [and] national public health or safety.” 42 U.S.C.
§ 5195c(e); see also 91 Fed. Reg. at 24,661-62 (listing factors).
“When the power goes out, life becomes difficult.” Nat’l Acads. of Scis., Eng’g
& Med., Enhancing the Resilience of the Nation’s Electricity System 9 (2017)
[hereinafter Nat’l Acads.]. Power outages can disrupt “[c]ritical social services” like
medical care, emergency services, and communications systems, “and lives can be
lost.” Id. Moreover, weather-related outages cost customers between $2 and $77
billion each year. U.S. Gov’t Accountability Off., GAO-21-423T, Electricity Grid
6

Resilience 4 n.9 (Mar. 10, 2021).9 That cost could balloon to over $480 billion by 2100.
Id. at 4. Outages prevent customers from operating appliances, computers,
electronics, machinery, and public transportation systems in residential, commercial,
industrial, government, and healthcare settings alike. Id. Though most power
outages occur on the local distribution grid, transmission outages have wider impacts
and create greater costs. Nat’l Acads., supra, at 26. Outages in one place can
propagate across the transmission system, causing cascading blackouts. Id.
System operators closely monitor transmission infrastructure to maintain the
careful balance between electricity generation and consumption. Sensors located at
substations and transmission lines transmit a variety of data that allows operators
to monitor system health. Nat’l Acads., supra, at 26. Utilities also regularly inspect
transmission infrastructure. Flaws or other physical damage increase the risk of a
large-scale cascading blackout. Id.
UAs pose substantial risks to transmission lines and substations and the
construction and utility workers who keep them operating. Workers already risk
electrocution, falls, and other hazards when working on or near transmission
infrastructure, especially if they are working at elevation. And much of this work is
performed with the assistance of helicopters, which requires careful coordination. UA
operation near transmission lines or substations adds a new risk factor. A UA might
collide with electrified infrastructure, helicopters, or workers, which could cause
injury or death. That could also cause costly outages for customers. To adapt,
9 https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-21-423t.pdf
7

electrical workers will have to either coordinate with UA operators or wait until the
UA has passed. There is currently no requirement for coordination between UA
operators and transmission project owners, meaning UA operation threatens the
timely completion of work to maintain or restore power.
Like the electrical infrastructure already covered by the proposed rule,
transmission lines and lower-capacity substations “are critical to regional energy
supply.” 91 Fed. Reg. at 24,669. Though the proposed rule already includes some
substations, it includes only the largest, ultra-high- and extra-high-voltage
substations. Off. of Elec. Delivery & Energy Reliability, supra, at 15. But substations
with capacities as low as 115 kilovolts are also involved in high-voltage transmission.
Id. They are as critical to continued transmission of electricity as 345- and 500-
kilovolt substations.
Allowing UAFRs for high-voltage transmission lines and 115-kilovolt
substations will avoid “fatalities, injuries, and property damage . . . and economic
losses from disruption or loss of operations.” 91 Fed. Reg. at 24,653. Therefore,
proposed Section 74.88(a) should be revised to cover high-voltage transmission lines
and to reduce the minimum capacity for electrical substations to 115 kilovolts:
§ 74.88 Energy sector.
A fixed site facility satisfies the requirements under § 74.54(c) if
the facility is a(n) —
(a) Electricity facility that meets the following criteria:
(1) The facility is a power-generation facility with a combined
nameplate capacity of 500 megawatts or greater of power;
(2) The facility is an electrical substation with a capacity of
8

500kilovolts 115kilovolts or greater of power; or
(3) The facility is an electrical substation with a capacity of
345kilovolts or greater of power in the Electric Reliability Council of
Texas a high-voltage transmission line with a capacity of 115kilovolts or
greater of power.
* * *
III. Construction and Utility Crews Should Have Priority Access to
Electrical Infrastructure.
The proposed rule would allow limited access to flight-restricted airspace,
including for commercial uses, agricultural operations, and package delivery. 91 Fed.
Reg. at 24,676-77. To have access, the UA operator would have to broadcast remote
identification and transition the UAFR in the shortest amount of time practicable.
14 C.F.R. § 74.250(a) (proposed). The UA operator would also have to provide notice
to the site manager. Id. § 74.255 (proposed). That notice would be required “as soon
as reasonably possible in advance of the operation.” Id. § 74.255(c) (proposed).
The FAA requested comments “on if there are circumstances where allowed
operations should not be allowed entry and transit through a UAFR.” 91 Fed. Reg.
at 24,677. With respect to electricity infrastructure, there are. For example, utility
crews must have rapid access to transmission infrastructure to maintain or restore
power. Nat’l Acads., supra, at 112. Construction crews should also have the
flexibility to complete sensitive operations around transmission infrastructure
without the risk of interruption from UAs. The same may be true for construction in
other critical infrastructure sectors.
Therefore, proposed Section 74.250(a) should be revised to authorize owners,
proprietors, or site managers of critical infrastructure to completely disallow UA
9

operation when necessary for temporary construction, maintenance, or repairs:
§ 74.250 Allowed operations.
(a) General. Unless otherwise authorized by the Administrator
unmanned aircraft may only operate within an unmanned aircraft flight
restriction if the unmanned aircraft meets the following requirements:
(1) The unmanned aircraft broadcasts remote identification in
accordance with 14 CFR part 89.
(2) The unmanned aircraft transitions the UAFR in the shortest
amount of time practicable.
(3) The unmanned aircraft is one of the operations described in
paragraphs (b)-(f) of this section.
(4) The unmanned flight restriction is a standard unmanned
aircraft flight restriction established under § 74.5.
(5) The owner, proprietor, or facility site manager of the fixed site
facility for which FAA issued an unmanned aircraft flight restriction has
not temporarily prohibited operation of some or all unmanned aircrafts
within the unmanned aircraft flight restriction due to construction,
maintenance, or repairs.
* * *
Proposed Section 74.255 should also be revised to require notice to and
coordination with the site manager at least thirty days before operation of a UA in
the UAFR. Advance notice and coordination would enable the site manager to
disallow UA operation if necessary to prioritize construction, maintenance, or repair
of the critical infrastructure:
§ 74.255 Unmanned aircraft flight restriction access
notification and coordination.
* * *
(c) Timeline for Notification. An operator must provide notice as
soon as reasonably possible no later than thirty days in advance of the
operation; unless the operation is conducted by or on behalf of a
government agency or law enforcement acting within the scope of their
10

legal authority then notification must be provided verbally as soon as
reasonably possible and written notification within seven calendar days.
(d) Coordination. Before conducting any operation, an operator
must coordinate with the fixed site facility site manager. The fixed site
facility manager may require the operator to alter the date, approximate
time, number of unmanned aircraft, and area of operations within the
unmanned aircraft flight restriction as a condition of access to the
unmanned aircraft flight restriction. The fixed site facility manager
may also temporarily prohibit operation of some or all unmanned
aircrafts within the unmanned aircraft flight restriction due to
construction, maintenance, or repairs.
IV. Conclusion
For the foregoing reasons, the IBEW respectfully requests that the FAA modify
the proposed rule to protect the safety of its members working on critical electricity
infrastructure projects, including high-voltage transmission lines and substations.
11

comments.commenter: Comment from Air Medical Operators Association (AMOA)

We support FAA actions to implement Congressional intent to protect US critical facilities including those intersecting the emergency, health care and transport sectors.
