comments.commenter: Comment from Alliance for Chemical Distribution
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
The Honorable Bryan Bedford
Administrator
U.S. Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue SW
Washington, DC 20591
Attention Docket ID No. FAA-2026-4558
Submitted via Regulations.gov
RE: Comments in Response to FAA Section 2209 NPRM: Designation - Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility Docket
ID No. FAA-2026-4558, 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (May 6, 2026).
Dear Administrator Bedford:
The Alliance for Chemical Distribution (ACD) respectfully submits the following comments in
response to the May 6, 2026, Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) request for comments on its
Proposed Rule, Designation - Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility Docket, Docket ID No. FAA-2026-4558 (“Section 2209 rule”).
ACD supports FAA’s efforts to fulfill Congress’s intent under the FAA Extension, Safety, and
Security Act of 2016 (FESSA),1 as amended 2 and to advance the Administration’s direction under
Executive Order 14305, Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty, by establishing a regulatory
structure governing unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs) around fixed-site critical
infrastructure. A clear, administrable, and risk-based framework will allow FAA to more effectively
manage unmanned aircraft systems (UAS)-related risks while continuing to enable the safe
integration of unmanned technologies into the National Airspace System (NAS).
Except for emergency, public-safety, or other operations expressly approved by the facility, no UAS
should operate over a fixed site facility that uses, manufactures, stores, transports, possesses or
distributes one or more hazardous-release chemicals, unless the flight is conducted by the facility
owner or operator, on its behalf, or under its prior authorization and continuing coordination.
Compliance with generally applicable FAA operating rules, including Remote ID requirements,
should not by itself confer a right to enter or transit airspace protected by a UAFR.
While earlier incidents cited by FAA accurately reflect baseline risks, the current environment is
materially different and ever-changing. Advances in UAS capabilities, combined with global
1 FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016
2 FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024

examples of their use against industrial infrastructure, demonstrate that risks are evolving rapidly.
These developments underscore the importance of establishing a proactive regulatory framework.
ACD strongly supports timely finalization of the Section 2209 rule so that both government and
industry are equipped with tools to address risks before a major incident occurs.
For ACD members—who represent the entire chemical distribution supply chain—the threat
environment has changed significantly. Unauthorized UAS activity is no longer sporadic or
incidental, and facilities are experiencing increasing frequency of incursions. These activities
elevate operational risk, create safety hazards, and generate concern among facility personnel.
Modern UAS capabilities, combined with global examples of their use against industrial assets,
underscore the need for proactive measures. While regulatory tools alone will not eliminate
malicious use, they are a necessary foundation for enforcement, deterrence of non-compliant
operators, and coordination with security partners. ACD strongly encourages the timely finalization
of the rule to ensure that action is taken before a significant incident compels a reactive response.
About ACD and the Chemical Distribution Industry
ACD supports and champions the chemical distribution experts the world depends on to safely,
reliably, responsibly, and sustainably move the chemical products essential to our daily lives. ACD’s
more than 400 chemical distribution industry members are primarily small, multi-generational
family-owned businesses. They provide critical chemical products to more than 750,000 end users.
As leaders of the over $41 billion chemical distribution industry, ACD member companies possess
extensive expertise, a strong commitment to safety and sustainability, and access to a vast array of
resources necessary to ensure chemicals are transported safely and responsibly whenever and
wherever needed. ACD owners and operators have a personal stake in the health, safety, and
security of their employees, companies, and communities. They demonstrate their dedication by
strictly following the highest standards in quality, safety, sustainability, and performance embodied
in the ACD Responsible DistributionTM framework.
The comprehensive Code of Management Practice, a core requirement of Responsible Distribution,
obligates each member company to maintain an active, continuously improving safety
management program focused on reducing risk and preventing incidents across all aspects of
chemical handling and transportation. This commitment is reinforced through strong employee
engagement, active participation in local communities, including collaboration with Local
Emergency Planning Committees, and rigorous adherence to a wide range of federal, state, and
local regulatory requirements.
These efforts enable ACD members to safely and reliably deliver essential chemicals to sectors
including agriculture, water treatment, pharmaceuticals, construction, energy, electronics, and
consumer goods. Because disruptions can quickly cascade across industries, chemical
distribution is foundational to U.S. manufacturing, critical infrastructure, economic growth, and
global competitiveness.
ACD members strengthen this network by ensuring essential materials are delivered safely,
securely, and efficiently to support critical operations and communities nationwide.
2

Importance of UAFRs to the Chemical Distribution Industry
ACD-member facilities operate complex, high-hazard environments that depend on predictable
and secure operating conditions. ACD members therefore do not support UAS operations over their
facilities unless the operations are conducted by the facility, on its behalf, or pursuant to its prior
authorization and continuing coordination. Any other aerial activity, whether unintentional or
deliberate, introduces unacceptable levels of uncertainty and can have cascading impacts on
public safety, raw material supply, and economic stability.
UAS incursions present multiple overlapping risks, including:
• Observation and mapping of sensitive assets and processes;
• Disruption to operations or interference with equipment;
• Delivery of illicit or dangerous payloads;
• Cyber-enabled exploitation of physical or digital systems; and
• Physical impact events that could trigger cascading consequences, such as spills of
hazardous substances or explosions as a result of an unplanned release.
Even earlier incidents cited by FAA, such as accidental drone crashes near refinery operations and
federal warnings regarding chemical facility targeting, reflect the types of risks that persist today.
However, current conditions are substantially more complex. Advances in autonomy, payload
capacity, and coordination have increased the potential severity of both accidental and intentional
incidents.
Congress explicitly identified chemical facilities in Section 2209 of FESSA as locations warranting
consideration for airspace protections. The rule should preserve that intent by ensuring these
facilities have a viable pathway to obtain UAFRs where warranted by risk.
Changing Threat Landscape
Compared to the conditions that existed when earlier incidents were documented, today’s UAS
environment presents greater challenges. These include systems that are more capable and widely
available, flight operations that are more advanced and include coordinated multi-drone activity,
and barriers to entry which have declined as a result of changing technologies or failure to
reauthorize standards which enforced facility security measures, such as the Chemical Facility
Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) program.
The CFATS program allowed CISA to identify 3,200 U.S. based facilities as high-risk by analyzing
increases and decreases in chemical inventory. CISA effectively monitored these facilities to
ensure security was maintained. Although CFATS expired in July 2023, the threat of chemical
terrorism remains. ACD finds it imperative that UAFRs become an accessible option to aid in
security focused on anti-terrorism for chemical facilities nationwide.
International developments further illustrate the potential consequences of inaction. Energy and
industrial infrastructure have become routine targets in overseas conflicts due to their strategic
value. While these events have occurred outside the U.S., they demonstrate how rapidly emerging
technologies can be applied to disrupt critical systems.
3

These evolving risks should inform FAA’s approach. A forward-looking framework must consider
not only historical incidents, but also credible future scenarios.
Role of UAFRs Within a Broader Security Strategy
ACD views UAFRs as a critical element within a broader, layered framework for managing risks
associated with UAS operations. Protecting critical infrastructure from evolving aerial threats
requires a comprehensive approach that extends beyond any single tool or regulatory measure.
This approach must include improving awareness among UAS operators regarding sensitive
airspace, establishing clear and enforceable limitations around high-risk facilities, and ensuring
that appropriate mechanisms exist to support timely response and enforcement actions when
unauthorized activity occurs. It also requires ongoing evaluation of mitigation authorities and
capabilities as technology and threat conditions continue to evolve.
Within this broader continuum, UAFRs serve an essential function by clearly defining protected
airspace around eligible facilities and establishing facility control as the default condition for
access. By creating a legally recognized boundary, UAFRs should enable facility operators and law
enforcement to distinguish facility-operated, facility-contracted, or facility-authorized flights from
all other operations. Unless an emergency or other narrowly defined public-interest exception
applies, a third-party UAS should not enter or transit the protected airspace without the facility
operator’s prior authorization and continuing coordination. This clarity supports more effective
situational awareness and enables appropriate action within existing legal authorities.
ACD further notes that the designation of a UAFR may play a meaningful role in informing future
policy decisions, including the evolution of counter-UAS authorities. Given this potential, it is
important that the framework for UAFR eligibility is sufficiently inclusive and responsive to real-
world risk conditions, ensuring that facilities facing credible security threats can access these
protections.
Benefits of UAFRs for Operational Innovation
In addition to improving safety and security, UAFRs have the potential to support advanced UAS
applications within protected environments.
By reducing uncontrolled third-party activity and clarifying airspace status, UAFRs can create
more predictable operating conditions for:
• Beyond visual line of sight operations;
• Automated or dock-based UAS systems;
• Continuous monitoring and inspection programs; and
• AI-enabled diagnostics and surveillance.
These use-cases can enhance safety, reduce operational risk, and improve efficiency across
industrial facilities. Improved situational awareness and clearer airspace controls can enable
facility operators to deploy UAS technologies with greater confidence while maintaining
compliance with FAA requirements.
4

Need for a Practical, Risk-Based Framework
For the regulatory framework to achieve its intended purpose, it must be grounded in the practical
realities faced by facility operators. ACD believes the final rule should prioritize a consequence-
based approach to risk that reflects the potential impact of an incident, rather than relying on
overly prescriptive or rigid criteria that may not capture real-world conditions. It is also important
that the rule aligns with existing federal regulatory programs to avoid duplicative requirements
that add burden without improving safety or security outcomes.
Given the diversity of critical infrastructure operations, the framework should provide sufficient
flexibility to accommodate different security postures, operational models, and resource
constraints across facilities. At the same time, the process for applying for and maintaining a UAFR
should be transparent, predictable, and efficient so that applicants clearly understand
expectations and can comply without unnecessary delay. Absent these considerations, overly
complex or burdensome requirements could discourage participation and limit access to UAFRs
for the very facilities that would benefit most from these protections.
Coordination with Security Agencies and Industry Stakeholders
ACD recognizes and appreciates FAA’s collaboration with Sector Risk Management Agencies during
development of the proposed rule. Continued coordination will be essential to ensure that the final
framework reflects real-world threat conditions and operational constraints. Ongoing engagement
with federal security partners, industry stakeholders, and UAS operators will be important for
refining implementation, protecting sensitive information, and minimizing unintended impacts on
legitimate operations. ACD encourages FAA to host regular stakeholder meetings, consider holding
joint exercises, and establish feedback mechanisms, all of which can help ensure implementation
remains effective, transparent, and responsive to operational realities. ACD also emphasizes the
importance of broad outreach across sectors. Clear communication of eligibility criteria,
application procedures, and operational requirements will be necessary to ensure widespread
understanding and compliance.
Transparency and Communication with Facility Operators
ACD supports FAA’s efforts to maintain ongoing communication with applicants and UAFR holders
throughout the lifecycle of the designation. Regular and transparent engagement between FAA and
facility operators can improve the efficiency of application review processes, enhance the quality
of security assessments, support effective coordination for authorized operations within UAFRs,
and facilitate timely and accurate notification processes. Given the active role that facility security
teams play in monitoring and responding to UAS activity, clear communication channels are
essential to successful implementation.
NPRM Refinements Needed to Strengthen Protection of Critical Infrastructure
§ 74.6. Special Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction Designation
The proposed rule introduces a Special Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (Special UAFR)
designation for locations presenting credible safety or security risks, generally tied to federal
ownership or sponsorship by a federal security or intelligence agency. The proposal also
contemplates that facilities currently subject to 14 CFR § 99.7 restrictions would retain those
5

protections and transition into the Special UAFR framework. While ACD supports the intent behind
establishing a more robust designation for high-risk sites, it is essential that FAA adopt a flexible
and inclusive approach when determining eligibility for Special UAFRs.
ACD emphasizes that many privately owned critical infrastructure facilities face risks that are
comparable to those at federally sponsored sites. Facilities regulated under established federal
security programs—such as the Maritime Transportation Security Act, Transportation Security
Administration Security Directives, or those that historically fell under the CFATS program—have
already been identified as high-risk locations due to the materials they handle or the role they play
in national security and economic stability. These facilities should be considered strong
candidates for Special UAFR designation given their demonstrated risk profiles.
More broadly, ACD notes that private-sector facilities have experienced credible UAS-related
threats in the absence of formal federal sponsorship. As currently structured, the Special UAFR
framework could lead to inconsistent outcomes if access is limited primarily to federally affiliated
sites without clear pathways for similarly situated private infrastructure. The preamble’s
discussion of critical infrastructure—defined as systems and assets, whether physical or virtual, so
vital to the United States that the incapacity or destruction of such systems and assets would have
a debilitating effect on security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or any
combination of those matters—closely mirrors the conditions described for Special UAFR
eligibility. This overlap underscores the need for a more cohesive and accessible framework.
To ensure consistent and equitable access, ACD recommends that FAA establish clear eligibility
criteria, defined sponsorship pathways, transparent review timelines, and robust procedures for
handling sensitive information. At a minimum, facilities subject to federal security regulations—
whether current or legacy—should be presumptively eligible for consideration under the Special
UAFR program. Without these clarifications, high-consequence private facilities may face barriers
to obtaining the level of protection warranted by their risk profile, particularly when they are
unable to secure sponsorship through existing § 99.7 processes.
By adopting a more flexible and clearly defined approach, FAA can ensure that the Special UAFR
framework fully supports the protection of both public and private critical infrastructure in
alignment with the intent of Section 2209.
§ 74.20. Obligation to Update
The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) proposes ongoing obligations for facilities to update
application information within five business days and to provide annual—and in some cases more
frequent—reporting on UAS activity. While ACD supports the FAA’s need for timely and accurate
information, the current approach could impose unnecessary administrative burden if applied
broadly to routine or non-substantive changes. For many facilities, particularly those already
managing complex regulatory requirements, the absence of a materiality threshold and the
potential for open-ended interim reporting requests create uncertainty and resource strain
without a commensurate security benefit.
To address this, ACD recommends that FAA focus reporting obligations on material changes that
directly affect a UAFR’s eligibility, scope, or administration, such as modifications to boundaries,
facility operational status, or key points of contact. In addition, FAA should extend the five-
business-day update timeline to a more practical reporting window, establish standardized
templates for both interim and annual submissions, and provide secure pathways for transmitting
sensitive information. These adjustments would allow FAA to obtain actionable data while
6

ensuring that compliance expectations remain clear, consistent, and operationally achievable for
facility owners and operators.
Furthermore, ACD is concerned that the proposed update requirement does not clearly identify the
triggering event for reporting changes associated with facility expansions, modifications, or new
infrastructure development. For example, if a distributor constructs a new tank farm, it is unclear
whether an update would be required when construction begins, when construction is completed,
when tanks are first filled, or when the facility becomes fully operational once again. Because
projects of this nature frequently span months or years, the lack of a defined reporting trigger
creates uncertainty regarding compliance with the proposed five-business-day notification
requirement. ACD therefore recommends that FAA establish clear, objective update triggers tied
to a material operational milestone, such as the date a new asset or facility component becomes
operational and relevant to the UAFR designation. Providing defined reporting thresholds and
triggering events would improve consistency across regulated entities, reduce unnecessary
administrative burden, and ensure that FAA receives information that is both meaningful and
actionable.
§ 74.50. General
The NPRM proposes that applicants submit required information through a web-based UAFR
Module in a form and manner determined by the Administrator. While ACD supports the use of a
centralized platform to streamline the application process, it is important that the scope of
information collected through this system be carefully tailored to balance efficiency with the
protection of sensitive data. Without explicit safeguards, the submission and storage of this
information could introduce increased risks associated with disclosure, cybersecurity, and
operational security.
ACD emphasizes that the information required for UAFR applications should be limited to what is
directly necessary for FAA to evaluate eligibility, risk, and operational impact. Collecting excessive
or highly detailed facility, operational, or security information not only increases administrative
burden, but also introduces additional risks associated with the storage and handling of sensitive
data. Broad or overly detailed submission requirements could create vulnerabilities if such
information is accessed, retained, or transmitted without sufficient safeguards.
To address these concerns, ACD strongly recommends that FAA clearly establish and
communicate robust protections for all information submitted through the UAFR process. This
should include explicit treatment of confidential business information (CBI), security-sensitive
information, and other operational details as protected from public disclosure to the fullest extent
permitted by law, including appropriate exemption from release under the Freedom of Information
Act. Given the sensitive nature of these submissions, it is essential that applicants have
confidence that their information will be handled securely and not exposed in a manner that could
create additional risk.
In addition, ACD strongly urges FAA not to require the submission of facility security plans,
vulnerability assessments, or other detailed security documentation as a condition of obtaining or
maintaining a UAFR. Such a requirement would create a significant disincentive for critical
infrastructure owners and operators to participate in the program and could ultimately undermine
the rule’s intended security benefits by discouraging otherwise eligible facilities from seeking
airspace protections. Moreover, the collection and transmission of detailed security plans
presents its own security risks, as these documents often contain highly sensitive information
regarding facility layouts, protective measures, access controls, and potential vulnerabilities. FAA
should instead limit submissions to information that is directly necessary to evaluate eligibility and
7

UAS-related risk, relying on certifications or high-level attestations, where appropriate, rather
than requiring disclosure of sensitive security plans. ACD believes that a streamlined approach will
both protect sensitive information and encourage broader participation by critical infrastructure
facilities, thereby enhancing the overall effectiveness of the UAFR program.
ACD also notes that existing federal programs utilize established protections for sensitive
infrastructure information, such as the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information framework.
Applying comparable protections within the UAFR process would further ensure that sensitive
submissions are properly safeguarded while enabling facility owners and operators to provide the
information necessary to support their applications.
By incorporating strong information-protection measures and maintaining a targeted,
proportionate approach to data collection, FAA can support both the security of critical
infrastructure facilities and the successful implementation of the UAFR program.
§§ 74.54, 74.81, Appendix A. Eligible Facilities and Chemical Sector Considerations
The NPRM establishes eligibility criteria for UAFRs based on a combination of factors, including
fixed-site status, designation as critical infrastructure, sector-specific considerations, the
presence of protective security measures, identification of vulnerable assets, and the potential for
regional or national-level impacts. For the chemical sector specifically, FAA proposes to rely on
the CFATS Appendix A list of Chemicals of Interest (COIs), including associated concentration
thresholds and screening threshold quantities, to determine eligibility for facilities handling
hazardous-release chemicals.
ACD supports FAA’s recognition of the chemical sector as critical infrastructure. ACD also
generally supports the proposed definition of a chemical sector fixed site facility as one that “uses,
manufactures, stores, transports, possesses or distributes one or more hazardous-release
chemicals at or above the minimum concentration percentages and screening threshold
quantities.” ACD agrees that the Appendix A framework can serve as a useful starting point for
identifying facilities that may present significant hazards. However, reliance on Appendix A
thresholds as a primary eligibility screen raises concerns regarding both flexibility and relevance.
The CFATS framework was developed for a different regulatory purpose and has not been
comprehensively updated to reflect current chemical manufacturing, storage, and distribution
practices, evolving risk management approaches, or the unique considerations associated with
UAS-related threats. As a result, strict adherence to these thresholds may exclude facilities that
present meaningful risk while including others based on criteria that do not directly translate to
aviation safety or airspace management considerations.
Chemical sector operations are highly dynamic and often involve complex, integrated processes
and distributed infrastructure. A facility’s risk profile is influenced not only by the presence or
quantity of listed chemicals, but also by site-specific factors such as process design, proximity to
populated areas, interdependencies within supply chains, and potential offsite consequences in
the event of a release, fire, or explosion. In addition, facilities may handle hazardous materials at
levels below CFATS thresholds while still experiencing repeated or credible UAS incursions that
elevate overall risk. ACD believes these realities cannot be fully captured through a static list or
fixed numerical thresholds alone.
ACD also emphasizes that the chemical sector is continuously evolving, with companies
developing and deploying new chemistries that may not appear on legacy lists such as Appendix A
8

but still present comparable hazards. Without a mechanism to account for these emerging
materials, the eligibility framework risks becoming outdated and unable to address new or
unanticipated risks. ACD recommends that FAA establish a process allowing facilities handling
novel or emerging chemicals to demonstrate eligibility through alternative, risk-based
justifications. This approach would ensure that the UAFR framework remains responsive to
innovation within the chemical sector and capable of addressing evolving risks over time.
To address these concerns, ACD recommends that FAA avoid applying numerical thresholds to
Appendix A chemicals for purposes of UAFR eligibility. A facility that manufactures, stores,
transports, possesses, or distributes any chemical included on the Appendix A list should be
eligible for consideration, regardless of the quantity or concentration present. Eligibility should
focus on the presence of the listed chemical and the potential safety, security, and consequence
risks associated with unauthorized UAS activity, rather than thresholds developed for a different
regulatory program. FAA should also preserve flexibility to account for new and emerging
chemistries that may not yet appear on Appendix A but could present comparable hazards or
critical infrastructure concerns as chemical technologies and supply chains evolve.
In addition, ACD encourages FAA to look to existing, actively maintained regulatory programs—
such as the Environmental Protection Agency’s Risk Management Program—which include
consequence analysis, hazard modeling, and risk management requirements that are more directly
aligned with evaluating potential release scenarios and their impacts. Leveraging these
frameworks, where appropriate, could provide a more current and operationally relevant basis for
assessing eligibility.
By incorporating flexibility beyond rigid thresholds and aligning eligibility with real-world risk
conditions, FAA can ensure that the UAFR program effectively captures high-consequence
chemical facilities and fulfills the intent of Section 2209 to protect critical infrastructure from
emerging threats.
§ 74.56 Protective Security
The NPRM proposes that facilities seeking a UAFR demonstrate certain baseline protective
measures, including restricted access, security personnel, monitoring capabilities, and the ability
to receive Remote ID broadcasts in the vicinity of the facility. While ACD supports the objective of
improving situational awareness, the proposed Remote ID-related expectations raise significant
practical considerations for facility operators. Implementing and maintaining Remote ID collection
and monitoring capabilities introduces technical, cybersecurity, data management, and cost
challenges that may not align with the diverse operational environments of industrial facilities. In
particular, overly prescriptive requirements—such as fixed sensor standards, undefined data
retention expectations, or expansive reporting obligations—risk driving investments in
technologies that may not be proportional to site-specific risks or compatible with existing
security systems and workflows.
These challenges are especially pronounced for small and mid-sized operators, which often lack
dedicated resources to procure, integrate, and manage Remote ID detection systems. Unlike
larger enterprises, these facilities must operate within constrained budgets and staffing levels,
while balancing multiple regulatory requirements. As a result, mandating comprehensive Remote
ID detection capabilities could inadvertently create barriers to participation in the UAFR
framework for facilities that nonetheless face meaningful security risks. To address these
concerns, ACD recommends that FAA establish clear and narrowly tailored expectations for any
9

Remote ID detection-related obligations, including defined data elements, retention periods,
reporting triggers, and submission formats. FAA should avoid mandating specific technical
configurations and instead provide flexibility for facilities to implement scalable, cost-effective
solutions, including the use of third-party or shared services, appropriate to their risk profile. In
addition, ACD encourages FAA to consider phasing in more advanced detection or data
requirements only after a facility has been granted a UAFR designation, rather than as a
prerequisite for eligibility. These adjustments would improve feasibility, reduce unnecessary
burden, and better align the rule with real-world operational capabilities while still advancing FAA’s
security objectives.
§ 74.58. Lateral Boundary
The NPRM proposes that UAFR lateral boundaries be narrowly defined, limited to the property lines
of the fixed-site facility, and not extend into areas already subject to permanent airspace
restrictions. While ACD appreciates FAA’s intent to minimize unnecessary encroachment into
navigable airspace, a strict property-line limitation does not fully reflect the operational and risk
realities of many critical infrastructure facilities. In practice, significant vulnerabilities often
extend beyond formal property boundaries, including process units located near perimeters,
interdependent systems that span multiple parcels, approach corridors that could be exploited by
unmanned aircraft, and consequence zones associated with potential incidents. As a result, a
boundary tied exclusively to property lines may leave critical areas insufficiently protected.
ACD emphasizes that Section 2209 directs FAA to consider restrictions for unmanned aircraft
operations in “close proximity” to eligible facilities, which supports a more flexible, risk-based
interpretation of appropriate airspace boundaries. To better align the rule with both statutory
intent and real-world conditions, ACD recommends that FAA allow for the inclusion of limited
buffer zones beyond facility property boundaries, where justified by demonstrated vulnerability
and potential consequence. Such an approach would enable applicants, in coordination with FAA
and relevant stakeholders, to propose boundaries that more accurately reflect operational risk
while maintaining appropriate oversight and consideration of impacts to other airspace users. A
risk-informed buffer option—applied judiciously and supported by clear justification—would
strengthen the effectiveness of UAFRs without unnecessarily restricting access to the NAS.
§ 74.64. UAS Security and Incident Response Plans
The NPRM proposes that applicants provide detailed information regarding facility security
measures, including descriptions of security perimeters and UAS-specific incident response
plans. While ACD recognizes the importance of demonstrating that facilities maintain appropriate
security capabilities, the level of detail contemplated raises significant concerns related to the
protection of sensitive information. Security plans, perimeter details, and incident response
procedures often contain highly confidential operational information that, if broadly shared or
stored within centralized systems, could introduce unintended vulnerabilities.
ACD is particularly concerned that requiring detailed disclosures as part of the application process
may deter facilities from providing complete information or discourage participation in the UAFR
framework altogether. It is critical that any submission requirements account for the need to
10

safeguard sensitive security information while still enabling FAA to assess whether applicants
meet the objectives of § 74.64.
To strike this balance, ACD recommends that FAA allow applicants to demonstrate compliance
with these requirements through alternative mechanisms that reduce the need for detailed
disclosure. Specifically, facilities should be permitted to provide executive-level certifications or
formal attestations from corporate leadership affirming that the facility maintains layered security
controls, defined security perimeters, and established UAS incident response procedures
consistent with regulatory expectations. This approach would allow FAA to verify that appropriate
safeguards are in place while minimizing exposure of site-specific vulnerabilities.
Adopting a more flexible approach to this requirement would support the dual objectives of
maintaining strong security practices and encouraging participation in the UAFR program, without
creating additional risks associated with the handling of sensitive information.
§ 74.66. Demonstration of Need
The NPRM proposes that applicants demonstrate the need for a UAFR by providing information on
historical UAS traffic patterns over the previous 24 months, along with facility-specific
vulnerability analyses, consequence assessments, and descriptions of how the UAFR would
integrate into existing security programs. While ACD supports a risk-informed approach to
evaluating need, the proposed requirements do not fully reflect the current capabilities and
operational realities of chemical manufacturing, storage, and distribution facilities.
Many facilities do not yet have access to mature, standardized, or consistently reliable UAS
detection systems, and therefore lack comprehensive historical data on UAS activity. Where such
data does exist, it may be incomplete, inconsistent, or of limited operational value. Requiring
extensive historical analysis as a precondition for eligibility risks placing undue burden on
applicants and may disadvantage facilities that face credible risks but have not yet had the
resources or capability to implement advanced detection technologies.
ACD is also concerned that requiring detailed submissions of facility-specific vulnerabilities,
security procedures, and consequence modeling could result in the aggregation of highly sensitive
information within centralized systems. Such aggregation presents significant cybersecurity and
operational security risks, particularly where the information involves critical infrastructure assets
and potential points of vulnerability.
To address these concerns, ACD recommends that FAA adopt a more flexible, risk-based approach
to demonstrating the need for a UAFR. Applicants should be permitted to rely on alternative forms
of justification that better align with sector realities, including existing risk assessments,
consequence-based analyses, and high-level descriptions of vulnerabilities, as well as executive
certifications or attestations developed in coordination with the appropriate Sector Risk
Management Agency. In addition, FAA should significantly narrow or eliminate expectations
related to historical UAS traffic data, recognizing the current limitations in detection capabilities
across the sector.
By reducing reliance on rigid data requirements and avoiding the centralized collection of detailed
vulnerability information, FAA can create a more practical and secure process that still enables
11

effective evaluation of risk while encouraging broader participation from facilities that would
benefit from UAFR protections.
§ 74.95. Transportation-Related Chemical Operations
The NPRM outlines eligibility for certain transportation-related facilities, including rail-secured
areas and other infrastructure with defined security controls. While ACD recognizes the
importance of these categories, the proposed approach does not fully account for the operational
realities of chemical manufacturing, storage, and distribution systems, which are often highly
integrated across facility boundaries.
Chemical operations do not function as isolated sites. Manufacturing facilities, storage terminals,
and distribution hubs are typically supported by interconnected infrastructure such as rail loading
and unloading areas, transfer systems, tank farms, and control systems that operate as part of a
unified process. These assets are essential to the safe handling, storage, and movement of
chemicals and are often located adjacent to or physically separate from the primary facility
footprint. Limiting UAFR consideration to narrowly defined facility boundaries without accounting
for these interconnected components risks leaving critical portions of the operational system
exposed to unauthorized UAS activity.
ACD therefore encourages FAA to clarify that transportation-related assets supporting chemical
manufacturing, storage, and distribution operations may be included within a UAFR where those
assets are operationally linked to the facility seeking protection. This should encompass
infrastructure such as rail spurs, storage tanks located on connected parcels, process control
systems, and other supporting components that are integral to the facility’s operations.
Recognizing the interconnected nature of chemical operations will ensure that UAFRs can be
applied in a manner that meaningfully reflects real-world risks and provides comprehensive
protection across the full scope of facility operations.
§ 74.250. Allowed Operations
The NPRM proposes to allow certain unmanned aircraft operations conducted under Parts 91, 107,
108, 135, and 137 to transit standard UAFRs, provided they meet requirements such as broadcasting
Remote ID, minimizing time within the restricted area, and complying with other applicable
conditions. While ACD supports FAA’s efforts to maintain access to the NAS for authorized
operators, a generalized access framework does not fully account for the unique safety and
operational risks presented within chemical manufacturing, storage, and distribution
environments.
Facilities operating hazardous processes must manage a range of site-specific risks, including the
potential for loss of control of a UAS, collisions with sensitive equipment, electromagnetic
interference with control systems, and ignition hazards in areas with flammable materials. In these
environments, even a minor UAS incident can have significant safety, environmental, and
operational consequences, including cascading impacts beyond the immediate facility. As such,
open or routine transit of third-party UAS operations—even those conducted by otherwise
compliant operators—may not be appropriate in all areas or under all conditions.
ACD also notes that the NPRM relies, in part, on existing pilot certification and security vetting
processes to justify access to UAFRs. However, pilot certification, operator vetting, Remote ID
compliance, or general authorization to operate within the NAS do not establish that a particular
12

operation is safe or appropriate over a specific chemical facility. These credentials address the
qualifications of the operator, but do not account for facility-specific operational, safety, or
security risks, nor do they substitute for the facility operator's authorization. ACD members
maintain responsibility for the safety, security, and continuity of operations at their facilities and
therefore must retain primary authority to determine whether non-emergency UAS operations
may occur over their sites. Current authorization frameworks may provide insufficient clarity to
facility operators and UAS pilots regarding these limitations. Additionally, while FAA references
forthcoming frameworks such as Part 108, these provisions are not yet finalized and should not be
relied upon as a basis for determining access standards at this stage.
To address these concerns, ACD recommends that FAA prohibit routine third-party transit through
UAFRs covering chemical facilities. Non-emergency access should be limited to operations
conducted by the facility owner or operator, on the facility’s behalf under contract or other agency
relationship, or pursuant to the facility operator’s express prior authorization and continuing
coordination. A generalized claim of operational convenience, compliance with Parts 91, 107, 108,
135, or 137, or a direction to minimize transit time should not override the facility operator’s
determination that an overflight presents an unacceptable site-specific risk.
Facility owners and operators are best positioned to understand site-specific risks and should
have authority to approve, condition, delay, or deny non-emergency UAS access based on
operational needs, maintenance activities, emergency response situations, or elevated security
conditions. Notice alone is not consent, and the absence of a facility response should not be
treated as authorization. This framework should preserve flexibility for facility-controlled
operations: UAS activities conducted by the facility, by a contractor or agent acting on its behalf,
or under its express authorization and continuing coordination—such as inspection, maintenance,
safety, or emergency response functions—should be accommodated through appropriate
exemptions or operational allowances, including relief from rigid transit requirements such as the
“shortest time practicable” standard when consistent with safe and coordinated operations.
Any exception to facility authorization should be narrowly defined and limited to exigent public-
safety, national-security, law-enforcement, or emergency-response operations for which advance
coordination is impracticable. Even in those circumstances, the operator should notify the facility
as early as operationally feasible, minimize exposure to hazardous process areas, and coordinate
with the facility incident command or security function when conditions permit. FAA should not
create broad exceptions for routine package delivery, infrastructure inspection for unrelated third
parties, aerial photography, mapping, data collection, or transit convenience.
By incorporating a more flexible, risk-informed approach to allowed operations, FAA can better
align the UAFR framework with the operational realities of chemical facilities while maintaining an
appropriate balance between access to the NAS and protection of critical infrastructure.
§ 74.255. UAFR Access Notification
The NPRM proposes that authorized UAS operators provide advance notice to facility site
managers, including detailed operational and identifying information. ACD supports improved
coordination and situational awareness, but notification should not create or imply a right of
access. For non-emergency third-party operations, submission of information should be treated
as a request for facility authorization, and the operation should not proceed unless the facility
affirmatively grants that authorization. The absence of an objection from a facility should not be
construed as approval. A notification-based framework that permits access absent facility
13

consent does not adequately address the risks presented by chemical manufacturing, storage, and
distribution environments.
ACD recommends that FAA adopt a more tailored, risk-informed approach to notification
requirements. In high-hazard environments, such as chemical facilities where UAS operations
could introduce risks related to loss of control, electromagnetic interference, ignition sources, or
operational disruption, enhanced advance notice and coordination should be required for third-
party operators. At the same time, routine operations conducted by, on behalf of, or authorized
directly by the facility should not be subject to repetitive manual notification requirements.
Instead, FAA should enable streamlined processes that recognize the controlled nature of these
activities.
To support this approach, ACD encourages FAA to establish a tiered notification framework that
differentiates between higher-risk third-party operations and lower-risk, facility-managed
activities. This framework should include the ability to implement automated or recurring
authorization mechanisms, such as pre-approved operator credentials and Remote ID identifiers,
allowing routine operations to proceed without duplicative notification burdens. Integration of
these capabilities into existing facility security operations’ workflows would further enhance
efficiency and situational awareness.
ACD also emphasizes the importance of providing facilities with a reasonable implementation
timeframe following UAFR approval. Facilities should have sufficient time to evaluate, procure,
and integrate appropriate Remote ID detection technologies that align with site-specific
operational needs, cybersecurity considerations, and existing infrastructure. Given the evolving
nature of detection technologies, facilities should retain flexibility to adopt solutions that are both
effective and proportionate, rather than being compelled to make accelerated procurement
decisions solely to meet immediate compliance requirements.
Finally, ACD underscores that enhanced notification mechanisms should not be interpreted as an
endorsement of routine overflight access. Except for narrowly defined emergency, public-safety,
law-enforcement, or national-security operations, UAS activity within a UAFR should be limited to
operations conducted by the facility, on its behalf, or pursuant to the facility's express
authorization and continuing coordination. FAA should make clear that compliance with
notification requirements, Remote ID requirements, or other operational rules does not
independently authorize access to a protected facility's airspace.
§ 74.70. Environmental Impact
The NPRM proposes that applicants provide information on environmental resources and, in some
cases, support site-specific analysis or National Environmental Policy Act-related documentation.
ACD is concerned that this approach extends beyond the intended scope of UAFR designations,
which are focused on airspace safety and security. Requiring individual facility applicants to
conduct or fund environmental analyses could delay urgently needed protections, duplicate
responsibilities already assigned to other federal agencies, and impose burdens unrelated to
facility operations. ACD therefore recommends that FAA address environmental considerations
through its own interagency coordination processes, rather than requiring site-specific analyses
from applicants as part of the UAFR process.
Maintaining Operational Use of UAS
It is critical that any restrictions on unauthorized UAS activity do not inadvertently limit beneficial
uses of UAS by facility operators. ACD members rely on unmanned aircraft for a range of critical
functions, including equipment inspection and maintenance; environmental monitoring and
14

compliance; emergency response and safety assessments; and operational efficiency and
reliability improvements. The final rule should ensure that facilities operating within a UAFR retain
appropriate authority and flexibility to conduct these activities safely and efficiently.
Implementation, Application Process, and Information Handling
Following issuance of a final rule, FAA should anticipate a substantial volume of UAFR applications
across multiple critical infrastructure sectors. To ensure consistent and timely implementation, it
will be important for FAA to establish clear, practical guidance that assists applicants throughout
the lifecycle of the UAFR process.
ACD encourages FAA to develop comprehensive implementation materials that outline
expectations for eligibility, documentation, and ongoing compliance. Clear guidance will be
particularly valuable not only for larger organizations with dedicated compliance resources, but
especially for smaller operators that may lack the capacity to navigate a complex or iterative
application process. Providing step-by-step clarity will help ensure that the benefits of the rule are
accessible across the full spectrum of eligible facilities.
As previously stated, ACD supports FAA’s development of a centralized, web-based UAFR Module to
manage application submissions and related activities. A streamlined digital platform can
significantly improve efficiency by allowing applicants to submit required materials, track
application status, and manage updates in a single location. To further enhance usability, FAA
should incorporate standardized templates within the system for key elements such as risk
descriptions, geographic boundaries, and supporting justifications. These templates would
promote consistency in submissions, reduce ambiguity, and facilitate more efficient review by FAA
personnel.
In addition to improving efficiency, the use of standardized templates would help minimize
administrative burden and support compliance with federal requirements governing information
collection. Consistent formatting and structured inputs will allow both applicants and FAA
reviewers to focus on substantive risk considerations rather than procedural formatting issues.
ACD emphasizes the importance of establishing clear and secure processes for submitting
sensitive information. UAFR applications may require facilities to provide proprietary data,
security-related details, or other information that must be protected from public disclosure. While
FAA has acknowledged that some applicants may provide classified or CBI to supplement their
submission, and adds that the draft Advisory Circular, Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions, offers
detailed instructions. However, these detailed instructions are missing from the draft proposal,
and it is essential that FAA provides secure submission procedures for CBI, especially within a final
rule that requires the disclosure of sensitive information from applicants to provide eligibility.
Ensuring robust safeguards for confidential and sensitive materials will be essential to maintaining
industry trust and enabling applicants to provide complete and accurate information in support of
their requests.
Moreover, ACD encourages FAA to provide reasonable implementation timelines and continue to
engage with critical infrastructure owners and operators as Section 2209 is implemented. A
15

phased approach will allow facilities to align internal procedures, acquire technology, review
cybersecurity, train personnel, and integrate security operations with the final rule’s requirements.
Finally, ACD recognizes that the proposed rule contemplates a public notice-and-comment
process for UAFR applications; however, we have significant concerns regarding the breadth of
information that may be made publicly available through such notices. To the extent FAA
determines that public notice is necessary, ACD strongly urges the agency to strictly limit the level
of detail disclosed in Federal Register postings and related materials. Information describing
facility locations, operational characteristics, vulnerabilities, or the basis for requesting protection
could create unintended security risks if broadly disseminated.
ACD believes that a more controlled review process—such as one limited to registered operators,
vetted stakeholders, or other mechanisms that restrict access to sensitive information—would
better balance transparency with security. Protecting the safety of the NAS and the integrity of
critical infrastructure must remain paramount, and unnecessarily wide distribution of sensitive
details could undermine those objectives.
Conclusion
ACD strongly supports FAA's efforts to implement Section 2209 through a clear, risk-informed
UAFR framework that protects critical infrastructure while preserving safe and beneficial facility-
controlled UAS operations. For the chemical distribution industry, effective UAFRs must establish
a clear default rule: except for narrowly defined emergency, public-safety, law-enforcement, or
national-security operations, no UAS should operate over an ACD member facility unless the flight
is conducted by the facility, on its behalf, or pursuant to its express prior authorization and
continuing coordination. This approach is essential to improving situational awareness, deterring
unauthorized activity, supporting enforcement, and protecting employees, communities, and
essential supply chains from evolving aerial risks.
ACD urges FAA to finalize a flexible, consequence-based rule that provides meaningful access for
high-consequence private-sector facilities, protects confidential and security-sensitive
information, avoids unnecessary administrative and technical burdens, and reflects real-world
chemical distribution operations. ACD appreciates the opportunity to comment and looks forward
to continued collaboration with FAA and its federal partners to advance a practical final rule that
strengthens critical infrastructure security and supports safe integration of UAS into the NAS.
Sincerely,
Brian E. Callahan
Senior Vice President, Government Affairs
Alliance for Chemical Distribution
bcallahan@acd-chem.com
(571) 482-3062
