comments.commenter: Comment from Dixie Aerial Photography Inc
comments.comment_text:
Re: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) – 14 CFR Part 74: Designation of Unmanned
Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) Over Critical Infrastructure
I am writing to express significant concerns regarding the scope and underlying logic of
proposed 14 CFR Part 74 establishing Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) over
designated critical infrastructure, specifically regarding dams and water management
facilities.
While protecting vital national infrastructure is a critical objective, blanket airspace bans
over facilities like dams create a false sense of security while disproportionately penalizing
compliant operators.
Key Arguments Against Blanket Restrictions on Dams
• Disproportionate Physical Threat Matrix (Waterborne vs. Airborne):
Standard small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (sUAS) operating under Part 107 or
Section 44809 typically weigh under 55 pounds and carry minimal payload. In
contrast, heavy motorized watercraft and large recreational or commercial vessels
can approach dams via open waterways carrying hundreds or thousands of pounds
of potential physical threat or hazardous materials. Creating stringent airspace
restrictions while leaving surrounding public waterways accessible highlights a
fundamental imbalance in actual threat assessment.
• Inefficacy of Spatial Restrictions Against Malicious Actors:
Regulatory designations do not create physical barriers. A bad actor intent on
committing a criminal act or causing structural harm will not be deterred by a FAA
airspace restriction (UAFR). Much like restrictions on physical items or tools,
restricting airspace only restricts law-abiding hobbyists, commercial inspectors,
photogrammetrists, and media personnel, while doing nothing to physically prevent
unauthorized or malicious flights.
• Chilling Effect on Lawful Aviation and Public Oversight:
Dams are frequently located in public recreation areas, state parks, and navigable
waterways where recreational flying, environmental monitoring, and media coverage
occur daily. Blanket 400-foot AGL restrictions over large swaths of public water and
land restrict safe, low-risk operations without demonstrating a commensurate safety
benefit.
Proposed Recommendations for the Final Rule
1. Require High-Burden Vulnerability Assessments for Waterway Assets:
The FAA should require facility applicants for dams to explicitly demonstrate why
airspace restrictions are necessary when ground and water access remain
unregulated.
2. Focus Regulations on Intent and Payload, Not Location:
Enforcement and security efforts should focus on kinetic threat mitigation and

malicious intent rather than penalizing passive transit or camera operations over
public waters.
3. Protect Transit and Public Space Overflight:
Ensure clear transit corridors along public riverways so operators navigating
surrounding airspace are not inadvertently criminalized.
Thank you for considering this input on balancing realistic threat vectors with the rights of
safe, compliant aviation stakeholders.

Dear FAA:
I certainly don't envy the position you are in, trying to balance airspace and drone safety while also protecting certain types of so-called critical structures.
My feelings are that the proposed rules are too restrictive and too confusing for the typical drone pilot to understand. I approach this statement as a journalist who uses his drones to provide information to the public to newspapers and publications in Colorado.
I am of the opinion that while drones shouldn't fly at ongoing fire scenes (which can result in problems for first responders), the public has First Amendment Free Press rights that shouldn't be squashed by additional government regulations.
If any or every building owner would be given to declare their location as "off limits" to drones, it would severely destroy the public's right to know. Futhermore, photojournalists who use drones, flying under Part 107, are told where they shouldn't legally fly by using available apps while planning their mission. It's my stance that additional regulations - or requiring a drone journalist to contact each agency for permission to photograph many limited-access facilities, would be a disservice and likely would be ruled illegal by the courts.
I stand with the National Press Photographers' Association, which said: "NPPA does not challenge the FAA’s authority to impose appropriate narrowly tailored restrictions where necessary to address documented safety and security concerns.”
The issue is not that there are rules surrounding drone operations in certain areas, those are expected, but that the FAA’s proposed rules would effectively open the door for operators of just about any infrastructure or infrastructure-related site to petition the FAA to restrict drone access. This includes sites related to things like communications, commercial operations, dams, energy manufacturing, food and agriculture, information technology, transportation systems, and water, among others. Many of these covered sites have direct and important relevance to the public interest and safety."
In addition, I have many acquaintances who are police officers, firefighters and involved in Search & Rescue. When lives are on the line, or when wildfires, floods, train derailments and other disasters occur, those who use drones in their line of work do not need an additional layer of bureaucracy to deal with when time is of the essence.
We live in a day and age when most people own a cellphone, which has picture-taking capabilities. Look at any newscast and you'll find photos of videos of emergency situations captured by the public's cellphones. The same "right to know" situation should not be impacted for a drone photojournalist whose position is to keep the pubic aware and involved. More than two centuries ago, Benjamin Franklin penned "Poor Richard's Almanac" in what's considered a foundation for the public to have a free press to bring them news and information. I request that the FAA stop this proposal to put handcuffs on the public's right to know, as well as preventing national airspace regulations from getting out of control.
Thank you.

comments.commenter: Comment from National Association of Manufacturers
comments.comment_text:
Christopher Phalen
Vice President, Domestic Policy
August 5, 2026
Docket Operations
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Room W58-213, West Building 5th Floor
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Comments of the National Association of Manufacturers; Designation-
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility (Docket Number FAA-2026-4558)
To whom it may concern:
The National Association of Manufacturers (NAM) respectfully submits these comments on
the Federal Aviation Administration's (“FAA” or “the agency”) proposed rulemaking
Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility (“the proposal” or “the proposed rule”) through which the agency is implementing
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (Section 2209). The
NAM appreciates the opportunity to provide input on this proposal and its implications for
the protection of critical infrastructure and the safe, efficient use of unmanned aircraft
systems (UAS) by manufacturers and industrial operators.
The NAM is the voice of the manufacturing community and the leading advocate for a policy
agenda that supports and empowers the 13 million people who make things in America. As
the largest manufacturing association in the U.S., the NAM’s membership includes
businesses of all sizes, across all industrial sectors, and in all 50 states. Manufacturers
collectively contribute $2.9 trillion to the U.S. economy—and right-sized, commonsense
regulations are critical to sustaining the manufacturing strength that underpins our nation’s
prosperity.
Manufacturers operate, support, and rely on a wide range of critical infrastructure facilities
that may be eligible for protection under the proposed framework, including chemical
facilities, energy production and transmission facilities, refineries, industrial manufacturing
sites, transportation infrastructure, and other facilities critical to the nation's economic and
national security. At the same time, manufacturers are active adopters of UAS technologies,
utilizing drones to support inspection, maintenance, environmental monitoring, emergency
response, security operations, and safety initiatives.
The NAM supports the FAA's efforts to establish a framework that protects critical
infrastructure from unauthorized UAS activity while preserving the ability of facility operators
to conduct legitimate, authorized drone operations. As the FAA finalizes this rulemaking, the
NAM respectfully requests that the agency ensure the framework remains risk-based,
operationally practical, and sufficiently flexible to support future technological innovation.
1

Support for a Risk-Based Section 2209 Framework
The NAM supports implementation of Section 2209 through a demonstrated-need approach
that evaluates applications based on facility-specific risk considerations and operational
requirements. The proposed process for designating unmanned aircraft flight restrictions
(UAFRs) is the cornerstone of the FAA’s implementation of Section 2209, providing the
mechanism to protect eligible facilities from unauthorized drone operations that present
legitimate safety and security risks. Restrictions should be targeted at facilities that present
legitimate security and safety concerns and should be supported by appropriate
documentation demonstrating the need for protection.
A risk-based framework will help ensure that flight restrictions remain appropriately tailored
to the security objectives established by Congress, while minimizing unintended impacts on
legitimate UAS operators and industrial activities. As the FAA gains experience
administering the program, the NAM recommends that the agency continue to evaluate
whether application requirements remain practical, scalable, and appropriately aligned with
the risks presented by individual facilities.
Facility Eligibility Considerations
The FAA’s proposed rule is intended to provide eligible critical infrastructure facilities with
an appropriate mechanism to seek airspace protections against unauthorized UAS
operations. As such, manufacturers request that the FAA clarify that eligibility
determinations may appropriately include large industrial manufacturing facilities that share
the operational, safety, and security characteristics of other critical infrastructure sectors
identified under the proposed framework. Facilities such as paper mills and other
permanent, complex industrial and transportation operations (such as railroad facilities,
added by Congress in the 2018 FAA reauthorization) often handle combustible materials,
regulated waste streams, wastewater treatment systems, biomass storage areas, heavy
industrial equipment, and continuous production processes that present unique safety and
security considerations.
Additionally, manufacturers request that the FAA consider expanding the lateral boundaries
beyond property lines for certain facilities and circumstances. Some examples of potentially
covered facilities could include: point-of-departure logistical facilities such as loading docks,
loading bays, staging areas, or marine terminals and port facilities; pipeline corridors; critical
electrical or water facilities, such as substations or treatment works, located outside of a
facility’s property line; or railyards or rail lines being used to transport critical materials.
Unauthorized UAS operations in close proximity to these facilities may create credible risks,
including disruption of the delivery of critical services like energy and water, fire hazards,
interference with industrial equipment and operations, disruption of environmental
management systems, and unauthorized surveillance of sensitive infrastructure and
processes. The NAM appreciated the FAA ensuring that the final rule provides sufficient
flexibility to recognize these risks when evaluating facility eligibility under Section 2209.
2

Consider the Use of Consequence-Based Eligibility in Addition to Facility
Classification
Beyond evaluating various factors to determine facility eligibility under Section 2209, the
NAM believes it would be most practical for the FAA system to also consider a
consequence-based eligibility framework. The current system is largely built around what a
facility is and whether that facility falls into a category authorized to receive drone
restrictions. However, manufacturers recommend that the FAA consider the potential
consequences of a successful malicious or unauthorized UAS event at these facilities.
For many industrial facilities, the consequences of an incident may extend beyond the
facility boundaries and include impacts to employees, surrounding communities,
environmental resources, transportation networks, regional supply chains, and emergency
response operations. Facility size, production capacity, regulatory designation, or other
measurement metrics alone may not adequately capture risks of this nature. A
consequence-based evaluation framework would help ensure protections are appropriately
applied and enforced where the greatest potential impacts exist.
Protect Current Safety Commitments and Recognize Existing Practices
Manufacturing facilities eligible for Section 2209 protections often conduct complex
industrial operations where safety is paramount, and these facility operators bear significant
responsibility for employees and the larger community. Unauthorized UAS activity can
introduce unnecessary risks to employees, contractors, emergency responders, neighboring
communities, and critical industrial processes.
Throughout the rulemaking, it is important for the FAA to recognize that appropriate
airspace protections support a broad range of safety objectives, including:
• Employee and contractor safety;
• Public and community safety;
• Process safety and operational reliability;
• Emergency response operations;
• Environmental protection; and,
• Security of critical industrial infrastructure.
Many facilities that may qualify for protection under the proposed framework already
operate under extensive federal security and access-control requirements, which are
designed to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive operations, hazardous materials,
critical infrastructure systems, and regulated manufacturing environments. For example,
facilities covered under the Maritime Transportation Security Act (MTSA) must implement
access-control measures through approved Facility Security Plans pursuant to 33 CFR §
105.255. Facilities registered with the Drug Enforcement Administration must maintain
effective controls against theft and diversion of controlled substances under 21 CFR
§1301.71. FDA-regulated manufacturing facilities operate under current Good
Manufacturing Practice requirements that restrict access to authorized personnel and
protect product integrity pursuant to 21 CFR Part 211. Similarly, facilities subject to
hazardous materials security planning requirements under 49 CFR §172.802 must
3

implement measures to prevent unauthorized access to hazardous materials and
associated operations.
Additional programs include Process Safety Management (PSM), EPA Risk Management
Programs (RMP), Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (where applicable), site
emergency response plans, mutual aid agreements, and other facility-specific risk
management measures.
The ability to effectively control access to sensitive facilities is a foundational element of
these regulatory programs. Unrestricted aerial access over critical infrastructure facilities
may undermine the ability of facility operators to fully implement federally mandated security
and access control measures. In some industrial environments, including facilities that
handle hazardous materials, combustible materials, or flammable substances, unauthorized
aerial activity may also introduce operational and safety risks that facility operators cannot
adequately manage. The FAA should recognize the important role that appropriately
tailored UAFRs can play in supporting broader critical infrastructure security objectives and
existing federal security requirements.
Detection Technologies Should Complement Airspace Protections
The NAM recognizes the important role that UAS detection, identification, and situational
awareness technologies play in supporting facility security and operational awareness.
These technologies can help facility operators identify other unauthorized drone activity,
improve incident response, and strengthen coordination with law enforcement and other
applicable authorities.
However, detection capabilities alone do not prevent, deter, or mitigate unauthorized UAS
operations. The ability to identify a drone after it has entered sensitive airspace does not
eliminate the potential security or safety risks associated with that intrusion. As the FAA
evaluates applications under Section 2209, the existence of detection technologies should
not be viewed as a substitute for unmanned aircraft flight restrictions UAFRs. Rather,
detection technologies and UAFRs should be viewed as complementary tools that together
strengthen the protection of critical infrastructure facilities.
Preserving Authorized Industrial UAS Operations
Protecting facilities from unauthorized aerial activity is an important objective, but the
implementation of the regulatory framework under Section 2209 NPRM should not
unintentionally disrupt authorized UAS operations that provide significant safety,
environmental, operational, and security benefits.
Manufacturers increasingly rely on drones to conduct inspections in difficult-to-access
locations, reduce employee exposure to hazardous environments, monitor facility
conditions, support maintenance activities, and improve operational efficiency. Many
companies have invested significant resources in developing safe and effective drone
programs, by establishing compliance procedures, obtaining FAA approvals, and integrating
UAS technologies into routine operations.
4

As such, manufacturers strongly encourage that the agency’s final rule ensure that facilities
receiving UAFRs retain the ability to conduct authorized operations, including activities
conducted by facility personnel, approved contractors, emergency response teams, and
other authorized operators. Existing FAA approvals, waivers, enterprise drone programs,
emissions monitoring activities, environmental compliance programs, and other authorized
operations should not be disrupted in the process of implementing this framework.
Across the manufacturing sector, facility-operated UAS should be recognized not as a risk
to be restricted, but as the increasingly important component of modern industrial safety,
environmental management, maintenance, and security programs that it is, and the NAM
believes these activities should be regulated as such.
Emergency Response Considerations
The ability to rapidly deploy UAS assets during emergencies is particularly important for
many industrial and manufacturing facilities. Manufacturers increasingly use drones during
emergency situations to improve personnel safety, enhance situational awareness,
accelerate incident assessment and response, and support emergency decision-making.
For instance, UAS technologies can provide critical capabilities during fire response
operations, hazardous material releases, gas detection and plume monitoring activities,
security incidents, search and rescue efforts, storm response activities, and other
emergency situations.
Additionally, industrial operators frequently deploy UAS resources to support neighboring
facilities, mutual aid organizations, local emergency management agencies, fire
departments, and other critical infrastructure partners during emergency situations. It is
essential to preserve the flexibility that allows for these necessary partnerships during
emergency situations.
The FAA should ensure that facilities operating under approved UAFRs retain the ability to
rapidly deploy authorized UAS assets during emergency situations, within their facilities or
alongside neighboring partners, without unnecessary administrative delays or procedural
barriers. Preserving operational flexibility during emergencies will help ensure that the rule
enhances security without inadvertently limiting critical response capabilities.
Administrative Practicality and Unfunded Airspace Management Obligations
Additionally, in this same spirit of providing sufficiently protective regulations that do not
hamper manufacturers’ ability to efficiently and safely proceed in their operations, the NAM
encourages the FAA to implement the program in a manner that minimizes unnecessary
administrative burdens or unfunded airspace management costs on applicants.
Some facilities may face challenges, through no fault of their own, in providing detailed
historical data regarding UAS activity or other similar information that may not currently be
tracked through existing compliance systems. Application requirements should remain
practical and focused on information necessary to support FAA decision-making, with
appropriate consideration given to operationally critical functions, such as safety operations,
emergency response functions, hazardous material management and site security, as well
as the use of UAS to support existing regulatory reporting requirements. Additionally, the
5

FAA should avoid creating circumstances in which facility operators become responsible for
ongoing airspace management activities.
On the management and cost front, manufacturers support a streamlined implementation
framework that does not shift ongoing airspace management responsibilities to facility
operators. Section 2209 designations should not create expectations that designated
facilities continuously monitor surrounding airspace, maintain specialized detection
infrastructure, or undertake reporting and enforcement functions beyond the scope of their
responsibilities. While many manufacturers employ security measures specific to their
operational needs, participation in the Section 2209 program should not depend upon
assuming responsibilities or costs beyond those that facility owners can reasonably meet
and that are necessary to request and maintain a designation.
Enterprise Program Considerations and Additional Benefits of UAFRs
As the program matures, the agency should also consider opportunities to support
enterprise-level or programmatic approaches for organizations operating multiple facilities
under common security, operational, and UAS management frameworks. Many
manufacturers and industrial organizations are leading the way and have developed mature
enterprise drone programs supported by FAA-compliant procedures, standardized training
programs, safety management systems, operational governance processes, and qualified
operating personnel and contractors.
The final framework should recognize the distinction between unauthorized operators and
trained, qualified operators conducting approved missions under established enterprise
UAS programs. A balanced framework to support enterprise programs provides
opportunities to reduce duplicative administrative requirements while maintaining
appropriate oversight, which will improve efficiency for applicants and the FAA.
Additionally, while the primary purpose of Section 2209 is to enhance the protection of
critical infrastructure facilities from unauthorized UAS activity, appropriately implemented
UAFRs can also provide secondary operational benefits for authorized facility operators. By
reducing unauthorized traffic and creating more controlled operating environments,
approved restrictions can improve operator identification, enhance situational awareness,
reduce uncertainty, and facilitate the continued deployment of advanced industrial UAS
capabilities. A well-designed and implemented framework should both enhance security
against unauthorized drone operations and enable the continued safe, efficient, and
responsible use of authorized industrial UAS across the manufacturing sector.
Supporting Future Innovation
Industrial UAS technologies continue to evolve, and the final rule should remain sufficiently
flexible to accommodate future advancements (including existing enterprise programs).
Manufacturers are increasingly evaluating and deploying technologies such as centralized
remote operations centers, autonomous inspections, dock-based deployments, integrated
robotics systems, artificial intelligence-assisted monitoring, advanced detection
technologies, enterprise-scale drone operations, and beyond visual line of sight inspection
capabilities. Future applications may also involve greater integration between UAS
platforms and broader industrial automation and robotics systems.
6

The final regulatory framework should remain technology-neutral and avoid unintentionally
limiting future capabilities that can improve both facility security and operational efficiency.
Maintaining flexibility will help ensure that facilities can continue adopting innovative
technologies while meeting the security objectives of Section 2209.
*****
The NAM appreciates the FAA’s efforts to implement Section 2209 and strengthen
protections for critical manufacturing and infrastructure facilities. As the agency finalizes this
rulemaking, manufacturers respectfully request that it ensures that the framework protects
facility security, preserves authorized industrial UAS operations, supports emergency
response capabilities, minimizes unnecessary administrative burdens, and remains flexible
enough to accommodate future technological innovation.
The NAM looks forward to continuing to work with the FAA throughout this rulemaking
process.
Sincerely,
Kirbie Ferrell
Director, Transportation and Infrastructure Policy
Christopher Phalen
Vice President, Domestic Policy
7

comments.commenter: Comment from National Electrical Contractors Association
comments.comment_text:
July 6, 2026
Comments of the National Electrical Contractors Association to “Designation: Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”
Docket Number: FAA-2026-4558
Introduction
The National Electrical Contractors Association (NECA) submits these comments in response to
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) for
Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFR) near designated facilities. NECA appreciates the
opportunity to provide feedback on how the proposed rule may negatively impact NECA
members performing critical transmission infrastructure work.
NECA is a national trade association and the leading voice of the $225 billion electrical
contracting industry that brings power, light, and communication technology to buildings and
communities across the United States. NECA collectively represents over 4,000 electrical
contractor members, employing over 500,000 electrical workers spread served over 118 local
Chapters across the country. NECA employs a unionized workforce with contracts collectively
bargained with the largest union of electrical workers in the world, the International Brotherhood
of Electrical Workers, AFL-CIO, CLC (IBEW).
NECA’s outside line contractor members build, maintain, and modernize the nation’s electric
power transmission and distribution system—high-voltage transmission lines, substations,
distribution circuits, and associated telecommunications and control infrastructure. They work
daily in utility corridors, along energized lines, and in proximity to critical infrastructure across
every region and terrain in the United States.
NECA members understand the real-world geometry, constraints, and hazards of working within
50 feet of infrastructure, including rotorcraft maneuvering needs, obstacle clearance, wire
environment complexities, and ground crew safety. Their combined experience with utility
aviation partners, UAS inspection programs, and utility safety protocols makes them uniquely
qualified to identify practical deconfliction measures, right-of-way clarifications, electronic
conspicuity needs, and dynamic coordination mechanisms that will allow UAS operations,
including BVLOS operations, and line workers to coexist safely.
Background
FAA’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) aims to enable expanded unmanned aircraft
system (UAS/drone) operations, both Visual Line of Sight (VLOS) and Beyond Visual Line of
Sight (BVLOS), near critical infrastructure unless a project or property owner meets a stringent
list of requirements for a UAFR. As written, the NPRM may allow UAS operators to fly near,
through, and around high-voltage transmission lines with near impunity.
Despite stating that, “Unmanned aircraft operating in close proximity to these facilities and
high-voltage transmission and distribution substations could surveil the facility's security

operations and potentially, either intentionally or unintentionally crash, into critical
components, causing damage to the system, as well as power outages, fires, and property
damage that may have a cascading impact to that Nation's power grid,” NECA is concerned that
the NPRM does not adequately protect our nation’s energy grid and the men and women who
work on high voltage systems every day.
Areas of Concern and Recommendations
1. Eligible Facilities
Under Section 74.88, eligible Energy Sector facilities are defined below:
Criteria. FAA proposes that energy sector facilities seeking a UAFR meet the following
minimum qualifications for their specified subsector:
Electricity Facility. The operator or proprietor of a fixed site facility within the electricity
industry may apply for a UAFR if it meets one of the following criteria: (1) the facility is a
power-generation facility with a combined nameplate capacity of 500 megawatts or greater of
power; (2) the facility is an electrical substation with a capacity of 500 kilovolts or greater of
power; or (3) the facility is an electrical substation with a capacity of 345 kilovolts or greater of
power in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas.
There are two principal areas of concern:
1. High-voltage transmission lines are not eligible for a UAFR; and
2. 500 kilovolts for an electrical substation is too high of a threshold for electrical substation
eligibility for a UAFR.
Not listing transmission lines as critical facility under the NPRM would allow actors - amateur,
professional, and those with maligned intentions all the same - the ability to operate UAS near
and within critical transmission corridors. The NPRM does adequately protect the health and
safety of electrical line workers building and maintaining the energy grid, who often work at
significant heights and with the use of manned helicopter flights.
In addition, a 500kilovolt threshold covers only a fraction of electrical substations in the country.
The purpose of a substation is to “step-down” the voltage so it can be safely distributed to
communities and ratepayers. It is a critical component of the larger grid, and 500 kilovolts would
only cover the absolute largest substations in the United States.
NECA Recommendations
• Include high-voltage transmission lines as eligible for a UAFR; and
• Lower the threshold for electrical substations to 230 kilovolts.
NOTE: This is the chief area of concern for NECA.

2. Demonstration of Need
Under Section 74.66, applicants must provide data and documentation relating to:
(a) Existing unmanned aircraft traffic patterns. Describe unmanned aircraft operations over the
fixed site facility during the last 24 months, where available. The description must include the
type of unmanned aircraft operation, if known; identify whether the operator is known to the
operators or proprietors; and quantify the total number of operations not associated with the
facility itself.
NECA is concerned that this is an exceedingly burdensome requirement for the energy sector,
particularly at a time when President Trump is seeking to lower energy prices for the American
people. As stated repeatedly in the NPRM, UAS are often difficult to distinguish, even in close
proximity.
Transmission corridors cover large geographic areas, and the inability of project owners to
accurately monitor and describe unmanned aircraft operations, particularly in rural areas, does
not diminish the importance of energy infrastructure to those communities. In fact, NECA holds
that transmission projects serving areas where monitoring is more difficult are even more
important to the lives and livelihoods of the communities they serve. Even if this could be
achieved at the scale needed for the energy grid, the monitoring and reporting costs may be
passed onto ratepayers.
NECA Recommendation
• Allow noted exceptions and flexibilities to the UAS reporting requirement, particularly
for facilities that cover a large geographic footprint and facilities in rural areas.
3. Allowed Operations
Under section 74.250, proposed paragraph (d), unmanned aircraft flying BVLOS would be
permitted to enter a UAFR under FAA proposed 14 CFR part 108 with either an FAA-issued
operating permit or certificate. This proposal is in keeping with the August 7, 2025, FAA
NPRM, Normalizing Unmanned Aircraft Systems Beyond Visual Line of Sight Operations.
The referenced part 108 NPRM would allow unmanned aircraft, including those conducting
commercial operations related to package delivery, the absolute right-of-way over manned
aircraft within shield areas. This includes near transmission lines.
Without edits to the references NPRM related to part 108, the proposed paragraph (d) prioritizes
general commercial operations, including package delivery, over the lives and livelihoods of

electrical workers and crews who conduct high-voltage transmission related work using manned
helicopters.
As noted repeatedly within the current NPRM of issue, UAS can be extremely difficult to
distinguish for even the most discerning eye. This was illustrated recently on Monday, July 26,
2026, when a flight landing at John F. Kennedy International Airport struck a drone.
Placing the burden of maneuverability onto manned helicopter crews working on live, high-
voltage transmission lines at altitude is extremely dangerous, and, without careful back-and-forth
with the energy sector, should not be permitted.
NECA Recommendation
• Strike paragraph (d) until such a time as there is a final Part 108 rulemaking and there
has been enough time to monitor for downstream impacts.
4. Access Notification
Under Section 74.255, UAS operators that qualify to fly within a UAFR must provide the below
notification to a project owner:
§ 74.255
Unmanned aircraft flight restriction access notification.
(a) General. Any person that operates or plans to operate an unmanned aircraft in accordance
with § 74.250 in an unmanned aircraft flight restriction must provide notice to the fixed site
facility site manager in a form and manner acceptable to the Administrator.
(b) Contents. The notice must include:
(1) Name, mailing address, email address, and phone number of the person providing notice;
(2) Name and on-site phone number of the person(s) operating the unmanned aircraft;
(3) Airman certificate number or 14 CFR Part 108 permit or certificate number the allowed
operation is being conducted under.
(4) Remote Identification Serial Number(s) associated with allowed operation.
(5) Unmanned aircraft registration number(s);
(6) Information identifying the unmanned aircraft flight restriction site;
(7) Date, approximate time, number of unmanned aircraft, and area of operations within the
unmanned aircraft flight restriction.
(8) Type of operation permitted in accordance with § 74.250.
(c) Timeline for Notification. An operator must provide notice as soon as reasonably possible in
advance of the operation; unless the operation is conducted by or on behalf of a government

agency or law enforcement acting within the scope of their legal authority then notification must
be provided verbally as soon as reasonably possible and written notification within seven
calendar days.
Of issue is the vagueness of “as soon as reasonably possible”. Whether it’s building or
maintaining a hospital, school, transmission line, or electrical facility, work stops when there is a
drone in the vicinity. It is a significant safety issue for workers on-site and a liability issue for
project owners.
In the energy sector, construction and maintenance work is planned well in advance, and crews
need to be mobilized to get the job done as quickly as possible and under budget.
If a UAS operator informs a project owner of a fly-through with 10, 5, or even 2 days notice, and
that fly-through conflicts with a planned construction or maintenance project, who bears the
burden of shutting down the site? In the case of the electrical grid, is that cost passed onto
ratepayers? What if this was the only date/time that the work could be done?
In addition, there is not a mechanism for a project owner to restrict covered UAS operations,
whether VLOS or BVLOS, during critical construction or maintenance periods. Similarly, there
is no burden on a UAS operator, who, once simply informing the project owner “as soon as
reasonably possible,” now has absolute right-of-way within the UAFR and through a planned job
site.
Recommendations
1. Require a specific time-period by which a UAS operator must inform a project
owner of a UAFR of a fly-through; and
2. Allow for denials by the project owners under specific circumstances, such as
construction or maintenance periods.

Re: Hermeus Corp. Comments to the Section 2209 NPRM on Restricting the Operations of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to Fixed Site Facilities (FAA-2026-4558)
To Whom It May Concern:
Hermeus Corporation (Hermeus) appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments to the
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) titled “Designation – Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in
Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility” implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and
Security Act of 2016 (hereinafter “NPRM” or “proposed rule”). Hermeus is appreciative of the
FAA’s work to propose a framework for establishing Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions
(UAFRs) as a mechanism to improve safety, security, and operational deconfliction in sensitive
airspace, and we have a few suggestions for improvement.
As an aerospace and defense technology company focused on the development of unmanned
high-Mach aircraft, we regularly conduct flight test activities at federal test ranges and military
installations that would be eligible to apply for and obtain a Special UAFR designation. The ability
to restrict unauthorized UAS activity in these sensitive environments can play an important role
in ensuring the safety and security of flight test activity occurring at these sites.
While Hermeus generally supports the proposed rule, we are concerned that the NPRM may
unintentionally create unnecessary barriers for legitimate non-government UAS operators
conducting authorized activities at facilities subject to Special UAFRs. Specifically, the proposed
framework appears to require approval from both the federal agency utilizing the Special UAFR
and the FAA before an authorized operation may occur. Hermeus respectfully submits that this
approach could create duplicative review processes, unnecessary delays, and operational
uncertainty. The final rule must ensure a streamlined and efficient process for authorized non-
U.S. Government operators to gain access to Special UAFRs.
Page 1 of 4

Docusign Envelope ID: 64B4D194-DB52-81A9-8185-F4D23B0D6AEF
Who We Are
Hermeus is a U.S. high-speed aircraft manufacturer focused on the rapid design, build, and test
of high-Mach and hypersonic aircraft for the national interest. The U.S. Government has partnered
with Hermeus to accelerate development and prototyping of high speed aircraft in a collaborative
strategy that accelerates fielding the most promising technologies for potential future military
use. In the near-term, the business is focused on building high-speed larger UA that sustainably
deliver asymmetric advantage to the Department of War (DoW) and allied partners. Utilizing an
iterative development approach to aircraft development, Hermeus’ high-Mach and hypersonic
aircraft aim to deliver capabilities at a pace not seen in the U.S. since the 1950s.
Hermeus has developed a rapid prototyping roadmap—the Quarterhorse Program—that aims to
build the talent and infrastructure required to deliver high speed capabilities. Hermeus deploys
integrated, hardware-rich, iterative development processes, which set the pace for our cadence
objective to design, build, and flight test one new vehicle per year. Our flight development program
incorporates lessons learned into each build, designing vehicles to meet specific objectives and
technology goals. This developmental flight testing often needs to occur at civil federal test
ranges and military installations.
The Final Rule Should Allow the Using Agency to Authorize Access Without Separate FAA Approval
Section 74.251 of the proposed rule establishes stricter access controls for Special UAFRs, which
protect highly sensitive facilities. As proposed, operations within Special UAFRs require both
permission from the government agency responsible for the site (“using agency”) and approval
from the FAA.
The NPRM’s proposed framework for accessing Special UAFR airspace appears to be premised
on the assumption that authorized non-government operations within Special UAFRs will be
relatively uncommon. In Hermeus' experience, this assumption may not reflect operational
realities. Many U.S. companies are actively supporting DoW, national security, and other federal
missions through the development, testing, demonstration, and evaluation of advanced UAS
technologies. These activities often occur as a civil operation and frequently require access to
military installations, federal test ranges, and other sensitive facilities that may be protected
through a Special UAFR. Such operations are becoming more common, and they are increasingly
central to the development of next-generation aerospace capabilities needed to advance defense
technology development and the nation's broader UAS industrial base.
For this reason, the final rule should recognize that authorized non-government operations may occur
regularly within Special UAFRs and should establish a process that facilitates, rather than impedes,
legitimate access. In a scenario where the federal entity for which a Special UAFR has been
established has authorized a proposed operation, separate FAA approval should not be required.
The entity sponsoring or utilizing the Special UAFR is generally best positioned to evaluate
mission requirements, operational compatibility with ongoing activities, local safety and security
considerations, range scheduling and resource constraints, and the overall safety and security
Page 2 of 4

Docusign Envelope ID: 64B4D194-DB52-81A9-8185-F4D23B0D6AEF
risks associated with permitting UAS operator access. Requiring an additional FAA approval after
the using agency has determined that an operation is appropriate provides limited additional
safety or security value while creating additional administrative burden for both operators and
the FAA. Delegating Special UAFR access approvals to the using agency directly would promote
efficient decision-making, reduce duplicative reviews, and ensure that access determinations are
made by the entity possessing the most complete understanding of the operational environment.
The approval process for accessing Special UAFR airspace in the final rule should also reflect the
fact that civil UAS operations occurring on federal installations are already subject to extensive
FAA review and approval under the current regulatory framework. To the extent that the final rule
requires FAA approval to access Special UAFRs, the FAA review and approval should occur in
conjunction with the issuance of any operational or airspace approvals necessary to enable UAS
operations at the federal installation.
The FAA Should Establish a Standardized Process for Special UAFR Access
Regardless of whether access is managed by the FAA or the using agency, operators should be
subject to a standardized and transparent process for requesting authorization to operate within
a Special UAFR.
Without clear and consistent procedures, operators could face different requirements depending
on which agency, facility, installation, or organization requested the Special UAFR. Such variability
could create confusion, increase compliance costs, and delay legitimate operations that support
public-interest, national security, or technological development objectives.
To improve predictability and transparency, the final rule should establish standardized
procedures applicable across all Special UAFRs, including, but not limited to:
• Standard application requirements;
• Uniform information submission formats;
• Designated points of contact;
• Consistent review criteria;
• Published response timelines; and
• Clear procedures for approval, denial, or appeal.
A standardized framework would benefit both operators and facility sponsors by reducing
uncertainty and ensuring a common understanding of the access process.
Page 3 of 4

Docusign Envelope ID: 64B4D194-DB52-81A9-8185-F4D23B0D6AEF
The FAA Should Develop a Template Special UAFR Access Request Form
To the extent that the final rule requires FAA approval to access Special UAFRs, to support
consistency and efficiency, Hermeus recommends that the FAA develop a single standardized
Special UAFR Access Request Form that may be used for all requests to operate within Special
UAFRs. Such a form could capture information commonly needed to evaluate proposed
operations, and in doing so, help streamline reviews, reduce administrative burden, facilitate
automation where appropriate, and promote uniform treatment of similarly situated operators.
Conclusion
Special UAFRs have the potential to be a highly effective tool for protecting sensitive facilities
and coordinating increasingly complex airspace operations. To realize that potential, however,
the FAA should ensure that access procedures are standardized, transparent, simple, and
delegated to the entities most capable of making informed operational decisions.
Thank you for considering these comments.
Respectfully Submitted,
Laurie Sussman
Associate General Counsel
Hermeus Corporation

I am concerned about these “national security” restrictions being put into place that prohibit those of us who use a drone as part of their commercial venture to do their job. I already have to follow FAA rules which is fine, but there is more and more restrictions being put into place as time goes on. It is restricting to those who have jobs to do. And, as time goes on, the restrictions get stricter and stricter to the point you cannot operate. I think it is not what myself and others who rely on drones to do their job needs. I am not in favor of this and hopes it does not pass.

Alanna St Laurent, Part 107 drone operator.

I oppose including the Food and Agriculture sector (§ 74.90) among the critical infrastructure facilities eligible for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).

There's no documented evidence that drones threaten the safety of animals, workers, or equipment at agricultural facilities. In fact, drone footage has exposed workers abusing calves, illegal and cramped calf hutches in violation of state law, and unlawful dead piles that pose public health risks — abuses that would otherwise stay hidden.

Drones aren't a safety risk at these facilities; they're one of the only tools holding them accountable. Please don't shield factory farms from public scrutiny — exclude the Food and Agriculture sector from UAFR eligibility.

Drones are needed to keep information on factory farms available.
What do they have to hide?

Hello, I am strongly against this new rule that could cause restriction of droning over certain facilities, specifically Factory farms. There is so much money behind keeping these Farms secret and the animal cruelty that is gone unchecked. I personally know many of the part 107 accredited Pilots currently droning legally over factory farms and one of the most heartbreaking facts that I have learned is they don't need to drone for hours to capture this cruelty. They see it the moment the Drone gets up in the air. The farm industry will claim that people and animals are not safe, but the rules of flying already address safety. The real reason Farms would like to limit drone access is so that they can continue to operate in secrecy, which is absolutely disastrous for Millions if not billions of animals. Please, keep safety as your number one priority, but don't fall for these industries' attempts to appeal to the FAAs mission of safety when it is clearly about their own mission of secrecy.

I OPPOSE allowing animal agriculture facilities, including factory farms and concentrated animal feeding operations, to obtain  Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions or UAFRs. Industrialized animal farming operations are designed to conceal the horrors taking place within their confines from public view, lest a compassionate public lose its taste for products derived from the bodies of tortured animals. In recent years, drone footage has exposed some of the appalling cruelty, false marketing claims, and environmental devastation that the animal agriculture industry would rather keep hidden. The industry is trying to sell the implementation of UAFRs as a safety measure. It is not. There is no documented case of a drone harming a person, an animal, or a piece of equipment at one of these facilities in the US. In truth, the powerful animal agriculture industry is trying to shield itself from scrutiny, which is the opposite of what the public interest requires.

I oppose UAFRs for the food and agriculture sector because claims of drone-related safety or security risks lack documented evidence. Drone footage promotes accountability by exposing pollution, waste breaches, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims.

I oppose allowing food and agriculture facilities to obtain Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs). Drone photojournalism is one of the only tools the public has to see inside factory farms. I personally have made decisions to cease purchasing from companies that were exposed by photojournalism. I believe the public has a right to know when companies are not operating ethically. There is a documented history of drone footage exposing false marketing claims, environmental violations, and animal welfare abuses. They need to be held accountable.
I ask the FAA not to develop gating criteria for this sector and not to grant UAFRs to food and agriculture facilities.

Similarly, an owner or operator of a facility that has 10,000 pounds or more of ammonia on its

One of the risks identified by owners of facilities with ammonia in their RMP/PSM risk

facility rooftops, or any on the exterior of their food manufacturing plants or food warehouses, which can

facilities be able to request and maintain an UAFR. The EPA, and specifically the Chemical Safety and
Hazard Investigation Board, and OSHA likely have detailed information of the magnitude and potential
consequences of a breach of the ammonia systems at many of the ammonia refrigerated manufacturing
plants and warehouses located throughout the country that can inform you of the critical need of these
facilities to have an UAFR. Finally, drones flying over and around refrigerated food manufacturing and
warehouse facilities also present a danger to maintenance personnel and contractors working on the
facility rooftops.
IL Minimum Qualifications for Food the Food and Agricultural Sector.
The FAA has indicated in the federal register publication that it has not developed criteria for the food
and agriculture sector. As such, FAA seeks comments on the following questions to inform the
development of the criteria for the food and agricultural sector:
1. What types of facilities within this sector should be considered for an UAFR? Specifically, those
that could have debilitating regional or national-level consequences.
2. What characteristics should be considered in the development of gating criteria for those
facilities?
3. Should the population served or regional or national economic impact be considered in the
development of gating criteria, and if so, what are appropriate thresholds?
The preamble in the federal register publication recognizes that potential safety and security
incidents, including espionage and terrorism at critical infrastructure facilities, are factors to be
considered in determining whether a facility is eligible for an UAFR. Unmanned aircraft flying over or
near certain types of infrastructure can pose a risk to the safety and security of both the facility and the
surrounding population. 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (May 6, 2026), pg. 24654-24655. Unmanned aircraft flying

Oregon Department of Aviation
3040 25th Street SE
Salem, OR 97302-1125

COMMENT
August 5, 2026
Department of Transportation
Federal Aviation Administration
Washington, D.C. 20024
Re: Re: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03
Dear Administrator Bedford,
The Oregon Department of Aviation appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Federal
Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking implementing section 2209 of the
FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016. ODAV strongly supports the overall structure of
the proposal.i
The proposed rule strikes an appropriate balance between protecting genuinely sensitive fixed
site facilities and preserving the public right of transit through the National Airspace System.
FAA has correctly recognized that unmanned aircraft flight restrictions should be applied
carefully, with defined eligibility, a demonstrated need, and continued FAA oversight. The
proposal avoids creating broad private no-fly zones, while still giving critical infrastructure
owners and operators a pathway to seek protection when the facts support it.ii
ODAV supports the rule because it is selective, evidence based, and still allows lawful overflight
by known operators. FAA should retain that structure in the final rule. ODAV recommends
targeted improvements to notification, Remote Identification validation, interoperability,
protection of sensitive information, state and local government operations, corrections-related
Special UAFRs, machine-readable data, and enforcement coordination.
Eligibility Should Remain Selective and Site Specific
ODAV particularly supports FAA's decision to limit unmanned aircraft flight restriction eligibility
to fixed site facilities that meet sector-specific criteria and then require applicants to
demonstrate that the restriction is necessary for aviation safety, protection of people and
Oregon Department of Aviation’s mission is to provide infrastructure, financial resources,
and expertise to ensure a safe and efficient air transportation system.

property on the ground, national security, or homeland security. Critical infrastructure status
alone should not be enough. The applicant should have to show why unmanned aircraft create
a specific safety or security concern at that site, how the restriction would address that
concern, and why existing measures are insufficient. FAA's proposed burden of proof is a
necessary protection against overdesignation and unnecessary restriction of lawful unmanned
aircraft activity.iii
ODAV also supports FAA's decision to reject overly broad corridor-based approaches, including
proposals that would have effectively treated every mile of railroad as eligible for restricted
airspace. That approach would have been inconsistent with the fixed site concept, difficult for
operators to understand, and disruptive to lawful aviation. The proposed rule is stronger
because it focuses on facilities whose disruption would have consequences beyond ordinary
local operational impacts.iv
ODAV also supports FAA's decision to limit communications infrastructure eligibility to facilities
whose disruption would have regional or national impacts. Communications facilities are
important, but not every communications facility should qualify for a federal airspace
restriction. The same principle should apply across sectors. Eligibility should focus on facilities
where the consequence is regional, national, or otherwise high enough to justify federal
airspace action.
Standard UAFR Access Should Preserve Lawful Overflight
ODAV supports FAA's decision to allow certain known and vetted operators to access Standard
UAFR airspace. The National Airspace System cannot be closed to lawful unmanned aircraft
operations simply because a facility qualifies for protection. Operations under Parts 91, 107,
proposed 108, 135, and 137, along with qualifying public aircraft operations, generally involve
operators that are known to FAA, subject to an applicable safety framework, and often subject
to Transportation Security Administration security threat assessment requirements.v
FAA's proposal to allow those operators to transit a Standard UAFR, while requiring Remote
Identification, notice, and shortest-practicable-time transit, is a sound balance between
security and continued integration. ODAV supports that approach and recommends that FAA
maintain it in the final rule.vi
ODAV also supports the notice-only structure for Standard UAFRs. Notice should not become
permission by another name. A facility owner should receive timely information about lawful
unmanned aircraft activity in or near the restricted volume, but the facility owner should not be
able to veto lawful operations that FAA has determined may access the airspace. This

distinction is essential for public safety, infrastructure inspection, emergency response, utility
work, aviation operations, news gathering, and other lawful uses.
Notification Should Use a LAANC-Like System
FAA should improve the notice process by using a system modeled on the Low Altitude
Authorization and Notification Capability. An operator should be able to draw or submit the
proposed flight volume, identify the aircraft and operator information required by the rule, and
submit the operation through a centralized FAA-recognized system. That system should
automatically notify the affected fixed site facility manager or designated contact. The system
should also allow the facility owner or operator to log in and view current and planned notices
affecting the site.vii Systems that are simple and easy to use contribute to higher rates of
compliance.
A LAANC-like notice system would reduce administrative burden, create a reliable record, and
help ensure that notices do not get lost in a general inbox or disconnected facility workflow.
FAA should make clear that notice must be operationally useful. The final rule should require
UAFR sponsors to maintain current points of contact, define where notices are received, and
establish internal procedures for handling them. If a facility receives a restriction but does not
maintain the ability to receive, review, and act on notices, the practical value of the restriction
is reduced.
FAA should also consider allowing authorized infrastructure owners to view notices through a
secure portal rather than relying only on direct message delivery. In some cases, a portal-based
operating picture may be the more reliable way for a facility to maintain awareness of lawful
operations in and around a protected volume.
Remote Identification Should Be Validated, Interoperable, and Operationally Reliable
ODAV supports FAA's use of Remote Identification as part of the proposed framework. Remote
Identification is the right foundation for this rule because it helps distinguish known, compliant,
and accountable operators from unknown or noncompliant activity. FAA's proposal
appropriately requires facilities seeking protection to have the capability to receive Remote
Identification messages from unmanned aircraft operating within or near the restriction.viii
FAA should strengthen that requirement in several ways. First, Remote Identification receiving
equipment used to support a UAFR should be third-party validated. FAA, in coordination with
the Department of Homeland Security, Federal Bureau of Investigation, other security partners
as well as a standards development organization such as ASTM, should establish or approve a
validation process for hardware and software used by restriction sponsors. Facilities should not

be allowed to install a single untested receiver and treat that as sufficient to meet the rule. The
equipment must be capable of reliably receiving, logging, retaining, and sharing relevant
Remote Identification data in the environment where the facility is located.ix
Second, each applicant should be required to complete a site-specific radio frequency study
before relying on Remote Identification data to support an application. Terrain, structures,
interference, antenna placement, receiver density, and site layout can materially affect
reception. A facility should not be granted a restriction based on assumptions about detection
coverage that have not been tested in the field.
Third, FAA should require interoperability. Remote Identification receiving systems used to
support a UAFR should be capable of sharing data with authorized systems and authorized
government partners, including FAA, the Department of Homeland Security, state partners,
approved unmanned traffic management providers, and approved flight information exchange
providers. The final rule should avoid creating isolated facility-specific systems that cannot
contribute to broader airspace awareness.
Fourth, FAA should allow facilities already covered by an existing qualified detection system to
rely on that system instead of requiring duplicative equipment purchases. The important
requirement should be capability, reliability, validation, and interoperability, not procurement
of a separate system solely to satisfy a checkbox.
ODAV supports the idea that other sensors may be layered with Remote Identification, but
additional sensors should remain optional unless FAA determines that a specific use case
requires them. Remote Identification should serve as the baseline. Other sensors, such as radio
frequency detection, radar, optical systems, acoustic systems, or integrated airspace awareness
tools, may be valuable in some environments, but a one-size-fits-all sensor mandate would be
costly and unnecessary. Where additional sensors are used, they should also be interoperable
and should support lawful data sharing with authorized entities.
Sensitive Facility Information Should Be Protected
FAA should further clarify how facilities will submit sensitive information in support of a UAFR
application and how FAA will handle public comment without inadvertently disclosing
exploitable security information. ODAV recognizes that the NPRM and draft advisory materials
describe a web-based module and processes for confidential business information, classified
information, controlled unclassified information, sensitive security information, and other
nonpublic material. FAA should make those procedures clear in the final rule or associated
guidance so applicants understand what information must be submitted, what will be withheld

from the public docket, and how the public can provide meaningful comments without
exposing vulnerabilities.x
This issue is especially important because UAFR applications may include facility vulnerabilities,
operating procedures, security plans, Remote Identification detection locations, radio
frequency coverage information, and incident response procedures. FAA should provide a
secure submission pathway for applicants and a parallel method for receiving sensitive public
comments or agency comments when those comments contain security-sensitive information.
The final process should support transparency and notice and comment while avoiding the risk
that bad actors could exploit information disclosed through the docket.xi
State and Local Government Operations Need Clear Carve-Outs
FAA should provide broader and clearer carve-outs for state and local government agencies
that operate unmanned aircraft for legitimate government purposes. These operations are
often time-sensitive and may include emergency response, urgent law enforcement activity,
search and rescue, disaster assessment, wildfire support, hazardous materials response,
environmental monitoring, wildlife monitoring, and other public missions. FAA has already
recognized that government agency and law enforcement operations may require operational
security and may need a different notice timeline. ODAV recommends that FAA expand and
clarify this concept in the final rule.xii
The final rule should preserve public agency ability to conduct urgent operations without delay
while still providing reasonable notice and post-operation documentation. A UAFR should not
unintentionally slow a time-sensitive government mission where the operator is acting within
legal authority and the aircraft is otherwise identifiable, accountable, and operated under an
applicable FAA framework.
Corrections Facilities and Special UAFRs
ODAV supports FAA's recognition that correctional facilities face a heightened unmanned
aircraft risk, particularly related to contraband delivery, surveillance, weapons, escape tools,
and cell phones. FAA correctly included state prisons within the Emergency Services Sector for
purposes of the proposed rule and recognized the documented UAS-related risks faced by
correctional systems.xiii
FAA should provide a mechanism for a state corrections agency to submit one coordinated
application or management package for correctional facilities operated by that agency, rather
than requiring entirely separate applications for every individual prison facility when the
facilities present common ownership, common operational control, common security concerns,

and common response procedures. FAA may still need facility-specific boundary,
environmental, Remote Identification, and risk information, but the process should allow a
state corrections agency to submit a consolidated package with facility-specific appendices.
That approach would improve efficiency, support consistency, and reduce administrative
burden.
FAA should also clarify how a consolidated state corrections package would interact with
Special UAFR procedures. If a state corrections agency seeks protection for multiple facilities
based on a heightened, recurring, and documented security risk, the final rule should explain
whether and how an agency sponsor, using agency role, and access procedure under proposed
section 74.251 may be applied across multiple correctional sites.xiv
Transportation Facilities, Bridges, Tunnels, and Rail Corridors
ODAV supports FAA's decision not to treat the national rail network itself as eligible restricted
airspace. FAA should retain the fixed site approach and continue to reject broad linear corridor
treatment unless Congress directs otherwise. Airspace restrictions over large linear networks
would be difficult for operators to understand, difficult to administer, and inconsistent with
continued unmanned aircraft integration.xv
ODAV also supports FAA's consideration of bridges and tunnels with more than 50,000 average
daily traffic as potentially eligible transportation facilities, but FAA should refine the category.
Eligibility should be limited to freestanding bridges and tunnel entrances where an unmanned
aircraft could create a specific safety or security concern. Elevated roadways, viaducts, and
ordinary grade-separated highway structures should not be treated as bridges for purposes of
this rule. FAA should further refine the threshold to avoid unintentionally sweeping in
transportation structures that do not present the type of fixed site risk section 2209 was
designed to address.xvi
Transit Standards Should Remain Performance Based
ODAV agrees with FAA that the Standard UAFR transit requirement should be performance
based. Requiring operators to transit the restricted volume in the shortest practicable time is
preferable to a rigid rule that could interfere with safety, deconfliction, emergency response, or
other operational needs. FAA should consider whether a minimum transit altitude, where
operationally feasible and consistent with safety, would provide an additional layer of
protection for some facilities. Any such altitude should remain performance based and should
not prevent lawful public safety, inspection, emergency, or facility-related operations that
require lower-altitude flight.xvii

Special UAFRs and Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Mitigation Authority
ODAV supports FAA's proposed treatment of Special UAFRs. Requiring an agency sponsor and a
credible security assessment is appropriate. Special restrictions should remain limited, justified,
and tied to a higher level of government security interest. ODAV supports the stricter access
requirements for Special UAFRs, including the requirement that non-using-agency operators
receive permission from the using agency and approval from FAA.xviii
ODAV does not support allowing critical infrastructure owners or operators to use counter-
unmanned aircraft mitigation technologies merely because they receive a UAFR. FAA is correct
that a restriction does not create authority to jam, spoof, seize, destroy, or otherwise interfere
with an aircraft. Mitigation authorities should remain limited to entities with specific legal
authority, appropriate oversight, and specialized training. If mitigation is allowed in connection
with a Special UAFR, it should be limited to authorized law enforcement, federal agencies, or
properly trained personnel operating under clearly defined legal authority and operational
procedures.xix
Machine-Readable UAFR Data and Interoperability
FAA should clarify that, once the rule is implemented, relevant UAFR data will be available to
drone operators in a machine-readable format. A publicly accessible website is helpful, but it is
not sufficient for scalable operations. Operators, approved service providers, unmanned traffic
management providers, flight information exchange providers, public safety users, and state
partners need timely, machine-readable airspace data to support planning, automation,
notification, compliance, and deconfliction.xx
Machine-readable data should include the location, vertical limits, activation period, site
identification number, applicable access provisions, notice requirements, and any public-facing
operational constraints. FAA should also establish appropriate security controls so sensitive
facility details are not released while operationally necessary airspace information remains
available to lawful operators.
Enforcement and State and Local Coordination
FAA should strengthen the enforcement pathway. A restriction is only meaningful if there is a
practical way to respond to violations. FAA should consider how state and local law
enforcement may support enforcement of UAFRs, or at a minimum, how FAA can create a clear
pathway for state and local agencies to document, report, and refer violations. State and local
personnel are often the first to receive reports, respond to facilities, preserve evidence, and

encounter operators. The final rule should include a practical process for information sharing,
evidence preservation, referral to FAA, and coordination with federal partners.xxi
FAA should also consider whether additional authority, delegation, memoranda of
understanding, cooperative agreements, or standardized referral procedures are needed to
allow state and local agencies to play an appropriate role. The final rule should make clear what
evidence FAA needs, how Remote Identification data should be preserved, how local case
reports should be transmitted, and what state or local personnel should do when an
unauthorized operation is detected inside a UAFR.
Coordination with the SAFER SKIES Act Interim Final Rule
FAA should clarify the relationship between Standard UAFRs, Special UAFRs, and the July 2026
Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice interim final rule implementing
the SAFER SKIES Act for state, local, Tribal, and territorial law enforcement and correctional
agencies. That interim final rule establishes a separate federal framework for certain counter-
unmanned aircraft system activities by eligible law enforcement and correctional agencies,
including training, certification, authorized technologies, airspace coordination, notification,
reporting, privacy, and oversight requirements.xxii
The final section 2209 rule should explain how a UAFR or Special UAFR designation interacts
with SAFER SKIES Act implementation. A UAFR should not be read as independent mitigation
authority. At the same time, where an eligible public safety or correctional agency is separately
authorized under the SAFER SKIES Act framework, FAA should clarify how UAFR boundaries,
notice systems, Remote Identification data, airspace approvals, and operational coordination
should fit together. Clear alignment will reduce confusion for state and local agencies, facility
owners, drone operators, FAA field personnel, and federal security partners.xxiii
Conclusion
In summary, ODAV strongly supports the proposed rule. FAA has created a thoughtful and
balanced framework that protects high-consequence fixed site facilities without unnecessarily
closing the airspace. The proposal appropriately limits eligibility, requires applicants to prove
need, preserves lawful overflight by known and vetted operators, requires Remote
Identification capability, preserves notice and comment, and limits Special UAFRs to cases
involving appropriate government sponsorship.
With targeted improvements to notification, Remote Identification validation, interoperability,
secure information handling, public agency carve-outs, corrections-related application
procedures, machine-readable data, SAFER SKIES Act coordination, bridge and tunnel criteria,

data sharing, and enforcement coordination, the final rule can provide a durable national
framework for protecting critical infrastructure while continuing to support safe unmanned
aircraft integration.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Sincerely,
Kenji Sugahara
Director
Oregon Department of Aviation

Black & Veatch

These comments are submitted on behalf of the following non-profit, public utility
Jacobs
Ramboll Americas organization: the Maryland Association of Municipal Wastewater Agencies
WRA (MAMWA) (the Association). The Association is comprised of local government
water and sewer utilities dedicated to protecting public health and the
GENERAL COUNSEL environment. They strive to provide affordable and cost-effective water and sewer
