AquaLaw PLC
The Association submits these comments in support of the proposed rule, while
urging that all public water and sewer treatment facilities be eligible for a UFAR
designation and that responses be provided to the questions the FAA has asked.

Docket Id: FAA-2026-4558
August 5, 2026
Page 2
The Association supports the Proposed Rule to Protect Drinking Water and Wastewater
Facilities
The Association’s members provide public drinking and wastewater service using highly
specialized treatment and distribution/collection facilities. The treatment facilities are highly
specialized and cannot be quickly replaced in the event of a failure or a terror-related attack.
Unmanned aircraft pose critical security, safety, and operational risks to water and wastewater
utilities. Drinking water and wastewater plants and their associated distribution and collection
systems are large and expansive and are, therefore, uniquely exposed to harm from unmanned
aircraft.
Any interruption to public water or wastewater treatment services can shut down some or all of
the affected community – potentially for an extended period.
Given the explosion in drone use to attack vulnerable public infrastructure in conflict zones around
the world, the Association agrees that authorizing our members to obtain a UAFR is an essential
tool to help counter the threat of unmanned aircraft attacks against water and wastewater facilities
– especially vulnerable and hard-to-repair treatment facilities. Most of those treatment facilities
have little or no redundancy capability.
The ability to obtain a UAFR from the FAA presents a solution that is unavailable under any other
avenue. Association members continue to work at the state level to prevent (and punish with
greater consequences) damage and unauthorized access to their facilities. The proposed rule
presents an opportunity to implement an effective, uniform tool to protect water and wastewater
operations and prevent damage from unmanned aircraft through the UAFR process.
The Association offers the following suggestions in response to the FAA’s specific questions on
the recommended eligibility criteria for UAFRs in the Water and Wastewater Systems Sector in §
74.96.
Types and Characteristics of Drinking Water and Wastewater Systems the FAA should
consider when Developing Criteria
The Association suggests that system types addressed in the proposed rule text should include:
(1) drinking water treatment plants that serve as a primary treatment facility for a
community water system (CWS) – especially larger systems;
(2) critical drinking water distribution facilities such as elevated storage tanks, reservoirs,
and intake structures for a CWS;
(3) publicly owned wastewater treatment plants;
(4) infrastructure such as pump stations, recharge facilities, booster facilities, and other
essential assets;
(5) related control facilities and SCADA infrastructure; and
(6) any chemical storage facilities.

Docket Id: FAA-2026-4558
August 5, 2026
Page 3
Important system characteristics to analyze should include (1) whether there is hazardous chemical
storage, particularly chlorine, ammonia, fluoride compounds, in large quantities; (2) the ability for
an unmanned aircraft to surveil and gather important information from the air at the facility and/or
cause physical damage at the site; and (3) the extent of the impact that a disruption of
water/wastewater service would cause to the communities served.
Consideration of Population Served and Appropriate Population Thresholds
The Association agrees that population served is an important consideration given the difficulty of
replacing (or finding alternative solutions for) larger scale water treatment facilities that may be
damaged by drone attack. Nevertheless, all water and wastewater treatment plants that fit the
definition of critical facility under 42 U.S.C. § 5195c(e) should be able to request a UAFR (as the
definition itself does not include a population cutoff). However, priority consideration should be
given to facilities serving larger populations or facilities with higher risk factors (such as those
serving critical national or regional facilities, agencies, or industries). While prioritizing eligibility
for a UAFR based on a high population metric could discount rural areas, we believe there are
greater opportunities for other local public utilities and the states to support smaller rural facilities
and populations than for major facilities serving large population areas.
We recognize the potential administrative burden for the FAA if every water and wastewater utility
simultaneously requested a UAFR. Population thresholds could therefore be used to establish
presumptive eligibility for a UAFR request. For example, a service population threshold of
100,000 or more people for both water and wastewater plants could be appropriate for establishing
presumptive eligibility to request a standard UAFR, while allowing smaller systems the
opportunity to demonstrate why they may warrant UAFR protection. In other words, a valid
demonstration of need, e.g. the lack of alternative sources or remoteness of the facility, should
allow utilities with smaller service populations to overcome any population criterion presumption.
Nevertheless, the FAA should prioritize UAFR consideration for facilities with larger populations
due to the potentially extensive safety and security impacts of disruptions to those systems.
Critical customers served by a drinking water/wastewater system may warrant
consideration when prioritizing UAFRs
Every water treatment facility serving a large community will have critical customers should it be
rendered inoperable. Truly critical national defense and other facilities will likely need to rely on
on-site backup water supply systems. In some cities, critical industries, hospitals, and schools may
have their own wells or storage systems to allow continued operation during service outages. So,
while we agree that in some cases critical customers may warrant prioritizing consideration of the
establishment of a UAFR for a particular facility, the reality is that all larger water plants will have
critical customers.

Docket Id: FAA-2026-4558
August 5, 2026
Page 4
Documentation of unauthorized drone flights over a drinking water or wastewater system
should be considered when prioritizing UAFRs but not considered as a necessary condition
for eligibility
Threat history should be considered when prioritizing the establishment of UAFRs but should not
be determinative of eligibility for a UAFR. Facilities that have had past incidents/threats should
be given UAFR establishment priority. However, again, past threats should relate to the
prioritization of the establishment of a UAFR, not to eligibility for a UAFR.
Additional Comments
Promulgating Water and Wastewater Sector Eligibility Criteria. Given the urgency and
importance of the safety and security associated with the proper provision of water and wastewater
service, the FAA should issue the Eligibility Criteria for the Water and Wastewater Systems
Section (§ 74.96) with the proposed rule text. Given the exponential expansion in unmanned
aircraft technologies and offensive uses, the FAA should move forward as efficiently and
expeditiously as possible. The FAA should identify the water and wastewater sector’s
prioritization criteria with the proposed rule – and not as a follow-up to the rule - to optimally
protect the provision of public water and wastewater services in the country.
Remote Sensing Technology. Applicants for UAFRs must submit information describing existing
security plans and measures under § 74.56(d) of the proposed rule, including the ability to receive
broadcast Remote Identification messages from unmanned aircraft. The Association supports this
measure to bolster the overall security of water and wastewater utilities but suggests that the FAA
provide accompanying guidance on appropriate ways to fulfill the Remote Identification
requirement, along with information on technical assistance to better help utilities meet and
understand this specific requirement.
Lateral Boundary Limitation. The proposed definition and limitations of a lateral boundary in §
74.58 may not accommodate the range of critical public water/sewer utility assets. The proposed
rule would set the lateral boundary at a facility’s property line. The final rule should ensure that
any UAFR covers all essential assets, such as elevated storage, chemical storage, and feed
locations. In some instances, establishing UAFR zones may make more sense than an individual
property-line approach, especially when multiple properties are in the same area. There should be
additional guidance/information about the flexibilities for water and wastewater systems with
regard to their sector and property line limitations so as not to undermine the true protective value
of a UAFR.
Five-Year Term. The Association supports the five-year permit duration (proposed § 74.200).
However, for water treatment facilities, we believe the permit duration should be 10 years, as these
facilities are so critical that we do not see UAFR zones being reduced or removed.
The Association appreciates the difficulty the FAA faces in balancing the optimal use of the
nation’s airspace with the protection of important utility infrastructure but urges the FAA to

Docket Id: FAA-2026-4558
August 5, 2026
Page 5
recognize that broad eligibility for UAFRs for water and wastewater utilities is essential to the
provision of public water and sewer service nationwide.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments. Please feel free to contact me with any
questions.
Sincerely,
Christopher Pomeroy
General Counsel

On behalf of the nearly 70 resort hotels across Nevada that we represent, including many of the
world’s largest integrated resorts, the Nevada Resort Association respectfully submits the following
comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
regarding the implementation of Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of
2016, which establishes a process for restricting unmanned aircraft operations in close proximity to
qualifying fixed-site facilities.
We support the FAA’s efforts to establish a consistent framework that protects critical infrastructure
from unsafe and unauthorized drone operations while preserving the many beneficial uses of
unmanned aircraft systems. As drafted, however, the proposed rule leaves a significant gap by
excluding many of the country’s highest-density tourism and entertainment destinations and venues.
Collectively, our members welcome more than 50 million visitors annually to Nevada, employ
hundreds of thousands of residents and host many of the nation’s largest conventions, sporting events,
mega concerts and massive public gatherings, such as our annual New Year’s Eve celebration. These
gatherings take place in venues that are not currently contemplated in the draft rule. Respectfully, we
urge the FAA to expand the rule to recognize these uniquely vulnerable facilities and protect the
millions of visitors, employees and residents who gather at these locations every day.
Expand Eligibility to High-Occupancy Tourism and Public Assembly Venues
The proposed rule appropriately recognizes that certain facilities warrant additional protection
because unauthorized drone operations present heightened safety and security risks. However, the
categories of eligible facilities are too narrow and omit some of the nation’s largest concentrations of
visitors and public gatherings for large scale events.

As drafted, the rule provides a pathway for certain amusement parks but not for integrated resort
properties, convention centers, stadiums, arenas or other large, high-profile public assembly venues.
There is likewise no mechanism to protect destinations such as the Las Vegas Resort Corridor, which
surrounds approximately four miles of Las Vegas Boulevard known colloquially as the “Las Vegas
Strip,” or the major tourism districts in Reno, despite the millions of visitors they attract each year
and the unique operational and security challenges they present.
The FAA specifically requested comments on whether additional facility types should be eligible for
protection. We respectfully recommend expanding eligibility to include:
• Integrated resort properties;
• Resort facilities meeting objective occupancy or visitor thresholds;
• Convention and exhibition centers;
• Stadiums and arenas; and
• Other large public assembly venues and tourism districts where significant crowds
routinely gather.
The FAA could establish objective eligibility criteria, such as maximum occupancy, annual
attendance, hotel room inventory or other measurable standards, which would provide a clear,
consistent framework for determining eligibility while clearly recognizing those facilities that present
elevated public safety and security considerations.
Safety, Privacy and Operational Risks
Unauthorized drone operations over large resort destinations present risks that extend beyond
traditional critical infrastructure concerns. Integrated resort properties combine hotels, entertainment
venues, restaurants, convention facilities, pools and outdoor gathering spaces, transportation
infrastructure and critical building systems into densely populated environments operating around the
clock. Unauthorized drone activity in these areas raises concerns regarding public safety, guest
privacy, noise and light disturbances, interference with emergency response activities, potential
conflicts with helicopters and other aircraft operating in the surrounding airspace and security
concerns associated with surveillance or unauthorized operations over sensitive resort
infrastructure. These risks become even more significant during major public events that attract tens
of thousands of attendees within a concentrated area in addition to the equally large number of
employees working in those spaces
Restrictions Should Extend Beyond Property Lines
The Nevada Resort Association encourages the FAA to establish reasonable buffers extending
beyond property boundaries for qualifying facilities. A restriction ending precisely at
a property’s boundary would permit drone operations immediately adjacent to venues where
thousands of people may be gathered, undermining the safety and security objectives of the rule. A
modest buffer surrounding qualifying facilities would provide a more practical and effective means of
reducing risks to the public.
District-Wide Designations
The Las Vegas Resort Corridor functions as a single destination comprised of adjacent resort
properties, entertainment venues, convention facilities, pedestrian bridges and transportation
infrastructure. Rather than requiring each eligible property to petition separately, the FAA should
allow certain high-density contiguous qualifying areas to seek a district-wide designation.
2

This approach would eliminate gaps in coverage, simplify compliance for drone operators and
provide a more efficient application process for the FAA.
Event-Based Flight Restrictions
The proposed rule permits either continuous restrictions or restrictions lasting up to 290 consecutive
days each year. This framework does not reflect the operational realities of venues that experience
heightened security needs during recurring special events and predictable periods of dramatically
elevated security needs. If the FAA does not allow for a blanket year-round restriction for qualifying
tourism districts, then FAA should provide a mechanism allowing approved facilities to activate
temporary flight restrictions during defined event periods, such as major scheduled sporting events,
New Year’s Eve celebrations, Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix race weekend, large tradeshows
and conventions and other major high-attendance events. Event-based activation would better align
restrictions with periods of elevated risk while minimizing impacts on lawful drone operations.
Public Safety and Emergency Operations
We also encourage the FAA to ensure that any final rule expressly preserves exemptions for
authorized public safety operations, including law enforcement, fire protection, emergency medical
services, disaster response and other governmental activities necessary to protect life and
property. Such exemptions should be clearly articulated to avoid unintended operational conflicts
during emergencies.
In closing, the Nevada Resort Association appreciates the FAA’s thoughtful efforts to modernize
drone safety regulations and establish a petition process for protecting critical infrastructure. We
respectfully encourage the FAA to expand the proposed rule to include integrated resort properties,
convention centers, stadiums, arenas and other large public assembly venues; authorize district-wide
designations for contiguous tourism corridors; provide reasonable buffers beyond property
boundaries; allow event-based activation of flight restrictions; and ensure appropriate exemptions for
public safety operations. These modifications would better reflect the evolving nature of America’s
most visited destinations while enhancing safety, protecting privacy, reducing operational risks and
supporting the safe integration of unmanned aircraft into America’s airspace.

I. A UAFR Is a Legal Instrument; Detection Is Its Indispensable Companion.
The FAA aptly describes a UAFR as a “virtual no trespassing sign.” A sign, however, does only
what signs do: it communicates a rule. It does not detect a violation, identify the violator, or alert
anyone that a violation is underway. A UAFR that is not paired with the ability to detect incursions
risks being a restriction whose violation goes unnoticed until after the harm has occurred: after the
contraband has been dropped, the surveillance flight completed, or the disruption caused. This
concern is sharpened by the transparency the framework rightly requires: because designated
Comments of SkySafe, Inc. — Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 Page 3 of 13

UAFRs must be published for operators to comply, the aggregate result is a public, government-
curated map of the Nation’s most sensitive facilities, each of which has attested to its own
vulnerability. A published restriction without a detection tripwire announces the target while
providing no means of knowing when it is being approached. The docket record already reflects
public reports of more than 300 drone seizures at FIFA World Cup match venues within the first
weeks of the tournament.4 Prominent, protected sites face incursions at volume; awareness, not
designation alone, enables response.
This is the central theme of SkySafe’s comments. For a UAFR to deliver the protection Section
2209 contemplates, the facility must be able to know, in real time, when an unauthorized aircraft
enters or approaches the restricted airspace, and to identify and attribute that aircraft. SkySafe
accordingly urges the FAA to treat detection as a core element of the protective posture that both
justifies and gives practical effect to the designation.
II. Proposed § 74.56(d) Should Require Detection of Non-Cooperative UA, Not Merely
Receipt of RID.
Proposed § 74.56(d) would require a facility to be capable of receiving and monitoring broadcast
RID messages from drones operating in or near the UAFR. SkySafe supports RID as a foundational
tool for airspace accountability. Standing alone, however, a protective-security standard limited to
RID receipt addresses the wrong population of aircraft.
By design, RID identifies cooperative operators who are complying with the law. The drones that
actually threaten a sensitive facility are precisely the ones that will not transmit compliant RID:
those flown by clueless, careless, or criminal operators. A facility able to “see” only RID-
broadcasting drones is, in effect, blind to the threat the rule is meant to counter. A monitoring
requirement satisfied entirely by RID receipt would give facilities a false sense of security while
leaving the most consequential incursions undetected. In response to the Agency’s specific request
for empirical data on the efficacy of Remote ID broadcast messages, SkySafe notes that it
maintains an extensive body of real-world RID reception data collected across its nationwide
detection network, and is prepared to provide this data to the Agency to support development of
the final rule.
SkySafe therefore recommends that § 74.56(d) require facilities to maintain the capability to
detect, identify, track, and characterize non-cooperative UA, in addition to receiving RID. This is
not an aspirational standard. Passive RF detection routinely identifies non-cooperative drones
(often including make, model, serial number, takeoff and landing locations, and the operator’s
position) without any cooperation from the operator, day or night and without reliance on line of

III. Detection Standards Should Be Performance-Based and Technology-Neutral, While
Recognizing the Advantages of Passive RF Detection.
SkySafe encourages the FAA to express any detection requirement in performance terms rather
than by prescribing a particular sensor architecture. Mandating a specific configuration (for
example, a “multi-sensor” system) would risk locking the rule against rapid technological change
and could impose cost and complexity without corresponding benefit. A better approach is to
define the outcomes a detection capability must achieve and to let facilities meet them with
whatever technology does so effectively. SkySafe suggests the following outcome criteria: the
ability to (i) detect both cooperative and non-cooperative UA; (ii) identify and characterize the
aircraft; (iii) localize the aircraft and, where feasible, the operator; (iv) operate persistently and
automatically; and (v) generate time-stamped, auditable records of activity.
Within a technology-neutral framework, SkySafe encourages the FAA to recognize, in the
preamble to the final rule and in any associated advisory material, the distinct advantages of
passive RF detection for this application. Passive RF detection emits no signal, and therefore raises
none of the spectrum-interference or authorization concerns associated with active sensing; it
operates in darkness and adverse weather and does not require line of sight; it can run continuously
and scale economically across wide areas; and, distinctively, it produces the attribution and
forensic data that connect an incursion to a specific aircraft and operator. These attributes make
passive RF detection particularly well suited to the persistent, wide-area protection the UAFR
framework envisions, whether deployed alone or as the backbone of a layered system.

V. The Demonstration of Need Should Not Impose a Two-Year Data-Collection Runway
on Facilities the Government Has Already Identified as Critical.
Proposed § 74.66 asks applicants to describe existing UA activity in close proximity to the facility
over the previous 24 months, where data is available. SkySafe supports grounding the
demonstration of need in objective, verifiable, sensor-collected data rather than anecdote; indeed,
SkySafe urges the FAA to require it. But the 24-month site-specific lookback, as proposed, would
have a perverse effect: because proposed § 74.56 requires facilities only to receive RID (a
capability few facilities have historically maintained), virtually no applicant will possess two years
of rigorous activity data at the time the rule takes effect. In practice, a facility that wishes to make
a data-supported showing must first deploy detection and then wait up to two years to accumulate
the record. For the Nation’s most sensitive sites, the proposal would thereby delay effective
protection by roughly two years after the rule is finalized. SkySafe recommends that the final rule
(a) make explicit that the lookback is not a data-collection gate, and (b) shorten the expected site-
specific observation window to no more than three months.
A three-month site-specific window is sufficient for four reasons. First, criticality is not in
question. The FAA, working with the Sector Risk Management Agencies, has already identified
approximately 125,000 high-priority fixed site facilities across the 16 critical infrastructure
sectors.8 For a facility on that list, the open question in the demonstration of need is UA exposure,
not whether the site matters. Second, networked and cross-site data substantiate need faster and
better than any single site’s log. SkySafe’s operational experience is that the most probative threat
evidence is often cross-site: the same operator or aircraft appearing at multiple facilities, patterns
of route-testing and rehearsal, and regional activity trends. Three months of site data, corroborated
by networked detection data and regional activity records, is a stronger evidentiary basis than 24
months of one facility’s isolated observations. The FAA should give explicit evidentiary weight
to such networked, cross-site, and third-party data in § 74.66. Third, a purely site-bounded activity
record understates the threat by construction. Modern UA sensors permit standoff surveillance: a
camera-equipped drone can observe a facility in detail from well outside any property-line UAFR,
without ever generating an “in close proximity” event in the facility’s log. A demonstration-of-
need standard that counts only overflights therefore systematically misses the surveillance activity
that most concerns security planners. Fourth, administrability. With 125,000 candidate facilities
and more than 9,000 applications projected over five years, a per-site, self-proven, 24-month
evidentiary model does not scale for applicants or for the FAA’s reviewers. Shorter site-specific
windows, standardized data formats, and networked corroboration are what make review at that
volume tractable.

In response to the Agency’s request for comment on eligibility criteria for the Water and

Section 2209 was enacted to address, and SkySafe recommends it be adopted as a criterion for

VII. Detection Should Extend a Reasonable Distance Beyond UAFR Boundaries.
The Agency has requested comment on whether a UAFR’s lateral boundaries should, in some
circumstances, extend beyond the fixed site facility’s property line. SkySafe recommends the FAA
resolve this question by distinguishing between the two functions a boundary might be asked to
serve. As a legal restriction, the UAFR is appropriately confined to the applicant’s property:
extending the prohibition into surrounding airspace would encroach on navigable airspace and
burden legitimate operations near, but not over, the facility. As a matter of security awareness,
however, the property line is the wrong boundary. Effective protection requires detecting and
assessing an approaching or loitering aircraft before it crosses into restricted airspace, while there
is still time to alert personnel, coordinate with law enforcement, and respond. The standoff
surveillance capability described in Section V makes the gap concrete: an aircraft observing the
facility from outside the boundary never enters restricted airspace at all. Detection limited to the
footprint of the UAFR would create exactly the blind spot a determined operator will exploit.

VIII. The Final Rule Should Require Retention of Detection Data for a Defined Minimum
Period.
The FAA has sought comment on whether retention of RID and detection data should be required,
and for how long. SkySafe’s answer is yes: the final rule should adopt a defined minimum retention
requirement, not merely permission to retain. Retention is not incidental to this framework; several
of the rule’s own obligations depend on it. The draft advisory material contemplates an annual UA
activity report from every UAFR holder covering both allowed and observed unauthorized activity,
a report that cannot be produced from data that was not retained. Renewal of a five-year
designation is an inherently retrospective showing of continuing need, made from the retained
record. Enforcement, whether civil or criminal, requires time-stamped, auditable evidence that
survives to the conclusion of proceedings. And the shortened, prospective demonstration of need
recommended in Section V above relies on the ongoing retained record in place of a long historical
lookback. A rule that mandates reporting, renewal, and enforcement while remaining silent on
retention would be internally incoherent.
SkySafe recommends: (a) a defined minimum retention period for detection and RID-receipt
records of no less than the annual-reporting and renewal cycle (SkySafe suggests no less than 24
months for routine records); (b) longer retention for incident-associated records, through the
conclusion of any related enforcement action or the term of the designation; and (c) express
recognition that retention may be performed by a certified third-party provider on the facility’s
behalf, consistent with the service model described in Section IV, so that the compliance burden
on facilities remains low.
On cost, which the Agency specifically asked commenters to address: the records at issue are
structured detection and RID-receipt data, consisting of timestamps, identifiers, positions, and
signal metadata. Storage of this kind is a negligible expense, orders of magnitude below the video

does not change materially whether the retention period is measured in months or years. Cost is
not a reason to leave retention unaddressed in the final rule, and where a facility retains through a
certified service provider, retention is simply a feature of the service rather than a separate expense
at all.
SkySafe recognizes that some commenters will raise privacy concerns about mandatory retention.
Those concerns are addressable and should not defeat the requirement. What would be retained is
aircraft telemetry and broadcast identifiers, which RID already makes publicly receivable by
regulatory design, not personal information; access should be limited to security, safety, and

The framework’s transparency provisions serve an essential function: a restriction operators cannot

and is prepared to provide the Agency with operational cost data from real-world detection
deployments to assist that analysis.
The conclusion to draw from a more realistic cost picture is not weaker requirements but affordable
compliance, which the certified service models described in Section IV deliver. Detection-as-a-
service spreads network costs across many subscribing facilities, bringing genuine non-
cooperative detection within a per-facility cost envelope far closer to the FAA’s estimate than
facility-owned systems ever could. An accurate cost analysis and an express service-provider
pathway are complements: together they make the rule both honest and achievable.
XI. Transit, Notification, and the Facility’s Role.
SkySafe supports allowing qualified, accountable operators to transit UAFRs, and recommends
that the access-notification process in proposed § 74.255 be capable of automation through
machine-to-machine and whitelist-based methods rather than manual, flight-by-flight notification.
Detection service providers are well positioned to perform the threat-discrimination function at the
heart of that process: a provider monitoring the airspace can distinguish a whitelisted, authorized
transit from an unknown incursion and notify the facility only when an aircraft has not been
cleared. The same RID credentials and manufacturer identifiers used for accountability can drive
an automated clearance process, including for operators conducting recurring flights. Coupled with
the real-time UAFR register recommended in Section IV, this closes the loop of a coherent system:
current restriction data flows to operators and facilities alike, authorized operations clear
automatically, and human attention is reserved for genuine anomalies.
SkySafe cautions, however, that a whitelist is only as trustworthy as the identifiers on which it is
keyed. Broadcast RID messages under the current U.S. means of compliance carry no
authentication: any transmitter can broadcast any serial number, including one enrolled on a
whitelist. A clearance process keyed to unauthenticated identifiers can be defeated by simple
impersonation, and the more privilege an identifier confers, the more attractive impersonation
becomes.
The solution is authentication, and it need not burden the general operator population. SkySafe
recommends that the final rule condition whitelist enrollment, and the streamlined transit clearance
that comes with it, on broadcasting authenticated RID: messages cryptographically signed with
credentials issued at enrollment. Japan’s Remote ID framework demonstrates that this is practical
at national scale today.10 Aircraft registration through the government’s DIPS platform issues a
signing key, and the aircraft broadcasts a signature over its identification data using the
Authentication message already defined in the same ASTM F3411 framework on which the FAA’s
10See Civil Aeronautics Act (Japan), as amended (mandatory aircraft registration and Remote ID, effective June 20,
2022). Registration through the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism’s Drone/UAS Information
Platform System (DIPS) issues a cryptographic signing key to the aircraft’s Remote ID equipment, and the aircraft
broadcasts a signature over its identification data.
Comments of SkySafe, Inc. — Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 Page 11 of 13

Remote ID means of compliance is based.11 No new broadcast standard is required. The message
type exists; the United States has simply not required it to be populated.
Structured this way, authentication scales naturally to fleets. Credentials may be issued at the
operator or manufacturer-code level (the four-character ANSI/CTA-2063-A manufacturer code),
so a fleet operator need not enroll each aircraft individually; trust attaches to the certificate rather
than to any particular identifier. This preserves the low-burden enrollment that high-volume
operators need while ensuring that the aircraft claiming a whitelisted identity is the aircraft that
was cleared. Operators who do not seek whitelist privileges face no new requirement:
unauthenticated broadcast RID remains the baseline for ordinary notification and transit under §
74.255. Conditioning privileges on authentication, rather than imposing new equipage mandates
on the entire fleet, is consistent with the direction of Executive Orders 14305 and 14307 to secure
the airspace without constraining lawful operations.
The framework should also define what happens after an incursion is detected. As proposed, the
rule assigns facilities an awareness function but establishes no channel through which that
awareness reaches an entity capable of acting on it. Referral to local law enforcement, standing
alone, is not such a channel; most local agencies lack the authority, tools, and training to investigate
airspace violations. SkySafe recommends that the final rule establish a standardized, electronic
incursion-reporting mechanism through which a UAFR holder or its detection service provider can
submit a structured incident record, including the aircraft track, any received RID data, and
associated timestamps, to the FAA for enforcement action under § 74.260, with routing to the
Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation for incursions implicating national
security, consistent with the interagency coordination directed by Executive Order 14305. A
defined referral pipeline converts detection from an alarm into the first step of an enforcement
process, and it ensures that the retained records described in Section VIII above serve their
evidentiary purpose. The 2026 FIFA World Cup demonstrated the model at national scale: more
than 1,600 unauthorized drones were detected attempting to enter restricted airspace around match
venues, enabling the seizure of over 700 aircraft and multiple federal prosecutions.12
Finally, SkySafe emphasizes, consistent with the NPRM, that a UAFR confers no authority to
interfere with, seize, or disable a UA. The facility’s role under Part 74 is, and should remain, one
of awareness: to detect, identify, and provide notification. SkySafe’s recommendations are
directed at making that awareness function as effective as possible. Questions of active mitigation
are governed by separate legal authorities and are beyond the scope of this rulemaking.
11ASTM F3411, Standard Specification for Remote ID and Tracking, defines an Authentication message type within
its broadcast message framework. The FAA’s accepted means of compliance for 14 C.F.R. part 89 is built on ASTM
F3411-22a, see 87 Fed. Reg. 49,520 (Aug. 11, 2022) (accepting ASTM F3586-22, an overlay of requirements to
ASTM F3411-22a), but does not require the Authentication message to be populated. Japan’s framework requires it.
12Federal Bureau of Investigation, How the FBI Keeps the Public Safe at Gatherings (July 15, 2026),
https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/special-event-security-part-two (reporting more than 1,600 unauthorized drones
detected attempting to enter restricted airspace around FIFA World Cup venues, with more than 700 seized).
Comments of SkySafe, Inc. — Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 Page 12 of 13

Conclusion
SkySafe appreciates the opportunity to comment and commends the FAA for advancing a
framework that will meaningfully improve the protection of critical infrastructure and other
sensitive facilities. SkySafe’s central message is straightforward: a UAFR is only as effective as a
facility’s ability to know when it is being violated; that ability depends on detection of non-
cooperative aircraft, sustained by retained data, delivered affordably through certified services,
and coherent with the low-altitude airspace architecture the FAA is already building. SkySafe
stands ready to serve as a technical resource to the Agency as it finalizes this rule, and would
welcome the opportunity to discuss these comments or to provide supporting operational data.
Respectfully submitted,
Grant Jordan
Chief Executive Officer
SkySafe, Inc.
Comments of SkySafe, Inc. — Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 Page 13 of 13

comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
Bryan Bedford
Administrator
Federal Aviation Administration
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Ave SE
Washington, D.C. 20590
Re: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility (Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03)
Dear Administrator Bedford:
The United States Golf Association, the PGA TOUR Enterprises, LLC, the Professional Golfers’
Association of America, the Ladies Professional Golf Association, and Augusta National, Inc.
(hereinafter “Golf Associations”) write to provide the following comments in response to the
Federal Aviation Administration’s (“FAA”) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NPRM”) on
“Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility,” which implements Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of
2016 (hereinafter “Proposed Rule”).1
As representatives of the major golf tournaments across the United States, we are deeply
concerned that golf tournaments, many of which attract tens of thousands of fans daily, are
excluded from coverage under the Proposed Rule, despite the significant and demonstrated
security risk and the lack of a consistent and predictable framework for the protection of golf
tournaments. Whereas other major sporting events, such as Major League Baseball, National
Football League, Division I college football games, NASCAR Cup, IndyCar, Champ Series
races, and others, have standing protection for their games, golf tournaments do not—even if
they host larger numbers of people than at other protected events. This creates a security gap for
golf tournament events. We urge the FAA to fill this gap before it issues the final rule.
I. Background on Golf Associations
The United States Golf Association (USGA): The USGA is a mission-based golf organization
whose purpose is to unify the golf community; to showcase the game’s best talent through the
U.S. Open, U.S. Women’s Open, and thirteen other national championships and our museum; to
provide unbiased global governance of the sport; and to advance issues important to golf’s
1 Federal Aviation Administration, Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close
Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility, 91 FED. REG. 24,650 (proposed May 6, 2026) (to be codified at 14
C.F.R. pts. 1, 74, 91, 107), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-05-06/pdf/2026-08943.pdf.
1

future, with a focus on driving sustainability, accessibility, and inclusion. The USGA also
manages day-to-day operations for the U.S. National Development Program, which helps
identify, train, and financially support top-tier American golfers, and the World Golf Hall of
Fame, which preserves and celebrates the legacies of the game’s greatest figures. As a nonprofit
association, our work and our team are driven to act for the good of the game.
PGA TOUR Enterprises, LLC (PGA TOUR): The PGA TOUR is a premier membership
organization for touring professional golfers. Its mission is to deliver the world’s most
compelling professional golf competition for players, fans, partners, and communities. PGA
TOUR members include the world’s greatest players, from 26 countries and territories. The
PGA TOUR hosts multiple signature tournaments, attracting high numbers of on-site attendees,
with individual events commonly attracting tens of thousands of spectators.
The Professional Golfers’ Association of America (PGA of America): PGA of America is one
of the world’s largest sports organizations, composed of more than 30,000 PGA of America Golf
Professionals, and hosts premier events including the annual PGA Championship, Women’s
PGA Championship, and Senior PGA Championship, as well as the biennial Ryder Cup (when in
the United States). Our events draw hundreds of thousands of on-site spectators and captivate
millions of fans around the world. Ensuring the public safety of fans and players is core to the
PGA of America’s not-for-profit mission of promoting enjoyment and involvement in the game
of golf and contributing to its growth by providing services to golf professionals and the golf
industry.
The Ladies Professional Golf Association (LPGA): Founded in 1950, the LPGA is widely
recognized as the longest-running women’s professional sports organization and serves as the
leading organization for women’s professional golf. Through the LPGA Tour; Epson Tour;
LPGA Professionals, with more than 2,500 members; and related golf-development initiatives,
the LPGA plays a central role in the professional golf ecosystem and in advancing women’s golf
globally. The LPGA has a direct interest in ensuring the public safety of major women’s
professional golf events and in ensuring sufficient airspace protection for its events.
Augusta National, Inc. (ANI): ANI operates Augusta National Golf Club, a private golf club for
its members located in Augusta, Georgia, and annually hosts the world-renowned Masters
Tournament, one of four men’s professional golf major championships, held during the first full
week in April and drawing tens of thousands of patrons every day over seven days. ANI also
hosts the final round of the Augusta National Women’s Amateur and the Drive, Chip and Putt
National Finals at Augusta National Golf Club. Each competition is an outdoor, open-air event
that is subject to ticketing and entry control procedures.
II. Unauthorized and Malicious Drones Present Significant Risks to Major Golf
Events
Golf tournaments are large, outdoor public gatherings that draw large crowds, often in the tens of
thousands per day. More than 200,000 fans regularly attend the U.S. Open and the PGA
Championship. Spectators travel across the country and around the world to attend golf
tournaments and often include senior federal, state, and local government officials; heads of
2

state; top business executives; sports and entertainment stars; and other high-profile individuals.
Tournaments hosted by our associations are nationally and internationally significant events
broadcast globally to millions of viewers.
Unlike stadiums and arenas, which generally have a defined, limited footprint and structural
buffer zones separating the venue from surrounding areas, golf tournaments take place across
hundreds of acres, often directly adjacent to residential neighborhoods. This poses distinct
security challenges, as drones can be easily launched from private property immediately next to
the course. The distance from launch to potential disruption is just a matter of a few feet. In
fact, there have been multiple cases in which drones launched from cars and private property
alongside a championship course have caused disruptions in play. The number of unauthorized
drones at championship tournaments has increased year over year.
The risks of a malicious attack or even inadvertent crashes causing significant casualties are
high. In June, authorities disrupted an alleged plot to attack one side of the White House-held
Ultimate Fighting Championship (“UFC”) event with explosive-laden drones to force panicked
spectators to exit the other side and then shoot at those seeking to depart.2 While the planned
attack was stopped, thanks in part to extensive work by the Federal Bureau of Investigation
(“FBI”), it highlights the vulnerability of open-air events to threats from the sky. During the
2026 World Cup, the FBI identified some 1,600 unauthorized drones and seized more than 700.3
The FBI has declared drones “a growing problem at special events.”4
Risks to golf include, but are not limited to, the following:
• A malicious actor using a drone with a payload could cause mass casualties, trigger
panic, and disrupt evacuation and emergency-response efforts across a large and difficult-
to-secure venue. The UFC example highlights that the threat is real.
• Drones can crash onto the course or areas where spectators are congregating—potentially
causing fatalities and significant injuries to spectators, players, caddies, volunteers,
vendors, and anyone else in attendance. Subsequent panic and the ensuing chaos can
result in follow-on fatalities and injuries as well.
• Surveillance drones and those with camera feeds enable unauthorized access to
tournament footage and violate tournament policies and entry controls. These drones can
also inadvertently lose control, causing significant injury and panic, even if accidental.
2 U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, FBI Arrests Two More Men in Washington and
Missouri in Connection with Planned Attack on Government Officials at White House UFC Event (June
22, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/fbi-arrests-two-more-men-washington-and-missouri-
connection-planned-attack-government.
3 Adam Leventhal, More Than 700 Illegal Drones Seized During the World Cup, Says FBI, N.Y. Times
(July 19, 2026), https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7452912/2026/07/19/more-than-700-illegal-drones-
seized-during-the-world-cup-says-fbi/.
4 Special Event Security, Part Two: How the FBI Keeps the Public Safe at Gatherings, Federal Bureau of
Investigation (July 15, 2026), https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/special-event-security-part-two.
3

Given the risks, unauthorized drones generally require play to stop, as security teams work to
assess the threat and protect the security and safety of all those in attendance. These disruptions
have implications beyond the obvious inconvenience. Such shutdowns have significant
economic consequences and can raise cascading security concerns, particularly for large
tournaments that are broadcast across the nation and globe.5
III. Insufficient Existing Protections
A. Flight Restrictions Are Administered Inconsistently
Despite these serious safety and security concerns, the golf industry has been consistently left out
of unmanned aircraft system (“UAS”) protections available to other major sports.
Football, baseball, and major car racing events are all covered by the FAA’s Sporting Event
Temporary Flight Restriction (“TFR”).6 Golf is not. The Sporting Event TFR is automatic—
covering a three-nautical-mile radius and 3,000 feet above ground for any stadium with a seating
capacity of 30,000 or more people during a Major League Baseball, National Football League, or
NCAA Division I Football game, even if the actual number of attendees falls well below 30,000.
The standing TFR also covers NASCAR Cup, IndyCar, and the Champ Series races. This
standing TFR is in effect from an hour before the scheduled event until an hour after the event
ends.
Golf tournaments are not covered by that standing protection, even when they draw crowds that
far exceed 30,000, and despite the added difficulties with securing open-air tournaments adjacent
to residential areas and without a stadium-like buffer zone. Instead, tournament organizers are
required to rely on the separate, case-by-case process for obtaining a TFR in the vicinity of a
major sporting event.
But this alternative process fails to address the needs of major golf events. It is a one-off, case-
by-case process that depends, in significant part, on the engagement of local authorities, rather
than a consistent assessment of risk or threat by the FAA. In fact, golf is not even mentioned in
the list of “major sporting event(s)” that could qualify for a temporary flight restriction pursuant
to FAA regulation regarding temporary flight restrictions around major sporting events.7 The list
includes World Cup Soccer, the Major League Baseball All-Star Game, the World Series, the
Sandia Classic Hang Gliding Competition, the Indianapolis 500 Mile Race, and the Kodak
5 Drones can also threaten the operational integrity of our competitions. Golf depends on a controlled and
quiet competitive environment. A low-flying drone can disrupt a golfer’s swing by shattering the silence
of the course. While not as significant as a catastrophic event that causes loss of life and injury, such
disturbances are still of high concern to our associations, as they interfere with the fair administration of
tournament play and competitive integrity.
6 Sporting Event Temporary Flight Restriction: FDC NOTAM 4/3621, Federal Aviation Administration,
https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/uas/resources/policy_library/Sports_TFR-UAS_Handout.pdf.
7 See 14 C.F.R. § 91.145.
4

Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta—but not a single golf tournament, despite the
significantly higher fan base and extended footprint of several major golf tournaments.8
In order for these one-off TFR requests to be successful, the request needs to come from and be
actively supported by state and local officials, along with federal officials. Protection thus often
depends on local resources and prioritization, rather than on an objective, national-level
assessment of the applicable safety and security risks by the agency responsible for managing the
national airspace.
This yields inconsistent results, even for events with similar threat profiles. In some
jurisdictions, public safety partners support a request for a TFR. In others, local law enforcement
may not have sufficient familiarity with the drone threat or with the TFR process to support such
a request. Local law enforcement also might not have the resources to prioritize, seek, and then
help enforce a TFR.
When the process works, and there is a TFR in place, our tournaments and fan base have
important protections in place, and unauthorized drone operators can be held to account. In
advance of the 2025 U.S. Open Championship at Oakmont Country Club in Oakmont,
Pennsylvania, for example, state, local, and federal law enforcement partners collectively
supported issuance of a TFR. When unauthorized drones violated the flight restrictions, the
operators were identified, located, and interviewed by the FAA and FBI, which in turn supported
ongoing deterrence efforts.
Conversely, local law enforcement in Los Angeles, California, declined to support the request for
a TFR in connection with the 2026 U.S. Women’s Open at Riviera Country Club. Soon into the
championship, a drone being used by a real estate agent to take pictures of a golf course-adjacent
house flew over the first putting green, causing a delay in play as security officials worked to
identify the source and assess the risk. In this case, the operator was friendly and cooperative
and agreed to stop flying until the end of the championship after being contacted by USGA
security personnel. But had the operator not voluntarily agreed to stop flying the drone, the
USGA would have had no recourse, as there were no restrictions in place. Had the drone
crashed—or even worse, operated with bad intent—the consequences could have been
devastating.
Over the course of the weeklong 2025 PGA TOUR Championship in Atlanta, Georgia, more
than 200 unauthorized drone flights entered the course boundaries. Although the course is
surrounded by an eight-foot exterior wall that limits unauthorized entry and ground-based
threats, the risk posed by these drones could not be controlled or mitigated, given the absence of
a TFR and associated deterrence capabilities. The PGA TOUR was limited in its recourse
options, and once again, opportunity was ripe for bad intent by unauthorized drone operators.
8 Id. § 91.145(a). While the list is non-exhaustive, golf’s absence from the list creates an added hurdle
that tournament organizers must meet—in terms of convincing the relevant decision-makers that a
particular event warrants protection.
5

B. Security Protections without Flight Restrictions are Insufficient
Each of our organizations prioritizes the safety and security of our tournaments. We work hard
to protect the many spectators, players, caddies, tournament officials, volunteers, vendors, media
personnel, employees, and others that attend our events—often spending millions of dollars on
security measures, including the best-in-class drone detection capabilities. At USGA national
championships, for example, it is not uncommon to spend $3 to $4 million on a single national
championship: $1 million to $1.5 million in private security costs, $1 million to $2 million in
reimbursements to state and local law enforcement, and $200,000 to $300,000 for aerial
surveillance, including drone-detection capability.
These investments are substantial. But they are insufficient without effective airspace
restrictions. Without restrictions in place, our associations cannot even prohibit local residents
from flying drones over our tournaments—nor do the kind of advanced education about the
applicable prohibitions that is so key to minimizing the risk of disruptions.
Without effective TFRs, our associations are left to respond to unauthorized UAS after the drone
has already flown over our event and to rely on the good faith and voluntary cooperation of the
drone operator. That is not sufficient. It leaves tens of thousands of fans vulnerable to a known
and significant risk. We need a predictable and nationally consistent framework to obtain flight
restrictions and thus provide critical protection for golf tournaments.
IV. Recommended Fixes to the Proposed Section 2209 Rule
The Proposed Rule presents a meaningful opportunity to fill an important gap and consistently
protect golf tournaments from the unauthorized and malicious use of UAS. However, critical
modifications are needed to include golf tournaments within the range of applicable protections.
A. Expand the Scope of “Commercial Facility” to Cover Golf Tournaments
The Proposed Rule’s preamble describes the category of covered “commercial facilities” as
including “various sites that draw large crowds for shopping, conducting business, entertainment,
or lodging.”9 Golf tournaments that draw large numbers of spectators would appear to fall within
this definition.
But in actuality, the Proposed Rule’s definition of a commercial facility eligible for an unmanned
aircraft flight restriction (“UAFR”) is narrowly crafted around amusement parks and little more.
Specifically, the definition is limited to a fixed-site facility that:
(a) Has an annual attendance that met or exceeded 2,500,000 visitors in the previous
calendar year;
(b) Has ticketing or entry control procedures;
(c) Is primarily outdoors and not enclosed;
(d) Is open to the public at least 120 days of the year;
9 Proposed Rule at 24,666.
6

(e) Is not a stadium or venue where the events may be covered by temporary flight
restrictions.10
Golf tournaments do not meet this definition.
• Golf tournaments have ticketing and entry control procedures. They also are primarily
outdoors and not enclosed—thus satisfying requirements (b) and (c).
• But golf tournaments are of limited duration. Given this limited duration, they do not
have an annual attendance in excess of 2.5 million visitors. They also are not open to the
public at least 120 days a year.
The exclusive focus on fixed-site facilities, like amusement parks, which operate on a more
permanent basis—and the exclusion of golf tournaments (and other similarly situated sporting
events)—leaves a gap. That gap is a mistake.
The stated justification for this approach also falls short. The preamble to the Proposed Rule
seeks to explain the narrow definition as follows:
[H]igh-risk fairs, parades, exhibitions, sporting events,
marathons, . . . etc. may be eligible to request temporary
flight restrictions from FAA. As these facilities host events
that are often temporary in nature (e.g., have a start and end
time), a temporary flight restriction is more appropriate than
a permanent or part-time UAFR. Certain major sporting
events also fall under a standing flight restriction for one
hour before and one hour after qualifying events.11
There are two key flaws with these claims:
First, it assumes that the process to obtain a temporary flight restriction for high-
risk temporary events, like golf tournaments, is always functional. As discussed
above, it is not.
Second, it seems to assume that the full array of key, major sporting events are
covered by the standing flight restrictions for sports. That also is not the case.
Golf tournaments are left out of that standing flight restriction, along with other
major sporting events, as discussed above.
At various points, the Proposed Rule seems to justify the almost exclusive focus on
amusement parks by pointing to Congress. In fact, the preamble specifically cites the
FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (“FAA Reauthorization Act”) and
states that:
10 Proposed Rule at 24,688 (proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.82).
11 Proposed Rule at 24,666.
7

Congress . . . identified specific categories of eligible
industries: critical infrastructure, such as energy production,
transmission, and distribution facilities and equipment; oil
refineries and chemical facilities; amusement parks; and
other locations that warrant such restrictions.12
But this is a misreading of the underlying statute. Congress identified both critical
infrastructure and amusement parks in the 2016 FAA Reauthorization Act and
subsequent amendments. Importantly, Congress has defined critical infrastructure as:
[S]ystems and assets, whether physical or virtual, so vital to
the United States that the incapacity or destruction of such
systems and assets would have a debilitating impact on
security, national economic security, national public health
or safety, or any combination of those matters.13
A drone attack on a golf tournament that causes significant loss of life and destruction
would have a debilitating impact on security and safety—and as much of a debilitating
impact as an equivalent attack on an amusement park.
RECOMMENDATIONS
• Amend the definition of “commercial facilities” and create an additional category of
short-term UAFR to cover golf tournaments of national or international significance
that anticipate significant attendance.
Create an additional category of “commercial facility” that (a) Has a daily
o
admission capacity of 10,000 or more; (b) Has ticketing or entry control
procedures; and (c) Is primarily outdoors and not enclosed.
Clarify that applicants would be eligible for part-time UAFRs only, timed to
o
last for the duration of the golf event and related activity—rather than the kind
of year-round UAFRs sought by other applicants.
• Allow for applications from tournament organizers to cover multiple sites that meet
the applicable criteria, thus enabling protections for tournaments that shift location
from year to year.
• Doing so will help ensure national-level oversight and thus a more reliable and
consistent framework for implementation of what are often one-off flight restrictions.
This will also bolster the enormous investment already expended by each
organization to provide for the safety and security of the golf tournament.
12 Proposed Rule at 24,654 (citing FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No.
114-190, § 2209(b)(1)(C), 130 Stat. 615, 634).
13 42 U.S.C. § 5195c(e).
8

• That said, the FAA should make clear that this is an additional path for obtaining
flight restrictions, designed to supplement the current processes for obtaining
restrictions over specific events. Put simply, our associations seek to supplement, not
override or supersede, existing processes for obtaining temporary flight restrictions.
B. Ensure that Flight Restrictions Include Sufficient Protections to Keep Out
Unauthorized Drones, While Continuing to Enable Use of Approved Drones
(i) Golf Associations Should Have Control Over What Drones Fly Over Our
Tournaments
The FAA should ensure that any flight restrictions enable tournament organizers to have advance
approval authority over which drones may operate within the protected airspace. Notice alone is
not enough.
Of concern, the standard UAFR envisioned under the Rule allows commercial and recreational
drones to fly over restricted airspace so long as they provide advance notice to the FAA and
facility manager, broadcast a remote ID, and transit the restricted area in the shortest time
practicable.14 This is insufficient to protect our tournaments from threats and significantly more
permissive than existing TFRs for sporting events and otherwise, which generally require
affirmative authorization or waiver to fly over a restricted area.
Broad automatic exceptions undermine the security purpose of TFRs, which work because they
enable tournaments to keep out unauthorized drone flights.
(ii) Tournament-Approved Drones Should Be Able to Carry Out the Full Spectrum of
Safety, Security, Broadcasting, and Other Authorized Roles
The Proposed Rule appears to require even facility-approved drones to be subject to the operational
conditions set out in the Rule—including the requirement that they transit the airspace in the
shortest time possible.15 This is inconsistent with the way our tournaments use approved drones
for safety, security, and inspection purposes; to create a broadcast feed and footage; and to video
events for posterity.
Put simply, our associations need the authority to (i) control the airspace over our courses—on a
temporary basis during golf tournaments where there are significant risks to the many fans, players,
volunteers, and others who are present; (ii) enable approved drones to carry out their important
security, public safety, broadcast, and related roles; and (iii) keep out unauthorized drones in order
to protect our players, volunteers, and spectators from the risk of disruption, crash, or—even
worse—malicious attacks.
14 Proposed Rule at 24,690 (proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.250(a)).
15 Id.
9

RECOMMENDATIONS
• The Rule should enable venue and tournament owners and other relevant parties to
fully control which drones can be present over the courses and how such drones
operate, albeit with emergency exceptions for law enforcement and public safety
purposes.
• To the extent commercial and recreational UAS operations are permitted over
restricted airspace, such flights should require express approval by the relevant
tournament organizer prior to operating.
• The Rule should explicitly authorize tournament organizers to maintain a list of
approved drones that are permitted to transit the protected airspace without
restriction.
V. Conclusion
We respectfully urge the FAA to revise the Proposed Rule to provide a predictable and
nationally consistent pathway for protecting golf tournaments from unauthorized drone
operations. These changes are essential to improving the safety, security, and integrity of golf
tournaments and their hundreds of thousands of fans. If you have questions or seek additional
input, please reach out to our counsel, Jennifer Daskal at Venable LLP (JDaskal@Venable.com
or 202-344-4975).
Sincerely,
United States Golf Association
PGA TOUR Enterprises, LLC
Professional Golfers’ Association of America
Ladies Professional Golf Association
Augusta National, Inc.

comments.commenter: Comment from New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
Ms. Michelle Ferritto
Office of Rulemaking
Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue SW
Washington, DC 20591
Re: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: “Designation – Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”)
Dear Ms. Ferritto:
The New York State Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) appreciates the opportunity to
submit comments in response to the above-referenced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)
concerning restrictions on the operation of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in close proximity to
critical fixed-site facilities.
Overview
MTA is North America's largest transportation network, serving a population of 15.3 million people
across a 5,000-square-mile travel area encompassing New York City and the surrounding areas of
Long Island, southeastern New York State, and Connecticut.
MTA appreciates FAA’s goal of streamlining regulations while maintaining safety and security. As
the operator of a large number of fixed-site public transportation facilities, many of which are in a
dense urban environment, MTA also supports the general goal of establishing rigorous safety and
security standards that UAS operators must adhere to. This includes establishing Unmanned
Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) for critical facilities as proposed in the NPRM.
While the FAA appropriately seeks to balance security, airspace access, and economic interests,
the protection of critical transportation infrastructure must remain paramount. MTA operates
infrastructure that is essential to public safety, regional mobility, and national economic activity,
making it an attractive target for malicious or disruptive operations of UAS. The FAA should ensure
that any limitation on UAFR eligibility does not diminish the ability to establish or maintain effective
protections around critical MTA facilities. Preserving robust authority to protect these assets is
essential to preventing unauthorized UAS activity that could disrupt operations, endanger the

Re: Docket Number FAA-2026-4558 (NPRM “Designation–Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”)
August 5, 2026
Page 2 of 5
traveling public, or create significant security vulnerabilities, while continuing to accommodate
authorized operations that serve legitimate public safety and infrastructure needs.
Accordingly, MTA makes the following recommendations:
I. Eligible Types of Public Transportation Facilities
A. Expand the eligibility criteria for a UAFR to include all public transportation
infrastructure, including, but not limited to, bridges, tunnels, yards, stations, transit
rights of way, and other facilities.
As proposed in the NPRM (proposed 14 CFR § 74.95), the scope of public transportation
facilities eligible for a UAFR is extremely limited, including only certain rail freight facilities,
electric substations supporting railroad catenary systems, highway bridges or tunnels
meeting minimum length and traffic requirements, and intermodal passenger facilities
handling three or more of the listed modes.
This tight scope would exclude protection of a wide range of other transportation
infrastructure that is equally essential to public safety, regional mobility, and national
economic activity. As noted in the Overview section above, unauthorized UAS activity
around any of this infrastructure could disrupt operations, endanger the traveling public, or
create significant security vulnerabilities.
For example, UAS operating around railroad rights-of-way endanger and delay passenger
train operations; when a UAS is sighted, operations must be adjusted in the interest of
safety. When a UAS lands within a railroad right-of-way or other hazardous location on
transportation agency property – including when a pilot attempts to retrieve the UAS –
operational impacts and safety hazards are even greater. In short, a UAS operating in close
proximity to any passenger facility, no matter how many modes it serves, endangers those
passengers, employees, operations, and infrastructure.
Similarly, bridges and tunnels that do not meet the size and traffic criteria proposed in the
NPRM can warrant UAFRs based on their locations and/or the cargo and passenger traffic
they handle. For example, a smaller bridge may warrant a UAFR because it is in a sensitive
location (e.g., neighboring an airport), where its shutdown for a UAS incident would impact
safety, regional mobility, and the economy.
Accordingly, MTA strongly urges FAA to expand the eligibility criteria for a UAFR to include
all public transportation infrastructure.

Re: Docket Number FAA-2026-4558 (NPRM “Designation–Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”)
August 5, 2026
Page 3 of 5
B. Ensure that all UAS operations in proximity to critical public transportation facilities
require approval in advance from the site operator (e.g., include in “Special” UAFS
category as currently defined in the NPRM).
As the proposed rule is written, the “Special UAFR” designation would require advance
approval from the site operator for any UAS flight. In contrast, for facilities assigned a
“Standard UAFR,” UAS operators could obtain blanket authorization to operate in proximity
to any such facility at any time, without the need for approval from the site operator.
As a result, the proposed “Standard UAFR” raises significant safety and security concerns
for public transportation infrastructure. In particular, those facility operators would have no
opportunity to either avert an unsafe flight plan or prevent excessive UAS traffic from
occurring at any given time. And regardless of the certifications UAS operators may hold,
increasing the number of flights around critical infrastructure inherently increases the
associated risk, including, for example, the potential catastrophic failure or collision of a
UAS and the resulting hazard to people and structures below.
As discussed above, all public transportation infrastructure, including but not limited to
bridges, tunnels, yards, stations, transit rights of way, and other facilities, constitutes
critical infrastructure that must be protected accordingly. Notably, transportation networks
such as MTA’s fall under at least three of the infrastructure sectors that the U.S.
Department of Homeland Security’s Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency has
deemed critical based on national security, economic security, safety, and/or public
health: Transportation, Government Services and Facilities, and Commercial Facilities.
Accordingly, allowing UAS operators to operate in close proximity to critical public
transportation facilities without prior notice to and authorization from the site operator
would risk the security and safety of the infrastructure, operations, employees, customers,
and local citizens. Requiring advance approval of all UAS flights around these
transportation facilities is essential.
Additionally, without a required approval process, the site owner would have no way of
determining in the moment whether a particular UAS flight was lawful (i.e., whether the UAS
operator was appropriately certified) without reporting all flights to law enforcement for
investigation. Notably, this undermines a streamlining intent stated in the NPRM – that “the
designation would help fixed site facilities and law enforcement distinguish between lawful
and unlawful operations in the vicinity of the facility and focus their resources accordingly.”
In contrast, if all public transportation facilities are included under the proposed “Special”
designation, only unapproved UAS flights would require action.

Re: Docket Number FAA-2026-4558 (NPRM “Designation–Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”)
August 5, 2026
Page 4 of 5
For these reasons, MTA urges FAA to ensure that UAS operations around all critical public
transportation facilities require approval in advance from the site operator (i.e., by including
them in the proposed “Special” designation).
C. For bridges and tunnels, clarify that the UAFR applies to the full footprint of the facility
to ensure all sensitive elements are included.
To ensure that all sensitive elements of a bridge or tunnel are included in a UAFR, MTA
recommends that FAA clarify that the area of a bridge or tunnel eligible for a UAFR includes
the full footprint of the facility. This extends beyond the structure length to include, as
applicable to the facility type, approaches, ramps, portals, plazas, towers, anchorages,
gantries, and support buildings or structures such as vent buildings and pump rooms.
II. Lateral Boundaries and Altitude Ceilings for UAFRs
To ensure adequate safety and security of fixed site facilities such as bridges and
tunnels, allow UAFR boundaries and altitude ceilings to be set according to each
facility's actual operating and security footprint, rather than setting limits based on
property lines or a pre-established ceiling.
In the NPRM, FAA asks whether the property line of a facility applying for a UAFR should be
the maximum perimeter of a UAFR in all cases or whether there are certain circumstances in
which lateral boundaries should expand beyond the property line. Additionally, the NPRM
anticipates a maximum ceiling for UAFRs of 400 feet above ground level (AGL); that limit
could be exceeded based on the height of the facility’s tallest component (to equal the height
of the tallest component plus 100 feet, rounded up to the next 50-foot increment).
MTA bridge and tunnel crossings sit over open water, public roads, and at times over shared
or borrowed property, so a strict property-line rule could leave significant exposure outside
the restriction. MTA requests that FAA permit UAFR boundaries and altitude ceilings to be set
according to each facility's actual operating and security footprint, rather than property lines
or pre-established ceilings.
III. UAS Operations By Site Owners
Ensure public transportation facility operators retain the ability to operate UAS at their
own facilities without FAA approval (regardless of the category of UAFR that may be
assigned).
MTA applauds the confirmation in the NPRM that the proposal would not preclude a facility
operator such as MTA from operating UAS at and around its own facilities. As stated in the

Re: Docket Number FAA-2026-4558 (NPRM “Designation–Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”)
August 5, 2026
Page 5 of 5
NPRM concerning the proposed Special UAFR designation, “Operations within Special UAFRs
require both permission from the government agency responsible for the site (‘using agency’)
and approval from the FAA Administrator. The using agency itself may operate within its own
Special UAFR without FAA approval.”
MTA urges FAA to retain this flexibility for public transportation facility operators in any
proposed rule.
Conclusion
While MTA supports the goals of streamlining regulations and generally facilitating UAS operations,
the safety and security of the nation’s critical infrastructure, and accordingly of its workforce and
citizens, must be paramount. At the same time, public facility operators must maintain the ability
to use UAS at their own facilities as required for effective operations.
As UAS technology continues to evolve and the number of operators continues to expand, MTA
urges FAA to retain key protections to prioritize safety and security. The recommended changes to
the proposal detailed above will help protect critical transportation facilities and services while
supporting expansion of UAS operations.
MTA appreciates FAA’s consideration of these comments.
Sincerely,
Jane Mellow
Director, Federal Affairs

ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING AND COMPUTER ENGINEERING SCIENCE
CHEMICAL ENGINEERING & MATERIALS SCIENCE
BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING
THE HENRY SAMUELI SCHOOL OF ENGINEERING
IRVINE, CALIFORNIA 92697-2625
Peter Burke, Professor
