pburke@uci.edu
http://www.burkelab.com
August 5, 2026
Docket Operations, M-30
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Room W12-140
West Building Ground Floor
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Comments on Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Designation: Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03; RIN 2120-AL33
Dear Administrator and Docket Operations:
I write in my personal capacity as an engineering educator and researcher. I am a Professor of
Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at the University of California, Irvine, with joint
appointments in Biomedical Engineering and Materials Science and Engineering, and a Fellow
of the IEEE. I have taught engineering for twenty-five years. I received the Distinguished
Faculty Award for Teaching from the UCI Academic Senate. I created and teach UCI's hands-on
unmanned aircraft course, in which undergraduates design, build, program, and fly their own
aircraft, and I led the student team that set a Guinness World Record for the farthest distance
controlling a drone. The views expressed here are entirely my own. They are not the views of
the University of California, the Irvine campus, or any unit thereof, and I do not speak for
my employer.
I write to oppose the proposed rule as drafted, and to urge the FAA to narrow it dramatically.
Summary of Position
The proposed Part 74 would build a permanent, nationwide architecture for excluding
unmanned aircraft from airspace over an enormous and ill-defined universe of private and
institutional property [1]. I do not dispute that a small number of genuinely sensitive sites
warrant protection. Nuclear facilities, military installations, correctional institutions, and the
White House are the obvious cases, and I support restrictions there.
The problem is everything else. As proposed, eligibility extends to all sixteen critical
infrastructure sectors identified in National Security Memorandum 22 [2]. That universe, by the
FAA's own description in this NPRM, includes more than four million miles of roadway, more

than 600,000 bridges, the entire freight and passenger rail network, the food and agriculture
sector, and, expressly, "institutions of higher education" [1, at 24,670, 24,672].
The scale is not a matter of inference. The FAA's own Regulatory Impact Analysis states that
approximately 125,000 fixed site facilities have already been identified as potentially "high
priority" for a restriction [1, at 24,679], and builds its cost estimate on a scenario in which more
than 9,000 of them obtain one [1, at 24,653]. The agency has not demonstrated that a problem
exists on anything approaching that scale, has not identified a single one of those facilities by
name, and has categorically excluded the largest and safest population of operators in the country
from any right of transit [1, at 24,690].
I respectfully ask the FAA to withdraw the proposed rule and repropose it with eligibility
limited to a short, expressly enumerated list of genuinely high-consequence facilities.
1. The FAA Has Not Identified the Problem It Is Solving
An agency proposing to close airspace should be able to say what harm it is preventing. This
NPRM does not.
The preamble asserts that "some stakeholders have become concerned about the safety and
security implication of unmanned aircraft flying in close proximity to certain type of facilities"
[1, at 24,650], and that Sector Risk Management Agencies "have identified the risks of UAS
activity over fixed critical infrastructure sites to include explosion or release of toxins... prison
contraband access, intelligence, surveillance, cyber intrusion, reconnaissance and a stop or delay
of operations" [1, at 24,679]. These are categories of imaginable harm, not findings of fact. The
NPRM contains no incident counts, no rates, no trend data, no comparison against the existing
baseline of authorities, and no analysis of which of these harms any airspace restriction would
actually prevent. The FPV Freedom Coalition, an FAA-recognized community-based
organization, makes the same observation in this docket, stating that it "cannot find any
substantiation to these claims" [3].
This omission is not a technicality. Section 2209 directs the FAA to create a petition process
under which applicants demonstrate need [4]. It does not direct the FAA to presume need across
sixteen sectors of the American economy. Where an agency restricts a public resource, the
burden of justification rests with the government. As the National Press Photographers
Association put it in this docket, "[p]ublic airspace is not the property of the applicant seeking
protection. It is a public resource subject to governmental regulation" [5].
If the FAA possesses data showing a pattern of unmanned aircraft causing the harms it lists,
it should publish that data and allow the public to comment on it. If it does not possess such data,
that is itself the answer to whether this rule is justified.
2. The Eligible Universe Is So Large That the Rule Is Not a Restriction but an Architecture
The NPRM proposes to define "critical infrastructure" by reference to 42 U.S.C. 5195c(e) [6]
and to include "systems and assets in all of the designated 16 critical infrastructure sectors"
identified in NSM-22 [1, at 24,685]. It then works through those sectors one by one, in proposed
§§ 74.81 through 74.96, setting out seventy-eight separately enumerated eligibility provisions
across sixteen sector sections and their subsectors [1, at 24,688–90].
Consider what the NPRM itself says is inside that universe. The highway and motor carrier
subsector "encompasses more than 4 million miles of roadway, more than 600,000 bridges, and
more than 350 tunnels" [1, at 24,672]. The transportation systems sector includes the aviation

subsector, freight rail, mass transit and passenger rail, maritime, and pipelines [1, at 24,671–72].
The food and agriculture sector, the commercial facilities sector, the financial services sector,
and the information technology sector are each in scope. The water and wastewater sector
reaches public water systems serving as few as twenty-five people [1, at 24,672].
NSM-22 does not support the use the FAA has made of it
The breadth described above rests entirely on one interpretive move: the FAA read "critical
infrastructure" in section 2209 to mean everything within the sixteen sectors designated by
NSM-22. That reading is incorrect. NSM-22 does not support it, and its own definitions
foreclose it.
First, NSM-22 disclaims legal effect of exactly this kind. It provides that "[n]othing in this
memorandum shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect... the authority granted by law to
an executive department or agency," and that it "is not intended to, and does not, create any right
or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity" [2]. NSM-22 is an internal
executive-branch coordination instrument. It rescinded and replaced Presidential Policy Directive
21, designates Sector Risk Management Agencies, and directs risk assessment and resilience
planning across the federal government. It is not a definition of regulatory eligibility, and it
cannot enlarge the authority Congress granted in section 2209.
Second, and more fundamentally, the proposed rule treats sector membership as
equivalent to criticality, and NSM-22 treats them as distinct. NSM-22 defines the two terms
separately and differently. A "sector" is "a collection of assets, systems, networks, entities, or
organizations that provide or enable a common function" [2]. Sectors are organized by common
function, which is what makes them useful for assigning a coordinating agency. "Criticality," by
contrast, is defined as "an attribute of an asset, system, or service that reflects its degree of
importance or necessity to stated goals, missions or functions" [2]. It is an attribute of a
particular asset, not of a category.
NSM-22 is explicit that these come apart, and it directs the government to do precisely the
work the FAA has skipped: effective risk management "necessitates identifying the criticality of
assets and systems within and across sectors" [2]. Criticality is something to be found inside a
sector, not something conferred by membership in one.
Third, NSM-22 supplies the instrument the FAA should have used, and the FAA passed
it over. The memorandum directs the National Coordinator to "regularly identify organizations
that own, operate, or otherwise control critical infrastructure that is prioritized based on the
potential for its disruption or malfunction to cause nationally significant and cascading negative
impacts to national security..., national economic security, or national public health or safety,"
which is the Systemically Important Entities list [2]. That standard is the operational analogue of
42 U.S.C. 5195c(e), which asks whether "the incapacity or destruction of such systems and
assets would have a debilitating impact" [6]. Had the FAA anchored eligibility to that concept,
the rule would be defensible. Instead it reached past the narrow, purpose-built instrument for the
broadest unit in the document.
The FAA's own analysis proves the point. Consider the food and agriculture sector. The
NPRM describes it as "approximately 1.9 million farms, over 700,000 restaurants, and more than
220,000 registered facilities in food manufacturing, processing, and storage" [1, at 24,669]. The
FAA then states, in terms, that it "could not identify a facility in this sector that was not already
captured by another sector or would rise to the level of national level debilitating impact" [1, at
24,669].

That is a finding that no facility in an entire NSM-22 sector satisfies the statutory test. It is
exactly what one would predict if sector membership and criticality were different things, which
is what NSM-22 says they are. And yet the sector remains in the proposed rule, as § 74.90, with
its criteria "[Reserved]" and the agency soliciting suggestions for how to populate them [1, at
24,689]. An eligibility category thus remains in the proposed rule although the analysis
supporting that rule identifies no facility that qualifies for it. That is not a close question of
judgment; it is an internal contradiction in the proposal, and § 74.90 should be struck.
The lesson generalizes. Sector membership tells you what kind of function an asset performs.
It tells you nothing about whether that asset's destruction would debilitate the United States. A
neighborhood restaurant and a water system serving three thousand people are both inside NSM-
22 sectors. Neither is critical infrastructure within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. 5195c(e), and
Congress did not authorize the FAA to close the airspace over either.
And for a significant part of that universe, there are no criteria at all
Proposed § 74.90, the food and agriculture sector, reads in its entirety: "A fixed site facility
satisfies the requirements under § 74.54(c) if the facility— (a) [Reserved]" [1, at 24,689].
Proposed § 74.96, the water and wastewater systems sector, is identical: "(a) [Reserved]" [1, at
24,689]. In both cases the preamble confirms it in terms: "FAA has not developed criteria for this
sector" [1, at 24,669, 24,672]. Two of the sixteen sectors have been carried into the proposed
regulatory text as empty brackets.
Elsewhere the criteria exist but do no work. A financial services facility qualifies if it "houses
C-suite or high-value personnel, or is located in urban centers or high-visibility areas," or if it has
"high-volume cash throughput" [1, at 24,689]. None of those terms is defined or bounded. The
Government Services and Facilities Sector, the one containing every school and university in the
country, supplies no threshold whatsoever, resting instead on an unspecified "comprehensive risk
assessment" [1, at 24,689]. I am not alone in reading it this way. The Foundation for American
Innovation, commenting in this docket, concludes that the rule "defines eligibility for 7 of 16
critical infrastructure sectors using open-ended language, undefined criteria, or no criteria at all,"
and singles out government services and facilities as the sector "leaving the most discretion to
the FAA" [7].
This matters concretely. The NPRM reports that there are approximately 42,624 community
water systems in the United States serving fewer than 3,301 people each [1, at 24,672]. Whether
any of them may close the airspace above itself is, at this moment, unknowable, because the
FAA has not written the rule that would decide it, and is nonetheless asking the public to
comment on the framework as though it had.
Soliciting input on how criteria should be drawn is not a substitute for having drawn them. A
proposed rule that leaves two of sixteen eligibility provisions blank has not given notice of what
is proposed for those sectors, and comment on them is not possible. Sections 74.90 and 74.96
should be withdrawn from this rulemaking and, if the agency wishes to pursue them, reproposed
with criteria the public can evaluate.
The projected scale
The FAA has quantified the overall scale itself, and the numbers are extraordinary. In the
Regulatory Impact Analysis, the agency states that the Sector Risk Management Agencies
"identified approximately 125,000 fixed site facilities in these sectors that may be high priority
for a UAFR," and adds that "[c]riteria are not yet fully established for all sectors... and thus

additional facilities may be identified" [1, at 24,679]. The agency's cost estimate is then built on
"a scenario of over 9,000 eligible fixed site facilities obtaining UAFRs" [1, at 24,653].
That is the scale of what is proposed: a pool of roughly 125,000 candidate sites, from which
the FAA's own working assumption is that more than nine thousand permanent exclusion zones
will be created. For comparison, the FAA's current National Security UAS Flight Restrictions
dataset, which comprises the standing 14 CFR 99.7 restrictions accumulated since the agency
began designating them over Department of Justice and Department of Defense facilities in
2019, contains on the order of 2,200 sites [8]. This rule contemplates multiplying the nation's
permanent drone exclusion zones several times over in a single rulemaking.
I do not think the public has understood that. I am reasonably well informed about this
subject, and I did not understand it until I read the Regulatory Impact Analysis.
Two further consequences follow.
First, the sheer number of sector-specific and subsector-specific criteria makes the rule
difficult to apply in practice. An operator trying to determine in advance whether a given piece
of ground is restricted must reason through sixteen sectors, at least eight named subsectors, and
seventy-eight qualification provisions. That is demanding for a commercial operator with
counsel, and it is not realistic for a student or a hobbyist.
Second, the NPRM sets no limit on the number of restrictions, their density, or their
cumulative effect. The Academy of Model Aeronautics made this point precisely in this docket:
"While individual restrictions may appear reasonable in isolation, the aggregate effect could
result in a patchwork of overlapping restricted areas that significantly reduces available airspace,
particularly in urban and infrastructure-dense regions" [9]. A rule that grants thousands of
individually plausible exclusions, with no ceiling and no cumulative-impact analysis, would not
restrict airspace at the margin. Over time it would shift the working presumption of the National
Airspace System, and I do not think that consequence has been squarely evaluated in the record.
I note that the sixteen-sector sweep was the FAA's choice, not Congress's command. Section
2209, as amended, names critical infrastructure such as energy production facilities, oil refineries
and chemical facilities, amusement parks, railroad facilities, and State prisons, and "other
locations that warrant such restrictions" [1, at 24,652][4]. Nothing in that text obliged the agency
to import the entire NSM-22 taxonomy. Executive Order 14305 directed the FAA to interpret
critical infrastructure "to the extent appropriate" consistent with 42 U.S.C. 5195c(e) [1, at
24,651][10]. The sixteen-sector scope is therefore a discretionary choice made in this
rulemaking, not a requirement imposed by Congress. It should be defended as a choice, or
narrowed.
3. Schools and Universities Are Within Scope, and Will Seek Blanket Bans They Cannot
Justify
I want to be precise here, because the drafting is easy to miss. The word "university" does not
appear anywhere in this NPRM. But in describing the Government Services and Facilities Sector
at proposed § 74.91, the FAA writes:
The education services and facilities subsector covers pre-kindergarten through 12th grade
schools, institutions of higher education, and business and trade schools. The subsector
includes facilities owned by both government and private sector entities [1, at 24,670].
Having brought every school and university in the United States, public and private, inside
the covered universe, the NPRM then gates eligibility with a single criterion: the facility must be

"[a] high-risk, high-security government facility with a national or homeland security role and
critical mission-oriented services along with a security level determination resulting from a
comprehensive risk assessment" [1, at 24,670].
It may be that this criterion is intended to be read narrowly, and that an ordinary campus is
not expected to satisfy it. If so, the final rule must say so in its text. An intention that appears
nowhere in the regulation constrains nothing, and it is the text that will be applied to
applications.
As drafted, it does not. Not one operative term in that sentence is defined. "High-risk," "high-
security," "national or homeland security role," and "critical mission-oriented services" are left to
case-by-case application, against a subsector the FAA has just finished defining to include every
institution of higher education in the country, public and private.
What will actually happen when this rule takes effect
I have spent twenty-five years inside a large research university, and I want to describe the
institutional behavior the FAA should expect, because I think the agency has not modeled it.
University and school administrators are, as a class, extremely risk-averse. They are
evaluated on incidents that occur, never on opportunities foregone. Presented with a federal
mechanism to exclude aircraft from the airspace over their property, the rational institutional
response, the one that carries no career risk and requires no analysis, is to apply. Not because
anyone has assessed a threat, but because applying is free, declining to apply is second-guessed
the moment anything goes wrong, and general counsel will advise that the option exists.
The consequence is predictable. If this rule is finalized as drafted, I expect a substantial
fraction of the roughly four thousand degree-granting institutions and many thousands of school
districts in the United States to file applications, and to file them quickly. Almost none of those
applications will rest on a documented threat assessment, because almost none of those
institutions has one. They will recite generalized concerns about privacy, about students, about
"vulnerability," and they will request a perimeter drawn at the property line of the entire campus.
The difficulty this creates falls on the FAA as much as on anyone. Faced with a large volume
of applications and no defined threshold, the agency would have little in the regulatory text to
cite in explaining a denial. A criterion that cannot generate a defensible "no" gives a reviewer
nothing to work with, and leaves the resulting decisions exposed to challenge whichever way
they go. Writing the standard now is what avoids that.
Nor does the rule offer any mechanism by which students, faculty, researchers, or the public
could contest a designation once it is granted.
This is not a prediction. Universities are already doing it, on no articulated threat at all
I do not offer the foregoing as speculation about institutional psychology. Universities have
already built exactly these bans, and the record of how they justified them is instructive.
The University of Michigan's Regents' Ordinance, Article XVI, prohibits operating, taking
off, or landing an unmanned aircraft "from on, or over" University property without a waiver
[11]. That is not a takeoff-and-landing rule; it is a ban on overflight. It applies not to a laboratory
or a stadium but to the entirety of the Ann Arbor campus, defined as "all Ann Arbor campus
property owned or leased or otherwise controlled by the Regents," and, where applicable, to the
Dearborn and Flint campuses as well [11]. It is, in other words, precisely the blanket, property-
line-to-property-line exclusion that I expect institutions to request under Part 74.

What is striking is the justification. In defending the ordinance, the University argued that
"allowing drone operation/surveillance of education facilities could increase the risk of privacy
breaches or malicious attacks to which universities are vulnerable" [11]. The court noted that
while "safety is no doubt one concern," the University "pointed to other concerns on which the
ordinance is focused, including the privacy of students and other persons on University property"
[11].
That is the entire showing. It is a statement that harm is conceivable. In the court's sixteen-
page opinion, there is no reference to a single drone incident at the University, no threat
assessment, no risk analysis, and no identification of any particular asset requiring protection.
The words "incident," "justification," and "rationale" do not appear in the opinion at all. A major
research university closed the airspace over three campuses on the proposition that something
bad could happen.
I want to be careful about what I am drawing from this case. I am not principally concerned
here with its preemption holding, though the Michigan Court of Claims did uphold the ordinance
and dismiss the challenge with prejudice on December 26, 2025 [11]. The doctrinal question of
whether a university is a "political subdivision" under Michigan's statute is a matter of state law
that will not govern this rulemaking [11][12].
The relevant point is behavioral, and it is directly predictive of what the FAA will face.
Given the opportunity, a university will ban drones over its entire footprint because it prefers not
to have them there, and it will defend that ban with generalized assertions of vulnerability rather
than any articulated threat. That is not an aberration. Grand Valley State University's policy
likewise prohibits operation "over University Property" absent prior written approval, and
requires applicants to disclose their "intended flight path" [13]. Institutions are already asking in
this docket: a director of safety and security for a large urban Southern California school district
writes that "[w]e would like the ability to limit drone/UAS flights over schools to approved
activities" [14].
These institutions are not acting in bad faith. They are doing what risk-averse organizations
do. The FAA's rule should be written in full expectation of it.
Some campus facilities do warrant protection. Campuses, as such, do not.
I want to be scrupulous here, because I am not arguing that no restriction over a school or
university could ever be justified, and I am emphatically not indifferent to the safety of children.
Some facilities located on university campuses present real and specific vulnerabilities.
Several dozen American universities operate licensed research reactors. Many host Department
of Defense and Department of Energy laboratories conducting classified or export-controlled
work, where the concern is concrete and statable: aerial imagery of a facility whose
configuration, equipment, or activity is itself protected information. Some operate academic
medical centers with rooftop helipads, where the aviation-safety concern is genuine and well
understood. Where an institution can identify a specific asset, name the specific harm, and
explain why that harm is not already addressed by existing authorities, a narrowly drawn
restriction over that facility may well be appropriate. I would support it.
That is a completely different thing from a restriction over a campus.
Being a school is not a threat. Being a school attended by children is not a threat. Children
are not made safer by a prohibition on overflight. A lawful operator at 200 feet endangers no one
on the ground, and an unlawful actor intending harm is not deterred by an additional regulatory

line he is already prepared to cross. A blanket exclusion over an entire campus does not
measurably improve the safety of anyone on it. What it does with certainty is make unlawful the
ordinary, useful, and overwhelmingly safe flying that happens on and around campuses: my
students' laboratory work, the high school robotics team on the athletic field, the local journalist
covering a protest, the roofer surveying a dormitory.
The distinction I am urging is between a restriction drawn around a research reactor and a
restriction drawn around a university. The first protects something identifiable. The second
protects a preference. Only the first should be available under Part 74.
The cost of getting this wrong falls on exactly the activity the country should want more of.
My students learn to fly outdoors, over open ground, on and around a campus. So do students at
every engineering school with a serious unmanned systems program, and so do the high school
robotics teams that feed those programs. The FPV Freedom Coalition warns in this docket that
"[s]chool based drone programs across the country are growing and may be forced to small,
indoors operations to avoid ever more-restrictive regulations from the FAA" [3]. American
aviation and computing were both built in substantial part by people who tinkered in garages and
on empty fields before they ever tinkered in laboratories. A rule that lets any campus in the
country close the sky above itself, on an undefined showing, forecloses that.
I would therefore ask the FAA to state plainly, in the regulatory text, that an educational
institution is not eligible for a UAFR on the basis of its educational function, its student
population, or the presence of minors, and that any application from such an institution must
identify the specific facility, the specific asset, and the specific threat said to require protection,
and will be granted, if at all, only as to that facility.
4. The Standard Should Be Specific and Articulable Facts, Not Preference and Not
Annoyance
The defect I have described in the education context is general. It runs through every one of
the sixteen sectors. The rule permits an applicant to obtain a permanent exclusion of aircraft from
public airspace on a showing that amounts to discomfort with drones. I want to propose the
standard that should replace it, and to explain why the analogy I am drawing is one of principle
rather than doctrine.
When a police officer stops and detains a person on the street, the officer's subjective unease
is not enough. The Supreme Court held in Terry v. Ohio that "in justifying the particular
intrusion the police officer must be able to point to specific and articulable facts which, taken
together with rational inferences from those facts, reasonably warrant that intrusion" [15]. The
Court has been explicit that this bar excludes the hunch: reasonable suspicion demands
"something more than an inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or 'hunch'" [16]. In Brown v.
Texas, the Court held a detention unconstitutional where officers could not point to "specific,
objective facts indicating that society's legitimate interests require the seizure of the particular
individual," and it has elsewhere condemned enforcement resting on "standardless and
unconstrained discretion" [17][18].
The principle underlying that body of law is simple and does not depend on the Fourth
Amendment. An official may not curtail the liberty of a citizen because the official dislikes that
citizen, is annoyed by that citizen, or would simply prefer that citizen were somewhere else. The
government must be able to say what specifically it fears, why it fears it here, and why the
ordinary rules are not sufficient. Generalized unease, however sincerely felt, is not a reason. It is
the absence of a reason.

I am not contending that a UAFR is a Fourth Amendment seizure, and I do not want to
overstate the analogy. The airspace above a property is not a person, and this rulemaking is not a
criminal-procedure case. But the FAA is not free of an analogous obligation, and it does not have
to look to the Fourth Amendment to find it. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, an agency
must "articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action including a 'rational connection between
the facts found and the choice made'" [19]. A determination that rests on an applicant's
generalized assertion that harm is conceivable, with no incident, no identified asset, and no
analysis of existing safeguards, does not satisfy that requirement. It is the administrative-law
equivalent of the hunch.
So the question I would put to the agency is this. If a police officer may not detain a citizen
for two minutes because the citizen's presence is unwelcome, on what theory may a private
institution permanently exclude that same citizen's aircraft from the public airspace above its
property because the aircraft's presence is unwelcome? The intrusion in the second case is
smaller in one sense and much larger in another: it is permanent, it operates against everyone
rather than one person, and it is imposed at the request of a private party rather than a sworn
officer.
The University of Michigan's justification, that drone operation "could increase the risk of
privacy breaches or malicious attacks to which universities are vulnerable" [11], is precisely the
kind of showing that would fail under Terry. It identifies no facts. It identifies no incident. It
describes a category of conceivable harm and asserts vulnerability to it. Under this NPRM as
drafted, that showing would very likely succeed.
I therefore urge the FAA to write into the regulatory text of § 74.54 an eligibility standard
requiring every applicant, in every sector, to point to specific and articulable facts
demonstrating:
• a particular asset or operation at the site that is vulnerable to unmanned aircraft, identified
with specificity;
• a documented history of relevant incursions, or a specific and credible threat, rather than a
generalized concern;
• the specific harm anticipated, and the mechanism by which an unmanned aircraft would
cause it;
• why existing authorities (Part 107 operating rules, Remote ID, temporary flight
restrictions, trespass and criminal law, and physical security measures) are insufficient; and
• why the geographic and vertical scope requested is the minimum necessary to address that
harm.
An applicant who cannot make that showing should not receive a restriction, and should not
be permitted to apply for a blanket one. This is not a burden on legitimate applicants. An
operator of a nuclear facility, a chemical plant with regulated quantities of hazardous material, or
a correctional institution with a documented contraband-delivery problem can satisfy every
element of it in a page. An institution whose real objection is that it would rather not have drones
overhead cannot satisfy any of it, which is the point.

5. The Restrictions Must Be Enumerated Exactly, Not Described in the Abstract
As set out above, the FAA knows approximately how many restrictions this rule will
produce: more than nine thousand, drawn from a pool of some 125,000 candidate facilities [1, at
24,653, 24,679]. What the agency has not disclosed is which ones, or where, or how large each
will be.
That asymmetry is the central procedural defect in this proceeding. The public is told the
aggregate and denied the particulars, and is then asked to comment. A commenter cannot
evaluate whether a designation over a specific refinery, rail yard, data center, or campus is
justified, because no list exists. Nor can a commenter assess cumulative effect on a given region,
because no map exists.
The proposal contemplates that designated restrictions will live in FAA Order JO 7400.12,
incorporated by reference at proposed § 74.30 [1]. As the FPV Freedom Coalition observed in
this docket, the referenced draft Order "appears not to have been published," and the Coalition
asks that the FAA "alert the public when this document is released and open the comment
window for comments to this document" [3]. The public is therefore asked to comment on a rule
whose operative content is a document it has not been given.
Notice-and-comment rulemaking presupposes that the public can evaluate what is proposed.
A framework described only in the abstract, with sixteen sectors, seventy-eight eligibility
provisions, two of them empty, and an unstated number of future designations, cannot be
meaningfully evaluated. I urge the FAA to:
• Publish the complete draft of FAA Order JO 7400.12 and reopen comment on it;
• Publish the list of the approximately 125,000 candidate facilities the Sector Risk
Management Agencies have already identified, disaggregated by sector, together with the
basis for the projection that more than 9,000 will obtain designations;
• Commit in the regulatory text to a single, authoritative, publicly accessible, machine-
readable database of every designated restriction, with precise coordinates, altitudes,
activation times, and expiration dates, integrated into B4UFLY and LAANC before any
designation becomes effective [9][5]; and
• Publish, for each granted designation, the written findings supporting it [5].
An operator cannot comply with a boundary that is not published. Neither can a professor
advising students where it is lawful to fly.
6. Excluding Recreational and Educational Operators Is Arbitrary
Proposed § 74.250 lists the operations permitted to enter a standard UAFR: Part 91
operations with an airman certificate or as a public aircraft operation; Part 107 operations;
proposed Part 108 operations; Part 135 operations; and Part 137 operations [1, at 24,690–91].
Recreational operations conducted under 49 U.S.C. 44809 [20] appear nowhere on that list.
The result is that the largest population of unmanned aircraft operators in the United States is
the only category categorically barred from transiting this airspace, while package delivery,
agricultural application, and commercial inspection flights may pass through.
The FAA offers no safety basis for that line, and the agency's own data cuts against it. By the
FAA's CY2024 Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Survey, recreational operators flew
approximately 21.7 million flights in that single year, alongside approximately 16.6 million Part
107 flights [21]. Against that volume, I am aware of no fatality involving a recreational electric

multirotor small unmanned aircraft in NTSB accident records, and the NPRM identifies none.
The FPV Freedom Coalition states in this docket that recreational multirotor operators have
"been logging more flight-hours than any other flyer or pilot of any aircraft without a fatality"
[3].
By contrast, the most serious documented bystander injury from a civil unmanned aircraft
operation in recent years did not involve a recreational operator at all. On December 21, 2024, at
a commercially operated 500-aircraft drone light show at Lake Eola in Orlando, Florida, a
malfunctioning aircraft struck a seven-year-old child, who required open-heart surgery; the
NTSB attributed the failure to a launch parameter file that had not been properly transmitted to
the fleet [22].
I do not offer that comparison to argue that commercial operations are unsafe. I offer it
because the NPRM draws a bright line that assumes the opposite of what the record shows, and
defends that line with no data at all.
The exclusion is not merely unfair to hobbyists. Section 44809 is the authority under which a
great deal of American educational flying is conducted: by students, by school and university
programs, and by community-based organizations chartered for exactly that purpose. Excluding
§ 44809 excludes classrooms.
This is not a fringe position. The Drone Service Providers Alliance, representing commercial
operators rather than hobbyists, asks the FAA in this docket to extend access to "Part 107, 49
U.S.C. § 44809 recreational operations, Part 108..., Part 135, Part 137, and any other FAA-
authorized operation," on the reasoning that access "should not be limited by operational
category" [23].
If the FAA's concern is conspicuity and accountability, the answer is the Remote ID
requirement it has already imposed in proposed § 74.250(a)(1) [1, at 24,690], not a categorical
bar on the operators with the best safety record.
7. The Regulation Should Foreclose the Abuses This Authority Has Already Produced
This comment is about the regulation, not about the agency. I raise the following episodes
only because each identifies a specific defect in the proposed text, and each is answered by a
specific change I recommend below.
The record is not partisan. These episodes span more than a decade and both political parties:
the earlier ones under a Democratic administration, the more recent under a Republican one. In
each, public airspace was closed on a stated safety rationale that the contemporaneous record
does not support. The proposed rule would create a permanent version of the same authority
while requiring less of an applicant than any of those episodes required.
In August 2014, under the Obama administration, at the request of St. Louis County Police,
the FAA restricted a thirty-seven square mile block of airspace over Ferguson, Missouri during
the protests there. The Associated Press subsequently obtained recordings of FAA telephone
conferences under the Freedom of Information Act. On those recordings, an FAA manager states
that the police "finally admitted it really was to keep the media out," and a manager at the Kansas
City center reports that county police "did not care if you ran commercial traffic through this
TFR all day long. They didn't want media in there" [24]. The St. Louis County police chief
publicly denied having sought to exclude the press, and cited reports of gunfire and a laser
directed at a police helicopter [24]. That denial belongs in the record alongside the recordings.
But the recordings are the FAA's own, and on their face they describe public airspace closed for

the purpose of excluding the press. That is an abuse of this authority. The bearing on this
rulemaking is direct: proposed § 74.54 would not have prevented it, because nothing in the
proposed eligibility criteria requires an applicant to identify an aviation hazard, and nothing
requires the agency to make a written finding that one exists.
In October 2016, again under the Obama administration, the FAA issued a series of
restrictions over the Dakota Access Pipeline protests near Cannonball, North Dakota, beginning
with FDC 6/6529, a seven nautical mile radius from the surface to 4,000 feet [25]. Documents
later released under the Freedom of Information Act show that the FAA air traffic control
specialist who first evaluated the request recommended denying it, writing: "I plan on denying
the request based on there being no hazard from the ground to [aircraft]" [25]. A subsequent
internal FAA document records that affected tribes were arguing the restriction "was driven not
by a genuine safety/security threat, but rather by the desire of the local [law enforcement agents]
handling the situation to prevent the protesters from using drones to surveil unlawful actions"
[25]. An FAA official wrote that the agency was "steering well clear of the First Amendment
arguments, which are well outside of our AOR" [25]. The FAA has defended the Standing Rock
restrictions on the ground that law enforcement reported unmanned aircraft operating
dangerously near police helicopters. That defense is in the record, and I do not attempt to resolve
the dispute. What is not in dispute is that the official who first evaluated the request concluded
there was no hazard to aircraft, and that the airspace was closed notwithstanding. The bearing
on this rulemaking is again direct: a technical finding of no hazard did not stop the restriction,
and the proposed rule does not require such a finding to be made, recorded, or answered.
Most recently, and now under a Republican administration, the FAA issued FDC 6/4375 on
January 16, 2026, a restriction with no fixed geographic boundary at all, prohibiting unmanned
aircraft within 3,000 feet laterally of the facilities and moving vehicles of the Departments of
Defense, Energy, Justice, and Homeland Security [26]. It was a no-fly zone that travelled with
unmarked government vehicles, that applied nationwide, and that no operator could locate in
advance in order to comply with it. A photojournalist petitioned for review in the D.C. Circuit
[26]. The FAA rescinded the restriction on April 15, 2026, replacing it with a non-punitive
advisory, FDC 6/2824 [26]. A comparable restriction had issued over greater Chicago three
months earlier, in October 2025: a fifteen nautical mile radius from the surface to 400 feet,
covering roughly 935 square miles, in effect from October 2 until October 12. The FAA cited
"special security reasons." Customs and Border Protection, asked to explain, said the restriction
was imposed "due to a credible threat of small, unmanned aircraft systems being used against
law enforcement." No evidence supporting that assertion was made public, and journalists who
requested it were not provided any [27].
That restriction's defect was not one of degree. A boundary defined by the current position of
unmarked vehicles cannot be located by an operator before flight, and a restriction that cannot be
complied with is not a safety measure. The bearing on this rulemaking: proposed § 74.58
governs lateral boundaries but nowhere requires that a boundary be publicly ascertainable in
advance by the operators bound by it. It should. The ability of citizens to observe and document
public events is not a value belonging to one party. Airspace was closed over Ferguson under
one administration and over federal immigration operations under another. A commenter who
objects to the first but not the second, or the second but not the first, has mistaken the issue. The
issue is that a standing authority to close airspace over newsworthy events, resting on a showing
that no one outside the agency reviews, will be used differently by different administrations. Part
74 would make that authority permanent, which is a reason to define it carefully now.

Mission creep in ordinary public events
Alongside that record, the agency's use of temporary flight restrictions over ordinary public
events has expanded well past anything recognizable as a national security rationale. In July of
this year, a no-drone zone covering a one-nautical-mile radius up to 400 feet was imposed over
the San Diego Convention Center and surrounding neighborhoods for the duration of Comic-Con
International, enforced with civil penalties reaching $75,000 and referral for criminal
investigation [28]. Comic-Con is a comic book convention. No national-security interest of the
kind section 2209 was enacted to address is served by closing the airspace above it, and none has
been publicly identified.
The bearing on this rulemaking is a drafting defect that I do not think has been widely
noticed, and I ask the FAA to address it expressly in the final rule.
Read one way, the proposal handles gatherings correctly. Proposed § 74.82 confines
commercial facilities eligibility to fixed sites with annual attendance of at least 2,500,000,
ticketing or entry control, primarily outdoor and unenclosed premises, and at least 120 open days
a year, and it expressly excludes "a stadium or venue where the events may be covered by
temporary flight restrictions" [1, at 24,688]. That is an objective, checkable standard, and it
correctly declines to convert transient gatherings into permanent exclusion zones. It also
demonstrates that numerically bounded criteria can be written for this rule, which makes their
absence from the Government Services and Facilities Sector, and the blank text at §§ 74.90 and
74.96, a choice rather than a difficulty. Section 74.82 should be the template for the rest of
subpart C.
But § 74.82 constrains only one of two routes to a designation, and the second route has no
criteria at all.
Proposed § 74.54 opens: "to be eligible to apply... an applicant must demonstrate the request
is for a facility that" meets the fixed site facility definition, meets the critical infrastructure
definition, satisfies a subpart C sector criterion, has protective security, has a vulnerable critical
asset, and would suffer "a regional or national-level debilitating impact" [1, at 24,686]. Every
one of those tests attaches to an applicant, meaning an operator or proprietor proceeding under §
74.15.
A federal agency is not an applicant. Under proposed § 74.5(a), a standard UAFR "may be
established for a specific location as requested by another Federal department or agency" [1, at
24,685]. Under proposed § 74.6(a), the FAA may designate a Special UAFR "[a]t the
Administrator's discretion or at the request of a Federal security or intelligence agency, the
Department of Defense, or the Department of Energy... when supported by a credible safety or
security threat" [1, at 24,685]. Neither provision requires a fixed site facility. Neither requires
critical infrastructure. Neither invokes § 74.54 or subpart C. Section 74.5(a) speaks of "a specific
location," not a facility, and § 74.6 requires only that a federal agency assert a credible threat.
That is how a gathering re-enters this rule. The restriction over Comic-Con was sought by
federal security agencies over a convention center. Nothing in proposed § 74.6 would prevent the
same agencies from obtaining a Special UAFR over the same location, for a five-year renewable
term, on the same assertion. Section 74.82's attendance threshold, outdoor requirement, and
express exclusion of event venues would not apply, because those limits govern applicants and
not agencies. The elaborate eligibility architecture of subpart C can be bypassed entirely by
routing the request through a federal agency instead of a proprietor.

The FAA also proposes to migrate existing 99.7 restrictions into Special UAFR designations
[1, at 24,659]. Those existing restrictions were issued under a standard no more demanding than
§ 74.6's, and their migration would confer permanence on restrictions never tested against any
facility criterion.
I therefore recommend that the final rule apply the substance of § 74.54 to agency-requested
designations under §§ 74.5(a) and 74.6, or, at minimum, require for each such designation a
written, publicly available finding identifying the specific facility, the specific threat, and the
reason existing authorities are inadequate. An eligibility standard that binds private applicants
but not the government is not an eligibility standard.
The 2026 FIFA World Cup is the clearest illustration. The FAA announced in advance that it
would impose match-day restrictions of a three nautical mile radius up to 3,000 feet over eleven
stadiums, and one nautical mile up to 1,000 feet over fan-event sites, with further restrictions at
team hotels, base camps, and training facilities [29]. By the agency's own account afterward, it
established "no-drone zones through nearly 250 temporary flight restrictions covering all match
venues, fan festivals, team hotels and training sites" [30]. Because the restrictions followed the
teams rather than the matches, they closed airspace over cities that hosted no World Cup games
at all, among them Boise, Idaho and Sandy, Utah, hundreds of miles from any match venue,
because a national team happened to be lodged there [31]. Nor were these brief. The base camp
and team hotel restrictions ran continuously, twenty-four hours a day, from June 1 through July
21, roughly seven weeks of standing closed airspace over ordinary American cities, tethered not
to any facility-specific risk but to the itinerary of a sporting event [31].
The enforcement statistics repay a close reading, because the government's own account of
them is more informative than the headline figure suggests. The FAA announced the results
under the headline "Successful Counter-Drone Efforts Helped Keep Millions of Fans Safe
During FIFA World Cup 2026, With More Than 700 Drones Seized," reporting that the FBI and
the Department of Homeland Security "seized more than 700 drones operating in restricted
airspace across all 11 U.S. host cities," and that "[e]ach unauthorized drone was treated as a
potential threat" [30].
"Treated as" is not a finding. It is a description of a posture in which every unmanned aircraft
in a large volume of airspace is presumed hostile until seized. That presumption is the thing this
rulemaking would make permanent and multiply, and it is worth examining what it actually
produced. On the question of what those seven hundred aircraft in fact were, the record is
explicit, and it comes from the government itself.
On July 31, 2026, the White House Deputy Assistant to the President and Senior Director for
Counterterrorism, asked about the full 700-drone total, stated that no weaponized drones were
seized [32]. The Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office confirmed
the same as to the 59 drones seized in Los Angeles [33]. The FBI likewise advised reporters in
North Texas that none of the drones seized around World Cup events there had been carrying
any dangerous payload [34].
So the figure is now fully characterized. More than seven hundred aircraft were confiscated
from the American public over roughly seven weeks. Not one of them was armed. Not one
carried a payload. No official has identified a single instance in which any of the seven hundred
was connected to an attack, a plot, or any hostile purpose whatsoever.
What the seven hundred appear to have been is indicated by the charging papers. On June 26,
2026, the United States Attorney for the Southern District of Texas announced that "[f]our

Houston area residents" had been charged for "flying drones into sensitive national defense
airspace without authorization" [35]. One complaint alleges that "law enforcement observed" a
defendant "operating a drone in restricted airspace in the vicinity of Polk and Chartres Streets in
Houston"; he is reported to have been filming footage for a family member's real estate business.
Another alleges a drone "flying in the TFR zone near 612 Live Oak Street in Houston" on June
11 [35]; that was reportedly a flight of roughly two minutes recording video of the operator's
church, on a day when no World Cup match was played in Houston [36]. The charge carries up
to a year of imprisonment and a fine of up to $100,000 [36]. In the Northern District of Texas,
the United States Attorney reported 94 drones seized and three operators charged [37].
These matters are pending, and the defendants are of course presumed innocent. But I want to
be precise about the role they play in my argument, because it is not the role a reader might
expect. I take the government's allegations at face value. Nothing I say here depends on any
defendant being innocent, or on any of these prosecutions being unfounded. My argument runs
the other way: it is strongest if the allegations are entirely true. Assume they are. Assume the
government proves every element. What it will have proven is that a man flew a camera over his
church for two minutes, and that another recorded footage of houses. Whether that conduct
violated a published restriction is a question for the courts, on which I express no view. What it
was, and what it was not, is the point.
I want to be equally careful about the obvious objection to all of this, because it is a fair one.
The obligation to check the airspace before flying rests on the operator. It does under
Part 107, and it does under 49 U.S.C. 44809, which conditions recreational flight on compliance
with airspace restrictions [20]. The FAA publishes restrictions by NOTAM and supplies
B4UFLY for exactly this purpose. An operator who fails to check, and flies into restricted
airspace, has violated the rule, and "the restriction was poorly justified" is not a defense to that
violation. I do not suggest otherwise, and I would not want a rule that invited operators to
substitute their own judgment for a published restriction.
My point is a different one, and it is addressed to the design of the rule rather than to the
culpability of any operator. A restriction that is well matched to a real threat catches the threat. A
restriction that produces seven hundred seizures, zero weapons, zero payloads, and a prosecution
docket consisting of church videography and real estate photography is not well matched to a
threat. It is capturing the wrong population, not because those operators bore no duty to check,
but because a rule whose entire measurable yield is the incidental capture of harmless people has
told the agency something important about its own calibration.
That distinction matters here because discoverability is a design variable the FAA controls,
and these restrictions differed sharply in how discoverable they were. I want to be accurate about
which was which.
The World Cup restrictions were discoverable. The base camp and team hotel restrictions
were fixed circles at fixed locations, each with a published NOTAM number, active continuously
from June 1 through July 21 rather than switching on and off with the match schedule [31]. An
operator who checked would have found them. What made them hard to anticipate was not
motion but distribution: roughly 250 restrictions nationwide, more than 100 of them at team
lodging and training sites, a substantial number of them in cities hosting no matches at all,
among them Boise and Sandy [30][31]. A pilot in Boise had no particular reason to associate his
city with a soccer tournament. That is a burden of discovery, not an impossibility, and it does not
excuse a failure to check.

The nationwide DHS restriction was different in kind. It attached to the facilities and moving
vehicles of four federal departments, including unmarked ones, so the boundary of lawful
airspace could not be located before flight by any amount of diligence [26]. An operator's duty to
check presupposes that checking can yield an answer. For the World Cup restrictions it could.
For that one it could not, and a restriction that cannot be complied with is not a safety measure.
The question this raises is what the restriction was drawn to capture. A seizure count and a
threat count are different measurements, and the government's own figures separate them
cleanly: seven hundred of the first, and, on the accounts above, none of the second. That is a
direct measurement of how a restriction of this breadth performs, and the result is not
ambiguous. Seven hundred confiscations that yielded no weapon and no payload indicate a
boundary drawn far wider than the risk it was meant to address. The remedy is to draw these
boundaries narrowly and publish them clearly, not to extend them to nine thousand permanent
sites.
The implication for this rulemaking should be stated without euphemism. Seven weeks of
restrictions of exactly the kind Part 74 would make permanent produced seven hundred seizures
and no weapons. That is the only field measurement available of what this instrument does, and
what it measures is cost with no corresponding benefit: a large number of lawful operators were
stopped, disarmed of their equipment, and in some cases prosecuted, and nothing in the public
record indicates that a single act of harm was prevented.
Part 74 proposes to take that instrument, make it permanent, and multiply it to more than nine
thousand sites. The predictable result is not more security. It is the same output at far greater
scale: seizures, forfeitures, and federal charges against people photographing buildings,
indefinitely, at nine thousand locations, with no evidence of a security return.
An agency proposing an expansion of that magnitude should be required to show that the
restriction prevents harm. This record does not show it. Until it does, the rule should not be
finalized.
Part 74 would convert temporary restrictions into permanent ones without re-justifying them
If this pattern were confined to genuinely temporary restrictions it would be troubling
enough. It will not be. This NPRM states that the FAA "plans to integrate all current eligible
99.7 SSIs that align with the intent of this section into Special UAFR designations," and explains
that "[u]nlike 99.7s, which are intended to be a short-term security measure, Special UAFRs will
provide a stable framework for flight restrictions with a term of five years" [1, at 24,659].
The consequence should be stated plainly. Restrictions adopted and justified to the public as
short-term measures would be converted into five-year, renewable designations, and their
number would grow substantially through petitions by private parties. Nothing in the proposal
identifies which existing 99.7 restrictions would be migrated, on what criteria, or subject to what
review. A short-term instrument and a standing one are justified differently, and a restriction that
was never tested against a permanent standard should not acquire permanence by administrative
transfer.
8. The Rule Is Bad for American Industry and Worse for American Education
This rule adds cost, delay, and legal uncertainty to every domestic operation while adding no
capability. It imposes on facility operators an obligation to field Remote ID receiving equipment
and to reconcile broadcast serial numbers against notifications [1, at 24,690]. As the FPV
Freedom Coalition observes, that requirement "changes the role of the UAFR operator/proprietor

to that of law enforcement without the appropriate authority," and "creates unnecessary liability"
[3].
The deeper cost is to the pipeline. The engineers who will build American autonomy,
avionics, and airframes are in high school and college right now, and many of them learn by
flying under § 44809 on open ground near a campus. A regulation that makes that flying
unlawful in an expanding and unpublished set of places does not merely inconvenience
hobbyists. It removes the on-ramp.

9. Recommendations
1. Withdraw and repropose. The eligible universe should be defined by an express,
exhaustive list, not by importing all sixteen NSM-22 sectors.
2. Limit eligibility to genuinely high-consequence categories (nuclear facilities, military
installations, correctional institutions, and comparable national security sites), and state that list
exhaustively in the regulatory text.
3. Stop treating NSM-22 sector membership as a proxy for criticality. NSM-22 defines a
sector by common function and criticality as an attribute of a particular asset, and directs that
criticality be identified within sectors. Eligibility should be anchored to the statutory test in 42
U.S.C. 5195c(e), which asks whether the incapacity or destruction of the specific asset would
have a debilitating impact, or to the Systemically Important Entities concept NSM-22 itself
establishes, not to the sector in which a facility happens to sit.
4. State expressly that educational institutions are not eligible for a UAFR on the basis of
their educational function.
5. Do not finalize any sector whose eligibility criteria are "[Reserved]" or undefined.
Proposed §§ 74.90 and 74.96 should be removed, and any sector resting on undefined terms such
as "high-value," "high-visibility," or an unspecified "comprehensive risk assessment" should be
reproposed with objective, size-bounded thresholds and a fresh comment period.
6. Adopt a "specific and articulable facts" standard in § 74.54, applicable to every
applicant in every sector, requiring identification of the particular vulnerable asset, a documented
incursion history or specific credible threat, the mechanism of anticipated harm, why existing
authorities are inadequate, and why the scope requested is the minimum necessary. Generalized
assertions of vulnerability, discomfort with unmanned aircraft, or a preference that aircraft not be
present should be expressly insufficient.
7. Prohibit blanket, property-wide designations for any applicant that has not made the
showing in Recommendation 6 as to each area to be covered.
8. Close the agency-request bypass. Proposed §§ 74.5(a) and 74.6 permit designations at
the request of a Federal department or agency without reference to § 74.54 or subpart C. Apply
the substance of § 74.54 to those designations, or at minimum require a written, publicly
available finding identifying the specific facility, the specific threat, and why existing authorities
are inadequate. Eligibility criteria that bind private applicants but not agencies do not constrain
the size of the restricted airspace.
9. Add 49 U.S.C. 44809 operations to § 74.250 as allowed operations, subject to the same
Remote ID and notification conditions imposed on other categories.
10. Publish the complete draft of FAA Order JO 7400.12 and reopen comment.
11. Cap and account for cumulative impact, including a published projection of the
number and density of expected designations and a mandatory cumulative-impact assessment.
12. Require a single public, machine-readable database of all designations, with published
findings, integrated into B4UFLY and LAANC before any restriction takes effect.
13. Limit lateral boundaries to the applicant's own property line and altitude to the
minimum necessary.
14. Shorten the term from five years to two, with renewal requiring a fresh evidentiary
showing under the same standard as an initial application.
15. Provide a public mechanism for affected parties to seek reconsideration, narrowing, or
termination of a designation.
16. Remove from the Advisory Circular any requirement that operates as a binding rule,
and subject such requirements to notice and comment.

Conclusion
I support protecting nuclear plants, military bases, prisons, and the White House from
unmanned aircraft. I do not support, and the record before the agency does not justify, a
permanent framework built on 125,000 candidate facilities and a working assumption of more
than 9,000 exclusion zones, under which four million miles of roadway, every bridge and rail
line, and every school and university in the United States may become eligible on an undefined
showing of "high risk," with not one of those sites disclosed to the public that is being asked to
comment on them.
The FAA should withdraw this proposal and repropose it with an exhaustive list of eligible
facilities, a real evidentiary standard, published boundaries, and access for the operators,
including students, whose safety record is the best in the National Airspace System.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Respectfully submitted,
Peter J. Burke, Ph.D.

Fellow, IEEE

To Whom It May Concern:
The National Association for Stock Car Auto Racing, LLC (“NASCAR”) submits the following
comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration’s (“FAA” or the “Agency”) and U.S.
Department of Transportation’s (“DOT”) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NPRM”) titled
“Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility” (hereafter the “NPRM” or “proposed rule”),1 implementing Section 2209 of the FAA
Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016.
NASCAR has long supported practical, risk-based security measures that keep sporting events,
large outdoor gatherings, and entertainment venues safe from unauthorized and potentially
malicious unmanned aircraft systems (“UAS” or “drones”) without unnecessarily restricting the
National Airspace System (“NAS”). Over the past two years, NASCAR events have recorded more
than 750 unauthorized drone incursions, highlighting the continued need for practical security
tools to address emerging airspace security hazards.
To the extent existing security measures such as the Sporting Events Temporary Flight
Restriction (“TFR”) (hereafter the “Sporting Events TFR”),2 and the TFR framework for large public
gatherings provided by 49 U.S.C. § 44812 (hereafter the “Large Public Gatherings TFR”),3 fail to
protect the country’s major motorsports venues and events such as the Daytona 500 at Daytona

(last visited July 13, 2026); see also Fed, Aviation Admin., Can I fly a model aircraft or UAS over a
stadium or sporting events for hobby or recreation?, https://www.faa.gov/faq/can-i-fly-model-aircraft-
or-uas-over-stadium-or-sporting-events-hobby-or-recreation (last visited July 14, 2026).

International Speedway, we appreciate the opportunity to continue to work with the FAA and other
stakeholders to address evolving threats while accommodating the diverse ways in which
motorsports events and facilities operate. Section 2209 is one potential mechanism for enhanced
security.
I. Background on NASCAR
NASCAR is the premier sanctioning body for stock car racing in the United States and one of the
largest motorsports organizations in the world. NASCAR owns and operates fifteen racetracks,
hosts major events in more than thirty markets annually, and sanctions races at thirty-five tracks
across the United States and Mexico. Race weekend events attract large in-person crowds—
frequently exceeding 100,000 participants—and are supported by a nationwide fan base
exceeding 70 million. Because NASCAR events regularly involve substantial coordination among
venue operators, public safety agencies, security personnel, and federal, state, and local
government partners, NASCAR has extensive experience planning and operating major sporting
events and the unique security considerations associated with them. Accordingly, NASCAR has
a strong interest in policies that help protect race venues and associated facilities from careless,
clueless, and criminal drone operators while supporting the safe and efficient use of the NAS.
II. Support for Existing Airspace Security Frameworks
NASCAR strongly supports the FAA's existing airspace-security frameworks, which provide
practical, risk-based tools for protecting major sporting events, large public gatherings, and other
activities that present elevated security concerns. NASCAR's experience with the Sporting Events
TFR demonstrates the value of clear, predictable, and repeatable airspace protections for major
public events. Rather than requiring event organizers to seek ad hoc restrictions for each
occurrence, the Sporting Events TFR provides an established mechanism that allows event
operators, security personnel, and government partners to plan around a known set of
protections. The current Sporting Events TFR expressly applies to NASCAR Sprint Cup races,
reflecting the longstanding recognition that major motorsports events present unique operational
and security considerations warranting enhanced airspace protections. NASCAR has long relied
on this framework and has seen firsthand the benefits of an approach that balances security
needs for large public gatherings and a predictable, reliable framework for sensitive sites with the
efficient use of the NAS.
NASCAR also appreciates the FAA’s use of the Large Public Gatherings TFR for concerts and
other major outdoor events that may present similar crowd-safety, security, and operational
concerns. As with the Sporting Events TFR, this framework recognizes that unauthorized UAS
activity near large public gatherings can create risks to people, property, event operations, and
public safety, and it provides an important tool for addressing those risks in appropriate
circumstances.

While these event-specific TFRs are helpful, clear security gaps remain. For example, the
Sporting Events TFR is time and geographically limited, and sometimes security measures are
needed outside of these narrow confines.
III. Addressing Remaining Security Gaps at Motorsports Facilities and Events
While the Sporting Events TFR provides important protections for NASCAR Cup Series race-day
events, many NASCAR facilities frequently support year-round operations—including testing,
training, and operational functions—that occur outside of race weekends and thus beyond the
scope of current TFR coverage. Certain facilities thus may face security concerns during periods
when no comparable protection is available.
To that end, NASCAR respectfully encourages the FAA to allow facilities that receive protection
through the Sporting Events TFR or Large Public Gatherings TFR to seek a UAFR during periods
when those protections are unavailable, recognizing that TFRs cannot overlap in time. For
example, facilities such as Daytona International Speedway may receive protection for certain
events yet continue to host testing, training, and other events throughout the year that present
comparable security concerns but fall outside the scope of existing TFR coverage. Similarly, non-
traditional events such as the NASCAR Chicago Street Race can present many of the same
security considerations as traditional motorsports events, including large public gatherings,
significant operational complexity, and substantial economic activity. The final rule should
therefore retain flexibility to allow the FAA to evaluate facilities and events holistically and
determine whether a UAFR or other protection options may be appropriate.
In the alternative, if the FAA determines that a UAFR is not the appropriate mechanism for these
circumstances, NASCAR encourages the FAA to consider other available mechanisms that would
allow NASCAR and similarly situated operators to protect their facilities as necessary. NASCAR
encourages the FAA to maintain sufficient adaptability within its existing authorities to ensure that
future motorsports events can continue to receive appropriate consideration based on their
specific operational and security characteristics rather than the particular configuration of the
venue. Whether through the existing Sporting Events and Large Public Gatherings TFRs, Section
2209, or other available security mechanisms, NASCAR believes that a flexible, risk-based
approach will best enable the federal government to address UAS-related security concerns.
IV. Conclusion
NASCAR appreciates the Administration’s continued focus on strengthening airspace security,
protecting airspace sovereignty, and advancing initiatives such as the SAFER SKIES Act and
Executive Order 14305, “Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty.”4 NASCAR shares the FAA’s
and the Administration’s interest in ensuring that airspace-security measures remain practical,
risk-based, and tailored to the specific circumstances presented by major events and sensitive

facilities. NASCAR appreciates the FAA's efforts to implement Section 2209 and the
Administration’s commitment to protecting sensitive facilities, major public gatherings, and large
sporting events from unauthorized UAS activity.
While the Sporting Events TFR and Large Public Gatherings TFR frameworks provide important
protections for many events, NASCAR respectfully encourages the FAA to consider additional
mechanisms to address circumstances in which those protections are unavailable. Section 2209
or another appropriate authority could help address remaining security gaps affecting motorsports
facilities and events. NASCAR would welcome the opportunity to continue working with the FAA,
DOT, and other stakeholders on practical approaches that support event security, protect large
public gatherings, and preserve the safe and efficient use of the NAS.

To Whom It May Concern:
On behalf of Airlines for America’s (A4A) members,1 we appreciate the opportunity to submit
these comments to the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) notice of proposed rulemaking,
Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility (NPRM).2 As a preliminary matter, aviation safety and security are of paramount
importance to A4A and its members. Moreover, as historic and full-time users of the National
Airspace System (NAS) dedicated to the safe and efficient transportation of passengers and
cargo, as well as operators of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), our members have a special
interest in the outcome of FAA’s rulemaking, support the rulemaking, and offer the comments
herein for the FAA’s consideration to improve and complete the rulemaking.
Fundamentally, we strongly support FAA’s objective to protect critical facilities from unauthorized
UAS activity. As with all regulations of aviation safety and security, the FAA should achieve its
objectives using a framework that is narrowly tailored, risk-based, and implemented in a manner
that preserves the unparalleled level of safety, efficiency, and flexibility of the NAS, while also
avoiding unintended consequences on airline operations, airport activities, emergency services,
and future aviation modernization initiatives.
Moreover, the FAA’s framework governing UAS operations in close proximity to designated fixed
site facilities should maintain robust deconfliction with manned aircraft operations and avoid any
introduction of new hazards or operational complexities for aircraft operating in the vicinity of
critical aviation infrastructure. Concurrently, the FAA should strike a balance: appropriately protect
designated fixed site facilities while also avoiding any unintentional prohibitions or overly
burdensome restrictions on UAS activities at aviation facilities (e.g., operated by airports, airlines,
and airport-authorized operators) that directly support aviation safety, maintenance, inspections,
construction, wildlife management, and emergency response functions.

Based on such principles, we offer the following suggestions:
• Aviation is a named subsector of the critical infrastructure transportation systems sector.3
In fact, the NAS is considered “one of the nation’s critical infrastructures—which is
comprised of air traffic control systems, procedures, facilities, aircraft and people who
operate and maintain them.”4 Thus, the FAA should explicitly designate essential aviation
facilities (e.g., commercial airports, air traffic control facilities, etc.) as part of the definition
of “transportation systems sector.”5
• Given the extraordinarily sensitive nature of the restricted airspace in close proximity to
fixed site critical infrastructure, we respectfully submit that the framework should, more
often than not but on a risk basis, require heightened approval process for allowing UAS
flights in such proximity, which may include agency and FAA-approval, perpetual vetting

infrastructure—the outage of which often has widespread impacts to national defense, the
safety of the American public, and the U.S. economy—should typically be subject to these
heightened procedures.
• In the same vein, because state and local law enforcement agencies and officers may be
using UAS to protect an especially sensitive designated fixed site facility, we recommend
that UAS operators seeking to operate within a restricted area coordinate directly with the
fixed site operator and the state or local law enforcement protecting the location, along
with further deconfliction measures (e.g., remote identification and following law
enforcement flight path instructions).
We thank the FAA for the opportunity to submit these comments and look forward to collaborating
with the FAA and other airspace users in the safe and efficient operation in the NAS and protection
of the critical infrastructure in the United States. Please contact Justin Madden at
jmadden@airlines.org and Haley Gallagher at hgallagher@airlines.org with any questions.

Haley Gallagher Justin Madden
Vice President, Security & Facilitation Vice President, Operations & Safety
AIRLINES FOR AMERICA AIRLINES FOR AMERICA

and-resilience/critical-infrastructure-sectors/transportation-systems-sector (last visited Aug. 3, 2026).
