comments.commenter: Comment from Associated Builders and Contractors
comments.comment_text:
VIA ELECTRONIC SUBMISSION
August 5, 2026
Docket Operations
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Ave. SE, Room W58-213, West Building 5th Floor
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558, Comments on the FAA’s Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, Designation: Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close
Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
Dear Sir or Madam,
Associated Builders and Contractors submits the following comments to the U.S.
Department of Transportation’s Federal Aviation Administration in response to the
above-referenced notice of proposed rulemaking published in the Federal Register on
May 6, 2026, at 91 Fed. Reg. 24650.
About Associated Builders and Contractors
ABC is a national construction industry trade association with 67 chapters and 24,000
members. Founded on the merit shop philosophy, ABC helps members offer a robust
employee value proposition, develop people, win work and deliver that work safely,
ethically and profitably for the betterment of the communities in which they serve.
ABC’s membership represents all specialties within the U.S. construction industry and is
comprised primarily of general contractors and subcontractors that perform work in the
industrial and commercial sectors for government and private sector customers.
Many ABC members use unmanned aircraft systems to survey, map, photograph and
inspect the construction of worksites, such as buildings, pipelines, power lines and land
that would otherwise be a physical challenge or cost-prohibitive to review. The
integration of UAS into the construction industry’s operations has increased safety and
efficiency in project delivery and created high-skill roles for the construction workforce.
Background
On July 15, 2016, the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 became law.1
Section 2209 directed the FAA to establish a process for operators and proprietors of
1 FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209, 130
Stat. 615, 638 (2016).
440 First St. NW, Suite 200 | Washington, DC 20001 | 202-595-1505 | abc.org

certain sensitive fixed-site facilities to request restrictions or prohibitions on unmanned
aircraft operations in close proximity to their sites.
On May 6, 2026, the FAA published the NPRM, Designation: Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility. The proposed rule would
establish a process for operators and proprietors of certain fixed-site facilities to request
an unmanned aircraft flight restriction designation.
ABC’s Comments in Response to the FAA’s Proposed Rule
ABC welcomes the FAA’s proposal to establish a process for facility owners to seek
airspace access limitations from the FAA based on credible safety and security
concerns. ABC strongly agrees that site and personnel safety and security is paramount
to U.S. national security, including that of America’s critical infrastructure.
At the same time, the FAA should ensure that UAFRs do not unnecessarily hinder safe,
lawful and site-related UAS operations that support construction, inspection,
maintenance, repair, emergency response and facility security.
ABC urges the FAA to clarify the allowed operations and access procedures for sites
with a Standard UAFR and Special UAFR designation as recommended below.
Standard Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction Designation
The NPRM would create a Standard UAFR designation with defined horizontal and
vertical limits around eligible fixed-site facilities. The designation would restrict
unmanned aircraft access unless an operation qualifies as an allowed operation under
the proposed rule.
Many fixed-site facilities that may qualify for a Standard UAFR rely on UAS for safe and
efficient construction, inspection, maintenance, repair, surveying, mapping, security and
emergency response. Construction contractors often use UAS to reduce the need for
workers to access elevated, energized, confined or otherwise hazardous areas,
including rooftops, cranes, scaffolding, bridges, towers, tanks, industrial equipment,
pipelines and other critical infrastructure.
The NPRM would allow certain unmanned aircraft operations within a Standard UAFR-
designated area, including operations under Part 107 with an airman certificate. To
operate within a Standard UAFR, the unmanned aircraft must broadcast Remote ID, the
operator must provide notice to the fixed-site facility site manager and the aircraft must
transit the UAFR in the shortest amount of time practicable.
ABC supports the FAA’s use of Remote ID as a conspicuity and identification tool.
Remote ID can help a fixed-site facility distinguish known and expected UAS operations
from unknown or unauthorized aircraft operating in or near the restricted airspace.
440 First St. NW, Suite 200 | Washington, DC 20001 | 202-595-1505 | abc.org

However, ABC is concerned the proposed “shortest amount of time practicable”
requirement does not fit owner-operated or owner-approved UAS operations conducted
for legitimate facility-related purposes. Construction, inspection, maintenance, surveying
and mapping operations often require hovering, grid flights, orbiting, repeated passes,
close visual inspection and other nontransitory flight profiles. These operations do not
merely pass through the UAFR; they are the reason the UAS operates at the site.
ABC urges the FAA to clarify in the final rule that the “shortest amount of time
practicable” requirement does not apply to UAS operations conducted by the UAFR
owner/operator, or by a contractor, agent or other third party approved by the
owner/operator, when the operation serves a legitimate site-related purpose and
complies with applicable FAA operating rules, Remote ID requirements and notice
requirements.
Specifically, the FAA should establish an express “owner-operated or owner-approved
site-sponsored UAS operation” pathway within the Standard UAFR framework. Under
this pathway, the FAA should permit a UAS operation within a Standard UAFR when:
• The UAFR owner/operator conducts the operation or approves a contractor,
agent or other third party to conduct it;
• The operation serves a legitimate facility-related purpose, including construction,
inspection, maintenance, repair, surveying, mapping, security, emergency
response, environmental compliance or asset management;
• The operator conducts the operation under Part 107 or another applicable FAA
operating authority;
• The unmanned aircraft broadcasts Remote ID, unless the FAA authorizes
otherwise; and
• The owner/operator or operator provides notice to the fixed-site facility site
manager under the final rule.
This approach would preserve the FAA’s authority over the National Airspace System
while recognizing that the fixed-site facility owner/operator can identify UAS operations
that are known, expected and necessary for safe facility operations. It would also
ensure that a Standard UAFR designation does not unintentionally impede construction,
inspection, maintenance and emergency response activities needed to keep critical
infrastructure safe and operational.
ABC also urges the FAA to allow standing, recurring or project-based notice for owner-
operated and owner-approved site-sponsored UAS operations. The FAA should not
require separate flight-by-flight notice for routine construction progress documentation,
inspections, mapping or maintenance activities when a standing or project-based notice
identifies the approved operator, aircraft registration, Remote ID serial number,
operating area, general purpose and duration of the project or recurring operation. This
approach would reduce administrative burden without materially affecting security.
440 First St. NW, Suite 200 | Washington, DC 20001 | 202-595-1505 | abc.org

Special Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction Designation
The NPRM would also create a Special UAFR designation for certain fixed-site facilities
with heightened safety or security needs. ABC recognizes that some facilities may
require more restrictive UAS controls because of national security, public safety or
critical infrastructure risks.
ABC members perform a significant portion of America’s military construction and may
need to use UAS at or near Special UAFR sites to perform construction, inspection,
maintenance, repair, surveying, mapping, emergency response and other facility-related
work. These operations support, rather than undermine, site security and operational
resilience and operations associated with federal agencies that are already subject to
requirements established by the American Security Drone Act of 2023, enacted as part
of the fiscal year 2024 NDAA.2
As proposed, the NPRM would require approval from the using agency for operations
within a Special UAFR. If an entity other than the using agency operates the UAS, the
proposal would also require FAA approval in a form and manner acceptable to the
administrator. ABC understands the need for enhanced review at Special UAFR-
designated sites, but the FAA should ensure that the final rule provides a clear, timely
and repeatable process for contractor UAS operations that support construction,
inspection, maintenance, repair and emergency response.
ABC urges the FAA to establish a specific pathway for contractor UAS operations within
Special UAFRs. Under this pathway, the FAA should allow contractors to operate UAS
within a Special UAFR-designated site when:
• The using agency approves the contractor to conduct the operation and, where
applicable, the site owner/operator supports or requests the operation;
• The FAA approves the operation when required under Section 74.251;
• The operation serves a legitimate facility-related purpose, including construction,
inspection, maintenance, repair, surveying, mapping, security, emergency
response, environmental compliance, outage support, turnaround work or asset
management;
• The operator conducts the operation under Part 107 or another applicable FAA
operating authority; and
• The operation complies with any site-specific security, operational, data-handling,
Remote ID or notice conditions imposed by the using agency or the FAA.
The FAA should also set reasonable timelines for reviewing contractor UAS approval
requests at Special UAFR-designated sites. Construction and maintenance work often
depend on tightly sequenced schedules, outage windows, crane picks, inspections,
2 National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Pub. L. No. 118-31, div. A,
title XVIII, subtitle B, 137 Stat. 136, 691 (2023).
440 First St. NW, Suite 200 | Washington, DC 20001 | 202-595-1505 | abc.org

weather conditions and safety-critical milestones. Delayed approval could disrupt
essential work at the same facilities the Special UAFR designation seeks to protect. The
FAA should provide an expedited process for time-sensitive work and emergency
response operations, including verbal or electronic approval followed by written
documentation when necessary.
Finally, the FAA should clarify that Special UAFR designations should not function as a
blanket prohibition on legitimate contractor UAS operations. The final rule should
distinguish between unknown or unauthorized UAS activity and known, vetted agency-
approved contractor operations that support construction, maintenance, inspection,
emergency response and facility security. A clear contractor approval pathway would
preserve the heightened protections of Special UAFR designations while ensuring that
critical facilities can safely use UAS to build, maintain, inspect and restore essential
infrastructure.
Conclusion
ABC appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on this matter and welcomes the
opportunity to work with the FAA to advance the safe operation of UAS as the
technology continues to evolve.
Respectfully submitted,
Kristen Swearingen
Vice President, Government Affairs
440 First St. NW, Suite 200 | Washington, DC 20001 | 202-595-1505 | abc.org

Passenger Vessel 103 Oronoco Street, Suite 200 Phone (703) 518-5005 pvainfo@passengervessel.com
Association Alexandria, VA 22314 www.passengervessel.com
4 August 2026
Docket Management Facility
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140
Washington, DC 20590
Re: Docket Number: FAA-2026-4558
Designation – Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility
As published in the Federal Register on May 6, 2026
Ladies and Gentlemen,
The Passenger Vessel Association (PVA) submits these comments in response to the
Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)
establishing a new 14 CFR Part 74 governing Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions
(UAFRs) at fixed site facilities. PVA is the national trade association representing
operators of U.S. and Canadian passenger vessels, including ferries, dinner and
excursion vessels, and other passenger-carrying vessels, along with the terminals,
landings, and piers that support those operations. Members operating Maritime
Transportation Security Act (MTSA)-regulated facilities have shared their experience
with unauthorized drone activity at their terminals, summarized below, and it directly
informs the positions PVA advances in this letter.
PVA supports FAA’s proposal to include the Transportation Systems Sector among
the critical infrastructure sectors eligible for UAFR designation. Passenger vessel
terminals, ferry landings, and cruise piers share many of the same vulnerabilities as
other transportation critical infrastructure, and our members report that unauthorized
drone activity at these facilities is not a hypothetical concern but an active,
documented, and in at least one instance physically injurious problem.
I. Background and Member Experience
Passenger vessel terminals, ferry landings, and cruise piers concentrate the traveling
public at fixed points of embarkation and disembarkation, alongside fueling and
machinery spaces, and in many cases already operate under MTSA-approved Facility
Security Plans and Coast Guard-verified threat assessments.
One member, an MTSA-regulated ferry operator serving Martha’s Vineyard and
Nantucket with five terminals, reported that Massachusetts State Police arrested an

individual after losing control of a drone near a docked vessel; the drone struck a
passenger in the head, causing serious injury, with charges currently pending. The
same member reported recurring incidents of drones operating erratically over
passengers and vehicles queued to board, and raised specific concern that drones
operating close to a vessel while moored could interfere with navigational equipment,
with attendant safety and commercial consequences for island-dependent ferry
service. The member also noted that unauthorized overflights provide detailed
imagery of terminal layouts and raised concern about the potential for drones to be
used to deliver a harmful payload against the traveling public.
A second member, operating Staten Island Ferry terminals and associated private
ferry landings in New York City, reported that the local USCG Sector New York / NYPD
Drone Detection Task Force has documented hundreds of unauthorized drone flights
per month in the vicinity of its terminals and landings. These overflights have triggered
security alerts and required notifications to the U.S. Coast Guard and the National
Response Center and have diverted security and operational personnel from posted
duties to conduct forensic review of camera footage and search for operators. This
member already maintains TWIC-based access control, designated security
personnel, and CCTV surveillance consistent with an approved Facility Security Plan,
and, given the sustained volume of documented activity and its existing law
enforcement drone-detection partnership, believes this record could support a Coast
Guard-sponsored request for Special UAFR designation.
Across both members, these MTSA-regulated facilities already have in place several
of the minimum-security elements the proposed rule would require, including access
controls, designated security personnel, and security monitoring. Neither member,
however, currently has Remote ID receiver capability in place, and both indicated that
this gap, rather than the other minimum requirements, is the element that would take
the time and investment to close.
Both indicated they conduct or would conduct legitimate Part 107 drone operations of
their own, for aerial inspection, safety monitoring, and marketing photography, and
therefore have a direct interest in ensuring that any UAFR framework remains
workable for authorized operators as well as protective against unauthorized ones.
II. PVA Recommendations on the Proposed Framework
Taken together, our members’ experience shows that not every documented safety or
security problem at a passenger vessel facility rises to the level the NPRM appears to
reserve for Special UAFR designation. PVA’s recommendations below are calibrated
accordingly.

● Clarify a Coast Guard sponsorship pathway to Special UAFR for MTSA-
regulated facilities, with Standard UAFR, including continuous designation, as
the appropriate tier otherwise. PVA understands that under proposed § 74.6,
Special UAFR eligibility for non-federal facilities depends on sponsorship by a
federal security or intelligence agency, such as DHS, DOD, DOE, or DOJ,
rather than on a facility's own Facility Security Plan or threat assessment
standing alone. PVA agrees this sponsorship-based structure is appropriate:
federal security agencies possess the operational authority and intelligence
resources needed to identify credible threats, and Special UAFR should remain
reserved for cases those agencies are prepared to vouch for. MTSA-regulated
ferry facilities already have an established security relationship with the Coast
Guard, a DHS component, which reviews and approves their Facility Security
Plans and, in some cases, participates directly in drone-detection efforts
alongside these facilities. PVA recommends that FAA clarify that the Coast
Guard may serve as the sponsoring federal security agency for Special UAFR
requests involving MTSA-regulated facilities, and that FAA coordinate with
DHS and the Coast Guard to establish a clear process by which a facility with
a well-documented pattern of unauthorized drone activity and an active law
enforcement drone-detection partnership can bring that record to the Coast
Guard's attention for consideration as a sponsored Special UAFR candidate.
For MTSA-regulated facilities that have experienced recurring unauthorized
drone activity and safety incidents but do not have this kind of sponsored
security record, PVA believes Standard UAFR, including a continuous, year-
round designation where warranted, is the appropriate and sufficient tool, and
we do not ask FAA to expand direct facility-level eligibility for Special UAFR.
● Flexibility on Remote ID receiver capability. PVA supports the Remote ID
receiver requirement in principle but asks FAA to clarify that a facility may
satisfy this element through participation in an existing regional drone detection
partnership (for example, a Coast Guard or municipal police Drone Detection
Task Force) rather than mandating standalone facility-owned equipment. We
also ask FAA to coordinate with DHS and the Port Security Grant Program so
that MTSA-regulated facilities pursuing UAFR designation can apply grant
funding toward detection and Remote ID equipment costs.
● Workable access provisions for authorized Part 107 operations. PVA supports
allowing FAA Part 107-certificated operators, including facility personnel
conducting inspection or marketing photography, to transit a UAFR subject to
Remote ID compliance and notification to the site manager. We ask FAA to
confirm that this notification mechanism can accommodate time-sensitive or

recurring operational needs (e.g., routine inspection near a facility located
within five miles of an airport) without requiring new authorization for each flight.
● Annual reporting is a reasonable and manageable obligation. Our members
already report drone incidents to state and local law enforcement, the Coast
Guard, and the National Response Center as a matter of course, and indicated
that an annual reporting requirement under a UAFR would not impose a
material additional burden.
PVA respectfully urges FAA to:
● Adopt the Transportation Systems Sector eligibility criteria as proposed,
recognizing passenger vessel terminals, ferry landings, and cruise piers as
covered facility types;
● Clarify that the Coast Guard may act as the sponsoring federal security agency
for Special UAFR requests involving MTSA-regulated facilities;
● Confirm that continuous, year-round Standard UAFR designation is available
to facilities with a documented, recurring pattern of unauthorized drone activity;
● Allow the Remote ID receiver requirement to be satisfied through participation
in an existing law enforcement drone-detection partnership, and coordinate
with the Port Security Grant Program to help offset compliance costs;
● Confirm that the notification mechanism for allowed Part 107 operations can
accommodate time-sensitive or recurring inspection and marketing needs
without a new authorization for each flight.
PVA appreciates FAA’s effort to implement section 2209 in a manner that balances
safety and security with the public right of transit, and we look forward to working with
FAA as this rulemaking proceeds.
Respectfully submitted,
Andrew Sargis
President, 2026

THE CHLORINE INSTITUTE
1300 Wilson Boulevard, Suite 525, Arlington, VA 22209
Phone: 703-894-4140 Fax: 703-894-4130
www.chlorineinstitute.org
Department of Transportation
Federal Aviation Administration
1200 New Jersey Ave. SE
Washington, DC 20590-0001
August 5, 2026
RE: Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility (FAA-2026-4558)
Dear Sir or Madam:
The Chlorine Institute (“CI” or “the Institute”) is a 200-member, not-for-profit trade association
representing the chlor-alkali industry worldwide. The Institute’s members account for the majority of
chlorine production capacity in the U.S., along with the majority of caustic soda, caustic potash, and
hydrochloric acid production, and one hundred percent of chlorine repackagers. The Institute’s mission
chemicals1 are used throughout the U.S. economy and are essential to public health, including water
purification, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and vinyl materials used in manufacturing and construction.
CI and FAA share a common interest in the safe and secure integration of unmanned aircraft into the
National Airspace System, including the protection of chemical manufacturing facilities from unmanned
aircraft that pose safety and security risks. In response to FAA’s Designation-Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility proposed rule (“Proposed Rule”), CI
respectfully submits the following comments and recommendations.
CISA and Sector Risk Management Agency Pre-Screening (§§ 74.15, 74.100)
The preamble describes FAA’s intent to coordinate with Sector Risk Management Agencies (SRMAs) on
security assessments for applications, but does not clearly describe when that coordination would occur
relative to an applicant’s submission. CI recommends FAA establish an optional pre-screening process
through which CISA, as the chemical sector SRMA, can review a draft application and provide an early
indication of whether the security justification is likely to be sufficient before an applicant commits to a
full submission.
1 CI’s mission chemicals are chlorine, sodium and potassium hydroxides, sodium hypochlorite, the distribution of
vinyl chloride monomer (VCM), and the distribution and use of hydrogen chloride.

P age | 2
Eligibility and Expedited Review for Priority Facilities (§§ 74.54, 74.66)
CI supports an expedited review for facilities with chemicals of interest (COI) on Appendix A of the
dormant Chemical Facility Antiterrorism Standard (CFATS). Appendix A is a starting point as a list of
substances; FAA should work with the chemical sector SRMA to evaluate and determine numerical
threshold values that are most applicable to today’s threat environment. CFATS was designed to address
security threats, which makes it the most logical existing regulatory text to use a vehicle for expedited
review.
Interim or Provisional Protection During Application Review
Proposed § 74.15 contemplates a multi-step review process, followed by a minimum 30-day comment
period. For facilities that can demonstrate an active or escalating threat, this process could leave a
documented vulnerability unaddressed for an extended period. CI recommends FAA consider a
mechanism for interim or provisional UAFR protection, where legally available and appropriately
supported, for applicants that submit a complete eligibility and need showing under §§ 74.54 and 74.66
while the remainder of the application remains pending.
Batch Review for Comparable Facilities (§ 74.52(b))
Proposed § 74.52(b) would limit each application to a single fixed site facility. Many chlor-alkali facilities
share comparable hazards, layouts, and security postures. CI recommends FAA consider allowing a
parent company or other single applicant to submit coordinated applications for multiple facilities with
substantially similar profiles, with FAA retaining discretion to evaluate eligibility and need individually
for each facility.
Tailored Public Comment Period for High-Consequence Facilities (§ 74.15)
A uniform 30-day comment period for every application, regardless of complexity, will compound the
resource and timeline burden FAA and applicants will face as the program scales. CI recommends FAA
retain the standard 30-day period for novel, complex, or contested applications, but adopt a shortened
15-day period for standardized applications submitted under the expedited RMP lane described above,
where the security need and proposed boundaries are not in dispute.
Website-First or Hybrid Notice Process for Standardized Applications
CI recommends FAA consider a website-first approach for standardized chemical-sector applications,
under which FAA posts the proposed UAFR boundaries and supporting non-sensitive information on its
public website concurrently with, or shortly before, Federal Register publication. This would give the
public and other airspace users earlier awareness of a pending restriction without requiring FAA to alter
its procedures for novel or complex cases.

P age | 3
Sector-by-Sector Application Status Dashboard
FAA’s regulatory impact analysis anticipates a significant volume of UAFR applications over the first five
years of the program. CI recommends FAA publish and regularly update a public dashboard showing the
number of applications received, pending, approved, and denied by critical infrastructure sector, to help
CI and other trade associations counsel members on realistic timelines.
Protection of Sensitive Security Information (§ 74.50)
CI appreciates that proposed § 74.50 contemplates a process for submitting confidential business
information and security-related materials with appropriate protections. CI recommends the final rule
or implementing guidance confirm how vulnerability assessments, asset layouts, detection-system
details, and other sensitive security information submitted with a UAFR application will be protected
from public disclosure, including in the public docket and in response to Freedom of Information Act
requests.
Lateral Boundary Limitations (§ 74.58)
Proposed § 74.58(b) would require the lateral boundary of a UAFR to lie entirely within the applicant’s
property line. For many chemical facilities, the most useful window to detect and respond to a hostile or
careless unmanned aircraft is before it reaches the fence line, particularly where process equipment sits
close to the property boundary. CI recommends FAA retain the property-line limitation as the general
rule, but create a narrow exception allowing the boundary to extend a limited distance beyond the
property line where an applicant’s security assessment demonstrates the additional standoff distance is
necessary for a meaningful detection and response window.
Remote ID Detection Costs and Enforcement Responsibility (§§ 74.56, 74.260)
Proposed § 74.56(d) would require every eligible facility to maintain, directly or through a contracted
service, the capability to receive broadcast Remote ID messages from unmanned aircraft — a capital and
ongoing operating expense that will be substantial for many chemical facilities. CI recommends FAA’s
final regulatory impact analysis fully account for this cost, including third-party monitoring subscription
fees and equipment maintenance. This detection requirement, however, does not by itself enable a
facility to act on what it observes: a UAFR does not create a physical barrier and does not authorize a
facility to use detection or mitigation technology absent separate legal authority, so facility operators
will often depend on timely response from FAA or law enforcement when they observe a non-compliant
aircraft. CI is also concerned that Remote ID compliance depends on operators broadcasting accurate
information in good faith, and operators with malicious intent have the least incentive to comply. CI
recommends the final rule or implementing guidance clarify which agency is expected to take primary
enforcement responsibility when a UAS operator is unidentified, fails to broadcast Remote ID, or is
otherwise operating in violation of a UAFR, and address how facilities and FAA should treat non-
broadcasting or unregistered aircraft for enforcement and risk-assessment purposes.

P age | 4
Chemical-Sector UAS Incident Reporting
FAA’s preamble notes that no comprehensive government-wide database of unmanned aircraft
incidents currently exists. CI recommends FAA coordinate with CISA, as the chemical sector’s SRMA, to
establish a protected reporting mechanism through which facility operators can report UAS sightings,
observed Remote ID status, flight behavior, and operational impact. Such a mechanism would support
FAA’s ongoing rulemaking and enforcement efforts while improving CI’s understanding of the evolving
threat across the chemical sector.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule and for your careful attention.
Best Regards,
Jack Pendlebury
Jack Pendlebury
Senior Project Engineer

Astrotech Space Operations(ASO) requests that airborne drone operations be prohibited in the vicinity of ASO's Titusville facility due to the nature of the operations in our facility, and the customers for which we perform those operations.

I am opposed to this potential set of rules to regulate unmanned aircraft from observing non-sensitive areas. These rules open up the ability of businesses that are otherwise rarely investigated by governmental agencies to break environmental and animal cruelty laws. There have been many instances of unmanned aircraft exposing violations on factory farms and industrial plants, which in turn caused these entities to cease and/or modify operations.

Do not pass this rule to suppress the rights of Americans to know how our food is raised and when the environment is being compromised.

comments.commenter: Comment from International Liquid Terminals Association (ILTA)
comments.comment_text:
The International Liquid Terminals Association (ILTA) submits these comments responding to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in the Federal Register on May 06, 2026.

ILTA represents more than 60 commercial operators of over 600 above-ground liquid storage terminals that handle a wide range of liquid commodities, including crude oil, refined petroleum products, chemicals, fertilizers, animal fats, and vegetable oils. These terminals represent a key piece of critical infrastructure within the United States’ energy, chemical, and transportation systems sectors. Among many things, terminals provide essential logistics services, support domestic and international trade, and foster the readiness of the United States armed forces by making fuels and liquid products available throughout the world.

As such, these facilities face concerning risks brought by unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), including surveillance, operational, cyber, and physical threats warranting an unmanned aircraft flight restriction (UAFR) over these critical facilities. ILTA broadly supports the mission and framework of this rulemaking but has identified specific concerns regarding the definition of facilities eligible to apply for a UAFR, along with other concerns relating to the provisions of this rulemaking.

DefendUAS Inc. submits the attached comments on the Section 2209 NPRM (Docket No. FAA-2026-4558). DefendUAS is a U.S. airspace security and drone-detection technology company developing infrastructure-mounted low-altitude sensing for urban airspace awareness. We support the FAA's effort to establish a uniform federal framework for unmanned aircraft flight restrictions, and our comments address the practical conditions under which the proposed protective security requirement in § 74.56(d) can actually be satisfied.
Our principal recommendation is that the Department open the public right-of-way and DOT-controlled roadside infrastructure to UAS detection equipment. Detection capability requires sensors positioned along the routes of approach to a protected facility, and in the United States those routes are streets and highways. The Department can address this through the utility accommodation and alternative-use mechanisms FHWA already administers under 23 C.F.R. Part 645 Subpart B and 23 C.F.R. § 1.23(c), through guidance to State DOTs, and through express treatment of Intelligent Transportation Systems roadway equipment. FHWA has applied comparable treatment to broadband and clean energy infrastructure.
We also recommend that the FAA: define the security monitoring requirement in performance terms — detection, tracking, and characterization — rather than by reference to Remote ID reception alone, given aircraft now fielded that operate without a radio command-and-control link; require detection capability effective against aircraft not broadcasting Remote ID; frame the coverage requirement around sufficient advance warning rather than a fixed geographic radius; recognize shared and hosted detection infrastructure so that designation remains attainable for facilities without large capital budgets; confirm in the preamble that § 74.56(d) does not require an applicant to hold mitigation authority; give materially greater evidentiary weight to technologically derived and characterized detection data; require non-proprietary export of detection events; address boundary flexibility for national security sensitive federal facilities through the proposed Special UAFR pathway; and refine the within-sector eligibility criteria and thresholds.
The full comments, including supporting discussion and citations, are attached.

August 4, 2026
Federal Aviation Administration
ATTN: Michelle Ferritto, Office of Rulemaking
800 Independence Avenue SW
Washington, DC 20591
Submitted via Federal Register only
RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Comments of Vertical Aviation International on the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
Dear Ms. Ferritto:
I. Introduction
Vertical Aviation International (VAI) respectfully submits these comments in response to
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding
Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility (for purposes of these comments, the “NPRM”).
VAI is the global trade association for the civil vertical aviation industry, with
membership representing nearly 1,300 businesses and more than 19,000 professionals
across 66 nations, including operators of helicopters, UAS, and next-generation vertical
aircraft. Because VAI represents helicopter operators, UAS operators, manufacturers,
emergency responders, infrastructure operators, and advanced air mobility
stakeholders, our members regularly operate on all sides of the operational scenarios
contemplated by this NPRM. VAI is dedicated to fueling the growth of the vertical
aviation industry through safety, advocacy, and education so that communities around
the world are strengthened by the power of vertical flight.
VAI supports the FAA’s objective of protecting critical infrastructure, sensitive facilities,
and the public from unsafe or unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations. We also
recognize Congress’ directive that the FAA establish a process through which certain
fixed-site facilities may request unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs).
However, VAI is concerned that the proposed framework does not adequately
balance security objectives, operational practicality, and the continued safe

Page 2 of 14
integration of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) into the National Airspace
System (NAS). As drafted, the proposal may impose substantial burdens on
facility operators while providing limited practical security benefit, particularly
where broad categories of operations are permitted access through a notification-
based process.
Throughout this NPRM, FAA relies heavily on notification as a means of
mitigating security and operational risks. However, notification alone does not
ensure operational coordination, deconfliction, or meaningful security protection.
VAI believes the final rule should place greater emphasis on coordination,
situational awareness, and risk management rather than relying primarily on
notice-based mechanisms.
VAI additionally encourages FAA to develop a comprehensive implementation and
education strategy for both eligible fixed-site facilities and aviation stakeholders. The
effectiveness of the proposed framework will depend heavily upon awareness and
understanding by facility operators, UAS operators, pilots, manufacturers, and public
agencies that may be affected by newly established UAFRs.
II. The Proposed Standard UAFR Structure Does Not Provide Meaningful
Security Benefits
The NPRM proposes that facilities seeking a Standard UAFR submit extensive
information regarding facility operations, security considerations, and justification for the
requested restriction. This information is intended to support FAA's evaluation and
would become part of the public regulatory process.
At the same time, the proposal allows numerous categories of UAS operations to
access Standard UAFRs upon providing notice to the facility operator. FAA expressly
states that operators meeting the applicable requirements may access a UAFR after
providing notification and that facility operators have no authority to approve or deny
access. Consequently, the practical effect of a Standard UAFR may be limited to
providing situational awareness rather than restricting operations.
VAI questions whether many facilities will perceive sufficient benefit to justify the
administrative burden, public disclosure obligations, and potential security risks
associated with obtaining a Standard UAFR. FAA should further evaluate whether the
proposed framework delivers meaningful protections commensurate with the effort
required of applicants.

Page 3 of 14
Rather than relying solely on notification-based access, FAA should consider a
coordination-based framework that allows facilities and operators to establish mission-
specific operating conditions, particularly where sensitive infrastructure, existing aviation
operations, hazardous materials, or emergency response functions are present.
III. New Technology Mandates May Be More Burdensome Than Helpful
VAI represents a broad range of aircraft manufacturers, operators, and technology
developers. As FAA considers implementation of Section 2209, the agency should
avoid establishing direct or indirect technology mandates that could unnecessarily
constrain innovation or create significant certification or compliance burdens.
In particular, VAI would oppose any requirement that manufacturers incorporate specific
technologies, such as geofencing systems or similar automated restriction capabilities,
as a prerequisite for operating near or within a UAFR. Such requirements would
represent a substantial departure from the operational framework currently governing
UAS operations and could have significant impacts on aircraft design, certification,
maintenance, and lifecycle support.
If FAA determines additional protections are necessary within a UAFR, those
protections should be addressed through operational requirements, coordination
procedures, or operator responsibilities rather than aircraft design mandates. This
approach preserves flexibility, promotes innovation, and avoids imposing technology
requirements that may become obsolete as operational concepts evolve.
The agency should further ensure that any future technological considerations remain
performance-based and technology-neutral rather than prescriptive.
IV. FAA Has Not Demonstrated That the Proposed Standard UAFR
Framework Materially Improves Security Outcomes
VAI is concerned that the NPRM does not adequately demonstrate that the proposed
Standard UAFR framework will meaningfully reduce the risks posed by malicious or
unauthorized UAS activity. The NPRM appears to assume that unauthorized operators
will self-identify by failing to comply with the notification requirements. However,
individuals intending to conduct malicious activity may simply ignore both the notification
process and the underlying UAFR restrictions, limiting the proposal's effectiveness as a
security measure.
The proposed rule places substantial obligations on fixed-site facility operators seeking
protection, including preparation of detailed applications, submission of potentially
sensitive information, and ongoing administrative responsibilities. At the same time,

Page 4 of 14
numerous categories of UAS operations may access Standard UAFRs through a
notification-based process that does not require facility approval.
As a result, the NPRM raises a fundamental policy question: what security benefit is
actually achieved by a Standard UAFR relative to existing authorities and operational
practices?
The FAA repeatedly notes that the proposal would help distinguish authorized operators
from unauthorized operators. However, VAI is concerned that the proposal primarily
affects compliant operators while providing limited deterrence against genuinely
malicious actors.
A bad actor intending to conduct surveillance, disruption, criminal activity, or an
intentional attack is unlikely to be deterred by a requirement to avoid a designated
UAFR or provide advance notification before entering one. By contrast, legitimate
commercial operators, infrastructure inspectors, surveyors, photographers, utility
operators, public safety agencies, and recreational users are likely to comply with the
rule's requirements.
Consequently, the proposal appears to impose the greatest burden on those operators
already inclined to comply with applicable regulations while offering uncertain benefits
against the very actors whose activities prompted Congress to enact Section 2209.
FAA should provide additional analysis demonstrating how the proposed framework
materially reduces risk and should explain why the anticipated benefits justify the
burdens imposed on facility operators, UAS operators, and the broader aviation
community.
V. FAA Should Ensure Section 2209 Implementation Remains Consistent
with National UAS Integration Objectives
The Administration, Congress, the FAA, and industry stakeholders have collectively
invested substantial resources toward the safe integration of UAS operations into the
National Airspace System, including implementation of Remote ID, expansion of beyond
visual line of sight operations, development of advanced air mobility concepts, and
establishment of scalable operational frameworks.
VAI is concerned that the NPRM does not sufficiently explain how the proposed UAFR
framework aligns with these broader integration objectives.
As drafted, the proposal could ultimately result in a nationwide network of facility-
specific UAFRs with differing operational impacts, notification requirements, and
coordination expectations. While VAI recognizes the need to protect genuinely sensitive
facilities, the agency should ensure that implementation of Section 2209 does not

Page 5 of 14
inadvertently create a fragmented operating environment that increases complexity for
legitimate operators while providing uncertain security benefits.
FAA should clearly articulate how the proposed framework supports both security
objectives and the long-term goal of enabling scalable, predictable UAS operations
throughout the National Airspace System. This should be done in connection and
collaboration with other UAS-related rulemaking, including Part 108. Further, to provide
fully informed comments to this NPRM, a final Part 108 rulemaking would be required to
evaluate this NPRM for completeness and cohesiveness.
VI. Mandatory Outreach / Education Strategy
The NPRM assumes that eligible facilities will be aware of the UAFR application
process and are capable of engaging with FAA to request protection. However, many
potentially eligible facilities have little to no routine interaction with the FAA and may be
unfamiliar with aviation regulatory processes.
VAI is concerned that implementation of the rule could result in uneven participation
among eligible sectors, with aviation-focused entities more likely to understand and
utilize the program than similarly situated facilities that operate outside the aviation
community.
FAA should develop a coordinated outreach strategy to ensure potentially eligible
facilities are aware of the UAFR program, understand eligibility requirements, and can
make informed decisions regarding participation.
Such outreach should include coordination with sector-specific federal agencies, state
agencies, and critical infrastructure partners that already maintain relationships with
facilities qualifying for protection under the rule. Examples may include the Department
of Energy, Department of Homeland Security, Department of Health and Human
Services, Environmental Protection Agency, Department of Agriculture, and sector-
specific regulatory authorities.
Absent such outreach, the effectiveness of the program may depend less on security
need and more on an applicant's familiarity with FAA processes.
Similarly, broad awareness of this rulemaking by aviation community stakeholders is
equally critical for success. With new obligations and facility applicants being
introduced, existing and future pilots need to understand UAFRs and their own unique
obligations around these flight restrictions.

Page 6 of 14
FAA should therefore develop an education and awareness campaign prior to
implementation, including guidance materials, stakeholder outreach, industry
engagement, and updates to pilot and operator educational materials to ensure that all
impacted stakeholders understand their responsibilities under the final rule.
Functionally, FAA could consider updating the TRUST Certificate Program and require
completion of a new version to include discussion of UAFRs, along with using B4YouFly
to disseminate information related to the new rulemaking.
VII. FAA Should Clarify the Relationship Between UAFRs and State and
Local Restrictions
As states, municipalities, and other local entities continue to enact laws and policies
affecting unmanned aircraft operations, FAA should clarify how federally designated
UAFRs interact with existing state and local restrictions. While VAI recognizes that
questions of federal preemption extend well beyond the scope of this rulemaking,
additional guidance regarding the relationship between federally-established UAFRs
and other applicable legal requirements would promote regulatory consistency and
improve operator understanding. Such clarification should be incorporated into the
FAA’s broader outreach and education efforts associated with implementation of the
final rule.
VIII. Public UAFR Designations Could Inadvertently Create an Unintended
Roadmap for Bad Actors
The NPRM would establish a publicly identifiable list of facilities that have been
determined to warrant special protection due to aviation safety, national security,
homeland security, or protection-of-property concerns.
While transparency is typically appropriate in aviation rulemaking, VAI is concerned that
the cumulative effect of publicly identifying protected facilities could inadvertently create
a consolidated map of sensitive infrastructure and operations that may attract the
attention of malicious actors.
FAA should explain how it evaluated this risk and whether alternative approaches were
considered. In particular, FAA should evaluate whether facility-specific information can
be protected from public disclosure, whether certain categories of facilities should
receive additional confidentiality protections, and whether publication of approved
UAFRs may undermine the security objectives the rule seeks to achieve.

Page 7 of 14
IX. Transparency When UAFRs are Modified
The NPRM establishes a public process for creation of a UAFR but appears less clear
regarding how subsequent modifications will be communicated to stakeholders.
Facilities may evolve over time through expansion, contraction, acquisition of adjacent
property, operational changes, construction of new infrastructure, or changes in security
posture. Such changes could materially affect the boundaries or operational impacts of
an existing UAFR.
FAA should establish a transparent process through which affected stakeholders can
readily identify proposed modifications to existing UAFRs and understand how such
changes may affect aviation operations. The agency should ensure that modifications
receive an appropriate level of public notice and opportunity for stakeholder
engagement, consistent with the objectives of transparency and predictability within the
National Airspace System.
Without a clear modification process, operators may face uncertainty regarding the
scope and applicability of existing restrictions.
X. Where UAFRs Contain Existing Aviation Operations, Coordination
Requirements Must be Strengthened
Many facilities that may qualify for UAFRs routinely support aviation activities that are
critical to public safety, infrastructure protection, and emergency response. Helicopter
operations associated with emergency medical services, wildfire suppression, utility
restoration, law enforcement, search and rescue, infrastructure inspections, and
disaster response frequently occur at low altitudes and often under time-sensitive
conditions, in and around the boundaries of what would be a UAFR.
Under the proposal, operators accessing a Standard UAFR generally need only provide
notification to the facility. While notification may improve situational awareness, it does
not facilitate operational coordination between aircraft operating within the same
environment. Notification alone does not ensure operational coordination, deconfliction,
or meaningful security protection.
VAI is concerned that the proposal could create circumstances where lawful, but
unanticipated, UAS operations occur in close proximity to existing helicopter activities,
increasing operational complexity and introducing avoidable safety risks. This concern
is particularly acute during emergency operations where mission requirements may

Page 8 of 14
evolve rapidly and where delays associated with resolving operational conflicts could
have significant safety consequences.
FAA should consider requiring a more detailed coordination process when proposed
UAS operations may interact with existing aviation activities. Such coordination could
include:
• Planned operating area;
• Planned altitude range;
• Operational time window;
• Communication procedures;
• Conflict resolution procedures when multiple operators intend to operate
simultaneously.
Absent such coordination, operators may receive notice of activity without sufficient
information to safely manage interactions with ongoing aviation operations, creating a
potentially deadly flight environment within a UAFR.
FAA should also carefully evaluate how route-based transit requirements would function
in practice. Unlike many traditional aviation operations, commercial UAS operations are
frequently conducted on demand, in response to changing operational needs,
environmental conditions, infrastructure inspections, emergency response
requirements, or customer requests. These operations often do not follow fixed
schedules or predefined routes.
To the extent FAA expects operators to identify specific transit routes through a UAFR,
the agency should ensure such requirements remain operationally practical and do not
inadvertently create unnecessary logistical burdens. Any routing expectations should
preserve operational flexibility while ensuring appropriate coordination with existing
aviation activities occurring within the UAFR.
Beyond coordination requirements, VAI believes that operations conducted in a UAFR
should be held to an elevated safety standard due to the increased likelihood of
interaction with sensitive facilities, critical infrastructure, and existing aviation
operations.
To aid coordination within a UAFR, proposed §74.250 could require that any UAS
operating within a UAFR must demonstrate the capability to effectively detect and avoid
other aircraft operating within or transiting the affected airspace. Such a requirement

Page 9 of 14
would be particularly important where the UAFR encompasses facilities that routinely
support helicopter operations.
Any detect and avoid requirements should either reflect or supplement the final Part 108
rulemaking and remain performance-based and technology-neutral. FAA should require
UAS operators intending to transit through UAFRs to demonstrate an ability to
effectively detect and avoid manned and unmanned aircraft operating within a UAFR
environment, through technology and operational mitigations.
At absolute minimum, FAA should require UAS operators seeking access to a UAFR to
demonstrate how they will maintain awareness of, and avoid, other aircraft operating
within the affected area and how conflicts will be identified and resolved prior to creating
a potential hazard.
XI. Additional Protections Must Be Afforded for Facilities with Existing
Aviation Operations
The NPRM appears to assume that all eligible facilities have similar operational needs.
However, many critical infrastructure facilities routinely host aviation operations that are
themselves integral to safety, security, inspection, maintenance, or emergency
response functions.
For these facilities, a simple notification-based access model may not adequately
address operational conflicts created by unanticipated UAS activity.
FAA should consider establishing a mechanism through which facilities demonstrating
regular aviation activity may qualify for additional operational protections. This could
include eligibility for a Special UAFR or an alternative operational framework requiring
enhanced coordination before access is granted.
Such an approach would better account for facilities where aviation activity is not
incidental but rather constitutes a core operational function.
FAA should also consider expanding eligibility for enhanced operational protections
beyond Level I trauma centers. Numerous hospitals and medical facilities that are not
designated Level I trauma centers nonetheless support critical helicopter operations,
including emergency medical transport, interfacility patient transfers, specialty medical
access, organ transport, neonatal transport, and disaster response activities.

Page 10 of 14
The safety concerns associated with unanticipated UAS activity near these facilities are
often comparable to those associated with designated trauma centers. FAA should
therefore consider whether medical facilities demonstrating routine helicopter operations
should be eligible for Special UAFR consideration regardless of trauma center
designation.
XII. Liquefied Natural Gas Facilities & Petroleum Storage Sites Should be
Awarded Additional Protections
VAI is concerned that the NPRM does not provide a clear pathway for liquefied natural
gas (LNG) facilities and petroleum storage sites to qualify for UAFRs despite the
significant operational and safety implications associated with the unauthorized UAS
activity at these locations.
Unlike many other industrial facilities, unauthorized drone activity around LNG and
petroleum storage infrastructure can have immediate operational consequences.
Reports from industry indicate that unidentified UAS operations frequently require
operators to suspend loading, transfer, or other critical activities while the source and
intent of the aircraft are assessed. These interruptions can create significant operational
disruptions, economic impacts, and potential safety concerns, even where no malicious
activity ultimately occurs.
Given the critical role these facilities play in the nation’s energy infrastructure and the
potential consequences of unauthorized activity, FAA should reevaluate whether LNG
facilities and petroleum storage sites should be expressly eligible for UAFRs or
otherwise establish gating criteria that appropriately recognize their unique operational
and security risks.
XIII. Clarity on How the Rule Applies to Facility-sponsored UAS Operations
The NPRM does not clearly address how facilities that routinely conduct their own UAS
operations would operate under the proposed framework.
FAA should clarify whether facility operators would be required to submit access
notifications for their own operations, whether standing authorizations may be
established, and how FAA intends to manage circumstances in which multiple facility-
sponsored UAS operators conduct routine operations within the UAFR.

Page 11 of 14
Absent additional clarification, the proposal risks creating unnecessary administrative
burdens for the very entities the rule is intended to protect, and could further
disincentivize fixed site facilities from applying for a UAFR.
XIV. FAA Should Consider Alternative Approaches That Better Balance
Security and UAS Integration
VAI supports efforts to address legitimate security concerns associated with
unauthorized UAS activity. However, the proposed framework appears focused
primarily on creating geographically restricted areas rather than developing
operationally integrated security solutions. Security restrictions are most effective when
paired with situational awareness, operational coordination, detection capabilities,
operator accountability, and practical enforcement mechanisms. Geographic restrictions
alone are unlikely to provide meaningful protections absent complementary security
measures.
The FAA should evaluate whether alternative approaches, including enhanced
coordination requirements, risk-based operational restrictions, integration with
authorized detection and mitigation programs, or targeted security frameworks for
particularly sensitive facilities, could achieve the same objectives with fewer impacts on
legitimate existing aviation operations.
As the FAA continues implementing Congressional directives related to UAS
integration, including beyond visual line of sight operations and advanced air mobility
initiatives, it is critical that security measures remain targeted, risk-based, and
operationally practical.
Relatedly, VAI encourages FAA and Congress to explore funding mechanisms that
would assist eligible facilities in implementing infrastructure necessary to safely and
effectively manage operations within a UAFR.
Many facilities that may qualify for a UAFR lack the resources, technical expertise, or
infrastructure necessary to maintain awareness of nearby UAS activity, coordinate with
operators, or identify potential unauthorized operations. Establishing a UAFR without
providing facilities with tools to understand what is occurring within the affected airspace
may limit the practical effectiveness of the program.
FAA should therefore evaluate opportunities to establish grant programs, cost-sharing
initiatives, or other funding mechanisms that support deployment of detection,
monitoring, communication, and coordination capabilities at eligible facilities. Priority

Page 12 of 14
should be given to facilities that routinely support existing aviation operations, including
hospitals with helipads / vertiports / UAS activity, emergency response facilities, utility
infrastructure supporting aerial inspection programs, wildfire response facilities, and
other locations where interactions between manned and unmanned aircraft present
heightened safety concerns.
Such investments may ultimately provide greater security and operational benefits than
expanding airspace restrictions alone while also improving situational awareness and
coordination among all aviation stakeholders.
XV. Conclusion
VAI remains concerned that the NPRM has not demonstrated that the proposed
Standard UAFR framework will materially improve security outcomes while
simultaneously introducing new administrative burdens, operational complexity, and
potential security vulnerabilities. The proposal appears to place substantial obligations
on facility operators and compliant UAS operators while providing limited deterrence
against malicious actors who are unlikely to comply with the rule's requirements.
While VAI supports the FAA’s objective of protecting critical infrastructure and sensitive
facilities from unauthorized UAS activity, the final rule must strike an appropriate
balance between security, operational safety, and continued integration of UAS into the
National Airspace System. Notification alone does not ensure operational coordination,
deconfliction, or meaningful protection for facilities that routinely support aviation
operations.
The most effective security framework is one that promotes coordination among
legitimate operators, provides facilities with meaningful situational awareness,
and preserves the ability of manned and unmanned aircraft to safely share the
National Airspace System.
Accordingly, VAI urges the FAA to revise the proposal to:
• Strengthen coordination requirements between UAS operators and facilities
hosting existing aviation operations;
• Require operators accessing a UAFR to demonstrate an ability to detect and
avoid other aircraft operating within the affected airspace;
• Expand consideration of enhanced protections for facilities with routine helicopter
and other manned aviation operations;

Page 13 of 14
• Maintain a technology-neutral approach that avoids unnecessary aircraft design
mandates while preserving flexibility for future innovation;
• Develop comprehensive outreach and education programs for both eligible
facilities and aviation stakeholders;
• Clarify the relationship between federal designated UAFRs and applicable state
and local restrictions to promote regulatory consistency and operator awareness;
• Establish transparent processes for creation and modification of UAFRs;
• Explore grant funding and other mechanisms to support deployment of detection,
monitoring, and coordination infrastructure at facilities operating within the UAFR
framework; and
• Reevaluate the eligibility criteria for critical energy infrastructure, including
liquefied natural gas and petroleum storage facilities, to ensure the final rule
appropriately addresses operational and security risks.
To the extent the FAA issues a final Part 108 rule prior to publication of a final Section
2209 rule, VAI encourages the agency to ensure the two regulatory frameworks operate
cohesively. Concepts such as detect-and-avoid, operational coordination, access
requirements, and operator responsibilities should be harmonized to avoid conflicting
requirements or unnecessary operational complexity.
VAI believes these modifications would better align the proposal with Congressional
intent, improve operational safety, enhance security outcomes, and support the
continued integration of manned and unmanned aircraft within the National Airspace
System.
VAI appreciates the opportunity to comment and would welcome the opportunity to
further engage with the FAA and industry stakeholders to support a fully justified and
operationally practical final rulemaking. To supplement these comments, please also
see Appendix A, where VAI directly answers some of the pointed questions FAA raised
in the NPRM.
With kindest regards,
Amber Harrison,
Director of Regulatory Affairs
Vertical Aviation International
amberh@verticalavi.org

Page 14 of 14
APPENDIX A – NPRM QUESTIONS
The attached responses are provided in addition to, not in lieu of, the broader policy
recommendations contained in the body of these comments.

Comments on Federal Aviation Administration Notice of Proposed Rulemaking “Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility” (FAA-2026-4558)
The Virginia Spaceport Authority (VSA), officially the Virginia Commercial Space Flight Authority, owns and operates the Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport (MARS) at Wallops Island, VA. MARS is one of only four public spaceports in the Nation, licensed by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), for vertical lift to orbit (FAA Launch Site Operator License No. LSO 02-007 (Rev 5)). VSA appreciates the opportunity to respond to NPRM FAA-2026-4558.

VSA supports the FAA's proposed rule establishing a process for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFR). Vertical lift spaceports are critical to assured access to space for the nation. Currently, there are only four public spaceports in the United States that are FAA-licensed for vertical launch to orbit. The vertical launch spaceports provide the bulk of support to launch critical national security missions. If the launch facilities and supporting infrastructures at the Eastern Range (Cape Canaveral Space Force Station/Kennedy Space Center), Western Range (Vandenberg Space Force Base), the VSA’s Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport (MARS) at Wallops Island, Virginia, or the Pacific Spaceport Complex at Kodiak, Alaska were disrupted or destroyed, the United States would lose the capability to replenish losses to critical space systems and services.

Therefore, spaceports and all their support facilities should be included as fixed site facilities in the FAA’s rule. VSA recommends that commercial spaceports licensed by the FAA for vertical lift to orbit and federally supported launch ranges be explicitly entered into one of the Nation’s Critical Infrastructure Sectors due to their importance to national security and the growing cadence of commercial launch operations. The FAA should also establish an expedited approval process for licensed launch sites to accommodate time-sensitive launch schedules and evolving operational requirements. These enhancements would strengthen protection of critical space transportation infrastructure while maintaining the safe and efficient use of the National Airspace System.
