Section 2209 NPRM for Restricting the Operations of Unmanned Aircraft in Close
Proximity to Fixed Site Facilities (FAA-2026-4558)
To Whom It May Concern:
Northeast UAS Airspace Integration Research Alliance, Inc. (NUAIR) appreciates the
opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and U.S. Department of
Transportation (DOT) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) titled “Designation – Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility” implementing Section 2209
of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (hereinafter “NPRM” or “proposed rule”).
NUAIR strongly supports the FAA’s efforts to address growing threats to critical infrastructure
from unauthorized and unlawful unmanned aircraft system (UAS) activity. These risks are real and
increasingly relevant across multiple sectors. At the same time, it is important to balance these security
needs with the need to enable lawful UAS operations that provide substantial societal and public safety
benefits. Safe, secure and scalable UAS operations will unlock vast economic and societal benefits
for millions of Americans across the nation. A framework that unduly restricts compliant operators risks
undermining the very operational efficiencies, safety enhancements, and economic gains that UAS
technologies are already delivering nationwide. In this regard, NUAIR appreciates the FAA’s clear
desire to ensure that airspace restrictions are proportionate to the risk and do not inadvertently impede
lawful operations.
I. Background on NUAIR
NUAIR is a nonprofit organization based in Syracuse, New York, and is driving economic
development through innovations in UAS and Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) in order to safely integrate
this technology into the National Airspace System (NAS). With support from Empire State
Development and the State of New York, NUAIR supports the harmonization needed to safely and
securely innovate airspace and advance aviation for the next century of flight. With more than ten
years of experience in UAS testing and validation, including managing operations at the New York
UAS Test Site, supporting state and local economic development, and training public safety officials,
NUAIR proudly drives airspace innovation in New York and advances mobility on a global scale.
NUAIR also regularly collaborates with private, state, federal, and military partners to test UAS flights
against various counter-UAS detection technologies in support of public safety and national security.

NUAIR has long been a leader in BVLOS operations, managing a 240-square-mile, highly
instrumented airspace in Central New York under a Part 107 sUAS-agnostic BVLOS waiver. To date,
NUAIR has conducted approximately 8600 BVLOS flights in controlled airspace in support of its safety
infrastructure and scaling of the industry. Recently, NUAIR was granted a Letter of Acceptance (LOA)
from the FAA to provide its surveillance-as-a-service infrastructure for routine BVLOS operations.
II. Key Areas of Support
NUAIR serves on the Board of the Commercial Drone Alliance (CDA), and we broadly support
comments submitted by the CDA in response to the NPRM. In particular, we endorse the CDA’s
comments in the following areas:
1. The importance of balancing security needs with ensuring airspace access for authorized and
compliant UAS operators.
2. Support for a tiered and risk-based approach to designating Unmanned Aircraft Flight
Restrictions (UAFRs) in the NPRM.
3. Support for the performance-based approach to enabling UAFR transit by compliant and
authorized UAS operators.
4. The challenges associated with flight-by-flight UAFR access notifications given the current and
growing scale of UAS operations, and the need to automate notification processes.
5. The need to clarify certain aspects of the UAFR application process.
6. The importance of implementing the proposed rule in a manner that does not impede a facility’s
ability to conduct its own UAS operations.
III. Enabling Drone Detection as a Service Models
NUAIR supports the NPRM’s proposal to require that fixed critical infrastructure sites have the
capability to receive and process UAS Remote Identification (Remote ID) broadcasts. Remote ID
provides a foundational layer of situational awareness, enabling infrastructure operators to identify and
differentiate compliant UAS operations from those that may warrant further scrutiny. This capability
represents a meaningful step forward in enhancing transparency and accountability in the airspace.
While Remote ID detection capabilities are essential, NUAIR emphasizes that Remote ID
detection alone is insufficient to address the full range of risks associated with unauthorized UAS
operations. Whether due to intentional disabling or the use of non-Remote ID compliant UAS, it is
likely that threats to critical infrastructure will involve noncooperative drones that do not broadcast
Remote ID. As a result, reliance solely on Remote ID risks creating gaps in detection precisely where
risk may be greatest. The final rule should require that facilities have the ability to identify and track

noncooperative UAS that are not broadcasting Remote ID. A comprehensive security framework for
critical infrastructure must incorporate both cooperative and noncooperative detection.
To support this objective, NUAIR recommends that the FAA establish a clear and scalable
regulatory framework for drone detection as a service. Many infrastructure operators will lack the time,
resources or technical expertise necessary to deploy and manage advanced UAS detection systems.
Surveillance- or detection-as-a-service (SAAS or DAAS) models would allow qualified third-party
providers to deliver standardized, reliable detection capabilities across a wide range of infrastructure
sites. Such a framework should define appropriate performance expectations, data handling
requirements, and operational parameters to ensure that detection services are both effective and
trustworthy. Establishing this type of structure would promote consistency and lower barriers to
adoption.
In developing this framework, NUAIR encourages the FAA to leverage the proposed Part 146
framework for regulating and certifying Automated Data Service Providers (ADSPs) and their services.
The proposed Part 108 rule correctly recognized that data is critical to enabling safe and scalable
beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) operations in the NAS, as the ability to operate BVLOS is
predicated on the fidelity and assurance of the data. The same is true for promoting security in the
NAS and the proposed Part 146 framework could be used as a model for establishing FAA oversight
of third-party detection service providers. The FAA’s Near-Term Approval Process (NTAP) also offers
a practical mechanism for evaluating and validating new services in real-world environments. NUAIR
went through the NTAP process and was granted a Letter of Acceptance (LOA) from the FAA to
provide its surveillance-as-a-service infrastructure for routine BVLOS operations. Applying similar
principles and processes to drone detection service providers would enable the FAA to ensure that
such systems meet consistent, performance-based standards while still supporting innovation and
rapid deployment. These approaches would promote confidence among both infrastructure operators
and the public.
IV. Ensure No Adverse Effect on Public Safety Drone Operations
NUAIR supports the FAA’s proposal to allow authorized commercial UAS operators to transit
UAFRs under defined conditions. Maintaining access for compliant operators is essential to ensuring
that beneficial commercial operations can continue without unnecessary disruption.
It is also critical that the proposed rule extend similar or greater operational flexibility to public
safety operators. Emergency response operations are inherently dynamic and time-sensitive, often
requiring rapid deployment in situations where advance notification is not feasible. In such scenarios,
requiring public safety operators to comply with standard authorization processes applicable to routine
commercial operations could introduce unacceptable delays. Accordingly, the final rule should provide
a clear mechanism that allows public safety operators to transit UAFRs when responding to active
emergencies, including circumstances where little or no prior notice can be provided to the FAA or the
affected infrastructure site. Emergency responders should be able to act decisively without
encountering procedural barriers that could impede life-saving missions.

V. Conclusion
NUAIR appreciates the opportunity to comment on FAA and DOT’s 2209 NPRM. We look
forward to collaborating with the FAA and DOT to shape a final rule that mitigates security threats
posed by unlawful UAS operations to critical infrastructure while preserving the significant benefits that
lawful UAS operations provide to American citizens.
Respectfully submitted,
NUAIR

comments.commenter: Comment from Commonwealth of Virginia UAS/CUAS Executive Committee
comments.comment_text: The Commonwealth of Virginia UAS/CUAS Executive Committee submits the attached comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016. We appreciate the FAA’s effort to formalize protections for fixed-site critical infrastructure through a new regulatory framework governing Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).

comments.commenter: Comment from The American Gas Association
comments.comment_text:
August 05, 2026
Submitted to the Federal eRulemaking Portal (www.regulations.gov)
Docket Operations
Room W58-213, West Building, 5th Floor
Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Washington, DC 20590
Re: Comments of the American Gas Association
Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558, RIN 2120-AL33, 91 Fed. Reg. 24650
(May 6, 2026).
The American Gas Association (AGA) respectfully submits the following comments in
response to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation (DOT)
proceeding referenced above. This Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), implementing
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (Section 2209),1 is vital
to securing critical infrastructure facilities from unmanned aircraft system (UAS) enabled
intrusions and malicious acts, and AGA and its members commend the FAA for its efforts
thus far to implement Section 2209. Although AGA shares our members’ concerns
regarding certain aspects of the NPRM, this proposed rule is an important initial step to
implementing Section 2209 and providing increased security for our nation’s critical
infrastructure facilities. Restricting the airspace above critical facilities and assets reduces
the risk of damage caused by UAS crash landings, hostile intelligence gathering, and UAS-
enabled attacks by malicious actors. AGA appreciates the opportunity to promote the
security of America’s critical energy infrastructure. To enhance the proposal’s
effectiveness, efficiency, and utility, we offer several recommendations aimed at expanding
the unmanned aircraft flight restriction (UAFR) eligibility criteria, revising the application
and notification requirements, and limiting the potential disclosure risk of sensitive
information. These recommendations are detailed below.
AGA, founded in 1918, represents more than 200 local energy companies that deliver clean
natural gas throughout the United States. There are more than 79 million
residential, commercial and industrial natural gas customers in the U.S., of
1 FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209, 130 Stat. 615, 634–35 (2016).

which 94 percent — more than 74 million customers — receive their gas from AGA
members. AGA is an advocate for natural gas utility companies and their customers
and provides a broad range of programs and services for member natural gas pipelines,
marketers, gatherers, international natural gas companies, and industry associates. Today,
natural gas meets one-third of the United States' energy needs.
Subpart C – Sector-Specific Requirements
§74.95 Transportation systems sector.
The eligibility criteria for natural gas assets and facilities should be expanded to
accommodate the best reading of the statute and ensure vulnerable facilities and
assets can effectively manage the risks associated with UAS intrusions and
malicious acts. While Section 2209 explicitly includes “distribution facilities and
equipment” as examples of critical infrastructure that may be eligible to apply for a
UAFR, as written, subpart C, Sector-Specific Requirements, renders all but a small
subset of distribution assets ineligible to apply for restrictions. AGA believes that the
best reading of the statute broadly grants application eligibility to critical
infrastructure, including infrastructure related to the safe and reliable distribution of
natural gas.2 While subpart C lists examples of facilities essential for the secure and
reliable provision of gas service, the list is far from comprehensive and ignores
facilities that would inspire significant disruptions if successfully targeted.3
AGA urges FAA to adopt an approach to eligibility that properly accounts for
potential downstream impacts of disruptions to facilities and assets and avoids the
use of absolute categories or facility descriptions that minimize applicant
discretion. This risk-based approach would ensure the eligibility of critical facilities
and preserve greater flexibility for the future. UAS is a nascent technology and the
ubiquity of flights and the threats introduced are not fully realized. By broadening
eligibility criteria to the maximum extent authorized by Congress in Section 2209,
FAA preserves the necessary flexibility to address future challenges in a developing
field.
FAA should capitalize on risk-based frameworks for determining whether a facility is
eligible to apply for a UAFR. For example, the critical facilities criteria in the
Transportation Security Administration (TSA) Pipeline Security Guidelines establish
sound, outcome-focused criteria that account for potential impacts to national
2“In this section, the term ‘critical infrastructure’ means systems and assets, whether physical or virtual, so
vital to the United States that the incapacity or destruction of such systems and assets would have a
debilitating impact on security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or any
combination of those matters.” 42 U.S.C. § 5195c(e) (2024).
3 “(d) Pipeline compressor station that is just upstream of electric power generating plants or major
metropolitan areas;… (g) Pipeline control station/room that is a sole source supply to cities, airports, and
national defense infrastructure;” §74.95 Transportation systems sector.

defense, key infrastructure, public services, reliable natural gas delivery, and
pipeline operations among other factors.4 Additionally, the TSA formally identifies a
key group of critical infrastructure owner/operators and regulates this community
via the Security Directives. 5 Facilities governed by the Security Directives should be
eligible to apply for a UAFR. The proposed rule’s current eligibility criteria consider
rigid facility categories rather than the operational importance of facilities and
assets. As currently written, the proposal fails to account for the variety of assets
and facilities most vulnerable to UAS disruptions and most necessary for the safe
and reliable delivery of natural gas.
Minimally, the transportation system eligibility criteria should be rewritten to
account for Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) facilities, peak-shaving facilities, city gates,
regulator stations, all compressor stations, and any pipeline control station or
facility housing gas control operations. A disruption to any of these facilities could
result in debilitating impacts on national security, economic security, or public
health and safety.
Broadened eligibility criteria help ensure that the facilities that most require UAFRs
are eligible to apply. Critical infrastructure owner/operators possess knowledge of
the unique risks and interdependencies across facilities and assets and would seek
protections according to operational necessity and the risk profile of specific
facilities. Given the extensive requirements, owner/operators would submit
applications for only facilities and assets most likely to benefit from UAFRs,
balancing the intention of the rulemaking and the administrative burden to both
applicants and the FAA. The UAS risk, likelihood, and impact will vary from operator
to operator and asset to asset, and UAFR application eligibility should reflect the
dynamism of the threat.
Subpart B – Minimum Requirements
§74.56 Protective security.
The designated security personnel requirement risks rendering critical remote
facilities and assets ineligible for UAFR protections. For example, remote regulator
stations may have limited or no full-time staff but remain vital to pipeline operations
and vulnerable to disruptions from UAS activity, like crashes or targeted vandalism.
The expectation that all eligible facilities maintain designated security personnel
fails to appropriately account for the diffuse and often remote nature of pipeline
4 Transportation Security Administration, Pipeline Security Guidelines (Mar. 2018, updated Apr. 2021),
available at https://www.tsa.gov/sites/default/files/pipeline_security_guidelines.pdf (last visited August 4,
2026).
5 Transportation Security Administration, Security Directives and Emergency Amendments, available at
https://www.tsa.gov/sd-and-ea (last visited August 4, 2026).

infrastructure. Many facilities may be vulnerable to drone incursions while being
difficult to access by traditional means.
The requirement that facilities maintain a remote identification sensing capability
also risks making critical sites ineligible to apply for protections under the proposed
rule. The expense of ruggedized hardware and of running power and connections to
remote assets or areas of a facility without the assurance that such measures will
result in a UAFR, makes scalable implementation financially and practically
difficult. In the absence of a UAFR, identification capabilities convey a limited
security benefit that is disproportionate to costs. Airspace awareness can be
established through a variety of means including spotting, both manually and via
cameras. Rather than mandating security measures that may disqualify facilities in
need of UAFRs, FAA should take into account applicant facilities’ adoption of
mitigations and measures appropriate to their unique operational realities and risk
environments.
§74.66 Demonstration of need.
To the degree possible, application materials should minimize the introduction of
new vulnerabilities. AGA is concerned by the UAFR application requirements in
§74.66 (b), to provide “the weaknesses or gaps that may be….exploited by
unmanned aircraft…Include information on the specific assets or elements of the
facility that may be exploited[,]” and (c) to “[d]escribe the consequences of the
vulnerability…if exploited.” Submitting this information would increase vulnerability
for applicants and could result in the creation of Sensitive Security Information,
triggering additional handling, safeguarding, and compliance obligations.6 AGA
adamantly opposes the collection and centralization of sensitive operational
and security-related information. FAA’s repository of vulnerabilities, gaps, and
consequences would create an enticing target for malicious actors seeking to
harm critical infrastructure. As emphasized by the recent Homeland Security
Information Network (HSIN) breach, critical infrastructure owner/operators are
concerned by the successful targeting of government databases and services.7
While a baseline or high-level depiction of the sensitive information may be
submitted or shared on screen for FAA’s evaluation, details should remain with the
applicant and not be removed by FAA physically or digitally.
All sensitive application information the FAA gathers, by any means, including
security information, confidential business information, vulnerability data, site
maps, and operational details, must be protected from unauthorized disclosure.
6 49 C.F.R Part 1520, Protection of Sensitive Security Information.
7 DiMolfetta, D. (2026, June 30). Hackers breached DHS information-sharing network, people familiar say.
Nextgov/FCW, available at https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/06/hackers-breached-dhs-
information-sharing-network-people-familiar-say/414534/ (last visited August 4, 2026).

Failure to adequately protect sensitive information undermines the purpose of the
rulemaking by diminishing the research threshold for malicious actors targeting
critical infrastructure.
To limit the administrative burden of processing applications and the risks of
documenting and gathering sensitive facility vulnerabilities, security gaps, and
consequences of successful exploitation, FAA should recognize the security and
safety determinations of other agencies and consensus standards bodies. AGA
requests a streamlined and simplified application process for facility owners whose
assets have already been identified by other agencies or consensus standards
bodies as warranting additional security and safety considerations. For example,
applicants for facilities and assets that meet TSA criticality criteria or are subject to
the TSA Security Directives should not have to provide much of the information
requested in §74.66, demonstrating the need for a UAFR.8 The economic and
operational impacts of disruptions to critical facilities and the need for enhanced
security measures are known by owner/operators and government agencies and
should not be reiterated or more broadly disseminated.
Additionally, AGA urges FAA to consider the high cost of drone detection technology
relative to the benefits in the absence of flight restrictions. Recognizing that many
operators, including those currently operating Radio Frequency Identification (RFID)
readers, may not have accumulated 24 months of traffic data by the time the UAFR
application process begins, AGA recommends amending §74.66 (a) to permit
submission of up to the most recent 24 months of available data. Additionally, the
potential unavailability of accurate or comprehensive traffic information should not
discount the importance of UAFRs to a facility’s security plan. In the absence of
protections today, facilities and asset owners have little incentive to document or
capture traffic above fixed site facilities. The substantial investment in drone
detection technology makes sense when an operator is reasonably assured of
mitigations, like a UAFR.
§74.68 Externalities.
The FAA is better positioned to account for the externalities, including costs,
disruptions, or other negative effects to manned and unmanned users of the
airspace, than facility owner/operators. FAA may leverage the public comment
process, interagency coordination, and airspace management tools to estimate
likely economic and operational impacts. UAFR applicants lack many of the tools
necessary for an accurate evaluation of impacts and the FAA should not shift this
responsibility to applicants.
8 Transportation Security Administration, Pipeline Security Guidelines, Table 1, “Critical Facilities Criteria”
(Mar. 2018, updated Apr. 2021).

Subpart D – FAA Evaluation and Determination
§74.100 Evaluation.
All materials made available to the public regarding potential or enacted UAFRs
should preserve the anonymity of applicants and the nature or function of protected
facilities and assets. To the degree feasible, information availability should be
limited to those with a demonstrated “need to know.” These safeguards minimize
unnecessary attention to facilities and assets and the exposure risk of information
that might be exploited by malicious actors targeting critical infrastructure.
Published information should be limited to only that which is minimally necessary
for UAS operators to abide by the UAFR.
In addition to facility criticality, consensus standards and the conditions that create
unacceptable safety hazards should inform UAFR eligibility and FAA determinations.
For example, the National Fire Protection Association Standard for the Production,
Storage, and Handling of Liquefied Natural Gas (NFPA 59A), references NFPA 70 and
requires electrical equipment in certain classified areas of LNG facilities to use
approved protection methods. 9 UAS operated above and within these facilities likely
fail to satisfy the standard and pose significant safety and operational risks.
As noted above, facility criticality and consensus standards should both inform
application eligibility and weigh heavily on the FAA’s UAFR determination. AGA urges
FAA to approve the applications of critical facility owner/operators, as determined
by TSA criticality frameworks, when feasible, and focus evaluations on the potential
impacts of disruption rather than asset types. FAA should weigh the potentially
damaging economic, operational, public safety, and public service impacts of UAS-
enabled disruptions when making UAFR determinations.
Subpart G – Access to Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions
§74.255 Unmanned aircraft flight restriction access notification.
Critical infrastructure owner/operators frequently use UAS to support maintenance,
security, regulatory compliance, and emergency response activities. To ease
administrative burden and facilitate the increasingly common and beneficial use of
UAS by critical infrastructure owner/operators, AGA recommends a standing
authorization for facility-authorized UAS and pilots.
9 National Fire Protection Association, NFPA 59A: Standard for the Production, Storage, and Handling of
Liquefied Natural Gas Chapter 11 (2026); National Fire Protection Association NFPA 70: National Electrical
Codes arts. 500-505 (2026).

Once a facility gains a UAFR, the owner/operator should be allowed to submit a list
of facility-owned, operated, or authorized UAS and pilots. These operations should
be exempted from the formal notification requirements proposed in § 74.255 that
could delay important operations, without added safety or security benefit. FAA
should create a secure and facility-managed list containing the information for
standing authorizations. Facilities should be able to add, modify, or suspend entries
as needed, and all information should be protected from disclosure.
Conclusion
AGA members support ongoing national efforts to enable UAS flights and believe this goal
is fully compatible with safeguarding critical facilities from intrusion. Most critical facilities
and assets detailed in these comments occupy a small footprint that UAS could easily and
quickly bypass without substantial flight path alterations. UAFRs help owner/operators
better distinguish legitimate traffic from potential risks, improving threat awareness and
informing possible mitigations. While advocating simplified compliance pathways for
facility-authorized flights, AGA advocates stronger third-party flight restrictions with fewer
exceptions to ensure facility safety. With expanded eligibility criteria, appropriate
information safeguards, streamlined requirements, and a simplified application process,
the rule could effectively balance critical infrastructure security concerns, airspace
efficiency, and the public right to transit.
Respectfully submitted,
Kimberly Denbow
Vice President, Security & Operations
American Gas Association

comments.commenter: Comment from Virginia Municipal Drinking Water Association
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
Via Regulations.gov
Docket Operations
U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT)
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE,
Room W58–213,
West Building 5th Floor,
Washington, DC 20590–0001
RE: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility (Docket Id: FAA-2026-4558)
Dear Ms. Ferritto,
We write on behalf of over fifty publicly owned water utilities in support of the FAA’s proposed
rule authorizing operators of fixed-site facilities to request and maintain an unmanned aircraft
flight restriction (UAFR). We believe it is especially critical that the final rule ensure that at least
all major water and wastewater treatment facilities will be eligible for a UAFR designation.
These comments are submitted on behalf of the following non-profit, public utility organization:
the Virginia Municipal Drinking Water Association (VMDWA) (the Association). The Association is
comprised of local government water utilities dedicated to protecting public health and the
environment. They strive to provide affordable and cost-effective water that meets all regulatory
requirements. Many members also operate wastewater utilities.
The Association submits these comments in support of the proposed rule, while urging that all
public water and sewer treatment facilities be eligible for a UFAR designation and that responses
be provided to the questions the FAA has asked.
The Association supports the Proposed Rule to Protect Drinking Water and
Wastewater Facilities
The Association’s members provide public drinking water and wastewater service using highly
specialized treatment and distribution/collection facilities. The treatment facilities are highly
specialized and cannot be quickly replaced in the event of a failure or a terror-related attack.
Unmanned aircraft pose critical security, safety, and operational risks to water and wastewater
utilities. Drinking water and wastewater plants and their associated distribution and collection
systems are large and expansive and are, therefore, uniquely exposed to harm from unmanned
aircraft.
Any interruption to public water or wastewater treatment services can shut down some or all of
the affected community – potentially for an extended period.
VIRGINIA MUNICIPAL DRINKING WATER ASSOCIATION, INC.
P.O. Box 51, Richmond, Virginia 23218-0051 │ (804) 716-9021 │ www.VMDWA.org

Docket Id: FAA-2026-4558
August 5, 2026
Page 2
Given the explosion in drone use to attack vulnerable public infrastructure in conflict zones around
the world, the Association agrees that authorizing our members to obtain a UAFR is an essential
tool to help counter the threat of unmanned aircraft attacks against water and wastewater
facilities – especially vulnerable and hard-to-repair treatment facilities. Most of those treatment
facilities have little or no redundancy capability.
The ability to obtain a UAFR from the FAA presents a solution that is unavailable under any other
avenue. Association members continue to work at the state level to prevent (and punish with
greater consequences) damage and unauthorized access to their facilities. The proposed rule
presents an opportunity to implement an effective, uniform tool to protect water and wastewater
operations and prevent damage from unmanned aircraft through the UAFR process.
The Association offers the following suggestions in response to the FAA’s specific questions on
the recommended eligibility criteria for UAFRs in the Water and Wastewater Systems Sector in
§ 74.96.
Types and Characteristics of Drinking Water and Wastewater Systems the FAA should
consider when Developing Criteria
The Association suggests that system types addressed in the proposed rule text should include:
(1) drinking water treatment plants that serve as a primary treatment facility for a
community water system (CWS) – especially larger systems;
(2) critical drinking water distribution facilities such as elevated storage tanks, reservoirs,
and intake structures for a CWS;
(3) publicly owned wastewater treatment plants;
(4) infrastructure such as pump stations, recharge facilities, booster facilities, and other
essential assets;
(5) related control facilities and SCADA infrastructure; and
(6) any chemical storage facilities.
Important system characteristics to analyze should include (1) whether there is hazardous
chemical storage, particularly chlorine, ammonia, fluoride compounds, in large quantities; (2) the
ability for an unmanned aircraft to surveil and gather important information from the air at the
facility and/or cause physical damage at the site; and (3) the extent of the impact that a disruption
of water/wastewater service would cause to the communities served.
Consideration of Population Served and Appropriate Population Thresholds
The Association agrees that population served is an important consideration given the difficulty
of replacing (or finding alternative solutions for) larger scale water treatment facilities that may
be damaged by drone attack. Nevertheless, all water and wastewater treatment plants that fit
the definition of critical facility under 42 U.S.C. § 5195c(e) should be able to request a UAFR (as
the definition itself does not include a population cutoff). However, priority consideration should
be given to facilities serving larger populations or facilities with higher risk factors (such as those
serving critical national or regional facilities, agencies, or industries). While prioritizing eligibility
for a UAFR based on a high population metric could discount rural areas, we believe there are
greater opportunities for other local public utilities and the states to support smaller rural facilities
and populations than for major facilities serving large population areas.

Docket Id: FAA-2026-4558
August 5, 2026
Page 3
We recognize the potential administrative burden for the FAA if every water and wastewater utility
simultaneously requested a UAFR. Population thresholds could therefore be used to establish
presumptive eligibility for a UAFR request. For example, a service population threshold of 100,000
or more people for both water and wastewater plants could be appropriate for establishing
presumptive eligibility to request a standard UAFR, while allowing smaller systems the opportunity
to demonstrate why they may warrant UAFR protection. In other words, a valid demonstration of
need, e.g. the lack of alternative sources or remoteness of the facility, should allow utilities with
smaller service populations to overcome any population criterion presumption. Nevertheless, the
FAA should prioritize UAFR consideration for facilities with larger populations due to the potentially
extensive safety and security impacts of disruptions to those systems.
Critical customers served by a drinking water/wastewater system may warrant
consideration when prioritizing UAFRs
Every water treatment facility serving a large community will have critical customers should it be
rendered inoperable. Truly critical national defense and other facilities will likely need to rely on
on-site backup water supply systems. In some cities, critical industries, hospitals, and schools
may have their own wells or storage systems to allow continued operation during service outages.
So, while we agree that in some cases critical customers may warrant prioritizing consideration
of the establishment of a UAFR for a particular facility, the reality is that all larger water plants
will have critical customers.
Documentation of unauthorized drone flights over a drinking water or wastewater
system should be considered when prioritizing UAFRs but not considered as a
necessary condition for eligibility
Threat history should be considered when prioritizing the establishment of UAFRs but should not
be determinative of eligibility for a UAFR. Facilities that have had past incidents/threats should
be given UAFR establishment priority. However, again, past threats should relate to the
prioritization of the establishment of a UAFR, not to eligibility for a UAFR.
Additional Comments
Promulgating Water and Wastewater Sector Eligibility Criteria. Given the urgency and
importance of the safety and security associated with the proper provision of water and
wastewater service, the FAA should issue the Eligibility Criteria for the Water and Wastewater
Systems Section (§ 74.96) with the proposed rule text. Given the exponential expansion in
unmanned aircraft technologies and offensive uses, the FAA should move forward as efficiently
and expeditiously as possible. The FAA should identify the water and wastewater sector’s
prioritization criteria with the proposed rule – and not as a follow-up to the rule - to optimally
protect the provision of public water and wastewater services in the country.
Remote Sensing Technology. Applicants for UAFRs must submit information describing
existing security plans and measures under § 74.56(d) of the proposed rule, including the ability
to receive broadcast Remote Identification messages from unmanned aircraft. The Association
supports this measure to bolster the overall security of water and wastewater utilities but suggests
that the FAA provide accompanying guidance on appropriate ways to fulfill the Remote
Identification requirement, along with information on technical assistance to better help utilities
meet and understand this specific requirement.

Docket Id: FAA-2026-4558
August 5, 2026
Page 4
Lateral Boundary Limitation. The proposed definition and limitations of a lateral boundary in
§ 74.58 may not accommodate the range of critical public water/sewer utility assets. The
proposed rule would set the lateral boundary at a facility’s property line. The final rule should
ensure that any UAFR covers all essential assets, such as elevated storage, chemical storage, and
feed locations. In some instances, establishing UAFR zones may make more sense than an
individual property-line approach, especially when multiple properties are in the same area. There
should be additional guidance/information about the flexibilities for water and wastewater
systems with regard to their sector and property line limitations so as not to undermine the true
protective value of a UAFR.
Five-Year Term. The Association supports the five-year permit duration (proposed § 74.200).
However, for water treatment facilities, we believe the permit duration should be 10 years, as
these facilities are so critical that we do not see UAFR zones being reduced or removed.
The Association appreciates the difficulty the FAA faces in balancing the optimal use of the
nation’s airspace with the protection of important utility infrastructure but urges the FAA to
recognize that broad eligibility for UAFRs for water and wastewater utilities is essential to the
provision of public water and sewer service nationwide.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments. Please feel free to contact me with
any questions.
Sincerely,
Christopher Pomeroy
General Counsel
Copy by email to:
VMDWA Board

RE: Docket Number FAA-2026-4558

The City of Chandler respectfully submits the following comments regarding the proposed FAA rule to restrict the operation of Unmanned Aircraft in close proximity to a fixed site facility.

As the City of Innovation, Chandler has long embraced emerging technologies to improve public service, community safety, and our resident’s quality of life. We fully support measures that aim to protect critical infrastructure and enhance aviation safety. However, it is imperative that restrictions do not unintentionally impede time-sensitive public safety operations by adding layers of approval to the authorization aviation process. Under current practice, Chandler Police and Fire operate drones under 14 CFR Part 107, with strict adherence to FAA safety requirements.

Drones have become an invaluable tool for Chandler Police and Chandler Fire that improve situational awareness, reduce risk to first responders, and ultimately save and preserve lives. The deployment of drones during high-priority critical incidents help provide intel on active emergency calls such as suspect searches, vehicle pursuits, active shooters, violent crimes, structural fires, hazardous incidents, and rescue operations. Routinely, drones are the first deployed resource providing real-time intel that directly supports safety for officers, first responders, and suspects.

Chandler first responders rely on immediate drone authorization and deployment without any burdensome administrative delay. The proposed restrictions near critical infrastructure may inadvertently create administrative delays in obtaining necessary airspace authorization under 14 CFR Part 107. Even a short administrative delay of a minute could then impact life-saving measures and pose a serious risk to first responders and residents.

The City of Chandler respectfully requests that agencies currently operating under 14 CFR part 107, maintain uninterrupted, seamless, and rapid access to the airspace necessary for emergency drone operations. Any future restrictions should prioritize preserving the current status quo and ability for first responders to deploy and operate drones during time-sensitive incidents.

Thank you for your consideration in advancing safety for both public safety and aviation.

I am writing to oppose the proposed restriction on drone flights over “fixed site facilities,” as currently drafted, because its vague scope could sweep in industrial animal agriculture operations and other privately-held sites that have a significant impact on public health, animal welfare, and the environment. Aerial observation from public airspace has become an important tool for journalists, whistleblowers, and concerned citizens to document conditions at facilities that are otherwise closed off from public view. Restricting this ability does not just protect legitimate security interests — it also removes one of the few independent ways the public can verify claims made by facility operators about their own practices. I urge the FAA to narrow the definition of “fixed site facilities” so that it targets genuine security-sensitive infrastructure (e.g., airports, power plants, government buildings) rather than functioning as a blanket shield for private industry from public scrutiny. Transparency and accountability should be weighed alongside safety and security when finalizing this rule.

I am writing to express strong opposition to the Federal Aviation Administration's proposed rule, "Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility," published under Regulations.gov Docket FAA-2026-4558. While protecting critical infrastructure is a legitimate safety priority, establishing Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) across potentially tens of thousands of fixed-site facilities in 16 broad industry sectors will balkanize low-altitude airspace below 400 feet AGL. By granting broad authority to restrict public airspace over extensive property footprints, this proposal creates a fragmented regulatory patchwork that severely impedes lawful commercial drone operators who rely on predictable flight corridors for infrastructure inspection, precision agriculture, and aerial transit.

Furthermore, the proposed rule’s mandatory site-manager notification requirements and strict operational limits—such as requiring transit in the "shortest amount of time practicable" and limiting non-transitory flight—disproportionately burden vetted, Remote ID-compliant commercial pilots while doing little to stop non-compliant or malicious actors who willfully disregard airspace designations. The agency's regulatory analysis acknowledges substantial compliance costs for applicants and operators but fails to demonstrate that virtual restrictions effectively mitigate airborne security threats. Rather than fostering the safe integration of unmanned aircraft into the National Airspace System, this framework introduces excessive operational friction and economic harm to the domestic drone industry. The FAA should instead maintain public right-of-transit in navigable airspace and rely on narrow, site-specific safety evaluations rather than establishing an overly broad airspace restriction mechanism.

This rule would let the largest, most powerful factory farms in the country ban drones from flying anywhere near their facilities. It's being sold as a safety measure. It is not. There is no documented case of a drone harming a person, an animal, or a piece of equipment at one of these facilities in the US. What drones have done is expose the repeated lies, cruelty, and pollution companies would rather keep hidden.

In one case, drone footage from a number of Pennsylvania egg facilities helped prove a company's "free roaming" hens had no real outdoor access at all — evidence that led to a $287,500 settlement in a federal consumer protection case. That kind of accountability only happened because the airspace over that facility was still open.

If this rule passes, such investigations could become impossible. No more aerial footage exposing false marketing claims. No more evidence of manure lagoons breaching after a hurricane. No more documentation of mass culling during a bird flu outbreak. No more way to check a company's story against reality. The bigger and more damaging the facility, the more protection it would get.
If you’re trying to hide something from the public, you probably shouldn’t be doing it.

comments.comment_text: International Bridge, Tunnel and Turnpike Association’s (IBTTA) Response to Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility

August 4, 2026
Docket Operations, M-30
U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT)
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Washington, DC 20590-0001
RE: Comment on the Federal Aviation Administration’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
– Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
(Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03)
To Whom It May Concern,
I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA)
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) concerning the establishment of Unmanned
Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) around certain fixed-site facilities. I am pleased to
see the FAA implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act
of 2016 and taking an important step toward closing a longstanding safety and security
gap through the establishment of a framework to protect eligible critical infrastructure
from unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations.
Recent conflicts have demonstrated the increasing role of low-cost Unmanned Aircraft
Systems (UAS) in surveillance and attacks against critical infrastructure, underscoring
the importance of ensuring that the final rule provides appropriate protections for
facilities facing credible security threats. While I support the overall approach proposed
in the NPRM, I believe there are several areas where the rule could be strengthened to
better address evolving security risks while remaining consistent with the FAA's
responsibility to preserve the efficient use of the National Airspace System.
Section 74.58(b)(1) – Lateral Boundary of UAFRs
Proposed § 74.58(b)(1) limits the lateral boundary of a UAFR to the property boundary
of the requesting fixed-site facility. While this approach is appropriate for most facilities,
it may unnecessarily limit the effectiveness of Special UAFRs established to address
credible national security or homeland security threats.
The NPRM explains that one of the primary benefits of a UAFR is enabling facility
operators and law enforcement to distinguish compliant aircraft from unauthorized
aircraft so they may focus resources on genuinely suspicious activity. That objective is
partially undermined if an unauthorized aircraft may lawfully approach immediately
adjacent to the facility before entering the Special UAFR.
Certain sensitive facilities may require additional stand-off distance to provide security
personnel sufficient time to detect, assess, and respond to unauthorized UAS activity.

This concern is particularly relevant where critical assets are visible or vulnerable
immediately beyond the property boundary.
I recommend that the FAA provide a limited exception allowing applicants for a Special
UAFR to request lateral boundaries extending beyond the property boundary when
justified by a facility-specific security assessment. Such requests should require the
applicant to demonstrate why the expanded boundary is necessary, identify the assets
requiring additional protection, and provide supporting analysis showing that the
requested dimensions are appropriately tailored to the identified threat.
Section 74.58(b)(2) – Overlap with Existing Airspace Restrictions
The NPRM preamble states that a UAFR may not overlap with an existing permanent
airspace restriction because such overlap "would be unnecessary and redundant."
While this rationale is appropriate in many circumstances, there are instances in which
overlapping protections may be warranted.
Some fixed-site facilities are located within permanent airspace restrictions that are not
continuously active. Although the restricted area is charted, the operational restrictions
associated with that airspace may only apply during certain activities or time periods.
Outside of those periods, unmanned aircraft may be permitted to operate in close
proximity to the facility even though the underlying security concerns remain.
In these situations, prohibiting overlap between a UAFR and an existing airspace
restriction may create an unintended gap in protection. While airspace restrictions are
often established to protect aircraft from hazardous activities or to protect those
activities from aircraft during periods of operation, a UAFR is intended to continuously
address safety and security associated with unauthorized UAS operations.
I recommend that the FAA revise § 74.58(b)(2) to permit overlap between a UAFR and
an existing permanent airspace restriction when the applicant demonstrates that the
overlap is necessary to address a continuing safety and/or security concern that is not
fully addressed by the existing airspace restriction. Such requests should remain
subject to the FAA's existing evaluation process and require the applicant to
demonstrate why overlapping protections are necessary.
Section 74.95 – Transportation Systems Sector (Commercial Spaceports)
The NPRM explains that commercial spaceports are adequately addressed through the
existing launch and reentry regulatory framework. While those regulations establish
comprehensive safety and security requirements for licensed launch site operations,
they are not intended to provide a persistent mechanism for restricting UAS in the
vicinity of a commercial spaceport outside of launch-related activities. As a result,

commercial spaceports remain vulnerable to unauthorized UAS surveillance or other
malicious activity during routine operations.
Commercial spaceports contain infrastructure that may be attractive targets for
malicious UAS activity even when launch operations are not occurring. Fuel storage
areas, hazardous materials, launch support equipment, communications infrastructure,
and other critical assets remain vulnerable to unauthorized surveillance or deliberate
attack outside active launch periods. A regulatory gap exists between launch-specific
protections and persistent UAS security concerns.
The NPRM recognizes throughout its discussion of critical infrastructure that unmanned
aircraft may be used not only to conduct physical attacks, but also to perform
surveillance of sensitive facilities in preparation for future malicious activity. Commercial
spaceports present many of these same vulnerabilities and therefore warrant
consideration alongside other transportation-sector facilities.
I recommend that the FAA add commercial spaceports as an eligible facility type under
proposed § 74.95, Transportation Systems Sector. Applicants should remain subject to
the same demonstration of need and risk analysis required of other applicants under the
proposed rule.
Respectfully Submitted,
Pete Frank

comments.comment_text:
SUBMITTED VIA REGULATIONS.GOV
DOCKET NO. FAA-2026-4558 August 4, 2026
Sean Duffy
Secretary
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue, SE
Washington, DC 20590
Bryan Bedford
Administrator
Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue, SW
Washington, DC 20591
Re: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03 / 26-03A; RIN 2120-
AL33; 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (May 6, 2026)
Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford,
Strategies for Ethical and Environmental Development (SEED) appreciates the opportunity to
comment on the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) proposed rule that would allow fixed
site facilities to obtain unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs) under proposed 14 C.F.R.
Part 74 (the Proposed Rule).1
SEED is 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization dedicated to creating an equitable and environmentally
sound future for animals, people, and the planet by advocating against the negative impacts of
industrial animal agriculture. Producing photographic and video evidence of the conditions on
and within animal agriculture facilities, including that obtained by drone, is an essential
component of our work. SEED regularly uses aerial photography (obtained lawfully via a Part
107 licensed operator who is required, as part of his employment, to follow all federal and state
laws and regulations) to (i) document evidence of potential discharges from farms in violation of
federal clean water and other environmental statutes, to (ii) verify producer marketing claims,
and to (iii) document animal treatment and welfare. In addition, SEED’s drone footage has been
utilized by several allied and partner nonprofits to further their public education and advocacy
goals.
As an animal and environmental advocacy nonprofit, SEED’s comments on the proposed rule
address a single question: whether facilities within the food and agriculture sector should be
eligible for UAFRs. They should not.
The FAA has correctly framed airspace restriction as an extraordinary remedy, available only
where an applicant demonstrates an important need arising from safety, protection of persons and
1 Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility, 91 Fed.
Reg. 24650 (proposed May 6, 2026) (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. pt. 74).

property on the ground, national security, or homeland security. Measured against that standard,
the record in this docket contains no evidence that unmanned aircraft have caused such harm at
an animal agriculture facility anywhere in the U.S. The industry commenters who urge the FAA
to extend UAFR eligibility to farms, feedyards, and slaughter facilities have collectively failed to
identify a single documented incident of a drone injuring a person, an animal, or a piece of
equipment at these facilities.
What they have identified is conduct they wish to stop, which is photography and videography of
their operations by journalists, advocates, and members of the public. That is not a safety
interest. It is a preference for secrecy, and the First Amendment does not permit a federal agency
to convert it into an airspace restriction.
The Proposed Rule would take a technology that has become one of the last means of
independent observation of industrial animal agriculture operations and condition its use at the
discretion of the facilities being observed. Public interest in these facilities is increasing, driven
by avian influenza and other zoonotic disease events, by recurring surface water contamination
from manure mismanagement, by intense water-usage during a time of severe drought, by
federal consumer-protection litigation over animal-welfare marketing claims, and by growing
concern over foreign ownership of American agricultural land. Reduced visibility at precisely
this moment serves no governmental interest identified by the FAA.
SEED respectfully urges the FAA to decline to establish eligibility criteria for the Food and
Agriculture Sector under the Proposed Rule, and to state expressly in the final rule that a UAFR
designation does not restrict lawful aerial documentation for journalistic, environmental, public
health, or animal welfare purposes, for the reasons articulated below.
Three comments in this docket address matters SEED does not repeat here. The joint comment of
FarmSTAND, We Animals, and Animal Outlook (FarmSTAND, et al.) (FAA-2026-4558-0596)
documents the photojournalistic record; the comment of the National Press Photographers
Association (NPPA) (FAA-2026-4558-0603) addresses procedural safeguards applicable to all
sectors; and the joint comment of the ACLU, CDT, EFF, and EPIC (ACLU, et al.) (FAA-2026-
4558-0568) addresses the cumulative effect of restrictions across the sixteen eligible sectors.
SEED adopts and endorses those comments and, where it relies on them below, cites them rather
than restating them.
I. There is No Present Safety or Security Risk at Animal Agriculture Facilities
a. The FAA’s standards for eligibility describe demonstrated need, not industry
preference
The notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) states that restricting airspace is an extraordinary
remedy, to be applied only when necessary, and that UAFR eligibility must be limited in order to
balance the safety and security concerns Congress identified against the national policy
objectives of preserving the public right of transit, maintaining airspace efficiency, and
integrating unmanned aircraft into the National Airspace System. Facilities meeting sector
criteria must additionally demonstrate that an important need justifies the remedy of restricting
airspace.
2

That framing is correct and creates an important distinction. The question is not whether animal
agriculture is economically significant, or whether the sector appears on a federal critical-
infrastructure list. The question is whether unmanned aircraft present a demonstrated safety or
security threat to these facilities such that closing the airspace above them is necessary. On the
record before the FAA, they do not.
The absence of supporting evidence is not an oversight by these commenters but instead reflects
an underlying reality. Aerial observation of open-air facilities is among the least intrusive forms
of information-gathering available. It involves no physical entry, no contact with animals, no
interaction with personnel, and no interference with equipment. The activity the industry seeks to
prohibit is, in operational terms, someone taking a photograph from public airspace.
b. The FAA’s own examples exclude agriculture entirely
In the “Statement of the Problem” section of the NPRM, the Agency catalogs the incidents
motivating this rulemaking process. Those examples involve oil refineries, an attack on an
electrical substation, chemical facilities, pipelines, and the use of drones to deliver contraband
into correctional institutions. Not one involves an agricultural facility. In fact, with regard to the
food and agriculture sector, the NPRM states that the “FAA … could not identify a facility in
this sector that was not already captured by another sector or would rise to the level of national
level debilitating impact.” Nor has the FAA developed criteria for determining whether food and
agriculture facilities qualify as eligible under the Proposed Rule.2
Here, the FAA has assembled the strongest available record of drone-related harm to critical
infrastructure facilities, and that record contains no agricultural incidents. The reason is not that
the FAA overlooked the sector, as the NPRM expressly lists Food and Agriculture as a sector for
which criteria may be developed. The reason is that the incidents do not exist, or are so rare that
their reference poses no meaningful support for the Proposed Rule.
The distinction between the facilities within the FAA’s record drone-related incidents list and the
animal agriculture facilities seeking eligibility is significant. A refinery presents catastrophic
ignition risk. A substation presents cascading grid failure risk. A correctional facility presents a
contraband-delivery method unique to drones. Each involves a mechanism by which a small
aircraft can produce disproportionate physical harm. A barn complex, a feedyard, or a manure
lagoon presents no comparable mechanism, and no commenter in this docket has identified one
that withstands even superficial examination.
c. The supporting comments confirm, rather than cure, the absence of evidence
Several animal agriculture stakeholders have filed comments in support of extending UAFR
eligibility to their sector as of August 4, 2026. Their submissions are worth examining closely,
because taken together they demonstrate that the industry cannot articulate a safety or security
rationale independent of its objection to being observed.
1. Biosecurity and disease transmission. The U.S. Poultry & Egg Association asserts that drones
may act as mechanical vectors, carrying viral particles on hulls and propellers onto clean farm
perimeters, and further contends that low-altitude drone operations can panic wild migratory
2 Id. at 24669.
3

waterfowl and drive them into contact with poultry facilities.3 The National Pork Producers
Council (NPPC) advances a parallel theory keyed to African Swine Fever.4 The Delmarva
Chicken Association (DCA),5 the North Carolina Poultry Federation (NCPF),6 the Sonoma
County Farm Bureau (SCFB),7 and the California Cattlemen’s Association (CCA)8 raise
variations on the same claim.
No commenter cites a single instance in which a drone transmitted disease to a livestock or
poultry operation anywhere in the world. This theory is offered without epidemiological support,
without any estimate of pathogen survival on an airframe, and without explanation of how a
drone operating at documentation altitude would deposit material on a facility at all. The
waterfowl-flushing theory is entirely unsupported by research and disintegrates under surface-
level inspection. If startling wild birds into contact with poultry houses were a genuine
transmission pathway, the same objection would apply to crop dusters, farm vehicles, hunters,
weather events, and the industry’s own use of agricultural drones, which many of these
commenters expressly wish to preserve.
Most tellingly, the United Dairymen of Arizona, writing in support of the rule, concedes that
drones “may not directly transmit disease,” and pivots instead to surveillance of facility layouts.9
That concession is the more accurate statement of the science and cannot be reconciled with the
biosecurity “concerns” the rest of the sector attempts to rely on.
Industry commenters simultaneously assert that third-party drones are a biosecurity hazard and
that their own drones (and those of their contractors) must remain free to operate over the same
facilities. A pathogen cannot distinguish between an airframe operated by a producer and one
operated by a journalist. If the biosecurity theory were a real threat, it would require restricting
the industry’s own operations, especially that of farm contractors, who often utilize the same
drones in surveying multiple facilities. That the industry wishes to retain the use of its own
drones establishes that biosecurity is not an actual concern.
Existing rules already govern proximity. Part 107 prohibits careless and reckless operation and
operation over people in certain categories, and the FAA has consistently applied its authority to
operations that harass or endanger. Operators may not approach people, animals, or equipment in
a manner that creates risk. The conduct the industry describes (low, aggressive flight near
animals and workers) is already prohibited. The conduct it actually seeks to prohibit (high,
stable, distant flight) presents no contact risk at all.
Drone operators observing farm conditions fly at altitude by necessity. Operators engaged in
journalism and advocacy have strong practical incentives to avoid disturbance. Disturbed
animals produce unusable footage and expose the operator to allegations of harassment,
certificate action, and civil claims. These operators, including SEED’s certified drone operator,
3 Comments of the U.S. Poultry & Egg Assn., Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0591 at 2.
4 Comments of the National Pork Producers Council, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0565 at 3.
5 Comments of the Delmarva Chicken Assn., Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0551 at 1.
6 Comments of the North Carolina Poultry Federation, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0549 at 1.
7 Comments of the Sonoma County Farm Bureau, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-1357 at 2.
8 Comments of the California Cattlemen’s Assn., Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0571 at 1.
9 Comments of the United Dairymen of Arizona, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0599.
4

work in an environment of intense industry scrutiny and legal risk where they cannot afford the
conduct they are accused of.
Finally, biosecurity concerns actually run in the opposite direction. Independent aerial
observation has repeatedly provided earlier and more complete public information about disease
events than operator self-reporting. If “biosecurity” becomes an accepted justification for
airspace closure without evidence of drone-related transmission, the practical effect will be to
reduce public visibility into disease response when it matters most.
2. Depopulation footage and market consequences. The U.S. Poultry & Egg Association
identifies drone footage of flock depopulation as potentially causing market devastation, trade
impacts, and supply chain vulnerability.10
The asserted harm here is not physical damage, safety, or security, but is instead the market and
reputational consequences of public disclosure about what happens at these facilities during a
disease event. Reputational and commercial injury flowing from truthful documentation is not a
safety or security risk within the meaning of Section 2209,11 and an agency may not restrict
speech in order to prevent the public from reacting to information about a matter of public
concern. Depopulation events during avian influenza or other disease outbreaks are matters of
substantial public interest. They involve federal insurance payouts, consumer price effects, and
animal welfare questions on a mass scale. The public’s interest in observing them is at its highest
precisely when the industry’s interest in concealing them is also at its highest.
3. “Weaponization” of aerial footage. The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association (NCBA)
asserts that public activists abuse drone technology, using intelligence gained as a “weapon”
against farms and ranches.12
NCBA offers no explanation of how aerial footage is “weaponized.” At its essence, this claim is
reduced to the simple complaint that the lawful documentation of agricultural operations may
result in regulatory complaints, litigation, media coverage, or consumer disapproval. Each of
those is a lawful civic consequence of truthful information reaching the public. A regulation
preventing citizens from generating information because officials or private parties may act on it
is not a valid safety measure.
4. The Fourth Amendment and state environmental inspection. NCBA argues that farm and
ranch operations should be treated as constitutionally protected curtilage, and that a state’s
authority to inspect property under the Clean Water Act should be exercised through on-site
review rather than aerial observation.13
This argument is foreclosed by settled law, and the FAA should reject it firmly. The curtilage
doctrine protects the area immediately surrounding a dwelling. It has never extended to
commercial agricultural operations spanning hundreds of acres. The Supreme Court has
reaffirmed the open fields doctrine, holding that open fields are not protected by the Fourth
Amendment and that curtilage is limited to the area to which the intimate activity associated with
10 U.S. Poultry & Egg Assn. Comments, Supra note 4.
11 FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209, 130 Stat. 615, 625 (codified at 49
U.S.C. § 40101 note).
12 Comments of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Assn., Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0573 at 1.
13 Id. at 2.
5

the sanctity of a home extends.14 The Supreme Court has also held that naked-eye aerial
observation from navigable airspace is not a search,15 and specifically, that EPA’s aerial
photography of a large industrial complex from navigable airspace was not a Fourth Amendment
search, reasoning that the open areas of an industrial plant complex are more comparable to open
fields than to the curtilage of a dwelling.16
NCBA thus asks the FAA to use its airspace authority to accomplish what the Fourth
Amendment does not require and what the Supreme Court has expressly declined to hold. Worse,
NCBA asks the FAA to do so for the stated purpose of insulating its members from “burdensome
liability and litigation.” An agency may not restrict a regulator or citizen’s ability to observe a
facility in order to reduce the facility’s exposure to enforcement of environmental or other laws
and regulations. That is not a security rationale, but a request that the FAA obstruct enforcement
of the Clean Water Act.
Notably, NCBA’s position is not shared by the state agriculture regulators who filed in support
of the rule. The Kentucky Department of Agriculture (KDA) expressly asks the FAA to preserve
exemptions for governmental inspections within any UAFR.17 The FAA should not adopt a
restriction on drone use that one supporting commenter demands and another supporting
commenter assumes will not apply.
5. “Aerial trespassing” and violent threat. NCBA characterizes drone overflight as aerial
trespassing and asserts that failing to adopt the rule would open the door for bad actors to
commit crimes, including releasing, injuring, or burglarizing livestock.18 CCA extends this
further, speculating that activists could use drones to intentionally drive livestock through
fencelines, and that criminals or terrorists could employ the same tactic to cause mayhem,
destruction, injuries, and deaths.19 NPPC devotes a substantial portion of its submitted comments
to assembling a history of animal-rights criminal extremism, including FBI testimony from 2004,
a study of arsons and bombings occurring between 1995 and 2010, a 2012 feedlot arson, and
various physical intrusions, and argues that drone documentation is the technological
continuation of that pattern.20
First, navigable airspace is subject to the exclusive sovereignty of the United States and a public
right of transit under 49 U.S.C. § 40103(a), and no federal cause of action for "aerial trespass"
exists in navigable airspace. Congress has vested the FAA with authority over navigable airspace
precisely because it is a public resource.21
Second, every incident cataloged by NPPC involves conduct that is already a serious crime
(arson, burglary, theft, breaking and entering, and property destruction) and none of it was
accomplished by drone. The Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act, state trespass and theft statutes,
federal arson law, and ordinary criminal enforcement all address the named conduct. There is no
relevance of a 20-year-old statement about physical intrusions, or of data that ends in 2010 (years
14 Oliver v. United States, 466 U.S. 170, 176, 180 (1984).
15 California v. Ciraolo, 476 U.S. 207, 213 (1986).
16 Dow Chemical Co. v. United States, 476 U.S. 227, 239 (1986).
17 Comments of the Kentucky Dept. of Agriculture, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0558 at 4.
18 NCBA Comments, Supra note 13, at 2.
19 CCA Comments, Supra note 9, at 2.
20 NPPC Comments, Supra note 5, at 4.
21 49 U.S.C. § 40103(a).
6

before consumer drones were commercially available), to a 2026 rulemaking proposal about
aerial photography. The argument’s structure is essentially that “some people who oppose our
industry have committed crimes, and some people who oppose our industry take photographs,
and therefore photography should be restricted.” That argument does not reach the safety and
security thresholds required to establish eligibility for a UAFR.
The potential scenarios depicted by the industry are purely speculative and deserve no weight.
CCA’s suggestion that activists might herd cattle through fences with drones is not supported by
a single documented instance. Its wildfire theory, that a lithium battery might ignite over
rangeland, rests on an FAA safety alert concerning the transport of lithium batteries as cargo
aboard manned aircraft, which is a materially different context, and identifies no rangeland fire
ever caused by a drone battery. Rulemaking on the basis of harms that have never occurred,
proposed by parties with a clear interest in the outcome, serves no legitimate governmental
interest in safety or security.
Finally, this argument is an explicit request for viewpoint-based restriction. NPPC and NCBA do
not ask the FAA to restrict all overflight. They ask it to restrict overflight by people whose
message they oppose, while preserving overflight by owners, producers, contractors, and
commercial operators. An agency that grants a restriction on that basis has not made a valid
safety or security judgment.
6. Animal stress and welfare. NCBA asserts that drone use raises serious concerns regarding
cattle safety and welfare, structural damage, and emergency management.22 CCA cites research
on livestock stress responses and claims that cattle may mistake drones for predatory birds, with
downstream effects on pregnancies, weight gain, and body condition.23 Grimmius Cattle
Company reports that a neighboring operation experienced a drone-triggered stampede in which
cattle were injured.24 The American Horse Council raises analogous concerns for equine
facilities, noting horses’ instinctive flight response.25
First, claims of concern over animal welfare are difficult to credit from an industry whose
confinement practices and animal neglect and mistreatment are the very subject the

V. Journalists, Advocates, and Members of the Public Who Gather Footage of
Animal Agriculture Facilities Are Engaged in Protected First Amendment
Activity
a. Creating photographic and video recordings of matters of public concern is
protected speech, including via drone
Federal courts have held that publication or disclosure of information is speech within the
meaning of the First Amendment.65 The federal courts of appeals have applied that principle
directly to recording. For example, the Ninth Circuit has explained that the act of making an
audio or audiovisual recording is necessarily included within the First Amendment’s guarantee
of speech and press rights, because the right to publish a recording would be largely ineffective if
the antecedent act of making it were unprotected.66
This principle has been applied to agricultural facilities specifically and repeatedly by federal
courts, as pointed out by FarmSTAND et al. in its comments.67 The pattern in these cases is
instructive and directly relevant here. Legislatures, at the urging of the same industry now before
the Agency, have repeatedly attempted to restrict documentation of animal agriculture facilities.
Courts have repeatedly held those restrictions unconstitutional. The present proposal would
accomplish through federal airspace regulation what those statutes could not accomplish through
state criminal law.
b. The restriction is content- and speaker-based as applied to the food and
agriculture sector
A UAFR granted to an animal agriculture facility would not operate as a neutral regulation of
airspace. By the express design of the Proposed Rule and the express request of its supporters,
agricultural producers, their contractors, and authorized commercial operators would still be
permitted to engage in drone operations. Only unauthorized operators (a category that in practice
means journalists, advocates, researchers, and members of the public) would be excluded.
That is speaker-based discrimination, and the supporting comments make the underlying content
preference explicit. DCA objects to footage gathered for investigations, documentaries, and
media campaigns.68 NCBA objects to footage used against farms and ranches.69 NPPC objects to
documentation by organizations it associates with an ideological movement.70 The distinction
being made is thus not between safe and unsafe flight, but between those who disagree with and
may publicize the resulting footage, and those who agree with it and will not.
Regulations that draw lines based on the message or the identity of the speaker are subject to
strict scrutiny, notwithstanding the government’s motive behind restricting said speech or

c. Even under intermediate scrutiny, the restriction fails
Assuming for the purposes of argument that a UAFR is content- and viewpoint-neutral, a time,
place, and manner restriction must serve a significant governmental interest, be narrowly
tailored, and leave open alternative channels of communication.72 None of these elements is
satisfied here either.
There is no significant governmental interest because there is no demonstrated harm. As set out
in Part I, no commenter has identified a single documented incident of drone-caused injury or
damage at an animal agriculture facility in the United States. An agency may not curtail speech
on the basis of speculation and conjecture; it must demonstrate that the harms it recites are real
and that the restriction will alleviate them in a material way.73
Nor is the restriction narrowly tailored. Drone operators who work for organizations like SEED
collect images and conduct newsgathering as part of their public advocacy and are expected to
follow all laws and regulations. These operators must obtain all licensing credentials required by
the FAA for commercial drone operation and are expected to operate in accordance with all FAA
and other federal and state rules as a requirement of their employment. Operators who fly
recklessly, at unsafe altitudes, beyond visual line of sight, or at night without certification,
present significant legal, operational, and reputational risks to these organizations. There is no
benefit to SEED in allowing reckless or unsafe flight, and allowing a drone operator to
negatively impact animal stress or welfare would violate its stated goals.
Either way, reckless and unsafe drone use is already prohibited; the FAA already has the tools
necessary to enforce against operators who violate Part 107. Closing the airspace to all
observation in order to reach a subset of hypothetical bad actors burdens substantially more
speech than is necessary, especially where no documented security risks have been identified
warranting such a severe restriction.
