The advance-notice requirement is also problematic. It requires a journalist to notify the subject
of the investigation, in advance, of the time and place of the newsgathering. No comparable
requirement exists anywhere in U.S. law, and its practical effect is the concealment of the site’s
potential violations before the drone operator even arrives. A notice requirement that permits the
subject of documentation to prepare for it does not preserve newsgathering; it defeats First
Amendment activity while appearing to accommodate it.
The requirement also functions as a licensing scheme administered by a private party with an
interest adverse to the speaker. Schemes vesting officials, much less interested private parties,
with discretion over First Amendment expressive activity, without narrow and objective
standards, are constitutionally suspect.74
Two additional burdens arise from the notice requirement. First, compelled disclosure of identity
and reporting plans, requiring an operator gathering information of public concern to disclose
their identity and planned activity directly to the facility being reported on, burdens anonymous
speech and associated privacy, and compromises confidential newsgathering. The Supreme
Court has protected anonymity in expressive activity,75 and the interest is at its strongest where
disclosure runs to a private party with reason to retaliate (via litigation, complaints against the
operator’s certificate, or otherwise). The FAA should not require journalists to identify
themselves to the subject of their reporting as a condition of lawful flight. SEED joins NPPA's
request that no waiver, authorization, exemption, or reconsideration procedure adopted under this
rule require journalists to disclose confidential reporting plans, sources, unpublished material, or
the anticipated content of future reporting. In the agricultural context that protection is not
abstract. An operator seeking authorization to document a facility would be disclosing the target
of an investigation to an agency that the facility's trade associations actively lobby, in a sector
whose comments in this very docket ask the FAA to distinguish operators by their intent rather
than their airmanship. The disclosure risk here runs in a specific and identifiable direction.
Advance notice also impedes documentation of breaking news or unfolding events. Lagoon
breaches during storms, fires, depopulation operations, and mass mortality events are not
scheduled, and a notice requirement attached to routine operations excludes reporting
specifically when public concern is heightened.
e. Granting UAFRs as proposed would confer a monopoly on aerial imagery of
the facilities in question
Under the Proposed Rule, owners, operators, and their contractors would retain access to drone
use while independent operators would not, meaning that a UAFR would not eliminate aerial
photography of a facility, but instead vests within said facility the exclusive ability to conduct it.
The consequence is that the only aerial imagery of these operations available to the public would
be imagery the facility itself chose to produce and release. In a sector where marketing materials
depict spacious and bucolic conditions and environmental sustainability, and where aerial
74 City of Lakewood v. Plain Dealer Publishing Co., 486 U.S. 750 (1988); Freedman v. Maryland, 380 U.S. 51
(1965); Larkin v. Grendel's Den, 459 U.S. 116, 122 (1982).
75 McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission, 514 U.S. 334 (1995); Talley v. California, 362 U.S. 60 (1960).
18

documentation has repeatedly proven otherwise, a government-conferred monopoly on drone use
is not a neutral security measure.
f. The chilling effect is concrete, not theoretical
Once a UAFR issues, unauthorized operation within it exposes the operator to civil sanctions and
potential certificate action. For working photojournalists and small nonprofit organizations, that
exposure is prohibitive. Advocacy organizations like SEED already refrain from lawful
recording of agricultural facilities where “ag-gag” laws have been passed, including laws later
held unconstitutional as violative of the First Amendment. Deterrence of protected activity by
threat of sanction is a cognizable First Amendment injury independent of any enforcement action
ever being brought.76
g. The retaliatory history requires caution
The animal agriculture industry has a documented record of attempting to penalize
documentation of its treatment of animals, its environmental compliance, and its operations as a
whole. “Ag-gag” statutes have been enacted and struck down across multiple jurisdictions. The
FAA should evaluate the present request against that history and recognize it as the latest
instrument in a sustained effort to foreclose observation and chill protected activity.
VI. Procedural Safeguards Must Be Written into the Rule Itself, Should the FAA
Proceed
Should the FAA retain food and agriculture sector eligibility over the objections set out above,
the safeguards that would constrain its use must appear in the regulatory text rather than being
left to future agency discretion. Comments filed in this docket by press-freedom and civil
liberties organizations (NPPA, ACLU et al.) identify structural deficiencies in the proposed
process that would bear directly on agricultural applications, and we adopt and endorse them
here.
a. The application process is one-sided as designed
NPPA identifies the structural defect in the application process: the FAA will have evaluated
need and impacts at the conditional-approval stage and will not revisit that determination de
novo after comment. SEED will not restate that analysis. What the FAA should note is what this
defect means for this sector specifically.
An agricultural UAFR application will assert facts about drone activity at a particular facility
(that activists have overflown it, that animals were disturbed, that biosecurity was compromised,
etc.). The parties in a position to test those assertions are the neighboring residents who live
downwind of the facility, the downstream water users, the state environmental regulators who
inspect it, and the journalists and organizations alleged to have caused the harm. None of them is
heard. The applicant's account of an incident at its own facility will stand unrebutted in the
administrative record, and the FAA will have made its need determination before anyone with
contrary knowledge learns the application exists.
76 Reno v. ACLU, 521 U.S. 844, 871 (1997).
19

That is a particular problem here because, as Part I demonstrates, the sector's public submissions
in this docket already contain unverified secondhand incident accounts, mischaracterized
research, and threat catalogs unconnected to drones. There is no reason to expect confidential
applications to be more rigorous, and every reason to expect them to be less. SEED therefore
urges the FAA to require public notice and a meaningful opportunity for comment before
approval, and to replace rolling application acceptance with periodic windows.
b. Designations must be publicly identifiable
Comments from NPPA and ACLU et al. both urge the FAA to establish a publicly searchable
database of designations. SEED endorses that request and adds one sector-specific reason for it:
agricultural UAFRs will cluster geographically. Poultry production in the Delmarva peninsula,
hog production in eastern North Carolina, dairy in the Central Valley and central Arizona, and
cattle feeding in the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles are each concentrated in a small number of
counties. A rolling, unpublished designation process in those regions will not produce a scattered
patchwork; it will produce contiguous regional exclusion zones, assembled one facility at a time,
with no point at which the cumulative effect is ever assessed. Only a public database makes that
visible before it is complete.
Compliance cannot depend on locating scattered Federal Register notices and agency advisories.
If the FAA moves forward with the Proposed Rule, SEED urges the Agency to establish a
federal public database for approved UAFRs identifying the facility, exact aerial boundary,
length of time, expiration, renewal, and the publicly releasable portion of the FAA’s findings.
c. Applicants must show that a restriction would actually work
The Proposed Rule requires applicants to describe vulnerabilities and the consequences of their
exploitation, and to explain how a UAFR would be integrated into existing security plans. It
should also require the applicant to demonstrate that the restriction would in fact ameliorate the
identified vulnerability.
SEED endorses NPPA's proposed findings requirement in full and does not restate it. SEED adds
one element specific to this sector: where an applicant's asserted vulnerability is that drone
imagery of its operations has generated or could generate adverse publicity, regulatory attention,
litigation, or consumer reaction, the FAA should state in its findings that it has identified that
assertion and given it no weight. At least sixteen supporting comments in this docket advance a
version of that claim. It will appear in applications, and it should be identified when it does.
The “threats” advanced by the supportive agricultural commenters (sabotage, contamination,
coordinated attack, theft) describe conduct that would not be prevented by a UAFR. Restrictions
bind compliant operators, not hypothetical malicious actors. Where the identified threat is one
that an airspace restriction cannot reach, the restriction imposes a burden without benefit, and the
applicant should be required to articulate how eligibility would reduce the threat risk.
VII. Conclusion and Requested Action
Permitting animal agriculture facilities to obtain UAFRs would eliminate a significant avenue of
public accountability and frustrate protected First Amendment activity while producing no
offsetting benefit to safety or security. The NPRM asks whether the share of the nation's meat,
milk, and eggs that a facility supplies should support eligibility. SEED's answer is that the
20

question is posed backwards: production share is a measure of how many people are affected by
what happens inside a facility, and therefore a measure of the public's interest in seeing it. Read
as the NPRM proposes, the criterion awards the strongest airspace protection to the facilities the
public has the greatest reason to observe.
Therefore, SEED respectfully requests that the FAA:
1. Decline to develop eligibility criteria for the food and agriculture sector under the
Proposed Rule. No comment in this docket identifies a documented incident of drone-
caused injury or damage at an animal agriculture facility in the United States, and a sector
that cannot produce one has not demonstrated the need the NPRM requires.
2. If the FAA nonetheless establishes eligibility for this sector, require each applicant to
demonstrate a specific and credible drone-related threat to its own facility, not
generalized sector concerns, not biosecurity assertions unsupported by transmission
evidence, and not the applicant's objection to being observed.
3. Preserve Part 107 operations within any granted UAFR without an advance-notice
requirement, so that notification cannot be used to anticipate and frustrate documentation.
4. Require enhanced public notice of agricultural UAFR applications, with meaningful
opportunity for comment by affected communities, journalists, and public interest
organizations, and publish the evidentiary basis for each grant.
5. State expressly in the final rule that a UAFR designation does not restrict lawful aerial
documentation conducted for journalistic, environmental, public health, or animal welfare
purposes, and does not limit federal, state, or local agency use of aerial observation in the
enforcement of environmental, food safety, or animal welfare law.
6. Require applicants to demonstrate that a restriction would actually mitigate the identified
vulnerability, not merely that a vulnerability exists and its exploitation would be serious.
7. Add the public interest in newsgathering and other First Amendment activity to the
factors the FAA weighs in evaluating an application, whether as an enumerated
consideration in the totality-of-the-circumstances review or as an externality under the
Proposed Rule, and recognize that journalism is among the uses protected by the public
right of transit.
8. Adopt the ACLU coalition's proposal to make the public interest in newsgathering an
express consideration in the totality-of-the-circumstances review, whether as an
enumerated factor or as an externality under the Proposed Rule. SEED adds that where
the applicant is an agricultural facility, the externality is measurable: the FAA can ask
what the facility has previously done to prevent ground-level observation of the same
conditions, since a facility already screened from roads and closed to visitors is asking
the airspace restriction to complete an existing information barrier rather than to address
a security gap.
9. Protect confidential newsgathering information from compelled disclosure in any waiver,
authorization, exemption, or reconsideration procedure adopted under this rule.

1. Executive Summary
Pierce Aerospace commends the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for its thorough,
well-structured, and visionary approach in Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) Docket No.
FAA-2026-4558 (14 CFR Part 74). By establishing a clear, standardized administrative
framework to implement Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016
(FESSA)—as amended by the FAA Reauthorization Acts of 2018 and 2024—the Agency
provides a crucial regulatory mechanism to protect national critical infrastructure while
preserving the public right of transit within the National Airspace System (NAS).
The FAA’s proposed rule directly aligns with the strategic objectives of Executive Order 14305,
Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty, and Executive Order 14307, Unleashing American
Drone Dominance. Together, these directives form a dual strategy: the "Sword" of domestic
commercial acceleration and the "Shield" of zero-trust low-altitude airspace security. Proposed
14 CFR Part 74 balances these mandates by establishing Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions
(UAFRs) while permitting authorized, vetted operators to transit restricted airspace.
Our public comment is anchored directly around the FAA’s explicit solicitation for empirical
evidence, technical data, and real-world feedback regarding Remote Identification (Remote ID)
power output, signal propagation, and receiver efficacy under proposed 14 CFR § 74.56.
Broadcast Remote ID under 14 CFR Part 89 serves as the baseline technical capability required
for fixed site facilities (FSFs) to establish airspace awareness, detect incoming aircraft, and
correlate authorized traffic.
Pierce Aerospace submits these comments as an experienced and operational contributor in
dual-use low-altitude airspace awareness, Remote ID tracking architectures, and Counter-UAS
(C-UAS) integrations. Having worked alongside the FAA, federal security agencies, the
Department of War (DoW), State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT) law enforcement, and
commercial enterprise operators, our perspective is grounded in Remote ID field testing,
operational deployment at scale, and rigorous engineering analysis.
A central finding of our empirical work is that Direct Broadcast Remote ID must continue as the
primary means of compliance for UAS, especially when considering the 2209 airspace security
mission. While Network Remote ID offers value as a supplementary, redundant data channel,
cellular-dependent networks introduce central single points of failure that make them unsuitable
as a primary surveillance mechanism for critical infrastructure protection. Direct Broadcast
Remote ID also paves the way for affordable and scalable electronic conspicuity, which is an
additional benefit that goes beyond 2209. Through ten years of experience in Remote ID
technology Pierce Aerospace remains consistent in its recommendations that Direct Broadcast
Remote ID be the primary means of compliance with Network Remote ID serving as a useful
supplement.

The OcuSync / Drone ID Technical Asymmetry
The footnote in the Remote ID Equation highlights a key market asymmetry. Proprietary
protocols—specifically DJI OcuSync / Drone ID—operate under higher-power FCC Part 15
digital transmission rules, broadcasting at power levels up to +33 dBm (2,000 mW) EIRP.

a limitation of open-standard physics, but an artifact of regulatory power restrictions. With
regulatory increases in broadcast power, Remote ID emitting drones can be seen just as easily
as DJI’s OcuSync / Drone ID emitting drones. The physics are proven.

Primary Compliance Standard: Broadcast vs. Network Remote ID
A core requirement for the success of Section 2209 UAFRs is absolute operational resilience.
Direct Broadcast Remote ID must serve as the primary means of compliance. Network Remote
ID provides useful supplementary and redundant information that can be correlated and fused
with Direct Broadcast Remote ID messages. Pierce Aerospace has supported this model for
years. The company can work with large fleet operators to synchronize APIs to whitelist
commercial UAS fleets over network connections. This provides an easy and effective way to
keep secure commercial and public-safety whitelists synchronized across networks while
remaining ready to detect those aircraft through Direct Broadcast Remote ID. Relying on
networks alone for primary critical infrastructure security introduces vulnerabilities and single
points of failure (SPOFs).
This vulnerability was underscored during the December 2020 bombing of an AT&T switching
facility in Nashville, Tennessee. The physical explosion disabled cellular networks, emergency
911 dispatch centers, and internet services across three states. The authors to this paper were
in Nashville when this bombing took place and saw the immediate loss of these networks
first-hand. Had airspace monitoring depended on Network Remote ID, entire regions would
have experienced a total air domain awareness blackout. Direct Broadcast Remote ID operates
as an independent, point-to-point RF architecture, ensuring continuous, uncompromised
visibility for law enforcement and critical infrastructure security even during major power grid
failures or cellular network disruptions. Direct Broadcast Remote ID technology and solutions
built with security in mind can continue to operate in degraded environments - as Pierce
Aerospace has successfully demonstrated with the DoW.

Consumer mobile devices, smartphones, and tablet computers already contained integrated

stakeholders. This was a good first step for Remote ID and it aligned very nicely with the low

cost and low power radio technology (dominated by Bluetooth and WiFi) already in mass use

adoption without reinventing the wheel or introducing economic burdens.
However, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth operate within unlicensed Industrial, Scientific, and Medical (ISM)
spectrum bands (2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz) governed by Federal Communications Commission
(FCC) Title 47 Part 15 rules and IEEE standards. These rules were originally promulgated to
regulate consumer electronics operating in close physical proximity to the human body—such
as desktop peripherals, handheld devices, and pocket-worn cellular phones. FCC Specific
Absorption Rate (SAR) limits and maximum permissible exposure (MPE) thresholds were
explicitly calculated to restrict RF radiation exposure to human tissue.
Applying consumer SAR-derived power limits to airborne uncrewed aircraft introduces a
fundamental technical disconnect that was exacerbated by the lack of a minimum power
requirement in Part 89. Drones fly tens, hundreds, or thousands of feet in the air and are far
removed from immediate human physical contact. Constraining airborne Remote ID transmitters
to radiation limits designed for pocket-worn devices artificially restricts their signal propagation
capabilities and significantly increases the cost of ground receivers designed to persistently
monitor the airspace for Remote ID emitting drones.
This regulatory friction created a stark technical asymmetry and market misunderstanding when
standard Remote ID broadcasts were compared to proprietary uncrewed aircraft Command and
Control (C2) links and proprietary tracking systems (about 20 times the power transmission for a
continuous video transmission link versus a transient RID broadcast message for most drones).
A notable example, as mentioned above, is DJI’s OcuSync protocol. It operates within the same
2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz frequency bands as Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, but it is classified as a digital
transmission system under higher-power FCC Part 15 rules - meaning it is following the same
physics, but with a regulator-approved higher power output because the IEEE standards and
FCC human exposure WiFi considerations were no longer taken into effect.
This allows OcuSync to utilize power amplification up to the full FCC ceiling of <33 dBm (2,000
mW) EIRP. This lets OcuSync deliver robust video and C2 links exceeding 6 to 12 miles.
Remote ID, not requiring a video or C2 link, is capable of achieving similar ranges.
DJI leveraged this elevated power ceiling to develop "Drone ID," a proprietary tracking protocol
transmitted via OcuSync signals and passively detected by DJI Aeroscope sensor units.
Because Drone ID transmits at significantly higher amplification levels than standard Wi-Fi or
Bluetooth Remote ID, DJI Aeroscope systems routinely detect aircraft at distances of 30 miles
or more in rural environments, and maintain multi-mile detection radii in dense urban settings.
These detection ranges that public safety has known for years with Aeroscopes are well within
the potential of Remote ID - the physics are the same, but today’s regulations and policy are
not.

Technical Power Summary of Remote ID Utility for BVLOS
Commercial Flight
Both this Part 74 rule and upcoming Part 108 rule for Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS)
operations represent a pivotal advancement for drone integration into the national airspace,
particularly enabling scalable delivery services that harmonize with critical infrastructure security
needs. Pierce Aerospace developed Remote ID solutions that can scale to monitor a NAS that’s
going to be operating with millions of drones simultaneously - a massive feat and requirement
for effectively serving the critical infrastructure stakeholders identified in 2209.
However, some industry comments (official and unofficial) have raised concerns that increasing
the minimum Effective Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP) for Remote ID (RID)
broadcasts—currently specified at 13 dBm for 2.4 GHz WiFi under ASTM F3411—would impose
unacceptable battery drain, thereby reducing operational range. Some OEMs, such as Elroy Air,
are making hybrid drones that use batteries plus another means of power where this draw
would be made even more insignificant.
This comment presents a step-by-step empirical energy consumption analysis demonstrating
that elevating RID transmit power to the FCC maximum of 30 dBm conducted (36 dBm EIRP)
results in virtually no impact on drone flight range, even in worst-case scenarios for delivery
drones flying BVLOS with packages and payloads, while dramatically enhancing the airspace
monitoring requirement for Part 74. Using empirically derived models and real-world drone
specifications, Pierce Aerospace refutes comments to the contrary and advocates for higher
power requirements to enhance detection reliability and overall safety performance without
compromising mission viability. Increasing the power, especially for Part 108 drones operating
BVLOS throughout airspaces that may encounter multiple critical infrastructure stakeholders
with UAFRs is a material improvement in that UAFR operator’s ability to monitor their airspace
with confidence.
Power Level Problem Statement
The FAA's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) for Part 108 establishes a framework for
routine BVLOS drone operations, including mandatory RID broadcasting for situational
awareness and collision avoidance. That NPRM, anticipated to be released soon as a final rule,
is critical for the understanding about how Remote ID will work for what will soon be the majority
of flight operations in the NAS.
Power levels are especially critical for delivery fleets operating over populated areas, where
extended detection ranges could mitigate risks to manned aviation and ground assets -
especially as Remote ID becomes the foundation for Electronic Conspicuity (EC). The ASTM
F3411-22a standard governs RID message formats and transmission, mandating WiFi or
Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) broadcasts with minimum EIRP levels of 13 dBm (2.4 GHz WiFi)
and 3 dBm (BLE). However, as we’ve explored above, FCC Part 15.247 permits up to 30 dBm

Operational Impact and Lateral Boundary Discussion Across the 16
Critical Infrastructure Sectors
Increasing Remote ID broadcast power strengthens security across the sixteen critical
infrastructure sectors defined by NSM-22 and 14 CFR Part 74. While we generally support
keeping airspace open and restricting Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) to
immediate facility areas, higher power outputs enable extended detection ranges. This grants
operators the flexibility to monitor compliant drones from a distance without unnecessarily
restricting flight paths. With this expanded range, UAFRs can remain compact, using geofencing
to manage compliant traffic while still effectively detecting and alerting on unauthorized aircraft.

to a Fixed Site Facility

/ Regulatory review.
Intended filing deadline: August 4, 2026
Submit via: https://www.regulations.gov (Docket FAA-2026-4558)

Date: August 4, 2026
Re: Comments on NPRM, Docket FAA-2026-4558
I. Identity and interest
CHAOS 1, Inc. (doing business as Chaos Federal, Inc.) (“CHAOS”) is a U.S. company
headquartered in Hawthorne, California (CAGE code 9JFR1). CHAOS builds ground-based
non-cooperative detection and airspace-awareness systems that detect and track
unmanned aircraft and fuse cooperative signals (Remote Identification and ADS-B) with
non-cooperative tracks for a single operational picture.
CHAOS submits these comments to support a risk-based, and performance-driven
implementation of 14 CFR Part 74 that recognizes independently validated, non-
cooperative airspace awareness as an acceptable means of satisfying protective security
and monitoring requirements for eligible fixed-site facilities. The final rule should establish
measurable surveillance outcomes rather than prescribe specific technologies, thereby
enabling innovation while ensuring effective protection of critical infrastructure. CHAOS is
not submitting these comments as a facility applicant, does not seek authority to interfere
with unmanned aircraft beyond existing statutory authorities, and does not advocate for
the FAA to mandate any specific vendor, product, or sensing modality.
II. Summary of position: shape eligibility toward real airspace awareness
CHAOS supports FAA’s proposal to implement section 2209 by creating a durable UAFR
process for eligible fixed-site critical infrastructure.
A UAFR that relies solely on a legal airspace designation and Remote Identification
(Remote ID) reception does not adequately address the range of threats that section 2209

was enacted to mitigate. While Remote ID provides valuable situational awareness for
compliant operators, it cannot detect non-cooperative unmanned aircraft, including those
that do not broadcast, transmit misleading identification, or otherwise operate outside
Remote ID requirements. These aircraft represent a significant portion of the security and
safety risks to critical fixed-site facilities.
Accordingly, protective security under proposed § 74.56 should adopt a risk-based,
performance-oriented approach that recognizes, for high-threat or high-consequence
facilities, security monitoring capabilities that provide independently validated detection
and tracking of both cooperative and non-cooperative unmanned aircraft. Such
capabilities may be provided through facility-owned or contracted services and should
complement, rather than replace, Remote ID reception to provide comprehensive airspace
awareness.
CHAOS respectfully recommends that the FAA structure the final rule and Advisory
Circular to establish a performance-based framework for protective security and airspace
monitoring by:
1. Maintaining the distinction that a UAFR is an airspace designation that does not by
itself authorize interference with unmanned aircraft beyond authorities otherwise
established by law;
2. Defining "security monitoring" in terms of measurable surveillance performance
and operational outcomes, rather than prescribed technologies. For facilities with
elevated or demonstrated risk, security monitoring should support continuous or
near-continuous situational awareness throughout the UAFR volume and include
the capability to detect, track, and distinguish both cooperative and non-
cooperative unmanned aircraft. Such capabilities may be provided through facility-
owned or contracted monitoring services.
3. Remote Identification reception remains necessary but is not treated as sufficient
monitoring for applicants whose security assessment shows a non-cooperative or
non-compliant unmanned aircraft. In such cases, complementary surveillance
capabilities should be recognized as an acceptable means of demonstrating
effective protective security.
Third-party detection logs and vulnerability assessments produced under
documented methodology are accepted as application evidence.
4. Accepting independently validated surveillance data, third-party detection logs, and
airspace vulnerability assessments developed using documented, repeatable
methodologies as acceptable application evidence. The Advisory Circular should
establish performance-based guidance for surveillance evidence, including data
quality, coverage, integrity, validation, auditability, and record retention, without
prescribing specific sensing technologies or vendors.

III. The public-interest case: Remote Identification is Necessary, but Not
Sufficient
Remote Identification (Remote ID) significantly enhances situational awareness for
compliant unmanned aircraft operations and represents an important foundation for the
safe integration of UAS into the National Airspace System. However, Remote ID alone
cannot provide comprehensive airspace awareness for the range of threats that section
2209 was intended to address. Non-cooperative unmanned aircraft, including those that
do not broadcast, transmit misleading identification, operate outside Remote ID
requirements, or otherwise cannot be reliably identified through cooperative means—
continue to present security and safety risks for eligible fixed-site facilities.
For facilities whose security assessment identifies elevated risks from non-cooperative
unmanned aircraft, protective security should be implemented using a risk-based,
performance-oriented approach. Rather than prescribing specific sensing technologies,
the final rule and Advisory Circular should recognize surveillance capabilities that provide
independently validated detection, tracking, and differentiation of cooperative and non-
cooperative unmanned aircraft throughout the UAFR volume. Such capabilities may be
provided through facility-owned or contracted monitoring services and should be
supported by auditable surveillance records suitable for compliance, periodic UAFR
reviews, and law-enforcement referral.
CHAOS does not advocate replacing or diminishing the role of Remote ID. Instead, CHAOS
recommends that the FAA recognize Remote ID as a foundational element of airspace
awareness while acknowledging that it may not, by itself, provide sufficient surveillance
performance for facilities facing elevated non-cooperative UAS risk.
IV. Preserve distinction between Airspace Designation and Counter UAS
Authorities
CHAOS strongly supports the NPRM's clear distinction that a UAFR is an airspace
designation and, by itself, does not authorize the detection, mitigation, disruption, or
interference with unmanned aircraft beyond authorities otherwise established under
applicable law. Maintaining this distinction in the final rule and accompanying Advisory
Circular is essential to preserving the FAA's role in managing the National Airspace System
while avoiding overlap or conflict with separate federal counter-UAS authorities.
Clear separation between (a) airspace designation, surveillance, and regulatory
compliance (b) operational response or mitigation authorities provides important
regulatory clarity for applicants, technology providers, law enforcement, and federal
agencies. CHAOS’s commercial and technical posture is detection and verified track
reporting. Surveillance capabilities that provide independently validated detection,
tracking, and reporting of cooperative and non-cooperative unmanned aircraft enhance
the effectiveness of UAFRs by supporting informed decision-making and timely referral of
unauthorized operations to the appropriate authorities.

V. Protective security (proposed § 74.56): Establish Performance based
Surveillance Requirements
Proposed § 74.56 would require restricted access, designated security personnel, security
monitoring, and capability (directly or through a contracted service) to receive broadcast
Remote Identification. CHAOS supports these foundational requirements and respectfully
recommends that the final rule, accompanying preamble, and Advisory Circular establish
a risk-based, technology-neutral, and performance-oriented framework that enables
applicants to demonstrate effective protective security through validated surveillance
capabilities commensurate with their assessed risk.
CHAOS requests the following in final rule text, preamble, or Advisory Circular:
1. For applicants whose security assessment identifies elevated or credible risks from
non-cooperative unmanned aircraft, "security monitoring" should be defined in
terms of measurable surveillance performance rather than prescribed sensing
technologies. The final rule should recognize continuous or near-continuous
situational awareness throughout the requested UAFR volume, including the
capability to detect, track, and differentiate both cooperative and non-cooperative
unmanned aircraft. These capabilities may be provided through either facility-
owned or contracted monitoring services.
2. Security monitoring and Remote ID reception should be permitted through qualified
contracted services that are fully integrated into a facility's security operations.
Applicants should be permitted to demonstrate compliance through equivalent
surveillance performance and should not be required to procure or operate
dedicated surveillance hardware where contracted services provide comparable
capability and operational effectiveness.
3. Remote ID reception should remain a foundational element of protective security
because it enhances situational awareness for compliant operations. However,
where an applicant's documented security assessment identifies risks from non-
cooperative or non-compliant unmanned aircraft, Remote ID reception alone
should not be presumed to satisfy the security monitoring requirement. In such
circumstances, applicants should be permitted to demonstrate compliance
through complementary surveillance capabilities that provide independently
validated detection and tracking performance.
4. Rather than identifying preferred technologies or vendors, the Advisory Circular
should establish objective criteria for demonstrating surveillance effectiveness.
Examples of acceptable evidence include:
o Geographic and vertical surveillance coverage appropriate to the requested
UAFR volume;

o Surveillance update rate, latency, availability, continuity, and outage
notification;
o Demonstrated capability to detect, track, and distinguish cooperative and
non-cooperative unmanned aircraft within a common operational picture;
o Documented validation methodology, data integrity, auditability, and quality
assurance processes;
o Data retention practices supporting § 74.20 compliance, periodic UAFR
review, and law-enforcement referral; and
o Documentation describing how surveillance capabilities are incorporated
into the applicant's security program while appropriately protecting sensitive
security information.
5. Remote Identification and track-data retention. FAA asked whether RID retention
should be required. CHAOS supports a published retention floor when RID and
track data support UAFR oversight and referral. A defined operational retention
period (for example, 90 to 180 days), with optional longer archive. If adopted, the
FAA should specify minimum retention periods, data formats, and documentation
expectations.
6. To support accurate, scalable, and interoperable implementation, the FAA should
publish UAFR boundary information in standardized machine-readable formats.
Digital boundary data would enable surveillance systems, flight-planning
applications, and contracted monitoring services to accurately ingest UAFR
geometries, reduce implementation errors, improve interoperability, and facilitate
consistent monitoring across a growing number of protected facilities.
CHAOS is not asking FAA to mandate radar, any proprietary modality, or any named
vendor. CHAOS is asking FAA to set performance-based monitoring criteria that reward
systems capable of non-cooperative awareness.
VI. Application evidence: accept proven detection records
Applicants will need to show unmanned aircraft activity and vulnerability. CHAOS requests
that FAA expressly accept:
1. Third-party surveillance records, detection logs, and airspace vulnerability
assessments developed using documented, repeatable methodologies should be
accepted as application evidence, subject to FAA and applicable Sector Risk
Management Agency (SRMA) review
2. Applicants should be permitted to submit redacted surveillance records, track
histories, and vulnerability assessments where public disclosure would
unnecessarily expose sensitive security information or increase operational risk.
The Advisory Circular should establish procedures that protect sensitive
information while providing the FAA with sufficient evidence to evaluate the
application.

3. The final rule should expressly recognize that pursuing a UAFR does not preclude
applicants from utilizing separately authorized surveillance or detection
capabilities available under other Federal, State, Local, Tribal, or Territorial (SLTT)
authorities. Airspace designation under Part 74 and lawful surveillance conducted
pursuant to other applicable authorities should operate as complementary
elements of a comprehensive protective security strategy rather than mutually
exclusive approaches.
Accepting rigorous third-party detection evidence accelerates credible applications and
favors applicants who already invest in real airspace awareness rather than procedural
compliance, thereby better supporting the safety and security objectives of Section 2209
while remaining fully consistent with the FAA's technology-neutral, performance-based
regulatory framework.
VII. Allowed operations inside a UAFR
CHAOS supports the NPRM's requirement that authorized operations within a UAFR
broadcast Remote Identification (Remote ID), as it enhances situational awareness and
enables facility operators to identify and distinguish compliant operations. However,
effective protective security requires a more comprehensive airspace awareness
capability. Because non-cooperative or non-compliant unmanned aircraft may not be
visible through Remote ID alone, applicants should be permitted to demonstrate
complementary surveillance capabilities that provide independently validated detection
and tracking of both cooperative and non-cooperative aircraft.
The final rule and accompanying Advisory Circular should recognize that Remote ID
reception and performance-based surveillance are complementary elements of an
effective security monitoring strategy. Together, they provide the situational awareness
necessary to distinguish authorized operations from potential threats, support timely
enforcement referral, and advance the safety and security objectives of Section 2209 while
remaining consistent with the FAA's technology-neutral, performance-based regulatory
framework.
VIII. Explicit non-asks (to prevent misreading)
CHAOS emphasizes that it is not requesting that the FAA:

• Expand or modify existing statutory authorities to authorize private entities to
detect, mitigate, disrupt, or otherwise interfere with unmanned aircraft beyond
authorities established under applicable law;
• Mandate or endorse any specific vendor, product, sensing technology, or
surveillance modality as a condition for UAFR approval;
• Require the use of any proprietary surveillance system or establish technology-
specific requirements in lieu of performance-based surveillance objectives; or
• Substitute a UAFR designation for the operational approvals, safety determinations,
or regulatory authorities required under other FAA regulations or federal statutes,
including operations conducted under 14 CFR Part 108, BVLOS operational
approvals, or Federal, State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT) counter-UAS
authorities.
IX. Offer of technical assistance
CHAOS welcomes the opportunity to engage with the FAA's Part 74 implementation team
to support development of technology-neutral, performance-based guidance for
protective security. CHAOS is prepared to provide technical input on surveillance
performance objectives, validation methodologies, integration of Remote Identification
with complementary surveillance capabilities, and evidence formats that support
consistent implementation of the final rule.
Respectfully submitted,
Sanjay Ralhan
VP Airworthiness & Certification
Aeronautics Division
Sanjay.ralhan@chaosinc.com
CHAOS 1, Inc.

COMMENTS OF THE CENTER FOR CROSS-SECTOR COORDINATION (CXC)
Regarding the Federal Aviation Administration's Proposed Rule,
"Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility"
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Executive Summary
The Center for Cross-Sector Coordination (CXC) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's proposed rule implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016.
CXC strongly supports the FAA's efforts to establish a transparent, practical process through which eligible fixed-site facilities may seek restrictions on unmanned aircraft system (UAS) operations where unauthorized activity could threaten public safety, economic security, or national resilience. Implementation of Section 2209 should, in CXC’s view, strengthen security and safety while minimizing unnecessary administrative burden, protecting sensitive facility information, and preserving the many legitimate uses of unmanned aircraft that themselves contribute to infrastructure safety, reliability, emergency response, and resilience.
America's critical infrastructure is increasingly defined by its interconnectedness. The systems that power our communities, move our goods, deliver clean water, enable communications, support healthcare, manufacture essential products, and sustain our economy operate as an integrated network rather than as isolated facilities. As a result, disruption affecting a single high-consequence asset can quickly cascade across multiple infrastructure sectors, amplifying operational, economic, and public safety impacts.
The rapid proliferation of increasingly capable and affordable UAS presents both extraordinary opportunities and evolving security challenges. While drones have become indispensable tools supporting infrastructure inspection, maintenance, emergency response, disaster recovery, and countless other beneficial purposes, they also introduce new vulnerabilities for facilities that provide essential services upon which the Nation depends. Protecting critical infrastructure from unauthorized or malicious UAS activity is therefore not solely an aviation issue; it is also a matter of homeland security, economic security, public safety, and national resilience.
As a national, nonpartisan organization representing critical infrastructure owners and operators, technology and solutions providers, and other security-and-resilience stakeholders, CXC believes this rulemaking presents an important opportunity to establish a durable, risk-informed framework that strengthens infrastructure protection while preserving the continued integration of UAS into the National Airspace System.
To strengthen implementation of Section 2209, CXC respectfully recommends that FAA:
1.Implement a risk-informed framework that emphasizes operational consequence, infrastructure interdependencies, and national resilience.
2.Recognize the variances across America's critical infrastructure by providing flexibility for differing facility types, operating environments, and security and safety considerations.
3.Design a simple, transparent, and scalable program that minimizes unnecessary burden, leverages existing Federal security programs, supports batch applications where appropriate, and limits information requirements to those necessary for informed decision-making.
4.Build upon existing Federal security and safety programs by streamlining review for facilities already recognized as high-consequence assets.
5.Ensure operationally meaningful protections through appropriately tailored stand-off distances and implementation of allowed operations that preserve the security value of UAS Flight Restrictions.
6.Enable portfolio applications for organizations operating multiple similarly situated facilities.
7.Protect sensitive facility information through data-minimization principles, self-attestation where appropriate, and safeguards against unnecessary public disclosure of sensitive facility information.
8.Maintain a technology-neutral framework that can adapt to emerging capabilities and evolving threats.
9.Support and leverage an enduring public-private partnership to contribute to continuous improvement of the Section 2209 program.
10.Recognize Section 2209 as one element of a broader counter-UAS strategy by continuing to pursue authorities, technologies, and partnerships that enable effective detection, identification, and mitigation of malicious UAS activity.
These recommendations are intended to strengthen implementation of Section 2209 while advancing a shared objective of government and industry: protecting America's critical infrastructure from evolving aerial threats while preserving the many benefits that unmanned aircraft systems provide to commerce, public safety, emergency response, and the Nation's long-term security and resilience.

August 5, 2026
Submitted via regulations.gov

Washington, DC 20590-0001
Attention: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03
Re: Comments in Response to FAA Section 2209 NPRM: Designation - Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility [Docket No. FAA-2026-4558]
To Whom It May Concern:
The Interstate Natural Gas Association of America (INGAA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on (NPRM) on Designation-
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility1. INGAA is a trade
association that advocates the regulatory and legislative positions of importance to the interstate natural
gas pipeline industry in the U.S. INGAA’s 28 members represent the majority of interstate natural gas
transmission pipeline companies in the U.S, as well as liquified natural gas (LNG) and natural gas storage.
INGAA’s members, which operate approximately 200,000 miles of interstate natural gas pipelines, serve
as an indispensable link between natural gas producers and consumers. INGAA member company assets
and operations are designated critical infrastructure under Presidential Policy Directive 21 (PPD-21),2 and
our members have a vested interest in securing their assets from both terrestrial threats and those
originating in the airspace above and immediately around their perimeter.
INGAA members appreciate FAA’s longstanding efforts to develop a regulatory framework that addresses
unmanned aircraft system (UAS) risks to critical infrastructure while supporting the safe integration of UAS
into the National Airspace System (NAS). This proposal, which implements Section 2209 of the FAA
Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA)3 as amended4, creates a process for operators of
certain fixed site facilities to establish unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs). This proposal is
especially significant for INGAA members given the considerable increase in the frequency of unauthorized
1 91 FR 24650 (May 6, 2026).
2 https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2013/02/12/presidential-policy-directive-critical-
infrastructure-security-and-resil/.
3 Public Law No: 114-190.
4 Public Law No: 118-63.

UAS activity over natural gas facilities in recent years. As such, INGAA supports FAA’s effort to establish a
regulatory framework for implementing Section 2209 and addressing UAS-related risks to critical
infrastructure. A final rule that is practical, implementable, and risk-informed is an important tool for
owners and operators to secure their operations while supporting the continued safe integration of UAS
into the NAS. INGAA’s comments below reflect an approach that supports national security and aviation
innovation while minimizing the regulatory hurdles for natural gas infrastructure owners and operators.
I. General Comments
INGAA appreciates the substantial effort undertaken by FAA to construct a proposal that considers the
concerns of critical infrastructure owners/operators, the Sector Risk Management Agencies (SRMAs), and
the commercial UAS community. Balancing the realities and commercial applications of UAS technology
with the need to protect critical infrastructure assets requires careful thought to the types of operations
undertaken at any given facility alongside the threat to health, safety, and the environment.
Accordingly, INGAA believes several aspects of the proposed rule would benefit from clarification, revision,
and refinement to ensure it meets the intended goals while being implementable across organizations of
all sizes. The rule must not be onerous for applicants, should be risk-driven, and should consider the
complexities and interdependencies of critical infrastructure operations. The amount of sensitive
information required by applicants, the lack of detail provided as to how that information will be
protected, and what information FAA intends to publish both as part of the notice and comment period
and once a UAFR is established, disincentivizes critical infrastructure operators from availing themselves
of this much needed regulatory framework.
FAA must also closely coordinate with key federal regulators of the critical infrastructure sectors to ensure
any requirements for UAFRs align with existing requirements. Within the midstream natural gas subsector,
this includes the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) for construction and siting, the Pipeline
and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) for safety, both the Transportation Security
Administration (TSA) and United States Coast Guard (USCG) for security requirements, and the
Department of Energy (DOE) as the Sector Risk Management Agency (SRMA) for the energy sector.
Further, as detailed below, certain requirements for the applicability of UAFRs do not account for
operationally critical assets. Within the natural gas industry, these are assets that may not meet the
proposed 500 MMcf/d threshold due to geographic limitations or operational efficiencies but are critical
for interconnects or other upstream compression. Adjacent facilities, including compressor stations owned
and operated by the same or different companies, and industrial clustering adds another layer of
complexity as one facility might not qualify for a UAFR, but a significant UAS incident at that facility could
have operational impacts at the adjacent facility that has a UAFR in place.
Indeed, UAS threats to critical infrastructure range from surveillance, operational disruptions, cyber-
enabled activities, and potential physical attacks against systems and assets. With more widespread
adoption of advanced UAS technologies, critical infrastructure owners and operators must contend with
these risks on a more proactive scale by addressing the potential threats of UAS activity in their corporate
and site security plans. Therefore, the framework established by this rule should be treated as a proactive
2

security measure rather than a reactive tool, considering that technology often outpaces regulation.
Rather than solely in response to demonstrable UAS concerns, UAFRs should be considered part of the
defense-in-depth, preventative security plan that critical infrastructure operators use to manage risks to
their people, assets, and the neighboring communities.
Importantly, the rule should also address the lack of commensurate enforcement mechanisms currently
available and the need for expanded counter UAS authorities. At present, impacted owners and operators
only have one recourse: to report suspicious UAS activity to state and local authorities and, even then,
those authorities are limited in their capacity to respond. Civil and criminal penalties vary across states,
and that is only if the UAS operator can be identified and found. FAA must use this rulemaking as a first
step toward scalable counter-UAS authorities for critical infrastructure owners and operators and should
work in concert with the Department of Justice (DOJ) on increasing penalties for nefarious UAS operators
that damage, destroy, or attempt to cause destruction to critical infrastructure assets and operations.
II. Subpart A – General
a. Obligation to Update (§ 74.20)
FAA proposes continuing obligations to update application information within five business days, annual
reporting of authorized and unauthorized UAS operations, and possible more frequent reporting when
requested by FAA. While reasonable, FAA should consider that – for a variety of reasons, including cost,
variability in the performance standards for Remote ID technology, and potential spectrum and wifi
interference with on-site equipment – many facilities may not have formal detection capabilities in place
at the time of application and so data on UAS flight patterns may only be based on observations and
reporting to state and local law enforcement. To that end, FAA should consider observed and reported
flights to be sufficient to meet the data requirement during the application process.
Similarly, the proposed five business days to update and open-ended interim reporting will impose
unnecessary administrative burdens on owners/operators, especially for any immaterial or routine
changes in UAS operations. FAA should instead propose a materiality threshold, standardized reporting
templates, and protected submission pathways to ensure the agency receives actionable updates without
additional compliance obligations.
b. Incorporation by Reference (§ 74.30)
INGAA understands that any closure of the NAS is a considerable challenge and that, under FAA
regulations5, all permanent NAS closures are subject to a notice and comment period. As such, FAA is
proposing that once a UAFR is conditionally approved, the FAA would publish the proposed UAFR in the
Federal Register for notice and comment for a minimum of 30 days, absent a good cause basis for forgoing
notice and comment.
However, FAA must appreciate that the very reason these sites are requesting UAFRs is due to the sensitive
nature of activities conducted at the facility; the risk to health, safety, and the environment that a UAS
incident would have at the facility; and the need to have additional security measures in place to protect

people and assets. In publishing proposed UAFRs in the Federal Register, FAA is publicly identifying these
sensitive sites even before the UAFR is permanently approved, providing nefarious UAS users with clear
targets alongside no criminal penalties.
FAA should clarify the type of information it intends to publish for notice and comment as part of any UAFR
application. Further, FAA should limit the information made available in the Federal Register for notice and
comment. INGAA strongly dissuades FAA from publishing any identifiable facility information, including
operator name, the type of facility, operations conducted at the site, any hazardous materials stored or
used at the site, any information on the facility’s security plans, and any information regarding the
potential consequences of a UAS incident at the facility. Providing that information publicly would grant
nefarious actors significant insight and visibility into critical infrastructure operations that could be
leveraged for counterintelligence, or to damage or destroy physical assets. INGAA reinforces the need to
coordinate with other federal regulators to assess the degree to which providing potentially sensitive
information to FAA for purposes of requesting a UAFR introduces additional risk to the facility and
company.
III. Subpart B – Minimum Requirements for Unmanned Aircraft Restriction
a. General (§ 74.50)
INGAA members realize that FAA needs facility and operational information to qualify for a UAFR. However,
as proposed, FAA would require considerable detail around security vulnerabilities at an applicant facility,
including consequences of a UAS incident and existing protective security measures. Although FAA has
created a system for applicants to submit security-related materials, the agency fails to define what
“appropriate security protections” are in place to ensure that the materials are handled properly and are
not breached.
Any time security or other sensitive information leaves company networks, risk is introduced. As FAA is
aware, in 2024, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) was the target of a
cybersecurity intrusion where malicious actors accessed the agency’s Chemical Security Assessment Tool
(CSAT), which contains highly-sensitive information on Top-Screen surveys, Security Vulnerability
Assessments, Site Security Plans, Personnel Surety Program (PSP) submissions, and CSAT user accounts.6
Despite being the federal agency charged with maintaining cybersecurity across the federal government
and for addressing cybersecurity risk in critical infrastructure, CISA’s own security controls were not
adequate to protect the potential exfiltration of sensitive security information for our nation’s highest risk
chemical facilities.
In recognition of these concerns, FAA should limit the level of specificity it is requiring of applicants and
consider holding a series of townhalls in which critical infrastructure owners and operators can understand
the security protections in place within FAA and the proposed submission system.
b. Protective Security (§ 74.56)

csat-ivanti-notification.
4

INGAA members believe it is reasonable for FAA to request that facilities applying for a UAFR have
protective security measures in place; however, as proposed, FAA states that it would require layered
security measures to protect from the threat of unmanned aircraft. It is unclear how applicants would
demonstrate their ability to protect from the threat of unmanned aircraft absent a UAFR since the airspace
above the facility cannot be secured. Additionally, it is not reasonable to expect critical infrastructure
owners and operators to enclose all their assets at a facility as some components, such as flaring
equipment, are operationally designed to be exposed. As addressed above, UAFRs themselves should be
considered part of the layered approach and based on owner/operator risk tolerance, rather than merely
a response to UAS incursions. To that end, INGAA encourages FAA to remove this as a condition of eligibility
for a UAFR, particularly if FAA will require sites with UAFRs to implement a Remote ID sensing capability.
With respect to Remote ID, INGAA members recognize that to deter UAS activity and report such activity
to law enforcement, detection capabilities are necessary. Nonetheless, INGAA encourages FAA to consider
that this might be cost, or potentially operationally, prohibitive at remote critical facilities. Remote ID
collection and monitoring requirements can also raise technical, cybersecurity, and data-management
issues for industrial facilities. Prescriptive sensor standards, unclear retention expectations, or broad
reporting obligations could require technology deployments that are not well aligned with site-specific
risks, existing security operations center workflows, or evolving Remote ID capabilities and performance
standards.
To address this concern, FAA should clearly define and limit any required Remote ID data collection,
reporting, and retention requirements, including required data elements, retention periods, reporting
triggers, and acceptable submission formats. FAA should likewise avoid creating prescriptive Remote ID
sensor standards or mandated technical configurations and instead allow facilities flexibility to implement
cost-effective solutions appropriate to their operational needs and risk environment. Any data retention
requirements should be narrowly tailored and designed to minimize unnecessary administrative, storage,
cybersecurity, and compliance burdens on facility operators.
Remote ID technology also frequently runs on the unlicensed spectrum, alongside millions of devices
including radios, telemetry, metering, and SCADA systems. It is unclear the impact that a potentially large-
scale implementation of Remote ID technologies might have on existing devices operating on that
spectrum. INGAA encourages FAA to work with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and federal
scientific bodies, such as the Department of Energy (DOE) National Laboratories, to assess and address
any potential operational reliability challenges that this requirement might present.
c. Lateral Boundary (§ 74.58)
INGAA members recognize that a lateral boundary for a UAFR is necessary to balance the security needs
of the facility alongside greater integration of UAS into the NAS. As proposed, FAA would require the lateral
UAFR boundary not exceed the operator or proprietor’s property boundary consistent with legal property
rights. While this would simplify the boundaries and reduce complexity for purposes of implementation,
for INGAA members, and many critical infrastructure operators, the UAS threat does not end at the
fenceline. For example, a UAS flying along the perimeter of a facility with a UAFR could lose control and
result in a safety and/or security incident at the facility. To provide an accidental buffer, INGAA
5

recommends FAA allow for an additional 100-yard radius along the perimeter, if requested. INGAA
members understand this may require coordination with a third-party legal owner of the adjacent
property, if it is not owned by the UAFR applicant.
Furthermore, INGAA also recommends FAA consider adjacent facilities or industrial clusters, and the
impact that a UAS incident at one facility may have on the adjacent facility, especially where there are
shared rights of way or interconnects along a pipeline system. For instance, in the below photograph, two
natural gas facilities operate within a one half mile radius of one another, separated only by a rural county
road. Based on the proposed requirements, the facility on the left of the photograph (Facility A) would be
covered as it meets the 500 MMcf/d processing threshold; however, the facility on the right of the
photograph (Facility B) is slightly under that processing threshold. Both facilities are owned and operated
by the same company, and both facilities have experienced a considerable rise in unauthorized and
suspicious UAS activity in recent months. In February 2026, this company reported five instances of large,
non-commercially available UAS, estimated to be approximately 8’ X 8’, flying at low altitude above these
two facilities between 8:00pm and 3:00am. These facilities also both maintain hydrogen sulfide on site for
natural gas processing, but under the levels recorded in Appendix A of the proposed rule.
Undoubtedly, an incident at one facility perpetrated by a UAS operator such as the one reported above
would directly impact the operations of the adjacent facility. It is with this real-time example in mind that
INGAA strongly encourages FAA to allow for adjacent facilities or industrial clusters to jointly apply for a
UAFR, even if one of the facilities does not meet all of the specific requirements (i.e. a processing threshold
just under 500 MMcf/d). FAA should also consider whether a federal sponsor, like the SRMA, could validate
geographic areas of criticality where groupings of facilities exist that might warrant a blanket UAFR. Doing
so will considerably reduce the risk of a significant incident resulting in danger to public safety, health, and
national security.
d. Altitude Ceiling (§ 74.60)
Similar to the lateral boundary, FAA must consider whether the altitude ceiling is sufficient to protect fixed
site facilities from UAS threats. In the proposal, FAA recommends a standard altitude ceiling of 400 feet
6

above ground level (AGL). However, FAA recognizes that facilities may have components taller than 300
feel AGL and thus proposes that UAFRs could extend vertically from the surface to the height of the
facility’s tallest component plus 100 feet, rounding up to the next 50-foot increment. FAA cites the example
of a smokestack reaching 310 feet AGL, whereby FAA would add 100 feet to the altitude and round up to
the nearest 50-foot increment, arriving at an altitude of 450 AGL.
INGAA members appreciate this flexibility and understanding that often asset infrastructure at facilities
varies in height. Still, INGAA believes that while 400 feet, or an additional ~150 feet, might be appropriate
for certain UAS and for surveillance purposes, any UAS operating a payload is likely to be able to inflict
damage onto the facility at that altitude. While INGAA members recognize that a UAS operator seeking to
cause disruptive impacts at a facility will likely ignore any UAFR, INGAA suggests FAA consider raising the
additional altitude exceedance to 200 feet AGL, rounded up to the next 50-foot increment. A higher
altitude ceiling would more sufficiently protect the tallest infrastructure from both surveillance activity
and any accidental UAS incidents.
e. Unmanned Aircraft System Security and Incident Response Plans (§ 74.64)
As stated above, INGAA members agree that it is reasonable to have security protections in place to
address vulnerabilities at the facility, but providing sensitive security information, including security and
incident response plans, outside the organization introduces unnecessary risk to the company and facility.
To that end, INGAA recommends that FAA allow applicants to satisfy portions of the requirement through
executive-level certifications or signed affidavits from corporate leadership affirming that the facility
maintains layered security measures, emergency response procedures, and UAS incident response
capabilities consistent with the objectives of Part 74. It is also worth reaffirming that FAA should commit
to describing the security protections in place at the agency that reduce the risk of sensitive security
information from being exfiltrated or compromised.
f. Demonstration of Need (§ 74.66)
INGAA members agree that FAA must balance the right of transit for UAS operators with the need to
ensure the safety and security of qualifying fixed site facilities. As proposed, FAA is requesting information
around four areas: (1) existing unmanned aircraft traffic in close proximity to the fixed site facility; (2) the
facility's specific vulnerabilities to unmanned aircraft traffic; (3) what would happen if an unmanned
aircraft were to exploit a vulnerability; and (4) how a UAFR would be integrated into a facility's security
plans to supplement existing security measures. This is a substantial amount of information that the
applicant may not be able or willing to provide in detail given operational and security sensitivities.
For example, FAA should consider that certain facilities may not have formal detection capabilities in place
and may not have actual data to support UAS flight patterns but can speak to observed patterns and
reporting to SLTT law enforcement. Especially in the early phases of implementation of the final rule, FAA
should consider observed UAS activity and reporting sufficient to meet the requirement detailing existing
UAS activity in proximity to the facility. Second, providing information around any specific vulnerabilities
at a facility and the consequences if a UAS were to exploit that vulnerability is highly sensitive information.
FAA should once more allow applicants to demonstrate need through alternative risk-based approaches
7

developed in coordination with the applicable SRMA, including executive certifications, consequence-
based assessments, existing vulnerability analyses, or sector-specific risk statements, without requiring
extensive facility-specific technical submissions.
Lastly, INGAA agrees that a UAFR would supplement a facility’s existing security plans; however, FAA’s
proposal is reactive, rather than affording owner/operators the opportunity to build UAFRs into their
layered security plans to proactively mitigate unauthorized UAS activity and the consequences of the UAS
risk to their unique facilities. Although FAA notes that none of the requirements of this provision are
dispositive, the agency also does not describe how the applications will be reviewed and how the data and
narrative information provided will be objectively balanced against the safe integration of UAS into the
NAS.
IV. Subpart C - Sector-Specific Requirements (Subpart C of Part 74)
INGAA appreciates that FAA identifies sector-specific criteria for fixed site critical infrastructure facilities
to qualify for a UAFR. INGAA members are unique in that they may fall under multiple sector categories,
including energy, transportation, maritime, and chemical. Some INGAA member assets, however, do not
appear to be recognized, or at a minimum, are not clearly identified within the proposed sector-specific
requirements.
Under the energy category, as proposed, natural gas facilities are inclusive only of natural gas processing
plants. FAA should revise this definition to include natural gas storage facilities and consider lowering the
processing threshold to account for more operationally critical assets. Further, although FAA does explicitly
mention natural gas compressors under the transportation category, it is worth noting that compressors
are also heavily utilized at processing facilities, creating confusion as to whether the 500 MMcf/d threshold
is applicable to all compressors or only at processing facilities. Still, the capacity of at least 500 MMcf/d
would exclude many operationally critical assets. INGAA recommends that FAA specify whether both
processing and transportation compressors are covered under either energy or transportation and lower
the threshold to 200 or 250 MMcf/d to allow eligibility for larger interconnects and other critical facilities.
INGAA further suggests that FAA consider including natural gas processing facilities that have potentially
hazardous chemicals onsite, even at levels under the Appendix A thresholds, as a UAS incursion could
trigger a life-threatening chemical release.
Within the transportation category, FAA includes pipelines and as noted, compressor stations, as part of
surface transportation. Specifically for compressor stations, FAA proposes compressors as eligible only if
they are “just upstream” of power generation or major metropolitan areas. FAA should both clarify what
it considers “just upstream,” and expand the scope to compressors that might not be “just upstream” of
power generation but have gravity assistance based on geographic location or significant on-site
horsepower that boosts capacity at the upstream compressor, making those facilities more critical to
operations than a compressor that might be “just upstream” of power generation. To simplify, FAA should
consider revising this provision to allow for pipeline owner/operators to identify which compressors are
critical and, through the UAFR application process, justify that criticality through the demonstrated need
for a UAFR.
8

Additionally, INGAA strongly encourages FAA to engage with TSA, the pipeline sector’s security regulator,
to align eligibility requirements under the surface transportation category with TSA’s “critical pipeline” list.
This list, while not shared publicly, is indicative of the varying types of pipeline assets that are considered
critical for national and economic security but might not meet certain arbitrary capacity or location
requirements. The owners/operators of those pipeline facilities are notified of their critical pipeline
asset(s) and, consequently, have both cybersecurity regulatory requirements7 as well as enhanced physical
security measures in place, as outlined in the TSA Pipeline Security Guidelines8. However, it is worth
reinforcing that TSA’s critical pipeline list may differ from the owner/operator’s operationally critical assets,
which are driven by the organization’s risk tolerance.
Furthermore, as proposed, liquified natural gas (LNG) facilities are not included under any sector-specific
requirements. LNG facilities, located both along waterways and inland, are large industrial facilities that
export, import, or store natural gas for domestic and global consumption. LNG facilities are frequent
targets for UAS activity. Recent geopolitical events have demonstrated that UAS attacks on LNG facilities
can cause significant short-term spikes in energy prices, hazardous environmental conditions, and forced
temporary closures9. Domestically, unidentified UAS activity has been routine at LNG facilities in the Gulf
of America and East Coast, often attributed to corporate espionage and environmental activists. Even if
accidental, a UAS incident at an LNG facility could cause considerable damage to assets, potentially
releasing highly flammable, cryogenic fuel resulting in explosions, toxic vapor releases, and possible
casualties. To that end, INGAA strongly encourages FAA to explicitly include LNG facilities (import, export,
and peak shaving) under either the energy or transportation categories within the sector-specific
requirements provision.
V. Subpart G – Access to Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (Subpart G of Part 74)
a. Allowed Operations (§ 74.250)
In demonstrating compliance with Executive Order 14307 Unleashing American Drone Dominance10, FAA
proposes that certain operations under Parts 91, 107, 108, 135, and 137 may access standard UAFRs if
they broadcast Remote ID, transition in the shortest time practicable, and satisfy other requirements.
While INGAA members understand the need to limit airspace restrictions, a generalized access framework
is likely to be insufficient in areas where accidental, reckless, or intentional malicious UAS activity could
create significant safety, environmental, operational, or cascading infrastructure consequences. Facility
operators are best positioned to understand the real-time facility conditions, and must have the tools to
coordinate, delay, or restrict operations when necessary.
Owner/operators of UAFR-covered facilities should have the ability to temporarily restrict, delay, or deny
non-essential operations when necessary to address operational conditions, maintenance activities,

FAA should likewise establish a more tailored access framework for certain sectors, such as energy and
