be limited and require advanced notification and coordination for non-emergency operations.
b. UAFR Access Notification (§ 74.255)
FAA is currently proposing that allowed UAS operators provide notice to the fixed site facility site manager
with operator contact information, certificate/permit numbers, Remote ID serial numbers, registration
numbers, site identification, date/time/area, and operation type. Notice must be provided as soon as
reasonably possible in advance, with alternative procedures for government or law enforcement
operations. While INGAA members appreciate the notification requirements, it is important to distinguish
between higher-risk third-party operations and routine facility-owned, facility-authorized, or contracted
UAS activities. To address this consideration, FAA could consider establishing an automated recurring
authorization or “whitelist” capability allowing facility-owned, facility-authorized, or contracted UAS
operations to operate under pre-approved Remote ID serial numbers, operator credentials, and
operational profiles without requiring repetitive manual notifications for routine operations. Such
capability should support integration into existing facility security operations center workflows and reduce
unnecessary administrative burdens for both operators and facility personnel.
VI. Conclusion
INGAA appreciates the opportunity to comment on this long-awaited and much-needed proposal to
mitigate the risk of unauthorized UAS activity above and around fixed site critical infrastructure facilities
in the United States. INGAA understands the importance of an operationally practical process for
establishing UAFRs, and the significance of issuing any restrictions in the NAS. Still, restricting unauthorized
UAS operations over high-risk critical infrastructure facilities provides an important layer within the
organization’s risk-based security framework. UAFRs can reduce the risk of accidental overflights of
sensitive locations, improve situational awareness for facility security personnel and law enforcement, and
better distinguish lawful operations from potentially suspicious or unauthorized activity.
INGAA members likewise believe the process for establishing and managing UAFRs should not be based
exclusively on the existing threat. As proposed, the rule is designed to limit UAFRs to only those high-
consequence facilities with established problematic UAS activity. A reactive approach to mitigating
nefarious UAS activity fails to account for how owners and operators determine risk at each of their unique
facilities. Rigid eligibility thresholds, including data demonstrating an existing, prolific UAS issue, may not
capture facility-specific consequences and downstream impacts should a UAS-related event occur, and
10

could unintentionally introduce risk by limiting the capability of owners and operators to implement
security measures based on their risk appetite.
In that regard, as FAA seeks to finalize this rule, the agency should likewise consider that critical
infrastructure owners and operators have no recourse beyond reporting unauthorized or malicious UAS
activity to state, local, and federal authorities. UAFRs are a critical part of deterrence, and FAA should treat
this rule as a first step toward smart and scalable counter-UAS authorities for critical infrastructure owners
and operators.
FAA must also be critically cognizant of the sensitivity of the information it is requesting from applicants.
Recent data breaches from federal networks point to the directed and intentional efforts of our adversaries
to exfiltrate information on and target our nation’s national and economic security. INGAA urges FAA to
adopt a “less is more” approach to requesting potentially vulnerable facility information. Similarly, INGAA
strongly encourages this same approach when determining the level of specificity provided when
publishing the conditionally approved UAFRs in the Federal Register and on the FAA’s website. If the
objective remains to ensure the security of our nation’s highest-risk facilities, FAA should continue to work
alongside industry in fulfilling that shared responsibility.
The improvements and clarifications requested would allow for UAFRs to be made available to facilities
where unauthorized UAS operations could create significant safety, security, environmental, or operational
consequences, while supporting authorized UAS operations and avoiding unnecessary administrative
burdens.

recognizes, would “reduce interagency redundancies and provide a streamlined application
process”;19 (iv) issuing either interim final rules or direct final rules while the FAA seeks public
comment on the UAFR designation; and (v) shortening the public comment period to 15 days.
Establishing the need for a UAFR should reflect the evolving threat landscape that
Congress intended to address. The new rules should include a presumption that there is a
“sufficient safety or security need” for UAFRs around data centers, absent information to the
16 See id.

(Proposed Rule 14 C.F.R. § 74.66).

https://www.oracle.com/data-centers (last visited June 30, 2026) (displaying pictures of data center

identification of assets that are vulnerable to UAS threats,23 UAS incident response plans for

comments.commenter: Comment from Skyports Drone Services Inc.
comments.comment_text:
Skyports Drone Services Inc.
Wilmington, DE
August 5, 2026
Federal Aviation Administration
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Washington, DC 20590
RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03; RIN 2120-AL33 - Designation-Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
Dear Sir or Madam,
Skyports Drone Services Inc. ("Skyports") appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the
Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking implementing Section 2209 of
the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 through the creation of Unmanned Aircraft
Flight Restrictions ("UAFRs") under proposed 14 CFR part 74.
Skyports supports the FAA's objective of establishing a clear, nationally consistent federal
framework for airspace restrictions near genuinely sensitive fixed-site facilities. A federal
framework is preferable to a patchwork of state, local, and facility-specific restrictions. At the
same time, the final rule could benefit from additional clarity to preserve practical access for lawful
commercial UAS operations, including Part 107 inspection and surveillance work and future Part
108 operations supporting infrastructure resilience, construction monitoring, logistics, and public
safety support.
Skyports' position is broadly aligned with AUVSI's comments. Security and access are not in
conflict if the final rule provides workable, risk-based access pathways, clearly bounded
restrictions, and operator-facing implementation tools. Skyports also believes FAA may find useful
examples in other UAS frameworks abroad, including infrastructure-notification practices and
geozone presentation in the UK and EU, without implying that those systems must be copied
directly.
Executive Summary
Skyports supports FAA's effort to create a uniform federal framework for UAFRs under Section
2209. A well-designed part 74 framework can improve critical infrastructure security while
preserving the commercial UAS operations that support infrastructure inspection, construction
safety, public safety response, and future BVLOS integration.
As FAA develops the final rule, Skyports encourages consideration of the following points:
• Standard UAFR notification should remain situational awareness, not facility permission, and
the rule text could state that distinction more clearly.
Skyports Drone Services Inc. | FAA-2026-4558 | Page 1

• The final rule could benefit from an explicit pathway for non-transitory missions such as
inspection, surveillance, construction monitoring, and other operations that require dwell time
inside or adjacent to a UAFR.
• FAA may wish to distinguish more clearly among notification, coordination, and permission so
that infrastructure-owner coordination does not become an unintended airspace veto.
• Boundary decisions may be more workable if they are tied to the security perimeter of the
critical asset rather than the full property line by default, with cumulative airspace-
fragmentation effects considered where UAFRs cluster.
• Special UAFRs may be most effective if kept narrow, evidence-based, and limited to genuinely
sensitive sites with documented national-security or homeland-security concerns.
• For public infrastructure and transportation corridors, the final rule could benefit from clearer
coordination pathways for property, right-of-way, emergency-management, and public-safety
issues, while preserving FAA's exclusive authority over airspace access and UAFR conditions.
• As UAFRs are published, Skyports believes it would be beneficial for operators to have access
to an FAA-operated planning tool that identifies each UAFR, its boundaries, its operating
conditions, the applicable contact route, and the action expected of the operator.
• The notification architecture may be more durable if it accommodates standing notifications,
automated or machine-readable workflows, and future integration with broader digital airspace
tools.
• FAA may also find value in confirming an access pathway for large UAS and future Part 108
operations when ATC-based surveillance and communication already provide continuous
federal situational awareness.
I. Introduction and Skyports' Interest
Skyports operates in the commercial UAS ecosystem and is directly affected by how UAFRs will
function in practice. Infrastructure inspection, construction monitoring, linear-asset survey,
surveillance, and recurring operational support often occur near the same fixed-site facilities that
may become eligible for a UAFR. The practical question for operators is therefore not simply
whether restrictions may exist, but whether the final framework allows lawful, low-risk operations
to continue in a predictable and scalable way.
Skyports agrees with AUVSI's broader view that a federal rule can replace today's fragmented
landscape with a clearer national baseline. That objective is important for both safety and
commercial planning. The final rule could be especially valuable if it gives operators confidence
that the published restriction, the access pathway, and the operational expectations are
understandable before flight rather than only after an operator reaches a site or contacts a facility
security desk.
II. Notification, Coordination, and Permission Should Remain Distinct
Skyports encourages FAA to preserve the NPRM's core premise that, for a Standard UAFR,
notification serves situational awareness rather than a facility-controlled approval process. That
principle is central to maintaining a federally consistent airspace regime. If it remains only an
Skyports Drone Services Inc. | FAA-2026-4558 | Page 2

implied concept, operators may still encounter field-level confusion where a facility responds to a
notification as though it were a request for permission.
The final rule could therefore benefit from a clearer distinction among three separate concepts.
Notification informs the relevant parties that a lawful operation will occur. Coordination supports
deconfliction, emergency response, launch or recovery logistics, and awareness of site activity.
Permission is a legal prerequisite that prevents a flight absent affirmative approval. Skyports
believes those concepts are not interchangeable and that the final framework will work better if
each is assigned a distinct role.
This distinction is also where practical lessons from other jurisdictions may be useful. In other
countries, infrastructure-owner notification practices can support deconfliction and emergency
arrangements without necessarily turning the infrastructure owner into the airspace decision-
maker. That example may help FAA refine how coordination can function in a Standard UAFR
without undermining federal primacy over access rules.
III. Recurring Commercial Operations Need a Practical Access Path
Many commercial operations near critical infrastructure are not simple transits. Inspection,
surveillance, mapping, thermal review, construction progress monitoring, and related tasks often
require hover, orbit, repeat passes, or slow movement within a defined work area. Skyports
believes the final rule could benefit from acknowledging that these are routine and legitimate use
cases rather than edge cases.
For that reason, FAA may wish to consider an explicit access pathway for non-transitory missions
where the operator is certificated, identifiable, and conducting a lawful commercial activity. A
framework designed only around the shortest-practicable-time concept may fit transit operations,
but it does not map neatly onto the mission profiles that support the infrastructure sectors this rule
is intended to protect.
Skyports also believes the final implementation could benefit from scalable notification options for
recurring operators. Standing notifications, fleet-based registration, or other repeat-use workflows
may be more proportionate than a fully manual per-flight process for operators conducting
frequent work over recurring service areas.
IV. Boundaries and Accountability Mechanisms Matter as Much as Eligibility
Skyports supports a rule in which a UAFR remains a last-resort airspace measure tied to
demonstrated need. In that context, boundary design is especially important. FAA may wish to
consider whether the default lateral boundary for many sites is better tied to the security perimeter
of the critical asset, or another site-specific operational boundary, rather than the full property line
by default. Large parcels often include parking, undeveloped land, or buffer areas that are not
closely related to the underlying security rationale.
Skyports also encourages FAA to consider cumulative effects where multiple UAFRs may cluster
along a corridor, within a suburban utility network, or around transportation infrastructure. Even if
each designation is individually reasonable, the combined result may materially constrain lawful
Skyports Drone Services Inc. | FAA-2026-4558 | Page 3

route planning, especially for inspection corridors and future BVLOS networks. The final rule could
benefit from a more explicit mechanism for weighing that aggregate impact.
Similarly, accountability during the life of a UAFR may be just as important as the initial approval
standard. Mid-term review, publication lead times, and predictable updates to public aeronautical
information may help ensure that an active UAFR remains justified and operationally
understandable throughout its term.
V. Public-Infrastructure Coordination and Special UAFR Narrowness
Skyports believes the final rule could be improved by recognizing a difference between general
private-site notification and coordination involving public infrastructure owners such as state
departments of transportation or other public asset managers. FAA's exclusive authority over
airspace access and UAFR conditions remains central, and any state or public-owner role should
be limited to property, right-of-way, emergency-management, and public-safety coordination
where bridges, tunnels, highways, rail corridors, or other public systems are affected.
At the same time, Skyports agrees with the principle that a permission-based model should remain
narrow. If a site truly requires a heightened approval regime, that may be more appropriately
addressed through a Special UAFR or another clearly defined high-sensitivity pathway rather than
by allowing ordinary Standard UAFR notification to drift into ad hoc permissioning.
For that reason, Skyports encourages FAA to keep Special UAFRs tightly limited to sites with well-
documented national-security or homeland-security concerns and to preserve a clear evidentiary
basis for any heightened access restrictions applied there.
VI. Operator-Facing Clarity Could Be Strengthened Through Better Public Tools
As UAFRs become established, Skyports believes it would be beneficial for operators to have
access to an FAA-operated planning tool that clearly identifies each published UAFR and the
actions associated with it. Experience from European and German geozone systems suggests that
operator usability improves when restrictions are shown in a map-based, operator-facing format
with clear status, conditions, and contact logic. Skyports offers those examples as useful
implementation references rather than as models FAA must replicate.
An FAA planning tool could improve compliance and reduce uncertainty if it allows an operator to
determine, before flight, whether a UAFR is Standard or Special, what its lateral and vertical
boundaries are, whether it is active, what operating conditions apply, whether the operator is
expected to notify, coordinate, or seek approval, and what contact route is relevant where contact
is required.
Skyports also believes machine-readable publication may become increasingly important as the
framework matures. Many mission-planning and airspace-management systems already rely on
digital data, and an operator-facing tool would be stronger if it is paired with data services that
support consistent implementation across planning platforms.
Skyports Drone Services Inc. | FAA-2026-4558 | Page 4

VII. Large UAS and Future Part 108 Operations Merit a Clear Pathway
Skyports supports AUVSI's concern that an access framework built solely around Part 89 broadcast
Remote ID may not map cleanly onto larger UAS or future Part 108 operations that already operate
with more extensive federal situational awareness. Where an operation is on an active flight plan, is
assigned a discrete beacon code, and remains in two-way communication with ATC, FAA may wish
to consider whether those conditions can satisfy the relevant awareness objective without
duplicative facility notification.
That approach would not expand access indiscriminately. It would simply recognize that some
operations already provide the federal visibility and operational discipline that the UAFR framework
is trying to achieve. Clarifying that pathway now could reduce friction for higher-end commercial
operations without weakening the rule's security purpose.
Conclusion
Skyports appreciates the opportunity to comment on this important rulemaking. Skyports supports
the development of a workable federal UAFR framework and believes the final rule could provide a
strong national baseline if it preserves practical access for lawful operators, keeps boundaries tied
to genuine need, distinguishes notification from permission, and provides clear public
implementation tools.
Respectfully submitted,
Skyports Drone Services Inc.
Skyports Drone Services Inc. | FAA-2026-4558 | Page 5

comments.commenter: Comment from National Association of Manufacturers
comments.comment_text:
Christopher Phalen
Vice President, Domestic Policy
August 5, 2026
Docket Operations
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Room W58-213, West Building 5th Floor
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Comments of the National Association of Manufacturers; Designation-
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility (Docket Number FAA-2026-4558)
To whom it may concern:
The National Association of Manufacturers (NAM) respectfully submits these comments on
the Federal Aviation Administration's (“FAA” or “the agency”) proposed rulemaking
Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility (“the proposal” or “the proposed rule”) through which the agency is implementing
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (Section 2209). The
NAM appreciates the opportunity to provide input on this proposal and its implications for
the protection of critical infrastructure and the safe, efficient use of unmanned aircraft
systems (UAS) by manufacturers and industrial operators.
The NAM is the voice of the manufacturing community and the leading advocate for a policy
agenda that supports and empowers the 13 million people who make things in America. As
the largest manufacturing association in the U.S., the NAM’s membership includes
businesses of all sizes, across all industrial sectors, and in all 50 states. Manufacturers
collectively contribute $2.9 trillion to the U.S. economy—and right-sized, commonsense
regulations are critical to sustaining the manufacturing strength that underpins our nation’s
prosperity.
Manufacturers operate, support, and rely on a wide range of critical infrastructure facilities
that may be eligible for protection under the proposed framework, including chemical
facilities, energy production and transmission facilities, refineries, industrial manufacturing
sites, transportation infrastructure, and other facilities critical to the nation's economic and
national security. At the same time, manufacturers are active adopters of UAS technologies,
utilizing drones to support inspection, maintenance, environmental monitoring, emergency
response, security operations, and safety initiatives.
The NAM supports the FAA's efforts to establish a framework that protects critical
infrastructure from unauthorized UAS activity while preserving the ability of facility operators
to conduct legitimate, authorized drone operations. As the FAA finalizes this rulemaking, the
NAM respectfully requests that the agency ensure the framework remains risk-based,
operationally practical, and sufficiently flexible to support future technological innovation.
1

Support for a Risk-Based Section 2209 Framework
The NAM supports implementation of Section 2209 through a demonstrated-need approach
that evaluates applications based on facility-specific risk considerations and operational
requirements. The proposed process for designating unmanned aircraft flight restrictions
(UAFRs) is the cornerstone of the FAA’s implementation of Section 2209, providing the
mechanism to protect eligible facilities from unauthorized drone operations that present
legitimate safety and security risks. Restrictions should be targeted at facilities that present
legitimate security and safety concerns and should be supported by appropriate
documentation demonstrating the need for protection.
A risk-based framework will help ensure that flight restrictions remain appropriately tailored
to the security objectives established by Congress, while minimizing unintended impacts on
legitimate UAS operators and industrial activities. As the FAA gains experience
administering the program, the NAM recommends that the agency continue to evaluate
whether application requirements remain practical, scalable, and appropriately aligned with
the risks presented by individual facilities.
Facility Eligibility Considerations
The FAA’s proposed rule is intended to provide eligible critical infrastructure facilities with
an appropriate mechanism to seek airspace protections against unauthorized UAS
operations. As such, manufacturers request that the FAA clarify that eligibility
determinations may appropriately include large industrial manufacturing facilities that share
the operational, safety, and security characteristics of other critical infrastructure sectors
identified under the proposed framework. Facilities such as paper mills and other
permanent, complex industrial and transportation operations (such as railroad facilities,
added by Congress in the 2018 FAA reauthorization) often handle combustible materials,
regulated waste streams, wastewater treatment systems, biomass storage areas, heavy
industrial equipment, and continuous production processes that present unique safety and
security considerations.
Additionally, manufacturers request that the FAA consider expanding the lateral boundaries
beyond property lines for certain facilities and circumstances. Some examples of potentially
covered facilities could include: point-of-departure logistical facilities such as loading docks,
loading bays, staging areas, or marine terminals and port facilities; pipeline corridors; critical
electrical or water facilities, such as substations or treatment works, located outside of a
facility’s property line; or railyards or rail lines being used to transport critical materials.
Unauthorized UAS operations in close proximity to these facilities may create credible risks,
including disruption of the delivery of critical services like energy and water, fire hazards,
interference with industrial equipment and operations, disruption of environmental
management systems, and unauthorized surveillance of sensitive infrastructure and
processes. The NAM appreciated the FAA ensuring that the final rule provides sufficient
flexibility to recognize these risks when evaluating facility eligibility under Section 2209.
2

Consider the Use of Consequence-Based Eligibility in Addition to Facility
Classification
Beyond evaluating various factors to determine facility eligibility under Section 2209, the
NAM believes it would be most practical for the FAA system to also consider a
consequence-based eligibility framework. The current system is largely built around what a
facility is and whether that facility falls into a category authorized to receive drone
restrictions. However, manufacturers recommend that the FAA consider the potential
consequences of a successful malicious or unauthorized UAS event at these facilities.
For many industrial facilities, the consequences of an incident may extend beyond the
facility boundaries and include impacts to employees, surrounding communities,
environmental resources, transportation networks, regional supply chains, and emergency
response operations. Facility size, production capacity, regulatory designation, or other
measurement metrics alone may not adequately capture risks of this nature. A
consequence-based evaluation framework would help ensure protections are appropriately
applied and enforced where the greatest potential impacts exist.
Protect Current Safety Commitments and Recognize Existing Practices
Manufacturing facilities eligible for Section 2209 protections often conduct complex
industrial operations where safety is paramount, and these facility operators bear significant
responsibility for employees and the larger community. Unauthorized UAS activity can
introduce unnecessary risks to employees, contractors, emergency responders, neighboring
communities, and critical industrial processes.
Throughout the rulemaking, it is important for the FAA to recognize that appropriate
airspace protections support a broad range of safety objectives, including:
• Employee and contractor safety;
• Public and community safety;
• Process safety and operational reliability;
• Emergency response operations;
• Environmental protection; and,
• Security of critical industrial infrastructure.
Many facilities that may qualify for protection under the proposed framework already
operate under extensive federal security and access-control requirements, which are
designed to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive operations, hazardous materials,
critical infrastructure systems, and regulated manufacturing environments. For example,
facilities covered under the Maritime Transportation Security Act (MTSA) must implement
access-control measures through approved Facility Security Plans pursuant to 33 CFR §
105.255. Facilities registered with the Drug Enforcement Administration must maintain
effective controls against theft and diversion of controlled substances under 21 CFR
§1301.71. FDA-regulated manufacturing facilities operate under current Good
Manufacturing Practice requirements that restrict access to authorized personnel and
protect product integrity pursuant to 21 CFR Part 211. Similarly, facilities subject to
hazardous materials security planning requirements under 49 CFR §172.802 must
3

implement measures to prevent unauthorized access to hazardous materials and
associated operations.
Additional programs include Process Safety Management (PSM), EPA Risk Management
Programs (RMP), Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (where applicable), site
emergency response plans, mutual aid agreements, and other facility-specific risk
management measures.
The ability to effectively control access to sensitive facilities is a foundational element of
these regulatory programs. Unrestricted aerial access over critical infrastructure facilities
may undermine the ability of facility operators to fully implement federally mandated security
and access control measures. In some industrial environments, including facilities that
handle hazardous materials, combustible materials, or flammable substances, unauthorized
aerial activity may also introduce operational and safety risks that facility operators cannot
adequately manage. The FAA should recognize the important role that appropriately
tailored UAFRs can play in supporting broader critical infrastructure security objectives and
existing federal security requirements.
Detection Technologies Should Complement Airspace Protections
The NAM recognizes the important role that UAS detection, identification, and situational
awareness technologies play in supporting facility security and operational awareness.
These technologies can help facility operators identify other unauthorized drone activity,
improve incident response, and strengthen coordination with law enforcement and other
applicable authorities.
However, detection capabilities alone do not prevent, deter, or mitigate unauthorized UAS
operations. The ability to identify a drone after it has entered sensitive airspace does not
eliminate the potential security or safety risks associated with that intrusion. As the FAA
evaluates applications under Section 2209, the existence of detection technologies should
not be viewed as a substitute for unmanned aircraft flight restrictions UAFRs. Rather,
detection technologies and UAFRs should be viewed as complementary tools that together
strengthen the protection of critical infrastructure facilities.
Preserving Authorized Industrial UAS Operations
Protecting facilities from unauthorized aerial activity is an important objective, but the
implementation of the regulatory framework under Section 2209 NPRM should not
unintentionally disrupt authorized UAS operations that provide significant safety,
environmental, operational, and security benefits.
Manufacturers increasingly rely on drones to conduct inspections in difficult-to-access
locations, reduce employee exposure to hazardous environments, monitor facility
conditions, support maintenance activities, and improve operational efficiency. Many
companies have invested significant resources in developing safe and effective drone
programs, by establishing compliance procedures, obtaining FAA approvals, and integrating
UAS technologies into routine operations.
4

As such, manufacturers strongly encourage that the agency’s final rule ensure that facilities
receiving UAFRs retain the ability to conduct authorized operations, including activities
conducted by facility personnel, approved contractors, emergency response teams, and
other authorized operators. Existing FAA approvals, waivers, enterprise drone programs,
emissions monitoring activities, environmental compliance programs, and other authorized
operations should not be disrupted in the process of implementing this framework.
Across the manufacturing sector, facility-operated UAS should be recognized not as a risk
to be restricted, but as the increasingly important component of modern industrial safety,
environmental management, maintenance, and security programs that it is, and the NAM
believes these activities should be regulated as such.
Emergency Response Considerations
The ability to rapidly deploy UAS assets during emergencies is particularly important for
many industrial and manufacturing facilities. Manufacturers increasingly use drones during
emergency situations to improve personnel safety, enhance situational awareness,
accelerate incident assessment and response, and support emergency decision-making.
For instance, UAS technologies can provide critical capabilities during fire response
operations, hazardous material releases, gas detection and plume monitoring activities,
security incidents, search and rescue efforts, storm response activities, and other
emergency situations.
Additionally, industrial operators frequently deploy UAS resources to support neighboring
facilities, mutual aid organizations, local emergency management agencies, fire
departments, and other critical infrastructure partners during emergency situations. It is
essential to preserve the flexibility that allows for these necessary partnerships during
emergency situations.
The FAA should ensure that facilities operating under approved UAFRs retain the ability to
rapidly deploy authorized UAS assets during emergency situations, within their facilities or
alongside neighboring partners, without unnecessary administrative delays or procedural
barriers. Preserving operational flexibility during emergencies will help ensure that the rule
enhances security without inadvertently limiting critical response capabilities.
Administrative Practicality and Unfunded Airspace Management Obligations
Additionally, in this same spirit of providing sufficiently protective regulations that do not
hamper manufacturers’ ability to efficiently and safely proceed in their operations, the NAM
encourages the FAA to implement the program in a manner that minimizes unnecessary
administrative burdens or unfunded airspace management costs on applicants.
Some facilities may face challenges, through no fault of their own, in providing detailed
historical data regarding UAS activity or other similar information that may not currently be
tracked through existing compliance systems. Application requirements should remain
practical and focused on information necessary to support FAA decision-making, with
appropriate consideration given to operationally critical functions, such as safety operations,
emergency response functions, hazardous material management and site security, as well
as the use of UAS to support existing regulatory reporting requirements. Additionally, the
5

FAA should avoid creating circumstances in which facility operators become responsible for
ongoing airspace management activities.
On the management and cost front, manufacturers support a streamlined implementation
framework that does not shift ongoing airspace management responsibilities to facility
operators. Section 2209 designations should not create expectations that designated
facilities continuously monitor surrounding airspace, maintain specialized detection
infrastructure, or undertake reporting and enforcement functions beyond the scope of their
responsibilities. While many manufacturers employ security measures specific to their
operational needs, participation in the Section 2209 program should not depend upon
assuming responsibilities or costs beyond those that facility owners can reasonably meet
and that are necessary to request and maintain a designation.
Enterprise Program Considerations and Additional Benefits of UAFRs
As the program matures, the agency should also consider opportunities to support
enterprise-level or programmatic approaches for organizations operating multiple facilities
under common security, operational, and UAS management frameworks. Many
manufacturers and industrial organizations are leading the way and have developed mature
enterprise drone programs supported by FAA-compliant procedures, standardized training
programs, safety management systems, operational governance processes, and qualified
operating personnel and contractors.
The final framework should recognize the distinction between unauthorized operators and
trained, qualified operators conducting approved missions under established enterprise
UAS programs. A balanced framework to support enterprise programs provides
opportunities to reduce duplicative administrative requirements while maintaining
appropriate oversight, which will improve efficiency for applicants and the FAA.
Additionally, while the primary purpose of Section 2209 is to enhance the protection of
critical infrastructure facilities from unauthorized UAS activity, appropriately implemented
UAFRs can also provide secondary operational benefits for authorized facility operators. By
reducing unauthorized traffic and creating more controlled operating environments,
approved restrictions can improve operator identification, enhance situational awareness,
reduce uncertainty, and facilitate the continued deployment of advanced industrial UAS
capabilities. A well-designed and implemented framework should both enhance security
against unauthorized drone operations and enable the continued safe, efficient, and
responsible use of authorized industrial UAS across the manufacturing sector.
Supporting Future Innovation
Industrial UAS technologies continue to evolve, and the final rule should remain sufficiently
flexible to accommodate future advancements (including existing enterprise programs).
Manufacturers are increasingly evaluating and deploying technologies such as centralized
remote operations centers, autonomous inspections, dock-based deployments, integrated
robotics systems, artificial intelligence-assisted monitoring, advanced detection
technologies, enterprise-scale drone operations, and beyond visual line of sight inspection
capabilities. Future applications may also involve greater integration between UAS
platforms and broader industrial automation and robotics systems.
6

The final regulatory framework should remain technology-neutral and avoid unintentionally
limiting future capabilities that can improve both facility security and operational efficiency.
Maintaining flexibility will help ensure that facilities can continue adopting innovative
technologies while meeting the security objectives of Section 2209.
*****
The NAM appreciates the FAA’s efforts to implement Section 2209 and strengthen
protections for critical manufacturing and infrastructure facilities. As the agency finalizes this
rulemaking, manufacturers respectfully request that it ensures that the framework protects
facility security, preserves authorized industrial UAS operations, supports emergency
response capabilities, minimizes unnecessary administrative burdens, and remains flexible
enough to accommodate future technological innovation.
The NAM looks forward to continuing to work with the FAA throughout this rulemaking
process.
Sincerely,
Kirbie Ferrell
Director, Transportation and Infrastructure Policy
Christopher Phalen
Vice President, Domestic Policy
7

comments.commenter: Comment from National Agricultural Aviation Association
comments.comment_text: The National Agricultural Aviation Association (NAAA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on FAA-2026-4558.

August 5, 2026
Submitted electronically via Federal eRulemaking Portal: www.regulations.gov
United States Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue, SE
West Building 5th Floor, Room W58-213
Washington, D.C. 20590
Re: DRONERESPONDERS® Comments on the Section 2209 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
on “Restricting the Operations of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to Fixed Site Facilities”
[Docket No. FAA-2026-4558]
To Whom It May Concern:
DRONERESPONDERS® appreciates the opportunity to submit comments in response to the
Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Section 2209 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking titled
“Restricting the Operations of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to Fixed Site Facilities.” We
appreciate the FAA’s diligent efforts to secure the National Airspace System (NAS) while maintaining
airspace access for authorized unmanned aircraft systems (UAS or drones).
In our comment, we will highlight the principles that DRONERESPONDERS® believes should govern
this rulemaking. We will highlight areas where we support the proposed rule as well as identify areas
where we believe improvements are necessary. Overall, DRONERESPONDERS® believes it is
critical that the final rule continue to allow for free and unencumbered access to the NAS for public
safety operators operating under the Part 91 UAS Public Aircraft Operations (PAO) or Part 107
framework. A failure to do so would hinder the ability of public safety operators to quickly and effectively
respond to time-sensitive and life-saving missions.
I. Standing
DRONERESPONDERS® is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit program under The Airborne International
Response Team (AIRT, Inc.) dedicated to convening public safety UAS programs under a single
collaborative organization. Together, our mission is to support first responders, emergency managers,
and search and rescue professionals by sharing research insights, developing standardized training,
and educating stakeholders to maximize the effectiveness and efficiency of drone technology in the
public safety sector. Through this forum, DRONERRESPONDERS® supports thousands of public
safety UAS programs nationwide. Guided by our Drones for Good® program, we promote the
responsible and positive use of unmanned aviation to solve societal challenges.
Public safety drone adoption has accelerated rapidly over the past two years, with U.S. public
safety programs increasing by about 50% to a total of 8,000 programs. Drone as a First Responder
(DFR) operations have also expanded dramatically, with approvals increasing from roughly 50 waivers
- 1 -

issued over a six-year period to over 1,000 approvals within a six-month span, with over 125 new DFR
waivers per month. Additional survey data indicates that public safety drone use is expected to triple
over the next five years.1 This growth reflects one of the most significant technological advances in
law enforcement and emergency response in decades, with clear benefits including improved life-
saving outcomes, faster incident resolution, safer operations, de-escalation of encounters, and more
efficient allocation of limited public resources. In short, drones help public safety officials save lives,
keep communities safer, be more responsive to emergencies, and de-escalate interactions with
potential perpetrators, while simultaneously allowing departments to better prioritize increasingly
limited resources, resolve incidents faster, and free up officers to respond to other calls.
II. DRONERESPONDERS® Perspective on the Section 2209 NPRM
DRONERESPONDERS® supports the FAA’s efforts to implement Section 2209 in a manner
that protects critical infrastructure and other sensitive facilities while preserving the ability of authorized
public safety operators to safely and efficiently access the NAS. As an organization representing
thousands of public safety UAS programs nationwide, DRONERESPONDERS® recognizes both the
security concerns underlying the proposed rule and the critical role that unmanned aircraft play in
emergency response, disaster management, search and rescue, and other public safety missions.
Public safety operators share the FAA’s objective of preventing misuse of UAS while ensuring that
public safety operators can continue to leverage these technologies to protect lives and property
nationwide. DRONERESPONDERS® thus supports a regulatory framework that strengthens airspace
security without unnecessarily constraining authorized public safety operations that provide substantial
public benefit.
DRONERESPONDERS® also believes that effective protection of fixed-site facilities requires
a layered and risk-based approach. Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) will provide a
critical legal framework that establishes clear operational expectations and accountability for airspace
users. However, legal restrictions alone cannot prevent intentional misconduct by actors who have no
intention of following the rules from the outset. For this reason, the UAFR framework should be viewed
as one component of a broader security strategy that incorporates airspace awareness, remote
identification (“RID” or “Remote ID”), detection capabilities, and other tools that allow facilities and
government authorities to better identify and respond to unauthorized drone operations. These
additional measures can work together to improve security while continuing to enable compliant
operators—to include public safety operators—to conduct legitimate missions in NAS.
Finally, DRONERESPONDERS® believes that the long-term success of the Section 2209
framework will depend on the FAA’s ability to implement restrictions in a manner that supports a
scalable and navigable low-altitude airspace environment. As the number of UAFRs expands
nationwide, the ability to manage the airspace more dynamically becomes increasingly important to
ensure that restrictions remain understandable, interoperable, and operationally manageable. Public
safety operators frequently conduct time-sensitive missions that require rapid deployment and the
ability to transit efficiently through the airspace. All authorized operators benefit from airspace
management systems that provide real-time awareness, prioritization, and coordination among users,
especially if those systems work in the background and don’t need direct operator intervention.
DRONERESPONDERS® therefore supports continued development of technologies and services
1 See Verizon Communications, Inc., Verizon Frontline 2025 Public Safety Communications Survey
(2025), https://www.verizon.com/about/sites/default/files/2025-Verizon-Frontline-Public-Safety-
Communications-Survey.pdf.
- 2 -

that facilitate efficient airspace access while maintaining appropriate security protections. As the FAA
advances related initiatives, including the development of UTM and Part 146 service-provider
frameworks, the agency should seek to leverage these tools in tandem with Part 74, which will
ultimately lead to a nationally consistent, technology-enabled approach to airspace management.
III. Areas of Support:
DRONERESPONDERS® largely supports comments submitted by the Commercial Drone Alliance
(CDA). In particular, DRONERESPONDERS® supports the following aspects of the proposed
rulemaking:
a. Balancing Security and Airspace Accessibility
DRONERESPONDERS® supports the FAA’s determination in the proposed rule that the
agency has the obligation to protect security interests, while also preserving pathways for authorized
UAS operations to take place. The proposed rule appropriately requires applicants to demonstrate a
safety, security, or national security justification for the establishment of a UAFR while preserving
pathways for authorized operations to transit restricted areas. This balanced approach helps protect
critical sites without unnecessarily limiting use of the airspace for legitimate operators. Labeling certain
sites ‘higher risk’ or giving something an ‘urgent’ tag necessarily heightens scrutiny and of course
interest from bad actors, but it’s important to use this designation intentionally – if everything is deemed
‘high risk’ then the designation loses its significance.
The FAA also acknowledges the merit of authorized, compliant operators by allowing Part 91
(PAO), 107, 108, 135, and 137 UAS to transit over UAFRs. DRONERESPONDERS® appreciates the
FAA’s acknowledgement of such operations, particularly Part 91 PAO public safety missions that rely
on airspace accessibility to effectively respond to time-sensitive emergencies. Public safety operators
are already vetted extensively as law enforcement and emergency response personnel, and therefore
carry very little risk by transiting UAFR airspace.
b. RID Detection Equipment Requirement for Fixed-Site Facilities
DRONERESPONDERS® supports the requirement for covered sites to be equipped with RID
detection equipment, ensuring increased airspace awareness and enforcement mechanisms.
Airspace awareness is the foundation of airspace security. It is fundamental for critical sites to be
equipped with and active in utilizing RID detection equipment that will help differentiate authorized
from unauthorized UAS in the airspace. This not only allows compliant operators to transit seamlessly
through authorized airspace, but also simultaneously highlights irregular activity and non-compliant
UAS in restricted areas. Additionally, the active monitoring of airspace activities will allow for critical
sites to provide proof for resulting legal enforcement actions for unauthorized UAS operations, and
provide better information to responding law enforcement officers to take appropriate action. As
detailed below, this provision could be even stronger if the resulting data collection is validated and
standardized.
c. Enabling Risk-Based UAFR Overflight
DRONERESPONDERS® supports the FAA’s implementation of a risk and performance-
based approach to enabling transit over UAFRs. The proposed rule allows certain authorized
- 3 -

operations to conditionally transit over UAFR areas. Proposed conditions include operators that
adhere to FAA regulations, are equipped and transmit RID, and follow necessary notification protocols.
Through this performance-based approach, operators are recognized according to their commitment
to safety and security protocols, and, as a result, enable the legitimate operators to navigate the
airspace. UAFR overflight is particularly important for public safety operators that require efficient
access to the airspace to conduct time-sensitive emergency response missions. As detailed below,
while we support the tiered approach to security, there must also be a streamlined approval process
for public safety operations to enter or transit Special UAFRs in addition to Standard UAFRs.
IV. Areas for Change and/or Clarification
a. Streamline Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction Access Notification
While DRONERESPONDERS® appreciates the FAA allowing authorized UAS to operate over
UAFRs, it is critical that the associated notification process is streamlined and modernized to enable
real-time airspace awareness and unencumbered access to the airspace for public safety operators.
Requiring pre-flight notifications for every public safety operation is not scalable for rapid
deployment of emergency response operations. Law enforcement and emergency response
personnel cannot delay operations to individually notify each UAFR site on route prior to deployment.
And while we appreciate the allowance for post-flight notification, in practice this does not meet the
full needs for public safety or the fixed site facility. There are an estimated 30,000 public safety flights
per day. At the rate of current DFR program growth, this number could rise to potentially 100,000
flights per day within the next three years. This estimation does not even account for tactical responses
outside of typical 911 emergency calls. The administrative burdens of non-automated notifications are
substantial and ultimately will not meet the needs of public safety or the fixed sites that need
protections. Additionally, public safety operators must be able to take direct routes in response to
emergencies without notification delays, because seconds can matter in life-saving missions.
The final rule should thus provide a streamlined, low-burden pathway for authorized public
safety operators to enter or transit UAFRs without creating administrative requirements that delay
response. DRONERESPONDERS® supports using RID and other elements already required of Part
91 PAO operators to facilitate UAS notification requirements for UAFR overflight. This could be through
automated notification systems, such as the FAA’s preexisting Low Altitude and Notification Capability
(LAANC) system, to enable real-time notifications between operators and covered sites. An alternative
is to utilize Remote ID to “white list” certain drone operations. Public safety operators could be “pre-
authorized” under the white-list system, which would allow registered drones from public safety
departments to operate without prior notification while remaining visible and identifiable to covered site
detection equipment. This is also an opportunity for fixed site facilities to leverage UTM capabilities
certified under Part 146, like network Remote ID, to filter known cooperating UAS operations from
unknown and potentially nefarious drones.
b. Leverage Enhanced Drone Detection Services and Data Aggregators
DRONERESPONDERS® believes that the FAA should establish a clear framework for
security monitoring equipment and/or services that leverage existing enhanced drone detection
technology. The capability to identify, track, and characterize non-cooperative UAS would generate a
- 4 -

more complete picture of the airspace, ensuring that covered sites are able to monitor the area
thoroughly, even if the UAS is non-compliant and failing to broadcast RID. The implementation of such
technology would make the airspace more secure, improving security of covered sites and maintaining
safety in the airspace as compliant operators transit over and around the UAFR. To do this, the FAA
should require fixed sites to leverage surveillance- or detection-as-a-service models, including
Network Remote ID-enabled services where appropriate, as forms of compliance with the detection
requirements in the NPRM. Such models would leverage subscription service solutions for a lower
cost to individual covered site facilities comparatively to each UAFR covered site purchasing their own
physical enhanced detection equipment, and could also serve to collect and aggregate site data
needed by federal security personnel to understand national trends and conduct nationwide threat
assessments. These service providers should be certified through the proposed Part 146 framework,
assuring data validity and standardization, appropriate cybersecurity measures, and interoperability
among airspace awareness systems. The FAA should also ensure that Part 146 service provider
frameworks support aggregated data collection and sharing across jurisdictions. Public safety
agencies should have timely and cost-effective access to relevant data to better understand cross-
jurisdictional trends, distinguish authorized public safety operations from unknown or non-cooperative
activity, and coordinate responses to potential threats.
V. Conclusion
DRONERESPONDERS® applauds the FAA’s efforts to balance the need to protect critical
infrastructure from criminal, careless, and clueless drone operators while also ensuring that legitimate
operators can safely and efficiently traverse the NAS. The safety and security of the American public
is foundational to the work of public safety entities, and we applaud the FAA for taking action to ensure
security of the people and critical sites while also enabling emergency response UAS operations to
respond to high-stakes public safety missions. DRONERESPONDERS® urges the FAA to modernize
notification systems to support time-sensitive emergency operations, as well as enhance detection
requirements to provide a detailed picture of the airspace for the benefit of both covered sites and
authorized UAS operators.
DRONERESPONDERS® appreciates the opportunity to comment on the FAA’s Section 2209
NPRM to support the enhancement of airspace security and airspace awareness systems for the
benefit of the American public. We welcome cooperation with the FAA as it finalizes this rulemaking
project to ensure that the final rule effectively secures fixed sites while maintaining a navigable
airspace for critical UAS operations.
Respectfully Submitted,
Chief Charles L. Werner (Ret.)
Director, DRONERESPONDERS®
Email: charles.werner@droneresponders.org
Website: droneresponders.org/
- 5 -

comments.commenter: Comment from International Liquid Terminals Association (ILTA)
comments.comment_text:
The International Liquid Terminals Association (ILTA) submits these comments responding to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in the Federal Register on May 06, 2026.

ILTA represents more than 60 commercial operators of over 600 above-ground liquid storage terminals that handle a wide range of liquid commodities, including crude oil, refined petroleum products, chemicals, fertilizers, animal fats, and vegetable oils. These terminals represent a key piece of critical infrastructure within the United States’ energy, chemical, and transportation systems sectors. Among many things, terminals provide essential logistics services, support domestic and international trade, and foster the readiness of the United States armed forces by making fuels and liquid products available throughout the world.

As such, these facilities face concerning risks brought by unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), including surveillance, operational, cyber, and physical threats warranting an unmanned aircraft flight restriction (UAFR) over these critical facilities. ILTA broadly supports the mission and framework of this rulemaking but has identified specific concerns regarding the definition of facilities eligible to apply for a UAFR, along with other concerns relating to the provisions of this rulemaking.

comments.commenter: Comment from Alabama Department of Corrections
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
SUBMITTED ELECTRONICALLY VIA WWW.REGULATIONS.GOV
U.S. Department of Transportation
Federal Aviation Administration
Docket Operations, M-30
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Room W58-213
Washington, D.C. 20590
Re: COMMENTS ON NOTICE OF PROPOSED RULEMAKING—“DESIGNATION—RESTRICT THE
OPERATION OF UNMANNED AIRCRAFT IN CLOSE PROXIMITY TO A FIXED SITE FACILITY”; DOCKET
NO. FAA-2026-4558; RIN 2120-AL33
Dear FAA Docket Operations:
Please allow this letter to serve as the official comment of ALABAMA DEPARTMENT OF
CORRECTIONS (the “Department”) on the FAA’s proposed rule1 implementing Section 2209
of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016.2 While the Department strongly
supports this long-awaited rulemaking, it writes these comments to explain why the
proposed rule would not adequately protect correctional facilities from the drone threats
that Congress directed the FAA to address—and what must change in the rule so that it
does.
ABOUT THE DEPARTMENT
The Department operates 26 CORRECTIONAL FACILITIES across the State of Alabama in
statewide regions where it maintains and oversees custody of NEARLY 22,000 INMATES with
a correctional staff of APPROXIMATELY 3,500 EMPLOYEES. Its 13 major correctional
facilities (“CF”)—i.e., BIBB CF, BULLOCK CF, WILLIAM E. DONALDSON CF, EASTERLING CF, ELMORE CF,
FOUNTAIN CF, WILLIAM C. HOLMAN CF, KILBY CF, LIMESTONE CF, ST. CLAIR CF, STATON CF, JULIA TUTWILER
PRISON FOR WOMEN, and VENTRESS CF—are its facilities most affected by drone incursions.
1 Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility, 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (proposed May 6, 2026) (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. pt. 74), Docket No.
FAA-2026-4558, RIN 2120-AL33 [hereinafter “NPRM”].
2 FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209, 130 Stat. 615 (2016)
(codified at 49 U.S.C. § 40101 note) [hereinafter “§ 2209”].

These figures bear directly on the burden this rule would impose. As proposed, each
UAFR is tied to a single fixed site facility, and the FAA interprets the statute’s “collective”
application option narrowly—covering only co-owners or co-operators of one facility, not
a single agency seeking coverage across its facilities.3 A corrections system of the
Department’s size would therefore be forced to file a separate application for each of its
26 facilities—an administrative burden the FAA should relieve through a multi-facility
application pathway (see SECTION VI below).
I. THE THREAT TO STATE PRISONS IS DAILY AND OPERATIONAL, NOT HYPOTHETICAL
Much of the national counter-drone conversation centers on hypothetical or
episodic threats—curious spectators and hobbyists drawn to a one-time event, or even the
occasional wrong-doer. Correctional facilities face something different: a daily,
operational threat from determined criminals. Bad actors use drones to deliver
contraband—narcotics, weapons, and cellular phones—directly over secure perimeters,
fueling violence, overdoses, and the operation of criminal enterprises from inside our
facilities. The FAA itself recognizes this threat in the NPRM.4 In CALENDAR YEAR 2025, the
Department documented ELEVEN (11) confirmed drone incursions and TWENTY (20)
contraband recoveries attributed to drone delivery. Representative incidents and figures
are set out in SECTION II below.
II. DOCUMENTED DRONE-CONTRABAND INCIDENTS AT THE DEPARTMENT’S FACILITIES
The following incidents and figures illustrate the drone-contraband threat at the
Department’s facilities.
BY THE NUMBERS | CALENDAR YEAR 2025:
• Confirmed drone incursions detected: 11
• Drones confiscated, seized, or brought down: 19
• Contraband recoveries attributed to drone delivery: 20
• Estimated value / type of contraband intercepted (drugs, weapons, cellphones): In
2025, the Department intercepted over 8 pounds of narcotics and over 200 electronic devices
resulting in a total contraband value of approximately $338,000.
EXAMPLE 1—Donaldson CF | Jefferson County, Alabama | June 12, 2026—At
approximately 5:20 P.M., a local civilian contacted the Department and informed staff
that a JSI delivery drone and duffel bag with contraband had been located about a mile
away from Donaldson CF. The Department proceeded to the location and recovered a
large red and black drone and a duffel bag containing approximately 3 pounds of
marijuana, 400ml of a suspected synthetic controlled substance, 35 cigars, 36 cell phones,
3 Although § 2209 itself permits operators or proprietors to apply “individually or collectively,” the
FAA interprets a “collective” request narrowly—as a request by more than one operator or proprietor for a
particular fixed site facility where more than one operator has an interest or exercises control. NPRM,
91 Fed. Reg. at 24661; see id. at 24652; proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.52. As proposed, each UAFR is therefore
tied to a single fixed site facility, and the rule provides no mechanism for one operator to cover multiple
facilities in a single application.
4 NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24656 (“Emergency Services Sector—State Prisons”); see proposed
14 C.F.R. § 74.87. The FAA acknowledges that “many incidents of unmanned aircraft being used to infiltrate
State prisons to deliver contraband such as cellphones, drugs, and weapons have been reported.”
2

7 sunglasses, 5 saw blades, 3 wi-fi devices, and 1 mobile wi-fi box. This event resulted in
the denial of contraband that would have increased the risk of harm and illegal activities
within one of the Department’s facilities. Additionally, intelligence was developed from
this incident that resulted in the arrest of a civilian charged with First Degree Conspiracy
to Promote Prison Contraband.
EXAMPLE 2—Fountain CF | Escambia County, Alabama | July 26, 2025—At
approximately 12:00 A.M., Department staff observed a vehicle entering state property
and subsequently flee from law enforcement officers. Law enforcement officers from both
the Department and a local police department pursued the fleeing vehicle for 5 miles
before cornering the driver. After the driver was taken into custody, a search of the vehicle
revealed a drone and a backpack containing contraband items. The driver was arrested
and charged with Attempting to Elude, Illegal Drone Use on Prison Property, and
Prohibited Activities.
EXAMPLE 3—Ventress CF | Escambia County, Alabama | July 26, 2025—At
approximately 9:11 P.M., a traffic stop was attempted on a suspicious vehicle in front of
Ventress CF. The vehicle fled from law enforcement authorities but stopped after law
enforcement conducted a rolling roadblock. During the traffic pursuit, the driver was
throwing items out of the window. Officers located a drone and contraband, resulting in
two civilian arrests, along with the following charges: Trafficking, First and Second
Degree Promoting Prison Contraband, Unlawful Possession of a Controlled Substance,
First Degree Unlawful Possession of Marijuana, and Transfer of Contraband by
Unmanned Aircraft.
III. THE DEPARTMENT SUPPORTS A TWO-TIER PART 74 FRAMEWORK
The Department commends the FAA for proposing a thoughtful framework under
a new 14 C.F.R. Part 74 and for creating two designation types—the Standard UAFR and
the Special UAFR.5 Congress expressly named prisons in Section 2209, and this
rulemaking is an important step toward giving correctional agencies a lawful means to
restrict the airspace over their facilities. The Department’s concern is not with the
structure, but how state prisons will be treated under this system and, in turn, whether it
will actually stop overflight of a prison.
IV. A STANDARD UAFR WILL NOT PROTECT A PRISON
As written, a Standard UAFR is too porous to protect a correctional facility.
Proposed § 74.250 allows operations under Parts 91, 107, 108, 135, and 137 to access the
restricted airspace so long as they broadcast Remote ID, transit in the “shortest
practicable time,” and notify the facility.6 In practice, that permits routine drone
overflight of the secure perimeter—precisely the vector used for contraband drops—and
bad actors intent on delivering contraband will not comply with a notification
5 See proposed 14 C.F.R. §§ 74.5 (Standard UAFR), 74.6 (Special UAFR); NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at
24656 (lateral boundaries within property lines; 400-foot AGL ceiling).
6 Proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.250; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24653 (allowing operations under Parts 91,
107, 108, 135, and 137 to access UAFR airspace over fixed site facilities where the operator broadcasts
Remote ID under 14 C.F.R. pt. 89, transits in the shortest practicable time, and notifies the facility under
§ 74.255).
3

requirement in any event. A Standard UAFR therefore does not solve the problem it is
meant to solve.
Only a Special UAFR actually restricts overflight. Proposed § 74.251 requires both
the permission of the responsible (“using”) agency and FAA approval before any
operation may enter the airspace.7 That facility-controlled access—not the Standard tier’s
notify-and-transit default—is what a prison needs. Yet the FAA has tied Special UAFRs
to federal security agencies, military departments, and a narrow “verified security
assessment” pathway modeled on the national-security instrument in 14 C.F.R. § 99.7.8
That framing signals the FAA does not intend to grant Special UAFRs to state prisons,
leaving them only the porous Standard tier. Such a result simply is untenable.
V. THE PROPOSED RULE CONFLICTS WITH SECTION 2209
Section 2209 does not merely authorize this rulemaking; it constrains it. In
directing that an application process be established, Congress directed that the
procedures “shall allow operators or proprietors of fixed site facilities to apply for
designation individually or collectively.”9 The word “shall” makes the collective-
application option mandatory, not discretionary, and it does not restrict it in any way.
Section 2209 provides, in relevant part:
SEC. 2209. APPLICATIONS FOR DESIGNATION.
(a) APPLICATIONS FOR DESIGNATION.—Not later than
180 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary
of Transportation shall establish a process to allow applicants
to petition the Administrator of the Federal Aviation
Administration to prohibit or restrict, including temporarily,
the operation of an unmanned aircraft in close proximity to a
fixed site facility.
(b) REVIEW PROCESS.—
(1) APPLICATION PROCEDURES.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—The Administrator shall
establish the procedures for the application for
designation under subsection (a).
(B) REQUIREMENTS.—The procedures shall
allow operators or proprietors of fixed site
facilities to apply for designation individually
or collectively.
(C) CONSIDERATIONS.—Only the following may
be considered fixed site facilities:
7 Proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.251; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24653 (operations within a Special UAFR
require both permission from the responsible government (“using”) agency and approval from the FAA
Administrator).
8 Proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.6; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24653 (Special UAFRs “available to federal
security agencies, military departments, and designated fixed-site facilities supported by verified security
assessments demonstrating credible threats,” paralleling 14 C.F.R. § 99.7, with five-year designations).
9 Section 2209(b)(1)(B).
4

(i) Critical infrastructure, such as energy
production, transmission, distribution facilities
and equipment, and railroad facilities.
(ii) Oil refineries and chemical facilities.
(iii) Amusement parks.
(iv) State prisons.10
The proposed rule cannot be squared with that Congressional directive. By tying
each UAFR to a single fixed site facility and construing “collectively” to reach only
multiple parties interested in one facility,11 the FAA has read the collective-application
option out of the rule for the operators who need it most—those, like state corrections
systems, that operate many facilities. An operator of 26 correctional facilities, such as this
Department, cannot “apply . . . collectively” in any meaningful sense if it must file a
separate application for each facility.
The proposed interpretation therefore does not “allow” collective application as the
statute requires; it forecloses it. That burden is not trivial: the FAA estimates that each
application will cost an applicant between $5,000 and $10,000 to prepare, and a
corrections system forced to file facility-by-facility would incur those costs many times
over.12 For the Department, that means an estimated $260,000 to obtain UAFRs across
all 26 of the Department’s facilities. And it imposes that cost at a time of severe, well-
documented staffing shortages across corrections, diverting scarce personnel and funding
from core security functions to duplicative, facility-by-facility paperwork.13
The statute likewise undercuts the rule’s decision to reserve meaningful,
overflight-restricting protection for national-security and military sites. Congress placed
“State prisons” on the list of eligible fixed site facilities alongside critical infrastructure14,
and authorized designations to rest on any one of four independent grounds—“aviation
safety,” “protection of persons and property on the ground,” “national security,” or
“homeland security.”15 Nothing in Section 2209 makes national security a precondition
for a protective designation. A rule that offers prisons only the porous Standard UAFR
while limiting the effective Special UAFR to national-security and military facilities
narrows grounds Congress made disjunctive and subordinates a facility category
Congress made eligible in its own right.
Worse still, § 74.6(a) makes a Special UAFR available only to facilities owned or
sponsored by federal security agencies or military departments, and it permits a non-
10 Id. (emphasis added).
11 See proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.52; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24661.
12 FAA, 2209 NPRM Regulatory Impact Analysis tbl.9 (May 2026) (Docket No.
FAA-2026-4558-0004).
13 See Safe Inside, Workforce Trends in State Departments of Corrections (Feb. 17, 2026),
https://safeinsideproject.org/report (50-state analysis supported by the U.S. Department of Justice,
Bureau of Justice Assistance, in partnership with the Correctional Leaders Association; finding that roughly
one in six corrections employees leave their jobs annually and that overtime spending has more than
doubled in many states since 2019).
14 See § 2209(b)(1)(C)(iv).
15 See § 2209(b)(2)(C).
5

federal site to qualify only “if sponsored by” the FAA or a federal intelligence or security
agency (i.e., DHS, DOD, DOE, or DOJ). A state department of corrections has no such
federal sponsor—so, however grave its documented drone threat, it is categorically shut
out of the only designation that stops overflight.
The FAA should conform the final rule to the statute by (i) providing a genuine
collective, multi-facility application pathway, and (ii) making an overflight-restricting
designation available to correctional facilities on the statutory ground of protecting
persons and property on the ground, without a national-security predicate. See SECTION VI
below.
VI. RECOMMENDATIONS
1. MAKE CORRECTIONAL FACILITIES ELIGIBLE FOR A SPECIAL UAFR—THE ONLY TIER THAT
ACTUALLY STOPS OVERFLIGHT.
Only a Special UAFR requires facility approval before a drone may enter
(§ 74.251); the Standard tier lets drones transit. The NPRM acknowledges a
Special UAFR “may be the appropriate airspace designation” for a state prison, yet
§ 74.6(a) lets a non-federal site obtain one only if a federal agency (i.e., DHS, DOD,
DOE, or DOJ) sponsors it—which a state department of corrections cannot do on
its own. The FAA should designate correctional facilities under the Special tier and
designate DOJ, already corrections’ counter-UAS partner under the SAFER SKIES
Act, as the sponsoring agency.
2. ALLOW A SINGLE AGENCY TO FILE ONE COLLECTIVE APPLICATION COVERING MULTIPLE
FACILITIES.
Proposed § 74.52(b) makes each application cover “only one fixed site
facility even if the operator or proprietor owns multiple eligible sites,” forcing a
statewide corrections system to file a separate application for every prison. hat
conflicts with Section 2209(b)(1)(B), under which the procedures “shall allow”
operators to apply “individually or collectively.” The FAA should revise § 74.52(b)
to let one operator file a single consolidated (portfolio) application across its
eligible facilities or, alternatively, provide a streamlined template for an agency
with many comparable sites.
3. HARMONIZE THE RULE WITH THE SAFER SKIES ACT.
Section 2209 dates to 2016, and this rule has been nearly a decade in the
making. In the meantime, Congress spoke again. The SAFER SKIES Act (passed
December 2025; implementing regulations effective July 1, 2026) now lets
corrections agencies mitigate drones posing a credible threat to their facilities. It
makes little sense to authorize corrections to bring a drone down while denying
them the airspace designation that makes it unauthorized in the first place. As the
FAA finally implements Section 2209, it should read the Special UAFR credible-
threat standard consistently with Congress’s most recent expression of intent.
6

4. IF ONLY A STANDARD UAFR IS GRANTED, THE FAA SHOULD STILL REQUIRE FACILITY
APPROVAL OVER THE SECURE PERIMETER.
Even under a Standard UAFR, the § 74.250/§ 74.255 notify-and-transit
allowance should not apply over a correctional perimeter—transit there should
require the facility’s approval.16
VII. CONCLUSION
The Department appreciates the FAA’s recognition of the acute drone threat to
correctional facilities. To deliver the protection Congress intended, the final rule should
do two things: (1) give correctional facilities access to an overflight-restricting Special
UAFR—with DOJ as the sponsoring agency—so that no drone may cross a secure
perimeter without the facility’s approval; and (2) honor Section 2209’s mandate by letting
a single agency apply for its facilities collectively in one filing rather than one per prison.
Read together with the SAFER SKIES Act, a rule so revised would give prisons what they
actually need and what would protect public safety: meaningful control of the airspace
above them.
Respectfully submitted,
s/ Greg Lovelace
