Echodyne Comments
Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility
Department of Transportation
Federal Aviation Administration
14 CFR Parts 1, 74, 91, and 107
[Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03]
RIN 2120-AL33
AGENCY: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation (DOT)
ACTION: Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM)
Introduction
Echodyne applauds the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for advancing
implementation of Section 2209 through this Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM). The
agency has appropriately recognized the growing need to protect critical infrastructure and
other sensitive facilities from unauthorized unmanned aircraft system (UAS or drone)
operations while preserving access to the National Airspace System (NAS) for legitimate
and authorized users.
Echodyne supports the FAA's risk-based approach and agrees that a uniform federal
framework is preferable to the patchwork of state, local, and facility-specific restrictions
that currently exist. This NPRM represents an important step toward providing certainty for
facility operators, security professionals, and drone operators alike.
However, airspace restrictions alone cannot provide the level of security needed as the
drone threat continues to mature and evolve. A UAS Flight Restriction (UAFR) can establish
legal boundaries, but it cannot independently detect, identify, track, assess, or respond to
unauthorized aircraft. The FAA should therefore ensure that the final rule encourages
deployment of layered airspace awareness architectures that provide both aviation safety
and security benefits that can be utilized by qualified entities and individuals.
The final rule should also recognize that qualified private-sector entities responsible for
protecting critical infrastructure must be able to participate meaningfully in detection and
tracking activities that support enforcement of UAFRs. While mitigation regimes remain

outside the scope of this rulemaking and require separate Congressional action,
effective airspace awareness is essential to realizing the security benefits Congress
envisioned under Section 2209. Restricting airspace without providing effective
mechanisms to identify and address actual threats risks creating a compliance regime that
affects lawful operators while doing little to deter malicious actors.
Echodyne's Perspective on Critical Infrastructure Sectors
Based on its work in the airspace awareness and facility protection space, Echodyne offers
the following observations on critical infrastructure sectors that align closely with those
identified in the NPRM.
The following are sectors in which ground-based radar and airspace awareness
technologies are deployed, or could readily be deployed:
• Energy generation and transmission
• Oil and gas infrastructure
• Chemical facilities
• Transportation infrastructure
• Ports and maritime facilities
• Airports and aviation facilities
• Telecommunications infrastructure
• Defense industrial base facilities
• Water and wastewater systems
• Food and agriculture facilities
• Public safety operations
• Federal facilities
• Critical manufacturing facilities
• Data centers
• Prisons/correctional facilities
• Healthcare facilities
• Stadiums and special event venues
• Other sensitive sites requiring persistent low-altitude airspace awareness
Across many of these sectors, Echodyne's radar systems provide persistent monitoring,
detection of cooperative and non-cooperative aircraft, support for counter-UAS (C-UAS)
operations, and situational awareness for authorized airspace users.
The FAA should ensure that the final rule permits facility operators to leverage proven,
capable, and readily available airspace awareness technologies that are already deployed
today rather than creating barriers that require entirely new security architectures.

Authorized Operations Within UAFRs
Echodyne supports the FAA's effort to preserve access pathways for legitimate operators.
The final rule should ensure that approved operations – including inspections, emergency
response, infrastructure monitoring, public safety missions, utility operations, and beyond
visual line of sight (BVLOS) operations – can continue safely and efficiently.
To accomplish this objective, the FAA should encourage the use of proven, capable
airspace awareness technologies that provide facility operators and security personnel
with confidence that authorized aircraft can be distinguished from unauthorized aircraft.
That requirement must include ground-based systems that meet the specifications above.
The Need for Layered Airspace Awareness
While mitigation authorities are beyond the scope of this rulemaking, detection and
tracking capabilities are essential to realizing the security benefits Congress envisioned
under Section 2209. The effectiveness of UAFRs ultimately depends on the ability of
authorized entities to identify, assess, and appropriately respond to unauthorized
operations through existing legal authorities and future frameworks established by
Congress. Echodyne views UAFRs as one component of a broader airspace security
architecture rather than as a standalone solution.
Effective protection requires persistent surveillance and situational awareness capabilities
capable of detecting both cooperative and non-cooperative aircraft. Ground-based radar
systems are one effective means of providing such independent surveillance of
cooperative and uncooperative aircraft regardless of equipage status, operator intent,
equipment functionality, weather, or time of day.
The FAA should explicitly state in the final rule that ground-based radar systems can
provide dual-use benefits that simultaneously support:
• Security operations around protected facilities
• C-UAS detection and assessment missions
• Situational awareness for authorized UAS operations
• Detection of non-cooperative aircraft
• Low-altitude airspace monitoring
• Support for scaled BVLOS operations
• Shared airspace awareness among public and private stakeholders

The FAA Should Encourage Dual-Use Infrastructure and Acknowledge the Need for
Future Mitigation Authorities
Airspace awareness technologies deployed to support Section 2209 facilities can provide
capabilities that extend well beyond facility protection.
The same infrastructure can support:
• C-UAS detection and assessment
• Shared low-altitude airspace awareness
• Emergency response operations
• Public safety missions
• Scaled BVLOS operations
• Advanced air mobility (AAM) integration
• Protection of critical infrastructure
The FAA should encourage facility operators to deploy dual-use systems capable of
supporting multiple public-interest objectives rather than narrowly tailoring deployments
to a single mission area.
Airspace restrictions alone do not prevent malicious actors from operating unmanned
aircraft near sensitive facilities. A UAFR establishes legal boundaries, but effective security
outcomes require the ability to detect, track, assess, and appropriately respond to
unauthorized aircraft activity.
For this reason, the FAA should acknowledge in the final rule that effective implementation
of Section 2209 will ultimately depend upon a layered security architecture that includes
detection and tracking capabilities and, where authorized by Congress and implemented
by appropriate federal agencies, carefully regulated mitigation authorities.
Many facilities eligible for protection under this NPRM are owned or operated by private-
sector entities responsible for critical national infrastructure, supported by professional
security organizations that routinely coordinate with federal, state, local, tribal, and
territorial (SLTT) authorities.
Echodyne encourages the FAA to coordinate with Congress, the Department of Homeland
Security (DHS), the Department of Justice (DOJ), and other relevant agencies to support
development of future frameworks that would permit qualified private-sector entities to
participate in appropriately authorized C-UAS activities under rigorous training,
certification, oversight, auditing, and accountability requirements comparable to those
applied to governmental operators.

Such a framework could be modeled on existing authorities available to federal agencies
and the recently granted authorities and associated requirements/training as part of the
SAFER SKIES Act in last year’s National Defense Authorization Act for SLTTs.
The final rule should acknowledge that:
• Airspace restrictions alone cannot stop malicious drone activity
• Detection and tracking capabilities are essential to effective enforcement
• Layered airspace awareness architectures improve both security and aviation safety
• Qualified private-sector security operators have an important role in critical
infrastructure protection
• Future mitigation frameworks should be developed with appropriate safeguards,
training standards, and federal oversight
A restriction without detection is difficult to enforce. A restriction without awareness does
not improve security. A restriction paired with layered detection, tracking, and
appropriately authorized response capabilities can provide meaningful protection for
critical infrastructure while preserving access to the NAS for legitimate operators.
Echodyne encourages the FAA to acknowledge in the preamble to this final rule that
effective implementation of Section 2209 will ultimately depend on a layered security
architecture that includes detection and tracking capabilities and, where separately
authorized by Congress and administered and overseen by the appropriate federal
agencies, carefully regulated mitigation authorities. Echodyne recognizes that this
rulemaking cannot provide such mitigation authority and that an act of Congress is
required; nonetheless, the FAA’s leadership in coordinating with Congress, DHS, DOJ,
and other agencies on the path forward would advance the security objectives
underlying Section 2209.
The FAA Should Recognize Radar-Derived Track Data as a Valid Source of Airspace
Awareness Information
As the FAA develops future architectures for UAFR notification, airspace awareness,
automated authorization, and broader low-altitude airspace integration, it should
recognize radar-derived track information as a valid and valuable source of operational
data.
Advanced radar systems can provide highly accurate tracking information for both
cooperative and non-cooperative aircraft and can supplement or validate information
received through Remote Identification (Remote ID), Automatic Dependent Surveillance –
Broadcast (ADS-B), UAS Traffic Management (UTM) systems, and other electronic

conspicuity technologies. Notably, ground-based advanced radar systems do not depend
on the aircraft’s willingness or ability to broadcast identification information, making it
a valuable tool for detecting non-cooperative or malfunctioning aircraft.
The FAA should ensure that future compliance frameworks remain flexible enough to
incorporate radar-derived surveillance data as an acceptable means of supporting:
• Situational awareness requirements
• Security monitoring requirements
• Automated notification architectures
• UAFR access verification
• Airspace deconfliction
• Future UTM implementations
• BVLOS safety services
Radar-derived track data can also help identify aircraft that are not broadcasting
identification information, are transmitting inaccurate information, or are otherwise
operating outside expected parameters.
As the agency continues implementation of advanced air mobility (AAM), BVLOS
operations, and digital airspace management systems, radar-derived surveillance
information should be viewed as a complementary and necessary data source that
strengthens overall system resilience and safety.
Conclusion
Echodyne commends the FAA for advancing implementation of Section 2209. The FAA
should ensure that the final rule remains focused on measurable security outcomes rather
than solely on geographic restrictions. To achieve those outcomes, UAFRs should be paired
with robust airspace awareness capabilities, and the rule should encourage deployment of
detection infrastructure that can serve multiple public-interest objectives, support safe
operation of authorized UAS activities, and recognize the important role that qualified
private-sector security operators can play in protecting critical infrastructure.
A layered approach – combining airspace restrictions, detection, shared situational
awareness, and, where separately authorized, appropriately regulated response
capabilities – will provide the strongest long-term foundation for both aviation safety and
national security.

Dear Ms. Ferritto,
On May 6, 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration proposed to enact an entirely new Part 74
to Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations ("Proposed Rule"), to implement the requirements of
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA). The Proposed Rule
would, for the first time, establish a process for applicants to request designation of restricted air
space for flights of Unmanned Aircraft over their facilities and to provide for flight restrictions in
such airspace. (91 Fed. Reg. 24650). Under the FESSA, the FAA may consider the following
factors when considering a request for an unmanned aircraft flight restriction (UAFR) zone:
aviation safety; protection of people and property on the ground; national security; and homeland
security.
Consistent with Executive Order 14305, Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty, the Preamble
to the Proposed Rule indicates that the FAA is proposing to limit facilities eligible for an UAFR
to those that are fixed site facilities and meet the definition of critical infrastructure in 42 U.S.C.
1

§5195c(e). Under that statute, " critical infrastructure" is defined as "systems and assets, whether
physical or virtual, so vital to the United States that the incapacity or destruction of such systems
and assets would have a debilitating effect on security, national economic security, national public
health or safety, or any combination of those matters." Under the proposed Part 74, the FAA
would consider whether an applicant could demonstrate that a UAFR is necessary for aviation
safety, protection of people and property on the ground, national security, or homeland security.
Venture Global supports the development of this UAFR program by the FAA as it represents a
significant step in protection of the nation's critical energy infrastructure, including facilities such
as those owned and operated by Venture Global to produce liquefied natural gas ("LNG") for
export. Venture Global was founded in 2013 and is a long-term, low-cost provider of American-
produced liquefied natural gas. Venture Global is operating, commissioning, constructing, and
developing multiple LNG export facilities in Louisiana, utilizing modular, mid-scale liquefaction
technology and an owner-led procurement and construction strategy, that seeks to reduce costs and
compress construction timelines to the benefit of its off-takers.
Venture Global's inaugural project, Calcasieu Pass, a 10.0 MTPA nameplate liquefaction
facility located in Cameron Parish, Louisiana, took Final Investment Decision (FID) in August
2019. Venture Global TransCameron Pipeline supplies natural gas to Calcasieu Pass.
Commissioning of Calcasieu Pass began in January 2022, and the first commissioning cargo was
loaded in March 2022 and delivered to Europe. Calcasieu Pass has continued to produce and export
LNG to more than 20 countries. The majority of the cargos have been delivered to Europe.
Thus, Calcasieu Pass continues to serve in the national interest by furthering national energy and
security goals by assisting in achieving the United States' commitment to the European Union to
provide U.S.-sourced natural gas to offset reductions in oil and natural gas that EU countries
previously acquired from Russia.
Venture Global took final investment decision (FID) on the first phase of its second
project, Plaquemines LNG, a 20.0 MTPA nameplate liquefaction facility in Plaquemines Parish,
Louisiana, in May 2022 and completed FID on the second phase in March 2023. Phase 1
of Plaquemines LNG began commissioning in May 2024 and exported its first LNG
commissioning cargo in December 2024. Venture Global Gator Express Pipeline supplies the
Plaquemines facility with natural gas.
In 2025, Venture Global began construction on its third project, CP2 LNG, a 20.0 MTPA
nameplate liquefaction facility that is being built adjacent to Calcasieu Pass. CP2 LNG is expected
to begin exporting its initial commissioning LNG cargos in 2027. The Venture Global CP Express
Pipeline System, which includes the Moss Lake Compressor Station in Calcasieu Parish,
Louisiana, will supply natural gas from sources in Texas and Louisiana to the CP2 LNG export
facility.
Venture Global has raised more than $100 billion in total capital since inception to support the
development of its projects. Since its founding, Venture Global has developed production capacity
of 68 MTPA that is in operation, in commissioning or under construction, of which more than 50
MTPA is subject to executed fixed price LNG long and medium-term Sales and Purchase
2

Agreements with a portfolio of high credit quality customers. Venture Global has targeted 100
MTPA total production capacity from its current and future LNG facilities.
Natural gas is a critical fuel source now and for the future and Venture Global intends to deliver
reliable and competitively priced LNG to the world. With lower cost LNG, more global, growing
economies will realize the environmental benefits of clean-burning natural gas. In addition to
improving the United States' balance of trade and strengthening relationships with our allies,
Venture Global's projects will support billions of dollars in new state and local revenue that will
have widespread positive economic impact and improve lives.
In addition to these benefits, the U.S. Department of Energy ("DOE") has consistently recognized
the geopolitical benefits of LNG exports. In its authorization for Plaquemines LNG to export LNG
to non-free trade agreement nations, for instance, DOE explained:
an efficient, transparent international market for natural gas with diverse sources of
supply provides both economic and strategic benefits to the United States and our
allies. Indeed, increased production of domestic natural gas has significantly
reduced the need for the United States to import LNG. In global trade, LNG
shipments that would have been destined to U.S. markets have been redirected to
Europe and Asia, improving energy security for many of our key trading partners.
To the extent U.S. exports can diversify global LNG supplies and increase the
volumes of LNG available globally, these exports will improve energy security for
many U.S. allies and trading partners.'
DOE's most recent authorization issued for the Venture Global CP2 LNG project, reached the
same conclusion2 and added the following more current observations:
• in light of the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, there continue to be concerns
about energy security for Europe and Central Asia, particularly given the relative
share of Russian natural gas supplied to those regions until recently, with continued
risk due to the now-expired agreement for the supply of Russian natural gas to
Europe.'
• Further, the European Commission recently proposed a legally binding ban on
European Union (EU) imports of Russian natural gas by the end of 2027, and
signaled that, to replace Russian supplies, the EU "could import more U.S. LNG"
among other measures.4
• Further, the United States has an increasingly important role in the EU's natural
gas supply. As the agreement allowing the transit of Russian natural gas through
Ukraine expired at the end of 2024, "[i]ncreasing LNG imports from trustworthy
global partners is key to fully eliminating the EU's reliance on Russian fossil fuels."
