In short, LNG produced by Venture Global LNG terminals is of critical geo-political importance.
Therefore, protection of LNG terminals from geo-political threats is crucial to national security
and national interests.
Recent world events have illustrated that LNG export operations and natural gas infrastructure are
at risk from drones that can be are weaponized by sophisticated nefarious actors. Further, the
increasing proliferation of drones and ease of public access to drone technology pose risk even
from those acting with good intentions, but who lack the knowledge or skill to avoid damage to
such infrastructure. While Venture Global facilities are designed to extremely high safety
standards, regulatory oversight of the type proposed in this rulemaking is necessary to protect
critical energy infrastructure to enhance local, state, and national security.
Indeed, Venture Global facilities have experienced several incidents involving drone incursions .
Venture Global is providing information on these incidents in a confidential submittal to the FAA
under this docket.
For these reasons, Venture Global strongly supports the basic structure and goals of the Proposed
Rule and urges the FAA to implement a program to create Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction
(UAFR) zones as promptly as possible. Venture Global is concerned about the cumbersome
process required by the Proposed Rule for facilities to supply vulnerability information and be
subject to FAA review and approval even where that same security and vulnerability information
has been reviewed by the Coast Guard and FERC. Venture Global requests that the FAA develop
a fast-track approval procedure for LNG terminals and other similarly situated facilities. In
addition, Venture Global offers the following comments for the FAA's consideration:
5

1. The FAA Should Act Expeditiously to Adopt UAFR Rules and Should Streamline
the Process for Approval of UAFRs.
It has been a decade since Congress enacted the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016
(P.L. 114-190) directing the FAA to establish an application process for owners and operators of
sixteen categories of critical infrastructure sites and amusement parks to request that FAA
designate surrounding airspace as "off-limits" to drones.13 Venture Global applauds the FAA for
initiating this critical program which has been delayed for so long and urges the FAA to complete
this rulemaking as soon as possible, consistent with legal requirements.
During this decade numerous safety incidents involving drones have been reported both domestic
and abroad. Drone use has proliferated and drone technology has become increasingly advanced.
As cited in a Congressional Research Report, terrorists have used drones to conduct
reconnaissance as well as to drop explosives. Both nations involved in the Russia-Ukraine war
have used drones extensively. Although small drones in the U.S. may seem incapable of mass
destruction, they could cause considerable impact if equipped with explosives or chemical,
biological, or radiological weapons.
To assist in combating these risks, the FAA should make every effort to streamline the proposed
procedure for establishing UAFRs. The procedure as proposed will take considerable time and
resources to implement as it requires a significant amount of information for the application, an
agency review process, publication of a proposed UAFR in the Federal Register, a 30-day
comment period, and final decision. The FAA should consider an abbreviated application process
that allows incorporation of risk assessments already undertaken by other agencies to substitute
for FAA review. For example, as discussed below, where a facility is regulated by the Maritime
Transportation Security Act, and has a Coast Guard approved Facility Security Plan, a UAFR
should be issued automatically upon submission of the boundary information and self-certification
that the facility has a Remote Identification detection program or equivalent. Other types of
facilities may also be good candidates for self-certification, with the FAA retaining the power to
modify or revoke the UAFR if evidence warrants such. The FAA could also consider a UAFR as
presumptively valid when it issues the public notice, with the UAFR to remain in effect unless
modified as a result of public comment.
2. The FAA Should Create an Automatic Approval Process for Facilities Subject to
the Maritime Transportation Security Act Regulations to the Extent Subject to an
Approved Coast Guard Facility Security Plan.
Proposed § 74.89(i) for the Transportation Sector extend potential eligibility for a UAFR to any
"facility regulated by the MTSA and currently has an active Facility Security Plan (FSP) or is
covered by Commandant [Coast Guard] approved Alternate Security Plan (ASP)." Venture
13 For more information on the background the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, see: Elias. B.. Frittelli,
J. Goldman, B., Jaikaran, C.. Marshall, J., and Parfomak, P.(May 23, 2025). Transportation Security: Background and Issues
for the 119th Congress, (Report No. R48543). Library of Congress, Congressional Research Service, available at:
https: ‘vm,.conszress.gov crs-product R48543s. Accessed July 2026.
6

Global's facilities at each of its terminals are regulated by the Maritime Transportation Security
Act (MTSA) and have Coast Guard approved FSPs.
The FAA proposes under new 14 C.F.R. § 74.56 the sites would be required to upload application
information concerning vulnerability assessments and information to demonstrate they meet all of
the following security requirements:
(1) Access to the facility, certain areas or key components must be restricted
(2) The facility must have designated security personnel
(3) The facility must have security monitoring
(4) Must include the capability, either directly or through a contracted service, to receive
broadcast Remote Identification messages from unmanned aircraft operating within or in
close proximity to the requested unmanned aircraft flight restriction.
MTSA-regulated facilities such as the Venture Global terminals were required to complete a
Facility Security Assessment (FSA) in accordance with 33 C.F.R. Part 105, Subpart C, to identify
and evaluates critical assets, critical infrastructure, potential threats to the critical assets and
infrastructures, and also to identify potential general facility security vulnerabilities. To address
the vulnerabilities identify in the FSA, the facility must then develop and submit a Facility Security
Plan (FSP) meeting the requirements of 33 C.F.R Part 105, Subpart D, to the Coast Guard for
review and approval. The FSP is also to specify requirements for training and periodic drills to
prepare for security incidents. The FSP, which must be approved by the Coast Guard, is valid for
five years, after which time the facility must submit an updated FSP for re-approval. The Coast
Guard conducts annual FSP audits/inspections to ensure that the facility is complying with the
FSP.
Venture Global requests that the FAA amend the proposed application process to provide that any
facility with an approved FSP will obtain an automatic UAFR upon submittal of information
defining the boundaries of the UAFR the and a certification that it has the ability to receive
broadcast Remote Identification messages from UAS in the vicinity. This UAFR would then be
publicly noticed as presumptively valid unless and until the FAA takes measures to modify the
UAFR. This process would build upon the already robust review process undertaken by the Coast
Guard and would allow the FAA to focus resources on other classes of facilities that are eligible
for a UAFR.
3. LNG Export Terminals Regulated by PHMSA Under 49 C.F.R. Part 193 Should
Be Specifically Added to Proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.88.
Under the FAA's proposal, only fixed-site (permanent, non-mobile) facilities that meet the
definition of "critical infrastructure" in 42 U.S.C. § 5195c(e), which includes sixteen (16) critical
infrastructure sectors identified in the National Security Memorandum (NSM-22) on Critical
Infrastructure Security and Resilience,14 may apply for a designation of an unmanned aircraft flight
restriction (UAFR) zone above their facility. In addition, facilities in these sectors would need to:
14 See: https: .www.cisa.gov:topics'critical-infrastructure-security-and-resilience national-security-memorandum-
critical-infrastructure-securitk -and-resilience.
7

• meet specific criteria designed to ensure UAFRs are available only to those facilities at
which drone operations above or near them present safety or security threats; and
• have at least one critical asset or component that is vulnerable to drone operations.
Proposed § 74.88 "Energy sector" lists what specific types of fixed facilities within the energy
sector that will qualify for establishment of a UAFR. It currently provides a list of three types of
facilities that includes electricity facilities, oil refineries, and natural gas facilities that process
natural gas into dry natural gas.15 This Energy Sector list does not specifically enumerate LNG
export terminals. As noted above, proposed § 74.89(i) for the Transportation Sector does extend
potential coverage under the program to any "facility regulated by the MTSA and currently has an
active Facility Security Plan (FSP) or is covered by Commandant approved Alternate Security
Plan (ASP)." Venture Global's dockside facilities at each of its terminals are regulated by the
Maritime Transportation Security Act and have FSPs. However, in order to ensure that the entire
LNG terminal, and not just the dockside and associated equipment are eligible for a UAFR,
Venture Global requests that the FAA add a new subsection (d) to this rule providing as follows:
(d) Liquefied natural gas facilities subject to the security requirements of 49 C.F.R.
Part 193.
LNG export terminals subject to 49 C.F.R. Part 193 are vital to national security and the national
economy and certainly should be categorized as "critical infrastructure." The term "critical
infrastructure" as used under NSM-22 means " the physical and virtual assets and systems so vital
to the Nation that their incapacity or destruction would have a debilitating impact on national
security, national economic security, or national public health or safety." Moreover, a significant
unmanned aircraft attack on key portions of an LNG facility could pose a risk to public health and
safety. The importance of security measures for LNG facilities is illustrated by PHMSA's
adoption of Subpart J of Part 193, which requires a plethora of security measures to protect the
safety of LNG facilities.
4. Establishing the Dimensions of UAFRs
a. Lateral Boundary
The Proposed Rule at 14 C.F.R. § 74.58 establishes the lateral boundary of a UAFR as not to
exceed the applicant facility property boundary. It states:
(a) The applicant must provide a description of the lateral boundary for the
requested unmanned aircraft flight restriction.
(b) The lateral boundary of the unmanned aircraft flight restriction must be
narrowly tailored to the specific security concern and may not:
(1) Exceed the fixed site facility property boundary; or
(2) Overlap in whole or in part with a permanent airspace restriction.
15 LNG facilities do not process natural gas into dry natural gas; instead, they liquefy natural gas for transport.
8

However, the FAA indicated that it would consider revising the rule to allow for asked for
expansion beyond the property line and requested comments on what distance beyond the property
line would be appropriate and why.
Venture Global suggests that the FAA adopt a provision that would provide for automatic
acceptance at the property boundary plus 100 feet as a minimum, with the ability of the applicant
to request extension based on particular safety and/or security factors. In the alternative, the FAA
could modify the proposed rule to provide that the horizontal extent of the UAFR is at the property
boundary effective immediately upon submittal of the application while any extended horizontal
zone is under review.
A 100-foot "halo" beyond the property boundary is necessary to enhance protection from both
intentional and inadvertent UAS incursions. Although FAA has adopted rules that require
certifications for operators who use of UAS for commercial purposes; thus ensuring such operators
are at least aware of the rules and have undergone a security threat assessment, such rules do not
apply to recreational UAS users, who do not undergo security assessments and may operate drones
at low altitudes. While many of these drones may be equipped with geofencing systems that allow
them to detect UAFR boundaries,16 there is no federal law requiring geofencing technology on
drones.
Venture Global employs flares at each of its LNG export terminals to control emissions from
startups, shutdowns, and maintenance activities requiring clearing of gases from the equipment.
In addition, each terminal has a marine flare to control gas-up and cool-downs from the LNG
vessels. Flying drones near an industrial flare stack is dangerous without proper planning as the
flare may have a zone of radiant heat which can also contribute to air turbulence in the area. Flares
can have a temperature of 1800°F or more at the flare tip, with an exit velocity of 65 feet/second
or more. The radiant heat could cause damage to the battery, electronic components and any plastic
components of the drone. Most drones cannot be safely operated if the air temperature in proximity
is 104 °F or more because higher temperatures can impair the functioning of their batteries and
electronics. Although this may be of greater concern for the vertical boundary of the UAFR, in
some cases, where a flare is near the property boundary, this could also be of concern for the
horizontal boundary. A damaged or out-of-control drone could then pose safety issues for the area
within the property boundary.
Further, electromagnetic interference and unpredictable wind shear or high winds are factors which
can contribute to drone control problems. Venture Global terminals are located on waterways
accommodating ocean-going vessels, which are also areas prone to significant winds and wind
changes. Due to these factors, a drone should not be allowed to operate right at the facility
boundary. A 100-foot zone would provide some buffer for damaged or out-of-control UAS to land
without damage to the terminals.
Property eligible for the UAFR should include any property under the control of the applicant,
including any parent company or corporate entity under common control. Further, the type of
16 As noted in the Congressional Research Service report cited at footnote 13, infra:• "It was reported in January 2025
that after previously integrating geofencing capabilities on its drones for about a decade, Chinese drone manufacturer
DJI, which controls about 70% of the civilian drone market in the United States, had chosen to make use of these
features optional on its drones."
9

property rights subject to protection should include leased property and rights-of-way (servitudes),
in addition to ownership of the land. This should specifically extend to rights-of-way or servitudes
for pipelines or other infrastructure crossing a public road or thoroughfare to connect one portion
of the covered facility to another.
b. Extent of Altitude Ceiling of UAFR
The Proposed Rule limits the height of the UAFRs to 400 feet above ground level unless a facility
contains structures exceeding 300 feet in height. In that case, an additional 100 feet would be
allowed above any structure exceeding 300 feet in height, rounded to the next highest 50-foot
increment. The proposed vertical limits appear to be based on the FAA's existing rules for effort
small Unmanned Aircraft System operating limitations in 14 C.F.R. Part 107, which generally
limit UAS to flying no higher than 400 feet above ground surface. However, UAS are capable of
flying to heights 3000 feet and above and have been known to pose risk to aircraft at those altitudes.
Venture Global believes a limit of 400 feet (with the ability to add an additional 100 feet if a
structure onsite is greater than 300 feet tall) is insufficient to fully protect its facilities from the
dangers posed by UAS.
Venture Global terminals contain flare stacks up to 197 feet tall with exit gas temperatures of over
1000°F; thus possessing a thermal plume that can rise higher than 400 feet. In addition, its hot oil
heater stacks are up to 160 feet tall, with exit temperatures that can be up to 450 °F. Each of
Venture Global's LNG terminals will also have communications infrastructure, cranes, and other
industrial assets that can exceed 150 to 250 feet in height. Under 14 C.F.R. §107.51(b), small UAS
may operate up to 400 feet above a structure's immediate uppermost limit. Thus, a drone could
legally fly at 400 feet, only 203 feet above one of Venture Global's flares while remaining
compliant with the vertical boundary in the Proposed Rule. This would pose an obvious danger to
the drone as well as to Venture Global employees on the ground or to equipment that may be
damaged by a falling drone.
The risk posed by drones flying at only 400 feet above Venture Global terminals is not solely the
danger posed by the drone's physical presence but also extends to the ability of the UAS to acquire
sensitive critical infrastructure information. A drone flying at just over 400 feet over its LNG
terminals, equipped with readily available high-resolution cameras with optical zoom capabilities,
thermal imaging systems, wireless signal collection technologies, and other advanced surveillance
devices would allow the drone operator to collect security sensitive information while remaining
in compliance with the proposed UAFR limits. In addition, some drones may be deployed with
equipment capable of disrupting wireless network or other communication systems that could
wreak havoc on terminal operations.
For these reasons, Venture Global requests that the FAA extend the vertical limit of a UAFR
ceiling to 800 feet as a default, with the ability of an applicant to request a higher vertical limit
based on site-specific conditions. While this measure would not eliminate all risks posed by UAS,
it would substantially strengthen the protectiveness of the rule.
10

5. Application Process - Protection of Submitted Sensitive Critical Energy
Infrastructure and Security Information
The proposed application process for establishment of a UAFR requires an applicant to provide
security and incident response plans and other potentially confidential and security sensitive
information such as a vulnerability analysis, information on the consequences of those
vulnerabilities and other operational information to justify the application. Venture Global has
concern about creating a central repository of such Security Sensitive Information that could be
subject to cyber-attack. Much of this information will already be protected under other federal
government programs. Instead of requiring that an applicant must submit this information, the
FAA should provide a procedure where the applicant can self-certify that the facility has
vulnerabilities to drone acquisition of information or physical harm and that such vulnerabilities
have been assessed as part of the requirements of another federal agency.
For example, Facility Security Plans (FSPs) under the MTSA are highly protected. As noted
above, Facility Security Plans and vulnerability assessments are protected by the MTSA rules (33
C.F.R. §105.400) which specify that such must be protected in accordance with 49 C.F.R. Part
1520 (U.S. DOT Rules for Protection of Security Sensitive Information for all Modes of
Transportation). There should be no need for the FAA to duplicate the review already performed
by the Coast Guard in its review and approval of the FSP.
For LNG facilities and interstate natural gas pipelines, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
("FERC") regulations protect Critical Energy/Electrical Infrastructure Information ("CEII") under
18 C.F.R. §388.113. Applicants for LNG export facilities as well as interstate gas pipelines and
compressor stations must submit detailed engineering and security sensitive information to FERC
in order to obtain authorization to operate under Sections 3 and 7 of the Natural Gas Act. FERC's
regulation 18 C.F.R. §388.113 provides detailed procedures for obtaining CEII designation for
sensitive information as well as procedures for sharing such information with other federal
agencies. The purpose of providing vulnerability information to the FAA is to allow the FAA to
determine whether such information justifies creation of a UAFR. The fact that FERC and the
Coast Guard have already protected such information is based on their expertise that such
information justifies protection.
Venture Global requests that the FAA include provisions in the final rule providing that facilities
subject to a FSP under the MTSA and LNG facilities subject to PHMSA 49 C.F.R. Part 193,
Subpart J, and FERC Natural Gas Act approvals automatically qualify for a UAFR to the extent
covered by a Coast Guard approved FSP or subject to CEII designation before the FERC without
providing vulnerability and consequence information. In the alternative, Venture Global requests
that the FAA allow an applicant to self-certify that it meets the safety and security criteria in to
qualify for a UAFR but without having to reveal sensitive security information on vulnerabilities
and consequences of those vulnerabilities.
At a minimum, the FAA should ensure that its regulations protect Security Sensitive Information
to the same extent as provided in the FERC regulations for Critical Energy and Electric
Infrastructure Information at 18 C.F.R. §388.113 to clearly protect any application materials from
11

public disclosure and to coordinate these procedures with the requirements from other federal
agencies with jurisdiction over the safety and security of LNG facilities.
6. Application Requirements- Remote Identification System
Current FAA regulations require nonmilitary drones to broadcast position information and a
unique identifier, referred to as a "Remote ID." In proposed Section 74.56, the FAA will require
that an applicant must demonstrate in its application that the facility has the capability, either
directly or through a contracted service, to receive broadcast Remote Identification messages from
unmanned aircraft operating within or in close proximity to the requested UAFR]. Venture Global
supports this proposed requirement with the flexibility that the applicant have the ability, directly
or through a contracted service, to receive broadcast Remote Identification messages. In addition,
because Remote Identification technology will not be able to detect illegal drones not broadcasting
their Remote ID, Venture Global requests that the FAA provide in the rule that it will allow more
advanced lawful passive approaches (acoustic, electro-optical, infrared, and multi-sensor fusion)
as an alternative if such systems provide an equivalent or superior means of meeting the proposed
requirement.
7. Potential Delays in Processing Applications
The sheer volume of comments on the Proposed Rule underscores the FAA's statement in the
Preamble to the Proposed Rule that it was concerned that the anticipated number of applications
would be significant, leading to delays in processing the applications. To avoid or minimize these
delays, and to the extent that the FAA does not adopt an automatic approval for facilities subject
to an FSP, Venture Global requests that the FAA consider a phased approach whereby applications
for significant energy and maritime critical sectors, including LNG export terminals are prioritized.
As noted above, facilities regulated under the MTSA with active FSPs could be processed first,
with acceptance of a self-certification approach. Similarly, LNG export facilities that have
demonstrated compliance with PHMSA/FERC requirements under 49 C.F.R. Part 193, Subpart J,
could be easily processed based on meeting those standards. A phased approach would allow FAA
reviewers to gain experience with facilities that should not require much additional information to
qualify for a UAFR, and then to proceed later with facilities that require a more detailed case-by-
case review because not already regulated under another federal agency's security requirements.
Venture Global further encourages the FAA to begin immediately with increasing its staffing and
technical expertise to meet the anticipated demand for UAFR designations.
8. Enforcement
Proposed Section 14 C.F.R. § 74.260 provides for criminal penalties, civil penalties, loss of
licenses and certifications for offenders. Venture Global requests that this provision be amended
to add the ability to issue a cease-and-desist order and/or to seek injunctive relief. This would
enable the FAA to address potential situations where probable cause exists that unlawful activity
is planned or imminent and to obtain an injunction against a repeat offender.
12

Conclusion
Venture Global appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Proposed Rule and appreciates the
efforts of the FAA to develop the Proposed Rule which marks a critical first step in establishing a
framework for a comprehensive airspace security system. We look forward to continued
cooperation with the FAA and other agency stakeholders to enhance the safety and security of our
facilities.
Sincerely,
%--rfi•,,i4w-t,i1,7t,btai.b.
Maureen N. Harbourt
Senior Counsel, Environmental and Regulatory
VENTURE GLOBAL LNG
13

In times of increased concern about animal welfare, I see no reason for giving the food and agriculture sector a type of special protection that would hide from the public how they conduct their business. The FAA has not identified an economic, national-security, public-health, or safety justification for allowing the food and agriculture sector to obtain flight restrictions. Drone footage supports accountability by documenting pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims. Do not develop criteria or grant these restrictions. Thank you.

In an age of growing surveillance, Factory Farms should not be immune. There is limited transparency when it comes to these massive operations, and drove footage is one vital tool we have to maintaining order and preserving our society's humanity. Do not prohibit drones from flying over factory farms.

An amusement park is not "critical infrastructure".  They are neither critical nor infrastructure under any meaning of either word.  The fact that it appears in the same sentence as energy production facilities seems to be evidence that theme park industry lobbyists are crafting this regulation to help their clients.  Disney has successfully kept aircraft away from its Orlando parks for decades under an outdated TFR.  Other theme parks are enamored with the idea of keeping their airspace free of photographers that do not pay them.  Other parks, like the now bankrupt Miami Seaquarium have employed SLAPP suits to prevent drone operators from exposing their abuse of animals onsite.  This regulation will help amusement parks, many of which keep animals for commercial profit, better hidden from people that care about animal welfare.  There is no legitimate reason to prevent air traffic of any kind over an amusement park.  I strongly urge you to remove amusement parks from the proposed regulation.

Private organizations that have critical infrastructure should absolutely have the right to restrict their airspace from members of the public flying UAS/drones overhead. For that matter, any private property owners should be allowed to restrict their airspace from penetration by non-government actors without a warrant.

comments.commenter: Comment from Humane World for Animals and Humane World Action Fund
comments.organization: Humane World for Animals and Humane World Action Fund
comments.comment_text:
1255 23rd St. NW, Suite 450
Washington, DC 20037
humaneworld.org
humaneaction.org
August 5, 2026
U.S. Department of Transportation
Docket Operations
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Room W58-213
West Building 5th Floor,
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Dear Ms. Ferritto:
On behalf of Humane World for Animals and Humane World Action Fund, we appreciate the
opportunity to provide comments on the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking regarding the establishment of Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) for
certain fixed-site facilities. Humane World for Animals is dedicated to protecting animals through
advocacy, investigations, public education and policy reform. Our work frequently involves
documenting conditions at animal agriculture facilities, commercial animal breeding operations, fur
farms and other animal-related enterprises that are often inaccessible to the public.
While we recognize the importance of protecting facilities where bona fide aviation safety, national
security, homeland security or public safety concerns exist, we are concerned that the proposed rule
could inadvertently restrict lawful aerial documentation that serves significant public interests. In
particular, agricultural operations and animal-related facilities that may seek UAFRs often operate
largely outside of public view. Drone technology has become an important tool for documenting
environmental conditions, animal welfare concerns, consumer protection issues and other matters of
public significance that would otherwise be difficult or impossible to observe.
Environmental accountability and landscape-level impacts
Large-scale agricultural operations can generate environmental impacts that extend far beyond
property boundaries. Improper waste disposal, including manure runoff, waste lagoon leaks,
unauthorized discharge into waterways, long-term carcass disposal, soil contamination, open burning
and improper chemical disposal, can affect surrounding ecosystems, neighboring communities and
public resources.
Many of these impacts are difficult—if not impossible—to assess from ground level. Aerial
observation provides a broader and more accurate understanding of how pollutants move across the
landscape and affect surrounding areas. Drone imagery can help identify waste runoff pathways,
impacts to streams and wetlands, vegetation stress, algae blooms and other indicators of
environmental degradation. It can also reveal conditions that would otherwise be obscured by
topography, fencing, buildings, vegetation or the remote location of facilities.

2
Importantly, environmental harm often occurs not only at the point where waste is generated or
disposed of, but throughout the larger watershed and ecosystem. Aerial perspectives help
demonstrate the full scope of these impacts and provide valuable information for public officials,
researchers, journalists and community members seeking to understand environmental conditions
affecting public lands and shared natural resources.
Demonstrative housing and husbandry concerns
Aerial surveillance also serves a unique role in documenting animal welfare conditions at facilities
housing large numbers of animals.
Many operations, including concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs), calf ranches, cattle
operations, equine facilities, fur farms and large-scale kennels, maintain hundreds or even thousands
of animals outdoors or in semi-outdoor environments. These animals may be exposed to extreme
heat, cold, precipitation and other environmental conditions that can significantly affect their health
and welfare.
Because views into these facilities are often limited, aerial documentation can provide important
insight into conditions that may warrant additional investigation. Drone imagery can reveal
overcrowding, inadequate shelter, improper carcass storage or disposal, failure to remove deceased
animals, accumulation of waste, fire hazards and evidence suggesting animals may lack adequate
access to food or water.
These observations can provide critical evidence that helps identify situations requiring review by
appropriate authorities. This type of transparency serves both animal welfare and broader public
health interests, particularly where animal housing conditions may affect disease transmission,
sanitation, food safety or environmental quality.
Transport and animal handling practices
Animals are especially vulnerable during transportation and loading operations. The process of
loading and unloading animals into transport vehicles presents heightened risks for injury, stress and
mishandling.
Many of these activities occur on private property and are not visible from public roads. Aerial
observation can help document practices that may raise concerns regarding animal treatment,
including the handling of non-ambulatory animals, abandonment, improper euthanasia, dragging of
animals or the use of excessively forceful handling methods. Drone footage has the potential to
provide objective documentation of activities that otherwise would occur entirely outside public
view.
Restricting access to aerial observation could significantly reduce transparency regarding animal
handling practices at precisely those moments when independent oversight is most needed.
Documentation of potentially unlawful activities
Drone surveillance can also play an important role in identifying activities occurring on the grounds
of licensed facilities that may nevertheless violate applicable laws or regulations.
Aerial imagery may reveal waste pits, burn sites, burial areas, improperly maintained waste storage
systems, unauthorized construction or other activities that warrant further investigation. It can also

3
help identify the housing of unregistered or prohibited animal species, improper food handling
operations, unlawful land uses or other conditions that may present risks to animals, workers,
neighboring communities or the environment.
In some circumstances, aerial documentation may even reveal evidence of unrelated unlawful
activity occurring on facility grounds, including substandard worker housing conditions or other
activities affecting human welfare and safety. Because such operations are frequently located in
isolated areas with limited public access, aerial observation may be among the few available
mechanisms for identifying concerns requiring additional scrutiny.
Consumer protection and transparency
Aerial documentation has become increasingly important in helping consumers evaluate claims made
by agricultural and animal-related businesses.
Consumers are often asked to pay premium prices based on representations regarding animal welfare,
humane treatment, environmental stewardship, housing conditions or husbandry practices.
Independent aerial observation may provide one of the only means through which those claims can
be evaluated.
For example, investigations have demonstrated circumstances in which drone footage has
contradicted public marketing claims regarding the conditions under which animals were raised.
Such documentation helps ensure that consumers receive accurate information and can make
informed purchasing decisions.
This concern is particularly relevant to the commercial dog breeding industry. Humane World for
Animals has documented increasing efforts by certain breeding facilities to visually obscure breeding
and housing conditions from public roads and neighboring properties. Yet consumers frequently
purchase animals based on representations that dogs are raised in family environments or maintained
according to high welfare standards. Drone technology has become one of the few available tools
capable of providing independent documentation of actual facility conditions and bringing
transparency to an industry that often operates with limited public visibility.
Community impacts and facility proximity
Aerial imagery also provides critical context regarding the relationship between agricultural facilities
and surrounding communities.
Many facilities are located in close proximity to residential neighborhoods, schools, daycare centers,
parks, conservation lands, wetlands and other sensitive areas. While maps may provide some
information, aerial documentation offers a uniquely effective way of illustrating the real-world
relationship between facilities and nearby properties.
This is particularly relevant for facilities such as fur farms, breeding operations and certain animal
agriculture enterprises. Aerial imagery can help document circumstances in which facilities housing
large numbers of animals are located immediately adjacent to homes, businesses, childcare facilities
or environmentally sensitive areas. Such documentation can also help illustrate the potential impacts
of waste management practices, odors, noise, runoff and other conditions affecting neighboring
communities.
Information regarding facility proximity and surrounding land uses is often important to discussions
concerning environmental quality, public health, community planning and regulatory compliance.

4
Restricting aerial observation of these facilities could reduce the public's ability to understand and
evaluate impacts occurring within their own communities.
Conclusion
Humane World for Animals and Humane World Action Fund support efforts to address legitimate
aviation safety and security concerns. However, the FAA should carefully consider the broader
public interests served by lawful drone operations before authorizing restrictions that could limit
transparency around agricultural and animal-related facilities.
Drone technology has become an important tool for documenting environmental conditions,
identifying animal welfare concerns, monitoring transport and handling practices, promoting
consumer protection and improving public understanding of how facilities interact with surrounding
communities. In many instances, aerial observation provides information that cannot be obtained
through any other practical means.
As the FAA implements Section 2209, it should ensure that the final rule is narrowly tailored and
does not inadvertently curtail lawful activities that support public accountability, environmental
stewardship, animal welfare, informed consumer decision-making and public awareness of issues
occurring at facilities that are otherwise largely shielded from view.
Respectfully submitted,
Rebecca Sutton Gillian Lyons
Specialist, Public and Corporate Policy Director, Regulatory Affairs
Farm Animal Protection Humane World Action Fund
Humane World for Animals

comments.commenter: Comment from Information Technology Industry Council (ITI)
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
Bryan Bedford
Administrator
Federal Aviation Administration
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Washington, D.C. 20590
Re: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility (Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03)
Dear Administrator Bedford,
ITI writes to provide the following comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration’s
(“FAA”) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NPRM”) on “Designation—Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,” which implements Section 2209 of
the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (hereinafter “Proposed Rule”).1
ITI represents 80 of the world’s leading information and communications technology (ICT)
companies. Our members manufacture the building blocks that power the digital infrastructure
undergirding the AI economy, including semiconductors, networking equipment, cooling systems,
and electrical solutions. Our members are also investing billions of dollars in expanding domestic
capacity for advanced semiconductor manufacturing and critical AI infrastructure like data
centers.
ITI strongly supports the FAA’s effort to address the threats posed by the unauthorized and
malicious use of unmanned aircraft systems (“UAS”) around critical infrastructure fixed site
facilities. We are concerned, however, that the rule as drafted creates some inadvertent, yet
significant security risks, while conversely failing to fully account for critical security needs. The
specific concerns are laid out below.
I. Significant Security Concerns Raised by the Proposed Rule
The proposed rule raises three acute security concerns:
1 Federal Aviation Administration, Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility, 91 FED. REG. 24,650 (proposed May 6, 2026) (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. pts. 1, 74, 91, 107),
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-05-06/pdf/2026-08943.pdf.

(i) Application Process: The Proposed Rule requires applicants to submit incredibly sensitive
information about facilities vulnerabilities and security plans that would, if leaked, hacked,
or otherwise shared would provide a how-to guide for malicious actors seeking to attack
critical infrastructure’s most sensitive facilities.2
(ii) Notice and Comment Period: The Proposed Rule creates a notice and comment period
that would reveal the location of facilities that have been conditionally approved for a flight
restriction, based on a FAA assessment of vulnerability and need, but before such flight
restrictions are in place – providing a roadmap of vulnerable but yet unprotected facilities
to attack.
(iii) Scope of Restrictions: Even once facilities are granted flight restrictions, facilities will be
unable to sufficiently manage threats in the airspace above their facilities. Commercial
and recreational drones will still be able fly over restricted airspace so long as they provide
advance notice and meet certain other criteria. Meanwhile, facility operators are restricted
in their ability to use their own drones for safety and security given new and unworkable
restrictions included in the proposed rule.
The following addresses each in more detail below.
A. Security Concerns Regarding the Application Process: § 74.66
The Proposed Rule would require applicants to “describe the weaknesses or gaps that may be
intentionally or unintentionally exploited” by a UAS and the consequences of those identified
vulnerabilities, if exploited by a UAS.3 Applicants are also required to describe current security
plans and how the flight restrictions would be integrated into those plans to reduce risk.4 These
provisions would require the sharing of highly sensitive data that, if made public (whether
intentionally or not), would give adversaries a how-to guide for attacking sensitive facilities.
The proposed rule does not include any details about how such information would be safeguarded.
There is no information on secure transmission protocols or safeguards. But even if subject to such
safeguards and other protections from public disclosure, the centralization of so much sensitive
and valuable threat information would create a honeypot that adversaries would almost certainly
seek to exploit and access. Increased cyber vulnerabilities in light of increasingly sophisticated AI
make these risks even more acute.
To address these risks, ITI recommends the following:
2 Id. at 24687 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.66(b), (c)).
3 See Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg at 24687 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.66(b), (c)). Vulnerability is defined broadly, as
“something in a fixed site facility's infrastructure, software systems, operations, or procedures that an unmanned aircraft
could exploit or inadvertently interfere with in a way that could harm the facility, impede the facility's mission, or present
a hazard to people or property.” Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24664.
4 Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24687 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.66(d)).

• Create a self-attestation process regarding vulnerabilities, consequences of exploitation,
and security plans. Require applicants to maintain documentation in support of the self-
certification, which can be reviewed by the FAA, in coordination with the relevant Sector
Risk Management Agency (SRMA).
• This would protect against the disclosure of vulnerabilities and reduce administrative
burdens. It also would involve the relevant SRMAs, which are best equipped to know the
relevant industry and support the FAA in any assessment of risk and need.
B. Security Concerns Related to The Notice and Comment Process
The Proposed Rule envisions a public notice and comment period for each unmanned aerial flight
restriction (“UAFR”), request that is conditionally approved, unless the agency has “good cause”
to forgo that period.5 This process creates significant security concerns and appears to be based
on a misguided application of rules governing manned aircraft to flight restrictions governing low-
altitude airspace.
The notice and comment period would effectively put a target on a facility’s back alerting the world
that it deems itself vulnerable, has requested the protection of a UAFR but does not have one. This
creates significant security risk.
To address these risks, ITI recommends the following:
• Eliminate the notice and comment provision.
• Replace the pre-designation notice and comment with a post-designation process for
interested parties that are negatively affected by a UAFR to raise their concerns and petition
to modify or lift the UAFR subsequent to UAFR issuance.
C. The Scope of Proposed Restrictions Are Insufficient In Light of the Threat
The standard UAFR includes several exceptions for commercial and recreational drones that
provide advance notice to the FAA and fixed site facility, broadcast a remote ID, and transit the
UAFR in the shortest time practicable.6 This is significantly less restrictive than existing TFRs,
which generally require affirmative authorization or waiver to fly over a restricted area.
5 Id. (to be codified at § 74.100(c)).
6 Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24690 (to be codified at § 74.250(a)).

Broad, automatic exceptions undermine the security purpose of the Rule. It would allow operators
with no relationship to the facility, no site-specific need, no facility authorization, and no separate
emergency or public safety justification to enter protected airspace.
Of additional concern, these requirements—including the provision that UAS fly over restricted
facility in the least amount of time practicable—apply to the facility’s own drones, including those
used for a wide array of critical safety, security, inspection, maintenance, repair purposes. UAS
carrying out safety and security functions will often hover, circle, conduct repeated passes, or
otherwise operate for a duration longer than the shortest amount of time practicable. All such
functions would be barred under the rule as drafted.
To address these risks, ITI recommends the following:
• When there is a UAFR in effect, require commercial and recreational UAS operations to
obtain express approval by the relevant facility prior to operating.
• Authorize facility managers to maintain a list of approved drones that are permitted to
transit the protected airspace without restriction, which is essential to enabling inspection,
emergency response, and other safety and security-related operations.
II. Clarification on whether data centers – in particular large AI compute data centers
– fall within the Subpart C eligibility criteria
The Proposed Rule reaches data centers in two places, and neither clearly covers AI compute
facilities. The Communications sector criterion (§74.83) covers data centers with peak traffic
throughput of at least 1 terabit per second. That metric fits carrier hotels and internet exchange
points. The scale of an AI compute campus shows up in critical power load and compute density,
and many of the most consequential facilities in the country could fail a traffic throughput test. The
Information Technology sector criterion (§74.93) refers to "certain data center facilities," and we
could not locate a published threshold or description of which facilities qualify. As a result,
operators cannot determine eligibility before investing in an application that itself requires
sensitive disclosures.
This fits squarely within what the FAA has asked for. The preamble expressly requests comment on
limiting UAFRs to the sixteen sectors and on the minimum criteria FAA should apply to facility types
within them. We request the FAA to clarify in the final rule whether data centers are eligible under
§74.83 or §74.93.
To address this issue, ITI recommends the following:
• The. FAA should add an explicit, separate eligibility metric for data centers tied to critical IT
load or dedicated power capacity in megawatts. FAA already uses capacity-based

thresholds elsewhere in Subpart C, including 500 MW for energy generation, so a
comparable, purpose-built metric for compute is in line with existing practice.
III. Clarification on the 24-month UAS activity requirement in § 74.66(a)
The Proposed Rule requires applicants to describe existing unmanned aircraft activity over the
preceding 24 months, qualified by "if available." That hedge suggests the FAA anticipated that
newer facilities would lack a long track record, but the rule does not specify what counts as an
acceptable substitute. This matters directly for newly commissioned facilities.
ITI requests the FAA to confirm that sector-wide threat assessments, SRMA input, or comparable-
facility incident data are acceptable substitutes for a facility's own historical record, and to confirm
that the absence of a 24-month incident history at a new-build site is not, on its own, grounds for
denial.
IV. Additional Technical Considerations
The Rule is premised, in part, on the continued use of Remote ID as the key technological means to
distinguish authorized and unauthorized drones. In light of evolving technology, the Rule should
create flexibility to enable the FAA to require either Remote ID, and associated detection
equipment or other equivalent technology, as approved by the FAA. This is needed to allow for the
technology to adapt over time, without requiring a new rulemaking.
ITI recommends the following:
• The FAA should not lock itself into Remote ID technology as the sole approved detection
technology.
• Instead, any requirement should reference Remote ID "or other technology designated by
the FAA for these purposes,” thereby preserving the agency's flexibility to update or
supplement these requirements as technology evolves, without the need to initiate a new
rulemaking proceeding.
We thank the FAA for the opportunity to comment on this important Proposed Rule. We look
forward to serving as a resource for the FAA on this subject and encourage you to reach out with
any questions or if additional input or materials would be helpful.
***

comments.commenter: Comment from Virginia Tech Mid-Atlantic Aviation Partnership
comments.comment_text:
August 5th, 2026
Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue SW
Washington, DC 20591
Re: Docket Number FAA- 2026-4558
Virginia Tech Mid-Atlantic Aviation Partnership comments regarding Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity
to a Fixed Site Facility
INTRODUCTION
The Virginia Tech Mid-Atlantic Aviation Partnership (MAAP) applauds the Federal Aviation
Administration (FAA) for continued progress toward integrating emerging aviation technologies into
the National Airspace System (NAS), including the recent Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) for
implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016. This rule
represents a critical step in advancing a more structured, transparent, and scalable framework for
enabling access to airspace over sensitive sites, while maintaining the safety and security of critical
infrastructure.
MAAP recognizes that the Section 2209 NPRM, in conjunction with other rulemaking efforts such as
the Part 108 BVLOS NPRM, reflects a broader shift toward enabling higher-density, more complex
operations—including uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) and advanced air mobility (AAM) within both
controlled and low-altitude airspace. As these operations scale, the ability to effectively define,
manage, and communicate airspace constraints will be essential not only for security purposes, but
also for maintaining efficiency and predictability for all airspace users.
As an FAA-designated UAS Test Site and FAA BEYOND partner, MAAP brings over a decade of
experience supporting the safe integration of new entrants into the NAS. This includes extensive
operational testing of beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) operations, development and validation of
detect-and-avoid (DAA) systems and Operations Over People (OOP) Means of Compliance, and
participation in UAS Traffic Management (UTM) - all in support of enabling novel UAS safety cases
and business models. Through these efforts, MAAP has developed a deep understanding of how to
balance regulatory, safety, and security needs with the need to enable new entrants and the public
benefit that follows. The Section 2209 NPRM is particularly relevant to MAAP’s work because it
directly affects how airspace access is defined and operationalized at low altitudes—where many
UAS and future AAM operations will occur. Effective implementation of Section 2209 will require
careful alignment with emerging traffic management paradigms, including ATC, UTM, and
automated data service providers. It will also require consideration of how airspace restrictions

interact with the need for automated, machine-to-machine, data services.
The potential security benefits of 2209 must be carefully balanced with the need to enable airspace
access. The proposed rule at best only makes lawful UAS operations transparent to the site operator.
However, it does not inherently address threats from nefarious UAS; which is arguably the primary
security risk. While having knowledge of the lawful flight operations is a helpful first step in
identifying nefarious UAS, it is far from being a comprehensive mitigation for protection of critical
infrastructure. Given this limited potential of 2209 to mitigate the broader risk, we believe that the
FAA should minimize impact on lawful UAS operators.
We respectfully offer the following comments in support of a framework that manages national
security needs while enabling continued innovation and safe integration of advanced aviation
operations into the NAS.
COMMENTS
I. Eligibility and Scope of UAFRs
A. §§74.54, 74.66 Sector Eligibility and Demonstration of Need
MAAP generally supports the FAA's decision to use definitions in 42 U.S.C. 5195c(e) to determine
UAFR eligibility for facilities within the sixteen critical infrastructure sectors identified in the NPRM.
However, the eligibility criteria is not entirely deterministic and depending on interpretation and
implementation details, has the potential to overly restrict significant portions of the NAS from lawful
aviation activities and to stifle economic and societal benefits of UAS.
The NPRM requests detailed vulnerability assessments and supporting analyses describing how
individual facilities may be susceptible to unmanned aircraft threats. While we believe the applicant
should be required to demonstrate need, the process should be managed in a way that does not
reveal sensitive information or inform bad actors.
Accordingly, MAAP recommends that the FAA:
1. Should develop a risk proportionate eligibility process that balances the potential security
benefits with the potential negative outcomes that could stifle or overburden legitimate UAS
operations.
2. Create a streamlined application process that does not unnecessarily duplicate existing
federal security programs and critical infrastructure oversight mechanisms.
3. Maintain the requirement for applicants to provide vulnerability assessments and summaries

but establish procedures that protect sensitive security and operational information from
unnecessary public or third-party disclosure. Where additional security validation is
necessary, the FAA should leverage confidential reviews performed by applicable Sector Risk
Management Agencies (SRMAs) to minimize duplicative reporting requirements and
safeguard sensitive information.
4. Create a streamlined pathway for facilities meeting predefined criteria. Such facilities should
be eligible for fast-track or conditional approval processes that reduce documentation
requirements while preserving FAA oversight.
II. Operations Permitted Within UAFRs
A. §§74.20, 74.56, 74.100 Digital Access, Situational Awareness and Web-Based Notification
For UAFRs to operate effectively at scale, FAA should develop a secure digital interface that 1) allows
facility operators to maintain awareness of authorized activity occurring in proximity to protected
facilities, and 2) enables automated notification processes for authorized airspace users. Robust and
easy to use digital interfaces are pre-requisite to enable the real-time, machine-to-machine
transactions required to successfully implement 2209 for both the fixed site security operators as
well as the airspace users.
III. Economic Impact on Airspace Users
FAA appropriately recognizes that UAFRs may impose costs and operational impacts on airspace
users. MAAP encourages the Agency to carefully consider these impacts as the number of UAFRs
expands nationally.
Restrictions that prevent legitimate operators from transiting a UAFR may result in:
• Increased route lengths;
• Additional flight time;
• Increased battery utilization;
• Greater maintenance requirements;
• Accelerated wear on life-limited components;
• Reduced operational efficiency.
These impacts may be especially significant for operators conducting infrastructure inspection, utility
patrol, package delivery, emergency support, agricultural operations, and other BVLOS activities. FAA
should therefore preserve transit opportunities whenever consistent with the security objectives of
the UAFR.

IV. Protective Security and Remote Identification
A. §74.56 Remote ID
MAAP recommends that FAA explicitly recognize network-based Remote ID as a means of satisfying
§74.56(d) security monitoring requirements. Network Remote ID provides centralized, real-time
aircraft identification and monitoring capabilities that improve situational awareness while reducing
the need for facility-specific surveillance infrastructure.
Because Network Remote ID data is centralized and interoperable across providers, it offers a
scalable and cost-effective solution for operators managing one or multiple facilities. For fixed-site
facilities, Network ID can support security monitoring objectives, facilitate correlation of aircraft
identity information with UAFR authorization data, and reduce infrastructure costs.
The FAA should avoid requiring Broadcast Remote ID as the sole authorized monitoring technology.
Broadcast Remote ID has known range and coverage limitations that may result in incomplete
awareness of aircraft operating near a facility, whereas Network Remote ID can provide a more
comprehensive and accessible means of supporting UAFR security objectives.
B. §74.56 Designated Security Personnel
FAA should clarify whether the requirement for designated security personnel requires continuous
onsite staffing or whether remote monitoring satisfies the requirement. This distinction is particularly
important for critical electric substations and similar facilities that do not maintain permanent onsite
personnel. A remote monitoring option should be explicitly permitted where appropriate
technologies and operational procedures are in place.
V. Environmental Impact Requirements
A. §74.70 Site-Specific Environmental Analysis
MAAP recommends eliminating the general requirement for applicants to prepare site-specific
environmental analyses under §74.70. Because a UAFR is an airspace designation rather than a
construction project or physical alteration of the environment, and because the FAA is already
conducting a programmatic environmental review of UAS operations and the UAFR framework. Site-
specific analyses should be required only where the FAA identifies extraordinary circumstances,
unique environmental concerns, or a credible potential for significant environmental effects.
Requiring such analyses for all applications would impose significant costs and delays with little
corresponding environmental benefit, particularly because critical infrastructure operators often lack
access to the detailed information necessary to assess impacts on adjacent properties, third-party
landowners, or environmental resources beyond their control. Moreover, it is difficult to see how

restricting drone operations over critical infrastructure for security purposes would, in most cases,
result in significant environmental impacts warranting project-specific review.
MAAP also opposes requiring applicants to bear the costs of FAA-selected consultants preparing
environmental documentation. The FAA should remain responsible for analyses necessary to support
federal decision-making, except in cases involving extraordinary circumstances that warrant
additional applicant participation.
VI. Duration, Renewals, and Administrative Efficiency
A. §74.210 Administrative Rollover Process
The NPRM's requirement for a complete reapplication every five years may impose unnecessary
administrative burden on owners of permanent infrastructure assets which typically remain fixed,
operational, and largely unchanged over long periods. MAAP recommends establishing an
Administrative Rollover process that balances the FAA's need to maintain accurate eligibility and
ownership records with a streamlined renewal process for existing UAFRs.
Under this approach, authorization could be renewed through a simplified digital certification
confirming that: (1) the facility remains operational; (2) ownership information remains current; (3)
the facility footprint has not materially changed; and (4) the basis for eligibility continues to exist.
Such a process would reduce unnecessary applicant burden while allowing the FAA to efficiently
verify continued eligibility and focus agency resources on applications involving substantive changes
or higher-risk circumstances.
VII. Costs and Paperwork Reduction
Many large utilities operate hundreds of facilities that could potentially qualify for UAFRs. At
estimated application costs ranging from several thousand dollars per site, system-wide participation
could become prohibitively expensive.
To reduce burden and promote participation, FAA should consider:
• Portfolio-based applications;
• Multi-site submissions;
• Consolidated documentation packages;
• Shared eligibility determinations;
• Streamlined renewal processes.
These measures would advance the objectives of the Paperwork Reduction Act while enabling

broader protection of critical infrastructure.
Conclusion
MAAP supports FAA's effort to implement Section 2209 and establish a scalable framework for
protecting critical infrastructure from unauthorized or malicious unmanned aircraft activity. However,
successful implementation depends upon balancing security objectives with operational practicality,
economic efficiency, and protection of sensitive infrastructure information.
MAAP respectfully recommends that the FAA:
1. Eliminate duplicative vulnerability assessment requirements.
2. Establish procedures that protect sensitive security and operational information from
unnecessary public or third-party disclosure
3. Leverage existing SRMA security reviews.
4. Establish streamlined application pathways.
5. Support network Remote ID and digital situational awareness tools.
6. Permit flexible monitoring solutions and remote security operations.
7. Limit environmental review obligations to extraordinary circumstances.
8. Implement administrative rollover mechanisms for permanent facilities.
9. Provide portfolio-based application options for large operators.
These modifications would enhance effectiveness, reduce burden, improve scalability, and better
support the protection of critical infrastructure while preserving the benefits of unmanned aviation
within the National Airspace System.
