COMMEN T S OF CTIA
CTIA1 respectfully submits these comments in response to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking (“NPRM”) issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (“FAA”) in the above-
captioned proceeding seeking comment on a process for operators and proprietors of certain
critical infrastructure facilities to request and maintain an unmanned aircraft flight restriction
(“UAFR”).2
I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY.
CTIA supports the FAA’s proposed UAFR process, which would implement Section
2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, as amended3 and would be
consistent with Executive Order 14305, “Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty.”4 Among
1 CTIA – The Wireless Association® (“CTIA”) (www.ctia.org) represents the U.S. wireless
communications industry and the companies throughout the mobile ecosystem that enable Americans to
lead a 21st century connected life. The association’s members include wireless providers, device
manufacturers, and suppliers, as well as apps and content companies. CTIA vigorously advocates at all
levels of government for policies that foster continued wireless innovation and investment. CTIA
represents a broad diversity of stakeholders, and the specific positions outlined in these comments may
not reflect the views of all individual members. CTIA was founded in 1984 and is based in Washington,
D.C.
2 Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,
91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (May 6, 2026) (“NPRM”); Extension of Comment Period, 91 Fed. Reg. 39568 (June
30, 2026).
3 Section 2209 directed the FAA to establish a process to allow applicants to petition the FAA to prohibit
or restrict UAS operations over critical infrastructure facilities. FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act
of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114–190, 130 Stat. 615 (2016) (“FESSA”).
4 Executive Order 14305 announced that “[i]t is the policy of the United States to ensure control over our
national airspace and to protect the public, critical infrastructure, mass gathering events, and military and

its key objectives, the FAA is seeking to “balance the safety and security concerns Congress
identified in section 2209 with the national policy objectives of ensuring the public right of
transit, preserving airspace efficiency, and integrating UAS into the [National Airspace System
(“NAS”)].”5 CTIA supports this effort and, in particular, the FAA’s proposal to permit UAS
operations within a UAFR if such operations fall into one of the categories enumerated in
proposed Section 74.250 – for example, operations pursuant to Part 107 (small UAS) or
proposed Part 108 (beyond visual line of sight (“BVLOS”) UAS flights).
As the FAA implements its proposals, it should avoid creating fragmented airspace that
would undermine UAS operations and the Administration’s goals of accelerating the safe
commercialization of drone technology and full integration of UAS into the NAS. At the same
time, the FAA should strike a balance that ensures the UAFR process does not inadvertently
undermine national security or the goals of the underlying legislation or Executive Order. To
that end, the FAA should modify the UAFR application process to protect from public disclosure
detailed descriptions, principally the precise physical location, of facilities that are not publicly
identified as critical infrastructure, such as wireless communications facilities. The Federal
Communications Commission (“FCC”) and Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) have
identified that communications infrastructure and wireless network information should be
protected from national security and business perspectives and have underscored the importance
of its confidentiality. The FAA should likewise ensure that such information remains protected
as part of the UAFR process.
sensitive government installations and operations from threats posed by the careless or unlawful use of
UAS.” Exec. Order No. 14305, § 3, 90 Fed. Reg. 24719, 24719 (June 11, 2025).
5 NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24651.
2

The FAA can also promote the balance of protecting critical facilities while encouraging
UAS deployments at scale by: (i) permitting UAS operators to use an electronic and/or
automated system for notifying UAFR holders about planned UAS operations permitted pursuant
to proposed Section 74.250; (ii) authorizing the use of network-based remote identification
(“Remote ID”) solutions as alternate means of compliance with the Remote ID requirement;
(iii) establishing a centralized, readily-accessible UAFR database that is updated in real time and
integrated into the FAA’s Notice to Airmen (“NOTAM”) database, Low Altitude Authorization
and Notification Capability (“LAANC”) system, and other official airspace data feeds
(anonymized as described below); and (iv) maintaining its determination that a UAFR does not
independently authorize the use of counter UAS (“C-UAS”) detection and mitigation systems,
such as jamming.
Finally, the FAA should expressly preempt state and local laws that attempt to regulate
the airspace above critical infrastructure. The FAA has exclusive jurisdiction to regulate UAS
operations in the NAS, but many states have enacted, and more are proposing, legislation
regulating such operations. Federal regulations should plainly preempt such state and local
efforts.
II. THE FAA SHOULD ENSURE THAT SENSITIVE INFORMATION ABOUT
CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE FACILITIES REMAINS PROTECTED AS
PART OF THE UAFR PROCESS.
CTIA generally supports the UAFR concept and urges the FAA to ensure that
implementation of the proposed process does not inadvertently undermine national security
interests by disclosing sensitive, non-public information about critical infrastructure sites. A
balanced approach for standard UAFRs that both promotes transparency in the process while
protecting sensitive sites would align with the FAA’s approach to special UAFR requests, where
3

the “FAA recognizes that notice and comment on the proposed special UAFR could increase the
risk of revealing threat assessments, security vulnerabilities, or operational timing
considerations.”6 As a result of these considerations, the FAA indicates for special UAFRs that
it “may limit the type of information provided in the NPRM in the interest of national or
homeland security.”7 These same concerns exist for certain facilities like communications
facilities and thus justify exempting from public notice the details that are made available about
them as part of the standard UAFR process. In particular, information about communications
infrastructure facilities that may not otherwise be readily known should be protected similar to
sites eligible for special UAFRs.
While the locations of some critical facilities such as fuel storage facilities, stadiums, and
similar critical sites may be public, the specific locations of some wireless communications
infrastructure may not be.8 Disclosing information about these assets in public notices or in a
central repository of vital critical infrastructure could provide a roadmap to be exploited by bad
actors. This would be inapposite to nationwide efforts to protect key infrastructure from cyber
and other security threats as well as the objectives of this effort. In the last several years, there
has been a spike in criminal activity that has directly impacted the availability of
communications services. From June 2024 to June 2025, there were 15,540 reported theft and
sabotage incidents, including copper theft and fiber cuts, targeting communications
6 Id. at 24659.
7 Id.
8 In the wireless context, information regarding cell sites and other wireless facilities is not generally
available in a publicly accessible centralized dataset. Although cell sites must be registered in the FCC’s
Antenna Structure Registration database if the site height exceeds 200 feet or the site is near an airport
glide path, most sites do not require registration. 47 C.F.R. §§ 17.4, 17.7.
4

infrastructure.9 These incidents can cause Internet, 911, and other communications services
outages and impose millions of dollars of costs on consumers, communications network
providers, and the economy.10 The FAA should work toward a balanced process that protects,
rather than worsens, the potential for attacks against communications networks.
In addition to being in the public interest, ensuring that information regarding
communications facilities remains protected is also consistent with the approach of other federal
agencies. The FCC has long held that information regarding cell site locations and network
vulnerabilities should be kept confidential. For example, the FCC has recognized that the
geographic coordinates of fixed wireless base stations may be sensitive to providers for business
or security reasons and thus it treats such information as presumptively confidential.11 Similarly,
the FCC has noted that information in wireless network outage reports “could be used by hostile
parties to attack [] networks, which are part of our Nation’s critical information infrastructure.”12
The FCC also has concluded that the “national defense and public safety goals” underpinning
outage reporting would be “seriously undermined if [the FCC] were to permit these reports to
fall into the hands of terrorists who seek to cripple the nation’s communications
infrastructure.”13
9 NCTA, CTIA et al., Protecting the Nation’s Critical Communications Infrastructure from Theft &
Vandalism, at 5-8 (last updated Oct. 2025), https://protectcci.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/10/CriticalAttacksReport_Oct25.pdf; see also Reply Comments of CTIA, FCC
Docket No. 21-346 et al., at 8-9 (filed Dec. 18, 2025) (“CTIA Dec. 2025 Comments”).
10 CTIA Dec. 2025 Comments at 8-9.
11 See Establishing the Digital Opportunity Data Collection, Third Report and Order, 36 FCC Rcd 1126,
1140 ¶ 33 (2021); id. at 1148-49 ¶ 55.
12 New Part 4 of the Commission’s Rules Concerning Disruptions to Communications, Report and Order
and Further Notice of Proposed Rule Making, 19 FCC Rcd 16830, 16853 ¶ 40 (2004).
13 Id. at 16855 ¶ 45.
5

DHS – the Sector Risk Management Agency identified by the FAA as responsible for the
communications sector14 – has similarly highlighted the importance of the communications
sector for supporting national security and emergency preparedness communications. Among
other things, it has stated that “[t]he confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the public
communication networks are a matter of national security and not merely a matter of
convenience.”15 It has also recognized that “[n]ation states, criminal groups, and lone hackers
are well aware of the significance of [information communications technology] infrastructure
vulnerabilities at multiple levels (e.g., network, service, application, and user).”16
These factors counsel against disclosing the precise location and specific vulnerabilities
of wireless communications infrastructure covered by a UAFR request. While the FAA states in
the draft Advisory Circular accompanying the NPRM that sensitive information would be subject
to the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (“PCII”) Program,17 neither the NPRM nor
the Advisory Circular provides further guidance or details as to how such critical information
will be protected as part of the UAFR application or approval process. This omission is
especially notable given that it is a well-established hurdle to qualify for PCII Program
protection. The FAA should adopt final procedures that clearly ensure sensitive national security
and business information surrounding wireless communications infrastructure for which an
owner or operator would like to pursue a UAFR would be protected.
14 See FAA, Advisory Circular, Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility, at 20 (May 6, 2026) (“Advisory Circular”),
https://www.regulations.gov/document/FAA-2026-4558-0006.
15 DHS, Communications Sector-Specific Plan: An Annex to the NIPP 2013, at 16-17 (2015) (emphasis
added), https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/nipp-ssp-communications-2015-508.pdf.
16 Id. at 17.
17 Advisory Circular at 12.
6

In particular, rather than require that all aspects of the standard UAFR request be publicly
disclosed, the FAA should consider limiting the type of information contained in the notice
seeking comment on certain categories of standard UAFRs in the interest of national or
homeland security, consistent with the approach proposed for special UAFRs. Among other
things, the FAA proposes to require an applicant for a standard UAFR to “submit information
demonstrating that its facility meets the eligibility criteria and that there is a safety or security
need for the UAFR” and to require applicants to describe “the nature of the facility’s assets, the
vulnerabilities of these assets to unmanned aircraft, and potential consequences or effects if an
unmanned aircraft exploited a vulnerability.”18 If the FAA agrees with the applicant that a
UAFR is warranted, it would “publish the proposal in the Federal Register for notice and
comment.”19 However, detailed descriptions of certain facilities, principally the precise physical
location of non-public communications facilities coupled with information regarding protective
security measures already taken and a description of vulnerabilities at the site,20 are especially
sensitive UAFR application elements that could be readily exploited by bad actors. The FAA
should omit these elements from public disclosure, which can be done while still promoting a
transparent UAFR review process.21 Publicly available information about granted UAFRs also
18 NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24652, 24656, 24661-62. The FAA also proposes to require applicants to
propose a vertical limit defined by an altitude ceiling for the requested UAS flight restriction, which
would be subject to the parameters of proposed rule § 74.60. To ensure that spectrum rights of
commercial wireless licensees are protected, the FAA should clarify that the boundaries of a UAFR are
specific to UAS operations and do not impact the rights of commercial wireless licensees to utilize their
spectrum to the full extent authorized by the FCC.
19 Id. at 24652, 24660.
20 See id. at 24686-87 (proposed rules §§ 74.52, 74.56, 74.66).
21 To the extent the PCII Program process will be used, the FAA should consider recommending that such
information be categorically protected as PCII. See 6 C.F.R. § 29.6; see also PCII Program Frequently
Asked Questions, CISA, https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/programs/protected-critical-infrastructure-
information-pcii-program/pcii-program-frequently-asked-questions (last visited July 28, 2026).
7

should not give the exact physical location of the site being protected or its security measures or
vulnerabilities.
By revising the UAFR process to omit sensitive information from public disclosure, the
FAA will help preserve the confidentiality of the critical infrastructure locations it seeks to
protect and avoid creating a roadmap of potential targets for bad actors.
III. THE FAA CAN BALANCE THE SAFETY OF THE NAS AND CRITICAL
FACILITIES WHILE PROMOTING UAS DEPLOYMENT AT SCALE.
CTIA applauds the FAA for seeking to balance safety and security concerns associated
with critical infrastructure with the need to promote UAS deployment at scale. As noted below,
this balance can be achieved best by: (i) permitting an automated, electronic notification process
for UAS operations within a UAFR; (ii) authorizing the use of network-based Remote ID
solutions; (iii) establishing a readily accessible UAFR database that is updated in real time; and
(iv) emphasizing that UAFR grants do not authorize C-UAS technology deployment or use.
A. The FAA Can Modify the Process of Notifying UAFR Holders of Planned
UAS Operations While Ensuring Critical Facility Owners’ Rights Remain
Protected.
CTIA supports the FAA’s proposal to permit commercial UAS operations within a
UAFR if such operations fall into one of the categories enumerated in proposed Section 74.250.
As the FAA notes, operations pursuant to proposed Section 74.250 should be permitted because
such operations have met rigorous FAA safety requirements and Transportation Security
Administration security threat assessments and the need for such operations outweighs the need
to restrict airspace access over critical infrastructure.22
22 NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24676.
8

The proposed rules would require UAS operators that do not have legal rights to the
property subject to a UAFR to notify UAFR holders prior to commencing operations permitted
under Section 74.250.23 Although it appears self-evident that operators with legal rights to
properties subject to UAFRs are exempt from the UAFR and therefore the notification
requirement, the FAA should eliminate any ambiguity by expressly clarifying this point in the
final rules.
The notice requirement provides an important protection for UAFR holders seeking to
safeguard critical infrastructure facilities, and the FAA should adopt an efficient process for UAS
operators to notify UAFR holders when Section 74.250 will be invoked. In this regard, to avoid
unnecessary delays associated with manually sending individual notifications to every UAFR
holder impacted by operations under Section 74.250, the FAA should permit UAS operators to
use an automated process to electronically send these notifications. The FAA has established
similar mechanisms in the past.24
If the FAA decides against establishing an automated notification mechanism as part of
the UAFR process, it should exempt from the notification requirement UAS disaster recovery
operations and special government interest waiver operations. When it comes to critical
infrastructure, time is of the essence immediately after a disaster and UAS often are deployed to
quickly assess damage so that restoration efforts can commence rapidly and efficiently. In some
cases, UAS may be used to temporarily restore communications service in disaster-stricken areas
so that people can reach loved ones during emergency circumstances. Rather than require
23 Id. at 24690-91 (proposed rule §§ 74.250, 74.251(a)) (requiring notice to the UAFR holder “in a form
and manner acceptable to the Administrator”).
24 For example, LAANC uses system-to-system interfaces with approved service providers to automate
the submission, processing, and dissemination of airspace authorization information.
9

critical infrastructure providers to divert resources toward manually notifying UAFR holders
about disaster-related operations, the UAFR rules should exempt from the notification
requirement UAS operations providing support to areas impacted by disasters.
Finally, CTIA agrees that the FAA should not intervene in private property disputes over
how the fixed site facility property should or should not be used.25 While property owners may
enter into agreements relating to such issues outside of the UAFR process, the FAA should
clarify in the final rule that applicants do not have exclusive airspace rights and thus may not
misuse the UAFR process to circumvent private contracts, including, for example, to restrict or
dictate the choices regarding drone hardware, software, or third-party vendors at a fixed site
facility.
B. The FAA Should Authorize Networked Remote Identification.
Given the importance of Remote ID to the proposed UAFR process, the FAA should
authorize the use of networked Remote ID. The proposed notification process would provide the
UAFR holder with the Remote ID Serial Number for the UAS that will be flown within the
UAFR. This Remote ID information will allow the UAFR holder to discern harmless UAS
operations from potentially nefarious operations. Reliance on Remote ID as proposed reinforces
the need for the FAA to permit commercial wireless networks to provide this functionality.
Networked Remote ID is an especially important functionality that commercial wireless
networks can support safely and efficiently, and at a greater range than unlicensed spectrum
currently used to comply with the broadcast-based Remote ID rule.26 Stakeholders have long
advocated for the FAA to permit Remote ID to operate on cellular networks, and the FAA should
25 NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24661.
26 See 14 C.F.R. § 89.320(g)(1); Remote Identification of Unmanned Aircraft, 86 Fed. Reg. 4390, 4405
(Jan. 15, 2021) (“Remote ID Final Rule”).
10

modify its Remote ID rules to allow for use of licensed commercial wireless networks—which
can support development of innovative uses and functions27—to serve as a viable alternate
means of compliance with the Remote ID requirement.
The FAA has an extensive record demonstrating the benefits that commercial wireless
networks can provide for Remote ID.28 Networked cellular communications can be relied on to
securely convey Remote ID information and improve the range of current Remote ID
communications.29 Commercial wireless networks can satisfy Remote ID requirements,
including transmitting all Remote ID data elements following the ASTM standard referenced in
the Remote ID rule.30
Stakeholders agree that commercial wireless networks can support Remote ID. For
example, a report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office (“GAO”) cites multiple
drone industry stakeholders stating that networked cellular-based Remote ID technology can
provide information “more robustly” than can be provided via broadcast.31 Other stakeholders—
27 See FAA, UAS Identification and Tracking (UAS ID) Aviation Rulemaking Committee (ARC) Final
Report, at 15 (Sept. 30, 2017) (explaining that licensed spectrum “is likely free from interference from
other applications implying a higher quality of service”).
28 See, e.g., Comments of CTIA, Docket No. FAA-2023-1256, at 2 (June 14, 2023) (“Engineered to carry
massive volumes of data to and from more than 300 million people across the country, networked cellular
can support diverse UAS activities with little risk of a ‘lost link’ to a ground station, including support for
[UTM,] which is essential to the future of UAS.”); Comments of Verizon, Docket No. FAA-2023-1256,
at 2 (June 14, 2023) (“Advanced digital wireless networks provide robust signals with high availability
and reliability to minimize the likelihood of lost links.”); Comments of Qualcomm Incorporated, Docket
No. FAA-2023-1256, at 2 (June 14, 2023) (“[M]odern 3GPP cellular technology standards [] can
accommodate low- and high-altitude drones operating BVLOS in congested and non-congested areas,
enabling expedited, cost-effective deployment of UAS.”).
29 See Comments of CTIA, Docket No. FAA-2019-1100, at 12 (Mar. 2, 2020) (explaining that
commercial wireless networks can provide “reliable broadcast of Remote ID messages outside of network
coverage, with low latency, high reliability, and superior security”).
30 Remote ID Final Rule, 86 Fed. Reg. at 4445.
31 GAO, GAO-24-106158, Actions Needed to Better Support Remote Identification in the National
Airspace, at 18-19 (June 2024) (“GAO Report”), https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-24-106158.pdf.
11

including AT&T, GSMA, Qualcomm, T-Mobile, and Verizon—have supported networked
cellular Remote ID due to security benefits and broad coverage available from existing
commercial wireless networks.32 As Qualcomm has explained, “[t]oday’s mobile cellular
networks that multiple national carriers have ubiquitously deployed and are constantly upgrading
to support increased capacity . . . can provide safe BVLOS operation[s] at any time of day and
over individuals not associated with the UAS flight.”33
Further, the FAA and stakeholders also have recognized the limitations with relying
solely on unlicensed, broadcast-based Remote ID technologies to enable advanced drone
operations.34 As commercial drone stakeholders have explained, “a broadcast-based signal is not
sufficient for providing real-time, networked data about drone location and status as needed for
advanced operations.”35 Limitations include the more-restricted range and less reliability of
unlicensed signals compared to licensed commercial wireless networks.36
Given the benefits of licensed commercial wireless networks, the more limited
capabilities of unlicensed signals, and the goal of advancing UAS deployment in the United
States, the FAA should take this opportunity to expand its Remote ID rules to allow for use of
licensed commercial wireless networks to independently support remote ID solutions, which can
support development of innovative uses and functions.
32 See Comments of AT&T Services, Inc., Docket No. FAA-2019-1100, at 2-3 (Mar. 2, 2020); Comments
of GSMA, Docket No. FAA-2019-1100, at 4-5 (Mar. 2, 2020); Comments of Qualcomm Incorporated,
Docket No. FAA-2019-1100, at 1-2 (Mar. 2, 2020) (“Qualcomm Remote ID Comments”); Comments of
T-Mobile USA, Inc., Docket No. FAA-2019-1100, at 3-4 (Mar. 2, 2020); Comments of Verizon, Docket
No. FAA-2019-1100, at 14-15 (Mar. 2, 2020); Remote ID Final Rule, 86 Fed. Reg. at 4408.
33 Qualcomm Remote ID Comments at 3.
34 GAO Report at GAO Highlights.
35 Id.
36 Id. at 18.
12

C. The FAA Should Maintain a Central UAFR Database That Is Updated in
Real Time and Utilized by Other UAS Databases.
In balancing the objectives of critical infrastructure security and UAS NAS access, the
FAA should establish a central database – updated in real time – containing all granted UAFRs.
A central database will help ensure that UAS operators do not inadvertently fly into UAFR areas
because they missed a public notice announcing the UAFR. CTIA thus supports the FAA’s
proposal to publish and maintain all UAFRs on the UAFR-Utility and to publish them “in the
Federal Register, UAS Data Delivery Service (UDDS), and FAA Order Joint Order (JO)
7400.12,” with JO 7400.12 being available online.37 Further, information regarding UAFRs
should be incorporated into the FAA’s NOTAM database, other official airspace data feeds, and
LAANC applications such as the B4UFLY Desktop and Mobile Applications. Automated
systems potentially could be created that would allow drone operating systems to interface with
the database and seamlessly obtain flight restriction information. Importantly, for the reasons
noted in Section II above, sensitive information should not be made public.
D. The FAA is Correct to Find That a UAFR Will Not Independently Authorize
Detection and Mitigation Measures.
CTIA applauds the FAA for recognizing that the proposed UAFR process would act like
a “no trespassing sign” and would not independently authorize specific C-UAS operations.38
Protecting the spectrum rights of wireless licensees and preventing harmful interference is also
necessary for UAS operations that rely on commercial wireless network connectivity, especially
systems that depend on licensed spectrum for preserving the integrity of command and control
37 FAA, Privacy Impact Assessment: Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions Utility UAFR-Utility, at 6
(May 2026), https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2026-05/Privacy%20-%20FAA%20-
%20UAFR%20Utility%20-%20PIA%20-%202026.pdf.
38 NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24657.
13

and payload links. This protection means a higher quality of service for consumers, enterprise
customers, and public safety customers that use services operating on licensed spectrum.
Interpreting the UAFR process as authorizing the use of C-UAS technologies would risk
reducing these protections and impeding the high quality of service wireless customers expect
from services on licensed spectrum. CTIA therefore fully supports the FAA’s determination that
the UAFR process does not independently authorize operators or facility proprietors to use
detection or mitigation technologies to interfere with unmanned aircraft (apart from entities with
separate statutory authority to use such systems).39
As the FAA notes, use of C-UAS detection or mitigation technologies remains subject to
existing federal laws. One such law is Section 333 of the Communications Act.40 Section 333 is
specific in its plain, express prohibition of willful or malicious interference, which undeniably
encompasses jamming. Section 333 is vitally important because jamming risks blocking or
degrading all nearby communications on the targeted spectrum, not just UAS communications.
For commercial wireless networks, that means potentially blocking 911 calls, first-responder
communications, Wireless Emergency Alerts, and other safety-related communications. This is
not a theoretical risk, but a predictable outcome – one that is at odds with the FAA’s public
safety goals in this proceeding.
The FCC recently clarified that Section 333 does not apply to the federal government
and, under the authority of the SAFER SKIES Act, interpreted that non-federal entities such as
state, local, Tribal, and territorial law enforcement and correctional agencies are entitled to
derivative immunity from Section 333 when jamming UAS under the authority of the SAFER
39 Id.
40 47 U.S.C. § 333.
14

SKIES Act.41 However, the FCC also clarified that “absent some other statutory source
exempting them from the provision, the non-federal actor would remain subject to section 333’s
prohibition against willful or malicious interference with communications of any licensed or
authorized station.”42 Thus, the use of jamming technologies by non-federal entities must not
interfere with non-UAS communications.
Based on the foregoing, CTIA urges the FAA to reiterate in its final rule that a UAFR
does not independently authorize use of detection or mitigation technologies and to retain the
language in proposed Section 74.56(d) stating that the “protective security” and “security
monitoring” provisions for a facility do not authorize “electronic interference or interception of
aircraft or navigation signals.” Such authority must be obtained separately from the UAFR
process.
IV. THE FAA SHOULD EXPRESSLY PREEMPT STATE AND LOCAL LAWS
THAT ESTABLISH UAS NO-FLY ZONES, INCLUDING AIRSPACE OVER
CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE.
CTIA urges the FAA to confirm that federal law preempts state and local laws that
attempt to establish UAS no-fly zones, including laws that attempt to regulate the airspace over
critical infrastructure facilities. The Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution states that “the
Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof . . . shall
be the supreme law of the land.”43 As noted by the Supreme Court, this gives Congress the
power to preempt state law.44
41 Application of Section 333 of the Communications Act to Development or Operations of Counter-
Unmanned Aircraft Systems for the Federal Government and under the SAFER SKIES Act, Declaratory
Ruling, DA 26-655, ¶ 13 (WTB rel. July 2, 2026).
42 Id. at 14.
43 U.S. Const. art. VI, cl. 2.
44 See, e.g., Arizona v. United States, 132 S. Ct. 2492 (2012).
15

There are three types of preemption: express preemption (when Congress specifically
preempts a state law);45 field preemption (when a federal framework of regulation is “‘so
pervasive . . . that Congress left no room for the States to supplement it’ or where a ‘federal
interest is so dominant that the federal system will be assumed to preclude enforcement of state
laws on the same subject’”);46 and conflict preemption (when state laws “conflict with federal
law, including when they stand ‘as an obstacle to the accomplishment and execution of the full
purposes and objectives of Congress’”).47
Congress has occupied the field with regard to regulating operations within the NAS.48
Consistent with this framework, Congress directed the FAA to integrate UAS into the NAS.49
Further, based on perceived security risks from drones, Congress directed the FAA to establish
processes for restricting UAS operations within the NAS above critical infrastructure in response
to requests from critical infrastructure owners.50 The FAA has acknowledged that Congress has
granted it field preemption to regulate aviation safety and airspace efficiency.51 The FAA thus
has exclusive jurisdiction to regulate operations in the NAS generally and over critical
infrastructure more specifically.52

47 Id. (quoting Hines v. Davidowitz, 312 U.S. 52, 67 (1941)).

50 FESSA, 130 Stat. 615.

The FAA has issued numerous letters to localities cautioning against the adoption of

UAS Fact Sheet, the FAA has made clear that laws banning drone operations are preempted.

2209 to protect airspace over critical infrastructure, some states and localities enacted laws

the airspace by aircraft are preempted. Outside those fields, the States are generally free to regulate—

some laws permitting the use of jamming.57 Numerous other states have pending legislation
proposing to regulate UAS operations over critical infrastructure.58 These laws intrude upon the
FAA’s exclusive authority to regulate UAS operations within the NAS.
Section 2209 expressly directs the FAA to establish a process to enable critical
infrastructure owners to protect the airspace over their facilities. This NPRM does just that and
state and local laws addressing this issue – even if well intended – are preempted.
V. CONCLUSION.
CTIA shares the FAA’s and Administration’s goals to support the development of
domestic UAS operations and protect critical infrastructure. A regulatory framework that
balances national security objectives with the public interest benefits associated with UAS
operations would best achieve these goals. By adopting a UAFR process consistent with these
comments, the FAA can strike the proper balance. Finally, to ensure that this carefully balanced
regulatory framework is not frustrated, the FAA should expressly preempt all state and local
laws and ordinances that attempt to regulate UAS operations over critical infrastructure.
CTIA and its members look forward to collaborating with the FAA to foster the
continued growth of the UAS industry while carefully protecting national security objectives.

As the owner and operator of critical electric infrastructure serving approximately 15 million people across Southern and Central California, SCE recognizes the importance of safeguarding assets that are essential to national security, public safety, and economic stability.

At the same time, utilities occupy a unique position within the aviation ecosystem. SCE's complete comments and recommendations are attached for the FAA's consideration. We appreciate the opportunity to participate in this rulemaking and look forward to continued engagement with the FAA and industry stakeholders as the agency develops a final rule.

Dear Administrator Bedford,
The Edison Electric Institute (“EEI”), American Public Power Association (“APPA”), Large Public
Power Council (“LPPC”), and National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (“NRECA”)
(hereafter the “Electric Utility Trade Associations” or “Associations”) provide the following
comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration’s (“FAA”) Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking on “Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity
to a Fixed Site Facility” (hereinafter “Proposed Rule”).1
The Associations support the FAA’s effort to address the threats posed by the unauthorized and
malicious use of unmanned aircraft systems (“UAS” or drones) around sensitive fixed site
facilities, including electric facilities. That said, the Associations have identified significant
practical and operational concerns with the way the Proposed Rule is currently drafted. The
Associations lay out these concerns, along with recommended solutions, below.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The implementation of section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016
represents an important opportunity to protect critical infrastructure, including the nation’s
electric sector, from the growing threat posed by the unauthorized and malicious use of UAS.
Such protections are vital to the electric sector, which undergirds the entire U.S. economy and
is core to the operation of all other critical infrastructure sectors.

PART I: RELEVANT BACKGROUND
A. BACKGROUND ON THE ELECTRIC UTILITY TRADE ASSOCIATIONS
1. Edison Electric Institute (EEI)
EEI’s member companies are the nation’s investor-owned electric utilities. Together, they
provide electricity to nearly 250 million Americans, operate in all 50 states and the District of
Columbia, and support over seven million jobs in communities across the country. EEI member
companies work every day to provide reliable energy to their customers at the lowest cost
possible. EEI member companies also form the backbone of our nation’s electric power
industry, which is essential to advancing our economic and national security priorities. Over the
next five years, investor-owned electric companies will invest more than $1.3 trillion to
enhance the electric grid, building critically needed new generation, transmission, and
distribution infrastructure required to power economic prosperity.
2. American Public Power Association (APPA)
APPA is the voice of not-for-profit, community-owned utilities that power 2,000 towns and
cities nationwide. Public power utilities are in every state except Hawaii; they collectively serve
over 55 million people in 49 states and five U.S. territories, and account for 15 percent of all
sales of electric energy (kilowatt-hours) to end-use consumers. APPA members seek to provide
the communities they serve with safe, reliable electric service at the lowest reasonable cost,
consistent with good environmental stewardship. This mission aligns the interests of the
utilities with the long-term interests of the residents and businesses in their communities.
3. Large Public Power Council (LPPC)
The LPPC represents 29 of the nation’s largest state and locally owned, not-for-profit public
power systems, serving 30.5 million Americans across 23 states and territories. LPPC’s members
include the larger, asset-owning members of the public power community and account for
approximately 90 percent of the transmission assets owned by public power. LPPC members
are also members of APPA.
4. National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA)
NRECA represents nearly 900 local electric cooperatives, including 63 generation and
transmission cooperatives that generate and transmit power and 832 distribution cooperatives
that provide electricity to the end of line co-op consumer members. Local electric cooperatives
power 56% of the nation’s landmass, serving 42 million Americans, and covering more public
lands and forests than any other type of utility. America’s electric cooperatives operate at cost
and without profit incentive. They are owned by the people that they serve and comprise a
unique sector of the electric industry. Due to their unique, not-for-profit business model,
cooperatives often operate on thin financial margins, and any increases in regulatory
compliance costs and liabilities are passed on to the end of the line consumer.

B. THE CRITICALITY OF THE ELECTRIC GRID
1. The Electric Grid
The nation’s electric grid is a complex, integrated system with thousands of interdependent
facilities, encompassing over 22,000 generators, 55,000 substations, 642,000 miles of high
voltage transmission lines, and 6.3 million miles of distribution infrastructure.4 These
components work together to serve as the backbone for public services, economic activity, and
other critical infrastructure sectors. The components of the grid are interdependent, such that
overall grid reliability depends on continued operation and coordination across the system.
Compromise of critical elements of this system can create substantial radiating harm. Critical
elements include both the large facilities covered by the definition of “electricity facility” in the
Proposed Rule and smaller facilities that play a central role in the grid’s network. Yet, smaller
facilities are excluded under the Proposed Rule’s unduly narrow definition of “electricity
facility,” despite their significance to public safety, national security, economic activity, and the
communities that depend on the grid’s continued functioning.
2. Regulation of the Electric Grid
Over two decades ago, in recognition of the critical role that electric grid reliability plays in
support of the nation’s economic and social welfare, Congress enacted section 215 of the
Federal Power Act in 2005, which transformed U.S. electric grid oversight by shifting from
voluntary industry standards to mandatory, enforceable federal reliability standards.5 This
statutory provision directs FERC to oversee a certified Electric Reliability Organization (which is
now NERC), and to approve mandatory, legally binding grid reliability standards for “bulk-power
systems.” Violators can be fined up to $1 million a day in civil fines.
The definition of “bulk-power system” recognizes the interconnected, networked way in which
the electric grid operates, and encompasses: (i) “facilities and control systems necessary for
operating an interconnected electric energy transmission network (or any portion thereof);” and
(ii) “electric energy from generation facilities needed to maintain transmission system
reliability.”6 The related definition of “bulk electric system,” which is a subset of the “bulk-
power system,” includes transmission elements operated at 100 kilovolts (kV) or higher—most
of which fall outside of the narrow definition of “electricity facility” under the Proposed Rule.7

In 2013, following a rifle attack on grid facilities, FERC adopted NERC Standard CIP-014, which
mandated key physical security standards for infrastructure deemed critical to grid operations.8
Standard CIP-014 applies to “Transmission stations and Transmission substations, and their
associated primary control centers, that if rendered inoperable or damaged as a result of a
physical attack could result in instability, uncontrolled separation, or Cascading within an
Interconnection.”9 Covered utilities include a range of transmission stations and substations
that fall below 500 kV, either because they meet specified criteria, are essential to meeting
nuclear plant interface requirements, or are defined as critical to the derivation of
Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits, the specific limits within a bulk electric system
that, if exceeded, could result in instability, uncontrolled separation, or cascading outages.10
Covered utilities are required to conduct an “evaluation of the potential threats and
vulnerabilities of physical attack to each of their” critical facilities that considers “unique
characteristics” of the critical facility, “prior history of attack on similar facilities taking into
account the frequency, geographic proximity, and severity of past physical security related
events,” and “intelligence or threat warnings received from” government agencies.11 The utility
must develop and implement a utility-specific physical security plan that addresses the specific
vulnerabilities identified.12
The Proposed Rule’s definition of “electricity facility” excludes the many facilities operating
below 500 kV that have been deemed critical by FERC and NERC.
3. The Associations’ Use of Drones to Meet Security Needs
In order to ensure the safe and reliable operation of the electric grid, the Associations’
members must regularly inspect power lines. Electric utilities continue to expand the frequency
and scope of these inspections in response to evolving regulatory requirements and increased
risk factors, caused by fires, extreme weather, and external threats. As investments in new
energy generation and grid integration infrastructure grow, inspection demands are expected
to continue to increase.

to-reach areas. The Associations’ members report cost reductions of up to 80 percent
compared to other inspection methods. UAS can access challenging terrain more quickly, more
safely, and more efficiently than traditional manned crews. UAS also can engage in repeatable
inspections, which increases accuracy. And they are particularly invaluable in the event of

C. THE SCOPE OF THE THREAT
The electric grid is central to the nation’s economic welfare, public health, and national
security. In fact, the electric grid serves an enabling function across all other critical
infrastructure sectors. This interdependence creates a distinct risk profile: grid disruptions can
cascade into water and wastewater systems, telecommunications, healthcare delivery, fuel
supply chains, emergency response, financial services, and transportation systems. As described
above, and in recognition of the importance of the electric grid, this administration declared
the “integrity and expansion of the Nation’s energy infrastructure . . . an immediate and
pressing priority for the protection of the Nation’s national and economic security.”13
1. Key Threats
Negligent and malicious drone use poses significant risk to the electric grid and all the Electric
Utility Trade Associations’ members. As the Proposed Rule recognizes, unauthorized and
malicious use of UAS can cause a combination of physical, surveillance, and cybersecurity
threats to the grid.14 As UAS technology becomes more sophisticated and more readily
available, often at very low cost, the risks spread, to include the following:
• Physical Risks: Drones with payloads can drop explosives from above, causing significant
damage. Drones can also crash into facilities (both intentionally and unintentionally),
causing potential explosions, wildfires, release of hazardous materials, damage to the
electric grid, and loss of life.
• Tech Failure Risks: Adding to the risk posed by malicious or negligent drone use,
technology failures, such as firmware or software issues, could cause a drone to crash,
resulting in damage to the facility, explosion, and wildfires.15
• Surveillance Risks: Drones can also be used to surveil facilities and their associated
structures. Such surveillance can be used by malicious actors to identify structural,

2. The Broader Costs
The misuse and malicious use of drones threatens not only the safety and reliability of the grid
itself but has potential for cascading impacts to many other critical industries and systems such
as hospitals, water distribution, and emergency services that rely on the electric grid. Even
temporary outages can cause massive disruptions to communities, businesses, and schools, and
possibly even lead to the loss of life.
Drone incidents will almost inevitably result in increased energy costs and decreased reliability,
as the Associations’ members work to address outages, manage system damage, rebuild
destroyed or exploited systems, face potential liability for drone-caused wildfires, and absorb
increased insurance rates as a result. This makes it hard to achieve the long-standing objective
of keeping costs down and reliability high, consistent with the administration’s priorities.21

PART II. ELECTRICITY INDUSTRY CONCERNS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
UAFRs are important tools that, if implemented effectively, could meaningfully minimize overall
risk to our nation’s electrical system. By establishing appropriate restrictions over sensitive
facilities, entities can protect their facilities from increasingly significant airborne threats, while
continuing to enable the productive use of drones for inspections, perimeter surveillance, and
other safety and security needs. Flight restrictions also enable entities to better distinguish
between compliant and non-compliant UAS operators and thus focus limited security and law
enforcement resources on addressing concrete threats.
The Associations are concerned, however, that the Proposed Rule, as currently drafted:
• Fails to account for key and critical portions of the electric sector;
• Establishes an unduly burdensome process that inadvertently creates new security
vulnerabilities; and
• Includes so many exceptions that it does not give critical infrastructure owners and
operators meaningful control over their airspace—thus undercutting the core purpose
of the Proposed Rule.
A. THE SCOPE OF COVERED ELECTRICITY FACILITIES FAILS TO PROTECT CRITICAL FACILITIES
The Proposed Rule’s definition of “electricity facility” excludes key facilities and distribution
systems that serve significant national security and homeland security interests, and are thus
highly vulnerable to the threat posed by the negligent and malicious use of drones. The
definition of “electricity facility” also fails to account for the reality of the way the electric grid
operates, as networked facilities that operate as an interconnected whole, and thus fails to
provide protections for key elements of this network.
1. Limited Definition of “Electricity Facility”
The Proposed Rule’s definition of “electricity facility” excludes key, critical facilities and
systems. The core definition of “electricity facility” includes just three types of fixed site
facilities eligible for a UAFR: (1) a power-generation facility with a combined nameplate
capacity of 500 megawatts or greater of power; (2) an electrical substation with a capacity of
500 kilovolts or greater of power; or (3) an electrical substation with a capacity of 345 kilovolts
or greater of power in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas.22
Other sections cover additional but narrow categories of electricity facilities. The Dams Sector
covers the narrow category of a “hydroelectric dam with a combined nameplate capacity of 350
megawatts or more of power and have produced 1,850,000 megawatt hours or greater during
the previous calendar year;” the Nuclear Reactors, Materials, and Waste Sector covers a
“nuclear power plant that is currently operating and generating electricity;” and the

2. Failure to Account for the Networked Reality of the Electric Grid
The Proposed Rule approaches protecting electric infrastructure by assuming a generation
facility-by-generation facility, substation-by-substation, and transmission facility-by-
transmission facility approach. For reasons discussed above, this does not reflect the reality of
how the electrical grid operates. The electric infrastructure is an integrated system of
generation facilities, substations, transmission facilities, and distribution facilities supporting
specific communities and regions. Owners and operators focus on security of the broader
network, not just single, discrete facilities. Risks and vulnerabilities are also spread across
networks, comprised of interconnected fixed sites.
There is, as a result, a dangerous mismatch between the Proposed Rule’s facility-by-facility
approach to securing airspace, the reality of how the electric grid operates, and the networks
that our members work to protect. The Associations urge that the definition of electric facilities
also account for networked facilities, thus better mapping the Final Rule’s protections to the
layout of facilities and security needs.
