B. THE APPLICATION PROCESS IS UNDULY BURDENSOME, COSTLY, AND CREATES INADVERTENT
SECURITY RISKS
The process and criteria for establishing a UAFR under the Proposed Rule ask for extremely
sensitive data that, if made publicly available, would create significant security risks. Other
parts of the process seek information that is simply not available. The Associations urge that
the final rule protect against the creation of a centralized database with sensitive vulnerability
and security information, include other essential protections for sensitive information, and
avoid unduly burdensome and costly data gathering exercises that could ultimately result in
increased costs to consumers.
The Proposed Rule would require UAFR applicants to submit information demonstrating a
safety or security need to justify the requested airspace restrictions. This includes: (i)
requirements to describe details, where available, about unmanned aircraft operations over the
fixed site facility in question during the last 24 months; (ii) detailed information about the
facility’s vulnerabilities; and (iii) detailed information about the consequences of those
vulnerabilities, if exploited.30 Each of these requirements poses a concern.
1. § 74.66(A) – Existing unmanned aircraft traffic patterns
The FAA proposes to require applicants to provide extensive information about UAS traffic
patterns over a given site in the past 24 months, where available, including the “type of
unmanned aircraft operation, if known; identify whether the operator is known to the
operators or proprietors; and quantify the total number of operations not associated with the
facility itself.”31
FAA states that it is seeking this information in order to establish “a baseline for existing traffic”
in order to “help FAA understand current operations over the facility [and to] create a
reference point for evaluating the effectiveness of the UAFR once it is active.”32 The agency
28 NERC, CIP-014-3, supra note 9.
29 See 18 C.F.R. § 388.113(c)(3); 10 C.F.R. § 1004.13(c)(3).
30 See Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24687 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.66).
31 Id. (to be codified at § 74.66(a)).
32 Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24664.
13

further states that it will “use this information to understand existing threats and hazards and
to evaluate the likelihood that a safety or security incident could occur.”33
This provision raises several concerns:
• First, it asks for information that most owners and operators of electrical facilities simply
do not have. Even if available in part, compiling this information would be labor
intensive, extraordinarily costly, and almost certainly incomplete. While the FAA
includes a caveat that this information is required “where available,” the Associations
are concerned that there will be an expectation that this information be provided, and
an implicit bias against those that fail to do so. This is an expectation that most electric
facilities cannot meet.
• Second, even if historical UAS activity data were to be available for a facility, the
Associations question the utility of such data, particularly given how quickly UAS
technology and associated threats are evolving. Put simply, two-year-old historical data
is likely to have limited relevance to current and future drone activity and risks;
requiring the FAA to review such data creates an unnecessary administrative burden,
with limited value. Moreover, the absence of prior drone activity is a poor measure of
future risk.
• Third, this kind of requirement raises broader concerns about the kind of costs utilities
are expected to bear in order to obtain a UAFR. The Associations recognize that once a
UAFR has been issued, applicants will be required to implement Remote ID detection or
equivalent technology to be able to receive data about unmanned aircraft operating
within or in proximity of the UAFR.
But they should not be required to invest in costly detection systems as a condition of
even applying for a UAFR prior to obtaining one. Of particular concern, utilities are
regulated entities that recover prudently incurred compliance costs through increased
rates. This is particularly important given the ongoing and significant concerns about
affordability and increasing electricity costs. A facility receiving a UAFR should not be
contingent upon the ability to afford air traffic detection technologies and personnel;
nor should it come at the expense of the ratepayer.
As discussed further below, the Associations are also concerned about a rule that
entrenches Remote ID as the sole detection standard and recommends additional
language that will enable broadcast requirements and detection systems to adapt to
evolving technology over time.
33 Id.
14

RECOMMENDATIONS:
• For initial applications, the FAA should ask for any known information about flight
patterns over a facility, should ask for historical data going back up to 12 months at
the most, and should make it clear in the text of the Rule that UAFR applicants should
not attempt to retroactively produce data that is not readily available.
• For renewal requests, the FAA should ask for data consistent with the Remote ID
requirement or similar detection technology.
• The FAA should require that applicants commit to implementing Remote ID or similar
detection technology if granted a UAFR; applicants should not be required to invest in
potentially costly detection systems unless they are granted a UAFR.
2. § 74.66 (B), (C), (D) – Vulnerability, Consequence, and Effect
The Proposed Rule would require applicants to “describe the weaknesses or gaps that may be
intentionally or unintentionally exploited” by a UAS and the consequences of those identified
vulnerabilities, if exploited by a UAS.34 Applicants are also required to describe current security
plans and how the flight restrictions would be integrated into those plans to reduce risk.35
These provisions would require the sharing of highly sensitive data that, if made public, would
give adversaries a roadmap of electrical facilities that may be vulnerable and how to attack
them. Moreover, even if the FAA never intends to make such data public, it would essentially
be creating a honeypot of valuable information that adversaries would seek to exploit and
access.
In fact, much of this information is separately recognized by FERC as Critical Energy/Electric
Infrastructure Information (“CEII”), pursuant to section 215A of the Federal Power Act, and thus
is subject to multiple protections in terms of how it is handled and shared.36
34 See Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24687 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.66(b), (c), (d)). Vulnerability
is defined broadly, as “something in a fixed site facility’s infrastructure, software systems, operations, or
procedures that an unmanned aircraft could exploit or inadvertently interfere with in a way that could
harm the facility, impede the facility’s mission, or present a hazard to people or property.” Proposed
Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24664.
35 Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24687 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.66(d)).
36 See 18 C.F.R. § 388.113.
15

RECOMMENDATIONS:
• The FAA should not require entities to share detailed information about
vulnerabilities and security plans. The FAA should instead establish a self-attestation
framework to establish need, vulnerability, and effective security plans, incorporating
the risk-based approach adopted in NERC and FERC security frameworks.
• A self-certification process would guard against the disclosure of vulnerabilities and
reduce administrative burdens. It also matches processes that have been successfully
used by agencies for many years.37
• The FAA should adopt a presumption of accuracy of self-attestation, should deny an
application only with clear evidence that the attestation is inaccurate or incomplete,
and should defer to the Sector Risk Management Agencies to the extent there is any
question as to need and vulnerability.
• Entities should be required to maintain documentation to support the self-
certification, which can be audited by the FAA, in coordination with the SRMA, as
necessary.
• The FAA should rely on existing NERC and FERC compliance structures wherever
feasible, rather than creating duplicative federal processes for validating security
need, vulnerability, or protective measures. This aligns with the administration’s
stated objective of alleviating burden by eliminating unnecessary regulation.38
37 In a recently issued Interim Final Rule, DHS and DOJ allow private correctional facilities and law
enforcement agencies to self-attest to compliance with Counter-UAS regulations. See Counter-UAS
Authority for State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial Law Enforcement and Correction Agencies, 91 Fed. Reg.
41466, 41488 (to be codified at 6 C.F.R. § 124.6(d)). Other agencies have similar self-attestation rules.
See 47 C.F.R. § 2.906 (requiring a manufacturer, importer, or integrator to certify that the equipment
complies with applicable FCC technical standards and other requirements); 18 C.F.R. § 292.207(a)
(allowing an owner or operator of a qualifying facility to self-certify that the facility meets the requisite
criteria without going through a formal FERC review process); Financial Industry Regulatory Authority
(FINRA) Rule 3130(b) (requiring the CEO or equivalent officer to certify annually that the entity has
policies and written supervisory procedures in place that are reasonably designed to achieve compliance
with applicable FINRA rules, MSRB rules, and federal securities laws and regulations); Sarbanes-Oxley
Act of 2002, 15 U.S.C. § 7241 (requiring regular certification or attestations to the SEC as to the accuracy
of financial disclosures); 17 C.F.R. § 40.2 (allowing a designated contract market or securities exchange
firm to list a new contract for trading without prior Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)
approval by filing a written self-certification that the product complies with the Commodity Exchange
Act and CFTC regulations); 32 C.F.R. §§ 170.15–.16 (laying out the requirements for self-assessment and
affirmation for the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Program of the Department of War).
38 Exec. Order No. 14192, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation, 90 Fed. Reg. 9065 (Jan. 31,
2025).
16

3. § 74.68 – Externalities
Under the Proposed Rule, the FAA would also require applicants to describe externalities
resulting from the proposed UAFR, including details about costs and disruption to other users of
the airspace.39 This is an unworkable requirement—one that would require electric facilities to
gather information about third parties’ activities and plans that they simply do not have access
to.
RECOMMENDATION: Delete the Proposed Rule’s requirement to describe externalities in the
application.
4. § 74.70 – Environmental Impact
Under the Proposed Rule, applicants would be required to identify and describe ten distinct
categories of sensitive land uses and other resources that are within, adjacent, or proximate to
the boundary of the proposed UAFR, and potentially generate an environmental assessment
about these adjacent facilities.40
Electric utilities simply do not have access to this kind of detailed information about third
parties. It is impracticable and unworkable to expect electric utilities to have this kind of
nuanced, detailed information about adjacent landowners and potential environmental impacts
on third parties outside their control. It is difficult to see how restricting drone operations in
electric airspace due to security concerns would result in a significant environmental impact.
RECOMMENDATION: Delete the Proposed Rule’s requirement to assess environmental impact
in the application.
5. § 74.56 – “Protective Security”
The Proposed Rule would require that an applicant has in place protective security, including
security monitoring.41 However, it does not specify what kind of monitoring is required. For this
to be workable, applicants should be able to demonstrate a risk-based approach to security
monitoring, including by demonstrating compliance with existing security frameworks, such as
the NERC CIP standards requirements discussed above or other federal government security
programs.
Given ongoing cost concerns, the Associations are also concerned about the potential for this
requirement to be interpreted to require investment in high-cost detection systems that most
39 Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24687 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.68).
40 Id. (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.70).
41 Id. at 24686–87 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.56).
17

of our members simply cannot afford. A multi-layered radio frequency, camera, and acoustic
detection system could cost upwards of half a million dollars per facility.42 These are costs that
will ultimately be borne by consumers. As a result, a detection system requirement should be
focused on the technologies needed to identify drones that are broadcasting Remote ID signals
or equivalent technology, to establish a baseline of lawful drone use at a given site.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Adopt a risk-based approach to protective security, commensurate with the nature,
sensitivity, and risk profile of a given facility.
• Applicants should be able to rely on compliance with existing NERC, FERC, or other
applicable security compliance frameworks as evidence of an effective security plan.
6. The FAA Should Allow Batched Applications
Given the interconnected nature of the grid and large number of facilities, the requirement that
individual applications be submitted for each individual facility is incredibly burdensome. The
FAA should instead allow a single applicant representing multiple locations to submit batch
applications for facilities with similar profiles. This would significantly decrease administrative
burden for FAA reviewers while streamlining the protection for similar facilities that each plan
to apply. The FAA could retain discretion to evaluate UAFR locations individually while saving
time by analyzing facilities with similar security plans, chemicals of interest, physical layouts,
and hazards. Ideally, the single applicant in the energy and chemical sectors would be the
parent company of the batch facilities. To address the potential administrative burden for both
the private and public sectors that would stem from a facility-by-facility approach to applying
for UAFRs, the FAA should create a system to allow applicants to submit consolidated or
programmatic applications where facilities or operations share similar characteristics, with
standardized criteria applied across qualifying assets.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Applicants should be permitted to submit a single application covering multiple
facilities or assets (e.g., substations, transmission corridors, or distribution systems)
that have common ownership, operate under a single operational plan, and meet the
requisite criteria within a defined service territory.
• This batched approach will streamline the number of applications a given entity will
need to submit, reduce the administrative burden on FAA, and enable consolidated
review of facilities with similar vulnerabilities and security plans.
42 WaveDone, Counter-UAS Cost-Benefit Analysis: Economics of Drone Defense (Mar. 12, 2026),
https://wavedone.com/counter-uas-cost-benefit-analysis-economics-of-drone-defense/.
18

• A batched application and designation process also would better align the UAFR
process with the manner in which utilities assess risk, develop security plans,
coordinate restoration activities, and manage interconnected infrastructure systems.
7. The Renewal Process Should Be Streamlined
While § 74.210 of the Proposed Rule establishes a renewal process requiring an applicant to
renew their request for a UAFR every five years, the text of that section lacks any additional
specificity as to the structure or content of that reapplication process.43 To prevent potential
lapses in protection, the FAA should adopt a streamlined process for renewal. This would
ensure an efficient UAFR renewal process that limits the burden on both applicants and the
FAA.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Establish presumptive renewals for applicants whose operations remain unchanged
from their original UAFR application.
• Create a short form certification for renewals using streamlined templates. These
templates should focus on addressing any material changes made since the last
application and avoid requiring the resubmission of previously approved information
as much as possible.
C. THE NOTICE AND COMMENT PROCESS RAISES SIGNIFICANT SECURITY RISKS AND RELATED
CONCERNS
The Proposed Rule envisions a public notice and comment period for each UAFR request that is
conditionally approved, unless the agency has “good cause” to forgo that period.44 This process
creates significant security concerns and appears to be based on a misguided application of
rules governing manned aircraft to flight restrictions governing low-altitude airspace.
1. The Notice and Comment Process Raises Significant Security Concerns
The notice and comment period would effectively put a target on a facility’s back—alerting the
world that it deems itself vulnerable, has requested the protection of a UAFR, but does not
have one. This creates significant security risk, which would be exacerbated if the notice
includes any of the sensitive information that the FAA seeks to collect from applicants.
43 Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24690 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. § 74.210).
44 Id. (to be codified at § 74.100(c)).
19

2. The Notice and Comment Process Creates Significant Administrative Burdens
Creating individual notice and comment periods for even a subset of all potential UAFR
requests will pose a significant administrative burden. It will require the FAA to publish the
proposed restrictions in the Federal Register (which itself requires several administrative steps),
provide for a 30-day review period, and then review and assess comments. This will inevitably
add time to the process and cause delays in decision-making, making it hard for the FAA to
finalize its review within the presumptive 90-day statutory deadline for making a final UAFR
determination.45
3. The Notice and Comment Process Should Be Replaced With a Mechanism for
Affected Third Parties to Seek Modification or Rescission Post UAFR Issuance
It appears that this provision is modeled after the requirements for designating controlled
airspace for civil aviation operations.46 Those provisions are intended to provide public input on
much more weighty and consequential government actions affecting manned aircraft and
commercial airspace. As applied to UAS operations at or below 400 feet, the potential
disruptions to third party operations are nowhere near as significant, and there is no equivalent
basis to require a notice and comment period for such UAFRs.
The FAA can—and should—create a mechanism for third parties to raise concerns and identify
specific externalities. But this process should be triggered only after a flight restriction has been
announced, so as to protect against the significant security concerns highlighted above.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Eliminate the notice and comment provision.
• Replace with a post-designation process for interested parties that are negatively
affected by a UAFR to raise their concerns and petition to modify or lift the UAFR
subsequent to UAFR issuance.
D. THE SCOPE OF RESTRICTIONS IS INSUFFICIENT AND RISKS UNDULY LIMITING THE PROACTIVE USE OF
DRONES FOR SECURITY AND SAFETY
The standard UAFR includes several exceptions for commercial and recreational drones that
provide advance notice to the FAA and fixed site facility, broadcast a Remote ID, and transit the
UAFR in the shortest time practicable.47 These provisions raise significant concerns:
45 See FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209(b)(2)(A), 130 Stat.
615, 634 (codified at 49 U.S.C. § 40101 note).
46 See 14 C.F.R. § 71.1 (establishing a notice and comment period for controlling commercial airspace).
47 Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24690 (to be codified at § 74.250(a)).
20

• First, they are overbroad and significantly less restrictive than existing temporary flight
restrictions (“TFRs”), which generally require affirmative authorization or waiver to fly
over a restricted area. Such authorization is typically available to entities with a
demonstrated need to operate in the restricted airspace, such as public safety agencies,
first responders, emergency-response personnel, or certain media operations.
The proposed UAFR, by contrast, authorizes a wide array of commercial and
recreational drone activity, with advance notice only. These kinds of broad, automatic
exceptions undermine the security purpose of the Proposed Rule. It would allow
operators with no relationship to the facility, no site-specific need, no facility
authorization, and no separate emergency or public safety justification to enter
protected airspace.
A UAFR with such broad exceptions will fail to provide the practical security benefit
Congress intended when it directed the FAA to establish this process.
• Second, the Associations are concerned that, as drafted, the Proposed Rule does not
include sufficient protections for facility-approved drones used for safety, security, or
inspections. As drafted, the Proposed Rule appears to require even facility-owned
drones to be subject to the operational conditions laid out by § 74.250(a), including the
requirement that they transit the airspace in the shortest time possible.
This is inconsistent with the way facility-owned drones are used. In practice, facility-
owned or authorized UAS may need to remain within a UAFR to perform legitimate
operational functions that require a UAS to hover, circle, conduct repeated passes,
follow electric infrastructure, or otherwise operate for a duration longer than the
shortest amount of time practicable.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Ensure fixed site facility owner/operators have meaningful control over the airspace
protected by UAFR.
• Commercial and recreational drone operations over defense critical electric
infrastructure, nuclear sites, and other critical elements of the electric infrastructure
pose an inherent risk and should be categorically prohibited.
• To the extent commercial and recreational UAS operations are permitted over
restricted airspace, such flights should require express approval by the relevant
facility prior to operating. Conversely, drones being used for emergency response and
public safety reasons should be permitted with notice to the facility owner/operator,
as the Proposed Rule envisions.
21

• The Rule should explicitly authorize facility managers to maintain a list of approved
drones that are permitted to transit the protected airspace without restriction, which
is essential to enabling routine inspection, maintenance, reliability, restoration,
vegetation management, emergency response, and security-related operations.
E. ADDITIONAL RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Provide Flexibility to Adapt to Evolving Technologies
The Proposed Rule is premised, in part, on the continued use of Remote ID as the key
technological means to distinguish authorized and unauthorized drones. In light of evolving
technology, the Final Rule should create flexibility to enable the FAA to require either Remote
ID and associated detection equipment, or other equivalent technology, as approved by the
FAA. This is needed to allow for technological developments over time without requiring a new
rulemaking.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
• The FAA should not lock itself into Remote ID technology as the sole approved
detection technology.
• Instead, any requirement should reference Remote ID “or other technology
designated by the FAA for these purposes,” thereby preserving the agency's flexibility
to update or supplement these requirements as technology evolves without the need
to initiate a new rulemaking proceeding.
2. Expand the Scope of Protected Areas Based on Security Needs
The Proposed Rule specifies that flight restrictions may not exceed the fixed site facility
property boundary.48 The final rule should also account for the fact that the risks posed by UAS
are not limited to direct overflight of a protected asset.
A drone operating just outside a facility boundary may still be capable of conducting
surveillance, identifying security vulnerabilities, interfering with operations, or delivering a
payload with precision. In many cases, the relevant security concern is not simply whether a
UAS crosses the vertical plane above a facility, but whether it is operating close enough to
create a credible threat to the facility, its personnel, or its supporting infrastructure.
48 Id. at 24687 (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. §§ 74.58, 74.60) (defining the lateral boundary and altitude
ceiling of the flight restrictions).
22

RECOMMENDATION: Enable applicants to apply for buffer zones, based on identified security
needs. The appropriate buffer zone will vary based on the size, configuration, location, and
risk profile of the facility.
3. Support Strong Enforcement
The Associations encourage the FAA to exercise active enforcement authority over drone flights
that violate restricted airspace. The final rule should enable and encourage critical
infrastructure and law enforcement to work together to enforce violations of UAFR restrictions.
F. CONCLUSION
The Electric Utility Trade Associations thank the FAA for the opportunity to comment on this
important Proposed Rule. The Associations look forward to serving as a resource for the FAA on
this subject and encourage the FAA to reach out to our counsel, Jennifer Daskal, at 202-344-
4975 or JDaskal@Venable.com, with any questions or comments.
Respectfully submitted,
Jennifer C. Daskal Aryeh B. Fishman
Venable LLP Edison Electric Institute
Partner Associate General Counsel
Jdaskal@venable.com afishman@eei.org
Latif Nurani Jonathan D. Schneider
American Public Power Association Stinson LLP
Senior Regulatory Counsel Counsel for the Large Public Power Council
lnurani@publicpower.org jonathan.schneider@stinson.com
Megan Olmstead
National Rural Electric Cooperative Association
Regulatory Affairs Director
megan.olmstead@nreca.coop
23

comments.commenter: Comment from The American Gas Association

comments.comment_text:
RE: Docket Number FAA-2026-4558

The City of Chandler respectfully submits the following comments regarding the proposed FAA rule to restrict the operation of Unmanned Aircraft in close proximity to a fixed site facility.

As the City of Innovation, Chandler has long embraced emerging technologies to improve public service, community safety, and our resident’s quality of life. We fully support measures that aim to protect critical infrastructure and enhance aviation safety. However, it is imperative that restrictions do not unintentionally impede time-sensitive public safety operations by adding layers of approval to the authorization aviation process. Under current practice, Chandler Police and Fire operate drones under 14 CFR Part 107, with strict adherence to FAA safety requirements.

Drones have become an invaluable tool for Chandler Police and Chandler Fire that improve situational awareness, reduce risk to first responders, and ultimately save and preserve lives. The deployment of drones during high-priority critical incidents help provide intel on active emergency calls such as suspect searches, vehicle pursuits, active shooters, violent crimes, structural fires, hazardous incidents, and rescue operations. Routinely, drones are the first deployed resource providing real-time intel that directly supports safety for officers, first responders, and suspects.

Chandler first responders rely on immediate drone authorization and deployment without any burdensome administrative delay. The proposed restrictions near critical infrastructure may inadvertently create administrative delays in obtaining necessary airspace authorization under 14 CFR Part 107. Even a short administrative delay of a minute could then impact life-saving measures and pose a serious risk to first responders and residents.

The City of Chandler respectfully requests that agencies currently operating under 14 CFR part 107, maintain uninterrupted, seamless, and rapid access to the airspace necessary for emergency drone operations. Any future restrictions should prioritize preserving the current status quo and ability for first responders to deploy and operate drones during time-sensitive incidents.

Thank you for your consideration in advancing safety for both public safety and aviation.

I oppose the inclusion of the Food and Agriculture sector (§ 74.90) amongst the critical infrastructure facilities that could obtain Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs)
It is crucial to counteract the secrecy of the industrial agriculture sector. Drone camera footage has been essential to expose deliberate acts of cruelty perpetrated on innocent animals on factory farms, otherwise there is no accountability for these actions and with no surveillance, workers at factory farms could commit acts of cruelty with impunity. As the majority of these huge animal factories have chosen not to install their own watchdog systems, drone surveillance is the only remaining method of responsible monitoring of potential animal welfare violations.
With properly licensed and trained drone operators there is no safety risk for the employees or animals. These drone operations provide an essential system of checks and balances on an industry with so much potential for cruelty and other health and safety violations.
Drone footage has been key in informing the public and possibly limiting the cruelty that I've seen in the footage.so far.
I've seen workers hitting and kicking calves, pulling on their noses with pliers and knocking them to the ground, dumping them from a trailer and shooting them in the head etc.
Please do not approve or allow any Fixed Site Facility Restrictions. That's what the animal agriculture sector wants so they can operate in secrecy with no accountability. Please don't let them hide behind any restriction!

As I understand it, passing this rule will likely allow farms and concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) to apply for (and be granted) the restriction of flying unmanned drones above those areas (including drones with video recording capabilities).

I support allowing the use of drones to fly above farms and CAFOs. Accountability is important - especially in industries that makes claims ("organic", "certified humane", etc.) but repeatedly fail to meet said claims. Drone use over farms and CAFOs helps to apply accountability in an industry that so desperately needs it.

We need transparency in how these operations conduct business, and we need verification that they meet the requirements set forth in their advertised certifications.

I see absolutely no benefit in restricting drone flights above these industries.

Because of this, I am against the passage of this new rule (or update to the existing rule).

Please consider to revise the proposed changes so that there is no restriction on drone use over CAFOs or farms.

Thank you.

These proposed rules would hinder our operations pertaining to immediate life and safety, of not only citizens but first responders as well. Those that intend to do illegal actions with their drones will not be hindered by these rules. This only hurts the law abiding pilots by restricting the national airspace.

I recommend limiting the restrictions to anyone without a FAA certificate ( 107 or 93)

The rule as proposed is a direct attack on freedom of speech and the transparency that the public requires in order to make informed decisions on controversial issu3s like the state of food sources in the US. I am against restricting drones from flying over or in close proximity to a fixed site facility.

comments.commenter: Comment from Los Angeles Philharmonic Association
comments.comment_text:
To Whom It May Concern:
The Los Angeles Philharmonic Association operating at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles has reviewed the proposed rulemaking including the new Part 74 of the Federal Aviation Regulations.
Upon our review, we find the requirement for commercial facilities to qualify for an unmanned aircraft flight restriction (UAFR) in the proposed §74.82 by having an annual attendance of at least 2,500,000 visitors to be unreasonable and excessive. We find that our concert venue is - like hundreds of other outdoor facilities in the United States that hold mass gatherings - vulnerable to the threat of unmanned aircraft system (UAS) activity despite having an annual attendance well below the proposed minimum of 2,500,000.
As the use of small UAS has proliferated over the past decade even with the publication of the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Part 107, our venue has observed dozens of instances of seemingly careless and clueless (if not criminal) operators flying over our facility and audiences, creating alarm amongst both our staff and audience members alike.
While our venue has averaged an annual draw of over one million visitors in the past 10 years (excluding 2020 and 2021 due to impacts from the Coronavirus-19 pandemic), we strongly urge the FAA to lower the attendance requirement to no higher than 500,000 in order to allow our venue as well as many like ours to be eligible to better protect mass gatherings critical to the economic health of the communities that we serve.
We appreciate the opportunity from the FAA to provide comment on this significant proposed rulemaking.
Banning drones essentially gives carte blanche to industrialists who flout the rules. Drones are necessary to monitor compliance with environmental, employment, and animal welfare regulations.

I oppose allowing the food and agriculture sector, including farming operations, to obtain unmanned aircraft flight restrictions. The FAA has shown no national-security, economic, public-health, or safety justification. Drone footage promotes accountability by documenting pollution, waste breaches, biohazards, animal-treatment concerns, and misleading claims. Factory Farms are using the FAA potential ban as a tool to hide their cruel and often illegal behavior.

The American Chemistry Council (ACC) appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, *Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility*, implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, as amended. ACC respectfully requests that the FAA consider the attached comments in developing the final rule.

RE: Opposition to docket number FAA-2026-4558
To whom it may concern,
Mercy For Animals, Inc. (“MFA”) submits this comment in opposition to the
development of eligibility criteria for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (“UAFRs”) over
Food and Agriculture Sector (“FAS”) facilities under this proposed rule.1 Although protecting
critical infrastructure is a legitimate goal, UAFRs over FAS facilities would impose an
unconstitutional burden on First Amendment-protected newsgathering, undermine transparency
and accountability in an industry that directly affects public health and welfare, and chill the
investigative work of advocacy organizations that serve the public interest. In response to FAA’s
three questions regarding the FAS sector,2 MFA urges FAA to: (1) finalize § 74.90 as
“[Reserved]”; (2) exclude the ability to be observed or photographed from the air as a qualifying
weakness in determining an FAS facility’s vulnerability; and (3) treat an FAS facility’s
regional/national economic impact as a factor weighing against, not in favor of, UAFRs.
1 Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility, 91 FED.
REG. 24,650 (May 6, 2026) (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. pts. 1, 74, 91, 107)
https://www.regulations.gov/document/FAA-2026-4558-0001.
2 The proposed rule mentions the following statement and questions:
FAA seeks comments on the following questions to inform the development of the criteria for the
food and agricultural sector: 1. What types of facilities within this sector should be considered for
a UAFR? Specifically, those that could have debilitating regional or national-level consequences.
2. What characteristics should be considered in the development of gating criteria for those
facilities? 3. Should the population served or regional or national economic impact be considered
in the development of gating criteria, and if so, what are appropriate thresholds? 91 Fed. Reg.
24,650, 24,669–70.

I. Interest of Commenter
MFA is an international nonprofit animal protection organization. MFA uses drone
imagery, captured by FAA-certified drone operators, to uncover the activities at FAS facilities
that are potentially unlawful and detrimental to public health and the environment. MFA’s
findings help reform corporate and government policies to improve biosecurity and public health
outcomes related to food production.
II. FAA’s own previous findings are correct and additional consideration discourages
extending UAFRs to FAS facilities.
FAA itself recognizes the absence of a demonstrated need to restrict drone operations
over FAS facilities. FAA acknowledges that it, “in consultation with the SRMAs, could not
identify a facility in this sector that was not already captured by another sector or would rise to
the level of national level debilitating impact.”3 In the absence of any demonstrated need,
developing criteria that would allow FAS operators to restrict airspace above their properties
would be arbitrary and inconsistent with FAA’s own stated principle that “restricting airspace [is]
a remedy to be applied only when necessary.”4
Indeed, FAA must proceed with caution and any UAFR proposal related to an FAS
facility faces a high burden: “restricting airspace is an extraordinary remedy that must be
balanced against the public right of transit.”5 The agency must consider “what effect, if any, the
UAFR would have on adjacent landowners and airspace users,” and anyone supporting a UAFR
needs to account for “the costs, disruptions, or other negative effects to users of the airspace,
including known traffic circumnavigating the facility.”6 “[I]n granting a UAFR to address one
risk,” the restriction must “not create a different concern for other stakeholders.”7 This comment
will describe how UAFRs of FAS facilities will help create many of the problems that FAA aims
to avoid.
III. The proposed access framework is incompatible with First Amendment-protected
investigations.
In the preamble, FAA admits that “first amendment activity, may require non-transitory
operations within a UAFR.”8 Yet the proposed rule’s access framework does not adequately
accommodate these vital activities: “Audiovisual recordings are protected by the First
Amendment as recognized ‘organ[s] of public opinion’ and as a ‘significant medium for the

These conditions are fundamentally incompatible with valuable investigations of FAS

necessary to document animal welfare violations, environmental contamination, and biosecurity

from multiple angles, not simply fly over as quickly as possible.
Second, requiring advance notification to the facility operator would defeat the purpose
of independent oversight. Advance notice would allow operators to conceal, mitigate, or
temporarily suspend the very conditions that journalists and advocates are seeking to document.
In a similar vein, an undercover journalist working as a prison guard and reporting on medical
neglect and violence in a prison,11 for example, would never give the prison a heads-up about his
arrival weeks in advance. Advance notification undermines the value of drone photography as an
oversight tool.
These First Amendment concerns discourage the creation of eligibility criteria for
UAFRs over FAS facilities. But even if FAA nonetheless develops UAFR eligibility criteria for
FAS facilities, the First Amendment should be top of mind. The agency should, at minimum,
exempt Part 107 operators engaged in First Amendment-protected newsgathering and
investigative work from the advance notification and transit-time requirements, and should
prohibit facility operators from interfering with lawful aerial documentation.

V. Conclusion
Investigative work using drones is vital First Amendment activity that furthers
Congress’s aims of “protection of people and property on the ground” by exposing the
biosecurity and environmental risks that FAS facilities pose to the public.33 UAFRs over FAS
facilities would violate the principles that should inform FAA’s rulemaking. As such, FAA
should reject such “extraordinary remed[ies].”34 Granting UAFRs for FAS facilities would
disarm nearby communities from advocating for their own wellbeing against the FAS operations
in their midst. Aerial imagery captures the geographic scope of contamination in a way that
ground-level observation cannot replicate.
For the foregoing reasons, Mercy For Animals respectfully requests that FAA decline to
develop eligibility criteria for the food and agriculture sector. The government’s own
epidemiologic data, MFA’s investigations, and peer-reviewed research all confirm that aerial
observation of FAS facilities serves public health and poses no demonstrated biosecurity risk. If
FAA nevertheless develops UAFR criteria, it should exclude the ability to be observed or
photographed from the air as a qualifying weakness in determining an FAS facility’s
vulnerability, treat an FAS facility’s regional/national economic impact as a factor weighing
against, not in favor of, UAFRs, and exempt Part 107 operators engaged in First
Amendment-protected newsgathering and investigative work from the proposed access
framework.

Comment Regarding Proposed 14 CFR Part 74
Docket No. FAA–2026–4558; Notice No. 26–03
RIN 2120–AL33
Patrick McKay, Esq.
August 5, 2026
I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the FAA’s proposal to establish Unmanned Aircraft
Flight Restrictions under proposed 14 CFR Part 74.
I am a longtime recreational unmanned-aircraft operator. I have flown fixed-wing
first-person-view aircraft since 2011 and DJI multicopters since 2017. I support reasonable,
evidence-based measures to protect facilities that face a genuine and unusual danger from
unmanned aircraft. I also generally support the comments submitted by the Drone Service
Providers Alliance regarding demonstrated need, access procedures, boundaries, private
mitigation, federal preemption, and the distinction between Standard and Special UAFRs.
The final rule, however, must be carefully limited so that it does not unnecessarily eliminate
recreational access to the National Airspace System. Because recreational operators generally
fly in parks, open fields, undeveloped areas, and other relatively scarce locations, even a
modest proliferation of low-altitude restrictions could leave hobbyists with few or no practical
places to fly in many communities.
1. The FAA should retain a strong distinction between Standard and Special
UAFRs
The proposed distinction between Standard UAFRs and Special UAFRs is appropriate and
should be retained.
Special UAFRs should be reserved for facilities facing a documented national-security,
homeland-security, corrections, or similarly exceptional threat. Examples may include certain
military installations, nuclear facilities, intelligence facilities, and correctional institutions with a
documented history of drone-delivered contraband.
Standard UAFRs should not become a routine benefit available to any facility that can describe
a hypothetical misuse of a drone. A Standard UAFR is still a closure of public navigable
airspace to an entire category of aircraft. It should therefore be treated as an extraordinary
remedy, not as an ordinary addition to a facility’s security program.

2
2. Eligibility must require a proven, site-specific, and uniquely
drone-related danger
The most important protection in the final rule should be a demanding demonstration-of-need
standard.
A facility should receive a UAFR only when it demonstrates all of the following:
1. A specific asset or operation at the individual site is unusually vulnerable to unmanned
aircraft;
2. The reasonably foreseeable consequences of a drone incident would be severe and
would have regional or national significance;
3. The danger is materially different from the ordinary possibility that someone could use a
vehicle, camera, computer, firearm, or other common technology to commit a crime;
4. Existing ground security, Remote ID, enforcement, physical hardening, operating
procedures, and other less restrictive measures cannot reasonably address the danger;
and
5. The requested restriction would materially reduce the identified danger.
The possibility that a criminal could use a drone for surveillance, trespass, vandalism, theft, or
another unlawful purpose should not, by itself, justify restricting airspace. Nearly every building,
business, residence, public event, or piece of infrastructure could make that claim. The relevant
question should be whether all ordinary drone operations, including lawful and responsible
recreational operations, create a unique danger that cannot be managed by narrower means.
The FAA itself recognizes that a UAFR may not deter a person who deliberately intends to
violate the law. That makes a strict eligibility standard especially important. A rule that primarily
changes the behavior of compliant operators should not impose widespread restrictions merely
because a noncompliant actor might commit a crime that the restriction itself is unlikely to
prevent.
Documented prior activity should also matter. An applicant should ordinarily be required to
provide verifiable evidence of drone incidents that caused, or came close to causing, a material
disruption, safety event, or security breach. Generalized concern, unidentified sightings,
speculation about surveillance, or the mere presence of recreational aircraft nearby should not
be enough.
3. The FAA must evaluate cumulative impacts, not merely each UAFR in
isolation
The proposed rule requires consideration of externalities associated with an individual
application. That is necessary but insufficient.
The FAA must also evaluate the cumulative effect of nearby UAFRs. A restriction that appears
small on a facility map can have a much greater practical effect when combined with other

3
restrictions, controlled airspace, airports, heliports, temporary flight restrictions, local park rules,
terrain, residential development, and the limited number of places where launching and
recovering a recreational aircraft is permitted.
This is especially important for energy and communications infrastructure. Electrical substations,
transmission and distribution equipment, cellular facilities, pipelines, rail infrastructure, and
related facilities are widely distributed throughout urban and suburban areas. They are
frequently located next to greenbelts, trails, parks, sports fields, reservoirs, flood-control areas,
and other open spaces where recreational operators may lawfully fly.
Allowing common facilities to obtain restrictions merely because they fall into a broad
infrastructure category could create overlapping or closely spaced restricted areas throughout a
city. The theoretical availability of isolated pieces of airspace would be of little value if there were
no practical location from which a hobbyist could launch, fly a safe pattern, and recover the
aircraft.
For every application, the FAA should therefore require a publicly available cumulative-impact
map showing:
● Existing and proposed UAFRs in the surrounding area;
● Public parks and recreational lands;
● Established model-aircraft fields and FAA-recognized identification areas;
● Known recreational UAS flying locations;
● Controlled airspace and other flight restrictions; and
● Remaining areas in which recreational flight would actually be practical.
The FAA should deny or reduce a proposed UAFR when its cumulative effect would materially
impair recreational access within the surrounding community.
4. Recreational operations under 49 U.S.C. § 44809 must be eligible to
access Standard UAFRs
Proposed § 74.250 would allow operations under Parts 91, 107, 108, 135, and 137 to enter
Standard UAFRs, subject to Remote ID and notification requirements. It does not extend the
same opportunity to recreational operations conducted under 49 U.S.C. § 44809.
That exclusion is unjustified and should be corrected.
A recreational operation is not inherently more dangerous merely because it is conducted for
recreation rather than compensation. The same aircraft may be flown by the same person over
the same route, with the same registration, Remote ID equipment, and operating limitations.
The safety or security of a facility should not turn on whether the pilot is being paid.
The final rule should allow a recreational operator to enter a Standard UAFR when the operator:
● Complies with 49 U.S.C. § 44809 and applicable FAA rules;

4
● Uses a registered aircraft when registration is required;
● Broadcasts Remote ID when required, or operates under another applicable FAA
authorization;
● Completes the required notification; and
● Complies with reasonable, nationally uniform operating conditions.
Special UAFRs may appropriately have more restrictive access requirements. Standard UAFRs
should remain accessible to lawful recreational operators on terms comparable to those
applicable to Part 107 operators.
The FAA should also protect established recreational flying locations. A UAFR should not
ordinarily be approved if it would overlap an FAA-recognized identification area, an established
model-aircraft field, or a public location with a documented history of lawful recreational UAS
use. Such a restriction should require an extraordinary and specifically documented justification.
5. The access system must be centralized, immediate, and
non-discretionary
I support the DSPA’s recommendation that the FAA use a LAANC-like process for Standard
UAFR access.
The process should be:
● Centralized and operated or supervised by the FAA;
● Available through a website and machine-readable interface;
● Capable of providing immediate confirmation;
● Free or available at nominal cost;
● Uniform across facilities and states; and
● A notification system, not a process through which a private facility may deny access at
its discretion.
A facility site manager may need notice of lawful operations, but a private facility should not
control public airspace or require a pilot to negotiate individually for permission. Submission of
the required information should be sufficient for an otherwise eligible operator to proceed.
The FAA should require each facility to maintain a current public point of contact, but the lack of
a response from that contact should not prevent an operation that complies with the regulation.
6. The “shortest amount of time practicable” standard must account for
fixed-wing aircraft
The proposed requirement that an aircraft transit a UAFR in the shortest practicable time
appears to have been written primarily with multicopters and commercial route operations in
mind.

5
Fixed-wing FPV aircraft cannot hover, stop, or make arbitrarily tight turns. They must maintain
airspeed and may require a substantial turning radius. Wind, terrain, signal quality, other aircraft,
and the need to maintain visual-line-of-sight compliance may also affect the safest route.
The final rule should therefore use language such as “without unnecessary delay and in a
manner consistent with safe operation” rather than requiring the mathematically shortest or
quickest transit.
The rule should also recognize that not every legitimate operation is a point-to-point transit. A
recreational fixed-wing aircraft flying from an adjacent park may need to turn near the boundary,
briefly follow a curved flight path, or maneuver to maintain separation from people and property.
Safe maneuvering should not be treated as loitering or suspicious activity.
7. Boundaries must be limited to the smallest area actually requiring
protection
I support proposed § 74.58’s general limitation to property boundaries, but the final rule should
go further.
The property line should be an absolute maximum for Standard UAFRs. No buffer should
extend over neighboring parks, streets, homes, trails, waterways, or other property. Within the
applicant’s property, the FAA should restrict only the smallest practicable polygon over the
particular asset shown to be vulnerable—not automatically the entire parcel.
Large industrial and utility properties may contain substantial open or undeveloped areas that
have no relationship to the asserted vulnerability. Restricting the entire property would be
broader than necessary.
The vertical limit should likewise be no higher than necessary. Standardized, clearly published
limits are preferable to complex facility-specific rules, but a default ceiling should not
automatically become the maximum ceiling for every application.
The FAA should also preserve usable corridors between adjacent facilities and should reject
configurations that create narrow traps, complex boundaries, or areas that are impractical for a
recreational operator to recognize while flying.
8. Standard UAFR status must not confer private counter-UAS authority
The final rule should state unequivocally that a UAFR does not authorize a facility owner,
employee, contractor, or private security provider to jam, spoof, intercept, seize, damage,
disable, or destroy an unmanned aircraft.
A pilot should not face a risk that private personnel will interfere with a control link or aircraft
merely because the facility believes the aircraft crossed a boundary. Any detection or mitigation
authority must remain limited to entities separately authorized by federal law.

6
The FAA should also require facilities to train security personnel that Remote ID reception does
not itself establish unlawful conduct and that a notification record is not permission for private
confrontation, pursuit, or interference.
9. The FAA should prevent fragmented state and local airspace restrictions
I support inclusion of explicit federal-preemption language.
The value of a federal Part 74 process would be undermined if states, counties, cities, special
districts, and individual infrastructure operators could establish additional exclusion zones,
stand-off distances, or flight restrictions based on the same facility-security concerns.
The final rule should confirm that regulation of flight and navigable airspace is an exclusive
federal function, while preserving traditional state and local authority over ground conduct,
landowner rules governing takeoff and landing, privacy, nuisance, reckless endangerment, and
generally applicable criminal law.
There should be one national airspace system and one authoritative source through which pilots
can determine where flight is permitted.
10. Each restriction should receive meaningful public notice, review, and
periodic reassessment
The FAA should retain Federal Register notice and comment for individual UAFRs rather than
relying solely on facility applications or an FAA webpage.
Local recreational pilots may possess information the applicant and FAA do not have, including
the existence of a model-aircraft field, commonly used park, flight corridor, public event,
emergency helicopter route, or other local condition.
Every proposal should include sufficient public information to permit meaningful comment on:
● The exact lateral and vertical boundaries;
● The facility’s non-sensitive justification;
● The proposed activation period;
● Nearby recreational land and flying locations;
● Other restrictions in the area; and
● The cumulative effect on local airspace access.
Standard UAFRs should expire unless the facility affirmatively demonstrates at renewal that the
original drone-specific vulnerability still exists, the restriction remains effective, and narrower
measures remain inadequate. Renewal should not be automatic merely because the facility
continues to meet a sector classification.

7
Conclusion
I support protecting genuinely sensitive facilities from demonstrated unmanned-aircraft threats. I
do not support transforming broad categories of common infrastructure into presumptively
restricted airspace.
The final rule should:
● Reserve UAFRs for site-specific, documented, and uniquely drone-related dangers;
● Require evidence of actual need rather than hypothetical criminal misuse;
● Evaluate cumulative effects on community access;
● Permit compliant recreational operations under 49 U.S.C. § 44809 in Standard UAFRs;
● Protect established recreational flying locations;
● Establish a centralized, immediate notification process;
● Account for the operating characteristics of fixed-wing aircraft;
● Limit restrictions to the smallest necessary boundaries;
● Prohibit any implication of private counter-UAS authority;
● Reaffirm federal control of airspace; and
● Require meaningful public review and periodic reassessment.
Recreational model aviation has existed safely for generations and provides education,
technical skills, community, and an entry point into aviation. The FAA can protect truly critical
facilities without making lawful recreational flight impractical across entire cities and suburban
communities. I respectfully ask the FAA to adopt a narrow, evidence-based final rule that
preserves that balance.
Thank you for considering my comments.

My name is Joseph Allman. I am a drone flight instructor and program administrator for a fleet of animal cruelty investigators who fly drones over industrial animal agriculture facilities to document the conditions of animals.

I write regarding Docket FAA-2026-4558. I oppose the inclusion of food and agriculture as a sector eligible to apply for UAFRs. The FAA expressly requested comment on the food and agriculture eligibility criteria.

I hold an FAA private pilot certificate (single-engine land), earned as a teenager after seven months of training. Manned aviation taught me the discipline behind this comment: though flying feels like magic, it isn't. Every flight is a chain of decisions with consequences down the line, people have died for the lessons in our study materials, and a good pilot learns to catch a bad decision in himself before he makes it. I brought that discipline to drones.

Direct Action Everywhere, where I run the drone program, documents conditions inside industrial animal factories, commonly called factory farms, which confine thousands to millions of animals in sheds. Some investigators lose their freedom for telling the stories of these animals, entering the farms, documenting conditions, and removing the sick and injured.

I set the standards for our drone program, whose mission statement is modeled on the FAA's own: to be the safest and most efficient program capable of documenting the conditions of factory farms. I created our checklist (attached), covering every phase of flight from preflight planning through landing and notetaking. Our students earn FAA certification and demonstrate proficiency in program flight standards to follow that checklist competently before I sign off on them flying over factory farms.

UAFR eligibility requires an applicant to demonstrate a documented vulnerability to what an unmanned aircraft can do. A camera recording from dozens to hundreds of feet away creates no such vulnerability. The payloads of our drones are no threat to animals, persons on the surface, or property. They are not weapons. They are cameras. They do not warrant classification as a "credible threat" to critical infrastructure.

The rule's defenders will point to the Standard UAFR transit allowance (proposed § 74.250), letting Part 107 operators cross a restricted area. But transit is defined as passing in the shortest practicable time, and documentation is the opposite of transit. Observing a facility to record conditions is the entire purpose of the flight. A Standard UAFR therefore forecloses lawful newsgathering over a covered farm while appearing to preserve access. A Special UAFR, which bars all operators absent the site owner's permission, forecloses it outright.

There have been days driving home after flying when I asked myself not whether the animals were okay, but how many bones I had just watched get broken, and whether there were any babies still alive in that dead-pile. There has never been a day when I wondered whether our drone had harmed an animal, or been a threat to the safety or security of a facility or its workers.

Local authorities and local farm owners will tell you otherwise. They have called into question my adherence to almost every drone rule there is. Flying beyond line of sight, at the wrong altitude, even killing a cow at a farm I was not surveilling. My drone at closest was 600 feet away from their fence according to flight logs. It was during that particular flight, that we saw a worker trying to push a calf with locked knees to the ground, in an area where months prior we saw baby calves thrown from a truck and shot in the head. And it was during that flight that a local sheriff told me in the same breath that I had killed a cow on a neighboring farm, and that our documentation was "propaganda."

Our flight investigations have captured harrowing footage at facilities across California. This work has produced coverage in the Los Angeles Times, Vox, the Modesto Bee, and the Turlock Journal (attached), led to the firing of a worker documented abusing calves, and generated law-enforcement referrals for animal cruelty. The threat these facilities seek to restrict is not to safety. It is to secrecy.

The difference between us flying and not flying is the difference between suffering animals being seen, as if they mattered, and enduring a pain-filled life, invisible.

It is the mission of the Federal Aviation Administration to uphold the safety and efficiency of the best national airspace system in the world. This administration has a duty not to animal agriculture, and not to government agencies captured by industry. It has a duty to the people. It has a duty to the system. The proposed rule, as written, allows factory farms to apply for flight restrictions. These flight restrictions would not be in the name of safety, but in the name of secrecy, falsehoods and the protection of corporate profits. Exclude food and agriculture from UAFR eligibility.

comments.commenter: Comment from Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
Submitted Online
Michelle Ferritto
Office of Rulemaking, Federal Aviation Administration
Department of Transportation
800 Independence Avenue SW
Washington, DC 20591
Dear Ms. Ferritto:
Comments on FAA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft
in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility [Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03]
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking to implement section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 regarding
the restriction of operation of unmanned aircraft in close proximity to fixed site facilities [Docket No. FAA-2026-
4558; Notice No. 26-03]. We especially appreciate the consideration and request for feedback on the restriction of
unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) at or near wastewater treatment systems and facilities, also known as Publicly
owned treatment works (POTWs). We strongly support the FAA’s efforts to protect critical infrastructure and
request that water and wastewater facilities of all sizes be designated eligible for standard unmanned aircraft flight
restrictions (UAFR).
The Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts (Sanitation Districts) are a local agency providing wastewater
and solid waste management services to approximately 5.5 million people in 78 cities and unincorporated areas of
Los Angeles County. Our mission is to protect public health and the environment through innovative and
cost-effective wastewater and solid waste management and, in doing so, convert waste into resources. The
Sanitation Districts’ wastewater treatment system includes 11 water reclamation and treatment plants of various
sizes, ranging in permitted capacity from 200,000 gallons per day to 400,000,000 gallons per day. The system also
includes over 1,400 miles of trunk sewers, 49 pump stations, and a seven-mile ocean outfall tunnel. These facilities
include seven wastewater facilities interconnected through a network of large trunk sewers known as the Joint
Outfall System.
POTWs often store and utilize large quantities of hazardous chemicals at their wastewater treatment and
reclamation facilities. The Sanitation Districts also utilize high-purity oxygen at one of our facilities and capture
large quantities of biogas to power a 22-megawatt onsite power plant and fuel vehicles at two fueling stations. Many
of our facilities have large, open-air footprints with security features that prevent unauthorized entrance from the
ground. However, the new age of readily available drones presents a threat for which our facilities and security
were not designed. These facility characteristics create unique vulnerabilities to UAS-related threats. Whether
unauthorized flights are actively hostile or simply recreational, UAS activity introduces operational and safety
hazards that current ground-based security measures cannot mitigate. In response to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking’s request for information specifically regarding water and wastewater facilities, we have focused our
comments on the Notice’s published questions related to the wastewater sector.
DOC 7869673

Michelle Ferritto - 2 - August 5, 2026
Wastewater systems are critical to ensuring clean water for communities throughout the country. The
Sanitation Districts recommend including all sizes of facilities in UAS no-fly zones. Water and wastewater systems
of all sizes face meaningful risks from unauthorized UAS operations. Large systems serving millions of people
present attractive targets for actors seeking widespread disruption, while smaller systems may be more vulnerable
due to limited security resources. Additionally, upstream facilities might directly serve smaller population sizes, but
disruptions to treatment processes could create downstream impacts on larger populations served by interconnected
networks of wastewater facilities, such as in our Joint Outfall System. In order to provide better service and ensure
access to clean water for their communities, water and wastewater systems of varying sizes are increasingly working
together through regional approaches. Providing UAS protections to agencies of all sizes supports better holistic
protection of water and wastewater systems, public infrastructure, and our communities.
Water and wastewater systems have extensively built infrastructure throughout their service areas. The
Sanitation Districts recommend focusing gating criteria on critical outdoor, above-ground components of POTWs
that would be most vulnerable to UAS. Such locations would include water reclamation and treatment units, such
as primary, secondary, and tertiary treatment systems, advanced treatment systems, water reclamation ponds, and
wastewater lagoons. Infrastructure such as pump stations could be considered due to their system criticality, but the
smaller footprints might mean there are little-to-no security benefits to UAS gating. The Sanitation Districts also
recommend providing standard UAFR for all water and wastewater systems regardless of specific critical
customers. Significant disruptions to POTW operations can cause raw sewage spills in neighborhoods and
waterways and present substantial public risks to local communities. If a POTW cannot operate, there are few
alternatives to safely manage sewage. Water and wastewater facilities are easily recognizable public infrastructure
and there is no public benefit to unauthorized private drone flights over these locations that would weigh against
more protective policies.
The Sanitation Districts recommend that the FAA does not limit gating criteria to water and wastewater
facilities or systems solely based on whether there is a history of unauthorized drone flights. As a public agency, a
substantial amount of information regarding our facilities and infrastructure is public and easily accessible. Satellite
images and GIS would make it possible to plan a drone attack without ever previously flying a UAS over a facility
or system for pre-attack surveillance. One unauthorized drone flight leading to an attack is one too many. Extending
UAS gating protection to all water and wastewater systems and ensuring POTWs can receive UAFRs would help
maximize protection and minimize potential threats from rule inception.
Thank you for the opportunity for the Sanitation Districts to provide sector-specific information and
feedback regarding the restriction of UAS at and near wastewater facilities. We strongly support the Administration
taking a strong defensive position in protecting critical infrastructure serving our communities throughout the
country. We respectfully request that the FAA designate all water and wastewater treatment facilities as fixed-site
facilities under Section 2209 and establish clear gating criteria for above-ground, outdoor critical treatment
infrastructure to make these facilities eligible for standard UAFRs. We appreciate your consideration of our
comments. If you have any questions about our comments, please contact me at paulacrowell@lacsd.org or
562-908-4288, extension 2714.
Very truly yours,
Paula Crowell
Chief Information Officer
Information Technology Section
