COMMENTS OF MELISSA RANK, PLS
Building an Implementable Section 2209 Framework
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 | Notice No. 26-03 | RIN 2120-AL33
August 5, 2026
VIA ELECTRONIC SUBMISSION
Docket Operations, M-30
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Room W58-213, West Building, 5th Floor
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Designation - Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
To the Federal Aviation Administration:
I submit these comments in my individual professional capacity. I use Altus Aviation Group as my independent
professional brand. The views expressed here are mine and do not represent any client, current or former
employer, or other organization.
I am a North Carolina Professional Land Surveyor with more than 25 years of experience in the geospatial and
design industry, including 17 years focused specifically on aviation. I have managed hundreds of airport
surveys across the United States and delivered numerous projects involving FAA-compliant aeronautical data,
airspace analysis, obstacle evaluation, obstruction analysis, and heliport surveys. My work has supported the
FAA, state departments of transportation, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, commercial-service airports,
general-aviation airports, and other public infrastructure owners.
I also served as principal investigator and project manager for an FAA research initiative addressing
geospatial data standards for heliports and vertiports. Much of my career has been spent at the point where
FAA requirements, geospatial data, airspace constraints, and real infrastructure decisions meet. That
experience directly informs these comments, particularly where the proposed framework depends on non-
aviation organizations to establish and maintain processes involving property interests, airspace boundaries,
operational notices, security information, monitoring, and regulatory compliance.
I support the FAA's effort to implement Section 2209 through proposed 14 CFR part 74. A fixed-site restriction
can be useful only if the designation, notice, data, monitoring, and maintenance systems work together. The
proposal is strongest where it preserves FAA control of the navigable airspace and requires a documented
safety or security need. It is less complete where the owner-side workload remains undefined, or the proposed
UAFR-Utility and draft guidance do not yet provide the standards, portfolio controls, and service expectations
needed for consistent administration.1
For a participating owner, Part 74 is not only an application for an airspace designation. It requires a standing
governance and administrative function. Applicants must establish authority over the facility and property
interests, define a precise airspace volume, document vulnerabilities and consequences, maintain security
and Remote Identification monitoring, develop UAS security and incident-response plans, receive operational
notices, update information, report activity, and renew the designation. Participation is voluntary, and these
duties attach only to applicants and UAFR holders. Even so, a voluntary program can fail if the process
assumes capacity that many eligible owners do not yet have.2

The FAA acknowledges that many fixed-site operators may have little prior experience with the agency or
aviation operations. That point should shape the final rule, Advisory Circular, and UAFR-Utility. Publishing a
rule is not the same as enabling implementation. The harder question is whether an eligible owner can
establish, maintain, and audit the institutional system behind a UAFR without acquiring airspace-control
authority that Congress did not assign to it.3
My central recommendation is straightforward: keep the FAA's substantive review and final decision facility-
specific, but do not require facility-by-facility administrative reinvention. The final framework should permit
common systems, shared capabilities, and portfolio administration while preserving an individual finding of
need and an individually defined airspace designation for each facility.
Summary of Requested FAA Actions
1. Keep the site manager's role notice-only. State in the regulatory text and system workflow that receipt,
acknowledgment, silence, or objection does not approve or deny an operation otherwise allowed under
proposed § 74.250.
2. Create an enterprise and portfolio intake pathway. Store common governance, security, monitoring, and
administrative information once, with site-specific records and a separate FAA decision for each requested
UAFR.
3. Clarify applicant authority and reuse existing security determinations. Define consensus and evidence of
authority for multi-party sites, and allow relevant federal or state security materials to be incorporated through a
protected annex.
4. Add a bounded consequence-based eligibility pathway. Retain sector thresholds as the normal screen, but
allow a fixed site to document comparable regional or national consequences without creating automatic
eligibility or approval.
5. Publish UAFR-specific geospatial, property, obstacle, and validation standards. Require machine-
readable geometry, defined reference systems, accuracy, metadata, and a clear relationship among property,
security, critical-asset, and requested airspace boundaries.
6. Resolve lateral and vertical boundary issues. Address narrowly tailored exceptions to property-line limits and
the conflict between proposed § 74.60 and lawful structure-proximity operations under § 107.51(b)(2), using
site-specific airspace analysis.
7. Create workable notice paths for real operations. Support facility-sponsored, destination, recurring,
contractor, and government emergency operations without turning notice into private permission or repetitive
manual processing.
8. Define Remote ID performance and protect sensitive data. Retain direct or contracted monitoring, establish
outcome-based acceptance tests, use role-based data views, and formalize Tribal, state, local, and Sector Risk
Management Agency coordination.
9. Revise the cost and applicant-timing analysis. Model concentrated multi-site costs, provide a good-cause
extension mechanism, and identify any available technical-assistance or funding pathways without assuming
owner capacity will be self-funded.
10. Establish readiness and accountability criteria. Pilot the UAFR-Utility with representative users and publish
service levels, continuity procedures, processing metrics, and auditable amendment, renewal, and
enforcement-referral workflows before broad intake.
I. Notice Is Not Permission (§§ 74.52, 74.250, and 74.255)
In the NPRM preamble, the FAA states that site-manager notice provides situational awareness and does not
confer authority to approve, disapprove, restrict, or prohibit an otherwise allowed operation. That is the correct
allocation. It keeps aviation authorization and enforcement with the FAA while giving a facility information
relevant to safety and security. Ohio DOT, the Oregon Department of Aviation, Florida Power & Light, and
SEED make materially similar points. Requests that would let an owner delay or deny navigable-airspace
access should not be adopted.4
FAA-2026-4558 | Page 2 of 9

The no-veto principle appears in the preamble, not in the proposed regulatory text. Proposed § 74.52(a)(4)
requires a site manager who will coordinate allowed operations with the public, and proposed § 74.255(a)
directs operators to provide notice to that manager. The preamble describes notice to both FAA and the site
manager, while the UAFR-Utility Privacy Impact Assessment describes access notice submitted through the
federal portal. Those are different workflows. Without one authoritative channel and vocabulary, facilities may
infer that they must vet credentials, approve routes, negotiate conditions, or maintain separate authorization
lists. Operators may infer the same thing.
The UAFR-Utility should receive and validate the required operator and aircraft fields, create a timestamped
record, and transmit the notice to the current site manager. Successful submission to the federal system
should satisfy the regulatory notice requirement. The facility may contact an operator about ordinary ground
access, site logistics, or an apparent discrepancy, but that communication should not become an airspace-
permission step. A suspected violation should be referred to the FAA or another authority designated by law.
Requested FAA action. Revise § 74.52(a)(4) to state that the site manager receives and administers notices
for operations allowed under §§ 74.250 and 74.255, but receipt, acknowledgment, objection, or non-response
does not approve or deny the operation. Make the UAFR-Utility the authoritative notice channel and define
correction, discrepancy, emergency, and outage procedures. Ground-access and property rights should
remain separate from navigable-airspace authority.
II. The FAA Decision Is Facility-Specific, but Many Applicants Operate Systems
Proposed § 74.52(b) permits one fixed site per application. That structure is appropriate for the FAA's airspace
decision. It is not an efficient model for every administrative function surrounding that decision. State
transportation departments, utilities, public authorities, ports, water agencies, and corporate owners may
share governance, legal authority, security policies, procurement, monitoring contracts, data systems, and
executive contacts across dozens or hundreds of facilities.
The record contains broad cross-sector support for portfolio or batch administration. DWR, AAPA, APTA,
CXC, CNPPID, NASEO, Florida Power & Light, INGAA, and The Chlorine Institute each identify some version
of the same problem: one owner may be required to repeat common information and maintain parallel
workflows for many sites. The sector details differ, but the design issue does not. An individual designation
may be necessary. An entirely separate administrative system for every site is not.5
The FAA can separate common enterprise information from site-specific facts. A parent profile should hold
signatory authority, governance, security standards, incident-response procedures, common contacts,
monitoring architecture, recordkeeping, and reusable documents. Each site record should hold the legal
interests, polygon, altitude, traffic history, vulnerability, consequence, externalities, environmental information,
local emergency contact, and requested activation period unique to that location.
Requested FAA action. Support enterprise profiles, delegated permissions, validated batch intake, common
records, facility contacts, bulk amendments, reporting across sites, renewal alerts, and a portfolio dashboard.
Preserve a separate administrative record and FAA finding for every requested restriction. A batch filing is an
intake method, not a request for a corridor or blanket restriction.
III. Applicant Authority, Eligibility, and Existing Security Programs Need Clearer
Treatment
A. Define applicant authority and consensus
Proposed § 74.52 requires contact information for operators and proprietors with legal interests in the facility,
and the preamble states that the FAA would not process an application until property-interest disputes are
resolved and the parties reach consensus. That may be workable for a single-owner facility. It may be
considerably more difficult for a port, transportation hub, industrial complex, leased facility, public right-of-way,
or property subject to multiple easements.6
FAA-2026-4558 | Page 3 of 9

The FAA should not adjudicate private property disputes. At the same time, an undefined consensus standard
may allow a minor or unrelated property interest to block a coordinated security decision even where state
law, governing documents, or a public authority assigns responsibility for the facility. The final rule needs to
distinguish authority to request an FAA airspace restriction from agreement on every underlying property
matter.
Requested FAA action. Define what constitutes consensus, what evidence establishes applicant authority,
and how the FAA will treat objections by tenants, easement holders, leaseholders, and other interests. Where
law or governing documents assign a public authority or facility operator responsibility for coordinated security,
permit that entity to act as the coordinating applicant, subject to notice to affected interests and the FAA's
independent review.
B. Use thresholds as screens and permit a bounded consequence showing
Objective sector thresholds can make a national program administrable, but a single capacity, population, or
modal threshold is not always a reliable proxy for consequence. Ports, utilities, bridges, tunnels, and other
infrastructure may have limited redundancy, long detours, cascading dependencies, or national-security
support functions even when one proposed threshold is not met. AAPA, Florida Power & Light, IBTTA, MDTA,
and TxDOT support consequence-based consideration. AASHTO, Ohio DOT, and the Oregon Department of
Aviation appropriately warn against turning the rule into broad corridor protection.7
Requested FAA action. Retain the sector criteria as the normal eligibility screen and add a transparent
alternative for a fixed site that documents comparable regional or national consequences using verifiable
evidence. FAA, not the sector or facility, should make the determination. The pathway should establish
eligibility to apply, not entitlement to a UAFR, and should not convert mobile assets, temporary events, or
linear rights-of-way into fixed sites merely because they are important.
C. Permit reuse of existing security determinations
Many intended applicants already operate under approved facility security plans, state energy-security plans,
vulnerability assessments, emergency-response plans, or sector-specific federal oversight. Requiring the
same findings to be recreated in a new FAA format adds work and can produce inconsistent descriptions of
the same risk.
Requested FAA action. Allow relevant security plans, governmental determinations, and Sector Risk
Management Agency assessments to be incorporated by reference or submitted through a protected annex.
Existing programs should not create automatic UAFR approval, but they should be accepted as evidence
where they address the same element. The FAA and relevant agencies should publish crosswalks showing
which existing materials satisfy Part 74 requirements.
IV. UAFR Geometry and Data Require Aeronautical Discipline
A UAFR is an airspace volume, not a property-management graphic. Every application should distinguish at
least four concepts: the applicant's legal property interest, the facility security perimeter, the critical assets to
be protected, and the requested UAFR geometry. Those boundaries may not coincide. Treating them as one
line can produce a restriction that is larger than necessary or too small to address the documented risk.
Airspace analysis, obstacle evaluation, and obstruction analysis depend on clear coordinates, reliable
elevations, defined reference systems, and traceable source data. The draft Advisory Circular permits
coordinates or an online drawing tool, but it does not yet state the horizontal datum, coordinate order,
minimum precision, accepted geometry types, closure and validity rules, vertical reference, metadata, or error-
handling process. Those are operational requirements, not drafting details. A shifted, invalid, self-intersecting,
or vertically ambiguous polygon can create a real airspace error.8
Requested FAA action. Publish a machine-verifiable UAFR geospatial specification before accepting
applications. Define accepted digital formats; horizontal and vertical reference systems; coordinate precision
and accuracy; polygon and multipolygon rules; treatment of holes, adjacent parcels, and noncontiguous areas;
property-boundary evidence; structure and obstacle attributes; elevation source; metadata; responsible party;
automated validation; version history; and update procedures. The 2017 FAA-Department of the Interior
procedure filed in the docket is useful evidence that standardized WGS 84 spatial files, metadata, validation,
contacts, and reporting are practicable. It is not controlling Part 74 precedent.
FAA-2026-4558 | Page 4 of 9

A. Keep the property boundary as the default, with documented exceptions
Proposed § 74.58 limits the UAFR to the facility property boundary, and the FAA asks whether limited
expansion may be appropriate. The default protects the public right of transit, but it may not fit waterside
assets, noncontiguous parcels, shared transportation facilities, security zones, or infrastructure separated by
public rights-of-way.
Requested FAA action. Retain the property boundary as the presumptive maximum, but allow a narrowly
tailored exception when the applicant demonstrates a specific vulnerability that cannot be addressed within
the property line, a direct security benefit, the legal and operational implications, the absence of a less
restrictive alternative, and acceptable effects on other airspace users. The FAA should retain final control over
the shape and minimize the resulting volume.
B. Resolve the structure-height and altitude-ceiling conflict
Proposed § 74.60 generally caps a UAFR at 400 feet AGL and allows a higher ceiling only when the tallest
component exceeds 300 feet. Separately, § 107.51(b)(2) allows a small unmanned aircraft operating within
400 feet of a structure to fly up to 400 feet above that structure's uppermost limit. A lawful Part 107 operation
may therefore be able to operate above a 400-foot UAFR near a structure that is 300 feet tall or less. A 250-
foot structure illustrates the mismatch: a Part 107 aircraft could potentially operate as high as 650 feet AGL
while remaining within the structure allowance.9
That does not establish that every UAFR should extend 400 feet above every structure. Such a rule could
unnecessarily affect crewed aircraft and other airspace users. It does establish that the proposed ceiling does
not fully align with the operating rule used to justify it.
Requested FAA action. Resolve the interaction between proposed § 74.60 and § 107.51(b)(2). Require a
site-specific vertical analysis where structure-proximity operations could defeat the intended protection, and
evaluate any higher ceiling against airports, heliports, crewed-aircraft routes, emergency operations, existing
airspace, and the minimum volume needed to address the documented risk.
V. Allowed Operations Need a Usable Notice Workflow (§§ 74.250 and 74.255)
The record shows legitimate operations that do not fit a one-flight, one-notice model: construction progress,
inspection, maintenance, survey, emergency response, airport and transportation work, deliveries to the
protected facility, and work performed by contractors on the facility's behalf. ABC, Florida Power & Light,
Houston Airport System, Marivin, Ohio DOT, SDDOT, TxDOT, and CALGRU provide concrete examples.10
The final rule should support facility-sponsored operations, operations whose destination is the protected
facility, recurring schedules, and named contractor fleets. A notice should be able to cover a bounded period
and operating area when the operator, aircraft, purpose, and responsible party remain current. Material
changes should require amendment. Individual notice should remain available for one-time or time-sensitive
operations.
Proposed § 74.250(a)(2) requires an allowed aircraft to transition the UAFR in the shortest time practicable.
That is a reasonable standard for transit. It should not imply that a properly notified inspection, survey,
emergency response, delivery, or other legitimate mission must be rushed or prohibited from hovering,
orbiting, descending, landing, or making repeated passes when those maneuvers are reasonably necessary.
The preamble recognizes the need for both transitory and non-transitory operations but leaves the regulatory
treatment unresolved.
Government and law-enforcement operations should retain the proposed emergency path: notice as soon as
reasonably possible, verbal notice when advance written notice is not feasible, and written notice within seven
calendar days. The system should generate a timestamped confirmation that a notice passed required-field
validation and was transmitted to the current site manager. That confirmation should protect the operator from
a later claim that the facility's inbox, staffing, or local workflow failed. It should not imply that the FAA approved
every operational detail.
FAA-2026-4558 | Page 5 of 9

Requested FAA action. Define facility-sponsored and facility-destination operations, permit recurring or
standing notice profiles for known operators and aircraft, and clarify that the shortest-time requirement
governs transit rather than the safe duration of a legitimate notified mission. State that successful transmission
through the FAA system satisfies notice and that facility acknowledgment is not required.
VI. Monitoring, Sensitive Data, and Consultation Need Defined Standards
A. Remote Identification is a baseline, not a private enforcement mandate
Proposed § 74.56(d) already allows a facility to receive broadcast Remote ID messages directly or through a
contracted service. That flexibility should be retained. Coverage, terrain, structures, radio-frequency
conditions, antenna placement, interference, receiver density, and network design will affect whether the
capability works. DWR, Ohio DOT, the Oregon Department of Aviation, INGAA, CXC, and ATIS support
clearer technical expectations and flexible implementation.11
A requirement to possess equipment is not the same as a requirement to achieve reliable situational
awareness. The FAA should define required outcomes for reception, availability, logging, verification,
interoperability, and authorized sharing. It should allow shared, centralized, contracted, and qualified
equivalent capabilities that meet the standard. A missing or unmatched broadcast should not, by itself,
conclusively establish a violation.
Requested FAA action. Publish acceptance tests appropriate to the site, interface specifications for matching
a notice to observed data, and a process for reporting suspected noncompliance. Define the purpose, fields,
retention period, access controls, cybersecurity, privacy treatment, and cost before imposing a monitoring-
record retention mandate. State clearly that a UAFR does not authorize a facility to detect beyond existing law,
mitigate, intercept, or interfere with an aircraft or signal.
B. Use layered access, data minimization, and a protected annex
UAFR applications can contain vulnerabilities, security plans, asset locations, contacts, operational patterns,
property records, and information about cultural or religious resources. FAA needs enough information to
evaluate eligibility and need. Sector Risk Management Agencies need protected security records. Site
managers need operational notices. The public needs boundaries, effective dates, non-sensitive findings, and
an opportunity to identify airspace effects. Those are not the same data set.
The UAFR-Utility Privacy Impact Assessment describes protected critical-infrastructure information handling,
public and nonpublic roles, audit logs, reporting, and a system still in development. The final rule and guidance
should translate that architecture into explicit data-governance requirements. AAPA, INGAA, Oracle, NCAI,
the Oregon Department of Aviation, The Chlorine Institute, and SEED identify material confidentiality,
transparency, and governance concerns.12
Requested FAA action. Create public, FAA adjudicative, Sector Risk Management Agency, restriction-
manager, and facility views. Minimize personal and security-sensitive information; define collection purpose,
access roles, retention, correction, audit, breach handling, and records disposition; and provide a protected
annex for legally protected submissions. Publish machine-readable boundaries, status, effective dates, and
enough non-sensitive reasoning to show how the FAA evaluated eligibility, need, externalities, and airspace
effects.
C. Formalize Tribal and intergovernmental coordination
The docket includes requests for government-to-government consultation, protection of sensitive Tribal
information, and clearer use of state energy-security plans and state risk assessments. FAA Order 1210.20
remains active and establishes the agency's Tribal consultation policy. Those obligations, and the role of state
agencies and Sector Risk Management Agencies, should not be left for an applicant to discover during an
individual filing.
Requested FAA action. Define consultation and intergovernmental coordination triggers in the final rule or
binding implementation procedures. Establish a process for proposed UAFRs that may affect Tribal lands,
interests, or sensitive resources, and explain how state agencies and Sector Risk Management Agencies will
contribute information without displacing the FAA's final airspace authority.
FAA-2026-4558 | Page 6 of 9

VII. Costs, Readiness, Administration, and Enforcement
A. Test the system before broad intake
The April 28, 2026 UAFR-Utility Privacy Impact Assessment describes the system as in development and
anticipates Authority to Operate by the end of the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026. The draft Advisory Circular
directs users to a generic FAA address rather than an operational UAFR-Utility address. These facts do not
establish a missed milestone. They do show that commenters did not have a completed public interface and
final operating instructions to test.13
Requested FAA action. Pilot the UAFR-Utility with representative owner types, including public, Tribal, small,
multi-tenant, and portfolio applicants. Before broad intake, test identity and roles, enterprise and site records,
geospatial validation, protected documents, notice transmission and confirmation, audit history, bulk reporting,
renewal alerts, accessibility, service levels, help-desk escalation, backup and recovery, and outage continuity.
Phase intake against demonstrated system and processing capacity while preserving a method for urgent
cases.
B. Give complex applicants a workable correction and reconsideration process
The proposed process includes application review, a Sector Risk Management Agency assessment,
conditional approval, at least 30 days of public comment, final review, and rulemaking. The FAA anticipates
delay letters because of application volume and resources. Applicants then have 30 days to correct specified
deficiencies or petition for reconsideration after a denial. A public agency or complex owner may need to
coordinate legal, security, property, procurement, and governing-body action within that period.
Requested FAA action. Provide at least 60 days to correct a deficiency or seek reconsideration, or authorize
a documented good-cause extension. Distinguish completeness from substantive review, provide one written
deficiency list when practicable, show status and decision milestones, and state when each response period
begins.
C. Validate concentrated owner-side costs
The FAA states that it lacks direct UAFR application-cost data and uses exemption work as a proxy,
estimating $5,000 to $10,000 per application. It separately provides an example of $2,800 in initial Remote ID
monitoring cost and $1,000 annually. Those assumptions do not separately quantify executive delegation,
legal and property review, GIS production, security planning, environmental documentation, procurement,
cybersecurity, training, records management, notice administration, incident reporting, or renewal.14
Applying only the FAA's unit assumptions to 100 facilities produces an illustrative five-year total of $1.28
million to $1.78 million: 100 applications, 100 initial monitoring deployments, and five annual monitoring
payments. This is not a forecast. Shared monitoring and portfolio administration may lower it, while omitted
enterprise and labor costs may raise it. The illustration shows why national averages can obscure
concentrated burdens within one owner portfolio.
Requested FAA action. Validate costs through structured interviews or user testing and report ranges by
owner type, task, and portfolio size. Explain which activities may be centralized, revise paperwork and small-
entity estimates, and identify whether existing technical-assistance or funding authorities can support public
and Tribal applicants. If no authority exists, state that limitation clearly rather than assuming that owner
capacity will be self-funded.
D. Make administration and enforcement auditable
Applicants need defined completeness checks, deficiency notices, status visibility, amendment and renewal
procedures, and a record of what the FAA relied on. Operators need authoritative, machine-readable notice of
active boundaries and effective periods. Facilities need a simple method to report suspected incursions
without being expected to make a legal determination.
Requested FAA action. Publish service targets and aggregate metrics for applications received,
completeness, processing time, approvals, denials, amendments, renewals, system availability, access
notices, discrepancies, and enforcement referrals, subject to appropriate security protections. Preserve an
auditable version history for each boundary, decision, notice, amendment, and renewal.

VIII. Conclusion
Section 2209 addresses a legitimate safety and security need. The public record does not support abandoning
a federal UAFR framework. It supports targeted changes that make the framework usable by the institutions
Congress intended it to serve.
The FAA should preserve individualized airspace review, public notice, and final federal authority. It should
also recognize that many applicants operate portfolios, rely on existing security programs, manage complex
property interests, and do not begin with aviation-specific staff or systems. A rule that requires each owner to
build the same governance structure from scratch will be slower, more expensive, and less consistent than
necessary.
A durable final rule must distinguish what remains site-specific from what can be standardized, shared, or
incorporated by reference. Notice must remain a federal workflow, not private permission. The rule should also
resolve the data, boundary, mission, monitoring, confidentiality, consultation, review, renewal, and
enforcement-referral issues described above.
These changes would preserve FAA control of the National Airspace System and prevent an owner veto over
navigable airspace. They would also make Section 2209 more consistent, defensible, and implementable.

Founded in 2013, DoorDash is a technology company with the mission to grow and empower local
economies. Through our platform, merchants like restaurants, grocery stores, convenience stores, and
virtually any other local business can connect with customers in their communities. Merchants use
DoorDash to meet new customers and grow their businesses, and customers discover new businesses and

DoorDash aims to integrate top-of-the-line logistics solutions into our commerce platform to meet rising

empowering local economies like never before. In 2022, DoorDash began collaborating with industry

In July 2026, DoorDash announced that it has earned Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal

DoorDash agrees with the overall concept for creating unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs) and
for authorizing flights through UAFRs. We note the critical underlying test for creating a new UAFR,
regardless of category of infrastructure, is that “the incapacity or destruction of such systems and assets
would have a debilitating effect on security, national economic security, national public health or safety,
or any combination of those matters.” [42 U.S.C. 5195c(e)]
DoorDash provides its comments in line with the following core principles:
● The criteria for approving and renewing UAFRs must be transparent, unambiguous, and
justifiable in relation to actual risk to infrastructure. Criteria that are open-ended or undefined
in the NPRM must be clarified prior to publication of the final rule. This will not only reduce
administrative burden on FAA, but will prevent unrelated facilities and infrastructure from being
swept into a given category. Over-designation of UAFRs where no security risk exists may cause
otherwise law-abiding UAS operators to unwittingly violate UAFRs, while also making it
difficult for FAA to enforce compliance.
● Allow for performance-based means of authorizing operations through UAFRs. Scalable
implementation of this final rule is critical to its success. FAA should fund multiple means of
authorization, with a preference toward automated tools, use of available technologies like
Network Remote Identification, and whitelists. Approval processes that require manual
coordination between UAS operators, UAFR site owners and/or the FAA will not be scalable, and
will result in significant burden for FAA while imposing negative economic consequences on
UAS operators who are grounded waiting for approval.
● Maximize use of industry consensus standards to support implementation. Consistent with
other recent FAA rulemaking activities, use of consensus standards enables faster and more
compliant implementation, since technical performance requirements are well understood, and
FAA only needs to accept standards as means of compliance, rather than writing their own
standards from scratch. Use of standards also ensures that geospatial data is understood, relayed
and interpreted correctly by automated systems, which promotes overall compliance.
● Implementation should be phased based on FAA’s ability to support the final rule.
Compliance deadlines should be based on FAA’s readiness, including workforce development and
deployment of new FAA-specific technology and data infrastructure. Premature compliance
deadlines could have negative economic impact for UAS operators who are unable to identify
UAFRs or are unable to request authorization to fly through UAFRs due to lack of available FAA
capabilities. Such de facto operational limitations would also contravene FAA’s statutory
authority to ensure the public’s right to access navigable airspace. Simply designating locations as
UAFRs does not obviate the fact that the airspace within a UAFR would otherwise be navigable.
Comments on Subpart A
§74.1. FAA proposes to define “operator or proprietor” as a person with ownership interest in a fixed site
facility. However, existing 14 CFR 1.1 defines “commercial operator” as someone who operates an
aircraft for compensation or hire; proposed 14 CFR 108.5 would define “operator” as a person who
conducts beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) UAS operators under that proposed part. Thus, adding a
non-aircraft-related definition of “operator” to 14 CFR 1.1 under the present proposed rulemaking would
2

diverge from established FAA precedent and commonly understood meaning of “operator” in an aviation
context. DoorDash proposes that FAA use only the term “proprietor” in relation to persons who own fixed
site facilities.
§ 74.6. The criteria for designating a “Special UAFR” appear to diverge from the overall intent of UAFRs
throughout the rest of proposed Part 24. It is clear that FAA’s intent is that standard UAFRs would persist
for years, and may optionally be seasonal – they are inherently long-term because the associated
infrastructure is permanent, with enduring ramifications on airspace usage and access to navigable
airspace. By contrast, Special UAFRs require a finding of a “credible safety or security threat.” This
phrase is commonly understood to be triggered by receiving information or intelligence with enough
details as to time, place and manner that it can be correlated with a specific location and not, for example,
every military base. But precisely because the term is so open to interpretation, it is also possible that well
intentioned government agencies could use any prior unexpired intelligence or information to claim that a
wide variety of government sites require a Special UAFR. FAA’s preamble indicates that a Special UAFR
could be created based on “a security assessment demonstrating credible risks.” On its face, this reads as a
broader and less specific basis for determination than the “credible safety or security threat” language
used in the proposed regulatory text; indeed, the preamble highlights the intended use is to cover
“persistent threats.”
FAA’s preamble provides meaningful interpretation of the intended use of Special UAFRs as a more
permanent form of restriction than Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs). However, given that the bar for
establishing the need for a Special UAFR is so low, DoorDash proposes that they be reviewed every two
years, rather than every five years. This review should include an updated risk and threat assessment so
that FAA can determine whether there is a legitimate ongoing security need to have a Special UAFR.
Further, DoorDash cannot readily find a definition or applicability criteria for the “certain fixed site
facilities” that would also be eligible for UAFRs. Without clear criteria, it would be possible for any
government property, land or area to be designated as a Special UAFR.

DoorDash seeks further clarity in the final rule related to multiple proposed categories as discussed in this

expansive interpretations of certain UAFR categories to protect sites that do not meet the statutory test
language identified by FAA in the preamble and quoted above. The result could be an arbitrary and
capricious designation of UAFRs without sufficient mechanisms to limit their proliferation.
DoorDash is supportive of FAA’s proposed lateral boundary limitations in § 74.58 so as not to exceed the
limits of the property boundary. This is reasonable and proportionate; adding buffers or standoff distances
to all UAFRs would unreasonably restrict navigable airspace near or adjacent to fixed sites, without any
clear risk reduction.

providers (ADSPs) that provide Network Remote ID services.5 This would ensure that Network Remote
ID services are deployed correctly to meet the needs of proposed Part 74. To ensure UAFR site
proprietors know about the proposed usage of Network Remote ID, DoorDash recommends that §
74.56(d) be updated to require monitoring of both broadcast and network remote identification. As further
guidance in an advisory circular, DoorDash recommends that FAA provide information about how UAFR
proprietors could identify FAA-authorized Network Remote ID display providers that they could use to
satisfy such a monitoring requirement.
Phased implementation based on FAA readiness
DoorDash is cognizant that implementing the full scope of Part 74 – including the ability to request the
creation of a UAFRs the ability to definitively know the locations of all UAFRs, the ability to notify
UAFR site proprietors of approved operators, and other elements of the proposed rule – require
substantial efforts to develop and deploy automated systems. Creating the automated processes and
deploying those systems and databases may take time. Therefore, DoorDash recommends that FAA adopt
a phased approach to Part 74 compliance that is tied to key technical milestones rather than specific dates.
For example, DoorDash recommends that UAS operators not be subject to enforcement action in relation
to Part 74 (including § 74.260(c), but also operator certificate enforcement provisions of part 107, 108,
5 In this specific recommendation, the Network Remote ID SPSO would contain explicit mention that it provides a
means of compliance to satisfy the operational requirements in § 74.250(a)(1) and § 74.255. This is because the
structure of proposed 14 CFR Part 146 is that services must support an operational requirement that can be traced to
regulatory text. Additionally, though not germane to this rulemaking, such an SPSO could also be a means of
compliance to the enhanced remote identification requirements in proposed Part 108.
8

135 and 137) until an authoritative, publicly available and machine-readable database of all UAFR
locations, including their boundaries, is available. Without such a database provided by FAA, it would not
be possible for UAS operators to determine whether a UAFR exists near their intended operating area,
and therefore whether they would need to make changes to their mission profile or notify a site proprietor.
In the case of Special UAFRs, site proprietors should continue to use existing processes for requesting
TFRs, since that data is already available to and consumable by UAS operators.
Additionally, DoorDash recommends that the notification requirements in § 74.255 only be phased in for
approved UAS operators once at least one scalable, automated means (e.g. Network Remote ID) is
recognized by FAA and a suitable number of ADSPs have been authorized under proposed Part 146. This
would prevent the administrative burden of UAS operators sending, and UAFR site proprietors receiving,
potentially dozens of notifications each day via phone, email, text or other human-centric means.

comments.commenter: Comment from Transportation Trades Department, AFL-CIO
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
The Honorable Bryan Bedford
Administrator
Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue, SW
Washington, DC 20591
RE: Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Administrator Bedford:
On behalf of the Transportation Trades Department, AFL-CIO (TTD), I am pleased to respond to
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding
the establishment of a process for operators and proprietors of certain fixed site facilities to request
and maintain an unmanned aircraft flight restriction. By way of background, TTD consists of 39
affiliated unions whose members work across all modes of transportation, including in aviation
and rail transportation.1 We are encouraged by the FAA’s efforts to promulgate this long-overdue
rulemaking. Additionally, we endorse the comments filed in this docket by our affiliate(s), the
Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen (BLET), the Transportation Division of the
International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers (SMART-TD).
Background
In order to address potential national and homeland security risks posed by the operation of UAS
in close proximity to certain fixed site facilities, Congress enacted section 2209 of the FAA
Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA). Section 2209 directed the FAA to create a
system under which operators or proprietors of these facilities are able to request unmanned aircraft
flight restrictions (UAFRs).
This rulemaking has been delayed for nearly a decade, and comes on the heels of multiple
Congressional mandates for action on this important issue. We are pleased to see the FAA issue
this NPRM and recognize the safety concerns inherent in the operation of unmanned aircraft in
close proximity to rail facilities.
1 Attached is a complete list of TTD’s affiliate Unions
Transportation Trades Department, AFL-CIO
815 16th St NW / 4th Floor / Washington, DC 20006
Tel: 202.628.9262 / www.ttd.org
Greg Regan, President / Shari Semelsberger, Secretary-Treasurer

Critical Transportation Infrastructure
We appreciate that the FAA has recognized the importance of securing fixed transportation
infrastructure sites through this proposed rule. Fixed site facilities throughout the transportation
network, including maritime ports, rail yards, and other intermodal rail facilities frequently
facilitate the movement of dangerous goods and passengers. Given the nature of these operations,
it is critical that these sites be eligible for UAFRs and Special UAFRs. Drone incursions into these
sensitive areas can pose preventable safety risks to employees and passengers, along with physical
and cybersecurity concerns.
UAS Activity in Close Proximity to Rail Yards
Congress rightly concluded that rail transportation facilities should be considered a fixed site
facility eligible for UAFRs and Special UAFRs. Rail workers routinely perform safety sensitive
tasks from which distractions can be deadly. Daily operations involve moving locomotives,
railcars, heavy machinery, hazardous materials, and complex switching operations. Drone
incursions in rail yards can easily divert focus and attention from this critical work and could
ultimately result in a preventable tragedy.
As SMART-TD notes in its comments in this docket, “A drone hovering over a switching
movement or operating near a crew member’s work location is not a harmless gadget. It is a foreign
object operating in a hazardous industrial environment. Every unnecessary distraction increases
risk. Every unnecessary risk increases the likelihood of injury or death.” As such, we encourage
the FAA to expand the criteria for rail fixed site facilities beyond rail facilities required by law to
have a rail secure area as defined in 49 CFR 1500.3, as is currently proposed. Major classification
yards, passenger terminals, locomotive servicing facilities, intermodal terminals, dispatching
support facilities, and locations where hazardous materials consists are routinely assembled or
stored may present equal or greater vulnerabilities despite not fitting within the proposed
framework. These areas should be eligible for UAFRs, as well.
Cybersecurity Risks
Many dangerous and hazardous goods are transported by rail on a daily basis. Not only does the
assembly of those consists require diligent focus by those working in the yard, but unauthorized
surveillance of those materials and their locations on the train pose serious security concerns.
These risks are heightened by the potential for UAS software to be hijacked or hacked. If an
unauthorized user is able to gain control of the device for nefarious purposes, sensitive and safety
critical information, such as the location of certain hazardous materials on a train, may be exposed.
Additionally, recent cybersecurity incidents in Minnesota have highlighted the need for heightened
cybersecurity measures at critical infrastructure facilities. According to the Federal Bureau of
Investigation (FBI), since late July 2026, Water and Wastewater Sector (WWS) utility companies
in at least seven states have reported cyber attack incidents, and some of that activity degraded

water operations. Operational effects reported to the FBI have included loss of pressure and
flooding.2 Pressure loss in water systems could potentially allow untreated ground water to seep
into pipes, resulting in health and safety risks to the communities served. While not the result of
unauthorized UAS activity, these incidents underscore the need for robust cybersecurity measures
at fixed site facilities.
We therefore encourage the FAA to consider requiring UAFR holders who intend to operate their
own drones at fixed site facilities to share the cybersecurity measures in place for their devices
prior to deployment.
Emergency Response Operations and Accident Investigations
We support limiting UAS operations in close proximity to rail yards and other critical
transportation infrastructure whenever possible. However, we urge the FAA to consider
maintaining exceptions for law enforcement operations, emergency response, and accident and
incident investigations.
Conclusion
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule and we look forward to working
with the FAA in the future.
Sincerely,
Greg Regan
President
2 https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2026/malicious-cyber-actors-targeting-water-and-wastewater-sector-
internet--facing-programmable-logic-controllers-causing-operational-disruptions

August 5, 2026
Via Electronic Transmission: Regulations.gov
Docket Operations
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue, S.E.
Room W58-213, West Building 5th Floor
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: WM Comments on FAA’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking entitled “Designation-
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”
(Docket No. FAA-2026-4558)
Dear Administrator Bedford:
WM is pleased to provide comments on the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA’s) Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) entitled “Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,” 91 Fed. Reg. 24,650 (May 6, 2026). WM is
North America’s leading provider of comprehensive environmental solutions, providing
collection, recycling, and disposal services to millions of residential, commercial, industrial,
medical, and municipal customers throughout North America. WM also has a growing network
of facilities that produce natural gas and electricity from landfill gas.
WM is both a significant owner and operator of critical environmental infrastructure and an
extensive commercial user of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) technology. Across our
network of facilities, WM utilizes UAS for monitoring facility operations and engineering,
surveying, construction management, operational planning, infrastructure inspections, and
emergency response activities. UAS technology thus has become an integral tool for enhancing
worker safety, environmental performance, and operational efficiency across WM’s network of
hundreds of active and legacy landfills, natural gas production facilities and infrastructure, and
power plants.
WM supports a framework that enables eligible facilities to seek site-specific protection from
third-party UAS operations while preserving access for WM-approved UAS used in furtherance
of operational, environmental, regulatory, and emergency-response activities. As FAA develops
its framework for restricting unauthorized UAS activity around sensitive facilities, it is essential
that the agency recognizes the role landfills and co-located infrastructure play in protecting
public health, managing environmental risks, and powering communities.
I. FAA Should Expressly Identify Landfills as Operations Eligible to Submit
Requests for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions.
WM urges FAA to list landfill operations alongside the other 16 critical infrastructure sectors
eligible to request unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs). These facilities meet the
statutory definition of “critical infrastructure” insofar as the interruption of waste sector
operations “would have a debilitating effect on . . . national public health or safety.” 42 U.S.C. §
5195c(e).

Landfills are complex industrial facilities that perform critical public and environmental health
functions through the management of municipal, commercial, industrial, and regulated waste
streams. Refuse pickup and disposal is widely recognized as an essential public health service
because these activities prevent disease, stop pest infestations, and control environmental
pollution. Indeed, federal agencies have recognized the critical role played by the waste
industry in this regard. See, e.g., U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Cybersecurity &
Infrastructure Security Agency, Office of the Director, “Advisory Memorandum on Ensuring
Essential Critical Infrastructure Workers’ Ability to Work During the COVID-19 Response,”
August 10, 2021 (identifying the waste sector as part of the critical infrastructure workforce).
The waste sector also supports many of the other critical infrastructure sectors identified in the
proposal, including the chemical sector, manufacturing, transportation, water and wastewater,
and healthcare and public health. For example, healthcare facilities have limited capacity to
safely store regulated medical waste, including infectious materials, sharps, pharmaceuticals,
and pathological waste. Timely waste collection, transportation, treatment, and disposal are
essential to prevent health and safety risks, maintain regulatory compliance, and ensure
hospitals, clinics, laboratories, and long-term care facilities can continue providing patient care.
A disruption in waste management services could constrain healthcare operations, increase
risks, and divert resources from essential patient services.
As landfill operations are subject to extensive and evolving federal and state laws and
regulations pertaining to environmental protection, health, and safety, a significant amount of
facility time and capital expenditure is related, either directly or indirectly, to regulatory
compliance and in safeguarding frontline communities. These facilities, which often are
hundreds of acres in size, operate extensive environmental control infrastructure, including
leachate collection and treatment systems, wastewater treatment infrastructure, stormwater
controls, landfill cover materials, environmental monitoring technologies, and other systems
designed to protect public health and the environment.
Landfill operators have come to rely on UAS technologies to regularly monitor advanced
engineering systems. WM routinely conducts authorized UAS missions across its landfill
network to support environmental monitoring, engineering inspections, operational planning,
and airspace management. These operations are integrated into WM’s standard landfill
management practices and provide teams with timely, high-resolution data to support
infrastructure planning and day-to-day operational decisions. Through routine drone surveys,
teams gain near real-time visibility into landfill conditions. In multiple locations, these capabilities
have improved operational efficiency and helped maximize available airspace, extending the
productive life of landfill assets while maintaining safe and compliant operations.
WM is increasingly encountering third-party and unauthorized drone activity around facilities.
Uncoordinated drone operations have the potential to interfere with authorized monitoring and
inspection missions and, in the event of an incident, could cause significant disruption to landfill
operations and to refuse disposal within a community. Like many industrial facilities discussed
in the NPRM, landfills contain exposed infrastructure, combustible and hazardous materials,
wastewater treatment systems, environmental control systems, and other sensitive industrial
processes. These operations face risks associated with unauthorized UAS operations,
including fires, operational interference, disruption of environmental management systems, and
releases of potentially harmful gases, liquids, and other waste streams. Disruptions to these
systems can have broader environmental, worker safety, public health, and community
consequences if operations are adversely affected.
2

Finally, landfills perform a public health function analogous to wastewater treatment facilities,
which are recognized as critical infrastructure. Both provide a controlled, highly regulated
means of managing waste streams that would otherwise pose significant risks to human health
and the environment. Just as wastewater treatment systems prevent the spread of disease,
protect water resources, and maintain sanitary conditions, landfills provide the secure disposal
capacity necessary to prevent waste accumulation that can attract disease vectors, contaminate
air, soil, and water resources, and threaten public health. Both systems are essential
components of a community’s infrastructure and support the continuous operation of homes,
businesses, healthcare facilities, and other critical services. For these reasons, landfills warrant
the same opportunity afforded to other critical infrastructure sectors to demonstrate a site-
specific need for additional protections where operational, safety, environmental, or public
welfare concerns justify a UAFR.
II. FAA Should Not Exclude Smaller Power Plants and Natural Gas Facilities under
Section 74.88.
WM is accelerating the growth of our energy business, building on decades of experience
converting landfill gas to electricity and natural gas. Today, WM owns or hosts over 130 power
plants and is on pace to have 24 natural gas facilities in operation by 2027. These investments
are expected to produce 28 Bcf of gas per year and generate approximately 300 MW of
electricity—capable of powering up to 1.7 million homes annually. Importantly, these facilities
are a significant source of baseload power for many rural communities. WM’s energy facilities
are also integral to our waste collection services. Natural gas produced from our landfills
constitutes a significant source of fuel allocated to our more than 13,500 natural gas collection
vehicles, ensuring regular access to waste pickup and disposal.
FAA has proposed that electricity facilities seeking a UAFR have a nameplate capacity of 500
MW or greater of power while limiting eligibility to natural gas facilities with processing
capacities of at least 500 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d) of natural gas. See 91 Fed. Reg.
at 24,669. Electricity and natural gas facilities co-located with landfill operations, although
smaller in size, perform many of the same energy production and fuel processing functions as
other energy facilities expressly identified in the proposal. As such, we recommend that FAA
evaluate the eligibility of smaller power plants and natural gas facilities on a case-by-case basis,
accounting for the potential disruption to nearby communities of incidents related to
unauthorized drone activities around these facilities.
III. Recommendations
As discussed above, WM respectfully recommends that (1) FAA expressly identify landfills as
operations that are eligible to submit requests for UAFRs and (2) avoid establishing minimum
levels of energy production under section 74.88 for operators of power plants and natural gas
facilities interested in seeking a UAFR. FAA also should be mindful to ensure that designation
of a UAFR not impede authorized UAS activities, which should remain fully available to facility
operators and other authorized personnel. If you have any questions, please feel free to contact
me at mwilso14@wm.com or 603-443-3088.
Sincerely,
Megan Wilson
Senior Manager, Business Solutions
3

August 5, 2026
Bryan Bedford
Administrator
Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue
Washington, DC 20591

Dear Administrator Bedford,
The California Farm Bureau (CAFB) appreciates the opportunity to comment in response to
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM)
concerning the operation of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in close proximity to fixed site
facilities.
For background, CAFB is a voluntary, non-profit organization made up of nearly 26,000
members across 54 counties and is the largest farm organization in the state. Established in
1919, we work for the betterment of family farmers, ranchers, and workers across California
and help support up to 2.5 million jobs and over $58 billion in crop value.
CAFB supports the FAA’s goal of providing a clearer and more consistent framework for UAS
in order to better protect our nation’s critical infrastructure. Our members are certainly no
strangers to the significant role technology plays in our industry, particularly as drones and
mechanization continue to grow in their importance. California agriculture has become an
early adopter of UAS technology for precision agriculture, crop monitoring, irrigation
management, pest detection, and livestock management.
Given its importance and variety of uses, our organization continues to back the usage of UAS
for agricultural and commercial purposes, and in no way do we wish to limit these valuable
agricultural applications. Rather, our concerns lie with unauthorized, non-agricultural
operations conducted without the knowledge or consent of the farm operator.
Unfortunately, many agricultural operations, particularly livestock, poultry, dairy, and other
animal production facilities, have experienced increasing incidents of unapproved drone
usage in recent years. Agricultural facilities have become targets of activist organizations that
use drones to record or surveil private agricultural property without the consent of the
landowner or farm operator.
Federal Policy | 2600 River Plaza Drive | Sacramento, CA 95833 | 916-561-5665 | www.cfbf.com

Unauthorized UAS should not operate close to livestock, poultry, or other animal operations
as repeated low-altitude flights can create unnecessary stress for animals, interfere with
standard agricultural operations, compromise biosecurity practices, and disrupt the safe
operation of working farms and ranches. To that end, FAA should particularly consider the
unnecessary risks posed to workers as well, as unauthorized drone usage over and around
workers and their equipment during planting, harvesting, livestock handling, and other duties
introduce an extra layer of hazards that workers and managers cannot fully account for.
In addition to being the nation’s largest agriculture producing state, California is also home
to many significant research and testing facilities, processing plants, and other critical food
infrastructure. Their existence helps ensure our state continues providing over a third of all
fresh fruits and vegetables to communities around the country. This is why we believe in the
ideal that ‘food security is national security’—which is similarly outlined as a core principle in
the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s own National Farm Security Action Plan (published in
July 2025). This was also evident through the critical workforce designations during the
COVID-19 pandemic.
This action plan also outlines several areas that are considered ‘at risk’ due to foreign
hostilities and agroterrorism. While it is our hope many of these threats remain low, just last
year, the U.S. Department of Justice charged two Chinese nationals with several crimes
relating to a smuggled-in fungus designated as a potential agroterrorism weapon. In addition,
California officials recently confirmed suspected cyberattacks on several water infrastructure
systems in which Iranian-backed hacker groups reportedly took credit for. We know these
potential threats only continue to grow, particularly as potential adversaries consider so-
called “soft” and other lower-security targets that could wreak havoc on our nation’s food
supply chain.
As such, CAFB respectfully encourages the FAA to consider whether a greater degree of
agricultural operations should be considered eligible for applying for the UAS flight
restrictions outlined in the NPRM. While we acknowledge that Congress primarily envisioned
critical infrastructure and sensitive government facilities to be the target of such exceptions
under the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, we believe the FAA should consider
the importance of our industry as it relates to national security. At the very least, the agency
should consider exemptions for agricultural operations where unique operational,
biosecurity, safety, or security concerns justify additional protection. Non-fixed site
agricultural operations may face risks comparable to other protected facilities and should
have an opportunity to demonstrate the need for additional safeguards where warranted.
Ultimately, CAFB supports the responsible and legal use of UAS and appreciates the FAA’s
goal of further protecting our nation’s critical infrastructure and security apparatuses. The
diversity in farming, ranching, and other agricultural practices in California help ensure our
Federal Policy | 2600 River Plaza Drive | Sacramento, CA 95833 | 916-561-5665 | www.cfbf.com

nation’s food supply chain remains running and we welcome any additional consideration to
expanding protections to such operations.
We thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposal and would be more than
happy to provide additional details as needed.
Regards,
Matthew Viohl
Director
California Farm Bureau
Federal Policy | 2600 River Plaza Drive | Sacramento, CA 95833 | 916-561-5665 | www.cfbf.com

Agreeing that there are infrastructures that could be deemed as critical. And I agree that those that are legitimately critical and could effect national security. The use a a general description would be dangerous to those with legitimate use of a UAS. An example. To generally say power stations rather than specifying actual locations that ARE critical. In a general use, then almost every block in a city or county could have a small switching station prohibiting flight throughout a large area, preventing lawful flights by those commercial UAV pilot. List Specific power stations, by location, not a blanket restriction.
Another solution is to create LAANC approval near or over critical infrastructure when a valid need is submitted, and with coordination with that facility,

My name is Lewis Bernier. I am a licensed drone pilot and a factory farm investigator with Direct Action Everywhere, where I help run our drone program. I write regarding Docket FAA-2026-4558. I oppose including food and agriculture (proposed § 74.90) among the sectors eligible to apply for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions. The FAA asked for comment on this eligibility, and my answer is that it does not belong in a safety rule.

I want to make three points: that this work is necessary and serves the public, that the FAA's existing rules already keep these facilities and the airspace safe, and that there is no record of drones like ours ever harming a farm.

Firstly, most Americans will never set foot inside a calf ranch, a hog barn, or a slaughterhouse. The companies that run them do not open their doors, and state trespass and ag-gag laws exist to keep the public out. A drone flown lawfully from public ground, done competently and within Part 107, is one of the only ways left to see what actually happens inside an industry that houses billions of animals. That is not a loophole. It is journalism, and it is exactly the kind of oversight the public depends on for an industry that feeds the country and largely regulates itself.

I know the value of this work because I have done it. I was the pilot who first captured footage at Agresti Calf Ranch in Stanislaus County, where our video showed workers kicking calves in the face and disbudding them with hot irons without pain relief. After the Los Angeles Times published it, the operation fired one of the workers. I have obtained other cruelty footage including at a calf ranch in Merced County linked to a major cheese company, and during a six-month drone investigation of California's largest calf-raising operation, Grimmius Cattle Company, which ran in Vox and gave the public a rare look at how dairy calves are actually raised. None of this footage would exist if the airspace over these facilities were closed. Every bit of it served the public interest.

Second, the FAA already has the safety rules it needs. Part 107 governs every flight we make. We stay below 400 feet, keep the aircraft within visual line of sight, do not fly over people, and never operate in a careless or reckless manner. Those are aviation safety rules, and they already keep both these facilities and the national airspace safe. A UAFR would add nothing to that safety. It would only hand a private company the power to switch off lawful, Part 107-compliant flight over its own property whenever it chooses.

The industry's objections are not really about aviation safety, and this rule is the wrong tool for them. Concerns about disease relate to with trucks, people, and equipment moving between farms, not a camera flying overhead that never lands on the property and never touches an animal. Biosecurity is the job of the USDA and the states, not the FAA. Worries about proprietary information and trespass are already covered by existing state and federal law. The FAA is an aviation safety agency, and none of these are aviation safety problems.

Third, and this is the point I keep coming back to as a pilot: there is no record of harm. Animal advocates have flown drones over farms for more than a decade. In all that time I am aware of no case, not one, in which an investigator's drone caused an aviation incident, injured a person or an animal, or damaged property. The harms the industry describes are hypothetical. The safety record is real, and it is spotless. You do not build a critical-infrastructure flight restriction on a threat that has never once materialized.

UAFR eligibility is supposed to rest on a documented vulnerability to what an unmanned aircraft can do. A camera recording from hundreds of feet away creates no such vulnerability. Our drones are not weapons. They are cameras, and the only thing they threaten is secrecy.

I ask the FAA to keep its rule anchored to genuine safety and security, where it belongs, and to exclude food and agriculture from UAFR eligibility.

Lewis Bernier

I oppose the inclusion of the Food and Agriculture sector (§ 74.90) amongst the critical infrastructure facilities that could obtain Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs).

The proposal highlights safety concerns (e.g. “protection of people and property on the ground”) as the key factor in considering requests for UAFRs. However, there is no documented evidence of drones at agricultural facilities threatening the safety or security of animals, workers, or farm equipment. To the contrary, recent drone footage at factory farms has revealed workers abusing animals (e.g. calves being kicked at Agresti Calf Ranch), illegal calf hutches with inadequate space (e.g. at Grimmius Cattle Company, in violation of California Penal Code 597t), and dead piles that violate environmental law and present a hazard to public health (e.g. at Vera Goat Dairy). Drones do not present safety concerns at these facilities; they expose them.

It is only because of drones that the public can see the reality of these factory farms, which can otherwise operate out of sight and free from accountability when they violate the law. I urge you not to shield these facilities from public scrutiny – please exclude the Food and Agriculture sector from receiving UAFRs.

Drone footage has been essential to exposing mistreatment of animals on factory farms. If animal agriculture businesses are able to obtain UAFR's, they would inevitably use it to keep extreme animal suffering and false advertisement hidden from consumers.

Regarding the proposed FCC rule to ban drones over factory livestock farms.

My name is Lauren Leigh Moore, a lifelong resident of Michigan. My comment is to urge you to NOT restrict drones from watching how businesses perform their livestock duties. If they are providing basic care & providing a decent life for these animals, they have nothing to fear. In fact they might use the drone footage as proof against lawsuits for mistreatment. If they are not, they should not be allowed to hide it, as it is immoral and illegal, is it not?

Why should these factory farms be allowed to hide what they’re doing?

As a journalist who covers environmental issues, I urge the FAA, in its proposed rulemaking, to strike a better balance between the security needs of infrastructure sites and the First Amendment rights of professional and citizen journalists. Drone imagery has helped me in my reporting to show the extent of water pollution from a development failing to control its runoff and by illustrating the proximity to impaired waterways of polluting municipal wastewater and industrial facilities. Those stories would not have had the same impact without the perspective provided by aerial views provided via drone. The proposed rule would grant flight restrictions to facilities in 16 broad sectors of the economy, so many that it could become virtually impossible for journalists to use drones in many areas. I urge you to set a high bar for granting restrictions, limiting the types of facilities eligible for restrictions and making determinations transparently in a way that journalists and other public stakeholders can be heard in whether restrictions are warranted on a case by case basis.

comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
VIA ELECTRONIC FILING
Federal Aviation Administration
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Room W58-213, West Building 5th Floor
Washington, DC 20590-0001
Re: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility, Docket No. FAA–2026–4558
Comments of the National Association of Broadcasters
The National Association of Broadcasters (NAB)1 appreciates the opportunity to comment on
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Notice) in the
above-referenced proceeding implementing section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety and
Security Act of 2016.2 The Notice seeks to establish a process by which certain fixed-site
facilities can apply for unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs), specify the
requirements for obtaining UAFRs, and limit the types of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS)
operations permitted within UAFRs. In our comments below, NAB discusses the potential
impact of the proposed rules on broadcasters who operate UAS for legitimate newsgathering
operations, and suggests modifications to the proposed rules to better accommodate these
operations.
I. INTRODUCTION
Over the last decade, broadcasters have increasingly used UAS to cover breaking news,
sports, natural disasters, and other newsworthy events. These operations typically provide
aerial video and imagery to support news coverage and the dissemination of emergency
information. For many local broadcast stations, UAS have become an essential part of their
newsgathering efforts, allowing them to offer their audiences unique and immersive
1 The National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) is the nonprofit trade association that
advocates on behalf of free local radio and television stations and broadcast networks
before Congress, the Federal Communications Commission and other federal agencies, and
the courts.
2 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (May 6, 2026).

perspectives into important news events.3 Broadcasters also have been leaders in
developing comprehensive training programs to ensure their personnel conduct UAS
operations safely and in full compliance with FAA regulations.4
In the Notice, the FAA proposes to create standard and special UAFRs, for which certain
facilities within 16 “critical infrastructure sectors” and government entities, respectively, can
apply to restrict the operation of UAS within set boundaries around their fixed-site facilities,
subject to certain exceptions.5 The Notice states that the FAA’s proposal is designed to
address growing concerns about the “safety and security implications” of UAS “flying in close
proximity to certain types of facilities,” while “ensuring the public right of transit, preserving
airspace efficiency, and integrating UAS into the [National Airspace System].”6
NAB supports the FAA’s efforts to ensure the safety and security of the national airspace
through reasonable restrictions on UAS operations near certain facilities. However, NAB

II. SECTION 74.250 SHOULD BE REVISED TO EXPLICITLY INCLUDE NON-TRANSITORY
NEWSGATHERING OPERATIONS WITHIN THE SCOPE OF ALLOWED OPERATIONS IN A

The Notice seeks comment on whether the proposed language at Section 74.250(a)(2) “is
broad enough to enable both legitimate transitory and non-transitory operations within a
UAFR, with the appropriate notification to the fixed site facility, while still preserving the
integrity of the airspace restriction.”7 The proposed Section 74.250 provides the
requirements by which certain UAS would be able to operate lawfully within standard UAFRs,
including that the UAS “broadcasts remote identification in accordance with 14 CFR part
89;” “[t]he unmanned aircraft transitions the UAFR in the shortest amount of time
practicable;” and the UAS operation is a permissible Part 91, 107, 108, 135, or 137
operation.8
The proposed rule does not sufficiently enable broadcasters’ non-transitory operations of
UAS in UAFRs, which as drafted requires UAS operating in a UAFR to “transition[] the UAFR in
the shortest amount of time practicable.”9 As the FAA acknowledged in the Notice, some
unmanned aircraft operations, such as “first amendment activity, may require non-transitory
operations within a UAFR.”10 When UAS are utilized in broadcasting, they usually are
engaged in such non-transitory operations like hovering, orbiting, or even loitering around a
facility in which a newsworthy event is occurring or developing, rather than merely transiting
over or through a restricted area.
Notably, the text proposed for Section 74.250(a)(2) does not explicitly include non-transitory
operations, and it requires completion of the UAS operation in the “shortest amount of time
practicable,” which contemplates UAS transit, thus providing little flexibility to broadcasters
in conducting their newsgathering UAS operations. While the Notice indicates that the FAA

The Notice further seeks comment on whether the proposed “lateral boundaries should be
reduced to less than the property line and what scenarios would be applicable to having less
than the property line for a UAFR.”22 Under the proposal in the Notice, Section 74.58 would
provide that “[t]he lateral boundary of the unmanned aircraft flight restriction must be
narrowly tailored to the specific security concern and may not: (1) [e]xceed the fixed site

restriction.”23 The Notice states that the purpose of the property boundary limitations “is to

broadcasters’ use of UAS for newsgathering purposes if fixed-site facilities decide to
reflexively set them at property lines. When broadcasters operate UAS to capture content,
they often orbit the UAS around the facility rather than transiting over the facility. Depending
on the size of the fixed-site facility’s property, broadcasters may need to orbit their
unmanned aircraft within the property lines to more clearly capture the sought-after content
at the facility. Further, there are several facilities eligible for a UAFR under the proposed rule
that would not need UAFRs up to their property lines, namely sports stadiums and arenas
with large complexes and parking areas, not all of which may be utilized in a given sporting
