I. Introduction
Southern Company respectfully submits these comments in response to the Federal
Aviation Administration’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking entitled “Designation - Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,” implementing Section
2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016.
Southern Company appreciates the FAA’s and broader Administration’s work to establish
a national framework for protecting critical infrastructure from unauthorized unmanned aircraft
systems operations. The protection of energy infrastructure is fundamental to public safety,
economic stability, emergency response, national security, and the daily lives of the customers
and communities Southern Company serves. As unmanned aircraft operations continue to
expand across the low-altitude airspace environment, a clear federal process for addressing
security concerns near qualifying critical infrastructure is both timely and important.
UAS are an important tool for advancing national priorities around energy infrastructure,
speed to power, and U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence. By enabling faster inspection,
monitoring, damage assessment, and restoration of electric infrastructure, UAS help utilities
deliver the reliability and responsiveness needed to support growing data center, advanced
manufacturing, and AI-related demand.
Southern Company supports the overall intent of the NPRM. The proposed framework
provides a meaningful foundation for designating unmanned aircraft flight restrictions near certain
fixed-site facilities and for creating clearer expectations for UAS operators, facility owners, and
government agencies. Properly implemented, UAFRs can help establish an enforceable legal
structure, improve awareness of sensitive locations, support compliance by lawful operators, and
provide an additional tool for addressing unauthorized activity near high-consequence
infrastructure.
At the same time, UAFRs should be designed and implemented with a clear understanding
of their practical role. Airspace restrictions are an important legal and informational tool, but they
are not, standing alone, a complete security solution. Restrictions will be most effective when they
are part of a broader framework that includes appropriate detection, identification, situational
awareness, reporting, and response capabilities. The final rule should therefore preserve the

security purpose of Section 2209 while recognizing that real-world protection of critical
infrastructure requires a layered and risk-based approach.
Southern Company also encourages the FAA to ensure the final rule remains workable for
the owners and operators of distributed infrastructure systems. Electric and natural gas
infrastructure includes fixed facilities, interconnected networks, linear corridors, and
geographically dispersed assets that must be inspected, maintained, monitored, and restored
under both routine and emergency conditions. These operational realities do not diminish the
need for security; rather, they underscore the importance of a framework that can provide
meaningful protection without unintentionally creating barriers to the activities that support
reliability, resilience, and public safety.
Southern Company offers the following comments from the perspective of a critical
infrastructure owner and operator with responsibility for protecting energy assets and maintaining
essential service. Southern Company also brings practical experience as a substantial user of
UAS technologies for infrastructure inspection, damage assessment, monitoring, and restoration.
This combined perspective informs the recommendations below: the final rule should be security-
focused, nationally consistent, risk-based, protective of sensitive information, administratively
clear, and capable of scaling with both infrastructure needs and the future growth of UAS
operations.
II. Southern Company Overview
Southern Company is one of the nation’s leading energy providers, serving approximately
nine million customers through a family of companies that includes state-regulated electric
utilities, natural gas distribution utilities, competitive generation, distributed energy infrastructure,
fiber optics, and wireless communications services. Through Alabama Power, Georgia Power,
and Mississippi Power, Southern Company provides essential electric service across Alabama,
Georgia, and Mississippi, supporting homes, businesses, hospitals, military installations,
emergency services, industrial customers, large load customers, public institutions, and other
critical community functions. With approximately 30,000 employees and capabilities that extend
across all 50 states, Southern Company’s operations are deeply connected to the reliability,
resilience, and security of the nation’s energy infrastructure.
Southern Company’s electric system includes approximately 46,000 megawatts of
generating capacity and a diverse resource portfolio that includes natural gas, nuclear, coal,
hydro, solar, wind, battery storage, and other energy technologies. The company’s transmission
operations include more than 27,000 miles of transmission lines, approximately 3,700
substations, and approximately 300,000 acres of right of way, all of which support the safe and
reliable movement of power across the Southeast. Southern Company also supports wholesale
energy customers through Southern Power, operates nuclear generation through Southern
Nuclear, provides distributed infrastructure solutions through PowerSecure, and maintains natural
gas distribution operations through Southern Company Gas. In addition, SouthernLINC Wireless
provides a mission-critical telecommunications network serving utility operations, public safety
agencies, transportation organizations, and other essential-service customers across the region,
delivering secure and resilient communications that support grid operations, emergency

response, and infrastructure reliability. Collectively, these assets and capabilities form an
interconnected energy and communications platform that is central to regional reliability,
emergency response, economic continuity, and national infrastructure resilience.
Protecting this infrastructure requires coordination across physical security, cybersecurity,
emergency preparedness, operational planning, regulatory compliance, field operations, aviation,
and system restoration functions. The company’s primary interest is ensuring that the final rule
meaningfully supports critical infrastructure protection while remaining practical for the entities
responsible for operating and maintaining those assets every day.
Southern Company uses UAS as an important operational tool to support infrastructure
inspections, vegetation management, environmental monitoring, storm damage assessment,
outage response, system restoration, situational awareness, security support, and data collection.
These operations can reduce risk to personnel, improve the speed and quality of inspections,
support faster restoration following severe weather, and help the company make more informed
asset-management decisions.
This dual responsibility to protect infrastructure and operate safely and efficiently with UAS
is central to Southern Company’s comments. Southern Company supports a framework that helps
protect sensitive facilities from unauthorized UAS activity. At the same time, the rule should
preserve the ability of infrastructure owners, their affiliates, and authorized contractors to conduct
necessary UAS operations in and around their own facilities and systems. A final rule that
accomplishes both objectives will better serve security, reliability, safety, and the public interest.
III. General Framework and Areas of Support
Southern Company supports the FAA’s effort to create a structured federal process for
UAFR designation. A federal framework is important because the airspace is national in character
and because UAS operators, infrastructure owners, public safety agencies, and commercial
entities need clear and consistent rules. Without a federal process, there is a risk that separate
state, local, or facility-specific approaches could develop in inconsistent ways, creating confusion
for operators and uneven protection for infrastructure.
Southern Company also supports the FAA’s risk-based approach. UAFRs should be
focused on facilities where the security need is significant and where the consequence of
disruption justifies airspace restriction. The proposed use of defined eligibility criteria, a
demonstration-of-need requirement, and a tiered structure helps ensure that restrictions are not
applied more broadly than necessary. This targeted approach is important to preserving both
security and access within the National Airspace System.
Southern Company supports the concept of sector-specific eligibility criteria because
critical infrastructure sectors are foundational to public safety, economic continuity, national
security, and the reliable delivery of essential services. These sectors differ in design, geography,
operational significance, vulnerability, interdependencies, and consequences of disruption. A rule
that recognizes those differences is more likely to result in appropriately tailored restrictions. The
final rule should continue to focus on infrastructure where the loss, disruption, or compromise of

a facility could produce meaningful downstream impacts to public safety, continuity of service, or
regional or national functions.
Southern Company also supports the FAA’s effort to tie UAFRs to existing security
measures. A UAFR should complement a facility’s broader security posture. In the energy sector,
facility protection is already addressed through a combination of physical security programs,
reliability obligations, emergency response planning, cybersecurity controls, operational
procedures, and coordination with government and law enforcement partners. The UAFR process
should recognize those existing frameworks and allow applicants to demonstrate how a requested
restriction would fit within their broader security program.
Southern Company further supports the general principle that UAFRs should be tailored
to the risk footprint of the facility. The proposed approach to limiting lateral boundaries to the fixed-
site facility boundary helps avoid unnecessary encroachment into surrounding navigable
airspace. Carefully tailored boundaries can support security objectives while reducing the
potential for unnecessary interference with lawful operations near, but not over, the protected
facility.
Southern Company also supports the FAA’s recognition that authorized UAS operations
should continue to be accommodated. Not all UAS activity near critical infrastructure is a security
concern. Many UAS operations are beneficial, planned, lawful, and conducted in support of the
facility owner, public safety, infrastructure reliability, or other public-interest functions. The final
rule should preserve these operations through clear access rules, practical notification
procedures, and appropriate allowances for facility-authorized activity.
Finally, Southern Company supports the FAA’s inclusion of public notice and input in the
UAFR process. Transparency can help ensure that UAFRs are appropriately tailored and that the
FAA understands the operational effects of a proposed restriction before final designation.
However, transparency must be balanced with protection of sensitive security, vulnerability, and
operational information. That balance is especially important for critical infrastructure owners that
may be asked to submit information that should not be placed in the public record.
IV. Recommendations and Areas for Clarification
A. UAFRs Should Be Understood as a Foundational Security Tool, Not a Complete Security
Solution
Southern Company supports the establishment of UAFRs as an important step in
protecting critical infrastructure from unauthorized UAS activity. A UAFR can help define where
certain operations are restricted, inform compliant operators, provide a basis for enforcement,
and support a shared understanding of sensitive airspace.
The final rule should also recognize the practical limits of any airspace restriction. A UAFR
can influence operators who know the rules and intend to follow them. It can also support
enforcement after a violation occurs. But a restriction does not, by itself, identify an aircraft,
determine intent, provide early warning, stop an aircraft, or resolve a security event in real time.

Operators who are unaware, careless, noncompliant, or intentionally malicious may not be
deterred by the existence of a restriction alone.
For that reason, the final rule should frame UAFRs as one layer within a broader critical
infrastructure security approach. Depending on the facility and risk profile, that broader approach
may include Remote ID reception, other detection or surveillance tools, security monitoring,
internal procedures, communications protocols, coordination with law enforcement, incident
response planning, and integration with existing facility security measures.
This framing is important for implementation. If UAFRs are treated as a complete security
solution, the rule may create a false sense of protection while imposing new constraints on
legitimate operators and disrupting essential operations needed to serve customers and
communities. If UAFRs are treated as a foundation that supports awareness, compliance, and
response, they can provide meaningful value as part of a layered security program.
Southern Company encourages the FAA to continue aligning this rulemaking with broader
federal work on UAS detection, identification, response, and mitigation. The security concern that
underlies Section 2209 is larger than airspace designation alone. A coordinated federal approach
will help ensure that UAFRs are useful in practice and that facility owners have a clear
understanding of how restrictions interact with other available tools and authorities.
B. The Rule Should Protect Sensitive Critical Infrastructure Information
Southern Company encourages the FAA to provide clear protections for sensitive
information submitted during the UAFR application, review, public comment, renewal, and
compliance processes. This is one of the most important implementation issues for critical
infrastructure owners.
Applicants may be asked to provide information concerning facility operations, security
posture, vulnerabilities, consequences of disruption, protective measures, incident history,
detection capabilities, response planning, and other site-specific details. For energy
infrastructure, this information is highly sensitive. If placed on the public record or disclosed
without appropriate controls, it could create new security risks and undermine the very purpose
of the rule.
Southern Company supports transparency in the designation process. Public input can
help the FAA understand how a proposed restriction may affect nearby airspace users,
communities, infrastructure operators, public safety agencies, and commercial UAS activity.
However, the public process should not require disclosure of detailed vulnerability information,
security plans, facility-specific risk assessments, or sensitive operational details.
The final rule should establish a clear process for separating public information from
protected information. Southern Company encourages the FAA to allow applicants to submit a
public-facing summary that describes the general nature of the request, accompanied by a non-
public appendix or supporting package containing sensitive materials. This approach would
support public review of the proposed airspace restriction while protecting information that should
not be broadly disclosed.

The FAA should also provide guidance addressing how sensitive materials will be
identified, marked, submitted, stored, accessed, shared, retained, and protected. Applicants
should understand what information will be made public, what information may be treated as
confidential, how interagency sharing will be managed, and what protections may apply under
applicable law and policy, including Freedom of Information Act considerations and protections
for security-sensitive critical infrastructure information.
Providing clear safeguards will improve the quality of applications. Facility owners will be
more able to provide candid and useful information to the FAA if they have confidence that
sensitive information will be adequately protected. Conversely, uncertainty around disclosure may
discourage participation or cause applicants to limit the detail provided in ways that make FAA
review less effective.
C. Protective Security Requirements Should Be Risk-Based and Should Recognize Existing
Security Programs
Southern Company supports the NPRM’s recognition that UAFRs should complement
existing protective security measures. A requested UAFR should not exist in isolation from the
facility’s broader security program. The final rule should, however, allow applicants to demonstrate
protective security in a manner that is proportional to the facility and consistent with existing
energy-sector security practices.
Critical infrastructure owners already operate within extensive security and reliability
frameworks. In the electric sector, facilities and systems may be subject to NERC reliability
standards, NERC Critical Infrastructure Protection requirements, physical security standards,
cybersecurity programs, emergency response plans, state requirements, internal corporate
security procedures, and federal guidance. These programs are not identical across every asset
because risk, function, and consequence vary by facility.
The final rule should allow applicants to rely on existing security programs as evidence of
protective security where those programs are relevant to the facility and requested restriction.
This would avoid duplicative documentation, reduce administrative burden, and allow the FAA to
evaluate UAFR requests in the context of a facility’s actual security posture.
Southern Company also encourages the FAA to clarify what is expected by the proposed
“security monitoring” requirement. The final rule should not be interpreted to require every
applicant to deploy the same type of detection system or to purchase high-cost, multi-layered
monitoring equipment regardless of risk. Monitoring expectations should be scalable and tied to
the nature of the facility, the requested restriction, and the security purpose of the UAFR.
Remote ID reception can provide an important baseline for identifying cooperative UAS
operating within or near a UAFR. It can help distinguish known or compliant aircraft from unknown
activity and can support a more informed security response. However, Remote ID is not a
complete detection solution because it depends on compliance by the aircraft operator and
functioning equipment. The final rule should recognize both the value and limitations of Remote
ID.

Southern Company encourages the FAA to preserve flexibility for applicants to use a range
of monitoring approaches. For some facilities, Remote ID reception and established security
procedures may be appropriate. For other higher-risk facilities, additional technologies or services
may be justified. A risk-based approach will better support security outcomes than a one-size-fits-
all requirement.
D. The Demonstration-of-Need Requirement Should Be Flexible and Based on Reasonably
Available Information
Southern Company supports the FAA’s proposal to require applicants to demonstrate a
safety or security need for a UAFR. This requirement is an important safeguard. UAFRs should
be granted based on risk and need, not as a default restriction or as a generalized means of
limiting access to low-altitude airspace.
At the same time, the final rule should preserve flexibility in how applicants demonstrate
need. Many critical infrastructure facilities do not currently have comprehensive historical UAS
detection records, continuous monitoring data, or the ability to reconstruct detailed UAS traffic
patterns over the prior 24 months. Some facilities may have incident reports, visual observations,
security records, Remote ID data, law enforcement contacts, or partial detection information.
Others may have limited historical information but still present significant risks because of the
nature and consequence of the facility.
Southern Company appreciates the NPRM’s use of a “where available” concept for certain
UAS activity information. The final rule should make clear that applicants are expected to provide
known and reasonably available information, not to create historical data that does not exist.
Applicants should not be expected to retroactively produce flight activity records or deploy new
detection infrastructure solely to recreate prior UAS activity.
The FAA should also avoid treating the absence of historical UAS activity data as evidence
that a facility lacks need. Past observations may be relevant, but they are not the only measure
of risk. UAS technology, operational patterns, and potential threat methods are changing rapidly.
A facility that has not documented frequent UAS activity in the past may still warrant protection
because of its criticality, vulnerability, location, operating characteristics, or the potential
consequences of disruption.
Southern Company encourages the FAA to accept a range of evidence in support of need.
Relevant information may include facility criticality, consequence analysis, known vulnerabilities,
security assessments, documented incidents, law enforcement information, operational
experience, existing regulatory security obligations, proximity to sensitive assets, available UAS
activity information, and qualitative risk analysis. This approach would preserve the integrity of
the designation process while recognizing practical differences among facilities.
E. The FAA Should Clarify When and How Detection or Remote ID Capabilities Must Be
Demonstrated
Southern Company recommends that the final rule or associated guidance clarify the
timing and evidence required to demonstrate Remote ID reception or other detection-related

capabilities. The NPRM recognizes the importance of such capabilities, but applicants will need
clearer direction to prepare complete and consistent submissions.
The FAA should specify whether evidence of Remote ID reception or other monitoring
capability must be provided at the time of initial application, during FAA review, before a UAFR
becomes active, or as a post-designation condition. Different timing may be appropriate
depending on the type of UAFR, the facility, and the nature of the requested restriction. Clear
guidance would reduce uncertainty and prevent avoidable delays.
The FAA should also identify examples of acceptable supporting materials. These could
include equipment descriptions, service provider documentation, coverage information, test
results, internal procedures, security plans, screenshots or system outputs, maintenance
procedures, or other reasonable evidence. Applicants should not have to guess what level of proof
is sufficient.
Southern Company also encourages the FAA to allow third-party service models where
appropriate. A facility should not necessarily have to own, operate, and maintain all detection or
monitoring equipment directly if equivalent capability can be provided through a qualified service
provider. Detection-as-a-service, surveillance-as-a-service, shared infrastructure, or other
managed service models may reduce costs, improve technical performance, and expand access
to useful monitoring capabilities.
The final rule should also remain flexible enough to accommodate future identification and
notification technologies. Broadcast Remote ID is an important current baseline, but low-altitude
airspace management is evolving. Future network-based identification, automated notification, or
other equivalent tools may provide more scalable awareness. The final rule should allow the FAA
to recognize alternative approaches that satisfy the same security and operational objectives.
F. The Application Process Should Be Clear, Efficient, and Proportionate
Southern Company supports the FAA’s effort to create a formal application process for
UAFR designation. A structured process will help ensure consistency, transparency, and
appropriate review. The usefulness of the framework, however, will depend heavily on whether
the process is understandable, efficient, and proportionate to the purpose of the rule.
Qualifying critical infrastructure owners should be able to seek UAFR protection without
unnecessary uncertainty or delay. The final rule should include clear instructions, standardized
submission tools, templates, and guidance that explain what information is required, what
information is optional, how sensitive information should be submitted, how the FAA will evaluate
applications, and how applicants can address deficiencies.
A centralized web-based platform would be useful for both applicants and the FAA. Such
a platform could standardize information collection, allow structured submission of maps and
supporting materials, provide a mechanism for identifying sensitive content, support public notice,
and improve the overall efficiency of the process.
The application process should also be calibrated to the statutory purpose of Section
2209. UAFR requests are security-driven airspace requests. The process should require enough

information for the FAA to evaluate eligibility, need, airspace effects, and security integration, but
it should not become so complex or burdensome that it discourages appropriate use of the
program. Providing appropriate information is necessary for a credible and risk-based process.
The key is ensuring that required information is clear, relevant, protected where sensitive, and
reasonably obtainable by the applicant.
G. Environmental and Adjacent-Land-Use Information Should Be Limited to What Applicants Can
Reasonably Know
Southern Company recognizes that the FAA may need to consider the broader effects of
a proposed UAFR, including potential impacts to nearby airspace users, surrounding land uses,
environmental resources, and neighboring communities. Southern Company supports a review
process that allows the FAA to understand the practical implications of a proposed restriction.
However, any requirement for applicants to identify or describe sensitive land uses,
environmental resources, or adjacent third-party conditions should be practical. Electric utilities
generally do not have detailed information about private property uses, third-party operations, or
landowner activities outside their ownership or control. Requiring applicants to develop detailed
information about adjacent properties could add uncertainty, cost, and delay without materially
improving the FAA’s review.
Southern Company recommends that the FAA limit applicant obligations in this area to
information that is reasonably available through the applicant’s own records, existing public
sources, or ordinary due diligence. Where more detailed environmental or adjacent-land-use
analysis is needed, the FAA may be better positioned to evaluate those issues using agency
expertise and federal, state, or local datasets.
The final rule or guidance should clearly define the level of detail expected. Applicants
should not be placed in the position of having to conduct open-ended investigations of third-party
land uses or environmental conditions outside their control. A practical approach would allow the
FAA to evaluate relevant impacts while keeping the application process focused and workable.
H. Facility Owners and Authorized Contractors Must Be Able to Conduct Necessary Operations
Within UAFRs
Southern Company encourages the FAA to clarify that facility owners, operators, affiliates,
and authorized contractors may conduct necessary UAS operations within UAFRs associated
with their own facilities, provided those operations comply with applicable operating rules and
appropriate safeguards. This clarification is essential to ensure that UAFRs protect critical
infrastructure without impeding the activities needed to inspect, maintain, secure, and restore that
infrastructure.
Owners use UAS for many activities that directly support safety, security, and operational
continuity. These include facility inspection, equipment monitoring, thermal imaging, LiDAR
collection, storm damage assessment, vegetation patrol, security observation, environmental
monitoring, outage response, and post-event restoration. These operations are often conducted

at the direction of the facility owner and may be necessary to evaluate conditions, identify hazards,
prioritize repairs, and restore service.
For 2026, Southern Company estimates approximately 2,555 UAS flights supporting
inspection and utility operations over its generation facilities alone, underscoring that facility-
authorized UAS activity is a recurring operational function that must remain predictable under a
UAFR framework. Many of these operations are not simple transits through restricted airspace.
They may require hovering, circling, repeated passes, low-speed flight, close visual inspection,
or sustained collection over a particular asset. A rule that clearly permits transit but does not
address facility-authorized non-transitory operations could create uncertainty for the very entities
the UAFR is intended to protect.
Southern Company recommends that the final rule or guidance expressly state that facility
owners and their authorized agents may conduct necessary UAS operations within a UAFR,
subject to applicable operating rules and appropriate safeguards. This clarification should apply
to routine operations and to time-sensitive circumstances, including storm response, outage
restoration, emergency repairs, and other reliability or public safety activities.
Such clarification would not weaken the security purpose of the rule. On the contrary, it
would strengthen the rule by ensuring that facility owners retain the tools needed to monitor,
maintain, and secure their own infrastructure.
I. Notification Should Be Automated, Standardized, and Designed to Avoid Turning Facilities into
Airspace Managers
Southern Company supports the concept of notification for authorized UAS access to
UAFRs, provided that notification is implemented in a way that can scale. A notification process
can improve awareness and help facility security personnel distinguish expected activity from
unknown or potentially concerning operations.
However, a manual notification process would be difficult to sustain across large volumes
of UAS operations and large numbers of facilities. Critical infrastructure owners are not designed
to function as real-time airspace management entities. A process that requires facility personnel
to manually receive, assess, respond to, and track routine access notifications could create
significant administrative burden without necessarily improving security outcomes.
Southern Company encourages the FAA to prioritize automated, standardized, system-to-
system notification methods. Digital interfaces, API-enabled tools, FAA-endorsed platforms, or
other automated mechanisms could allow operators to provide timely, verifiable notice while
reducing friction and improving consistency. Automation would also help ensure that facilities
receive the information they need without requiring active management of every compliant
operation.
An effective notification framework should be designed around exception-based
awareness. Facility personnel should be able to focus on unknown, unexpected, noncompliant,
or potentially concerning activity rather than manually processing routine lawful operations. This

approach would better align with how security organizations manage risk and would be more
practical as UAS operations scale.
The FAA should also consider how automated notification could integrate with future
airspace data services, Remote ID information, UAS Traffic Management concepts, and other
digital airspace tools. A standardized digital ecosystem would improve compliance, reduce
burden, and better support both security and operational efficiency.
J. The Final Rule Should Account for the Cumulative Effect of Multiple UAFRs
Southern Company supports the use of UAFRs where justified by risk and need. However,
the FAA should consider how the cumulative effect of multiple UAFRs may shape low-altitude
airspace over time, particularly around infrastructure networks.
Energy infrastructure is not limited to isolated facilities. Generation plants, substations,
transmission systems, distribution networks, natural gas assets, and related facilities operate as
part of interconnected systems. UAS operations often follow infrastructure corridors or move
between multiple assets as part of a single inspection, patrol, or restoration mission.
As additional UAFRs are established, especially across multiple sectors, the low-altitude
airspace environment may become increasingly segmented. If access, notification, and mapping
systems are not scalable, even well-justified site-specific restrictions could collectively complicate
recurring infrastructure operations, emergency response, public safety missions, and other
beneficial UAS activity.
Southern Company encourages the FAA to evaluate UAFR implementation not only on a
site-by-site basis, but also in terms of broader airspace functionality. The final rule should preserve
practical pathways for authorized operators, ensure that UAFR data is available in usable digital
formats, and support automated planning and notification tools that can account for multiple
restrictions across a route or operating area.
This is particularly important for routine BVLOS operations and future higher-density UAS
activity. A framework that works for a small number of restrictions may not work once UAFRs
become more numerous. Building scalability into the final rule now will help avoid operational
challenges later.
K. The UAFR Framework Should Be Compatible With Dynamic Airspace Management
Southern Company encourages the FAA to design the UAFR framework with the future
airspace environment in mind. UAS operations are moving toward greater automation,
repeatability, networked operations, and routine BVLOS missions. This trend will likely continue
as federal rules evolve and as infrastructure operators expand the use of UAS for inspection,
monitoring, and response.
Static restrictions and manual coordination processes will not be sufficient for that
operating environment. As the number of UAFRs increases and as UAS operations become more
frequent, the system will need digital tools capable of communicating constraints, supporting route

planning, enabling automated notifications, and helping operators comply with applicable
restrictions in near real time.
Southern Company encourages the FAA to ensure that UAFR data is structured,
accessible, current, and compatible with digital flight planning and airspace management tools.
UAFRs should be integrated into broader FAA airspace data systems in a way that supports both
operator compliance and facility awareness.
The final framework should also be flexible enough to work with future UAS Traffic
Management capabilities, automated data service providers, digital mapping services, Remote ID
information, and other airspace information services. This will help ensure that UAFRs remain
useful as technology and operating models evolve.
L. Sector-Specific Criteria Should Remain Targeted but Clear
Southern Company supports the FAA’s use of sector-specific eligibility criteria to focus
UAFRs on facilities with significant security or societal importance. Sector-specific criteria can
help prevent overuse of UAFRs and ensure that restrictions are directed toward facilities where
disruption could have meaningful consequences.
At the same time, the final rule should ensure that eligibility criteria are clear and
administrable. Critical infrastructure owners should be able to determine whether a facility may
qualify without unnecessary ambiguity. Where thresholds are based on capacity, voltage, function,
ownership, operational role, interconnection significance, or consequence of disruption, the FAA
should provide guidance explaining how those criteria will be applied.
Southern Company encourages the FAA to recognize that infrastructure significance may
not always be captured by a single numerical threshold. Certain facilities may have importance
based on system role, geographic location, interdependencies, restoration constraints, or the
customers and services they support. The final rule should preserve a path for the FAA to consider
facility-specific circumstances where appropriate, while maintaining a high threshold that prevents
unnecessary restrictions.
This balance is important. UAFRs should not become a broad mechanism for restricting
low-altitude airspace around ordinary infrastructure. But the rule should also avoid excluding
facilities that present legitimate security concerns simply because their importance is not fully
reflected by a single metric.
M. Public Notice Should Be Meaningful While Protecting Sensitive Details
Southern Company recognizes the FAA’s inclusion of public notice and comment before
UAFR designation. Public input can help identify operational concerns, airspace impacts, nearby
uses, or other issues the FAA should consider.
However, the final rule should ensure that public notice provides enough information for
meaningful comment without disclosing sensitive facility details. For example, public materials
may appropriately identify the general location and airspace dimensions of a proposed UAFR, the
type of restriction requested, and the general basis for the request. Public materials should not

disclose detailed vulnerability assessments, security procedures, response plans, sensitive
diagrams, or information that could assist a bad actor.
Southern Company encourages the FAA to create a public comment process that is
structured and secure. Applicants should have clear instructions for submitting public and non-
public materials. The FAA should also have a process for redacting or withholding sensitive
information before publication. This will allow public review to serve its intended purpose without
creating avoidable security risk.
N. Remote Pilot Training and Guidance Should Address UAFRs
Southern Company encourages the FAA to update relevant remote pilot training, testing,
and guidance materials once the UAFR framework is finalized. The effectiveness of UAFRs will
depend in part on operator awareness and understanding.
Remote pilots should know how to identify UAFRs, understand applicable operating
limitations, determine whether an operation is allowed, provide any required notice, and comply
with access conditions. This information should be incorporated into FAA guidance, safety
materials, knowledge test references, and Airman Certification Standards where appropriate.
Clear education will improve compliance by lawful operators. It will also reduce inadvertent
violations and help ensure that UAFRs function as intended: guiding compliant operators away
from restricted areas or through appropriate access procedures, while supporting enforcement
against unauthorized activity.
O. Cost and Implementation Should Remain Scalable and Proportionate
Southern Company encourages the FAA to consider implementation costs and
administrative impacts throughout the final rule. Application preparation, mapping,
documentation, security review, Remote ID reception, detection capabilities, notification
procedures, renewals, and ongoing compliance can all create costs for infrastructure owners.
Southern Company does not oppose reasonable application requirements or the need to
provide supporting information. A credible UAFR process requires the FAA to evaluate eligibility,
need, security integration, and airspace effects. However, requirements should be proportionate
to the purpose of the rule and should avoid unnecessary duplication or uncertainty.
In the electric sector, costs associated with compliance and infrastructure operations may
ultimately affect customers. Southern Company is focused on customer affordability, rate stability
and customer value and supports rulemaking that aligns with those priorities. A scalable and
proportionate framework will support participation while avoiding unnecessary cost pressure. The
FAA can help achieve that outcome by allowing applicants to rely on existing security programs,
submit reasonably available information, use standardized digital tools, protect sensitive
materials, and adopt monitoring approaches suited to the facility’s risk profile.
V. Recommended Refinements & Clarifications
Southern Company recommends that the FAA consider the following refinements in the final rule
or associated guidance:

1. Continue coordinating the UAFR framework with broader federal efforts related to UAS
detection, identification, response, and mitigation.
2. Establish clear procedures for protecting sensitive critical infrastructure information
submitted during the application, review, public comment, renewal, and compliance
processes.
3. Allow applicants to submit public-facing summaries with non-public sensitive appendices
or supporting materials.
4. Clarify how sensitive materials will be handled, stored, shared, retained, and protected,
including how applicable disclosure laws and policies will be applied.
5. Confirm that protective security requirements may be satisfied through a risk-based
approach that recognizes existing physical security, cybersecurity, reliability, emergency
response, and compliance programs.
6. Clarify the meaning of security monitoring and avoid interpreting the rule to require
identical or high-cost detection systems at every facility regardless of risk.
7. Recognize Remote ID reception as a useful baseline for cooperative aircraft awareness
while acknowledging that Remote ID does not address all unauthorized or malicious
operations.
8. Clarify when applicants must demonstrate Remote ID reception or detection-related
capabilities and what documentation will satisfy that requirement.
9. Allow applicants to use qualified third-party service models, including detection-as-a-
service or surveillance-as-a-service, where appropriate.
10. Preserve flexibility to recognize future identification, notification, or detection technologies
that meet the FAA’s safety and security objectives.
11. Make clear that demonstration-of-need requirements may be satisfied using known and
reasonably available information, including qualitative risk information, documented
incidents, facility criticality, vulnerabilities, consequence analysis, and available UAS
activity data.
12. Confirm that applicants are not expected to retroactively create historical UAS traffic
records that do not exist or deploy detection systems solely to reconstruct past activity.
13. Avoid treating the absence of historical UAS activity data as evidence that a facility lacks
a legitimate security need.
14. Provide a clear, efficient, and proportionate application process supported by standardized
templates, guidance, and a centralized digital submission platform.
15. Limit environmental and adjacent-land-use information requirements to information
reasonably available to the applicant or obtainable through existing public sources.

16. Clarify that facility owners, operators, affiliates, and authorized contractors may conduct
necessary non-transitory UAS operations within UAFRs associated with their own
facilities.
17. Clarify that facility-authorized operations include inspection, monitoring, maintenance,
security, storm response, outage restoration, environmental monitoring, and other
reliability or public safety activities.
18. Clarify that “shortest amount of time practicable” allows safety-based deviations for detect-
and-avoid maneuvers, lost-link procedures, weather, obstacle avoidance, emergency
conditions, or other operational contingencies.
19. Clarify that “as soon as reasonably possible” is a flexible standard that accounts for
emergency, on-demand, storm response, public safety, and other time-sensitive
operations.
20. Prioritize automated, standardized, system-to-system notification processes that provide
facility awareness without requiring critical infrastructure owners to manage routine
airspace coordination manually.
21. Consider the cumulative effect of multiple UAFRs on low-altitude airspace access,
especially for infrastructure corridors and recurring utility operations.
22. Ensure UAFR data is accurate, current, digitally accessible, and compatible with flight
planning, notification, and airspace management tools.
23. Design the UAFR framework to be compatible with future dynamic airspace management,
UAS Traffic Management concepts, automated data services, and BVLOS operations.
24. Provide clear guidance on sector-specific eligibility criteria and preserve the ability to
consider facility-specific circumstances where justified by risk and consequence.
25. Update remote pilot training, testing, and guidance materials to address UAFR
identification, access, notification, and compliance requirements.
VI. Conclusion
Southern Company appreciates the FAA’s leadership in advancing a framework to
address unauthorized UAS operations near critical infrastructure. The NPRM is an important step
toward creating a national, risk-based process for protecting sensitive fixed-site facilities while
preserving the safe and beneficial use of UAS in the National Airspace System.
Southern Company supports the intent of the proposed rule and encourages the FAA to
refine the framework so that it delivers meaningful security value, protects sensitive information,
and remains practical for the owners and operators of distributed infrastructure systems. The final
rule should recognize that UAFRs are most effective as part of a layered security approach; that
critical infrastructure information must be protected; that application and monitoring requirements
should be clear and proportionate; and that authorized facility operations must remain workable
under both routine and emergency conditions. With these refinements, the final rule can

strengthen critical infrastructure protection while supporting the safe, scalable, and responsible
integration of UAS technologies that contribute to energy reliability, system resilience, and public
safety.
Southern Company appreciates the FAA’s leadership, as well as the Administration’s
commitment to advancing policies that strengthen the security and resilience of the nation’s critical
infrastructure while enabling the continued growth of the UAS industry. By prioritizing this
rulemaking, the FAA and Administration have taken an important step toward addressing
unauthorized UAS activity around sensitive facilities and establishing a more consistent national
framework for risk-based airspace protections. Southern Company is grateful for the opportunity
to contribute to this effort and looks forward to continued collaboration with the FAA and other
stakeholders to ensure the final rule achieves its security objectives while supporting innovation,
operational effectiveness, and the safe integration of UAS technologies across the National
Airspace System.

comments.commenter: Comment from U.S. Chamber of Commerce
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
Docket Operations
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE
Room W 58-213
West Building Fifth Floor
Washington, D.C. 20590 -0001
Re: Comments on the Federal Aviation Administration, Department of Transportation ;
Notice of Proposed Rulemakin g; Designation -Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility (Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 )
To Whom It May Concern :
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce (the “Chamber”) welcomes this opportunity to
comment on the Federal Aviation Administration ’s (“FAA”) notice of proposed rulemaking
(“NPRM”) on Designation -Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity
to a Fixed Site Facility (“Section 2209 Rule”).1
The Chamber thanks the FAA for proposing to establish a process for the
restriction of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (“UAS”) operations in the airspace in proximity
of certain fixed site s and implementing Section 220 9 of the FAA Extension, Safety and
Security Act of 2016 . The stated objectives of the NPRM align with the Chamber’s strong
support for satisfying Congress’ directive in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 and in
other laws , supporting homeland security through protecting sensitive fixed site facilities
from unauthorized drones , and advanc ing the Trump Administration’s deregulatory
agenda and drone priorities as detailed in Executive Order 14 305, Restoring American
Airspace Sovereignty .2
Although the Chamber believes the Section 2209 Rule will have tremendous
benefit once it is finalized and implemented, we believe important changes must be
included in a Final Rule. Importantly, it must strike a balance between two imperatives: (1)
effectively protecting fixed -site critical infrastructure facilities and other sensitive sites,
while preserving the safety and efficiency of the National Airspace System (“NAS”); and
1 Designation -Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility , Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, 91 Fed. Reg. 24650, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 (rel. May 6, 2026) (“NPRM”).
2 Exec. Off. of the President, Exec. Ord. 1430 5, Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty (2025).

(2) sustaining thousands of authorized UAS operations that are saving lives, inspecting
infrastructure, and creating economic growth.
The Section 2209 Rule is critical to advance homeland security and enable a
process to protect against terrorism, espionage, safety hazards to ground operations,
and other criminal and illicit activities, while also recognizing the immense value and
benefit that authorized drone operations can provide. The use of drones in conflicts in
Ukraine and across the Middle East has underscored the vulnerabilities of energy,
chemical, rail, electric utility, amusement parks, data centers, and other sensitive sites to
surveillance and potential attack by drones. Domestically, these are not hypothetical
risks, given the number of close calls and sightings adjacent to sensitive sites including
electric utility infrastructure, oil refineries, chemical facilities, and correctional facilities.
Additionally, large -scal e gatherings at events such as the FIFA World Cup have proven to
be a public safety challenge because of hundreds of drone incursions, resulting in
arrests of drone operators and confiscation of many unauthorized drones.
Due to delayed federal action, over two dozen states have enacted legislation that
would establish restrictions, creating a confusing patchwork of state laws for the drone
and critical infrastructure industries and hinder ing FAA’s oversight over the national
airspace system. Finalizing and implementing the Section 2209 Rule , coupled with
federal preemption of similar state, local, and tribal laws ,3 would help to address these
issues by providing a single, nationwide program to protect critical infrastructure and
other sensitive sites.
The core security concern surrounding illicit drone activity is not only the
unauthorized flights themselves, but who is conducting them and why. We respectfully
urge the FAA to simplify the Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (“UAFR”) application
proces s and reconsider eligibility requirements, take steps to protect confidential and
highly sensitive security information, digitize the airspace and sharing of information at
scale, and consider the possible conflicts and limitations within the UAFR framewor k.
We further encourage the FAA to implement UAFR in a manner that protects
critical facilities while accommodating authorized aviation, public safety, and FAA -
approved UAS operations through risk -based and operationally feasible mechanisms.
I. Standard UAFR Application Process and Eligibility Requirements
A. Streamlin e the Application Process
3 The FAA acknowledges that it has field preemption authority to regulate airspace efficiency. See
https://www.faa.gov/uas/resources/policy_library/UAS_Fact_Sheet_2023.pdf.
2

The FAA's application and Standard UAFR maintenance requirements would
create an unnecessary, burdensome process for facilities with sensitive and
comprehensive security plans. In fact, unnecessarily complex application requirements
could actually undermine the goal of protecting in -need facilities. The Chamber
recommends streamlining application requirements and the process needed to obtain a
UAFR designation.
Allowing batch applications from eligible operators with multiple fixed -site
facilities and removing the environmental impact assessment in a Standard UAFR
application would help expedite the Standard UAFR review process and reduce FAA’s
workload. FAA should also ensure that aviation -related critical infrastructure, including
airports, FAA air traffic facilities, aviation fuel infrastructu re, and other facilities
supporting commercial air transportation, are appropriately considered within the
eligibility framework.
B. Reconsider Eligibility Requirements
In certain sectors, the Proposed Rule determines eligibility based on sector -
specific criteria and rigid numerical thresholds. The Chamber recommends adopting a
risk-based, case -by-case pathway that would allow the FAA and the applicable Sector
Risk Manage ment Agency (“SRMA”) to consider facilities that present significant
vulnerability and national security risk if left unprotected. For example, fixed site
facilities in the energy and chemical sectors may not meet the required numerical
thresholds for eligibility despite demonstrating serious risk and vulnerability to unsafe or
illicit UAS operations.
II. Protect Confidential and Sensitive Information
The NPRM requires applicants seeking a UAFR designation to submit highly
detailed operational, security, infrastructure, vulnerability, and emergency response
information. Even if protected from public disclosure, this information essentially creates
a potential roadmap for adversaries seeking information on the nation’s critical
infrastructure vulnerabilities and security plans. Even with the most robust cybersecurity
and other protections against disclosure, the risk of breach remains, creating extensive
vulnerabilities for the nation. Malicious actors could easily harvest and weaponize this
data, using this pre -packaged intelligence to disrupt facilities, compromise public safety,
or interfere with existing security operations.
We recommend establishing clear rules and standards to protect against disclosure
of any proprietary or sensitive information applicants are ultimately required to submit in
support of UAFR applications.
3

The Final Rule should clearly state a presumption that materials submitted in
support of UAFR applications containing confidential business information or other non -
public security -related information will be maintained confidentially, exempt from other
regulatory enforcement, civil litigation, and public disclosure, as well as protected from
disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act (“FOIA”) and similar public disclosure
laws to the fullest extent permitted by law, including appli cable exemptions protecting
trade secrets and confidential commercial information, sensitive records compiled for
law enforcement or that contain sensitive security information, and privileged and
deliberative governmental materials.
Additionally, the Final Rule should establish clear safeguards and cybersecurity
standards governing the secure submission procedures, including secure electronic
transmission systems, access controls, encryption requirements, storage, handling of
sensitive materials, and other cybersecurity safeguards reasonably designed to prevent
unauthorize d access, disclosure, alteration, or dissemination of submitted materials.
Lastly, the Final R ule should limit the information publicly disclosed by the FAA
during the notice -and-comment process and in any final determination to only basic,
non-sensitive information sufficient and reasonably necessary to provide meaningful
public notice and comment without revealing sensitive operational or security -related
details, specifically the general location, dimensions, duration, and general purpose of
the proposed UAFR. Public disclosures must not include confidential or security -
sensitive information regarding a site’s vulnerabilities, security measures, infrastructure
limitations, or emergency response procedures where such disclosure could further
increase risks to the safety and security of the applying facility.
In this context, the Chamber recommends that the FAA consider adopting
safeguards modeled on the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency’s ( “CISA ”)
Protected Critical Infrastructure Information ( “PCII ”) Program 4, including restrictions on
disclosure, dissemination, and use of information submitted in support of UAFR
applications. Doing so would help ensure that applicants can provide the information
necessary to support UAFR requests without creating additional cy bersecurity or
national security risks.
III. Digit ization of the Airspace and Information Sharing
UAS are effective due to their high degree of automation and the ability to
respond to conditions based on the availability of digital information. We recommend
4 Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency, Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII) Program , U.S.
Department of Homeland Security . See https://www.cisa.gov/resources -tools/programs/protected -critical -
infrastructure -information -pcii-program.
4

that the Final Rule state that Standard UAFR information (including lateral boundaries
and altitude ceilings) is available in an accessible, machine -readable, and standardized
format that can be readily incorporated into existing aviation, airport, and UAS
operational systems. This approach will avoid relying on manual processes and meet the
needs of operators that depend on the availability of digital information to input into
their automated systems. The Final Rule should also ensure that all Standard UAFRs are
easily accessible in one integrated location and that they feed into a Notice to Air
Missions (“NOTAM”) system.
We also recommend allowing commercial operators to submit a single "standing
notification" covering certain operational service areas, rather than requiring manual per -
flight submissions. The FAA has already contemplated a solution that would require one -
time submission of airman certificate number(s) and remote ID serial number(s) to the
FAA to be “included on a developed ‘whitelist’” that would be made available to fixed -site
facilities. The FAA should adopt this concept as a core operational mechanism fo r
implementing access to UAFRs while maintaining oversight and accountability for
airspace decisions. For a high -tempo commercial UAS network conducting thousands of
daily flights, manually submitting flight details for every individual transit flight brea ks
the automation loop, introduces human error, and acts as a de facto capacity cap on the
industry. For higher risk facilities where UAS mishaps, electromagnetic interference, loss
of control, ignition risks, or operational disruptions could create signifi cant safety,
environmental, or cascading infrastructure consequences, a tiered approach should be
implemented so commercial operators will know where individual flight notifications are
required.
For day-to-day monitoring of UAS flight operations, a fixed site facility should be
able to rely on broadcast or network -based Remote ID or successor technology . The
remote viewing capability of network -based Remote ID will allow a fixed site facility to
replace the proposed manual web portal with automated, machine -to-machine
communication s. This aligns with tech industry standards for data interoperability, cloud
integration, and scalable software ecosystems.
The Final Rule should also require an automated notification system that utilizes a
standardized and instantaneous process integrated directly with Low Altitude
Authorization and Notification Capability (“LAANC”) or an equivalent system. The FAA
should enc ourage a centralized, standardized notification architecture utilizing digital
platforms and secure data exchange. Any automated notification architecture should
preserve FAA authority over airspace access determinations and support coordination
5

with affected aviation stakeholders where appropriate. The FAA's LAANC framework
provides a proven model for how automated notifications and approvals can be
implemented at scale. Network -based Remote ID would ultimately provide a more
scalable means of id entifying, authenticating, and tracking authorized operations,
especially as Beyond Visual Line of Sight (“BVLOS”) operations already occurring under
Parts 107 and 135, and will occur under proposed Part 108, will soon become more
prevalent. The FAA should also consider leveraging emerging service -provider
frameworks, including Part 146 Automated Data Service Providers, to support automated
notification capabilities. The Final Rule should permit multiple compliance pathways,
including: (1) flight -specific n otifications; (2) standing notifications for recurring
operations; (3) pre -approved or whitelisted operator programs for public safety agencies;
and (4) future network -based identity and notification solutions facilitated through FAA -
approved service provi ders.
IV. Consider P ossible Limitation of UAFR s
A. Temporary Flight Restrictions
As drafted, the NPRM prevents commercial facilities that have been granted
Temporary Flight Restrictions (“TFR”) from applying for a UAFR , even if the TFR protects
less than the geographic entirety of the facility. Section 74.82(e) (Commercial Facilities
Sector) states that, to qualify as a fixed -site facility, a location may not also be “a
stadium or venue where events may be covered by temp orary flight restrictions.”
This language unnecessarily excludes certain facilities , such as large entertainment
venues that are subject to TFRs or other FAA protections , from the definition of an
eligible Commercial Facilities Sector facility.
Many qualifying venues have legitimate operational and security concerns that
the FAA has already recognized through temporary, event -specific, or area -specific flight
restrictions. However, because those restrictions are limited in duration, scope, or are a
covered, affected facilities should remain eligible to seek UAFR protections to address
ongoing security risks not fully mitigated by existing FAA restrictions. For example, a TFR
may protect only a portion of a facility, while other areas of the same pr operty remain
exposed to unauthorized UAS activity and could benefit from complementary UAFR
protections. Facilities that require temporary flight restrictions or whose protections
cover only a subset of the entire property may present some of the strongest
justifications for enhanced UAFR protections due to the scale, visibility, density, or
recurring nature of the security risks involved. Because TFRs are typically event -specific
and time -limited, they serve a different purpose than UAFRs, which are intended to
address continuing operational and security risks that exist outside discrete events or
protected periods. The existence of a TFR therefore should not automatically prevent an
6

otherwise eligible facility from seeking additional UAFR protections where FAA
determines such protections are operationally justified and compatible with existing
airspace management requirements .
The rule should provide greater clarity that nothing in the UAFR framework
disturbs, limits, or otherwise affects existing FAA authorities, including Temporary Flight
Restrictions, Special Security Instructions, or other aviation safety or security -related
restrictions. The Chamber requests that the Final Rule expressly clarify that existing FAA
protections do not preclude a facility from applying for or receiving a Standard or Special
UAFR , that nothing in the UAFR framework disturbs, limits, or otherwise affects existing
FAA operational authorities, restrictions, or approvals, and that UAFRs supplement,
rather than replace, such existing authorities. The existence or availability of FAA
protections should not disqualify facilities facing recurring or long -term UAS security
threats from obtaining more durable UAFR protections.
B. Facility Owner Access for Drone Operations
Although facility owners do not own or control the airspace above their facilities,
the Final Rule should clearly preserve the ability of facility owners , their authorized
agents , and anyone with a legitimate business interest in the site (e.g. a contract party)
to conduct UAS operations in support of inspection, maintenance, monitoring, security,
and emergency response functions. UAFRs should enhance facility security, not impede
the very drone operations that help facilities operate safely and securely.
At the same time, critical infrastructure operators should not be expected to
become airspace managers. The Final Rule should minimize administrative burdens on
facility operators while improving their ability to identify potentially unauthorized aircraft.
The FAA should support scalable approaches such as standing notifications, recurring
access arrangements, and auto mated mechanisms for compliant operators that routinely
conduct inspection, maintenance, or security operations within or through the same
Standard UAFRs .
To that end, FAA should establish a secure, facility -managed whitelist through the
UAFR Module or another FAA -approved system. Once a UAFR has been designated, the
operator or proprietor, acting through its designated representative or site manager,
should be permitted to submit and update information identifying facility -owned, facility -
operated, contracted, or otherwise facility -authorized UAS operators and aircraft.
C. Public Safety and Drone -As-First -Responder Access
The Final Rule should clarify that nothing contained in them will restrict
authorized federal, state, local, and tribal public safety agencies to transit through and
7

operate within Standard and Special UAFRs when conducting legitimate operational and
select training missions while maintaining appropriate coordination with FAA
requirements and applicable airspace procedures . The Final Rule should also explicitly
authorize public safety operators to conduct operations within, not merely transit
through, UAFRs when responding to emergencies or other time -critical incidents .
D. Expanding Eligibility for a Special UAFR
The Proposed Rule limits eligibility for Special UAFRs to federal facilities, military
operations, intelligence -related operations, and certain non -federal facilities deemed to
support national or homeland security. This framework does no t account for the
substantial public safety and security threats faced by large outdoor public venues and
amusement parks, which attract dense public gatherings and present heightened
vulnerability to unauthorized or malicious UAS activity.
The Proposed Rule recognizes that the purpose of the Special UAFR framework is
to address heightened operational, safety, and security risks that cannot be adequately
mitigated through a Standard UAFR alone. Those same vulnerabilities exist at large
outdoor public venues, amusement parks, destination entertainment venues, and sports
complexes that routinely host tens of thousands of guests in highly concentrated
outdoor environments.
Unauthorized drone operations over these facilities present serious and escalating
threats, including risks of collision with infrastructure, potential interference with public
safety personnel, potential intentional acts designed to create panic or mass disruption,
and the potential use of drones as weapons or delivery systems for harmful payloads.
These threats are not hypothetical, and the number of security incidents caused by
unauthorized drone incursions, intentional disruptions, reckless operations, and drone
malfunctions that occur over densely crowded venues continue to increase nationwide.
The Proposed Rule also does not clearly define the threshold necessary to qualify
for a Special UAFR. The Final Rule, as discussed in further detail below, should establish
clear criteria focused on the elevated risks associated with large outdoor public venues
and amusement parks, specifically unauthorized drone operations over large public
gatherings, iconic or symbolic locations that attract heightened unauthorized or
malicious UAS activity, and operational or structural conditions that increase both the
likelihood and potential consequences of a mass casualty event .
The Final Rule, including Proposed §§ 74.6 and 74.66, and discussions of eligibility
for Special UAFRs in the Supplemental Information sections, should expressly provide
that eligible fixed -site facilities presenting heightened security or public -safety risks
should be permitted to apply for a Special UAFR . We recommend the Final R ule focus on
8

whether the applicant demonstrates that unauthorized UAS activity presents elevated
risks of mass casualty events, public panic, interference with emergency response
operations, or other substantial security threat s. We also recommend that the Final Rule
clarify that the e xistence of a TFR should not prevent an otherwise eligible facility from
seeking Special UAFR protections. In keeping with the Proposed Rule’s intent to limit the
use of Special UAFRs, we recommend that this designation be used sparingly and only in
circumstances where the applicant has provided a sufficient and compelling showing of
the heightened security or public -safety risks described above.
Additionally, we recommend that Section 74.6(b) (Special UAFR Designation –
Characteristics) remove the requirement that a Special UAFR “must have a designated
using agency.” Retaining this requirement as drafted limits Special UAFR eligibility to
facilities associated with federal, military, intelligence, or other governmental operations
and would effectively exclude private -sector critical infrastructure facilities that may
satisfy the heightened operational and security risk standard warranting Special UAFR
protections.
V. Conclusion
The Chamber appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and
welcomes continued engagement with the FAA and the U.S. government on these
important issues to ensure homeland security , preserve the safety and efficiency of the
NAS, and restore American airspace sovereignty .
Sincerely,
Jordan Crenshaw
Senior Vice President
Chamber Technology Engagement Center
U.S. Chamber of Commerce
9

comments.comment_text:
Attached, please find the signatures of 15,815 Friends of the Earth supporters:
Re: Exclude CAFOs and slaughterhouses from eligibility for drone flight restrictions
Administrator Bedford,
The FAA should not create a process that allows industrial animal facilities or
slaughterhouses to shield their operations from public view.
Americans have a right to know how their food is produced, especially when large
Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations (CAFOs) and slaughterhouses can impact
nearby communities, air, water, and public health.
Drone footage is an important tool for transparency. It gives journalists and nearby
residents a safe, lawful way to document the scale and impacts of these large industrial
facilities, including animal welfare conditions, environmental pollution, and whether
facilities are complying with the law. This information helps hold both industry and
government accountable. Restricting lawful drone access would make it harder for the
public to understand what is happening at these facilities.
I urge the FAA not to create a process that allows industrial animal facilities or
slaughterhouses to block lawful drone flights over their operations. Please protect the
public's right to transparency and accountability.
Sincerely,

Re: Exclude CAFOs and slaughterhouses from eligibility for drone flight restrictions
Administrator Bedford,
The FAA should not create a process that allows industrial animal facilities or
slaughterhouses to shield their operations from public view. Americans have a right to
know how their food is produced, especially when large Concentrated Animal Feeding
Operations (CAFOs) and slaughterhouses can impact nearby communities, air, water, and
public health. Drone footage is an important tool for transparency. It gives journalists and
nearby residents a safe, lawful way to document the scale and impacts of these large
industrial facilities, including animal welfare conditions, environmental pollution, and
whether facilities are complying with the law. This information helps hold both industry and
government accountable. Restricting lawful drone access would make it harder for the
public to understand what is happening at these facilities. I urge the FAA not to create a
process that allows industrial animal facilities or slaughterhouses to block lawful drone
flights over their operations. Please protect the public's right to transparency and
accountability. Thank you
Sincerely,
Julie Carll
Chambersburg, PA 172028053

drone use can help document land use, infrastructure, environmental conditions, and
other matters of legitimate public concern while operating within existing federal aviation
regulations.Large industrial livestock and food processing facilities can have significant

carefully balanced against the public's interest in transparency and access to information.I

comments.commenter: Comment from National Association of State Aviation Officials (NASAO)
comments.organization: National Association of State Aviation Officials (NASAO)
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
The Honorable Bryan Bedford
Administrator
Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue, SW
Washington, DC 20591
RE: Comments on FAA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking – Designation—Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility (Docket No. FAA–2026-4558)
Dear Administrator Bedford:
On behalf of the National Association of State Aviation Officials (NASAO), I appreciate the opportunity
to share these comments to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in response to the Request for
Comments to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) on Designation—Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility (Docket No. FAA–2026-4558).
NASAO is the nationally recognized voice for the public interest in aviation on behalf of the states and
territories. NASAO represents state government aviation agencies of all 50 states, Guam, and Puerto
Rico, who, as part of their many responsibilities, make decisions on funding aviation systems and airport
infrastructure at our nation's more than 3,300 public-use airports.
NASAO supports the FAA’s efforts to implement Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and
Security Act of 2016 and establish a national framework governing unmanned aircraft system (UAS)
operations near fixed site facilities. NASAO appreciates that this framework avoids the creation of broad
privately controlled flight restrictions while providing a defined pathway for critical infrastructure owners
and operators with legitimate security concerns.
While NASAO supports this framework, we urge the FAA to ensure that its implementation does not
impede state government aviation agencies from conducting legitimate public missions. State government
aviation agencies regularly perform operations that serve the public interest, including emergency
response, disaster recovery, infrastructure inspection and assessment, surveying and mapping, traffic
monitoring, and construction monitoring. Many of these missions are time-sensitive and require UAS
operations. Notification requirements that may work in routine operational contexts may not be workable
during urgent infrastructure events where immediate response is critical.
For these reasons, NASAO urges the FAA to provide meaningful flexibility for state government aviation
agencies conducting legitimate public missions. This should include ensuring that any requirement to
transition or transit in the shortest amount of time practicable does not impede these operations. NASAO
also encourages the FAA to clarify that a Standard Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (UAFR) does
not prohibit a state-owned or state-operated transportation infrastructure owner from conducting
compliant UAS operations necessary to inspect, maintain, or operate that infrastructure, and the
National Association of State Aviation Officials

(202) 925-1337 • www.nasao.org

established state government operators have a workable pathway to access Standard UAFR airspace while
appropriate security protections are maintained.
NASAO appreciates the continued engagement and longstanding partnership with the FAA. Thank you
for your consideration of NASAO’s comments and I encourage the FAA to carefully consider the input
submitted by the individual states. Please do not hesitate to reach out to me or Jessica Nagasako

comments.commenter: Comment from Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International (AUVSI)
comments.organization: Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International (AUVSI)
comments.comment_text:
AUVSI Comment on Proposed Rule: Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions Near Fixed Site
Facilities
Docket: FAA-2026-4558 | Notice No.: 26-03 | RIN: 2120-AL33 Citation: 91 Fed. Reg. 24650
(May 6, 2026) Submitted by: Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International
(AUVSI)
AUVSI | 3100 Clarendon Blvd., Suite 1200 | Arlington, VA 22201

Executive Summary
AUVSI supports FAA's effort to establish a single federal framework for facility-based drone
restrictions under Section 2209. Security and access are not in conflict: the proposed rule
can protect genuinely critical infrastructure while preserving workable access for
certificated commercial operators, but only if several provisions are tightened in the final
rule. The recommendations below track the order of the comment and identify where
regulatory text, not preamble language, is needed.
AUVSI's principal recommendations are:
1. Make the operator access carve-out operationally real (Section II). Codify in the
regulatory text of § 74.250 that notification is situational awareness only and that facility
managers may not approve, deny, or condition compliant access; confirm that eligibility
turns on documented vulnerability rather than drone-traffic volume; and add an explicit
access provision for non-transitory operations, with conditions defined separately from the
§ 74.255 transit notification requirement.
2. Leverage existing digital infrastructure (Section III.D), including ASTM F3411 Remote ID,
