I. Introduction and Organizational Interest
AUVSI is the world's largest nonprofit association dedicated to advancing uncrewed
systems, autonomy, and robotics. AUVSI's membership spans thousands of organizations
across the full UAS ecosystem: commercial operators, manufacturers, technology service
providers, public safety agencies, agricultural operators, infrastructure inspection firms,
and advanced air mobility developers.
Members of AUVSI operate near critical infrastructure facilities routinely and at scale. They
conduct utility inspection, pipeline monitoring, precision agriculture, emergency response,
infrastructure survey, and commercial delivery missions, many of which require repeated
access to the same geographic areas as facilities eligible for designation under this
proposed rule.
AUVSI has supported Section 2209 implementation since the statute's enactment in 2016
and has engaged FAA at each stage of this rulemaking. A well-designed Part 74 framework
can replace the current patchwork of state, local, and facility-level airspace restrictions
with a clear, uniform federal standard that serves both the security objective Congress
directed and FAA's statutory mandate to integrate UAS into the National Airspace System
(NAS). AUVSI's comment reflects the operational experience of its membership and is
organized to give FAA specific, actionable positions and, where appropriate, proposed
regulatory text updates.
AUVSI's overarching position is that security and access are not in conflict. The proposed
framework can protect genuinely critical infrastructure while preserving meaningful access
pathways for certificated commercial operators, provided FAA codifies the right structural
safeguards. Every recommendation in this comment flows from that framing, grounded in
FAA's dual mandate under Section 2209, Executive Order 14305 (“Restoring American
Airspace Sovereignty,” June 6, 2025), and Executive Order 14307 (“Unleashing American
Drone Dominance,” June 6, 2025).
AUVSI | 3100 Clarendon Blvd., Suite 1200 | Arlington, VA 22201

AUVSI commends FAA for two foundational principles expressed in the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking (NPRM) that should carry through to the final rule: that a UAFR is a tool of last
resort, and that facility managers have no authority to approve, deny, or restrict compliant
operator access. AUVSI's recommendations are designed to ensure these principles are
enforceable in the regulatory text, not left to preamble interpretation alone.
A third principle follows from the first two and should be made equally explicit: a UAFR
establishes a legal boundary; it does not itself detect, identify, track, assess, or respond to
unauthorized aircraft. The security value of a UAFR depends entirely on the detection and
response infrastructure surrounding it, infrastructure the rule does not create and whose
absence the rule cannot cure. This distinction is consequential for how FAA and facility
applicants should understand what a UAFR accomplishes. Designation is not a security
solution; it is a legal predicate for one. AUVSI urges FAA to acknowledge this limitation in
the final rule preamble so that facility applicants do not treat UAFR designation as a
substitute for investing in appropriate and legal detection and response capability, and so
that the scope of designations is calibrated to what the legal boundary can actually achieve
rather than to a security outcome the rule has no mechanism to deliver.
II. The Operator Access Carve-Out Must Be Operationally Real
Proposed § 74.250
A. Notification Is Situational Awareness, Not Permission: Codify It
The proposed rule creates an access pathway for certificated operators under § 74.250,
conditioned on Remote ID broadcast and advance notification under § 74.255. FAA states
in the preamble that facility managers have no authority to approve, deny, or restrict
compliant access and that notification is for situational awareness only. AUVSI supports
this framework and urges FAA to codify it in the regulatory text.
Preamble-only protections will not hold in practice. Without it, a Part 107 operator notifies a
facility security desk and receives a response purporting to deny or condition access, there
would be no regulatory text to point to. The operator would face compliance uncertainty
that preamble language cannot resolve at the field level. FAA should add language to §
74.255 stating explicitly that receipt of notification does not confer on a facility manager
any authority to approve or deny compliant operations, and that FAA retains sole
enforcement authority over UAFR access. In addition, a manual process imposes a similar
burden on facility managers, who would also benefit from a more efficient, automated
notification procedure. The case for codification runs in both directions, not just the
operator's. This mirrors the pre-LAANC practice of drone operators calling airport towers
directly for airspace access: a manual process that did not scale and that FAA ultimately
replaced with automation.

The NPRM's requirement that a llowed operators transit a Standard UAFR “in the shortest
practicable time” raises the question of whether hovering or non-transitory operations are
permitted within a UAFR. FAA invited comment on the scope of § 74.250's allowed
operations category. AUVSI urges FAA to clarify in the final rule that individual UAFR
designations may not impose facility-defined operational constraints, including restrictions
on hovering or landing, beyond those established by Part 74 itself.
B. Vulnerability, Not Activity Volume, Is the Eligibility Standard
FAA has stated that documented vulnerability to debilitating disruption, not drone traffic
volume near a facility, is the gating variable for UAFR eligibility. AUVSI asks FAA to make this
explicit in the regulatory text and to provide clear guidance that applicants may not use
observed drone activity, including safe and authorized commercial operations, as evidence
of a threat warranting a UAFR. FAA should also clarify that the routine presence of small
commercial UAS performing mapping, inspection, surveying, or documentation work near a
facility is not, without more, evidence of a security threat and should not weigh in favor of
designation.
The NPRM confirms that the Administrator retains final authority to deny a UAFR even
where a facility meets all eligibility criteria. At 91 Fed. Reg. 24652, the preamble states that
the Administrator “retains final authority to determine whether to approve, deny, or cancel”
any UAFR, and at 91 Fed. Reg. 24653 describes airspace restriction as “a remedy to be
applied only when necessary” to be weighed against FAA's broader statutory mandates.
AUVSI urges FAA to give this authority operational content in the final rule. The NPRM
identifies no factors that would guide denial where an applicant clears the eligibility
threshold. Without that guidance, facility applicants will treat eligibility as entitlement. FAA
should list in the final rule the circumstances that support denial of an otherwise eligible
application, such as disproportionate impact on NAS access, availability of non-airspace
security alternatives, or aggregate UAFR density. Articulating those factors now is what
transforms the last-resort standard from text into practice.
C. Non-Transitory Operations Require Explicit Protection
The “shortest practicable time” standard in § 74.250(a)(2) was written for transiting
operations. It does not accommodate infrastructure inspection, agricultural survey, law
enforcement support, or other missions requiring sustained presence inside a UAFR. FAA
has acknowledged this gap and is soliciting comment on whether the current language is
adequate. See 91 Fed. Reg. 24677 (May 6, 2026).
AUVSI submits that it is not. Inspection of a transmission line running through a UAFR,
survey of water treatment infrastructure, precision agricultural survey, construction
progress documentation, roof or facade inspection, drone-as-first-responder operations in
response to an incident at an eligible facility, and other recurring mapping or inspection

missions all require dwell time , repeated passes, or hovering that cannot be characterized
as a transitory pass. FAA should add a separate access provision for authorized non-
transitory operations, with conditions tied to the nature of the mission and the operator's
certificate authority rather than a transit-time standard that does not fit the use case.
At a minimum, the rule should direct FAA to define the specific conditions for this separate
non-transitory provision, tied to the nature of the mission, so that facility managers receive
equivalent situational awareness without expanding the transit notification obligations that
apply to the broader universe of point-to-point operations.
Further, FAA should clarify the transit language for point-to-point operations to prevent an
overly constraining interpretation that could be read to require the fastest speed and
shortest distance available. Language such as “transits the UAFR expeditiously” better
captures the intended standard than “shortest practicable time,” which invites exactly that
kind of operational minimization reading.
III. FAA Should Build a Scalable, Automated Notification Framework
Proposed § 74.255
A. Per-Flight, Manual Notification, Will Not Scale
The proposed § 74.255 notification requirement asks operators to submit flight-specific
information to a facility manager before each operation in a UAFR. For operators
conducting dozens or hundreds of daily flights across delivery routes, inspection corridors,
or first-responder deployments, this requirement is administratively unworkable at
commercial scale.
The burden falls on the wrong population. Compliant commercial operators using aircraft in
certificated operations are precisely the class the notification framework should
accommodate efficiently. Operators intent on evading detection are unlikely to be deterred
by a manual notification obligation, while compliant commercial operators will bear the full
administrative burden. A manual per-flight requirement imposes friction on safe operators
without providing incremental security benefit.
AUVSI does not oppose the notification concept. Giving facility managers situational
awareness of compliant operations near their sites is appropriate. The problem is the
mechanism. AUVSI urges FAA to build the notification requirement around scalable,
automated alternatives. The final rule should state that the notification pathway must be
automated, machine-readable, and predictable enough to support routine commercial
operations at scale. A requirement that exists on paper but cannot be exercised in practice
provides none of the situational awareness benefit FAA intends.
B. Remote ID Whitelisting Is the Right Long-Term Architecture
AUVSI | 3100 Clarendon Blvd., Suite 1200 | Arlington, VA 22201

FAA has solicited comment on the feasibility of Remote ID-based automated notification as
an alternative to per-flight submissions. See 91 Fed. Reg. 24678 (May 6, 2026). AUVSI
supports this direction and recommends that FAA commit to a whitelisting framework in
the final rule.
Under a whitelisting approach, an operator registers fleet serial numbers and certificate
credentials with FAA through a federal registry, drawing on FAA's existing authority to
establish UAS registration and identification systems. During operations, the aircraft's
Remote ID broadcast serves as automated notification. The facility receives continuous
situational awareness without per-flight interaction. FAA retains enforcement authority. The
operator's compliance burden is proportionate to the risk the operation actually poses.
A whitelist should be a complete substitute for per-flight notification under § 74.255, not a
supplement to it. Facility managers receive the situational awareness Congress intended.
Access is not contingent on facility manager action. AUVSI recommends that FAA treat this
framework as a final rule commitment, with implementation timelines to be developed
through supplemental guidance, rather than deferring the architecture question to a future
rulemaking.
FAA could condition whitelist eligibility on current aircraft registration, certificate authority,
Remote ID or approved equivalent identification capability, and an FAA-managed
revocation mechanism for operators that lose eligibility or violate access conditions.
Facility access to the system should be limited to status verification and operational
awareness necessary for the UAFR, without exposing unnecessary operator, customer,
route, or mission-sensitive data.
Critically, the whitelisting framework should be technology-neutral as to the mechanism
through which facility awareness is achieved, even as Remote ID broadcast remains the
primary and default compliance pathway. Situational awareness can be delivered through
Remote ID broadcast, ADS-B transponder data coordinated through flight plans, operation
intent data from flight management systems, or other lawful channels that provide facility
management with real-time operational awareness, provided each source meets the same
availability and reliability standard. Structuring the framework to accept multiple qualifying
inputs into a common awareness layer keeps the concrete, implementable ask, Remote ID
whitelisting, intact as FAA's default answer, while avoiding a rule that becomes obsolete as
identification and communication technology evolves.
The data standard for what satisfies notification must also be clear. ASTM F3411 defines
the Remote ID message set, including both broadcast Remote ID and network-based
Remote ID, that provides aircraft identification and position data in real or near-real time.
Remote ID broadcast, or network-based Remote ID where elected, is the appropriate data
layer for UAFR notification: it gives facility managers situational awareness of compliant
operations near their site with no exposure of strategic planning data. FAA should state in

the final rule that compliance with Part 89 Remote ID broadcast requirements, including
network-based Remote ID as provided under § 89.305, satisfies the § 74.255 notification
requirement for Standard UAFR operations, without requiring separate strategic
deconfliction data as part of that showing.
C. A Standing Notification Provides a Near-Term Bridge
While whitelist infrastructure is developed, FAA should allow an interim alternative: a
standing notification covering an operator's defined operational service area, valid for a
fixed period such as 90 days. The operator registers once per cycle with its certificate
credentials and route area. Operations within that area during the period are covered. This
is operationally feasible now, consistent with FAA's situational awareness goal, and does
not require new infrastructure.

UTM operation intent data: Operation intent data already exchanged across the UTM

IV. UAFR Boundaries Must Be Right-Sized and Terms Must Include Accountability
Mechanisms
Proposed §§ 74.20, 74.58, 74.68, 74.100, 74.200
A. Lateral Boundaries Should Align with the Security Perimeter of the Critical Asset
A UAFR's lateral boundary should reflect the footprint of the critical asset, not the broader
property boundary of the facility seeking the designation. Large suburban properties
frequently include parking areas, buffer zones, and undeveloped land with no relationship
to the security rationale that justifies the UAFR. Restricting airspace over those areas is not
consistent with the last-resort standard or the vulnerability-based eligibility criteria in the
proposed rule.
AUVSI recommends that FAA require applicants to justify proposed boundaries with asset-
specific evidence, define the default lateral boundary as the immediate physical security
perimeter of the critical asset, and require documented, site-specific justification for any
extension beyond that perimeter.
Broadcast Remote ID, and where available network Remote ID, can give a facility
situational awareness over a wider area than the UAFR boundary itself. FAA should
recognize this in the final rule: a facility with adequate monitoring capability has reduced
justification for an expanded UAFR footprint, and the final rule should make clear that
airspace monitoring capacity is a relevant factor in assessing whether a requested lateral
boundary is the smallest practicable consistent with documented protection needs.
B. FAA Should Require a Cumulative Airspace Fragmentation Assessment
The individual UAFR approval process does not account for cumulative airspace impact.
Eligible facility types such as energy substations, water treatment plants, and healthcare
facilities can be densely clustered in suburban environments. A series of individually
justified UAFRs in a concentrated area can combine to create a contiguous restricted zone
AUVSI | 3100 Clarendon Blvd., Suite 1200 | Arlington, VA 22201

that blocks commercial delive ry routes, inspection corridors, or emergency response
paths, even if no single UAFR is overbroad standing alone.
AUVSI recommends that FAA amend § 74.100 to require a cumulative airspace
fragmentation assessment before any UAFR is approved in an area where other UAFRs exist
or are pending. The legal basis for this requirement rests on FAA's broad authority to
manage the national airspace system in the public interest under 49 U.S.C. § 40103(b),
which requires FAA to develop plans and policy for the use of navigable airspace. The APA
arbitrary-and-capricious standard independently supports considering cumulative effects
when individual approvals are made under a common framework. This assessment should
evaluate whether the proposed UAFR, in combination with existing or pending designations,
would produce a disproportionate restriction on NAS access relative to the security benefit
of the individual designation. To the extent FAA concludes it is not legally compelled to
weigh cumulative effects for individual airspace actions, AUVSI urges it to adopt the
assessment as a discretionary best practice within its authority to manage the national
airspace system, allowing the agency to capture the benefit of cumulative review without
having to resolve the scope of any mandatory duty.
C. The Five-Year Term Requires a Mid-Term Review Mechanism
The proposed five-year maximum term is a sound structural limit. However, five years
without a proactive interim check creates conditions for designations to persist after the
security rationale that supported them has lapsed. If a facility's annual activity logs show
no unauthorized drone incidents, or if a facility fails to submit its annual reports, FAA
should not have to wait for the five-year renewal cycle to address a stale designation.
AUVSI recommends that FAA add a mandatory two-year mid-term performance review to §
74.200, drawing on the annual operational reports already required under § 74.20(b) and
giving structure to the ongoing review the Administrator may already conduct under §
74.20(c). If annual reports reflect no unauthorized drone activity or are not filed, FAA should
have clear authority to initiate a show-cause proceeding to review the continued
justification for the designation, with notice to the facility manager and an opportunity to
respond before any provisional suspension takes effect. AUVSI also recommends that the
renewal process require the same evidentiary showing as initial designation, so the last-
resort standard is not eroded by a more lenient renewal threshold.
D. Operators Need Clear Publication Timelines and a Transition Grace Period
An operator cannot plan routes around restrictions that do not appear in the aeronautical
data sources they use. AUVSI recommends that the final rule establish a minimum lead
time between UAFR designation and enforcement effectiveness, that UAFRs be required to
appear in NOTAM systems before enforcement begins, and that FAA specify the update
latency standard for reflecting UAFR boundaries in aeronautical charts and EFBs.

existing airspace restriction patchwork to Part 74, during which operators acting in good-

V. Special UAFRs Must Stay Narrow, Federal Primacy Must Be Explicit, and Operators
Need a Challenge Mechanism
Proposed §§ 74.6, 74.68, 74.251
A. Special UAFRs Must Remain Narrow
The Special UAFR tier carries consequences substantially more severe than Standard
UAFRs: potential criminal liability under 49 U.S.C. § 46307, dual FAA and Department of
War access requirements, and designation as national defense airspace. These
consequences are appropriate for the narrow class of genuinely sensitive federal and
national security facilities for which they were designed.
AUVSI urges FAA to limit Special UAFR eligibility to sites with documented national security
threat assessments. AUVSI also urges FAA to require a fresh evaluation under the Part 74
standard before any existing 14 CFR 99.7 Special Security Instructions are carried forward
into the Special UAFR tier. See 91 Fed. Reg. 24651 (May 6, 2026). The NPRM proposes to
integrate only “appropriate” existing 99.7 SSIs into the Special UAFR framework, but does
not define what makes a legacy SSI appropriate for conversion. Carry-forward without a
fresh Part 74 vulnerability-based evaluation would import designations made under a
different standard and a different statutory authority, bypassing the eligibility criteria that
are the foundation of Part 74. The final rule should clarify that “appropriate” means
satisfaction of the Part 74 standard, and that no legacy 99.7 designation is grandfathered
into Special UAFR status without that evaluation.
B. Federal Primacy Must Be Explicit
FAA should state that Part 74 preempts state, local, tribal, territorial, or facility-level
requirements that purport to create, enforce, or condition UAS flight restrictions in
navigable airspace around covered critical infrastructure facilities outside the Part 74
framework. FAA's exclusive authority over the navigable airspace under 49 U.S.C. § 40103 is
well established, but state legislatures have repeatedly attempted to regulate drone access
near critical infrastructure in ways that conflict with that authority. Part 74 provides the
opportunity to replace that patchwork with a uniform federal standard limited to UAFR-type
airspace restrictions, but only if the preemptive effect is explicit in the regulatory text.
AUVSI asks FAA to include this preemption statement in the final rule, grounded in FAA's
exclusive airspace authority and reinforced by the administration's drone policy directives
under Executive Order 14305 (“Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty”) and Executive
Order 14307 (“Unleashing American Drone Dominance”). If FAA is not prepared to declare
AUVSI | 3100 Clarendon Blvd., Suite 1200 | Arlington, VA 22201

express preemption in the regu latory text, AUVSI urges it at a minimum to state affirmatively
that Part 74 occupies the field of UAFR-type airspace restrictions and reflects a strong
federal interest in a uniform national standard, language a cautious agency can adopt and
on which operators and courts can still rely.
This is not an untested step. AUVSI has worked for years with legislatures across the
country to align state drone regulation with FAA's exclusive airspace authority, and that
work has produced state-level recognition of federal preemption in multiple states,
consistent with the FAA's own guidance on this question. Mississippi's Uncrewed Aircraft
Systems' Rights and Authorities Act (Miss. S.B. 1246, signed into law March 2023) codifies
that ultimate authority over state airspace rests with the FAA and bars local ordinances that
regulate the ownership or operation of nonrecreational unmanned aircraft. South Dakota's
S.B. 169, signed into law in March 2024 after passing unanimously in the Senate and by a
wide margin in the House, similarly reaffirms FAA authority over air navigation and safety
and forecloses conflicting local regulation. Arizona's preemption statute, Ariz. Rev. Stat. §
13-3729, likewise bars municipalities from enacting ordinances regulating the ownership or
operation of unmanned aircraft. This state-level recognition of federal primacy tracks the
FAA's and DOT's own position: the FAA's State and Local Regulation of Unmanned Aircraft
Systems Fact Sheet, issued July 14, 2023 by the DOT General Counsel and FAA Chief
Counsel, affirms that state or local laws aimed at regulating aviation safety or airspace
efficiency are subject to federal preemption.
An explicit Part 74 preemption statement, limited to UAFR-type airspace restrictions, would
consolidate that progress into a single, durable federal standard rather than leaving it to
accrete state by state.

initiated changes; they do not address operator-initiated review. Filling that gap is what

D. FAA Should Address How Part 74 UAFRs Interact with Other Federal Agency Airspace
Regimes
The proposed rule does not address how a Part 74 UAFR designation interacts with
airspace restrictions already in place at facilities regulated by other federal agencies.
Nuclear power plants are subject to NRC drone security requirements under 10 C.F.R. Part
73. Dams and flood control infrastructure are managed by the Army Corps of Engineers
under authorities that may generate independent airspace equities. Certain facilities near
military installations may have existing Department of War equities relevant to Special
UAFR applications. No coordination mechanism between FAA and these agencies is
established in the proposed rule, and no guidance is provided on which agency's
requirements govern in the event of a conflict.
An operator near a nuclear facility that complies with Part 74 notification and access
requirements may face a separate and potentially inconsistent set of obligations under
NRC's drone security regime. AUVSI asks FAA to address, in the final rule or supplemental
guidance, how Part 74 UAFRs interact with existing airspace restrictions imposed or
coordinated by NRC, Army Corps of Engineers, and the Department of War, and which
regulatory framework governs where they conflict.

Water/Wastewater
Proposed §§ 74.90, 74.96
FAA has not finalized eligibility criteria for two of the sectors with the heaviest commercial

FAA has directly solicited comment to inform the development of both. See 91 Fed. Reg.
24670, 24673 (May 6, 2026). AUVSI urges FAA to build criteria grounded in demonstrated
vulnerability and regional or national consequence, not sector membership, property type,
or activity volume alone.
A. The Standard Should Be Demonstrated Vulnerability and Consequence, Not Category
Membership

An eligible facility should be on e whose disruption would cause debilitating harm to
regional or national food security, water supply, or public health at a scale that justifies
federal airspace restriction. The criteria should require applicants to demonstrate both that
the specific physical asset is genuinely susceptible to disruption by UAS and that disruption
of that asset would produce regional or national harm, not merely local operational
inconvenience.
Category membership alone should not establish eligibility. The universe of facilities within
these sectors is vast, and many are routine commercial environments where UAS
operations are beneficial, common, and low-risk. Criteria that default to sector
membership rather than demonstrated vulnerability will sweep in facilities that do not
warrant federal airspace restriction, creating UAFR environments in the same areas where
precision agriculture, crop survey, and infrastructure inspection missions occur daily
without incident. That risk is particularly acute here, because food/agriculture and
water/wastewater are also environments in which small commercial UAS routinely perform
beneficial, low-risk inspection, mapping, and survey work without incident, precisely the
kind of activity overly broad eligibility criteria would sweep in.
AUVSI also recommends that FAA require applicants to demonstrate that existing physical
and procedural security measures are insufficient before a UAFR is warranted, consistent
with the last-resort standard.
B. Food and Agriculture: Criteria Should Reflect Supply Chain Consequence and Asset-
Level Susceptibility
For § 74.90, AUVSI recommends that eligibility criteria focus on two questions: whether the
specific physical assets of the facility are genuinely susceptible to severe disruption by
UAS, and whether disruption of those assets would produce consequences at regional or
national scale.
General agricultural land, standard food processing operations, and facilities serving
primarily local markets do not meet that standard. Facilities that process, store, or
distribute food at a scale where disruption would affect regional or national supply chains,
and that have specific exposed physical vulnerabilities to UAS interference, are the
appropriate targets for designation.
C. Water and Wastewater: The Eligibility Standard Should Reflect Redundancy, Capacity,
and Interdependency

Out.

NRF passionately advocates for the people, brands, policies and ideas that help retail

In the NPRM, the FAA proposes a process for owners and operators of critical
infrastructure to request FAA-imposed drone flight restrictions, known as Unmanned Aircraft
Flight Restrictions (UAFRs), over their properties. Critically, it also proposes to allow a subset
of already highly regulated drone operators, including those flying under Part 135 and the future
Part 108 (“allowed operators”), to transit most areas protected by UAFRs by providing prior
notice, thus protecting such facilities from overflight by higher-risk drone operators while still
ensuring that needed airspace is available to “allowed operators” that provide important public
benefits and represent minimal or no risk to critical infrastructure.

NRF Supports the following areas of the NPRM –
Limit the lateral boundaries of a UAFR to a facility’s property lines.
NRF supports the proposal in § 74.58 to anchor UAFRs’ lateral boundaries to fixed-site

geographic boundaries, altitude parameters and activation schedules in a machine-readable
format via API and allow time for drone operators to comply with new restrictions.
Expiration of UAFR after five years unless renewed or canceled.
NRF supports the proposal in § 74.200 that UAFRs will expire after five years unless
renewed or the requestor cancels them in accordance with § 74.210. We also support the
proposal that would allow the FAA to terminate or modify UAFRs it deems no longer necessary

petition for modification or cancellation of an existing UAFR; under proposed § 74.215, only the

NRF has concerns with the following areas of the NPRM –
Lack of an express federal preemption statement in the Final Rule.
Unfortunately, the NPRM is silent on the issue of federal preemption. This is a significant
gap in the NPRM. Multiple states have enacted critical infrastructure overflight restrictions that
impose criminal penalties on drone operators regardless of FAA authorization, undermining the
certainty and public benefits that federal preemption provides other aviation sectors.
The NPRM’s preamble acknowledges that Congress enacted § 2209 to direct the FAA to
establish a restriction framework, not to ratify existing state approaches; state laws imposing
parallel restrictions on the same conduct should yield. Failure to address preemption in the Final

400 feet above a correctional facility. It contains no sunset clause, no exception for FAA-

implementation. The FAA should therefore include a clear statement in the regulatory text
declaring that Part 74 preempts state and local laws that restrict or prohibit unmanned aircraft

The TRC welcomes this statutorily-mandated rulemaking to protect fixed sites, including railroad

domestic and international security landscape continues to evolve, we applaud actions taken to
protect critical infrastructure, workers, supply chains, and the public. Rail yards certainly fall into
these categories. As we saw during the 2021 supply chain crisis, freight rail capacity is key to the
health of the American supply chain and by extension the entire American economy. Additionally,

The TRC’s primary concern with this rulemaking is ensuring that railroad employees can quickly

guess whether a drone operating above or near their work location is being operated by the railroad,
a contractor, a government agency, a member of the public, or a person intending to cause harm.

For this reason, the FAA should establish a secure verification system — we suggest a public record
of registered drone flights — through which railroad personnel, affected employees, emergency
responders, and appropriate government agencies can determine whether a drone operation within
a UAER has been approved. At a minimum, the system should identify the general location and
approved time of the operation, the identity or category of the authorized operator, and a point of
contact for reporting safety or security concerns. Planned drone operations conducted by a railroad,
contractor, government agency, or other authorized operator within an occupied work area must
comply with this reporting. Employees who observe drone activity should have a simple and im-
mediate means of determining whether the operation is authorized.

Further, the FAA should establish a simple, direct, and accessible reporting process through which
railroad employees, labor organizations, railroads, contractors, and members of the public may
report unauthorized or unsafe drone activity. Railroad employees should not be required to submit
these reports only through their employer or local supervisor. Employees and their designated rep-
resentatives should be permitted to report directly to the appropriate federal agency when a drone
creates a safety or security concern, interferes with railroad operations, enters an occupied work
area, or appears to be operating without authorization.

roadway workers, track inspectors, bridge workers, signal employees, mechanical employees,
cranes, roadway maintenance machines, moving trains, occupied equipment, energized electrical
systems, or other safety-critical work. Reports should also be accepted when drone activity dis-
tracts employees, interferes with a job briefing or established work zone, compromises an employ-
ee's ability to safely perform assigned duties, interferes with communications or visibility, causes

Mr. Bryan Bedford (3) August 5, 2026

work or train movements to be suspended, or creates concern that employees or railroad operations
are being improperly monitored.

The reporting form should allow the reporting party to provide the date, time, and location of the
incident, a description of the drone and its operation, available remote ID information, photographs
or video, and an explanation of how the activity affected employees, equipment, train movements,
inspections, maintenance activities, or other safety-critical operations. The form should also permit
labor organizations to submit reports on behalf of affected employees or to identify a pattern of
repeated unsafe drone activity at a particular facility or work location.

Each report should generate a confirmation or tracking number so the reporting party can verify
that the complaint was received and referred to the appropriate agency. The FAA should coordinate
with TSA, FRA, and local law enforcement, as appropriate, when a report involves railroad secu-
rity, employee safety, interference with railroad operations, or a possible violation of federal law.
Railroad employees and labor representatives who submit good-faith reports should not be subject
to retaliation for raising a legitimate safety or security concern.

In addition to meaningful enforcement penalties serving as a deterrent to unauthorized drone op-
erations, railroads must be prepared to respond rapidly when a drone creates a safety or security
concern. As part of this rulemaking, railroads and other qualifying fixed site owners should be
required to file a written drone safety, security, and incident response plan with the FAA and TSA,
as appropriate.

The plan should establish procedures for determining whether a drone is authorized, notifying
affected employees, suspending work or train movements when necessary, communicating with
the FAA, TSA, FRA, and local law enforcement, preserving available evidence, and determining
when operations may safely resume. The plan should also address loss of communication or con-
trol; flyaway events; crashes; battery fires; drones fouling track; and contact with electrical, signal,
bridge, or other railroad infrastructure.

Affected employees should receive appropriate training on the plan and should be permitted to
initiate the applicable reporting or emergency response procedures when an immediate safety or
security concern exists, including halting operations, without fear of retaliation. Railroad employ-
ees and their representatives should also be consulted in the development and periodic review of
plans that directly affect occupied work areas.

Finally, the TRC holds that authorization to operate an unmanned aircraft within a UAFR should
not be interpreted as authorization to replace inspections, observations, or other safety-critical du-
ties that are required by federal regulation or railroad operating rules to be performed by qualified
railroad employees. The FAA's approval of an unmanned aircraft operation should be limited to
the safe use of the national airspace and should not be construed as approval to substitute drone
technology for work that has historically been performed by railroad employees governed by the

Mr. Bryan Bedford (4) August 5, 2026

Federal Railroad Administration or other applicable federal requirements. The FAA should coor-
dinate with the FRA to ensure that implementation of this rule does not create uncertainty regard-
ing existing railroad safety regulations or the responsibilities of qualified railroad employees.

These reasonable requirements would significantly improve protections for railroad employees
and the public from both unauthorized drone activity and unsafe authorized operations. UAFRs
should protect critical infrastructure without creating privately controlled airspace in which rail-
roads may conduct drone operations without meaningful notice, accountability, worker protec-
tions, or federal oversight. We urge the FAA to include these safeguards in the final rule.

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this docket and look forward to working with the
FAA on this and other issues in the future.

Sincerely,

YEA £ Clu

Re: Comments on the FAA’s Proposed Rule: Designation - Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed-Site Facility, Docket No. FAA-
2026-4558
To Whom It May Concern:
The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers (AFPM) appreciates the opportunity to comment on
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA’s) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), “Designation -
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”1 implementing
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA), as amended.2
AFPM supports the FAA’s efforts to establish a regulatory framework to address unmanned aircraft
system (UAS) risks to critical infrastructure while maintaining the safe integration of UAS into the
National Airspace System (NAS). AFPM has long supported implementing FESSA Section 2209 and
recognizes the importance of a risk-informed and operationally practical process for establishing
unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (UAFRs). AFPM appreciates the FAA’s coordination with Sector
Risk Management Agencies (SRMAs), industry stakeholders, and security partners throughout
development of the Proposed Rule. AFPM’s efforts to secure critical infrastructure airspace date back to
FESSA 2016, when our advocacy led to the creation of the original Section 2209. AFPM has since had
extensive engagement with the FAA, Department of Homeland Security (DHS), National Security
Council (NSC), Congressional offices, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), congressional
offices, and other critical infrastructure stakeholders to support implementation of Section 2209.3
FAA’s Section 2209 framework marks an important first step toward protecting the airspace around
critical infrastructure, but it does not yet reflect the seriousness of the threat. For refineries, petrochemical
facilities, and connected energy infrastructure, an unauthorized drone is not a nuisance—it can present a
1 91 Fed. Reg. 24,560 (May 6, 2026).
2 FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209, 130 Stat. 615, 649–52 (2016), as amended by
FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Pub. L. No. 118-63 (2024).
3 AFPM has also partnered with other trade associations and coalitions, including the Chamber of Commerce, and other critical
infrastructure organizations. AFPM has also consistently discussed drone issues within the Chemical and Oil and Natural Gas
Sector Councils, encouraging DOE and DHS CISA to engage with FAA to promulgate regulations protecting our nation’s most
vital critical infrastructure sites. AFPM also was a member of the Critical Infrastructure Partnership Advisory Council (CIPAC)
Unmanned Aircraft Systems Security Working Group, assisting in the development and review of DHS drone detection response
guidance documents.
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 1

real safety, security, homeland security, and operational risk. The proposed rule creates a regulatory
framework to restrict airspace but still leaves facility operators largely dependent on calling local law
enforcement and waiting for a response after an unauthorized flyover has already occurred. That approach
creates, at best, a false sense of security. FAA should strengthen the final rule by adopting AFPM’s
suggestions and supporting Congressional efforts to provide critical infrastructure operators with more
effective, practical tools to prevent and respond to unauthorized UAS activity in restricted airspace,
including a pathway for appropriately authorized facility operators to prevent and respond to unauthorized
UAS activity in restricted airspace, including a pathway for appropriately authorized facility operators to
mitigate or intercept drones that unlawfully enter protected airspace.
AFPM believes several aspects of the Proposed Rule would benefit from additional clarification,
refinement, and operational flexibility to ensure the framework can be implemented effectively across the
energy, chemical, and petrochemical sectors. In particular, the final rule should reflect the scale,
complexity, and interconnected nature of critical infrastructure operations while avoiding unintended
impacts to lawful UAS operations. AFPM’s comments are intended to support a practical implementation
approach that strengthens aviation safety, national security, and protection of people and property without
creating unnecessary regulatory burden or operational uncertainty for critical infrastructure owners and
operators.
Section 2209 was enacted to provide a practical pathway for fixed-site critical infrastructure facilities to
obtain UAS flight restrictions where drone operations present safety, security, homeland security, or
national security risks. The FAA’s final rule should therefore avoid rigid eligibility screens or application
requirements that prevent vital energy, refining, petrochemical, and connected storage and transportation
assets from seeking protection. AFPM’s recommendations are intended to make the rule implementable,
protective, and flexible enough to reflect real-world industrial risk.
I. Executive Summary of Principal Recommendations
AFPM strongly supports the FAA’s effort to implement Section 2209 of FESSA and establish a practical
framework for restricting UAS operations near critical infrastructure. However, several elements of the
proposal should be revised to ensure the program is risk-informed, operationally practical, protective of
sensitive information, and accessible to facilities that face legitimate UAS-related threats. Our principal
recommendations are as follows:
A. Expand eligibility through a risk-informed approach and pre-existing security
programs
FAA’s use of rigid eligibility thresholds in the energy and chemical sectors would exclude facilities that
are vulnerable to significant safety, security, economic, and national security risks from UAS. AFPM
recommends that FAA remove the categorical throughput and production thresholds, include connected
facilities (e.g., terminals, LNG facilities, tank farms, marine docks, rail loading areas, and pipeline assets),
and establish a case-by-case eligibility pathway so all at-risk energy sites can demonstrate UAS related
risk and consequence. For the chemical sector, Appendix A may be an appropriate filter but should not
be the exclusive gateway to eligibility. FAA should additionally leverage existing security programs and
directives to expedite facility eligibility and UAFR determinations – without duplicative application
burdens.
B. Create clear and flexible pathways for special UAFRs
AFPM supports the proposed special UAFR framework, but eligibility and review procedures remain
unclear. FAA should provide high-consequence private sector facilities with clear qualification criteria
and clarity on how sponsorships are maintained for “special” UAFRs. AFPM believes refineries and
petrochemical facilities should be strongly considered for special UAFR designation.
C. Refine Remote ID detection and data requirements
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 2

Remote ID sensing and detection technologies remain uneven in performance, range, cybersecurity, and
operational reliability. The FAA should not make existing Remote ID sensing capability a condition
precedent to UAFR approval. Instead, FAA should allow facilities to obtain UAFR approval based on
existing protective security measures and a reasonable post-designation implementation plan for Remote
ID sensing capability. The FAA should also clarify that the absence of 24 months of UAS detection data
is not, by itself, a basis for denying the application.
D. Ensure UAFR boundaries are protective
AFPM recommends that UAFR polygons cover the entirety of critical infrastructure facilities and that
sites have the option to expand outward to meet section 2209’s statutory mandate to create airspace
restrictions in “close proximity to” fixed site critical infrastructure – not directly above or within the
property boundary. Having the option to create a buffer will protect facilities from the safety and security
risks of UAS that may extend beyond the facility boundary. AFPM additionally recommends flyovers be
increasingly restricted for UAFRs with unique risks that regular flights would exacerbate (e.g.,
turnarounds, equipment blowdowns).
E. Reduce administrative and application burdens for all stakeholders
FAA should limit unnecessary compliance and application burdens to streamline protections for critical
infrastructure. This includes limiting the environmental review and externalities requirements and
allowing FAA and public experts to provide input through internal review and public comment.
F. Protect sensitive security and operational information
UAFR applications may require disclosure of highly sensitive facility information. FAA should provide
strong protections for confidential business information, security-sensitive information, vulnerability
assessments, and operational data, while limiting the amount of detailed security information required
from applications.
Please view Section VI for the full set of AFPM recommendations.
II. The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers
The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers4 is a national trade association representing U.S.
manufacturers of transportation fuels, petrochemicals, and midstream energy products. AFPM’s members
produce the vast majority of the nation’s gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, heating oil, and petrochemicals that are
necessary for all sectors of the U.S. economy and a vital part of our nation’s critical infrastructure. The
organization serves as a leading voice for the refining and petrochemical sectors on issues involving
energy security, economic growth, manufacturing competitiveness, safety, and environmental
stewardship.
Congress deliberately ensured that oil refineries and chemical facilities are not just included in Section
2209, but are treated as high-risk, priority critical infrastructure when FAA evaluates whether to grant
drone flight restrictions.5 Therefore, protecting those facilities from unauthorized or unsafe UAS
operations is directly tied to security, emergency preparedness, supply chain resilience, worker safety and
energy and petrochemical production.
III. Statutory Background
4 American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers - https://www.afpm.org/about-us/about-us
5 FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209(c), 130 Stat. 615, 633 (2016) (identifying
factors the FAA must consider when evaluating requests for UAS facility restrictions).
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 3

Before Section 2209, the FAA had broad authority over U.S. airspace but lacked a standardized
mechanism for operators of critical infrastructure and other sensitive fixed-site facilities to obtain
standing, facility-specific protections from UAS operations.6 Congress enacted Section 2209 to fill that
gap, recognizing that emerging UAS operations presented distinct safety, security, and infrastructure-
protection concerns not fully addressed by existing airspace tools.7 Section 2209 supplements the FAA's
existing authority under 49 U.S.C. § 40103 by directing the FAA to establish a process through which
eligible fixed-site facilities may request restrictions on UAS operations in close proximity to those
facilities for aviation safety, protection of people and property, national security, or homeland security
purposes.8 The NPRM implements that directive through a new Part 74 framework governing UAFRs for
qualifying critical infrastructure facilities.9 Accordingly, the proposed rule should be evaluated against
Section 2209's core purpose: providing a clear and administrable process to protect qualifying facilities
from persistent UAS-related risks while preserving the safe and efficient use of the National Airspace
System.
IV. Importance of Restricting UAS over Critical Infrastructure
The threats from unauthorized drone flights over refineries and petrochemical sites are real. Critical
infrastructure facilities face an evolving range of risks associated with UAS, including surveillance,
operational disruption, cyber-enabled threats, contraband delivery, and potential physical, weaponized
attacks against sensitive systems and assets. As UAS technology becomes increasingly accessible,
capable, and widely adopted, owners and operators of critical infrastructure require practical tools to help
manage risks to staff, assets, intellectual property, and operations. There has been a steady increase of
unauthorized drone flights above our member sites, with one-third of facilities reporting an increase in
UAS overflights over their airspace in the last year according to a recent critical infrastructure industry
survey.10 These unauthorized and potentially dangerous flights have grown from isolated small-drone
incidents to larger and more coordinated flights involving aircraft hovering near process units, storage
areas, and other sensitive operational assets. These operations create safety risks if a UAS loses control
from unintended interference, collides with equipment, drops a payload, or distracts facility personnel
during operations. Recent overseas conflicts have demonstrated that UAS can be used to surveil, disrupt,
and attack energy and industrial infrastructure, reinforming the need for a protective domestic framework
before a serios incident occurs. AFPM recognizes that no regulation, standing alone, will deter a
determined malicious actor. But UAFRs will deter careless and reckless operators, provide law
enforcement and prosecutors with a clear legal basis to act against violators, and allow facility security
personnel to distinguish authorized operations from suspicious activity. Regulations implementing
Section 2209 must be finalized quickly so government and the private sector are not forced to react after a
potentially tragic event.
Restricting unauthorized UAS operations over certain high-risk fixed-site facilities can provide an
important layer within a broader, risk-informed security framework. Properly implemented UAFRs can
help reduce inadvertent overflight of sensitive locations, improve situational awareness for facility
6 49 U.S.C. § 40103(a)–(b).
7 FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209, 130 Stat. 615, 634; Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed-Site Facility, 91 Fed. Reg. 24,650, 24,651 (May 6, 2026).
8 Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed-Site Facility, 91 Fed. Reg. 24,650,
24,651-2.
9 Id., 91 Fed. Reg. 24,653-54.
10 This survey was conducted in June 2026 in partnership with 14 energy and chemical trade associations. 33 companies
representing 3,560 facilites responded.
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 4

security personnel and law enforcement, and better distinguish lawful operations from potentially
suspicious or unauthorized activity.
At the same time, any UAFR framework should remain practical, risk-informed, and appropriately
tailored to the operational realities of critical infrastructure environments. The process for establishing
and managing UAFRs should strengthen security while also ensuring facility owners and operators can
continue to safely and efficiently conduct lawful UAS operations in support of inspection, maintenance,
emergency response, safety, environmental monitoring, and operational continuity activities. The final
framework should provide clear, predictable, and operationally achievable requirements that enhance
security without creating unnecessary administrative burden or limiting the ability of critical
infrastructure operators to leverage UAS technologies to support safe, reliable, and resilient operations.
A. Importance to AFPM Member Facilities
Refineries, chemical manufacturers, and midstream facilities face increasing risks from unauthorized
UAS activity, creating clear demand for Section 2209 protections. Incursions from UAS overflights
consistently pose a threat to the safety and security in and around a facility’s fenceline, whether
intentional or unintentional. Within the preamble itself,11 the FAA’s NPRM cites a 2015 UAS crash near
a New Jersey refinery and a 2022 FBI warning regarding potential terrorist attacks using UAS against
Louisiana chemical facilities and pipelines.12
The risk environment has grown substantially since those incidents. Between 2016 and 2024, the
recreational UAS fleets increased from approximately 1.1 million to 1.87 million aircraft – a 70%
increase,13 while the commercial fleet grew from ~42,000 to ~960,000 aircraft during the same
timeframe.14
Refineries, chemical manufacturers, and midstream facilities today are seeing a vast increase in
suspicious and reckless fly-overs using advanced operations that increase onsite risk. About 80% of
facilities have reported flyovers, and with a third of all respondents reporting increasing incursions.
Recent attacks against refineries and other energy infrastructure in the ongoing Russia–Ukraine conflict
further demonstrate the potential consequences of malicious UAS operations.15 While those incidents
occurred overseas, they underscore the importance of implementing Section 2209 in a manner that
provides a clear, practical, and risk-based pathway for refineries and other critical infrastructure sites to
obtain appropriate UAS protections consistent with congressional intent. The proposed designation of
restricted airspace over critical infrastructure is a necessary first step, but without the ability of the facility
to take action, this first step will ultimately fail to comprehensively protect our nation’s vital facilities..
B. Local Security Event, Cascading Damages
The FAA should consider not only the direct impacts of a UAS incident on a single facility, but also the
broader consequences for interconnected fuel and chemical supply chains. As the FAA recognizes, energy
infrastructure operates through a highly integrated network of refineries, pipelines, terminals,
11 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 24,655 (May 6, 2026).
12 Id.; “Drone Crashes Into Truck Outside New Jersey Oil Refinery,” CDL Life, November 20, 2015. Accessed July
7, 2026, at http://www.cdllife.com/2015/drone-crashes-into-truck-outside-new-jersey-oil-refinery/. [5]
https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/30/europe/russia-tuapse-oil-refinery-strikes-pollution-intl-cmd.
13 Compendium to FAA Aerospace Forecast Fiscal Years 2025–2045: Emerging Aviation Entrants—Unmanned Aircraft Systems
and Advanced Air Mobility, Federal Aviation Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation (2025),
https://www.faa.gov/data_research/aviation/aerospace_forecasts/2025-uas-and-aam-full-document.pdf.
14 Id.
15 https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/30/europe/russia-tuapse-oil-refinery-strikes-pollution-intl-cmd
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 5

transportation assets, and end users, meaning disruptions at a single facility can have effects far beyond
the facility fence line.16
U.S. refiners and associated terminals are also critical suppliers to the U.S. military supporting substantial
deliveries of military fuels. 17 Specific to the Navy, more than 800 million gallons of avjet and 100
million gallons of navy-spec fuel were awarded in contracts in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.18
FAA’s energy and chemical sector overview did not assess the impact of possible refinery interruptions
on military operations and readiness. Impacts to the fuel supply line can drastically reduce the readiness
of U.S. military operations. Instead, FAA focuses on a specific aspect of military operations, defense
industrial base sectors for contractors and subcontractors, choosing to only restrict those airspaces.
In the sector overview, FAA states “The [defense industrial base] sector provides products and services
that are essential to mobilize, deploy, and sustain military operations.”19 It is undeniable that both energy
and chemical sectors provide products “essential to mobilize, deploy, and sustain military operations” and
as such, should see FAA prioritization.
C. Executive Orders on Airspace Sovereignty, Drone Dominance, and American
Energy
On June 6, 2025, the Administration issued two landmark UAS executive orders that together affirm the
importance of protecting critical infrastructure while maintaining a competitive UAS economy: Restoring
American Airspace Sovereignty and Unleashing American Drone Dominance.20 Restoring American
Airspace Sovereignty recognizes that “criminals, terrorists, and hostile foreign actors” are weaponizing
UAS against critical infrastructure, while Unleashing American Drone Dominance seeks to make the
United States the global leader in drone technology by streamlining regulations, expanding drone
operations, and promoting the development and deployment of American-made drones. Together, these
policies support targeted protections for high-consequence facilities while creating controlled
environments in which legitimate UAS can safely operate.
Likewise, Executive Order 14,154, Unleashing American Energy, which establishes national interest in
affordable and reliable energy to rebuild the nation’s economic and military security.21 Section 2(c) of the
action specifically states that it is the policy of the United States “to protect the United States’s economic
and national security and military preparedness by ensuring that an abundant supply of reliable
energy is readily accessible in every State and territory of the Nation.”22 Achieving the Administration’s
goal of fully unleashing American energy requires recognizing that reliability, accessibility, and security
are inherently linked, and that providing Section 2209 UAFRs to refining and chemical facilities supports
the continuous and dependable delivery of energy to communities across the United States. FAA should
weigh the President’s objectives on energy prosperity when reviewing related facility UAFR applications.
Fewer UAS incursions equate to fewer operational challenges and therefore increased energy reliability.
Providing Section 2209 protections to refining and chemical facilities is consistent with that objective
16 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 24,669 (May 6, 2026).
17 U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Military Jet Fuel Kerosene-Type Net Deliveries to U.S. Military Consumers by
Prime Supplier, California (Series ID: KD0VMIR501), Petroleum & Other Liquids Data, accessed July 14, 2026,
18 Defense Logistics Agency (DLA), “DLA Energy Awards Fiscal 2020 Fuel Contracts During COVID-19,” August 11,
2020, https://www.dla.mil/About-DLA/News/News-Article-View/Article/2314515/dla-energy-awards-fiscal-2020-fuel-contracts-
during-covid-19/.
19 See 91 Fed. Reg. at 24,650 (May 6, 2026).
20 https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/06/restoring-american-airspace-sovereignty/ and Unleashing American
Drone Dominance – The White House
21 https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/unleashing-american-energy/
22 Exec. Order No. 14,154, § 2(c), Unleashing American Energy (Jan. 20, 2025).
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 6

because it helps reduce safety and security risks at facilities that support critical energy, manufacturing,
and defense supply chains.23
V. Key Areas of Support
A. Establishing a Section 2209 Implementation Framework
AFPM fully supports FAA’s effort to satisfy the Administration’s Executive Order 14305, Restoring
American Airspace Sovereignty, and Congress’s Section 2209 of FESSA 2016 in establishing a workable
regulatory framework for implementing restricted airspaces in close proximity to fixed site critical
infrastructure. In creating a final rule that is clear, administrable, and risk-informed, FAA can successfully
address UAS-related risks to critical facilities, while also supporting the continued safe integration of
UAS and future technologies into the NAS.
Comprehensive critical infrastructure protection from UAS requires a holistic approach, beginning with
pilot education about hazardous facility airspaces, legally protecting those airspaces, UAS mitigation in
the event of a criminal act through law enforcement or owner/operator, and everything in between. Part
74 UAFRs provide a key piece in this complex FAA initiative. By creating a legal barrier around eligible
facilities, owners and operators will have a clear indicator of whether the UAS flight is a legal or criminal
act and then decide how to act in compliance with current mitigation authorities. Part 74 UAFRs may also
be a selection criterion in future mitigation authorities, so it’s essential that all facilities who need this
option be eligible to receive coverage.
In addition to future mitigation coverage, AFPM supports an implementation framework that creates
expanded opportunities within protected industrial airspaces. UAFRs will have the benefit of establishing
controlled operating environments that serve as hot spots for facility-led BVLOS flights, dock-based
operations, autonomous monitoring programs, and AI-assisted inspection and security surveillance. These
future possibilities will flourish from reduced third-party traffic, improved operator identification,
enhanced situational awareness, and greater operational certainty. Delivering UAFRs into the NAS will
deliver clear and measurable benefits to all stakeholders and the FAA.
B. Risk-Informed Protection of High-Consequence Fixed Site Facilities
AFPM supports FAA’s goal to protect specific high-risk facilities where unauthorized UAS may create
safety, security, environmental, operational, or cascading infrastructure concerns. FAA’s definition of
critical infrastructure adheres to this goal by using the 42 U.S.C. 5195c(e) definition when selecting
facilities for UAFRs:
“Systems and assets, whether physical or virtual, so vital to the United States that the incapacity
or destruction of such systems and assets would have a debilitating effect on security, national
economic security, national public health or safety, or any combination of those matters.”
The final rule and implementation should preserve FAA oversight in designation, while allowing
eligibility and implementation decisions to account for facility-specific vulnerabilities, consequences, and
operational realities.
The proposal’s inclusion of “special” UAFRs (SUAFRs) is a promising advancement in risk-informed
protections. Entities with credible safety and security threats where operational integrity can be
compromised are able to receive significant airspace restrictions through partnership with security and
intelligence agencies. AFPM supports this special airspace and is enthusiastic about member sites being
considered for these designations.
23 Id., Exec. Order No. 14,154, § 2(c).
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 7

C. Coordination with SRMAs, Security Partners, and Industry Stakeholders
AFPM appreciates FAA’s coordination with Sector Risk Management Agencies (SRMAs) during the
development of this proposal and believes that continued coordination is essential to ensure that a final
rule matches the risks critical infrastructure faces. Partnerships with security experts and industry
stakeholders are crucial in finalizing Part 74. These groups, throughout the comment process and
implementation period, can assist in protecting sensitive information, minimize unintended impact to
lawful UAS operations, and find a balance that is practical for complex industry facilities to comply with.
AFPM notes that it is imperative that FAA conducts outreach to all sectors of critical infrastructure and
UAS operators so that there is little confusion on the final rule requirements and application processes.
D. Transparency with Critical Infrastructure
In addition to communications through the rulemaking process, AFPM supports FAA’s efforts to
maintain transparency with owners and operators throughout the application process and active UAFR
time period. AFPM member security teams are heavily involved in protecting their facilities from UAS
threats, and continuous FAA communications can assist in timely application evaluations, effective
security assessments to UAS operations, and successful notification procedures per § 74.255 UAFR
Access Notification.
VI. Modifications Required to Enhance Critical Infrastructure Security and Resilience
As stated above, this proposal is an important step towards protecting critical infrastructure from drone
attacks; however, the proposal will not by itself accomplish Congress’s goal of hardening critical
infrastructure. That said, designation of no-fly zones is an important first step, and AFPM believes the
process of implementing that first step may be improved. AFPM presents the following modifications in
order of significance, beginning with the threshold question of eligibility, which determines whether a
critical infrastructure facility may seek Part 74 protection and proceeding through boundary, access,
information protection, and administrative issues.
A. Eligibility and Sector Coverage
1. General Eligibility (§ 74.54)
FAA proposes general eligibility based on fixed site facility status, critical infrastructure, sector-specific
criteria, protective security, vulnerable critical assets, and regional or national-level debilitating impact.
§ 2209 reflects Congress’s intent to permit refineries and petrochemical facilities to petition for a UAFR
designation. § 2209(a) provides that a “fixed-site facility” may submit such a petition, and Congress
expressly included oil refineries and chemical facilities within that term’s definition. 24 By specifically
identifying these facilities, Congress demonstrated that they should have a meaningful opportunity to seek
UAFR protections. Arbitrary eligibility thresholds based on facility output or other requirements that
prevent qualifying facilities from submitting a petition would therefore undermine the statutory design.
Such restrictions would not merely affect whether a designation is granted; they would limit the ability of
expressly identified facilities to apply in the first place.
AFPM stresses that rigid eligibility thresholds may not fully capture facility-specific risk, regional
consequence, supply-chain interdependence, or the operational realities of integrated energy, chemical,
and petrochemical assets. A case-by-case pathway would allow FAA and the applicable SRMA to
consider facilities that present significant vulnerability or consequence even when they do not fit neatly
24 § 2209(b)(1)(C)(ii)
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 8

within a numerical threshold. Additional locations that require consideration are terminals, tank storage
facilities, and LNG plants.
To encompass the full impacts of UAS risks to facilities, FAA should include a case-by-case pathway for
facilities that are not automatically eligibly through other considerations but who are able to demonstrate
risk, vulnerability, and consequence even if they do not meet a specific numerical threshold. This pathway
could be implemented through SRMA sponsorship of a standard or special UAFR.
Further AFPM feedback is detailed in sections VI.B Chemical Sector, § 74.81), VI.C (Energy Sector, §
74.88), and VI.D (Transportation Systems Sector, § 74.95) below.
2. Chemical Sector (§ 74.81)
The FAA proposes eligibility for facilities using, manufacturing, storing, transporting, possessing, or
distributing hazardous-release chemicals at or above minimum concentration percentages and screening
threshold quantities listed in Appendix A of the former Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards
(CFATS) program. Appendix A includes chemicals of interest, concentration thresholds, screening
quantities, and release categories adapted from 6 CFR Part 27 with FAA and SRMA modifications.
FAA should use Appendix A as a starting point, not a gatekeeper. Facilities that fall below a screening
threshold may still present significant UAS-related risk based on process conditions, storage
configurations, proximity to populations, critical supply-chain role, prior suspicious UAS activity, or
Lother consequence factors. Solely relying on the Appendix A list could create an inflexible and
potentially outdated eligibility screen that is not tailored to aviation safety, airspace management, or
UAS-related consequence analysis. Retaining the Appendix A framework could exclude high-
consequence facilities while requiring others to rely on chemical lists and thresholds developed for a
different regulatory purpose. For example, FAA should strongly consider sites that may have COIs below
the threshold level but documented numerous suspicious drone incursions. FAA should also strongly
consider offsite community-impact risks associated with high-consequence chemical operations and
releases, facility-specific information regarding hazardous materials, chemical inventories,
concentrations, process conditions, storage configurations, proximity to populations, and consequence
potential, even where the facility does not meet a specific Appendix A threshold.
AFPM strongly supports FAA's use of risk-based criteria to identify facilities eligible for UAFR
consideration. However, FAA should recognize that facilities subject to the Maritime Transportation
Security Act (MTSA) already have undergone a federal determination that they present security risks
warranting enhanced protective measures. Facilities regulated under MTSA are required to conduct
vulnerability assessments, implement access controls, maintain incident response procedures, and operate
under Coast Guard oversight through an approved Facility Security Plan (FSP) or Coast Guard-approved
Alternative Security Program (ASP). As a result, MTSA applicability is a significantly more reliable
indicator of security risk than arbitrary production, throughput, or chemical-threshold criteria.
FAA's proposal recognizes MTSA-regulated maritime facilities as eligible for UAFR consideration within
the Transportation Systems Sector. However, FAA has not adequately explained why MTSA-regulated
refineries, petrochemical facilities, LNG facilities, and waterfront chemical facilities, many of which
operate under the same federal maritime security framework, may be excluded based solely on throughput
thresholds or Appendix A screening criteria. These facilities face comparable security risks, are subject to
comparable federal security obligations, and often perform transportation, storage, transfer, and
distribution functions that are operationally integrated with the maritime transportation system.
Because MTSA-regulated facilities already have been identified by the federal government as requiring
heightened security measures to address significant security risks, FAA should treat MTSA status as
prima facie evidence that a facility warrants consideration under Section 2209. This approach would
ensure consistent treatment of similarly situated facilities, better align the rule with existing federal
security determinations, and allow FAA to evaluate facility-specific risk through the UAFR application
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 9

process rather than categorically excluding facilities based on thresholds that may not accurately reflect
consequence or vulnerability.
Proposed Revision
Appendix A may be used as an initial screening tool for determining whether a facility is eligible for
UAFR consideration.
Appendix A shall not serve as the exclusive basis for determining eligibility where an applicant
demonstrates that facility-specific hazards, materials, operations, concentrations, storage configurations,
or potential consequences warrant further review.
Where Appendix A includes criteria derived from prior Federal chemical security frameworks, including
the former Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards program, the Administrator shall recognize that
such criteria may no longer reflect current chemical security risks, facility operations, chemical uses,
concentrations, or threat conditions.
The Administrator may allow a facility that does not meet a specific Appendix A threshold to seek
eligibility through a risk-informed supplemental review.
In conducting such review, the Administrator may consider chemical types, quantities, concentrations,
process conditions, storage configurations, proximity to surrounding populations, potential off-site
consequences, critical supply chain functions, emerging industrial uses, or other safety, security,
environmental, operational, or public safety factors.
The Administrator shall coordinate with the applicable Sector Risk Management Agency, and where
appropriate affected industry stakeholders, when evaluating, updating, or supplementing Appendix A
criteria.
The Administrator may update Appendix A criteria, consistent with applicable law, to account for
changes in chemical risks, UAS technology, threat conditions, facility operations, industrial practices, or
national and homeland security considerations.
The Administrator shall deem a facility eligible to apply for a UAFR where the facility is regulated under
the Maritime Transportation Security Act (MTSA) and maintains an active Coast Guard-approved
Facility Security Plan (FSP) or is covered by a Commandant-approved Alternative Security Program
(ASP).
3. Energy Sector (§ 74.88)
FAA proposes eligibility for power-generation facilities, certain electrical substations, and specifically oil
refineries converting crude oil into petroleum product with capacity of 100,000 barrels per day or more,
and natural gas processing facilities meeting capacity criteria.
The proposed energy-sector criteria rely on high throughput thresholds, including 100,000 barrels per day
for petroleum facilities and 500 million cubic feet per day for natural gas facilities. The FAA's Regulatory
Impact Analysis, indicates that only 64 petroleum refineries would qualify for UAFR designation, despite
there being approximately 124 active refineries operating in the United States. This means that the
proposed threshold would exclude nearly half of the Nation’s refining sector from applicability before the
FAA conducts any facility-specific risk assessment.
Throughput is but one small part of a refineries security risk profile and is not an appropriate metric for
designating no-fly zones over refineries. A refinery or LNG facility below a proposed threshold may
handle hazardous, flammable, explosive, or high consequence materials; support regional fuel supply;
connect to critical pipeline, terminal, or marine operations; or operate near populated areas. A disruption
at a lower throughput facility may have serious consequences depending on the facility’s function,
location, interdependencies, and consequence profile. For example, three refinery examples are listed

below that have a refining capacity well below the 100,000 bpd threshold, yet each of the facilities are
essential to the local economy based on the proximity and specialized product they produce.
• Example 1, approximately 60,000 bpd– Produces high-value specialty products including
lubricating base oils, waxes, solvents, and process oils used in industrial, automotive, and
manufacturing markets.
• Example 2, approximately 27,000 bpd: – Produces naphthenic base oils used in transformer

• Example 3, approximately 9,000 to 10,000 bpd– Produces naphthenic lubricating oils and

These facilities may not be large by crude-throughput measures, but disruption could affect specialized

Refineries with capacities below 100,000 bpd are not inherently lower-risk facilities. Many support
military and critical infrastructure operations, handle hazardous and flammable materials, operate
complex industrial processes, and provide products that are difficult to replace through other domestic
sources. Accordingly, FAA should not adopt any criteria that excludes refineries based on non-pertinent
calculations.
The proposed threshold for a minute number of facilities effectively creates a disparity in access to
Section 2209 protections whereby thousands of critical manufacturing facilities may petition for
consideration while dozens of critical energy infrastructure facilities are categorically excluded. Given the
Administration's recognition that reliable energy supplies are essential to economic and national security,
FAA should reconsider whether refinery throughput is an appropriate screening criterion for access to the
UAFR application process.
As we stated in Section VI.B (Chemical Sector, § 74.81), FAA lists MTSA locations as an eligibility

Many refineries and petrochemical sites are regulated by MTSA based on their function as waterfront

Eligibility under this section shall not be conditioned on the facility meeting a minimum production,

• Fire or explosion events;
• Toxic or hazardous material releases;
