B. Scope of Restriction
1. Lateral Boundary (§ 74.58)
FAA proposes that the UAFR lateral boundary be narrowly tailored to the specific needs of each facility,
not exceed the fixed-site facility property boundary, and not overlap with permanent airspace restrictions.
However, Congress used the phrase “close proximity to” rather than “directly above” or “within the
property boundary.” FAA should give effect to that statutory language by allowing a risk-based buffer
where necessary to address hazards that do not stop at a fence line.
AFPM emphasizes that a property-boundary-only approach may not adequately address UAS risks where
vulnerable assets, consequence zones, approach corridors, or connected operational systems extend
beyond a formal property line. Chemical, petrochemical, refining, oil, and gas facilities regularly extend
beyond their strict property boundaries. Many AFPM member sites are connected or adjacent to other
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 13

critical infrastructure. Thus, FAA must account for connected operations to a refinery or chemical facility,
such as process units, tank farms, loading racks, terminals (including marine terminals), rail operations,
utility corridors, pipelines and pipeline interconnections, control rooms, and flare systems.
Conversely, FAA should also recognize that the appropriate boundary may differ by facility and should
be based on the specific hazard, operational, and public safety profile of the site rather than a one-size-
fits-all formula.
To address these concerns, the FAA should permit applicants to define lateral boundaries based on site-
specific risk considerations, including the extent of operational areas, locations of hazardous materials,
potential consequences of an incident, existing security measures, and surrounding land-use
characteristics. A narrowly tailored, risk-based buffer option would better align the UAFR boundary with
actual safety and security considerations while preserving FAA oversight and stakeholder coordination.
Detailed maps could be submitted by applicants to support expanded UAFR boundaries.
Question: If FAA does not allow UAFRs to extend beyond the property line, how might that
heighten the risk to some kinds of facilities?
Property-line-only UAFRs may not adequately protect critical infrastructure because UAS operating
immediately outside a facility boundary can still create surveillance, security, and dropped-object risks to
personnel and equipment inside the facility.
To analyze the safety risk of non-buffered UAS flights to personnel and equipment, AFPM utilized a
dropped object calculator25 to find the exact energy (in Joules) of items dropped from a controlled
distance and the consequence result when falling on a worker. We used the assumption that free falling
UAS will not fall in a straight line and that there are permitted flyovers in certain areas of a facility. We
also used the assumption that personnel at the facility are wearing full PPE and that the object is blunt
(sharp objects, such as UAS, produce worse outcomes).
Our calculation showed that if a 0.55 lbs. drone26 were to fall from a height of 400ft,27 the resulting
impact would produce 298.28 Joules of energy and could create a fatality-level dropped-object hazard,
depending on impact location, object geometry, velocity, and surrounding conditions. This can be
exacerbated when 1) the UAS has a vertical velocity, 2) the UAS shape contains sharp edges, and 3) the
permitted flyover height is beyond 400ft per equipment height extension.
Falling objects represent a well-documented hazard across industrial environments, where elevated
operations, material handling, and maintenance activities routinely introduce risk to personnel below.
Effective mitigation requires a layered approach, including engineering controls, administrative
restrictions, and personal protective equipment, alongside site-specific risk assessments that account for
height, object characteristics, and operational conditions. Facilities comply with robust OSHA regulations
that mitigate such risks.
Our analysis shows that even the smallest registered UAS can introduce credible and fatal dropped-object
hazards, particularly when operating overactive operation areas, hazardous material locations, and
personnel-dense locations. When in free fall, it is also unlikely that a UAS will fall in a direct pathway
down. If UAFR boundaries are created strictly on fence or property lines, the safety risk remains for both
the personnel and equipment on or near the exact boundaries.
25 DROPS, E-DROPS Calculator, DROPS Online, available at: https://www.dropsonline.org/drops-guidance-and-
resources/drops-calculator/e-drops-calculator/ (last accessed June 30, 2026).
26 0.55lbs (250g) or heavier is the weight threshold for registration through the FAA for recreational or commercial purposes.
Weights increase drastically when including payloads, advanced cameras, and other technologies.
27 Ceiling height for Class G airspace. The height can be higher depending on surrounding equipment.
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 14

When drafting Section 2209 of FESSA 2016, Congress deliberately used the term “close proximity”. This
intentional language suggested that facility-specific determinations were necessary to properly protect
facilities, rather than a uniform FAA-boundary. FAA should conform with the statutory text with these
risks in mind when finalizing how lateral boundaries should be determined.
Proposed Revision
The lateral boundary of a UAFR shall be limited to the area necessary to address the safety, security,
operational, or public consequence risks associated with the fixed-site facility.
In determining the appropriate lateral boundary, the Administrator may consider the facility’s property
boundary, hazardous material storage areas, process areas, loading and unloading operations, utility
corridors, terminals, pipelines, pipeline interconnections, emergency response access points, critical
assets, security requirements, and other facility-specific factors relevant to the requested designation.
The Administrator may approve a lateral boundary that differs from or extends beyond the property
boundary when the applicant demonstrates that the requested boundary is necessary to address facility-
specific safety, security, operational, emergency response, or public safety concerns.
The applicant may support the requested lateral boundary through maps, diagrams, descriptions, risk-
based summaries, or other information acceptable to the Administrator. Where detailed boundary
information would reveal sensitive security, proprietary, or operational information, the Administrator
may allow the applicant to submit generalized, redacted, or otherwise protected information.
The lateral boundary shall be no broader than necessary to accomplish the safety or security purpose of
the UAFR while preserving access to navigable airspace to the extent practicable.
2. Allowed Operations (§ 74.250)
The FAA proposes that certain operations under Parts 91, 107, 108, 135, and 137 may access standard
UAFRs if they broadcast Remote ID, transition in the shortest time practicable, and satisfy other
requirements. The FAA should distinguish between transitory operations that merely pass through a
UAFR and operations over or near hazardous process areas, emergency response activities, flaring,
blowdowns, turnarounds, or other temporary high-risk conditions. A generally authorized UAS operation
may still be unsafe at a particular facility, at a particular time, and in a particular operating area.
AFPM emphasizes that a generalized access framework is insufficient for hazardous process areas in
chemical and energy sectors where UAS mishaps, loss of control, electromagnetic interference, ignition
risks, or reckless operations could create significant safety, environmental, operational, or cascading
infrastructure consequences. Facility operators continuously observe that UAS fly overs are not safe from
refinery conditions and regularly recover lost UAS from their properties.
Refineries and chemical facilities support a broad array of routine and non-routine operations, during
which even a risk-assessed UAS operation may present significant hazards to the facility operations and
even the commercial unmanned aircraft itself. Due to the reactive, and sometimes emergency, nature of
flaring and unit blowdowns, it is nearly impossible to accurately determine when a third-party UAS could
path through vented gases, both amplifying the emergency and interfering with facility response.
On a broader timescale, turnarounds and maintenance operations also present examples of how a simple
flyover poses increased risk. A refinery turnaround is a planned, extensive maintenance shutdown where a
refinery temporarily halts operations to inspect, repair, and upgrade equipment, ensuring long-term safety,
efficiency, and reliability. During this process, facilities see increased personnel numbers onsite,
temporary configurations creating non-routine ops, and larger equipment (e.g., cranes) in use. UAS
interference can prolong this process, leading to costly adjustments, injury to personnel or aircraft, and
delayed fuel supplies to the nation.

Indeed, incumbent electronic and electromagnetic signals, extreme atmospheric conditions, and shared
communication frequencies within a refinery or chemical facility have the possibility to unintentionally

personnel regularly recover UAS within their fencelines. The unique complexity of AFPM member sites
proves that regular flyovers present high risks of drone failure and danger.
As shown in our dropped object analysis in Section VI.E (Lateral Boundary), the existence of an
authorized operation does not eliminate the underlying safety risks associated with UAS malfunctions,
loss of control events, or airborne conflicts. Even a small UAS can create a credible risk of serious injury

Within allowed licensed operations, FAA’s justification for allowing overflights is TSA’s background

Operators or proprietors of covered facilities should have the ability to temporarily restrict, delay, or deny

Similar to UAS operation notifications, FAA should also distinguish between facility-authorized UAS

3. UAFR Access Notification (§ 74.255)
FAA proposes that UAS operators provide notice to the fixed-site facility site manager with operator
contact information, certificate/permit numbers, Remote ID serial numbers, registration numbers, site
identification, date/time/area, and operation type. Notice must be provided as soon as reasonably possible
in advance, with alternative procedures for government or law enforcement operations.
AFPM supports the proposed requirement that facility owners/operators receive notice whenever a non-
facility UAS is authorized to operate within restricted critical infrastructure airspace. It is paramount to
have clear lines of communication between FAA, third-party UAS operators, and facilities from start to
finish when a UAFR is active and thus an increased risk in flyovers was predetermined. However, FAA’s
preamble is unclear in exactly how the notification system is to be calibrated. For example, third-party
UAS operators are instructed to notify the UAFR facility manager “as soon as reasonably possible” in

ambiguous language creates the potential for scenarios in which a UAS operation is authorized through a
standard UAFR process, while affected critical infrastructure facilities remain unaware of the
authorization and may mistakenly interpret the activity as negligent or malicious. A third-party UAS
operation may be physically closer to the UAFR facility, thus giving significantly less time between the
facility notification and planned flyover, leading to a falsely-identified negligent flight by facility security
personnel.
Clarity is also needed for facilities that fly their own UAS as part of routine or ad hoc operations. It is
unclear whether UAS flown by the facility are required to submit a notification, thus creating a redundant
and counterproductive regulatory requirement to “notify themselves.”
Additionally, per the nature of a UAFR and the facility’s responsibility in maintaining one, effective UAS
detection technology is essential in managing permitted flyovers. Without reliable detection, a similar
scenario of mistaken UAS identification could take place similar to that of delayed notifications.
AFPM requests that the FAA establish a tiered and risk-informed notification framework for UAFRs
dependent on critical infrastructure sector, particularly for chemical, petrochemical, fuel, and energy-
sector facilities where UAS mishaps, electromagnetic interference, loss of control, ignition risks, or
operational disruptions could create significant safety, environmental, or cascading infrastructure
consequences. AFPM recommends enhanced advance-notification requirements and coordination
procedures for third-party operations over or near critical infrastructure areas, while supporting
streamlined or automated notification pathways for facility-authorized operations. The outcome of
enhanced notifications could be a fixed timeframe in which third-party operator must notify the UAFR
manager or an agreement between the two parties.

4. Facility-Authorized UAS Whitelist (§§ 74.250 and 74.255)
The proposed access and notification framework does not provide a clear mechanism for a fixed-site
facility with an approved UAFR to identify facility-owned, facility-operated, contracted, or otherwise
facility-authorized UAS that may routinely operate within the restriction. Proposed § 74.255 would
require advance notice containing operator-, aircraft-, and operation-specific information. Although
FAA’s preamble contemplates a possible whitelist based on one-time submissions by UAS operators, that
approach does not expressly allow the operator or proprietor of the UAFR facility to establish and
maintain the authoritative list of UAS operations the facility has approved.
Critical infrastructure facilities increasingly use autonomous, remotely supervised, dock-based, and
beyond visual line of sight operations to support inspection, maintenance, construction, security,
environmental monitoring, regulatory compliance, emergency response, and operational continuity. These
operations may occur frequently, on short notice, or automatically in response to alarms, equipment
conditions, or other operational needs. Requiring a separate access submission or operation-specific
notification for each flight could delay safety-critical activities, impose unnecessary administrative
burdens, and cause facility personnel to treat known facility operations as unidentified activity.
The final rule should preserve FAA’s authority over the NAS and all otherwise applicable aviation
requirements while clearly distinguishing facility-authorized operations from operations conducted by
unrelated third parties. Once a facility has communicated to FAA that an operator and unmanned aircraft
are authorized by the facility, that submission should satisfy the UAFR-specific access and notification
requirements for the scope and duration identified by the facility.
FAA should establish a secure, facility-managed whitelist through the UAFR Module or another FAA-
approved system. Once a UAFR has been designated, the operator or proprietor, acting through its
designated representative or site manager, should be permitted to submit and update information

C. Application and Information Protection
1. Remote ID Detection (§ 74.56(d))
AFPM supports Remote ID as one component of a layered UAS security framework, but the FAA should
not make existing Remote ID sensing capability a condition precedent to UAFR approval. Many facilities
have not previously had a practical legal or operational reason to purchase UAS detection systems, and
the market for Remote ID sensing remains uneven in range, performance, cybersecurity, spoofing risk,
and integration with facility security operations.
FAA proposes that eligible facilities have restricted access, designated security personnel, security
monitoring, and capability to receive broadcast Remote ID messages within or near the requested UAFR.
AFPM notes that FAA’s approach requiring Remote ID monitoring will notably lead to numerous critical
infrastructure locations procuring detection systems simply to satisfy the eligibility requirement rather
than selecting technology that is reliable, secure, effective, and the best fit for the operating facility’s
environment. This concern is heightened further in that Remote ID broadcast modules and facility
Remote ID detection technologies are not mature and still present difficulties for accurate
detection/compliance. Remote ID undoubtedly has a short broadcasting range, even when compliant with
FAA’s § 89.320 minimum performance requirements. The maximum broadcasting range of modules
limited to Bluetooth is only about 2km,28 which is permissible over small facilities with exceptional
detection equipment, but for bottom-line, mobile detection, this opens the possibility for inaccurate
overflight assessments. Even in the high-end detection technologies, Remote ID broadcasts can prove
spotty and raise concerns about non-compliance by the pilot, inaccuracies in detection, or more malicious
actions such as spoofing.
Spoofing is a significant concern of facility security personnel. Spoofing describes the action of falsifying
identification data through unencrypted broadcast to appear legitimate or mislead positioning.29 It is
understood that Remote ID information is intentionally unencrypted for accessibility purposes, but this
opens the door to a false sense of security in restricted airspaces. A bad actor, for example, could
find/detect authorized “whitelisted” serial numbers and spoof those IDs to freely fly over restricted
airspace.
Facility security personnel are hesitant to fully trust Remote ID compliance, but AFPM understands it is a
necessity for maintaining standard UAFRs. However, countering this with prescriptive sensor standards,
unclear retention expectations, or broad reporting obligations could require technology deployments that
28 American Model Aeronautics Association (AMA), Advanced Flight System Committee Remote ID Module Status Report (Mar.
19, 2024), https://www.modelaircraft.org/sites/default/files/documents/AMA_RID_Module_Status_Report.pdf.
29 Remote ID spoofing can inject fake serial IDs, broadcast false locations, and even inject non-existent drones (or “ghost
drones”) over facilities, similar to VPNs and IP addresses.
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 20

are not well aligned with site-specific risks, existing security operations center workflows, or evolving
Remote ID capabilities.
AFPM instead requests that FAA clearly define and limit any required Remote ID data collection,
reporting, and retention requirements, including required data elements, retention periods, reporting
triggers, and acceptable submission formats. AFPM requests that FAA avoid creating prescriptive
Remote ID sensor standards or mandated technical configurations and instead allow facilities flexibility to
implement cost-effective solutions appropriate to their operational needs and risk environment. Any data
retention requirements should be narrowly tailored and designed to minimize unnecessary administrative,
storage, cybersecurity, and compliance burdens on facility operators.
Importantly, the FAA should not require acquisition or deployment of Remote ID sensing capability as a
condition precedent to UAFR approval. Instead, FAA should allow facilities to obtain UAFR approval if
they maintain appropriate protective security measures and submit a reasonable plan to acquire Remote
ID sensing capability within a defined period after approval. FAA could provide a reasonable
implementation period for detection in a facility’s conditional approval, such as two years following
UAFR acceptance. This would allow facilities to evaluate available systems, avoid poor investments, and
align procurement with emerging federal standards or guidance. During such a period, FAA could then
limit, delay, or condition non-facility UAS operations that would be otherwise allowed within the UAFR
until the facility procures the detection technology.
Retrospectively, up until the publication of FAA’s section 2209 NPRM and DOJ’s publication of the
Safer Skies Act IFR, there were little legal actions facility owner/operators or law enforcement could take
to counter hazardous UAS flights over critical infrastructure. At the time, there was little practical
justification for many facilities to invest in UAS detection technology. Even where resources were
available, the market for detection systems remained relatively immature, offering limited confidence in
reliable detection performance while operating within an uncertain and grey legal and regulatory
framework.30 Requiring facilities to have already deployed Remote ID sensing capability would penalize
facilities for not purchasing technology before there was a clear regulatory framework in which that
technology could support enforceable UAFR protections. Facilities care about drone security, but
impracticable, expensive detection systems would not be additive to their already existing UAS security
plans.
Proposed Revision
A fixed-site facility seeking a UAFR shall maintain protective security measures appropriate to the
facility’s risk, operations, and requested designation. Such measures may include restricted access to the
facility, restricted access to key areas or components, designated security personnel, security monitoring,
incident reporting procedures, and coordination with appropriate law enforcement, emergency response,
or security partners.
A fixed-site facility shall not be required to acquire, install, or contract for Remote Identification sensing
capability as a condition precedent to approval of a UAFR.
An applicant may satisfy the Remote Identification sensing element of this section by demonstrating that
the facility maintains layered protective security measures and has developed a reasonable plan to
evaluate, acquire, install, or contract for Remote Identification sensing capability within a period
specified by the Administrator, not to exceed two years following approval of the UAFR.

During the Remote Identification sensing implementation period, the Administrator may limit, delay, or

alternative access coordination process.

2. Demonstration of Need (§ 74.66)
FAA proposes that applicants submit information on existing UAS traffic patterns in close proximity to a
facility over the previous 24 months where available, vulnerabilities to UAS incursions, consequences of
such incursions, and how the UAFR would integrate into security plans. Only then will facilities
determined to have sufficient safety or security threats be designated to maintain a UAFR.
FAA should not require a facility to experience, document, or wait for a specific UAS incident before
becoming eligible for protection. Section 2209 is intended to prevent safety and security consequences,
not merely respond after they occur. As stated in Section VI.G (Remote ID detection), many facilities do
not yet possess detection systems that can standardize UAS flight information to submit for a UAFR.
Until FAA’s proposed rule was published and SAFER SKIES Act was enacted, facilities had no incentive
to procure expensive technologies that could accurately produce this data. Advanced detection systems
are available on the market, however without a legal basis to act on such incursions or mitigate in the
event of a threat, facilities have had little reason to deploy them on site. While such information may be
useful for analyzing facility airspace, depending on the complexity of detection system, the proposed
demonstration requirement places too much emphasis on past data. Therefore, the absence of 24 months
of UAS traffic data should not be treated as evidence that a UAFR is unnecessary.
Additionally, requiring extensive facility-specific vulnerability and consequence submissions could create
significant information aggregation and cybersecurity risks. Facilities should not be required to disclose
detailed vulnerability assessments, consequence modeling, security gaps, or proprietary operational
information to prove that UAS overflight could present a credible safety or security concern. Nor should
facilities be required to wait for an incident, attempted overflight, or a specific threat stream before
becoming eligible for protection. FAA should rather allow applicants to demonstrate need through facility
characteristics, hazardous material inventories, critical functions, process safety concerns, consequence
potential, operational hazards, sector threat information, prior suspicious UAS activity, or federal/SRMA
validation. Past security regulations could be considered as well, such as MTSA or CFATS.
Lastly, for collection and storage of sensitive information, AFPM requests that FAA avoid creating a
centralized repository containing detailed facility vulnerability information, operational security data,
security procedures, and consequence assessments across the critical infrastructure community due to the
significant cybersecurity, operational security, and information aggregation risks such a database creates.
Proposed Revision
An applicant may demonstrate need for a UAFR through a risk-informed showing that unauthorized or
uncoordinated unmanned aircraft operations could create elevated safety, security, environmental,
operational, economic, or public safety risks to the fixed-site facility.
The demonstration of need may include information regarding the facility’s mission, hazardous material
inventories, process safety risks, critical infrastructure functions, operational sensitivity, potential
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 22

consequences, documented sector risks, prior suspicious or unauthorized unmanned aircraft activity, or
other information acceptable to the Administrator.
Information describing unmanned aircraft operations in close proximity to the facility during the previous
24 months may be submitted where available and shall be considered additive to the applicant’s
demonstration of need. The absence of comprehensive 24-month unmanned aircraft traffic data shall not,
by itself, be a basis for denial of a UAFR application.
An applicant may satisfy the unmanned aircraft traffic information element through available records,
partial data, security observations, incident reports, law enforcement notifications, facility reports, or a
statement explaining that such data is not reasonably available.
The Administrator shall not require an applicant to submit detailed vulnerability assessments, security
plans, consequence analyses, threat intelligence, or proprietary operational information unless necessary
to evaluate the application.
Where such information is necessary, the Administrator may accept summaries, certifications, Federal
agency or Sector Risk Management Agency validation, references to existing regulatory information,
redacted materials, or protected submissions in a form and manner acceptable to the Administrator.
3. UAFR Module Security (§ 74.50)
As published its Proposed Rule, FAA would require applicants to submit required information in a form
and manner acceptable to the Administrator, using a web-based UAFR Module.
The UAFR Module may collect highly sensitive facility, operational, security, and vulnerability
information. Unless FAA expressly protects such information and provides secure submission and
handling procedures, applicants may face increased disclosure, cybersecurity, and operational security
risks when participating in the UAFR process.
AFPM requests that all information, including confidential business information (CBI), security-sensitive
information (SSI), facility vulnerability data, site diagrams, operational details, and other sensitive facility
information submitted through the UAFR process be expressly protected from public disclosure to the
fullest extent permitted by law, through applicable FOIA exemptions and protected-information regimes.
AFPM additionally requests FAA limit the amount of security information required for applications.
Entire physical security plan submissions are unnecessary, burdensome, and will prolong the application
review process. AFPM strongly urges FAA to limit information to drone response plans or simplified
proof of security protocol similar to § 74.64. FAA should apply Protected Critical Infrastructure
Information (PCII), Sensitive Security Information (SSI), Confidential Business Information (CBI), or
comparable protections, as applicable, to sensitive information submitted by companies seeking UAFR
protections.
4. UAS Security and Incident Response Plans (§ 74.64)
The Proposed Rule states that a flight restriction should not be the first line of defense to address UAS
threats against facility vulnerabilities. FAA proposes that applicants provide UAS security and incident
response plans and descriptions of security perimeters in a manner acceptable to the Administrator.
AFPM agrees that UAFRs are not the first line of defense in a secure airspace, but emphasizes that
detailed security plans, perimeter descriptions, and incident response procedures are highly sensitive and
could create operational security concerns if submitted broadly or retained in centralized repositories.
FAA should instead allow applicants to satisfy this requirement through submitting plan summaries,
certifications, or other means deemed acceptable by the Administrator. These alternatives will still prove
facilities have taken actions to minimize UAS vulnerabilities while reducing administrative burden for
both FAA reviewers and applicants.
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 23

Additionally, FAA should consider that UAS security and incident response plans be satisfactory if part
of a broader security plan and not a standalone document specific to UAS incursions. The proposed
requirement could be interpreted as requiring facilities to create a new standalone plan, even where UAS
procedures are already incorporated into existing security, emergency response, crisis management,
business continuity, or incident command programs.

5. Obligation to Update (§ 74.20)
FAA proposes continuing obligations to update application information within five business days, annual
reporting of authorized and unauthorized UAS operations, and possible more frequent reporting when
requested by FAA.
Additionally, FAA proposes that the owner/operator has a responsibility to report any material change in
circumstances that affects the need for a restriction, including shutdowns or temporary lapse in services.
The proposed five-business-day update obligation and open-ended interim reporting authority could
impose unnecessary administrative burden if applied to immaterial or routine changes. A materiality
standard, standardized reporting templates, and protected submission pathways would help ensure FAA
receives actionable information without creating avoidable compliance uncertainty for facility owners and
operators.
AFPM notes that the term “material change in circumstances” may encompass a broad range of
operations that commonly occur at refineries and chemical facilities. Examples include planned
turnarounds, maintenance outages, unit shutdowns, and other temporary changes. These examples should
not lead to a modification in UAFRs or facilitate a burdensome reporting requirement. In some cases,
temporary downtimes increase overall safety of the facility and require increased security of the site’s
airspace.
To ensure FAA receives fulsome and accurate information from UAFR facilities, FAA should extend the
proposed five-business-day reporting requirement and limit interim updates to material changes that
directly affect UAFR eligibility, scope, or administration, such as changes to UAFR boundaries, facility
operational status, designated site manager information, or facility decommissioning. AFPM also requests
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 24

that FAA establish clear reporting templates, define required reporting elements for both interim and
annual submissions, and provide protected submission pathways for sensitive or security-related
information.
FAA should also clarify what a “material change in circumstances” is to UAFR holders and incorporate a
definition that does not overly burden FAA and owner/operators. FAA can distinguish between routine or
temporary operational changes and material changes in the definition that meaningfully alter the facility’s
eligibility. FAA should also provide sector-specific examples in the final rule preamble or Advisory
Circular so UAFR holders can consistently comply without the need for over reporting. Clear definitions
and examples will assist FAA in managing UAFR modifications without unnecessary administrative
burden or harmful lapses in airspace restriction.
Proposed Revision
A “material change” is a change that materially affects UAFR eligibility, boundary scope, site-manager
contact information, facility ownership or control, facility decommissioning, or the justification for the
restriction. Routine maintenance, planned turnarounds, temporary unit outages, short-term production
changes, and other ordinary-course operational changes should not trigger a (FAA extended)-X business-
day update requirement unless they materially affect the UAFR itself.
6. Externalities (§ 74.68)
FAA would require applicants to describe costs, disruptions, or negative effects to airspace users and
efforts to reduce or limit those effects.
In the Proposed Rule, FAA assumes that facility owners and operators have comprehensive knowledge of
regular third-party UAS operations over and near their property. This is erroneous, as facility owners and
operators do not have the tools, data, authorities, or technical expertise to evaluate broader aviation
externalities, including impacts to UAS operators, nearby airspace users, aviation routes, or FAA airspace
management priorities. Chemical, petrochemical, refining, oil, and gas facilities are experts in their
operations, hazards, security posture, and potential consequences of unauthorized UAS activity, but as
authorities currently stand, site personnel do not have this prior knowledge to adequately fulfill this
requirement as proposed. Requesting facility applicants to perform this analysis would also increase cost,
delay applications, and create inconsistent submissions without improving FAA’s decision-making. It
may also discourage high-risk facilities from applying for UAFR protections because they are being asked
to analyze issues that are properly within FAA’s responsibility as the national airspace regulator.
FAA, not the individual facility applicants, is best positioned to assess impacts on navigable airspace,
UAS operators, aviation routes, nearby airports, emergency response aviation, and broader airspace
management. Applicants should provide facility-specific risk and consequence information, while the
FAA should provide aviation externalities through its internal airspace review, interagency coordination,
and public comment process. That said, even the largest refinery is quite small in the context of drone
diversion around the UAFR. In other words, the costs or disruptions from a drone operator having to route
around a facility UAFR is de minimis.
Proposed Revision
The Administrator shall evaluate the externalities associated with a proposed UAFR as part of FAA’s
internal review of the application.
An applicant shall not be required to conduct or submit a formal externalities analysis regarding impacts
to navigable airspace, aviation users, UAS operators, aviation routes, or broader airspace management
considerations.

An applicant shall provide information within its expertise that is reasonably necessary for FAA’s review,
including facility operations, safety or security concerns, hazardous materials, potential consequences,
operational sensitivities, and the facility-specific need for the requested UAFR.
In conducting the externalities analysis, the Administrator may consider the potential impacts of the
proposed UAFR on airspace users, aviation access, allowed operations, emergency response access, and
other airspace management considerations.
The Administrator may also consider the potential public safety, environmental, economic, homeland
security, national security, and national resilience consequences associated with unauthorized or
uncoordinated unmanned aircraft operations at the fixed-site facility.
FAA may consider whether tailored boundaries, access procedures, standing authorizations, or other
conditions can reduce impacts to legitimate airspace users while preserving the safety and security

7. Environmental Impact (§ 74.70)
The FAA proposes that applicants provide information on sensitive land uses, resources, and other
documents that may require site-specific analysis for environmental assessment under the National
Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) and other applicable environmental laws, regulations, and
Executive orders prior to designating a UAFR.
AFPM emphasizes that individual UAFR applications are intended to address airspace restrictions for
safety and security purposes, not to create a facility-level environmental review program. A UAFR is a
FAA airspace designation; it does not authorize construction, facility expansion, ground disturbance, new
emissions, or changes to industrial operations. Requiring applicants to conduct or finance site-specific
environmental analysis could delay security protections, duplicate federal agency responsibilities, and
impose costs unrelated to the applicant’s operational control without adding any extra environmental
benefits.
AFPM requests that FAA remove the requirement for individual fixed-site facility applicants to conduct
or support site-specific environmental impact analysis as part of the UAFR application process. Instead,
FAA should coordinate with appropriate federal agencies, such as the Environmental Protection Agency,
Department of the Interior, and other relevant land-management or environmental authorities, if there is
substantiated need to identify environmentally sensitive areas and address any related airspace
considerations through separate federal processes or airspace-designation mechanisms. FAA should
additionally apply categorical exclusions or streamlined review procedures when appropriate, given that
airspace flight restrictions generally do not create physical environmental impacts. To the extent
environmental considerations are relevant, FAA should also consider that UAFRs may reduce the risk of
incidents involving facilities that handle hazardous, flammable, explosive, or toxic materials by reducing
unauthorized or uncoordinated UAS activity near those facilities.

The Administrator shall conduct any required environmental review for a proposed UAFR as part of

An applicant shall not be required to prepare or submit a standalone environmental analysis for a UAFR
that does not authorize construction, ground disturbance, new emissions, facility expansion, or changes
to facility operations.
Where environmental information is necessary for FAA’s review, the applicant shall provide only facility-
specific information reasonably necessary to support the Administrator’s evaluation.

The Administrator may allow an applicant to satisfy environmental information requests by referencing
existing Federal, State, local, Tribal, or territorial environmental, safety, emergency response, or
regulatory submissions, where appropriate.
The Administrator may apply a categorical exclusion or other streamlined environmental review
procedure where the proposed UAFR does not result in direct physical environmental impacts.
In evaluating the proposed UAFR, the Administrator may consider the protective purpose of the
restriction, including whether the UAFR may reduce risks associated with unauthorized or uncoordinated

VII. Other Opportunities to Improve 14 CFR Part 74
A. Implementation Guidance, Templates, and Secure Submission Procedures
After final rule promulgation, FAA should develop clear implementation guidance and maintain ongoing
stakeholder engagement to support the large volume of applications expected across industry sectors.
Clear guidance will help ensure a consistent and efficient application process for both large organizations
with dedicated compliance resources and smaller businesses with limited regulatory expertise. AFPM also
encourages FAA to leverage the UAFR Module to create a streamlined, user-friendly application process
and utilize standardized templates to improve consistency, reduce administrative burden, and support
compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act. FAA should furthermore consider incorporating
specialized staff and planned workshops to assist critical infrastructure during the implementation period.
Applicant assistance for submissions and maintaining approved UAFRs would streamline proper
applications and reduce time spent on rejections/resubmissions.
In addition, FAA should establish secure and clearly documented procedures for submitting sensitive
information that may be required as part of the application process. While FAA acknowledges that
applicants may need to provide Confidential Business Information (CBI) or Sensitive Security
Information (SSI), the draft rule does not adequately explain how such information should be submitted
and protected. AFPM recommends FAA provide explicit instructions and continue engaging stakeholders
after implementation to identify operational challenges, clarify expectations, and ensure the program
remains effective, secure, and practical for regulated entities.
B. Batch Application Process
FAA proposes in § 74.52(b) that each UAFR application be limited to one single fixed-site facility.
AFPM recommends FAA remove the single facility limitation and instead allow a single applicant
representing multiple locations to submit batch applications for facilities with similar profiles. A batch
application and designation process would significantly decrease administrative burden for FAA
reviewers while streamlining the protection for similar facilities that each plan to apply. Within the batch
application, FAA could retain discretion to evaluate UAFR locations individually but then would
additionally be saved work hours by analyzing facilities with similar security plans, chemicals of interest,
physical layouts, and hazards. Ideally, the single applicant in the energy and chemical sectors would be
the parent company of the batched facilities.
C. Phased Implementation
FAA should provide reasonable implementation timelines and continue engagement with critical
infrastructure owners and operators as Part 74 is implemented. A phased approach would allow facilities
to align internal procedures, technology acquisition, cybersecurity review, personnel training, and security
operations center integration with the final rule’s requirements.
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 27

D. Protect Existing FAA Approvals and Waivers
AFPM requests that a final Part 74 not negatively impact currently authorized UAS-enhanced programs.
As stated earlier, AFPM members have long incorporated UAS technologies and pilot teams within their
operations. Part 74, while imperative for site security and emergency response may unintentionally inhibit
operations that currently comply with FAA regulations. Examples include Part 107 FAA waivers for
BVLOS, approved enterprise drone programs, emission monitoring programs, and company emergency
response operations.
E. Fairness Between Mature Programs and New Programs
AFPM suggests FAA avoid unintended disincentives based on maturity of facility drone and security
programs. Facilities should not face disproportionate application burdens relative to less-developed
programs and sectors.
F. Preserve Future Technology Flexibility
AFPM recommends FAA finalize requirements that don’t restrict emerging security technologies or
facility operations. Examples include autonomous operations, AI-assisted monitoring, advanced detection
systems, future enterprise UAS platforms, and evolving Remote ID capabilities.
G. Ongoing Stakeholder Engagement
Following finalization of the Section 2209 rule into implementation, AFPM recommends FAA maintain a
robust and ongoing critical infrastructure engagement process to ensure effective implementation and
continuous improvement of the UAFR framework. FAA should establish regular forums, workshops, and
listening sessions to gather feedback on operational challenges, technological developments, and
emerging security concerns. Continued engagement will help the FAA identify unintended consequences,
clarify compliance expectations, assess the effectiveness of designated restrictions, and adapt guidance as
the UAS and counter-UAS landscape evolves.
VIII. Cost Analysis Considerations
A. Regulatory Notices and Analyses
FAA estimates that the primary cost burden associated with the proposed UAFR framework would be the
application process and minimum Remote ID sensing capability requirements. FAA estimates application
preparation costs between approximately $5,000 and $10,000 per facility and estimates Remote ID
monitoring capability costs using an example system priced at approximately $2,800 upfront and $1,000
annually. FAA also estimates government review costs at approximately $1,000 per application but
acknowledges uncertainty associated with implementation and administration of the program.
In our survey representing 14 energy and chemical trade association members, over half of the
respondents that own detection technology reported costs above $5,000 annually to maintain. One third of
the same respondents with detection technology reported that annual costs were above $10,000. A portion
of respondents did not own detection technology, as we stated in our request for procurement flexibility,
but the cost data of those that do present a detection environment where the average technology costs are
well above the estimated $1,000. AFPM requests FAA reanalyze and substantiate the initial and annual
cost of detection technology to account for operative technologies critical infrastructure locations are
managing. We encourage FAA to look beyond vendor performance claims and consider the experience of
facility owners and operators, who must ultimately bear the costs, resource demands, cybersecurity
considerations, and operational burdens associated with implementing these technologies at scale.
The NPRM cost estimates may also significantly understate the practical costs associated with facility-
level implementation, including staffing, security operations center integration, cybersecurity reviews,
policy and procedure development, legal review, contractor support, employee training, recurring
AFPM Comments on FAA Section 2209 NPRM | Page 28

monitoring and reporting obligations, technology upgrades, maintenance, data retention, and operational
coordination with FAA and external operators.
IX. Conclusion
AFPM supports FAA’s long-awaited implementation of Section 2209 and urges FAA to finalize a rule
that is protective, administrable, and practical for high-consequence private critical infrastructure. To
meet Congress’s intent, the final rule should avoid using rigid eligibility thresholds, property-line-only
boundaries, or technology prerequisites that exclude facilities facing legitimate UAS-related risks.
Instead, FAA should adopt a risk-informed framework that allows energy, refining, petrochemical,
chemical, and connected transportation assets to demonstrate need; protects sensitive security and
operational information; distinguishes facility-authorized operations from third-party operations; and
provides clear implementation guidance, templates, and secure submission procedures.
These refinements will better protect critical infrastructure while preserving lawful UAS operations and
the safe integration of drones into the National Airspace System. Most importantly, FAA should
recognize that restricted airspace alone cannot fully protect critical infrastructure if facility operators
remain unable to respond to unlawful incursions once they occur.
If you have any questions regarding these comments, please contact Matt Fuller at mfuller@afpm.org.
Respectfully submitted,
Matthew Fuller
Senior Policy Analyst, Regulatory Affairs

Re: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
Dear Ms. Ferritto,
The Animal Agriculture Alliance (the Alliance), and the undersigned organizations appreciate
the opportunity to comment on the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) “Designation-
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”
published in the Federal Register on May 6, 2026, by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
Collectively, the Alliance and the undersigned organization support the NRPM which establishes
a process for operators and proprietors of certain facilities to request and maintain an
unmanned aircraft flight restriction. Further, we believe that the NRPM represents an
important step toward protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening biosecurity, and
safeguarding the nation's food supply while allowing for the continued responsible use of
unmanned aircraft systems.
Drones have become valuable tools for agriculture. Producers routinely use unmanned aircraft
to monitor crops, inspect infrastructure, assess livestock, and improve operational efficiency.
However, like many emerging technologies, drones can also be misused. As drone technology
has become more affordable and accessible, animal rights activist organizations and other
groups have increasingly incorporated drones into campaigns targeting farms and food
production facilities. These operations often involve capturing aerial footage for so-called
investigations, documentaries, media campaigns, or coordinated activist efforts designed to
generate public attention rather than provide complete context.
The concern extends well beyond privacy. Low-altitude drone activity around livestock and
poultry operations can cause unnecessary stress for animals, disrupt normal farm operations,
and raise legitimate biosecurity concerns, just to name a few. Aircraft moving between
multiple agricultural sites have the potential to contribute to disease transmission risks if not
operated responsibly. During a time when the United States continues to face animal disease
threats including Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) and New World Screwworm (NWS),
we believe that strengthening agricultural biosecurity and reducing unnecessary aerial activity
around sensitive livestock, poultry, and food facilities is a reasonable precaution.

The NPRM also supports broader food security objectives. America's livestock and poultry
farms, along with meat, poultry, dairy, and food processing facilities are essential components
of the nation's critical infrastructure, employing hundreds of thousands of dedicated workers
and providing protein to millions of people around the world, and should be facilities
considered for a UAFR. Disruptions caused by unauthorized surveillance, repeated drone
activity, or security incidents can have consequences that extend beyond individual farms or
food producing facilities and may negatively impact consumer confidence, supply chains, and
the resiliency and safety of the U.S. food system.
Further, the unauthorized use of unmanned aircraft could be used to unlawfully gain
proprietary information on new agricultural innovations or even target the safety of the food
supply, from either domestic or foreign perpetrators. Providing operators of eligible facilities
with a clear process to request unmanned aircraft flight restrictions is a practical way to help
reduce these risks while preserving legitimate commercial, governmental, and authorized
drone operations.
Specifically, the Alliance has monitored activist tactics for decades and has observed a growing
use of drones alongside other activities such as surveillance, coordinated campaigns, and, in
some cases, trespassing. While the vast majority of drone operators act responsibly and
lawfully, the increasing use of drones by groups targeting agricultural operations underscores
the need for a clear regulatory framework that enables vulnerable facilities to request
additional protections when justified.
For these reasons, the Animal Agriculture Alliance and the undersigned member organizations
support the FAA's NPRM and encourage the Agency to expedite finalization. Strengthening
protections around eligible facilities will improve agricultural security, support biosecurity
preparedness, protect critical food production infrastructure, and reinforce the resilience of the
nation's food system while maintaining responsible access to the benefits of drone technology.
Thank you in advance for your consideration, and we are available to provide additional
information if it would be helpful to the Agency’s efforts.
Respectfully submitted,
Animal Agriculture Alliance
American Feed Industry Association
National Chicken Council
National Milk Producers Federation
National Pork Producers Council
National Turkey Federation
The Meat Institute
United Egg Producers
U.S. Poultry and Egg Association

Comment on the FAA’s Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Submitted by: Ryan Baker, CEO, Arch Aerial LLC
Date: August 5, 2026
Houston, Texas

Arch Aerial is a U.S. drone services provider focused on aerial data collection for energy, construction, and infrastructure asset operators. Arch Aerial appreciates the FAA's efforts to protect genuinely sensitive critical infrastructure while maintaining the safe integration of unmanned aircraft into the National Airspace System.

As a commercial UAS service provider, we encourage the FAA to ensure that any UAFR framework does not create unnecessary administrative burdens for operators conducting inspections and other services on behalf of critical infrastructure owners and operators. Many of these missions occur multiple times per week as part of recurring maintenance, integrity management, environmental monitoring, and compliance programs. The final rule should provide a practical mechanism that allows authorized commercial operators working directly for, or under contract with, critical infrastructure owners to continue these operations without excessive paperwork or repeated approval processes. Additionally, any required approval or notification process should be predictable, timely, and scalable to support both routine recurring operations and time-sensitive industrial work. The rule should also avoid disrupting existing inspection programs by introducing approval timelines that are incompatible with established operational schedules. If a critical infrastructure operator already conducts weekly or biweekly inspections, the authorization process should not require weeks or months to obtain approval, resulting in interruptions to safety, integrity management, or regulatory compliance activities. Consideration should also be given to recurring or standing authorizations for trusted commercial operators performing ongoing work on behalf of critical infrastructure owners.

Finally, the FAA should avoid imposing unnecessary restrictions on certificated Part 107 operators and future Part 108 operators that already comply with FAA operational, training, and safety requirements. These operators have demonstrated their ability to conduct safe commercial operations and should be afforded a streamlined path to continue supporting the nation's critical infrastructure while preserving the security objectives of this rule.

comments.comment_text:
Josh Stein Leslie Cooley Dismukes
Governor Secretary

Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov

Federal Aviation Administration

Re: Comments on Notice of Proposed Rulemaking — “Designation to Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”; Docket No.
FAA-2026-4558; RIN 2120-AL33
Dear FAA Docket Operations:
The North Carolina Department of Adult Correction (“the Department”) submits these comments
on the FAA’s proposed rule1 implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and
Security Act of 2016.2 The Department strongly supports this long-awaited rulemaking, but writes
to explain why the rule as proposed would not adequately protect correctional facilities from the
drone threat Congress directed the FAA to address—and what must change so that it does.
About the Department
• Correctional facilities operated: 57.
• Total incarcerated population: More than 32,000.
• Correctional staff: More than 10,000.
• Geographic footprint / regions served: 46 out of 100 counties.
• Facilities most affected by drone incursions: Closed custody facilities.
These figures bear directly on the burden this rule would impose. As proposed, each UAFR is tied
to a single fixed site facility, and the FAA interprets the statute’s “collective” application option
1Designation to Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility, 91 Fed.
Reg. 24650 (proposed May 6, 2026) (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. pt. 74), Docket No. FAA-2026-4558, RIN 2120-
AL33 [hereinafter NPRM].
2Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209, 130 Stat. 615
(2016).
FROM THE OFFICE OF:
MAILING ADDRESS:
Orlando L. Rodriguez
5201 Mail Service Center
General Counsel
Raleigh, NC 27699-5201

narrowly—covering only co-owners or co-operators of one facility, not a single agency seeking
coverage across its facilities.3 A corrections system of the Department’s size would therefore be
forced to file a separate application for each of its 57 facilities—an administrative burden the FAA
should relieve through a multi-facility application pathway (see Section VI, Recommendations).
I. The Threat to State Prisons Is Operational and Not Hypothetical
Much of the national counter-drone conversation centers on hypothetical or episodic threats—
curious spectators and hobbyists drawn to a one-time event, or even the occasional wrong-doer.
Correctional facilities face something different: a daily, operational threat from determined
criminals. Bad actors use drones to deliver contraband—narcotics, weapons, and cellular phones—
directly over secure perimeters, fueling violence, overdoses, and the operation of criminal
enterprises from inside our facilities. The FAA itself recognizes this threat in the NPRM.4 In 2026,
with minimal detection capabilities at only six facilities, the Department documented at least 10
drone incursions.
II. Drone Incursions at the Department’s Facilities
While the number of documented drone incursions to date is modest, this is most assuredly due to
the minimal detection coverage that has been deployed to date. The Department is actively working
to expand detection capabilities. With expanded detection, incidents of the drone-contraband threat
at the Department’s facilities will only become more evident.
III. The Department Supports a Two-Tier Part 74 Framework
The Department commends the FAA for proposing a thoughtful framework under a new 14 C.F.R.
Part 74 and for creating two designation types—the Standard UAFR and the Special UAFR.5
Congress expressly named prisons in Section 2209, and this rulemaking is an important step
toward giving correctional agencies a lawful means to restrict the airspace over their facilities. Our
concern is not with the structure, but how state prisons will be treated under this system and, in
turn, whether it will actually stop overflight of a prison.
IV. A Standard UAFR Will Not Protect a Prison
As written, a Standard UAFR is too porous to protect a correctional facility. Proposed §74.250
allows operations under Parts 91, 107, 108, 135, and 137 to access the restricted airspace so long
3Although Section 2209 itself permits operators or proprietors to apply “individually or collectively,” the FAA
interprets a “collective” request narrowly—as a request by more than one operator or proprietor for a particular fixed
site facility where more than one operator has an interest or exercises control. NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24661; see id.
at 24652; proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.52. As proposed, each UAFR is therefore tied to a single fixed site facility, and
the rule provides no mechanism for one operator to cover multiple facilities in a single application.
4NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24656 (“Emergency Services Sector—State Prisons”); see proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.87. The
FAA acknowledges that “many incidents of unmanned aircraft being used to infiltrate State prisons to deliver
contraband such as cellphones, drugs, and weapons have been reported.”
5See proposed 14 C.F.R. §§ 74.5 (Standard UAFR), 74.6 (Special UAFR); NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24656 (lateral
boundaries within property lines; 400-foot AGL ceiling).
Page 2 of 7

as they broadcast Remote ID, transit in the “shortest practicable time,” and notify the facility.6 In
practice, that permits routine drone overflight of the secure perimeter—precisely the vector used
for contraband drops—and bad actors intent on delivering contraband will not comply with a
notification requirement in any event. A Standard UAFR therefore does not solve the problem it
is meant to solve.
Only a Special UAFR actually restricts overflight. Proposed §74.251 requires both the permission
of the responsible (“using”) agency and FAA approval before any operation may enter the
airspace.7 That facility-controlled access—not the Standard tier’s notify-and-transit default—is
what a prison needs. Yet the FAA has tied Special UAFRs to federal security agencies, military
departments, and a narrow “verified security assessment” pathway modeled on the national-
security instrument in 14 C.F.R. § 99.7.8 That framing signals the FAA does not intend to grant
Special UAFRs to state prisons, leaving them only the porous Standard tier. That result is
unacceptable.
V. The Proposed Rule Conflicts with Section 2209
Section 2209 does not merely authorize this rulemaking; it constrains it. In directing that an
application process be established, Congress directed that the procedures “shall allow operators or
proprietors of fixed site facilities to apply for designation individually or collectively.”9 The word
“shall” makes the collective-application option mandatory, not discretionary and it does not restrict
it in any way.
Section 2209 provides, in relevant part:
SEC. 2209. APPLICATIONS FOR DESIGNATION.
(a) APPLICATIONS FOR DESIGNATION.—Not later than 180 days after the date of
enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Transportation shall establish a process to allow
applicants to petition the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration to prohibit
or restrict, including temporarily, the operation of an unmanned aircraft in close proximity
to a fixed site facility.
(b) REVIEW PROCESS.—
(1) APPLICATION PROCEDURES.—
6Proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.250; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24653 (allowing operations under Parts 91, 107, 108, 135,
and 137 to access UAFR airspace over fixed site facilities where the operator broadcasts Remote ID under 14 C.F.R.
pt. 89, transits in the shortest practicable time, and notifies the facility under § 74.255).
7Proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.251; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24653 (operations within a Special UAFR require both
permission from the responsible government (“using”) agency and approval from the FAA Administrator).
8Proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.6; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24653 (Special UAFRs “available to federal security agencies,
military departments, and designated fixed-site facilities supported by verified security assessments demonstrating
credible threats,” paralleling 14 C.F.R. § 99.7, with five-year designations).
9Section 2209(b)(1)(B), Pub. L. No. 114-190, 130 Stat. 615 (2016) (codified at 49 U.S.C. § 40101 note) (emphasis
added).
Page 3 of 7

(A) IN GENERAL.—The Administrator shall establish the procedures for the application
for designation under subsection (a).
(B) REQUIREMENTS.—The procedures shall allow operators or proprietors of fixed
site facilities to apply for designation individually or collectively.
(C) CONSIDERATIONS.—Only the following may be considered fixed site facilities:
(i) Critical infrastructure, such as energy production, transmission, distribution facilities
and equipment, and railroad facilities.
(ii) Oil refineries and chemical facilities.
(iii) Amusement parks.
(iv) State prisons.10
The proposed rule cannot be squared with that Congressional directive. By tying each UAFR to a
single fixed site facility and construing “collectively” to reach only multiple parties interested in
one facility,11 the FAA has read the collective-application option out of the rule for the operators
who need it most—those, like state corrections systems, that operate many facilities. An operator
of 57 prisons, such as this Department, cannot “apply…collectively” in any meaningful sense if it
must file a separate application for each facility.
The proposed interpretation therefore does not “allow” collective application as the statute
requires; it forecloses it. That burden is not trivial: the FAA estimates that each application will
cost an applicant between $5,000 and $10,000 to prepare, and a corrections system forced to file
facility-by-facility would incur those costs many times over.12 For our Department, that means an
estimated $285,000-$570,000 to apply to obtain UAFRs across all 57 of our facilities. And it
imposes that cost at a time of severe, well-documented staffing shortages across corrections,
diverting scarce personnel and funding from core security functions to duplicative, facility-by-
facility paperwork.13 Simply to apply for a UAFR, state agencies would have to develop detailed
procedures and protocols around real time intrusion notifications and other reporting requirements,
for each of its facilities. It is also worth noting that the FAA estimates these technical requirements
would also add to the costs to the agency in addition to those described above (close to $3,000 per
site – not including infrastructure modifications that would be necessary for installation nor the
annual costs for services). Presently, the Department’s vacancy rate among correctional officers is
estimated to be 25%. The time, effort and resources individual facility applications would require
10Id.
11See proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.52; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24661.
12FAA, 2209 NPRM Regulatory Impact Analysis tbl.9 (May 2026) (Docket No. FAA-2026-4558-0004).
13See Safe Inside, Workforce Trends in State Departments of Corrections (Feb. 17, 2026),
https://safeinsideproject.org/report (50-state analysis supported by the U.S. Department of Justice, Bureau of Justice
Assistance, in partnership with the Correctional Leaders Association; finding that roughly one in six corrections
employees leave their jobs annually and that overtime spending has more than doubled in many states since 2019).
Page 4 of 7

would almost certainly add to this existing strain. Moreover, there is no guarantee of UAFR
approval even once the onerous prerequisites of the application process are met.
The statute likewise undercuts the rule’s decision to reserve meaningful, overflight-restricting
protection for national-security and military sites. Congress placed “State prisons” on the list of
eligible fixed site facilities alongside critical infrastructure14, and authorized designations to rest
on any one of four independent grounds—“aviation safety,” “protection of persons and property
on the ground,” “national security,” or “homeland security.”15 Nothing in Section 2209 makes
national security a precondition for a protective designation. A rule that offers prisons only the
porous Standard UAFR while limiting the effective Special UAFR to national-security and
military facilities narrows grounds Congress made disjunctive and subordinates a facility category
Congress made eligible in its own right.
Worse still, §74.6(a) makes a Special UAFR available only to facilities owned or sponsored by
federal security agencies or military departments, and permits a non-federal site to qualify only “if
sponsored by” the FAA or a federal intelligence or security agency (DHS, DOD, DOE, or DOJ).
A state department of corrections has no such federal sponsor—so, however grave its documented
drone threat, it is categorically shut out of the only designation that stops overflight.
The FAA should conform the final rule to the statute by (i) providing a genuine collective, multi-
facility application pathway, and (ii) making an overflight-restricting designation available to
correctional facilities on the statutory ground of protecting persons and property on the ground,
without a national-security predicate. See the recommended changes below.
VI. Recommendations
1. Make correctional facilities eligible for a Special UAFR — the only tier that
actually stops overflight.
Only a Special UAFR requires facility approval before a drone may enter (§74.251); the Standard
tier lets drones transit. The NPRM acknowledges a Special UAFR “may be the appropriate
airspace designation” for a state prison, yet §74.6(a) lets a non-federal site obtain one only if a
federal agency (DHS, DOD, DOE, or DOJ) sponsors it — which a state department of corrections
cannot do on its own. The FAA should designate correctional facilities under the Special tier and
designate DOJ, already corrections’ counter-UAS partner under the SAFER SKIES Act, as the
sponsoring agency.
2. Allow a single agency to file one collective application covering multiple
facilities.
Proposed §74.52(b) makes each application cover “only one fixed site facility even if the operator
or proprietor owns multiple eligible sites,” forcing a statewide corrections system to file a separate
application for every prison. That conflicts with Section 2209(b)(1)(B), under which the
procedures “shall allow” operators to apply “individually or collectively.” The FAA should revise
14See Section 2209(b)(1)(C)(iv).
15See Section 2209(b)(2)(C).
Page 5 of 7

§74.52(b) to let one operator file a single consolidated (portfolio) application across its eligible
facilities, or provide a streamlined template for an agency with many comparable sites.
3. Harmonize the rule with the SAFER SKIES Act.
Section 2209 dates to 2016, and this rule has been nearly a decade in the making. In the meantime,
Congress spoke again. The SAFER SKIES Act (passed December 2025; implementing regulations
effective July 1, 2026) now lets corrections agencies mitigate drones posing a credible threat to
their facilities. It makes little sense to authorize corrections to bring a drone down while denying
them the airspace designation that makes it unauthorized in the first place. As the FAA finally
implements Section 2209, it should read the Special UAFR credible-threat standard consistently
with Congress’ most recent expression of intent.
4. If only a Standard UAFR is granted, the FAA should still require facility
approval over the secure perimeter.
Even under a Standard UAFR, the §74.250/§74.255 notify-and-transit allowance should not apply
over a correctional perimeter—transit there should require the facility’s approval.16
5. The proposed rule should be revised to further clarify that it does not
preempt state laws that restrict drone operations in order to protect critical infrastructure
facilities or other sensitive sites within a State’s boundaries.
On December 3, 2022, gunfire attacks on two Duke Energy substations in Moore County, North
Carolina left thousands of citizens without power. While that incident involved firearms, the
conflict in Ukraine shows drones can similarly threaten state and national security. Ensuring states’
authority to enforce trespass and related criminal laws would prevent future offenders from later
challenging crucial state-level protections.
The Department is concerned that current or future state criminal trespassing laws prohibiting the
use of UAS around correctional facilities and other critical infrastructure could trigger a conflict
preemption review. Based on prior FAA guidance, the restrictions contemplated should not
implicate field preemption, because any such criminal trespassing laws would not concern airspace
safety or impair the reasonable use of the airspace. However, there is a concern that such laws may
trigger review for conflict preemption. Thus, the Department recommends that the FAA
acknowledge that states may impose criminal trespassing sanctions or other similar criminal laws
so long as they do not conflict with the limitations provided in the proposed rule. Specifically, if
the state laws, without intending to regulate aviation safety or efficient use of airspace, incorporate
definitions of “critical infrastructure” or “prohibited spaces” broader than the site categories in the
Rule in order to protect sensitive locations in the state that the FAA’s Rule does not otherwise
address. Such an acknowledgement in the rule would allow states to enact or enforce targeted
legislation without concern for creating or enforcing laws that have to be repealed, and it would
be consistent with the prevailing federal appellate precedent on this issue. See Nat’l Press
Photographers Assoc. v. McCraw, 90 F.4th 770, 795-98 (5th Cir. 2024).
16Proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.255; NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24653.
Page 6 of 7

VII. Conclusion
The Department appreciates the FAA’s recognition of the acute drone threat to correctional
facilities. To deliver the protection Congress intended, the final rule should do two things: give
correctional facilities access to an overflight-restricting Special UAFR — with DOJ as the
sponsoring agency—so that no drone may cross a secure perimeter without the facility's approval;
and honor Section 2209’s mandate by letting a single agency apply for its facilities collectively, in
one filing rather than one per prison. Read together with the SAFER SKIES Act, a rule so revised
would give prisons what they actually need and what would protect public safety: meaningful
control of the airspace above them.
Respectfully submitted,
Orlando L. Rodriguez
General Counsel
North Carolina Department of Adult Correction
214 W. Jones Street
Raleigh, NC 27603
Leslie.Dismukes@dac.nc.gov
