Re: Comments of the News Media Coalition regarding the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking Concerning Restricting the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close
Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
The News Media Coalition (“Coalition”) consists of more than fifteen news media
organizations, including local and national newspapers, broadcasters, cable networks,
websites, wire services, photojournalists, and nonprofits, that provide Americans each day
with the news they need. In addition, the Coalition’s members represent one of the sectors of
the economy that is most engaged with the development of sound Unmanned Aircraft
System (“UAS”) regulations and best practices.1 While the member companies compete in
markets across the country, they have come together for more than a decade in the unified
belief that preserving the right to gather news, including by UAS, is not a competitive
obligation but one of universal, and great, civic importance.
The Coalition hereby submits these comments regarding the Federal Aviation
Administration’s (“FAA”) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding Restricting the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility.2
1 Coalition members are listed below on page 7.
2 See Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a
Fixed Site Facility, 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (May 6, 2026) (to be codified at 14 C.F.R. Parts 1,
74, 91, and 107) (the “NPRM”).

Docket Operations, M-30
August 5, 2026
Page 2
INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY
UAS today are powerful tools for safe and effective newsgathering, and news
organizations employ and contract with UAS pilots and journalists to tell stories of both
local and national import. In contrast to many UAS use cases, however, the media’s current
UAS operations tend to be short-range—usually extending far less than one mile from
launch point. Moreover, while many UAS operations follow a designated flight plan from
Point A to Point B, news media operations require flexibility to follow the news as it
evolves.
The Coalition appreciates that the expansion of UAS operations may increase risk.
The Coalition believes, however, that in adopting a final rule regarding the designation of an
Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (“UAFR”), the FAA must provide for a balance of the
First Amendment rights to gather and report the news with on-the-ground concerns.
As more fully described herein, the Coalition writes to address several points
regarding the NPRM, including of most importance, the FAA’s proposal that any UAS
transiting an area covered by a UAFR be required to do so “in the shortest amount of time
practicable.” See, e.g. NPRM at 24690, Section 74.250(a)(2). The Coalition encourages the
FAA to more explicitly protect First Amendment UAS activities by making clear that UAS
operated by news organizations and journalists within a UAFR need not be limited in
duration, so long as the UAS is otherwise complying with all applicable rules and
regulations.
In addition, the Coalition encourages the FAA to modify several other aspects of its
proposed rule, including the following:
• To ensure that UAFRs are approved through a deliberative process, the FAA
must require that any fixed site facility seeking a UAFR make specific
showings before granting the designation.
• The FAA must provide the public with a meaningful opportunity to comment
prior to the grant of a UAFR. The Coalition encourages the FAA to not only
publish proposed UAFRs in the Federal Register but also to maintain a
website accessible to the public.
• The FAA should require agencies who receive heightened Special UAFRs to
publicly report denials of requests for permission from UAS operators to
transit the UAFR.

Docket Operations, M-30
August 5, 2026
Page 3
• The FAA should develop a process by which the public can challenge
existing UAFRs, and a mechanism for the public to provide information
relevant to the FAA’s ongoing supervision of the UAFR.
ARGUMENT
The Coalition recognizes that certain facilities may present particularly acute
concerns for the operation of UAS, and it supports the broad framework proposed by the
FAA. The Coalition, however, encourages the FAA to make several important
modifications to its proposal prior to adoption of the final rule.
I. The FAA should permit newsgathering UAS operations greater flexibility to
operate within a UAFR beyond “the shortest amount of time practicable.”
Of most concern is the FAA’s proposal to require that any UAS activity within a
UAFR be completed “in the shortest amount of time practicable.” NPRM at 24690, Section
74.250(a)(2). While the Coalition agrees with the FAA’s assessment that a “performance-
based objective” is more flexible than “operational restrictions for operations within a
UAFR” that would categorically prohibit things like “hovering,” it does not agree that the
FAA’s proposal is “broad enough to enable both legitimate transitory and non-transitory
operations within a UAFR.” Id. at 24676.
A. Regardless of intent, the plain language of the proposed rule prohibits non-
transitory operations and operations taking longer than necessary to
traverse the UAFR
Throughout the NPRM, the FAA states that it aims to “balance the mandate to ensure
public right of transit” with the “mandate to create a process for UAFRs.” Id. at 24660
(emphasis added). While the proposed rule purports that the FAA intends to permit “non-
transitory operations,” including First Amendment operations, within UAFRs, see id. at
24676, the language of the proposed rule is quite explicit in the opposite. Rather, as the draft
rule makes clear, UAS “may only operate within” a UAFR if the UAS “transitions the
UAFR in the shortest amount of time practicable.” Id. at 24690, Section 74.250(a)
(emphases added). That is, the proposed regulation explicitly contemplates that a UAS not
transiting in the shortest practicable duration could be found in violation of the regulation,
thereby subjecting its operator to both civil and criminal penalties. Id. at 24691, Section
74.260.
To state the obvious, news events rarely take place in a linear manner. It therefore
makes little sense to require news organizations to operate UAS in linear lines, traversing a
UAFR from Point A to Point B. And despite the FAA’s representation that it intends to

Docket Operations, M-30
August 5, 2026
Page 4
permit UAS engaged in First Amendment activity to conduct “non-transitory” operations,
that intent is in direct conflict with the express, unambiguous language of the draft rule. And
as the FAA is no doubt aware, courts are skeptical of permitting an agency’s intent to trump
the unambiguous language of a regulation. See, e.g., Advanced Energy United, Inc. v. FERC,
82 F.4th 1095, 1114 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (“This Court affords substantial deference to [an
agency’s] interpretation of its own regulations, unless the agency’s interpretation is plainly
erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation.”) (emphasis added; cleaned up).
The FAA should make explicit that UAS registered to news organizations may
operate within UAFR without traversing in the “shortest amount of time practicable” and
may instead conduct “non-transitory” operations.
B. The proposed rule fails to provide adequate guardrails and guidance for
fixed site operators to report UAS activities to law enforcement
The proposed rule also contemplates that operators of facilities covered by a UAFR
will be the primary point of contact to engage law enforcement if the operator believes that a
UAS is behaving in an unlawful manner. See, e.g., NPRM at 24651 (“Another benefit is that
the designation would help fixed site facilities and law enforcement distinguish between
lawful and unlawful operations.”). The Coalition believes that this scheme carries a
substantial risk that facility operators may claim that a news organization’s UAS is being
operated in an unlawful manner to shut down a journalist’s activities and prevent news
reporting, rather than to mitigate real risks to security.
The rule already contains three provisions that should reassure the security for fixed
site facilities: (1) only certain, professional UAS operations will be permitted within UAFRs
id. at 24690, Section 74.250(b)-(f); (2) any UAS operating within a UAFR will be required
to broadcast their Remote ID, which the facility must have the capability to monitor in real
time id. at 24690, Section 74.250(a)(1); and (3) any UAS seeking to operate in a UAFR will
be required to provide notice to the operator of the facility within the UAFR, further
ensuring that its operator will be able to triangulate and identify whether a UAS operating
above a UAFR is behaving lawfully. Id. at 24691, Section 74.255(c).
The FAA must include in the final rule explicit direction that if the UAS operator has
provided the required notice to the facility of the operation and is otherwise complying with
all applicable laws and regulations, the FAA should presume that the UAS is operating
lawfully. The final rule also should provide that any search or seizure of a UAS by law
enforcement, absent additional indicia of unlawful behavior, would run the risk of
constituting an unlawful search and seizure in violation of the Fourth Amendment. A law
enforcement investigation should not be triggered merely because a fixed site facility claims
that the UAS was not operating at a properly high rate of speed to transit the UAFR.

Docket Operations, M-30
August 5, 2026
Page 5
Absent explicit, and robust, protections for First Amendment activity within UAFRs,
the final rule risks precluding a significant portion of newsgathering operations out of fear of
interference by law enforcement for merely taking longer to transition than the facility
manager believes is “practicable.”
II. The FAA should modify several other aspects of its proposed rule
The Coalition also encourages the FAA to modify several additional elements of its
proposed rule.
First, the Coalition urges the FAA to strictly enforce its intent that before a facility
can obtain a UAFR, the facility must articulate a clear need for the restriction. Id. at 24686,
Section 74.54. As the FAA is aware, the categories of facilities that are eligible to seek
approval for a UAFR are incredibly broad, including everything from “amusement parks,
theme parks, and zoos,” to corporate headquarters of financial services facilities that house
“C-suite or high-value personnel,” to “food and agricultural” facilities and data centers. Id. at
24688, Sections 74.82, 74.89, 74.90, and 74.93(a). Absent strictly enforcing a requirement
that facilities provide concrete rationales, supported by evidence and data as appropriate, the
FAA risks creating a de facto nationwide “no fly zone” for UAS.
Second, while the FAA proposes to publish proposed UAFRs in the Federal Register
for notice and comment of at least 30 days prior to final approval, the proposed process
raises significant concerns that the FAA will preordain the decision before the notice-and-
comment period. Specifically, the FAA states that upon conditional grant of a UAFR—
which triggers the Federal Register publication—it “would have already considered the need
for and impacts of the requested UAFR,” and that comments would only inform the FAA’s
decision to the extent they raise “any new issues or unforeseen consequences.” Id. at 24673
(emphasis supplied). The FAA must provide the opportunity for robust public comment
before permitting private enterprise to restrict flight in the nation’s airspace. The FAA must
be willing to complete a de novo review of the proposed UAFR informed by public
comment.
Third, the FAA questions whether it should publish proposed UAFRs in the Federal
Register or on a website. The Coalition, however, encourages more transparency not less.
While the FAA is correct that at least some sector of the public “is familiar with the federal
register notice and comment process,” id. at 24674, at least as large a sector of the public has
never heard of the Federal Register and does not know how to find information in the
Federal Register. The FAA therefore should publish proposed UAFRs for comment in the
Federal Register and it should ensure that there is a public website that maintains a database

Docket Operations, M-30
August 5, 2026
Page 6
of all applications, proposed UAFRs and active UAFRs to provide fulsome public
transparency.
Fourth, and also in the name of transparency, the Coalition encourages the FAA to
require agencies whose facilities are protected by the heightened Special UAFRs to publicly
report denials of requests to operate within the UAFR. Affording agencies broad discretion
to restrict airspace, see id. at Section 74.251, without any corresponding requirement to
disclose when the agency has not granted UAS permission to operate within the UAFR, risks
agencies exercising their authority in an arbitrary and unequitable manner.
Fifth, while the FAA contemplates that UAFRs will be “subject to ongoing review by
the Administrator, id. at 24686, Section 74.20(c), the FAA does not provide any mechanism
by which the public may challenge an existing UAFR, or even a mechanism by which the
public may inform this “ongoing review.” There are a number of reasons why an existing
UAFR may no longer be warranted, whether due to changed circumstances or bad acts by
the fixed site facility operator, and the public must be provided the opportunity to challenge
an existing UAFR that is no longer serving its intended purpose.
CONCLUSION
Society is seeing, time and again, how news organizations, through UAS operations,
shed light on newsworthy events in a way, and on a scale, not previously thought possible.
These news reports not only serve journalists’ audiences, but also fill a critical role in the
emergency response system, allowing local law enforcement entities to enlist the help of
journalists to provide vital, timely information to ensure public safety during crises.
An increasingly flexible regulatory framework can both enhance the safety and
security of drones while encouraging innovative and important journalism. The FAA must
ensure, however, that its rules do not impede innovation. The Coalition appreciates the
opportunity to participate in this important regulatory process, and it encourages the FAA to
ensure that its UAFR regulations do not unintentionally impede the majority of news
organizations from engaging in these operations, by placing a thumb on the ability of
journalists to operate their UAS in the vicinity of important, and newsworthy facilities.
Sincerely,
Charles D. Tobin
Emmy Parsons

Date: July 6, 2026
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 Notice No. 26-03 Re: Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
To the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA):
This comment is submitted in response to the FAA's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)
implementing Section 2209, 91 FR 24650 (May 6, 2026), within the comment period as extended to
August 5, 2026 by Notice No. 26-03A, 91 FR 39568 (June 30, 2026). We strongly support the FAA’s
initiative and write from the perspective of stakeholders committed to advancing American airspace
sovereignty through the safe, secure, and lawful integration of UAS into the National Airspace System.
Establishing clear boundaries to protect sensitive locations from careless or unlawful unmanned aircraft
systems (UAS) is a vital step forward for the low-altitude ecosystem.
While the creation of Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) provides an essential legal tool to
distinguish between authorized operations and unauthorized threats, there are areas where the proposed
rule is vulnerable to legal challenge. To ensure this critically important rule is enforceable and can
withstand judicial scrutiny, we respectfully offer the following constructive recommendations to strengthen
the rule’s statutory alignment, administrative record, and technological security.
1. Advancing Airspace Sovereignty Through Legal Designation We commend the NPRM’s alignment
with Executive Order 14305, "Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty," which prioritizes protecting
critical infrastructure and sensitive installations. By establishing clear horizontal and vertical boundaries
(generally capped at 400 feet AGL), the UAFRs create a necessary "virtual no trespassing sign". While
the UAFR does not independently authorize counter-UAS (C-UAS) mitigation, it gives site operators and
law enforcement a vital, much-needed legal framework to distinguish between compliant operators and
unauthorized aerial threats, allowing them to focus their enforcement resources accordingly. This
framework has taken on new significance since publication of the NPRM. The DHS and DOJ joint Interim
Final Rule implementing the SAFER SKIES Act (FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act, Pub. L.
119-60, Div. H, Title LXXXVI; 6 U.S.C. 124n) took effect July 1, 2026 and was published July 6, 2026 at
91 FR 41466, with comments due September 4, 2026. It authorizes certified State, local, Tribal, and
territorial (SLTT) law enforcement and correctional agencies to conduct C-UAS operations, including
mitigation, subject to training, authorized-technology, airspace-coordination, and reporting requirements.
We note that under section 124.9 of that rule, FAA review of a proposed C-UAS operation is expressly
coordination rather than approval. The UAFR is the airspace-designation layer that should interlock with
that mitigation framework. We recommend the final rule explain how UAFR designations will interoperate
with SLTT C-UAS operations, including whether unauthorized operation within a UAFR may inform a
"credible threat" determination under the Interim Final Rule, and how the rule’s real-time air traffic control
notification procedures for mitigation actions will function within UAFR airspace.
2. Aligning Facility Eligibility with Statutory Authority to Ensure Durability To help ensure the final
rule withstands judicial review after Loper Bright, we recommend the FAA closely align the scope of
eligible facilities with the statutory text Congress enacted. In Section 929 of the 2024 FAA
Reauthorization Act, Congress explicitly amended Section 2209 to add state prisons while deliberately
removing the catch-all phrase “other locations that warrant such a restriction”.
By importing all 16 of the National Security Memorandum 22 (NSM-22) "critical infrastructure sectors"
(which includes unlisted facilities such as corporate headquarters, financial trading floors, and IT data
centers), the rule invites claims of regulatory overreach. Opponents will argue the FAA is expanding its
mandate beyond the explicitly named statutory sites (such as energy facilities, chemical plants, and
prisons). We encourage the FAA either to limit eligible facilities in the final rule to categories expressly

160 Newtown Rd, Suite 302 877.601.1860
Virginia Beach, VA 23462 droneup.com
identified in Section 2209, as amended, or to provide a category-by-category explanation showing how
each covered facility type falls within Congress’s delegation.
3. Clarifying the FAA's Exclusive Jurisdiction over Special UAFRs We fully support the creation of
Special UAFRs to protect our most sensitive federal and military installations from credible threats.
However, under proposed § 74.251, access to Special UAFRs requires the permission or approval of the
"using agency".
To protect the rule against claims of unlawful subdelegation of authority, we recommend the FAA clarify
the mechanics of this provision. Congress granted the FAA exclusive jurisdiction to manage the navigable
airspace under 49 U.S.C. 40103. The final text should make clear that the "using agency" may provide
security assessments, mission-specific information, and recommendations, but that the FAA retains final,
non-delegable authority to approve, deny, condition, or revoke access to the National Airspace System
under standards stated in the rule. Recent operational experience underscores this concern. In June
2026, the FAA amended its FIFA World Cup security NOTAMs to route operator access requests through
a DHS point of contact, with no published decision standards or service-level response timelines, after
commercial operators holding valid airspace authorizations were grounded by the initial restrictions. To
avoid replicating that outcome under § 74.251, the final rule should require published decision criteria,
defined response timelines for access requests, and a clear statement that final authority rests with the
FAA Administrator.
4. Fortifying the Administrative Record for Rule Mechanics To ensure the rule’s operational
requirements are not deemed arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act, the FAA
should expand upon the scientific or risk-based justifications for its specific metrics. For instance, the
NPRM proposes a "part-time" flight restriction capped at 290 consecutive days. The FAA should explain
the evidentiary or operational basis for the 290-day threshold, including why that duration reasonably
distinguishes temporary or part-time restrictions from restrictions requiring different treatment, so that the
final rule reflects reasoned decision-making under the Administrative Procedure Act.
Additionally, proposed § 74.250 requires authorized drones to transit restricted airspace "in the shortest
practicable time," a requirement that may limit hovering, loitering, or other observational uses within a
UAFR. We support this security measure, but recommend the FAA explain in the final rule how the transit
requirement is tailored to safety and security needs and how the authorization process preserves
reasonable access for protected activities, including newsgathering, where consistent with facility
security. The FAA also now has operational and litigation experience that was unavailable when the
NPRM was drafted. Public reports indicate more than 600 drone seizures near FIFA World Cup venues
as of July 2026. In January 2026 the FAA issued NOTAM 6/4375 restricting UAS operations near
Department of Homeland Security facilities and mobile assets; after a petition for review was filed in the
U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit raising First Amendment, vagueness, and Administrative
Procedure Act claims, the FAA rescinded that restriction in April 2026 and replaced it with an advisory
notice. That sequence is instructive here: an airspace restriction that lacks published boundaries, decision
criteria, and access procedures is difficult to sustain. We encourage the FAA to incorporate this 2026
enforcement and litigation record into the administrative record supporting the final rule’s access, transit,
and newsgathering provisions.
5. Requiring Trusted Compliance Infrastructure and Enforcing FCC Covered List Restrictions. The
practical enforcement of airspace sovereignty depends on trusted compliance infrastructure. The
Department of Transportation has already recognized, in other safety-critical transportation contexts, that
enforceable rules often require reliable electronic records capable of verifying compliance rather than
relying solely on operator assertions. The same principle should guide UAFR implementation. Legal
restrictions alone will not allow fixed-site facilities, law enforcement, or the FAA to distinguish lawful
operations from unauthorized threats unless the supporting identity and monitoring architecture is reliable,
machine-readable, and resistant to manipulation. Accordingly, the FAA should ensure that UAFR
implementation is supported by authenticated Remote ID reception, audit-ready access records, and
tamper-resistant operational data sufficient to verify whether an aircraft was authorized, whether it
remained within the terms of authorization, whether the aircraft identity can be reliably attributed to the

160 Newtown Rd, Suite 302 877.601.1860
Virginia Beach, VA 23462 droneup.com
responsible operator, and whether such records are retained for a defined period sufficient to support
enforcement and judicial review.
The practical enforcement of airspace sovereignty also relies on ensuring that the technological
capabilities of fixed-site facilities are secure, trusted, and interoperable with federal enforcement needs.
Under proposed § 74.56, eligible facilities must maintain protective security that includes passive RF, Wi-
Fi, or Bluetooth equipment capable of receiving Remote ID broadcasts. The federal restrictions governing
that class of equipment changed fundamentally after this NPRM was drafted, and the final rule should be
written against the current framework rather than the entity-based framework that preceded it.
On December 21, 2025, an interagency national security determination concluded that foreign-produced
unmanned aircraft systems and UAS critical components present an unacceptable risk to national
security absent a contrary determination by the Department of War or the Department of Homeland
Security. Implementing that determination and Section 1709 of the FY2025 National Defense
Authorization Act, Pub. L. 118-159, the Federal Communications Commission on December 22, 2025
added to the Covered List all UAS and UAS critical components produced in a foreign country, together
with the communications and video surveillance equipment and services identified in Section 1709(a)(1)
(Public Notice DA 25-1086). "UAS critical components" expressly include data transmission devices,
communications systems, flight controllers, ground control stations, navigation systems, sensors and
cameras, batteries and battery management systems, motors, and associated software. The restriction is
therefore categorical and origin-based rather than limited to any single manufacturer. Because the
covered categories include the radiofrequency and data-transmission components from which Remote ID
sensing equipment is built, the protective security requirement of proposed section 74.56 cannot be read
in isolation from them.
We strongly support this framework and oppose efforts by foreign UAS manufacturers, including through
the petitions for review now pending in the U.S. Courts of Appeals, to circumvent or narrow these national
security restrictions. We recognize that the FCC, in its July 2, 2026 actions supporting SAFER SKIES Act
implementation, waived certain equipment authorization requirements and granted temporary spectrum
authority for C-UAS systems on the Authorized Systems List. Our recommendation is accordingly focused
on supply-chain trust rather than authorization paperwork: the FAA should require, to the extent within its
statutory authority and in coordination with the FCC, the Department of Commerce, and DHS, that
sensing equipment, networking hardware, ground control and monitoring software, and third-party
security monitoring services procured or used by covered facilities for UAFR monitoring be screened
against the FCC Covered List and other federal restrictions on covered communications or surveillance
equipment, even where equipment authorization requirements are otherwise waived. A waiver of
equipment authorization is a procedural accommodation; it is not a supply-chain risk determination, and
the final rule should not permit it to function as one. Recent FCC actions also demonstrate that
grandfathering windows for covered equipment can close. On June 26, 2026, the FCC prohibited the
continued importation and marketing of previously authorized equipment from Covered List entities
designated in 2024 or earlier (DA 26-635), and in PS Docket No. 26-184 the Commission has proposed
extending that prohibition to foreign-produced UAS and UAS critical components (DA 26-742; 91 FR
48108, comments due August 31, 2026). Separately, the Commission's Third Report and Order adopted
July 23, 2026 (FCC 26-50) bars authorization of devices containing covered logic-bearing hardware
components and revises the definition of "critical infrastructure" on remand, a definition that will govern
how use-based restrictions apply to the facilities this rule designates. On July 21, 2026, the Commission
removed the December 31, 2026 termination date for conditional approvals of foreign-produced UAS and
UAS critical components, conditioning continued validity on adherence to an approved onshoring plan,
and extended the Blue UAS Cleared List and domestic-end-product exemptions to January 1, 2028 (DA
26-761). These actions extend availability; they do not confer permanence. The final rule should therefore
caution facilities against building UAFR monitoring infrastructure on equipment subject to near-term
regulatory expiration. Allowing America's most sensitive critical infrastructure sites to use compromised,
foreign-made technology to monitor UAFRs creates an unacceptable national security vulnerability, and
FAA and FCC policies should be harmonized so that UAFR monitoring infrastructure does not depend on
equipment or services that federal law identifies as posing an unacceptable national security risk.

160 Newtown Rd, Suite 302 877.601.1860
Virginia Beach, VA 23462 droneup.com
Two further points bear on the final rule. First, many facilities eligible for UAFR designation will procure
monitoring equipment using federal grant or contract funds and are therefore already subject to the
American Security Drone Act of 2023, Pub. L. 118-31, which since December 22, 2025 has prohibited the
use of federal funds to procure or operate covered foreign entity UAS, implemented through FAR subpart
40.2 and FAR 52.240-1 and, for federal financial assistance, through OMB Memorandum M-26-02.
Because Executive Order 14305 directs federal C-UAS grant support, the final rule should state this
restriction plainly so that facilities encounter it before procurement rather than after. Second, the
Department of Commerce's information and communications technology and services rulemaking for
unmanned aircraft systems, 90 FR 279, remains at the advance notice stage; when finalized on the
model of the connected vehicles rule, 90 FR 5620, it will reach the software, firmware, and cloud service
layers that equipment authorization does not. We recommend the FAA commit to coordinating UAFR
monitoring guidance with that rulemaking rather than treating FCC equipment authorization as the sole
measure of trust. Finally, because perimeter security at these sites increasingly relies on unmanned
ground vehicles and other connected autonomous platforms, a category to which the FY2026 National
Defense Authorization Act extended covered entity procurement prohibitions, we recommend the FAA
articulate the trust requirement in technology-neutral terms rather than confining it to Remote ID reception
hardware.
6. Conclusion We commend the FAA for taking this foundational step to protect critical infrastructure and
restore American airspace sovereignty. By refining the rule’s statutory scope, clarifying FAA decision-
making authority over Special UAFR access, coordinating UAFR designations with the SAFER SKIES C-
UAS framework, explaining the evidentiary basis for operational metrics, incorporating the 2026
enforcement and litigation record, addressing First Amendment considerations, harmonizing monitoring-
technology requirements with the current country-of-origin restrictions on foreign-produced UAS and UAS
critical components, and stating plainly the federal procurement restrictions that already bind facilities
purchasing monitoring equipment with federal funds, the FAA can finalize a robust, legally sound
framework that will secure our skies for years to come.
If you have any questions or wish further discussion, please contact Jonathan Daniels, VP of
Governance, Risk and Compliance at jonathan.daniels@droneup.com
Sincerely,
John Vernon
CEO

COMMENTS OF OFFICES OF ATTORNEYS GENERAL OF NEW YORK,
ARIZONA, CALIFORNIA, COLORADO, DELAWARE, NEW JERSEY,
NORTH CAROLINA, AND VERMONT
August 5, 2026
via www.regulations.gov
William “Liam” McKenna Michelle Ferritto
Chief Counsel Office of Rulemaking
Federal Aviation Administration Federal Aviation Administration
800 Independence Avenue SW 800 Independence Avenue SW
Washington, D.C. 20591 Washington, D.C. 20591
Re: Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close
Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility, 91 Fed. Reg. 24,650 (May 6, 2026)
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558
Dear Liam McKenna and Michelle Ferritto:
The Offices of the Attorneys General of New York, Arizona, California,
Colorado, Delaware, New Jersey, North Carolina, and Vermont (the AGs)
respectfully submit these public comments on the Federal Aviation Administration
(“Administration” or “FAA”)’s notice of proposed rulemaking titled Designation—
Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility (the “Proposed Rule” or the “Rule”), which the Administration published in
the Federal Register on May 6, 2026.1 The Proposed Rule would “establish[] a
process for operators and proprietors of certain fixed site facilities to request and
maintain an unmanned aircraft flight restriction” (“UAFR”) and also “identifies the
types of operations that are allowed in the [UAFR].”2
The AGs have six principal suggestions for critical revisions to the Proposed
Rule.
First, the FAA should clarify that the Rule would not have the effect of
preempting current or future state laws or regulations that restrict operation of
drones in low-altitude airspace in the proximity of state-defined critical
1 Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility, 91 Fed. Reg. 24,650 (May 6, 2026). On June 30, 2026, the FAA published a
notice in the Federal Register granting the Office of the New York State Attorney General’s
request to extend the deadline for public comments on the Proposed Rule through August 5,
2026. 91 Fed. Reg. 39,568 (June 30, 2026).
2 Proposed Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. at 24,650.

infrastructure sites, even where a State’s definition of “critical infrastructure” in
this context includes site categories not covered by the FAA proposal.
Second, the FAA should clarify how it will provide a secure channel for
facilities to submit sensitive information in support of their applications for a
UAFR, and for FAA to receive public comment on those applications, in order to
avoid the risk that bad actors will exploit such information if it is publicly disclosed
by FAA.
Third, the FAA should provide broader carve-outs to State and local
government agencies that operate unmanned aircraft for various legitimate
government purposes, often on highly confidential or time-sensitive missions, such
as for emergency response actions, active law enforcement operations and
authorized investigative activities, and environmental and wildlife monitoring.
Fourth, the FAA should provide a mechanism in the Rule for State
corrections agencies, which face a heightened need to restrict their airspace from
drones to prevent contraband-related interference, to submit a single application
under proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.251 that would allow all correctional facilities
operated by that State agency to be protected by a “Special UAFR” under the Rule,
without the need for multiple applications for a UAFR by each individual prison
facility.
Fifth, the FAA should clarify the interplay between State and local agency
implementation of Standard UAFR and Special UAFR designations for certain
facilities, and the requirements of the July 6, 2026 Interim Final Rule under the
Safer Skies Act issued by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S.
Department of Justice, which “authorizes State, local, Tribal, and territorial law
enforcement or correctional agencies to conduct counter-unmanned aircraft system
(‘‘C–UAS’’) operations.”3
Finally, the FAA should clarify that, once the Rule is implemented, the FAA
will make relevant UAFR data available in machine readable format to drone
operators, including to State and local agencies, by integrating the data into the
most common FAA and commercial software products for drone pilots.
3 See Counter-UAS Authority for State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial Law Enforcement and
Correctional Agencies, 91 Fed. Reg. 41,466 (July 6, 2026).
2

I. FAA Should Further Clarify That the Proposed Rule Does Not
Preempt State Laws That Restrict Drone Operations in Order
to Protect Critical Infrastructure Facilities or Other Sensitive
Sites Within a State’s Boundaries.
In the decade since Congress in 2016 directed the Administration to
“establish a process to allow applicants to petition the [FAA] to prohibit or restrict
the operation of an unmanned aircraft in close proximity to a fixed site facility,”4
multiple states have adopted laws that criminalize or otherwise restrict knowing
operation of drones in the vicinity of certain kinds of critical infrastructure or other
sensitive sites within the state.5 Other states may adopt similar laws in the future.
These state laws are an exercise of traditional state police power, intended to
protect sites on the ground from improper encroachments or interference by drones.
Congress did not intend the FAA’s regulations implementing section 2209 to
preempt such state laws. The AGs urge the FAA to further clarify that state laws
and regulations—including state laws imposing restrictions on drone operations in
the airspace of categories of sensitive sites beyond those covered by the Rule—are
not preempted under any theory of preemption.
As courts have recognized, “the Federal Aviation Act [of 1958], which . . .
remains the foundation of federal aviation law today, contains no express
preemption provision.” Sikkelee v. Precision Airmotive Corp., 822 F.3d 680, 692 (3d
Cir. 2016). In 2024, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals held that a law enacted by
the State of Texas that made it “illegal to fly a drone above sensitive sites like
critical infrastructure facilities, prisons, and large sports venues” was not field
preempted by the Federal Aviation Act or any FAA regulations thereunder. See
Nat’l Press Photographers Assoc. v. McCraw, 90 F.4th 770, 795-98 (5th Cir. 2024).
The Fifth Circuit reasoned that “the FAA has expressly declined to preempt all
state regulation of drones. In promulgating a final agency rule on drone regulation,
the agency stated, ‘The FAA . . . reviewed the comments and . . . decided that
specific regulatory text addressing preemption is not required in the final rule.’”
McGraw, 90 F.4th at 796.6
4 FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. No. 114-190, § 2209, 130 Stat.
615, 635 (2016).
5 See https://www.dronelaws.us/federal-preemption#state-ci (“Roughly fourteen states have
enacted drone-specific critical infrastructure statutes that we have been able to verify
against authoritative sources.”).
6 The Fifth Circuit was quoting the FAA’s statement in its 2016 final rule, Operation and
Certification of Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems, 81 Fed. Reg. 42,064-01, 42,194 (June
28, 2016).
3

The Fifth Circuit in McGraw discussed the FAA’s State and Local Regulation
of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Fact Sheet, which was last issued by FAA’s
Office of Chief Counsel and the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of
General Counsel in July 2023 (the “2023 FAA Fact Sheet”).7 Id. at 797. The court
emphasized that based on the 2023 FAA Fact Sheet, “‘security-related restrictions
over open-air water treatment facilities or certain types of critical infrastructure’
are likely not to be preempted, particularly if the restrictions are ‘limited to the
lower altitudes.’” Id. (quoting 2023 FAA Fact Sheet at p.6). The court concluded that
given that discussion in the 2023 FAA Fact Sheet, the challenged Texas provisions,
“which prohibit drone flights less than 400 feet over critical infrastructure, are thus
expressly permitted, not preempted.” Id.8
Congress, in enacting section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and
Security Act of 2016, did not in any way indicate that the UAFR procedures that it
was directing the FAA to establish would have the effect of preempting existing or
future state laws. In fact, in providing a statutory definition of “fixed site facilities”
eligible to submit a petition for drone restrictions, Congress included a catch-all by
including “other locations that warrant such restrictions,” in addition to listing
specific categories of fixed facilities, i.e., “critical infrastructure, such as energy
production, transmission, and distribution facilities and equipment; oil refineries
and chemical facilities; and amusement parks.”9 This indicates that congressional
intent was not to insist upon an exclusive or static definition of “fixed site facilities.”

FAA has the exclusive authority to regulate aviation safety and the
efficient use of the airspace by aircraft; the public relies on FAA
regulations for direction and clarity. Attempts by State and local
governments to regulate in the fields of aviation safety and the efficient
use of the airspace by aircraft are preempted. Outside those fields, the
States are generally free to regulate—even by enacting laws that affect
aviation—as long as their laws do not conflict with FAA regulations, are
not aimed at regulating aviation safety or airspace efficiency, and do not
relate to the prices, routes, or services of commercial air carriers. FAA
anticipates this proposed rule would reduce regulatory confusion in the
national airspace for unmanned aircraft access.11
This provision of the Proposed Rule cites to the 2023 FAA Fact Sheet, paraphrasing
the Fact Sheet as stating that “laws aimed at objectives other than aviation safety
or airspace efficiency—such as privacy—that do not impair the reasonable use by
UAS of the airspace would likely not be subject to preemption.”12
The AGs are concerned that the Rule’s reference to hypothetical conflicts
between state laws and FAA regulations—reflected in the clause “as long as their
laws do not conflict with FAA regulations”—is vague without additional context or
examples, and could contribute to, rather than reduce, “regulatory confusion in the
national airspace for unmanned aircraft access.” 91 Fed. Reg. at 24,656.
State laws that impose restrictions on the operation of drones in the vicinity
of critical infrastructure sites, like the Texas law at issue in McGraw, may
incorporate definitions of “critical infrastructure” that differ from those to be
codified in the FAA Rule. Additionally, such state laws may include protections for
other sensitive sites that do not strictly qualify as “critical infrastructure” under a
state’s own statutory or regulatory definition of that term. The lack of a perfect
overlap between the FAA’s delineation of “critical infrastructure” site categories in
the Rule and a state’s delineation of “critical infrastructure” in its state drone
restrictions law should not be a basis for a finding that such a state law is
preempted by FAA regulations.
Additionally, the absence of any conflict between the Rule and a state law
like that at issue in the McGraw case is illustrated by the fact that a drone operator
would be able to comply with any flight restrictions under the Rule and with such a
state drone law. The Rule itself does not, upon promulgation, automatically

and Security Act, the statute directed FAA to establish “procedures [that] shall
allow operators or proprietors of fixed site facilities to apply for designation
individually or collectively.”28 In the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Congress
amended section 2209 to include State prisons in addition to the initial list of
critical infrastructure site categories that could seek a UAFR.29
The Proposed Rule highlights the need to protect State prisons from the risks
of drone-introduced contraband and related concerns:
Unmanned aircraft pose a significant challenge for State prisons. Many
incidents of unmanned aircraft being used to infiltrate State prisons to
deliver contraband such as cellphones, drugs, and weapons have been
reported. Unmanned aircraft threaten existing security protocols and
perimeter control, and they can also be used to conduct surveillance.30
Richardson, 208 F.3d 626, 629 (7th Cir. 2000). The AGs’ understanding is that “time-
sensitive” drone missions will include those to prevent harm to persons or protected natural
resources, to prevent the destruction of relevant evidence or the escape of a suspect, or to
prevent some other consequence improperly frustrating legitimate law enforcement efforts.

V. FAA Should Confirm That State and Local Agencies That Have
Obtained “Mitigation Certification” Under the Safer Skies
Interim Final Rule Have Lawful Independent Authority to
Conduct Counter-UAS Operations Within Any Standard UAFR.
Counter-UAS measures are the strategic, operational, and technical actions
used to detect, track, identify, mitigate, and neutralize unauthorized or hostile
drones.
The Proposed Rule clarifies that the establishment of a UAFR “does not
authorize the use of detection or mitigation technologies to interfere with
unmanned aircraft” and that “the UAFR alone does not create a physical or
electromagnetic boundary to prevent unauthorized access. However, facilities with
independent authority to operate such systems may continue to do so lawfully, and
manufacturers may leverage the publicly available UAFR database.”34 Further, as
to Special UAFRs, “[f]acility operators with separate statutory authority to deploy
counter-UAS technologies may continue existing practices; however, this proposed
rule does not grant or expand such authorities.”35
The AGs recommend that the FAA explicitly confirm that State, local, Tribal,
and territorial (SLTT) agencies holding a “Mitigation Certification” under the Safer
Skies Interim Final Rule (IFR) possess lawful, independent authority to conduct
counter-UAS operations within at least Standard UAFR-designated airspace. The
joint DOJ and DHS Safter Skies framework—which went into effect on July 1,
2026—provides vetted State, local, Tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies
with the active electronic and kinetic tools needed to legally disrupt, disable, or
seize threat drones. Without explicit alignment in the FAA’s Rule’s final text, State
and local agencies potentially risk facing regulatory ambiguity or conflicting federal
enforcement actions when looking to actively neutralize a drone threat inside an
FAA-approved UAFR.

Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility”; Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; RIN 2120-AL33
Dear Administrator Bedford:
On behalf of its membership, the Correctional Leaders Association (“CLA”) submits these comments on the FAA’s
proposed rule to implement Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016. As you may know,
CLA members are the highest appointed chief executive corrections officials and leaders for each U.S. state
corrections agency, the Federal Bureau of Prisons, U.S. Armed Services Corrections, any U.S. Territory, Possession
and/or Commonwealth, the District of Columbia, and several large jail systems including New York City, Philadelphia,
and Los Angeles County. All told, CLA members represent over 400,000 corrections professionals and have
command authority over 8 million incarcerated people, parolees, and felony probationers. CLA welcomes this
rulemaking and supports the FAA’s decision to build a durable framework for restricting drone operations over
vulnerable sites. We offer these comments in a spirit of partnership: we support the rule, and we urge the FAA to
close the gaps that would, as drafted, deny the nation’s prisons the one protection that would actually keep drones off
their perimeters.
II. Background
A. Corrections Confronts a Daily, Operational Drone Threat
For most of the public, the drone-safety conversation is about the occasional hobbyist or a crowd drawn to a stadium
or a special event. For most eligible facilities, the concern is what a drone might someday do—the threat is
hypothetical. For corrections it is neither hypothetical nor occasional; it is daily and relentless. Across CLA’s
membership, criminal networks fly drones over secure perimeters to deliver narcotics, weapons, and cellphones into
prison yards—cargo that fuels overdoses, assaults, and the remote operation of criminal enterprises from inside
prison walls. The FAA acknowledges this reality in the NPRM. Because the threat is continuous and nationwide, it
cannot be solved one facility or one agency at a time; it is precisely the harm Congress had in mind when it placed
prisons on the Section 2209 list. Illustrative incidents and aggregate figures from CLA member agencies appear in
Part B below.
B. The Threat by the Numbers: Data from Member Agencies
Drone-borne contraband is a widespread and worsening problem in state prisons nationwide, and the experience of
CLA’s member agencies bears that out. The following figures are offered as representative examples of that broader
pattern, not as its outer limits. Georgia’s Department of Corrections recorded 491 drone-related contraband incidents
at state prisons in calendar year 2025—and has already recorded more than 300 in 2026, a pace that would far
exceed last year’s record. According to public reporting, South Carolina’s Department of Corrections logged 273
drone-smuggling incidents across its 21 prisons in 2025, and officials intercepted a single drone carrying 464 grams
of fentanyl—by the director’s account, enough to kill everyone in the facility. These are not isolated events. Public
reporting documents the same pattern in prison systems across the country—from New York to California to the
federal prison system—confirming that drone-borne contraband is a national problem, not a regional one. For
corrections agencies nationwide, this is a nightly reality.

II. CLA Supports the Two-Tier Framework—But Only a Special UAFR Protects a Prison
CLA supports the two-tier structure—Standard and Special UAFRs—that the FAA proposes under the new
Part 74. But for a correctional facility, the two tiers are not interchangeable: only a Special UAFR—which bars
any drone from entering without the facility's permission—will actually keep an unauthorized drone from
crossing a prison fence. A Standard UAFR, which allows operators to transit the airspace on notice, will not.
Correctional facilities therefore need the protection the Special tier provides—and as proposed, the rule
denies it to them.
A. The Standard Tier As Currently Drafted Cannot Protect a Prison
The Standard UAFR will not stop overflight. Under proposed § 74.250, aircraft operating under Parts 91, 107, 108,
135, and 137 may enter the restricted airspace so long as they broadcast Remote ID, cross in the “shortest
practicable time,” and notify the facility. For a prison, that is no protection at all: it authorizes exactly the low, brief
overflight used to drop contraband, and the smugglers CLA’s members confront will never file the notice the rule
contemplates. Only the Special UAFR imposes a real gate—§ 74.251 bars any operation from entering unless the
responsible (“using”) agency grants permission and the FAA approves. Facility-controlled access of that kind is what
a correctional perimeter requires. The difficulty is that the rule all but closes that gate to prisons.
B. The FAA Should Make Special UAFRs Available to State Corrections Departments
Proposed § 74.6(a) makes a Special UAFR available to facilities owned or sponsored by federal security agencies or
military departments, and lets a non-federal site qualify only if it is sponsored by the FAA or a federal intelligence or
security agency such as DHS, DOD, DOE, or DOJ. The Department of Justice appears on that list, but the rule
creates no process by which a state department of corrections may seek or obtain sponsorship—no criteria, no
application channel, and no obligation for any federal agency to respond. The FAA compounds the problem by
modeling the Special pathway on the national-security instrument in 14 C.F.R. § 99.7. The suggestion is that the only
designation capable of stopping overflight is, in practice, unavailable to the very facilities Congress singled out for
protection. This restriction is not only unworkable; it departs from the statute itself. See Section III below.
The FAA’s supplemental request for data on the costs UAS operators would incur to transit—or to be excluded
from—UAFRs invites exactly the comparison that should decide this issue. A correctional facility is a compact, well-
defined site; for a commercial operator, the cost of a perimeter exclusion is the marginal expense of routing a flight
around it—typically a detour of seconds. For the facility, the cost of permitting transit is measured in fentanyl,
weapons, and cellphones delivered over the fence. Whatever the data show about transit costs generally, they
cannot justify preserving a transit allowance over correctional facilities. At other fixed site facilities, an overflight and
an attack are different events; at a prison they are the same event—a contraband drop takes seconds and is
indistinguishable, until the package falls, from a lawful transit. A transit allowance over a prison perimeter does not
merely tolerate an inconvenience; it licenses the precise maneuver the restriction exists to prevent.
To be sure, Congress has recently recognized the corrections drone threat. The FAA need not decide in the abstract
whether prisons face a credible drone threat; Congress has answered that question. The SAFER SKIES Act
authorizes state, local, tribal, and territorial law-enforcement and corrections agencies—after training and
certification—to detect, track, and mitigate drones that pose a credible threat to correctional facilities. It is difficult to
reconcile a federal statute that empowers corrections to bring down a threatening drone with a rule that withholds the
airspace designation needed to make that drone’s presence unlawful in the first place. The two should work together.
Reading the Special UAFR’s credible-threat standard in harmony with the SAFER SKIES Act also points to the
natural federal partner for correctional facilities: the Department of Justice, already corrections’ counter-UAS partner
under that Act, is well positioned to serve as the sponsoring agency § 74.6(a) requires.

III. The Proposal Conflicts with Section 2209: It Denies Collective Applications and Imposes a National-Security
Precondition Congress Did Not Enact
Section 2209 does more than authorize this rulemaking; it sets terms the FAA must honor. It provides, in relevant
part:
SEC. 2209. APPLICATIONS FOR DESIGNATION.
(a) APPLICATIONS FOR DESIGNATION.—Not later than 180 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the
Secretary of Transportation shall establish a process to allow applicants to petition the Administrator of the
Federal Aviation Administration to prohibit or restrict, including temporarily, the operation of an unmanned aircraft
in close proximity to a fixed site facility.
(b) REVIEW PROCESS.—
(1) APPLICATION PROCEDURES.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—The Administrator shall establish the procedures for the application for designation
under subsection (a).
(B) REQUIREMENTS.—The procedures shall allow operators or proprietors of fixed site facilities to
apply for designation individually or collectively.
(C) CONSIDERATIONS.—Only the following may be considered fixed site facilities:
(i) Critical infrastructure, such as energy production, transmission, distribution facilities and equipment,
and railroad facilities.
(ii) Oil refineries and chemical facilities.
(iii) Amusement parks.
(iv) State prisons.
First, Congress required a genuine collective option. As the text makes plain, the FAA’s procedures “shall allow
operators or proprietors of fixed site facilities to apply for designation individually or collectively.” The proposed rule,
however, ties each UAFR to a single fixed site facility—each application covers “only one fixed site facility even if the
operator or proprietor owns multiple eligible sites”—and reads “collectively” to mean only that several parties
interested in one facility may join a single request. A “collective” option limited to parties who share an interest in a
single facility does no work that “individually” does not already do; the FAA’s reading renders the word superfluous.
For CLA’s members—agencies that each operate dozens of prisons—that reading writes the collective option out of
the rule. A department responsible for dozens of facilities cannot apply “collectively” in any meaningful sense if the
rule forces a separate application for every institution. The burden is not hypothetical: the FAA’s own Regulatory
Impact Analysis estimates that a single application will cost roughly $5,000 to $10,000 to prepare, so a statewide
system would multiply that cost many times over—and would do so while corrections agencies nationwide are
managing severe, well-documented staffing shortages. The FAA should honor the statute by creating a genuine
portfolio pathway that lets one agency cover all of its facilities in a single, consolidated application.
Second, Congress did not make national security a precondition. It listed “State prisons” as eligible fixed site
facilities in their own right, alongside critical infrastructure and other categories, and it directed the Administrator to
weigh four distinct considerations—aviation safety, protection of persons and property on the ground, national
security, and homeland security—none of which is a prerequisite to the others. By offering prisons only the porous
Standard tier while reserving the effective Special tier for national-security and military sites, the proposal collapses
those distinct considerations into one and demotes a facility category Congress made eligible on its own terms.
“Protection of persons and property on the ground” fits a prison exactly, and it carries no national-security predicate.
Nor can the Standard tier alone satisfy the statute: a designation that expressly permits transiting overflight does not
“prohibit or restrict” drone operations over a prison in any sense Section 2209(a) contemplates.

IV. Recommendations
1. Create a collective, multi-facility (portfolio) application pathway
Proposed § 74.52(b) forces a statewide corrections system to file a separate application for every prison. The
FAA should instead let a single correctional agency cover all of its facilities through one consolidated (portfolio)
application, supported by shared materials—which is what Section 2209’s “individually or collectively”
command requires, and the change that is critical to CLA’s multi-facility members.
2. Guarantee correctional facilities an overflight-restricting UAFR.
On a qualifying application, a correctional facility should receive a UAFR under which no unmanned aircraft
may operate over the secure perimeter without the facility’s approval. The FAA can deliver that protection by
either of two routes:
(a) Open the Special tier.
Section 74.6 should not be limited to federal and military facilities. The credible-threat/ verified-security-
assessment pathway must clearly cover state, local, and tribal correctional facilities; a documented pattern of
drone-contraband incursions should satisfy the credible-threat showing; and the rule should establish a defined
process by which the Department of Justice—corrections’ counter-UAS partner under the SAFER SKIES Act—
serves as the § 74.6(a) sponsor.
(b) Fix the Standard tier.
Replace the § 74.250/§ 74.255 notify-and-transit model with facility approval before any operation may cross a
correctional secure perimeter.
3. Right-size the restricted airspace.
Allow correctional applicants to extend the lateral boundary beyond property lines where secure-perimeter
buffer and launch-standoff distances warrant; the default 400-foot AGL, property-line limit is a poor fit for
contraband delivery launched from just outside the fence line.
4. Recognize corrections as the ideal, low-burden implementer.
Correctional facilities are small, fixed sites with clearly defined footprints, which makes overflight restrictions
easy to contain without disrupting legitimate traffic in the national airspace system. CLA is committed to
disciplined, professional implementation across its membership and offers to partner with the FAA as a model
for safe state and local practice.
5. Streamline applications, protect sensitive information, and avoid an equipment precondition.
Provide a streamlined pathway, model application templates, and technical assistance; protect security-
sensitive application materials from public disclosure; and do not condition a designation on a facility’s prior
acquisition of Remote ID detection equipment.
6. Provide durable designations and an expedited interim pathway.
Congress directed the Secretary to establish this application process within 180 days of Section 2209's
enactment in July 2016. Nearly a decade has passed, and drone incursions at correctional facilities have
multiplied year after year. Every additional year without a final rule is another year of contraband deliveries that
no facility can lawfully prevent. CLA urges the FAA to finalize the rule promptly, create low-burden renewal,
and offer an interim or expedited designation mechanism for correctional facilities pending full Part 74
implementation.
CLA Headquarters PO Box 102 Iona, Idaho 83427
Phone 208-557-8264
www.correctionalleaders.com

Executive Committee Regional Representatives
President, Lindsay Wallace Northeast, Dan Martuscello
Vice President, Bobby Lumpkin Southern, Tyrone Oliver
Treasurer, Laurel Harry Midwest, Jeff Zmuda
Past President, Rob Jeffreys Western, Dan Shannon
V. Conclusion
CLA represents the correctional leaders who live with this threat every day. We ask the FAA to make two things true
in the final rule: that a prison which applies can actually keep drones off its perimeter, and that a single agency can
protect all of its facilities through one collective application, as Section 2209 requires. Aligned with the SAFER SKIES
Act, a rule so revised would give the nation’s correctional facilities the airspace protection Congress intended. CLA
stands ready to serve as a resource and partner throughout the rulemaking and the implementation of Part 74. We
urge the FAA to finalize this rule with our recommended changes forthwith.
Respectfully submitted,
Kevin Kempf

To Whom It May Concern:

The Williams Companies, Inc. (“Williams”) appreciates the opportunity to comment on
the Federal Aviation Administration’s (“FAA”) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking implementing
Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, which would establish a
process for operators of certain fixed site facilities to petition for unmanned aircraft flight
restrictions (“UAFRs”). Williams is one of the nation’s largest energy infrastructure companies,
owning and operating interstate natural gas transmission and gathering pipelines, compressor
stations, natural gas processing plants, underground storage, and liquefied natural gas (“LNG’’)
facilities. Williams’ assets are designated critical infrastructure under Presidential Policy Directive
21, and Williams has a direct interest in protecting its facilities, personnel, and neighboring
communities from threats originating in the airspace around its sites. Williams also routinely
operates its own and contracts unmanned aircraft to inspect, monitor, and maintain those assets,
giving it a dual perspective on this rulemaking.

Williams is a member of the Interstate Natural Gas Association of America (“INGAA”’)
and supports, and incorporates by reference, the comments INGAA is submitting in this docket.
Williams submits these separate comments to speak from the perspective of an owner and operator
of oil and natural gas infrastructure, and to underscore four points of particular importance to this
sector.

Docusign Envelope ID: CBE01867-B143-8AF3-83C7-1B580B13E297

I. The Final Rule Should Expressly Recognize Oil and Natural Gas Infrastructure

As proposed, the energy category’s definition of “natural gas facilities” reaches only
natural gas processing plants and applies a single 500 MMcf/d capacity threshold. Criticality
across the natural gas system, however, is not defined by processing capacity alone. Other parts of
the value chain, including storage fields, interconnects, and compression, can have a material
impact on the reliable delivery of energy even where they fall below the proposed threshold or
outside the processing-plant category. Williams respectfully urges the FAA to:

¢ include natural gas storage and LNG facilities (import, export, and peak-shaving)
within the sector-specific requirements;

* lower the 500 MMcf/d threshold to 200-250 MMcf/d so that critical interconnects and
similar assets are eligible;

¢ allow owner-operators to identify and justify their operationally critical compressors
through the application process, and clarify that both processing and transportation
compressors may qualify;

* recognize processing facilities that maintain hazardous chemicals on site even below
the Appendix A thresholds, given the potential for a UAS incursion to trigger a
dangerous release; and

¢ align eligibility with the Transportation Security Administration’s “critical pipeline”
list and coordinate with TSA as the pipeline Sector Risk Management Agency.

This consequence-based approach is consistent with the risk-based, performance-oriented
mindset of the industry, and it would ensure the rule protects the full range of oil and natural gas
infrastructure rather than an arbitrarily narrow slice of it.

II. “Less Is More”: The Volume of Data the FAA Requests May Create More Risk Than
the Restriction Prevents

Williams’ most significant concern is the sheer amount of sensitive information an
applicant must submit, and what the FAA would then publish. A UAFR is meant to reduce risk to
a facility, yet the proposal would require applicants to document facility vulnerabilities, the
consequences of a UAS incident, and existing protective measures, and it contemplates publishing
proposed UAFRs and site information in the Federal Register for notice and comment before any
restriction is even approved. For a highly sensitive facility, that concentration and publication of
data can create more risk than the restriction is designed to prevent, in effect mapping the site for
a bad actor. Every time such information leaves company networks, risk is introduced; the 2024
intrusion into the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s Chemical Security
Assessment Tool underscores that even federal security agencies cannot guarantee its protection.
Williams therefore urges the FAA to adopt a “less is more” approach:

¢ clearly define and strictly limit the information published for notice and comment, and
exclude facility type, on-site operations, hazardous materials, security plans, and
consequence information;

¢ limit the level of specificity required of applicants; and

* permit executive-level certifications or affidavits in lieu of detailed security and
incident-response plans.

Docusign Envelope ID: CBE01867-B143-8AF3-83C7-1B580B13E297

If the data burden is too high, operators will simply decline to use the framework,
ultimately defeating the rule’s purpose. Calibrating what is collected and what is published is
essential to making this a rule that critical infrastructure operators can actually use.

III. The Rule Should Clarify Enforcement and a Facility’s Right to Protect Its Restricted
Airspace

Even where a UAFR is granted, it is not clear how the restriction will be enforced or what
a facility may lawfully do to protect the airspace it has been given. Today, an operator’s only
practical recourse is to report unauthorized activity to state, local, and federal authorities whose
capacity to respond is limited, whose penalties vary, and who can act only if the operator is
identified and located. A restriction without a meaningful enforcement mechanism offers limited
protection. Williams urges the FAA to expand on how UAFRs will be enforced, to clarify what
facilities may and may not do to detect and respond to incursions into their restricted airspace, and
to treat this rule as a first step toward scalable counter-UAS authorities for critical infrastructure,
working with the Department of Justice to strengthen penalties for those who target it.

IV. The Rule Must Preserve Facility Operators’ Control of Their Airspace

Williams urges the FAA to ensure that a facility operator retains clear authority to
temporarily restrict, delay, or deny non-essential third-party unmanned aircraft operations within
its restriction during emergencies, hazardous processes, maintenance turnarounds, or elevated
threat conditions. The operator on site is the only party with real-time awareness of when
conditions on the ground make an overflight dangerous, and in those moments an otherwise-
authorized flight can turn a routine operation into a safety event. A general access framework that
the operator cannot pause in real time does not reflect how these facilities are run. Williams
likewise relies on its own and contracted unmanned aircraft for inspection, maintenance, and
emergency response, and asks that the rule preserve those authorized operations.

V. Conclusion

Williams supports the FAA’s effort to establish a practical, risk-informed UAFR
framework and appreciates the opportunity to comment. Williams urges the FAA to expressly
recognize oil and natural gas infrastructure, to adopt a “less is more” approach to the data it collects
and publishes, to clarify enforcement and operators’ rights to protect their restricted airspace, and
to preserve facility-authorized drone operations. Williams stands ready to serve as a resource as
the FAA finalizes the rule.

Respectfully submitted,

Grounding the Skies: The Case Against the FAA's Proposed Critical Infrastructure Drone Restrictions
Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03 (91 FR 24650)

On May 6, 2026, the FAA proposed a new category of permanent, privately-triggered airspace restriction: the Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restriction (UAFR). It sounds narrow — a process for owners of "critical infrastructure" to ask the government to keep drones away. In practice, it lets thousands of private landowners carve permanent, federally enforced no-fly zones out of public airspace, backed by criminal penalties, with only a thin layer of public oversight.

1. It privatizes a public resource

Navigable airspace is a public trust. In United States v. Causby (1946), the Supreme Court held the skies above the immediate reaches of private land belong to the public for passage, and 49 U.S.C. § 40103(a)(2) codifies "a public right of transit through the navigable airspace."

The UAFR program inverts that default. Private operators petition FAA to seal off airspace above their land — FAA itself estimates over 9,000 such petitions will be granted. Once approved, that airspace is closed to the public except for narrow, permission-gated exceptions. A public commons is being converted, facility by facility, into a patchwork of privately-requested exclusion zones.

2. "Critical infrastructure" is defined too broadly

The rule imports all sixteen NSM-22 sectors — chemical, communications, energy, finance, healthcare, IT, transportation, water, and more — covering nearly the entire built economy, not the narrow list Congress specified in 2016 (energy, refineries, chemical plants, amusement parks, railroads, state prisons). FAA also invites comment on expanding to additional sectors, making the "critical infrastructure" label an open door rather than a limit.

3. Rulemaking driven by executive order, not statute

Section 2209's actual text is modest. Yet the NPRM repeatedly cites Executive Order 14305, Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty, as the rationale for interpreting "critical infrastructure" far more broadly than Congress's statutory list. When an executive order — not legislation — expands a regulation carrying criminal penalties, that raises real separation-of-powers concerns.

4. Special UAFRs can bypass public review

Standard UAFRs at least require Federal Register publication and 30 days of comment. But "Special UAFRs," lasting up to five years, can skip notice-and-comment whenever FAA finds "good cause." Violations there can be prosecuted as national defense airspace violations under 49 U.S.C. § 46307. The public can be excluded from airspace, under threat of prosecution, based on a designation they never had a chance to see or contest.

5. It criminalizes people who never saw a sign

A UAFR creates no physical marker — it exists only on a government website pilots must consult before every flight, FAA's own "virtual no trespassing sign." Yet unknowing violation can trigger civil or, in Special UAFR zones, criminal liability. Imposing criminal exposure for crossing an invisible boundary sits uneasily with basic due-process notice principles.

6. Chilling effect on newsgathering and oversight

Energy, chemical, and government-facility sectors are exactly where environmental and accountability journalism relies on drone footage. A rule letting the facilities being scrutinized request their own criminally-enforced no-fly zones hands the entities most interested in avoiding scrutiny a new tool to keep cameras away.

Conclusion

Reckless or malicious drone flights near sensitive sites are a real problem, and Congress did direct FAA to address it. But this proposal goes well past that mandate — converting public airspace into a privately-petitioned exclusion system, defined broadly enough to cover most of the economy, partly justified by executive order rather than statute, criminally enforceable against people who never saw a boundary, and in its most restrictive form shielded from public comment. A narrower rule tied to Congress's actual statutory list, with real notice requirements, could address the legitimate security concerns without this level of overreach.

COMMENTS OF NCTA –
THE INTERNET & TELEVISION ASSOCIATION
NCTA – The Internet & Television Association (“NCTA”)1 submits these comments in
response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NPRM”) in the above-referenced proceeding
concerning the Federal Aviation Administration’s (“FAA’s” or “Administration’s”) proposal to
establish a process for restricting operation of unmanned aircraft systems (“UAS” or “drones”) in
close proximity to certain fixed site facilities that meet the definition of “critical infrastructure.”2
NCTA urges the Administration not to exclude cable operators’ broadband communications
networks and associated facilities from this process.
1 NCTA – The Internet & Television Association represents the U.S. cable industry, whose
members own and operate broadband, video, and voice communications networks serving the
vast majority of American homes and businesses. These networks are integral to emergency
communications, public safety, healthcare, education, commerce, and national security, and have
repeatedly demonstrated their critical role during national emergencies, including the COVID-19
pandemic and major natural disasters, when broadband providers worked alongside utilities and
government agencies to restore essential connectivity and support affected communities. NCTA
members also deploy unmanned aircraft systems to build, inspect, maintain, and restore
communications networks. See About NCTA, https://www.ncta.com/about/about-us; After the
Storm, https://www.ncta.com/industry/initiatives/after-the-storm.
2 Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility, Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; Notice No. 26-03 (May 6, 2026) (“NPRM”).

I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY
NCTA and its members share the Administration’s goal of ensuring the security and
resiliency of U.S. critical infrastructure while fostering an environment in which the growing
UAS market can continue to innovate and thrive. As cable operators and major broadband
communications providers, NCTA members also provide critical communications services that
enable public safety, national security, emergency response, and other functions necessary to
maintain modern American life. As such, NCTA members have a vested interest in protecting
critical facilities from disruption or compromise due to drone interference.
The NPRM recognizes communications operators among the sixteen critical
infrastructure sectors eligible to apply for unmanned aircraft flight restrictions (“UAFRs”), but,
based on an apparent misunderstanding, inaccurately distinguishes cable operators’ broadband
communications networks and facilities from all other segments of the communications sector.3
The NPRM mistakenly characterizes cable as “primarily support[ing] the distribution of
television and internet services, which are considered less critical compared to large scale
telecommunications and broadcasting which are essential for emergency communications, public
safety, and national security.”4 NCTA respectfully submits that this is incorrect. Modern cable
networks are broadband communications networks that integrate hybrid infrastructure (including
wireless, wireline, and cable components) to deliver critical communications services, including

III. THE PROPOSED EXCLUSION OF CABLE FACILITIES IS INCONSISTENT
WITH FEDERAL CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE POLICY
Consistent with the varied roles discussed above, federal law and longstanding federal
critical infrastructure policy have recognized cable as a central component of the
communications sector and of the nation’s critical infrastructure. Cable infrastructure
traditionally falls within the statutory definition of critical infrastructure used in the NPRM and
underlying Executive Order 14305, which covers “systems and assets, whether physical or

U.S. communities, creating redundancy and resiliency for other communications modalities and
Wi-Fi connections, and in many U.S. homes ensuring that Americans can communicate through

For these reasons, federal agencies have prioritized cable among the nation’s most critical

IV. THE FAA SHOULD APPLY A TECHNOLOGY-NEUTRAL APPROACH TO
COMMUNICATIONS INFRASTRUCTURE
Rather than excluding communications providers, facilities, or network technologies
from protections afforded to similarly situated operators, the Administration should rely on the
established definition of critical infrastructure and the U.S. government’s longstanding
characterization of the communications sector to establish eligibility for the UAFR program. It
should evaluate communications facilities based on their function and the consequences of
disruption to those facilities. Cable facilities must be treated consistently with their
communications sector counterparts in this regard. The Administration should adopt rules that
protect the entire critical infrastructure community from threats to their networks, not just certain
segments of it.

The proposed definition of Operator or Proprietor is overbroad, granting UAFR application
