IX. Amusement Park Remote ID Monitoring Obligations Should Be Limited to
Operating Hours and Defined High-Risk Periods.
Proposed § 74.56 would require an applicant to show protective security measures, including
restricted access, designated security personnel, and security monitoring.78 For purposes of that
security monitoring requirement, proposed § 74.56(d) would require the capability, either
directly or through a contracted service, to receive broadcast Remote ID messages from
unmanned aircraft operating within or near the requested UAFR, using equipment compatible
with Part 89.79 FAA explains that UAS may be difficult to detect visually or audibly and that
Remote ID sensing capability would help a fixed site facility establish awareness of airspace
around the facility and detect allowed operations under proposed § 74.250.80
IAAPA supports reasonable Remote ID monitoring as part of a UAFR security framework.
However, FAA should clarify that any monitoring obligation for amusement parks may be scaled
to operating hours, scheduled events, and defined high-risk periods. A year-round, 24-hour
monitoring expectation would be disproportionate for seasonal parks, parks that operate only on
weekends or holidays during portions of the year, and facilities whose UAS risk is concentrated
during guest operating periods. Scaling the monitoring obligation to operating hours and defined
high-risk periods reflects only where continuous Remote ID sensing capability is necessary; it
does not suggest that the UAFR's restrictions on unauthorized or unallowed UAS operations
relax during non-operating hours, nor should it be read to permit commercial or third-party
operations within the UAFR at any time absent the approvals otherwise required by this
comment. The relevant safety concern is the protection of guests, employees, attractions, and
operational infrastructure during periods when the facility’s UAS-related exposure is present or
materially heightened.
FAA’s own proposed framework supports this clarification. The NPRM recognizes part-time
UAFRs and states that such restrictions may operate on a seasonal basis for 290 or fewer
consecutive days.81 The same logic should apply to monitoring obligations. Where a UAFR is
seasonal, part-time, or tied to scheduled operating periods, the Remote ID monitoring obligation
should likewise be tied to the periods during which the risk justifying the UAFR exists, unless
FAA determines that additional monitoring is necessary based on site-specific facts.
FAA should also recognize the practical limitations of Remote ID as a security mitigation.
Remote ID is a valuable situational-awareness tool that can help identify compliant operators
conducting legitimate operations, but it should not be treated as the primary security measure
supporting a UAFR. Operators engaged in intentional malicious, disruptive, or criminal activity
are also the least likely to broadcast compliant Remote ID, meaning continuous monitoring
imposes a real operational burden while providing limited protection against the threat actors that
most justify a UAFR in the first place. Remote ID should be understood as one layer within a
broader security framework, and UAFR eligibility and protection should not become overly
78 91 Fed. Reg. at 24686-87 (proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.56(a)-(c)).
79 Id. at 24687 (proposed 14 C.F.R. § 74.56(d)).
80 Id. at 24662-63.
81 Id. at 24663-64.
23

dependent on a mitigation that is effective primarily against compliant operators rather than the
actors a UAFR is designed to guard against.
This clarification would preserve FAA’s ability to require appropriate monitoring where justified,
while avoiding an unnecessary year-round, 24-hour burden for facilities whose UAS-related risk
is tied to defined operating periods.
* * * * *
Thank you for your consideration of these comments. IAAPA appreciates the opportunity to
share our views on these important issues and welcomes further engagement with FAA as the
agency works toward a final rule that protects guests, employees, property, and aviation safety
while preserving appropriate UAS operations.
Respectfully submitted,

Todd Andrus
Vice President and Executive Director

comments.commenter: Comment from The Commercial Drone Alliance
comments.comment_text:
August 5, 2026
Submitted electronically via http://www.regulations.gov
United States Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue, SE
West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140
Washington, DC 20590
Re: CDA Comments to the Section 2209 NPRM on Restricting the Operations of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to Fixed Site Facilities (FAA-2026-4558)
To Whom It May Concern:
The Commercial Drone Alliance (CDA) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments in
response to the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) and U.S. Department of Transportation’s
(DOT) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) “Designation – Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility” implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension,
Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (hereinafter, “NPRM” or “proposed rule”). The NPRM is an important
step in creating a low altitude airspace ecosystem that protects important national security assets from
the dangers of careless and criminal drone use while still enabling authorized, compliant drone
operations.
The CDA has long supported and advocated for policies focused on confronting misuse of
drones. Our members believe that drone innovation and security are two sides of the same coin and
must advance together. Unauthorized drone operations present risk to the National Airspace System
(NAS) and people and property on the ground, while hampering the significant safety and efficiency
benefits that safe and compliant commercial and public safety drone operations bring to the American
public. Protecting our nation’s critical infrastructure and sensitive fixed sites from unauthorized drones
is an essential component to enabling safe, scalable drone operations in the NAS.
Page 1 of 17

I. About the Commercial Drone Alliance
The CDA advocates for U.S. leadership in advanced aviation and actively participates in
legislative, regulatory, and policy efforts to facilitate the safe and secure development and expansion
of domestic commercial drone operations. The CDA works with all levels of government to collaborate
on policies for industry growth and educates the public on the safe and responsible use of commercial
drones to achieve economic benefits and humanitarian gains. We bring together commercial drone
manufacturers, end-users, service providers, advanced air mobility companies, drone security
companies, and vertical markets including oil and gas, precision agriculture, construction, security,
communications technology, infrastructure, newsgathering, filmmaking, and more.1
Several CDA member companies, including those serving on the CDA Board, are critical
infrastructure entities that operate fixed site facilities. These facility operators seek to protect their
facilities while also using drones to support their operations, and therefore offer a unique perspective
on the need for balance within this regulatory effort.
II. First Principles
In this comment, the CDA discusses the implications of this NPRM on our members, including
civil and public UAS operators, manufacturers, data service providers, vertical market end users, drone
security companies and critical infrastructure fixed-site facility operators. In providing our comments,
CDA was guided by several first principles:
1. Improving airspace awareness around critical infrastructure requires a multi-layered
approach. The CDA strongly supports the FAA’s and broader Administration’s efforts to
improve airspace awareness around our nation’s critical infrastructure. Airspace restrictions
are an important first step in providing a legal and regulatory framework for airspace use.
Ultimately, UAFRs function primarily as legal and informational barriers—they do not provide
any inherent capability to detect, intercept, or stop clueless, careless, and criminal drone
operators. While UAFR designations can effectively guide lawful operators, they are inherently
limited when actors either carelessly or intentionally disregard those rules. Effective airspace
awareness will require a layered approach that combines restrictions with detection,
1 Learn more at https://www.commercialdronealliance.org. CDA Board members include: Choctaw
Nation of Oklahoma, DoorDash, Florida Power & Light, Hidden Level, Honeywell, NUAIR, Ondas,
Percepto Robotics, Skydio, SkySafe, Southern Company, uAvionix, Wing, and Zipline International,
Inc. General members include: Aerolane, Airspace Link, Inc., American Fuel & Petrochemical
Manufacturers (AFPM), ANRA Technologies, Ascent AeroSystems, AT&T, Aura Network Systems,
Inc., AX Enterprises, Brinc Drones, Inc., Dedrone by Axon, DEXA, Dominion Energy, Drone Service
Providers Alliance, DRONERESPONDERS, Edison Electric Institute (EEI), End State Solutions LLC,
Flock Safety, Flying Lion, Inc., GroWings Robotx, Kelly Hills Unmanned Systems, Lumenier,
Matternet, Merlin Labs, Mid Atlantic Aviation Partnership (MAAP), Mitsubishi Electric Innovation
Center, New York Power Authority, Pilot Institute, Pyka, Inc., Qualcomm Incorporated, Safe Pro
Group, Inc. Sustainable Skylines, Syracuse Regional Airport Authority, USI, Verge Aero, Virginia
Innovation Partnership Corporation (VIPC), Wingtra, and Xelevate Solutions.
Page 2 of 17

identification, and intent discernment capabilities. Federal guidance and operational
experience emphasize that detection systems—e.g., radar, radio frequency sensing, optical
or other technologies—are necessary to maintain situational awareness, identify unauthorized
operations, and ultimately distinguish compliant from non-compliant operators.2 Without these
complementary capabilities, restrictions alone simply reduce the amount of navigable airspace
available to legitimate operators.
2. It is possible to enable the good while preventing the bad. Unauthorized drones present
a real and growing risk to sensitive locations, as illustrated by the security successes
throughout the month-long World Cup event, including the detection of approximately 1,600
illegal drone incursions into restricted airspace around event stadiums.3 Protecting critical
infrastructure is a national priority and has only become more important as this technology
evolves. CDA has long supported the underlying legislative intent of Section 2209 for precisely
this reason. In a similar vein as many other policies with a nexus to national security, such
efforts must strike an appropriate balance between maintaining security and preserving civil
liberties—in this case, protecting vital assets without unnecessarily constraining access to the
NAS for legitimate, safety-enhancing, and economically beneficial UAS operations.
Commercial and public safety UAS operations conducted in compliance with FAA regulations
do not, in themselves, present a security threat. Rather, these operations are part of an
increasingly structured, identifiable, and accountable operating environment. Authorized
operators adhere to regulatory requirements such as Remote Identification (RID) and various
other requirements contained in applicable operational and airspace approvals, which
collectively enable transparency and traceability within the NAS. Principal security risks arise
from uncertainty, including the inability to readily determine whether a given UAS operation is
authorized, who is operating it, and whether it is operating in accordance with applicable rules.
Addressing these uncertainties will unlock an appropriately calibrated approach to discern bad
actors while preserving the ability of responsible operators to conduct authorized missions that
benefit the American public.
3. Dynamic airspace management is essential to achieving drone dominance. Commercial
drone operations are rapidly transitioning from remotely piloted, mission-specific activities to
highly autonomous, networked systems capable of executing repeatable operations with
minimal human intervention. Advances in AI-driven navigation, obstacle detection, and
mission management are enabling drones to conduct complex BVLOS flights, perform
continuous inspections, and operate as part of coordinated fleets rather than as isolated
aircraft. The upcoming Part 108 rule is expected to support routine, scalable operations in
2 Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. (2025). UAS detection technology guidance for
critical infrastructure. U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Available at
https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/DetectionTech_20251030_508.pdf.
3 Federal Bureau of Investigation. (2026, July 15). How the FBI keeps the public safe at gatherings.
[Press release]. Available at https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/special-event-security-part-two. Director
Kash Patel announced in an X post that the FBI seized over 700 drones near FIFA airspace.
Page 3 of 17

which a single operator may oversee multiple drones simultaneously, further accelerating
operational density. Low altitude airspace is evolving, and a dynamic airspace ecosystem is
essential to enabling scaled, highly automated commercial drone operations in the United
States. As contemplated in the FAA’s UAS Traffic Management (UTM) architecture, a real-
time, data-driven airspace construct capable of allocating access, imposing constraints, and
resolving conflicts will be critical to enabling routine beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS)
operations. Static airspace, case-by-case approvals, and manual implementation processes
will not support the integration of highly automated BVLOS operations into the NAS. The
proposed Part 74 UAFR framework underscores the importance of dynamic airspace by
enabling thousands of geographically discrete, potentially overlapping airspace constraints.
Without dynamic allocation, prioritization, and real-time constraint management, the
cumulative effect of UAFRs risks fragmenting the airspace into operationally unworkable
segments. Dynamic airspace will be critical to preserving the safety and security objectives of
the NPRM while also enabling scalable authorized drone operations at scale.
4. A federal framework for airspace management is needed. A uniform federal framework for
designating and managing UAFRs will help prevent the emergence of a fragmented, state-by-
state patchwork of airspace rules. As the rulemaking recognizes, UAFRs are intended to
create a consistent, nationwide process by which eligible fixed-site facilities can request
restrictions based on defined criteria. In the absence of a clear federal framework, states and
localities have understandably sought to impose their own restrictions on low-altitude
operations, creating legal uncertainty for commercial drone operators who must navigate
varying (and sometimes conflicting) jurisdictional requirements. Consistent UAFR eligibility
and access criteria will enhance compliance, reduce administrative barriers, and create a
predictable framework for both facilities and drone operators. This becomes more important
as eligibility for UAFR designations expands across a wide range of critical infrastructure
sectors, because the airspace becomes more segmented operationally as the number of
UAFRs grows. With that expansion, the need for predictable and operationally feasible transit
pathways becomes paramount; otherwise, even well-intentioned restrictions risk creating a
patchwork of constrained airspace that could impede critical UAS missions and hamper the
United States’ domestic drone dominance priorities.
III. General Areas of Support
The CDA appreciates and supports various facets of the NPRM. In particular:
1. General Framework and Intent of Security Restrictions. The CDA supports the general
framework and intent of the UAFR concept, with a focus on protecting fixed sites that have
demonstrated need, UAS-specific vulnerabilities, and regional- or national-level impact if
disrupted. The CDA generally supports the following specific elements:
a. The application of sector-specific eligibility criteria to ensure that protections are
focused where they are most needed—on infrastructure whose loss or disruption could
Page 4 of 17

have significant downstream societal or economic effects. In this respect, the sector-
specific criteria reinforce that UAFRs should be applied selectively, based on
demonstrated importance and risk, rather than as a generalized tool for limiting access
to the NAS. As discussed further in Section IV.10 below, certain sector-specific
eligibility thresholds lack clarity and could potentially leave some at-risk facilities
ineligible to apply for a UAFR.
b. The requirement to affirmatively demonstrate the need for a UAFR designation, which
ensures that airspace restrictions are grounded in objective, risk‑based justifications
and that UAFRs are deployed as targeted tools to mitigate demonstrated
vulnerabilities, rather than as a default mechanism that could unnecessarily constrain
access to the NAS. At the same time, the FAA should ensure that the “demonstration
of need” requirement is implemented in a manner that is efficient, predictable, and not
unduly burdensome for applicants, particularly for facilities with legitimate and
time‑sensitive security concerns.
c. The requirement to demonstrate how an airspace restriction complements existing
security measures. As previously stated, airspace restrictions are one layer of a
security strategy, and this requirement is essential to ensuring that critical
infrastructure facilities are leveraging multiple layers in their protection procedures.
d. The tiered framework for UAFRs reflects a risk-based approach to securing ground-
based infrastructure. Not all fixed-site facilities present the same level of vulnerability
or security concern and therefore should not be subject to uniform restrictions. By
establishing distinct categories, the proposed rule appropriately differentiates between
such facilities and imposes heightened restrictions where appropriate and tailors
restrictions to the specific risk profile of each facility, rather than imposing broad
limitations across the low-altitude airspace environment. While we generally support
the tiered UAFR approach, as discussed below in Section IV.9, aspects of the
designation process for Special UAFRs lack sufficient detail and warrant additional
clarity.
e. UAFR lateral boundaries based on fixed-site facility property lines appropriately
calibrates restrictions to the specific risk footprint of the underlying asset. By limiting
the lateral extent of a UAFR to the facility’s property boundary, the proposed rule
ensures that restrictions are tailored and do not unnecessarily encroach on
surrounding navigable airspace. This precision promotes operational predictability and
generally aligns with the ‘guns, guards, and gates’ principle of traditional physical
security practices.
f. The requirement to monitor and receive RID broadcasts from drones operating within
or near the fixed-site is foundational to effective, real-time airspace awareness and
enforcement. RID detection capabilities are already incorporated into most, if not all,
detection systems currently in use across the industry. By ensuring that facilities can
Page 5 of 17

observe compliant drones transmitting identification data, the proposal helps
distinguish authorized operations from unknown or potentially unauthorized activity,
thereby reducing uncertainty and enabling more targeted security responses. As
discussed further below in Section IV.5, RID detection alone is not sufficient to fully
address the spectrum of security risks identified in the NPRM, because RID detection
depends on cooperative compliance. As discussed further in Section IV.6, limiting
detection awareness solely to the immediate UAFR footprint may likewise undermine
the security objectives of the proposed rule.
g. The NPRM’s commitment to a transparent notice and comment process for
establishing UAFRs will ensure that both the government and facility understand the
full impact of each proposed restriction before being finalized. Transparency in this
process is particularly important given the localized nature of facility-specific
restrictions and ensures that UAFRs are tailored, evidence-based, and consistent with
national airspace policy. At the same time, as discussed further below in Section IV.3,
the CDA recommends the FAA takes appropriate measures to safeguard security-
sensitive information provided by the UAFR applicants during both the initial evaluation
and public notice and comment stages of the vetting process. The CDA also supports
the use of a centralized web-based platform for the feedback process and any steps
the FAA can take to streamline the application and information collection processes
for facilities applying for UAFRs, as detailed further in Section IV.2.
2. Balancing Security Needs with Airspace Access. The CDA agrees with the FAA’s position
in the proposed rule that the agency has an affirmative obligation to balance the need to protect
safety and security interests with maintaining access to the NAS for authorized operators,
including drones flown for the facilities’ business needs. The NPRM itself reflects this dual
mandate by requiring that any requested UAFR be justified based on aviation safety, protection
of people and property, or national or homeland security concerns, while still preserving
pathways for authorized operations under defined conditions. More broadly, the FAA has
consistently recognized that integrating UAS into the NAS requires a regulatory framework
that manages risks without unnecessarily constraining beneficial operations, ensuring that
innovation and operational access evolve alongside appropriate safeguards. For example,
FAA-authorized operators—such as those conducting operations under Parts 107, 108, or
135—adhere to a set of safety requirements and undergo vetting that collectively provide a
level of accountability and traceability that distinguishes them from authorized actors. The
proposed rule appropriately reflects this principle by creating a structured mechanism to
impose targeted, evidence-based restrictions, rather than broad or indiscriminate limitations.
The FAA should take care to ensure that application and eligibility criteria are sufficiently
rigorous to prevent over-designation of UAFRs, particularly with respect to Special UAFR
designations, which could impose significant operational complexity on operators navigating
a large number of restricted locations. Accordingly, maintaining a risk-based threshold for
approval will help ensure that restrictions are limited to facilities presenting genuine security
concerns, while avoiding unnecessary system-wide burdens. In this respect, the NPRM
Page 6 of 17

appropriately reflects the FAA’s risk-based regulatory model and captures the FAA’s core
responsibility to steward the airspace in a manner that simultaneously promotes utilization,
safety, and national security.
3. Performance-Based Approach to Enabling UAFR Transit. We agree with the NPRM’s
performance-based construct to enabling compliant operator transit through UAFRs, as it
reflects an appropriately flexible and risk-based regulatory framework. Rather than imposing
categorical prohibitions, the NPRM allows certain authorized operations to transit restricted
airspace subject to defined conditions, including adherence to FAA regulations, RID, and
notification protocols. This approach ensures that access to the airspace is determined by the
operator’s demonstrated ability to meet objective performance and safety standards, rather
than by rigid classifications that could unnecessarily restrict legitimate operations. By focusing
on outcomes—such as safe, identifiable, and controlled operation within or through a UAFR—
the proposed rule helps enable commercial and public safety operations that benefit the
American public, while still protecting sensitive facilities from malicious or unknown activity. As
discussed further below in Section IV.8, certain performance-based requirements warrant
additional clarification.
IV. Areas for Change and/or Additional Clarification
Consistent with the first principles outlined above, the CDA offers the following proposed
updates and points of clarification that we believe will help promote the safety and security objectives
of the NPRM, as well as the agency’s broader efforts to enable safe, scalable and increasingly
autonomous commercial drone operations in the NAS.
1. Automate and Streamline UAFR Access Notification
The CDA supports the proposed notification framework requirement in § 74.255 for qualified
UA operators to transit through Standard UAFRs. However, it is critical that the notification process be
automated to the greatest extent possible, and prioritize and facilitate solutions involving systems
talking to systems. The ultimate outcome should reduce burdens on the critical infrastructure operators
to understand and respond to drone traffic over their facilities, as well as support the integration of
highly automated BVLOS operations at scale in the NAS. Given the volume, geographic dispersion,
and real-time nature of low-altitude UAS operations—particularly over critical infrastructure and
industrial sites as they play an increasingly crucial role in equipment maintenance and monitoring—a
manual, case-by-case notification processes would impose significant administrative burdens on both
operators and facility owners, undermining the intended utility of the UAFR construct. Interoperable
detection, surveillance, and data-sharing capabilities, such as API-enabled systems or network-based
Remote ID, should be leveraged to filter compliant from non-compliant operations and manage
notifications to facilities of both authorized and unauthorized drones.
Page 7 of 17

A. Automating Notifications
An automated, federated, and standardized notification architecture—such as API-enabled
integrations or FAA-certificated data service providers—would facilitate timely, verifiable
communication, reduce friction in obtaining access, and promote consistent compliance across both
UAS operators and UAFR sponsors. Absent such automation, the notification requirement risks
becoming a de facto barrier to lawful operations rather than a scalable safety or security safeguard.
The FAA’s Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability (LAANC) system provides
one clear and proven model that could be replicated for automating notifications. By enabling near
real-time, automated authorization and notification exchanges between operators and airspace
stakeholders through digital platforms and API-enabled integrations, LAANC has already
demonstrated how standardized automation can facilitate compliance while supporting operational
efficiency. A comparable, FAA-endorsed approach for UAFR access that is platform-agnostic or
otherwise accessible without requiring the adoption of any one particular commercial service would
similarly enable timely, verifiable communication, reduce friction in obtaining facility access, and
promote consistent, scalable compliance across operators. The FAA could also consider extending
LAANC to capture and route operational intent near UAFRs to facility managers with little to no new
infrastructure being needed.
Beyond systems like LAANC that are already in place under Part 107, the FAA should also
seek to leverage systems and digital services that will come online under Part 108 to automate the
exchange of information between operators and facilities. For example, Part 108’s proposed
framework for strategic deconfliction contemplates the exchange of operational intent data, including
intended flight paths, across a networked data architecture developed by the industry at no cost to
government. The final rule should leverage the operational-intent4 information architecture that would
already be supported by third-party service providers regulated through the proposed Part 146
framework to satisfy, or substantially automate, notification requirements under the Part 74 rule. The
FAA should encourage a standardized, machine-readable mechanism through which the appropriate
data could be made available to facilities. This approach would minimize administrative burden on
operators, improve the timeliness and accuracy of notifications, and provide facilities with greater
situational awareness than a standalone notification process. Additionally, leveraging data streams
already required for most UAS operating under Part 108 would create a scalable and efficient
notification framework that advances both the objectives of Part 108 and Part 74, while sharing cost
burden fairly across UAS operators and fixed site facilities.
Specifically, the proposed Part 146 framework for certifying Automated Data Service Providers
(ADSPs), which will be foundational to enabling scaled operations under the Part 108 rule, could be
leveraged to certify surveillance, detection, or network Remote ID service providers offering automated
notification services. Because Part 146 was written as an extensible regulatory framework, it could
easily be leveraged to certify and authorize such services, with operational requirements on both fixed
4 In proposed § 108.5, FAA defined operational intent as a volume-based representation encapsulating
the intended flight path for a UAS operation and comprising one or more overlapping or contiguous
4 dimensional volumes defined by length, height, width, and a beginning and ending time.
Page 8 of 17

site facilities and UAS operators imposed in Part 74 similar to the operational requirements imposed
in proposed Part 108. Ultimately, we note that it is likely more important for fixed sites eligible for
UAFRs to be notified of unauthorized operations through a UAFR, rather than authorized operations.
Such solutions already exist and are being successful deployed around sensitive sites currently, and
thus have been proven effective. We strongly encourage the final Part 74 rule to leverage such
solutions for the benefit of both the critical infrastructure and UAS operator communities. The benefits
of leveraging Part 146 for this framework are described in further detail below under recommendation
5.
B. Utilize a Whitelist Database
A general theme among our critical infrastructure members is that critical infrastructure
facilities have neither the time and resources nor expertise to be in the airspace management
business, and that the proposed rule must not force overly burdensome administrative requirements
onto facilities. To further enhance and simplify an automated notification construct, the system should
incorporate a centralized, FAA-managed or FAA-endorsed database of pre-cleared (i.e., “whitelisted”)
UAS that are eligible for streamlined access across Standard UAFRs. Under such an approach,
operators could register UA identifiers—such as RID credentials, registration numbers, and/or
manufacturer serial numbers—into a verified system that is managed or credentialed by the FAA.
Under this approach, a detection service provider would only need to notify the facility if a detected
drone is not cleared through the whitelist. This construct would streamline the threat discrimination
process and alleviate the need for facilities to continually monitor and manage ongoing notifications
for a high volume of flights.
C. Enable Alternative Approaches to Flight-by-Flight Notifications
Some commercial drone operators may conduct hundreds or potentially thousands of flights
in a given day, some of which may need to transit through Standard UAFRs on a regular basis
(depending on how prevalent facility designations are). The final rule should accommodate alternative
approaches to providing notifications which do not necessitate providing specific RID credentials,
registration numbers, and/or manufacturer serial numbers for each individual drone and/or flight that
may need to transit through a UAFR. For operators with a need for reoccurring flights through a UAFR,
a “standing notification” process would be more appropriate and less burdensome on all involved
parties, rather than a continuously reoccurring flight-by-flight notification process. For operators that
manufacture their own drones, a whitelist process could work effectively without the need for operators
to provide individualized serial numbers for each drone. The FAA’s RID serial number is constructed
using an ANSI/CTA-2063-A format, which includes a constant 4-character (Manufacturer Code)
assigned by ICAO. The 4-digit manufacturer code could be leveraged to provide a streamlined and
effective means to clearly identify authorized operators permitted to transit through Standard UAFRs.
Additionally, the final rule text should be as performance-based as possible to enable machine-to-
machine solutions, such as those currently developed and deployed to support UAS operations in a
UTM environment. For example, network Remote ID could provide a streamlined alternative for many
facilities using a surveillance- or detection-as-a-service provider.
Page 9 of 17

2. Ensure a Clear and Efficient UAFR Application Process
We support the FAA’s effort in the NPRM to establish a formal process for designating UAFRs,
but we would emphasize that the effectiveness of this framework will depend in large part on the
usability and efficiency of the application process. To ensure that qualifying critical infrastructure
entities can obtain needed protections without undue delay, the FAA should adopt a streamlined,
transparent, and proportionate approval process that avoids imposing unnecessary administrative
burdens on facility applicants. In particular, the designation process should be carefully calibrated to
the statutory purpose of Section 2209 and should not trigger complex or protracted ancillary
requirements—such as extensive environmental review processes—that would be misaligned with the
operational and security-driven nature of UAFR requests. An overly burdensome application
framework risks discouraging appropriate use of the program while diverting resources away from
targeted risk mitigation, ultimately undermining the rule’s intended security benefits.
3. The UAFR Application Process Must Safeguard Safety and Security Sensitive
Information
Several of our critical infrastructure members raised concerns that the NPRM does not provide
sufficient clarity or assurance regarding the protection of sensitive information submitted as part of the
UAFR application process. As proposed, applicants are expected to provide detailed data regarding
facility operations, security posture, vulnerabilities, and incident response planning—information that,
if disclosed, could inadvertently create security risks. The proposed rule does not clearly address how
such information will be protected, secured, stored, retained, or accessed, including in the context of
interagency information sharing. For example, would application material be exempt from disclosure
under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)? Absent a clear and robust FOIA exemption framework,
facilities may face a material risk that highly sensitive site-specific security and vulnerability information
could be subject to public disclosure. This uncertainty may deter participation in the program or
undermine the integrity of the application process. The FAA should therefore establish explicit
safeguards governing the handling of UAFR application data, including clear confidentiality
protections, limits on dissemination, defined retention policies, and assurance that sensitive security
information will be appropriately protected from public disclosure.
4. Clarify the UAFR Application Phase for Demonstrating Proof of Detection
Capabilities
The NPRM is unclear as to when, within the UAFR application process, an applicant must
demonstrate proof of RID detection capabilities. While the proposed rule recognizes the importance
of such capabilities to justify the designation and ensuring ongoing compliance, it does not specify
whether evidence of detection capabilities must be included at the time of initial application, during
FAA review of the application, or as a post-designation condition. The final rule should provide clear
guidance on the timing and evidentiary expectations for demonstrating detection capabilities to ensure
consistency across applications and to avoid uncertainty that could delay or complicate the designation
process. The CDA recommends that applicants be required to demonstrate detection capability at the
time of application and to maintain that capability as an ongoing condition of the designation. Doing
Page 10 of 17

so would promote consistency across applications, reinforce the evidence-based demonstration of
need discussed below, and ensure that the protective measures justifying a UAFR remain in place
throughout its term.
5. Require or Encourage the Use of Detection Equipment
The protective security requirement in proposed § 74.56(d) would require facilities to have
security monitoring capable of monitoring and receiving broadcast RID messages from drones
operating within or in close proximity to the UAFR. Because malicious or careless operators may not
transmit RID, a monitoring standard limited to RID detection only would not necessarily provide enough
information to create an airspace awareness picture that fully enables discernment of lawful from
unlawful operations. The final rule should require, or at minimum strongly encourage, facility operators
to deploy detection technologies that are capable of identifying, tracking, and characterizing non-
cooperative UAS, including beyond the boundaries of the facility or UAFR. While RID provides a
foundational tool for airspace awareness and accountability, its effectiveness depends on the ability
of facilities to detect and distinguish non-compliant operations in real-time and early enough to
implement emergency response activities if warranted. The use of detection systems with
characterization capabilities, irrespective of the particular sensing modality employed,, would provide
a more complete air picture and ensure that UAFRs are not reliant solely on compliance with RID
broadcast requirements. Incorporating this capability into the Part 74 framework would align facility
operator responsibilities with evolving FAA identification requirements and help ensure that UAFRs
function as a credible and effective mechanism for protecting sensitive sites.
To support facility access to enhanced detection capabilities, the FAA should establish a clear
framework that enables surveillance- or detection-as-a-service (SAAS or DAAS) models. The financial
costs associated with mandates for detection capabilities can be defrayed through the availability of
service models which do not require facilities to own their own detection equipment. Accordingly, the
final rule should expressly permit facilities to satisfy any detection or monitoring requirement through
a certified third-party service provider, rather than requiring facilities to procure and operate their own
equipment. This approach would lower the cost of compliance, accelerate adoption, and allow critical
infrastructure operators—who have neither the time nor the expertise to be in the airspace-
management business—to obtain effective detection without building it in-house.
Additionally, the FAA should strongly consider leveraging the Part 146 architecture to authorize
these services, as this framework provides numerous advantages to both the government and
industry. First, the maturity of this existing architecture, which has been effectively demonstrated
already through the FAA’s Near Term Approval Process, offers a path to faster implementation and
reduced short-term costs. Second, it leverages industry consensus standards to ensure
interoperability and system-agnostic data standardization, which is necessary to support the United
States’ stated airspace sovereignty priorities. A standard already exists for network Remote ID, which
also accelerates implementation. Finally, it compels cybersecurity and data validation procedures,
ensuring that facilities are using trusted, certificated service providers which collect data based on an
accepted standard and communicate between other services and detection capabilities in a secure
Page 11 of 17

fashion. All of these benefits in combination promote a nation-wide, industry-developed networked
architecture for low altitude airspace awareness.
6. Extend Detection Capability Beyond the Immediate Boundaries of the UAFR
The final rule should also require or strongly incentivize the deployment of detection equipment
and services that extend airspace awareness capabilities beyond the immediate boundaries of the
UAFR. Detection capabilities limited strictly to the confined footprint of a facility risks creating blind
spots in the surrounding airspace, thereby reducing the ability of facility operators to anticipate and
respond to approaching or transiting UA that may imminently enter restricted airspace. By contrast,
detection capabilities that extend into the surrounding airspace would enable earlier identification,
tracking, and assessment of potential UAS threats, supporting a more effective security posture and
facilitating coordinated, proportional responses where appropriate. Requiring a reasonable buffer for
detection beyond UAFR boundaries would better align the Part 74 framework with practical operational
realities and help ensure that UAFRs function as proactive—not merely reactive—tools for protecting
sensitive facilities. Short of a requirement, facilities with such detection capabilities beyond their facility
boundaries should be viewed more favorably in the UAFR application process.
7. A UAFR Applicant’s Demonstration of Need Should be Based on Verifiable UAS
Activity Data
The CDA supports the proposed requirement in § 74.66 that an applicant for a UAFR
designation must demonstrate a sufficient safety or security need for designating the airspace,
including the requirement to characterize existing UAS activity near a facility. This requirement is an
important safeguard to ensure that designations are grounded in actual, evidence-based risk rather
than speculative concerns. However, the NPRM does not clarify how such operational data should be
collected or validated, creating a risk of inconsistent and potentially unreliable submissions.
To address this gap, the final rule should require the use of objective, verifiable data, rather
than anecdotal or human observations alone. While visual reports or incident recollections may have
some contextual value, they are inherently limited in accuracy, completeness, and repeatability. By
contrast, technology-based detection systems can provide time-stamped, auditable data on UAS
activity, including frequency, location, and movement patterns, thereby supporting a more rigorous
and defensible assessment of actual risk. Establishing a requirement or preference for such data-
driven methodologies would promote consistency across applications, enhance the credibility of UAFR
designations, and better align the framework with modern technological capabilities. Relatedly, the
final rule should address the retention of such data by clarifying that facilities may retain time-stamped
detection and airspace-activity data for a reasonable period to support the demonstration of need,
post-incident forensics, and ongoing security operations, subject to appropriate privacy and data-
handling safeguards.
Finally, in assessing the need for a UAFR, the FAA should also clarify that lawful and compliant
UAS operations, considered alone, do not constitute a security risk or threat and therefore should not
Page 12 of 17

be used as a sole basis to justify airspace restrictions. While such operations may inform the broader
operating environment, restrictions should be grounded in demonstrated safety or security risks rather
than the mere presence of UAS activity.
8. Clarify Certain Performance-Based Requirements for UAFR Access
The CDA generally supports the NPRM’s performance-based requirements for transiting
through Standard UAFRs; however certain aspects should be clarified in the final rule. There are also
opportunities to better future-proof the proposed performance-based requirements.
• Enable Network RID solutions. Under § 74.250 (a)(1), UAFR access is predicated on
broadcasting RID. Broadcast RID is an appropriate baseline, however the final rule
should be flexible enough to accommodate potential future alternative approaches
that achieve the same goal, e.g., the use of network RID.
• Clarify “As Soon as Reasonably Possible”. Under proposed § 74.255(c), Timeline for
Notification, an operator must provide notice “as soon as reasonably possible in
advance of the operation.” We believe this standard is an appropriate performance-
based required, but the advisory circular should clarify that the standard does not
impose any temporal limits and that “as soon as reasonably possible” might mean
less than a minute in some scenarios. For example, many package delivery flights are
performed on-demand following a customer order. Many public safety operations are
also effectively on-demand flights. In such scenarios, the operator may have little or
no advance notice of when flights will occur, and the “as soon as reasonably possible”
standard must be interpreted in a manner that reflects this reality. Such scenarios also
highlight the need for automated notification processes as outlined in (1) above, to
ensure that facilities’ detection systems, notification procedures, and response
activities are also designed to provide facilities with only the information they need.
• Clarify transiting the UAFR “in the shortest amount of time practicable”. Under
subparagraph (a)(2) of proposed § 74.250, Allowed operations, UA transiting a UAFR
must do so in the “shortest amount of time practicable.” This is an appropriate
standard; however, the advisory circular should clarify that safety of flight is ultimately
the FAA’s primary concern, and clearly state that this regulatory text is meant to
account for maneuvers or contingency procedures conducted in furtherance of
operational safety. For example, a detect-and-avoid (DAA) maneuver or automated
lost-link contingency procedure may dictate a flight path other than the most
expeditious direct route through a UAFR. The advisory circular could provide
guidance accounting for such scenarios.
Page 13 of 17

• Clarify when UAFRs become effective and enforceable. While the NPRM preamble
contemplates that restrictions apply once a UAFR “goes into effect,”5 the rule text does
not clearly define the timing of effectiveness or enforcement. The FAA should clarify
in the regulatory text when UAFRs become effective and incorporate a defined
transition period between publication and enforcement to allow operators to
incorporate new restrictions into flight planning systems and for facility owners to
validate implementation. We recommend an implementation period of not less than
seven (7) days between a final UAFR being issued and going into effect to enable
UAS operators to update route planning systems and software. This will also give
operators a chance to notify the FAA of any discrepancies or programming errors
encountered with digitized UAFR data.
9. Clarify the Special UAFR Designation Process
While we generally support the tiered UAFR approach, the final rule must provide greater
clarity regarding the standards, process, and limitations governing designation of Special UAFRs. As
proposed, the NPRM leaves significant ambiguity around the eligibility criteria, required evidentiary
showing, and decision-making framework for non-federal sites seeking Special UAFR designations.
This ambiguity creates uncertainty for facility operators and UAS stakeholders alike. The final rule
should more clearly define the narrow scope of circumstances under which Special UAFRs for non-
federal sites are appropriate and guard against incremental expansion beyond those limited, high-
sensitivity use-cases contemplated in the NPRM.
We agree that certain non-federal fixed-sites may face unique security threats that warrant a
more restrictive Special UAFR designation; however without appropriate guardrails, there is a risk that
the availability of federal agency sponsorship could function as a de facto loophole, enabling broader
categories of facilities to obtain Special UAFR status irrespective of whether they meet a rigorous,
risk-based threshold. To preserve the integrity and credibility of the Part 74 framework, the FAA should
establish transparent, objective criteria, require a documented and reviewable justification for each
designation, and ensure that federal sponsorship is not treated as a substitute for substantive eligibility,
but rather as one factor for consideration within a constrained and well-defined approval process.
10. Clarify the Basis for Sector UAFR Eligibility
The NPRM identifies 16 fixed-site facility sectors eligible to apply for UAFR designation;
however, the FAA does not sufficiently explain the basis for selecting these particular sectors or the
criteria used to differentiate them from other potentially sensitive facilities. While we are generally
agnostic as to the inclusion or exclusion of any specific sector, the final rule should provide a clear,
risk-based justification for sector eligibility, grounded in established principles of aviation safety and
national security. Historically, federal protections for sensitive facilities—such as nuclear power plants
and mass gathering venues—have been informed by the presence of robust physical security
5 Designation-Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility,
91 Fed. Reg. 24650, 24652 (May 6, 2026).
Page 14 of 17

measures (i.e., “guns, gates, and guards”), which both reflect and reinforce the criticality of those sites.
To the extent such facilities employ strong ground-based deterrence and access controls, it is
reasonable to recognize that threats may shift to the air, thereby justifying tailored UAS restrictions.
The final rule should consider aligning sector eligibility with these historical analogs by focusing
on facilities that maintain substantial, layered physical security measures and that present a clear
nexus to aviation safety or security vulnerabilities. Extending standard UAFR eligibility to facilities with
such established security postures may provide a principled and administrable basis for inclusion. At
the same time, regardless of which sectors are ultimately deemed eligible for UAFRs, the final rule
should ensure that UAFR designations are limited to facilities that are genuinely sensitive and that
present a substantiated risk profile, rather than broadly extending eligibility in a manner that dilutes
the integrity and effectiveness of the Part 74 framework and the original legislative intent of Section
2209.
11. Clarify and Better Tailor Site-Specific Criteria
The CDA supports the NPRM’s overarching effort to employ site‑specific criteria to ensure that
UAFR designations are reserved for facilities with a demonstrable security need. A tailored,
criteria‑based approach is preferable to categorical or overly broad designations, and—if properly
calibrated—can promote both risk-based prioritization and transparency in the designation process.
At the same time, several of the proposed criteria appear insufficiently grounded in established risk
frameworks or existing federal classifications, raising concerns that the resulting designations may be
both under- and over-inclusive.
In particular, certain eligibility thresholds appear arbitrary or misaligned with other federal
standards. Specifically, the CDA has the following concerns:
• The NPRM’s reliance on the National Inventory of Dams database does not correspond to the
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s framework for identifying high- and significant-hazard
dams, potentially excluding infrastructure that presents greater downstream risk while including
facilities of comparatively lesser concern.
• The NPRM’s treatment of nuclear facilities appears to omit protection during outage periods,
despite the fact that outages may present unique safety, security, or vulnerability considerations.
The criteria applicable to electric transmission infrastructure also lacks sufficient clarity to ensure
consistent application, creating uncertainty as to which assets qualify.
• The NPRM’s approach to chemical facilities raises similar concerns. By incorporating Chemical
Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) status and a 100,000 barrel-per-day throughput
threshold, the proposed criteria risk excluding a substantial portion of facilities that present
meaningful risk profiles but nonetheless fall below these thresholds or outside CFATS coverage.
As a result, a significant share of U.S. refining capacity—and other potentially sensitive facilities—
would be categorically ineligible to seek protection, notwithstanding legitimate security
considerations.
Page 15 of 17

The CDA encourages the FAA to revisit these thresholds and align them more closely with risk-based
federal frameworks, ensuring that eligibility criteria are both rationally grounded and sufficiently flexible
to capture facilities that warrant protection.
12. Facilities Must Be Able to Operate Their Own Drones
Critical infrastructure entities operate drones on a daily basis for legitimate, safety-critical, and
efficiency-enhancing purposes. For this reason, UAFR designations must be implemented in a manner
that does not impede a facility’s ability to conduct its own UAS operations. Many facilities rely on
routine drone operations for inspection, monitoring, maintenance, and security functions that directly
support safe and compliant operations. Facilities may also rely on drone delivery to support both critical
and routine operations, including the delivery of essential supplies such as medical materials, and the
rule should ensure such operations are not inadvertently disrupted. Absent clear and workable
allowances for facility owner/operator drone use—UAFR restrictions risk unintentionally degrading,
rather than enhancing, overall safety and resilience. The FAA should therefore clarify in the final rule
that facility operators (and their authorized agents) retain the ability to conduct UAS operations within
designated areas, subject to appropriate safeguards, to ensure that the rule supports rather than
constrains critical operational use cases.
13. Incorporate UAFR Requirements into the Airman Certification Standards for Part
107 Remote Pilots
The CDA supports the proposed framework allowing authorized commercial UAS operators,
including, but not limited to, Part 107 operators, to transit through Standard UAFRs under defined
conditions. To the extent that new regulatory requirements, including those in this proposed rule,
touch upon an operator, the FAA’s airman certification framework should include a training and
knowledge requirement addressing those regulatory requirements. To help ensure Part 107 operator
compliance with the proposed UAFR framework, Airman Certification Standards (ACS) for Part 107
Remote Pilots should be updated to cover UAFR requirements contained in the Final Rule.
14. Enforcement and Penalties Should Account for Inadvertent Brief Incursions
Operational contingencies such as DAA maneuvers and automated lost-link procedures
should be accounted for in the context of § 74.260, Enforcement and penalties. The enforcement
posture for UAFR incursions in such scenarios should be distinguished from incursions by clueless,
careless, or criminal actors. The same should be true for brief momentary incursions that may be
unintentional or stem from environmental conditions like wind. While the criminal penalties in
subsection (a) of § 72.260 are predicated on knowing and willful violations, the same standard does
not exist for civil penalties under subsection (c). As a general matter, brief unintentional incursions
should not automatically give rise to civil liability.
Page 16 of 17

15. Streamline or Automate Communication of UAFRs to Operators
To promote compliance with UAFR designations, the FAA should explore opportunities to
streamline or automate the process by which operators are made aware of UAFRs. There are existing
tools and standards which could be leveraged as part of the FAA’s implementation activities.
V. Conclusion
The CDA appreciates the FAA’s consideration of these comments and its continued leadership
in advancing a comprehensive framework to address the security risks posed by unauthorized UAS
operations near critical infrastructure. We support the FAA’s efforts to implement Section 2209 in a
manner that is risk-based, transparent, and operationally workable, and we look forward to continued
engagement with the FAA and other federal stakeholders as this rulemaking progresses.
Ultimately, we share a common objective: to ensure the effective protection of our nation’s
most sensitive facilities while preserving and enabling the safe, scalable use of drone technologies
that deliver significant benefits to the American public.
Lisa Ellman
Chief Executive Officer
Commercial Drone Alliance

Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
Dear Administrator Bedford:
TechNet is the national, bipartisan network of technology CEOs and senior executives
that promotes the growth of the innovation economy by advocating for a targeted
policy agenda at the federal and 50-state level. TechNet’s diverse membership
includes over 100 dynamic American businesses ranging from startups to the most
iconic companies in the world and represents over five million employees and
countless customers in the fields of information technology, artificial intelligence, e-
commerce, the sharing and gig economies, advanced energy, cybersecurity, venture
capital, and finance. Several of our members develop and deploy unmanned aircraft
systems, autonomous logistics technologies, cloud computing services, advanced
communications networks, and other technologies that are transforming
transportation, infrastructure, and the broader economy.
TechNet appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Federal Aviation
Administration’s (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Designation-Restrict the
Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility. TechNet
supports the FAA’s efforts to implement Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety,
and Security Act of 2016 by establishing a transparent, nationally uniform process for
restricting unmanned aircraft operations around qualifying critical infrastructure
facilities. The proposal represents an important milestone in integrating security
considerations into the National Airspace System while preserving the significant
public benefits that commercial unmanned aircraft provide.
The United States is entering a period of rapid growth in advanced aviation
technologies. Commercial unmanned aircraft are becoming an increasingly important
component of the nation’s transportation and logistics infrastructure. They enable
faster delivery of essential goods, improve inspection of critical infrastructure, support
emergency response, expand access to healthcare in underserved communities, and
Aust in • Boston • Chicago • Denver • Harrisburg • Olympia • Sacramento • Silicon Valley • Tallahassee • Washington, D.C.
Washington, D.C.

strengthen American competitiveness in advanced aviation technologies. The United
States has an opportunity to lead the world in commercial drone operations, but
realizing that opportunity depends upon maintaining a regulatory framework that
protects safety and security while preserving innovation, operational flexibility, and
the efficient use of the national airspace.
TechNet has long supported a national regulatory framework for unmanned aircraft
that is performance-based, technology neutral, and scalable. Such a framework should
rely upon objective safety outcomes rather than prescriptive operational
requirements, encourage innovation through automation and digital interoperability,
and preserve the FAA’s longstanding role as the sole regulator of the nation’s
navigable airspace. The proposed rule advances many of those objectives by replacing
a growing patchwork of state and local approaches with a comprehensive federal
process governing restrictions around fixed-site facilities.
We particularly support several foundational aspects of the proposal:
First, the NPRM establishes a standardized federal process through which owners and
operators of eligible critical infrastructure facilities may request Unmanned Aircraft
Flight Restrictions (UAFRs). Rather than allowing disparate restrictions to proliferate
across jurisdictions, the proposal appropriately centralizes these decisions within the
FAA, ensuring that security determinations affecting navigable airspace are made by
the agency Congress charged with managing the National Airspace System.
Second, the proposed distinction between Standard and Special UAFRs appropriately
balances legitimate security interests with the continued growth of commercial drone
operations.
Third, the proposal appropriately limits restrictions to qualifying facilities that satisfy
statutory eligibility criteria and establishes mechanisms through which restrictions
may expire, be modified, or be terminated. These provisions recognize that access to
navigable airspace should remain the default and that restrictions should exist only
where justified by demonstrated security considerations.
While TechNet strongly supports the overall direction of the proposal, several
modifications would improve the Final Rule’s effectiveness, reduce unnecessary
burdens on commercial operators, and further Congress’ objective of establishing a
comprehensive federal framework for drone operations around critical infrastructure.
I. The Final Rule Should Expressly Affirm Federal Authority Over Airspace
Restrictions.
TechNet requests that the Final Rule include an express discussion of federal
preemption. Congress directed the FAA to establish the process governing restrictions
on unmanned aircraft operations near fixed-site facilities. In carrying out that
directive, the FAA is creating a comprehensive federal regulatory framework governing
where and under what circumstances unmanned aircraft may operate around critical
2

infrastructure. Once finalized, Part 74 will establish nationally applicable eligibility
criteria, application procedures, operational restrictions, transit rights, and
enforcement mechanisms. This framework should govern uniformly throughout the
United States.
Numerous states have enacted laws restricting drone operations around critical
infrastructure that vary considerably in scope, geographic coverage, operational
requirements, and criminal penalties. Several of these statutes contain no mechanism
for harmonization once the federal Section 2209 process becomes effective. As a
result, a commercial operator complying fully with FAA regulations could nevertheless
face liability under state law for conducting an operation the FAA has expressly
authorized.
This uncertainty undermines one of the central purposes of the NPRM: creating a
predictable national framework governing drone operations around critical
infrastructure. Commercial operators cannot efficiently plan interstate operations if
compliance with federal aviation regulations does not provide confidence that those
operations may proceed without conflicting state restrictions.
The FAA possesses exclusive authority to regulate the safe and efficient use of
navigable airspace under 49 U.S.C. § 40103. The agency has consistently recognized
that state and local governments may not regulate aviation safety or airspace
management in ways that conflict with federal law. The Final Rule should reaffirm
those longstanding principles by making clear that Part 74 establishes the governing
federal framework for restrictions on unmanned aircraft operations around qualifying
facilities.
Accordingly, TechNet respectfully recommends that the FAA include an express
statement in the Final Rule confirming that Part 74 provides the comprehensive
federal framework governing operational restrictions near fixed-site facilities and that
conflicting state or local requirements regulating where unmanned aircraft may
operate in navigable airspace are subject to established principles of federal
preemption. Providing this clarity will reduce regulatory uncertainty, facilitate
interstate commerce, and ensure that commercial operators can confidently rely upon
FAA authorizations when conducting lawful operations throughout the National
Airspace System.
II. The Final Rule Should Enable Automated, Scalable Compliance.
The NPRM appropriately recognizes that owners and operators of fixed-site facilities
should receive advance notice when qualified commercial operators intend to transit a
Standard UAFR. TechNet supports this objective. However, the notification framework
contemplated by the proposed rule should be implemented in a manner that reflects
the highly automated nature of modern commercial unmanned aircraft operations.
Unlike traditional aviation, commercial UAS operations frequently involve large
numbers of short-duration flights that are planned, dispatched, monitored, and
adjusted through automated software systems. Delivery networks, infrastructure
3

inspections, utility operations, and similar services depend upon digital workflows
capable of managing thousands of operations each day. Requiring manual, flight-by-
flight notifications through web portals or other non-automated processes would
impose unnecessary administrative burdens, increase opportunities for human error,
and constrain the scalability of commercial operations without materially improving
security.
The Final Rule should therefore permit notification and approvals through automated,
interoperable digital systems. The FAA should encourage the development of
standardized electronic interfaces that allow qualified operators to transmit required
information in a secure, machine-readable format while providing facility operators
timely operational awareness. Such an approach would improve compliance, reduce
administrative burden for both operators and facilities, and better position the
regulatory framework to accommodate future growth in commercial UAS activity.
The FAA should also provide flexibility regarding how recurring operations are
communicated and approved. Many commercial operators routinely conduct similar
operations over the same geographic areas pursuant to established operational
procedures. The Final Rule should allow for a standing notification process that
accommodate recurring or ongoing operations where appropriate, rather than
requiring duplicative submissions for substantially identical activities. For day-to-day
monitoring of commercial UAS flight operations, a fixed site facility can use broadcast
or network-based Remote ID. The remote viewing capability of network-based Remote
ID will allow a fixed site facility to receive advanced notification of UAS operations
using that technology prior to any transit of a UAFR.
Adopting a technology-neutral, automated notification framework is consistent with
the FAA’s longstanding preference for performance-based regulation. Rather than
prescribing a particular software platform or communications protocol, the agency
should establish functional objectives that allow industry to develop interoperable
compliance solutions capable of evolving alongside advances in commercial UAS
technology.
III. UAFR Information Should Be Published in Machine-Readable Formats.
A modern regulatory framework depends not only on clear operational requirements
but also on timely access to accurate digital information. Commercial UAS operators
increasingly rely upon automated flight planning software that integrates multiple
sources of aeronautical information before and during flight. Temporary flight
restrictions, controlled airspace authorizations, weather conditions, Remote ID
information, and other operational data are routinely processed by software systems
to support safe and compliant operations.
The same approach should govern implementation of Part 74. When the FAA
establishes, modifies, renews, or terminates a UAFR, the relevant information,
including geographic boundaries, altitude limitations, effective dates, expiration dates,
and operational classifications, should be made available in standardized, machine-
4

readable formats capable of being incorporated directly into commercial flight planning
systems. Providing digital access to these data will improve compliance while reducing
the administrative burden on both regulators and operators. Operators should not be
required to manually interpret maps or individually update software systems
whenever restrictions change. Likewise, facility operators benefit when commercial
operators have immediate access to accurate restriction information before planning
flights.
IV. Eligibility Criteria Should Remain Narrowly Tailored to Demonstrated
Security Risks.
TechNet supports the FAA’s decision to limit eligibility for UAFRs to facilities identified
by Congress and to require applicants to demonstrate legitimate security needs before
restrictions are established. At the same time, the Final Rule should ensure that
eligibility criteria remain appropriately tailored so that UAFRs protect facilities
presenting genuine security concerns without unnecessarily restricting access to
navigable airspace.
Because access to navigable airspace is a public resource, restrictions should remain
the exception rather than the rule. Facilities seeking UAFRs should demonstrate why
the requested restriction is necessary in light of the specific security risks associated
with the protected asset.
The FAA should avoid interpretations that would allow broad categories of commercial
properties or ancillary infrastructure to qualify for restrictions absent a demonstrated
nexus to the statutory purposes underlying Section 2209. Overly expansive eligibility
determinations could result in a proliferation of UAFRs that collectively reduce the
availability of low-altitude airspace for legitimate commercial operations.
Similarly, applicants should not be permitted to rely upon lawful commercial drone
activity itself as evidence that additional restrictions are necessary. Existing traffic
analyses should distinguish between unauthorized operations and FAA-compliant
commercial operations conducted pursuant to applicable regulations. The growing
presence of authorized commercial flights reflects successful integration into the
National Airspace System rather than an increased security threat.
V. UAFR Boundaries Should Be No Broader Than Necessary to Address
Demonstrated Security Needs.
TechNet agrees that UAFRs should generally be geographically limited and should
avoid unnecessarily restricting access to surrounding airspace. The NPRM
appropriately proposes that Standard UAFRs ordinarily correspond to the boundaries
of the protected facility rather than extending arbitrary buffer zones into surrounding
communities. This represents a significant improvement over numerous state
approaches that establish fixed-radius restrictions without regard to operational
necessity.
5

Nevertheless, property boundaries will not always represent the narrowest area
necessary to protect the critical asset. Some facilities encompass substantial
undeveloped property, parking areas, or other land that presents little relationship to
the underlying security concern. In such circumstances, the FAA should retain
flexibility to establish lateral boundaries that more closely correspond to the
operational security perimeter while continuing to protect the facility itself.
This approach appropriately balances security and efficiency while recognizing that
every facility presents unique operational characteristics.
VI. The FAA Should Consider the Cumulative Effects of Multiple UAFRs.
Although individual UAFRs may be appropriately justified, the FAA should also consider
the cumulative impact that multiple restrictions may have on the availability of
navigable airspace. Commercial drone operations depend upon connected
transportation corridors rather than isolated operating areas. Numerous adjacent or
overlapping UAFRs could unintentionally create extensive areas where commercial
operations become impracticable despite each individual restriction being
independently reasonable.
Accordingly, before approving new restrictions, the FAA should evaluate whether the
cumulative effect of existing and proposed UAFRs would materially impair access to
surrounding communities or interfere with the continued development of commercial
low-altitude transportation networks. Considering cumulative impacts would further
the FAA’s statutory obligation to ensure both safety and the efficient use of the
National Airspace System while preserving the significant public benefits associated
with commercial unmanned aircraft operations.
VII. The Final Rule Should Establish Workable Procedures for Special
UAFRs.
TechNet supports the creation of Special UAFRs for facilities presenting unique
national security considerations. Providing additional protections for particularly
sensitive locations is consistent with Congress’ objectives and appropriately recognizes
that certain facilities require heightened safeguards.
The NPRM, however, provides relatively little guidance regarding how qualified
commercial operators may obtain authorization to enter Special UAFRs when
legitimate operational needs arise. The Final Rule should establish transparent
procedures describing application requirements, decision-making criteria, anticipated
processing timelines, and mechanisms for addressing emergency or time-sensitive
requests. Clear procedures will provide certainty to both operators and government
agencies while reducing unnecessary administrative delays.
Most importantly, the FAA should retain responsibility for overall airspace
management even where another federal agency serves as the using agency for a
Special UAFR. Maintaining centralized FAA oversight is essential to preserving the
6

uniform administration of the National Airspace System and ensuring consistent
treatment of similarly situated operators.
VIII. The Final Rule Should Protect Authorized Operations from Improper
Counter-UAS Interference.
The NPRM appropriately recognizes that Part 74 does not itself authorize owners or
operators of fixed-site facilities to detect, disrupt, or mitigate unmanned aircraft.
TechNet strongly supports maintaining this distinction. The authority to regulate the
use of counter-UAS technologies rests with Congress and the federal agencies
specifically authorized to exercise those authorities. Nothing in Part 74 should be
construed to expand those authorities or create uncertainty regarding their
application.
As commercial drone operations continue to expand, many critical infrastructure
operators will employ passive detection technologies to improve situational
awareness. Those systems can play an important role in identifying unauthorized
aircraft while also confirming the presence of FAA-authorized commercial operations.
The FAA should encourage facility operators to use available identification information,
including Remote ID, together with submitted notification information, before
concluding that an unmanned aircraft presents a security concern.
Finally, the FAA should encourage the reporting of any interference with authorized
commercial operations through existing aviation safety reporting mechanisms. Such
information will assist the agency in evaluating implementation of the Final Rule and
identifying opportunities for continued improvement as commercial operations
expand.
IX. The FAA Should Preserve Appropriate Oversight of Existing UAFRs.
TechNet supports the proposal establishing a finite duration for UAFRs and allowing
the FAA to modify or terminate restrictions when circumstances change. These
provisions appropriately recognize that restrictions on access to navigable airspace
should remain tied to continuing operational necessity. The Final Rule should build
upon this framework by encouraging periodic reassessment of existing restrictions to
ensure they continue to serve the purposes for which they were established. Security
risks, facility operations, surrounding development, and commercial aviation
technologies will inevitably evolve over time. In addition, parties whose operations are
materially affected by an existing UAFR should have a meaningful opportunity to
request that the FAA review whether modification or termination is warranted.
TechNet is not suggesting the FAA revisit every UAFR on a fixed schedule. Rather, we
encourage a flexible process that allows restrictions to evolve alongside changing
operational realities while preserving the agency’s discretion to determine whether
continued restrictions remain appropriate.
7

X. Conclusion
TechNet appreciates the FAA’s thoughtful efforts to implement Section 2209 through a
nationally uniform regulatory framework that strengthens security while preserving
the continued growth of commercial unmanned aircraft operations. The proposed rule
represents an important step toward replacing an increasingly fragmented regulatory
landscape with a comprehensive federal process that appropriately balances the
protection of critical infrastructure with the efficient use of the National Airspace
System. With the modifications described above, the Final Rule can better accomplish
Congress’ objectives by providing regulatory certainty for facility operators,
commercial drone operators, and the public alike.
TechNet appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and looks forward to
continued engagement with the FAA as it finalizes this important rulemaking.
Sincerely,
Linda Moore
President and CEO
8

COMMENTS OF THE
