Pursuant to the schedule established by the Federal Aviation Administration (“FAA”)
in the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NPRM”) dated May 6, 2026, and subsequently
extended on June 30, 2026, the Association of American Railroads (“AAR”) respectfully
submits these comments.1
AAR is an industry association representing the interests of North America’s
railroads, and includes the six U.S. Class I freight railroads, Amtrak, scores of U.S. short line
and regional freight railroads, and other commuter railroads. AAR’s freight railroad
members account for the vast majority of U.S. freight rail mileage, employees, traffic, and
revenue, while Amtrak accounts for the majority of intercity passenger trips. As operators
of UAS, law enforcement entities, and owners and operators of critical infrastructure,
1 See FAA, Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site
Facility, NPRM, 91 Fed. Reg. 24650 (May 6, 2026)(“NPRM”).
1

railroads have a strong interest in ensuring the safe and efficient integration of unmanned
aircraft systems into the airspace. And, as critical infrastructure owners and operators,
railroads must have a means of protecting their fixed site facilities (“FSF”) as contemplated
by Congress in section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016, as
amended (“section 2209”).2
BACKGROUND
By linking businesses and consumers domestically and abroad, America’s railroads
have played an essential role in America’s economic development for nearly 200 years.
Early on, railroads provided a means for previously inaccessible areas to be developed; for
mineral, timber, and agricultural products to get to market; and for the developed and
undeveloped areas of a growing nation to be bound together. Our nation’s railroads remain
indispensable today, serving nearly every industrial, wholesale, retail, resource-based
sector of the U.S. economy, while also moving passengers to, through, and from nearly
every region of the country. Freight railroads carry everything from grain and fertilizers to
groceries and produce; coal and steel to automotives and plastic resins; and a vast array of
other chemicals (including those chemicals of interest listed in Appendix A to the NPRM),
energy products, and intermodal containers and trailers filled with goods that line the
shelves of retail stores and wholesalers nationwide. Railroads also carry security sensitive
2 See Section 2209, FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016 (“FESSA”), Public Law 114–190 (July 15,
2016); Section 369, FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 (“FAARA”), Public Law 115-254 (Oct. 5, 2018) (Congress
specifically amended section 2209 to include “railroad facilities”).
2

and hazardous materials and products that are necessary for national security, providing
clean drinking water, growing American crops, and manufacturing domestic products.
Given the volume of rail freight (some 1.5 billion tons and 28 million carloads and
intermodal units in a typical year) and the long distances that freight moves by rail (nearly
1,000 miles on average), freight railroads’ direct role in the U.S. economy is immense.
However, freight railroads benefit the public in many other ways too:
• Safety. Moving freight by rail is also extremely safe. The train accident rate in
2025 was down 39 percent from 2000; the employee injury rate was down 52
percent; and the grade crossing collision rate was down 25 percent. Last year saw
record lows for the derailment rate, the equipment-caused accident rate, and the
Class I employee injury rate.
• Affordability. The affordability of freight rail saves rail customers billions of
dollars each year while enhancing the global competitiveness of U.S. products,
including grain, ores, forest products, and energy commodities from rural America.
Average rail rates (measured by inflation-adjusted revenue per ton-mile) were 46
percent lower in 2025 than in 1981. Millions of Americans work in industries that are
more competitive in the global economy thanks to the affordability and productivity
of America’s freight railroads.
• Fighting Highway Congestion and Reducing Highway Costs. Because a single
train can replace several hundred trucks, railroads reduce highway gridlock and the
need to spend taxpayer funds on highway construction and maintenance.
• Re-Investments. Unlike trucks, barges, and airlines, America’s freight railroads
operate overwhelmingly on infrastructure they own, build, maintain, and pay for
themselves. From 1980 to 2025, they spent more than $860 billion of their own
funds — well over $1.4 trillion in today’s dollars — on capital expenditures and
maintenance expenses related to their networks, including the protective measures
for these assets. “Crumbling” might describe some U.S. infrastructure but not
freight rail.
• Economic Impact. Rail is a major driver of economic activity, generating $233
billion in total economic output in 2023. For every $1 invested in rail transportation,
an additional $2.50 is generated elsewhere, highlighting railroads’ powerful ripple
effect. The industry supports close to 750,000 jobs nationwide through supply
chains and consumer spending.
• Good-Paying Jobs. The over 135,000 railroad employees are among America’s
most highly compensated workers. In 2024, the average U.S. Class I freight rail
3

employee earned total compensation of approximately $163,000. By contrast, the
average compensation per full-time equivalent U.S. employee in 2024 was
$102,000, just 63 percent of the rail figure. The median tenure of railroad employees
is about 14 years, compared to 3.9 years for private sector workers.
• Global Trade. In inflation adjusted dollars, the value of U.S. exports of goods
increased roughly 55 percent from 2007 to 2025, while the value of imports of goods
-
rose some 50 percent. Without freight railroads, this could not have happened.
Exports and imports are often produced or consumed in rural areas far from ports
and national borders. Railroads ship these products safely, efficiently, and cost
effectively.
• The Environment. On average, railroads are three to four times more fuel
efficient than trucks, meaning that moving freight by rail instead of truck saves
enormous amounts of fuel and reduces greenhouse gas emissions by up to 75
percent.
• Expanded passenger rail. Freight railroads provide a crucial foundation for
passenger rail. More than 70 percent of the miles traveled by Amtrak trains are on
tracks owned by other railroads (mainly freight railroads).
Protecting the national asset that is the nation’s railroads is integral to the continued
realization of these benefits.
America’s railroads currently are only scratching the surface of UAS capabilities.
UAS are helping railroads inspect tracks and bridges, ensure safety, enhance security, aid
law-enforcement activities, respond to disasters, and improve the protection of critical
infrastructure. However, as railroads begin to utilize UAS more, so do others, and that
utilization can often interfere with safe and efficient railroading. If UAS users encroach
upon railroad facilities, it can distract railroad employees from their duties, especially
those operating trains, whose situational awareness is key to safe railroading. Over the last
year, railroads have averaged 38 incursions of UAS into the airspace above the railroads’
facilities each month. Members have also reported the utilization of UAS by cargo thieves
to monitor trains and plan their attacks. AAR, therefore, greatly appreciates the rule finally
4

being proposed, after nearly a decade; however, AAR believes there are key improvements
that should be made prior to finalization of this rule.
COMMENTS
I. “Railroad Facilities” Must be Included as Eligible for Protection with UAFRs.
Railroad-owned facilities must be eligible for a UAFR. The protection of railroad
facilities, both freight and passenger, with UAFRs is not only integral to the realization of the
continued benefits of railroads to the nation’s economy, but were specifically mandated by
Congress. The NPRM recognizes that Congress specifically intended railroads’ facilities to
be protected, stating “[i]n the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 (FAARA), Congress amended
section 2209 to include railroad facilities.”3 Yet, the NPRM thwarts congressional intent by
ignoring freight railroad-owned facilities, and instead focusing on only those identified by a
shipper or receiver. Specifically, the NPRM restricts eligible freight “railroad facilities” to ‘‘a
secure location(s) identified by a rail hazardous materials shipper or rail hazardous
materials receiver where security-related pre-transportation or transportation functions
are performed or rail cars containing the categories and quantities of rail security-sensitive
materials are prepared, loaded, stored, and/or unloaded.’’4 Similarly, it confines passenger
“railroad facilities” to only those intermodal passenger facilities where there are three or
3 NPRM at 24650.
4 Id. at 24672 (citing 49 CFR 1500.3) (emphasis added). With decisions left to the shipper or receiver to
identify FSFs for a UAFR, the NPRM could result in zero freight railroad-owned facilities being protected by a UAFR.
5

more transportation modes and electric substations for catenary.5 This narrowing of the
proposed rule ignores the majority of passenger and freight railroad facilities, prohibits
freight railroads from applying for UAFRs, and thwarts Congress’ intent to protect all types
railroad facilities. This is simply unacceptable.
America’s railroads worked closely with the committees of jurisdiction in both the
House and Senate in 2018 to ensure that “railroad facilities” were specifically included in
the protections provided by section 2209.6 Railroads must be able to identify places like
yards, passenger stations, maintenance facilities, bridges, tunnels, certain tracks, and
other railroad facilities that are subject to security risks and apply for those facilities to be
protected with UAFRs.7 For freight railroads, failure to do so will leave the security of this
vital American infrastructure to shippers and receivers whose interests may not be aligned
with the freight railroads and whose knowledge of railroads’ operations and protective
measures are minimal. For passenger railroads, their protection is only for their stations
with three or more modes of transportation and electric substations for catenary.8 Both
types of railroads are left with very little control or opportunity to protect their facilities.
AAR therefore strongly requests that the final rule make clear that freight railroads (not just
5 NPRM at 24672.
6 See FAARA, section 369.
7 The NPRM protects certain highway bridges and tunnels but would not protect railroad bridges or
tunnels. See NPRM at 24672.
8 With the exception of one small railroad with minimal trackage, no freight railroads in the United States
are powered by catenary. Catenary power is, however, utilized by some passenger and commuter railroads.
6

railroad shippers and receivers) and passenger railroads be able to apply and identify any
of their own facilities as FSFs under the proposal.
II. Railroad Tracks Must be Included as Eligible FSFs, at Least on a Temporary or Part-
time Basis.
Railroad tracks are “permanent, non-mobile facilities.”9 Yet, FAA claims that it
“does not believe that issuing UAFRs over potentially 140,000 miles of track is consistent
with Congress’s direction under section 2209 or FAA’s statutory mandate to ensure public
right of access and the safety and efficiency of the NAS. Moreover, FAA is concerned that
airspace restriction on this scale would be inconsistent with its obligation to integrate
unmanned aircraft into the airspace.”10 AAR disagrees, and believes that FAA should not
disqualify railroad tracks, on the front end, from eligibility a UAFR.
FAA’s concerns about integration of UAS are misplaced. The NPRM itself allows a
wide variety of UAS operations in Standard UAFRs, so there is simply no inconsistency
between protecting railroad tracks (at least, part-time) and integrating UAS into the NAS.11
While FAA may not want all railroad tracks covered by a Standard UAFR, the FAA ultimately
retains the right to grant a UAFR and in so doing impose restrictions, or not. Indeed, FAA
9 NPRM at 24651 (stating that “FAA interprets ‘fixed site facilities’ to mean permanent, non-mobile
facilities”).
10 Id. at 24671.
11 Id. at 24690-91 (proposed 49 CFR 74.250, allowing numerous UAS operations even in airspace protected
by a standard UAFR); see infra section IV (discussing AAR’s concerns with the various operations allowed in
Standard UAFR).
7

contemplates part-time protections for certain FSFs, albeit on a seasonal basis.12 The rule
should not, on the front end, assume that no railroad tracks can be protected.
FAA’s exclusion of railroad tracks is also illogical. FAA recognizes there is significant
risk at shipper and receiver facilities for certain materials. Notably, for the chemical sector,
FAA recognizes the need to protect the public from the release of certain chemicals. FAA,
however, makes the irrational distinction that protections be limited for certain chemicals
“[i]n transportation containers used for storage not incident to transportation, including
transportation containers connected to equipment at a facility for loading or unloading and
transportation containers detached from the motive power that delivered the container to
the facility.”13 This distinction raises numerous questions. Why is the risk distinction made
upon detachment from the locomotive (in the case of railroads)? And why only when at the
facility for loading and unloading?
The risk of release does not decrease when a locomotive is attached. Precisely
when the locomotive is attached and the train is traversing the railroad tracks is when the
risk of release can increase. Logically the risk of these chemicals being released –or the
risk of any number of railroad-transported goods being released– does not abate when a
train is moving those materials. While railroads are the safest way to transport goods over
land, in many instances, the act of transporting the material – not when sitting at a shipper
12 See NPRM at 24656 (noting a “part-time UAFR would be active for up to 290 consecutive days per year,
providing flexibility for applicants with seasonal or non-year-round operational needs.”). AAR envisions that
protecting tracks could be done on a temporary basis depending upon what is being transported. This would
require FAA to revisit its unwillingness to “grant a UAFR for single days or for multiple consecutive groupings of
days within a year.” NPRM at 24663.
13 Id. at 24692 (Appendix A) (emphasis added).
8

or receiver’s facility – increases the exposure to surrounding communities through which
railroad tracks pass. It is because of these risks that for certain railroad-transported
materials the Transportation Safety Administration (“TSA”) has promulgated regulations
regarding rail routing and the protection of certain areas from release when transporting
goods by rail.14 In addition to TSA regulations, the movement of toxic-by-inhalation (“TIH”)
and other hazardous materials is governed by an extensive set of DOT safety regulations
that are intended to minimize the risks of transporting hazardous materials by rail.15 While
these regulations help to ensure safe and secure rail transportation, they do not protect the
railroad facilities or public from threats posed by UAS. That is the role of this rule. So, for
FAA to write-off railroad tracks without considering these risks is concerning. AAR suggests
that railroads be allowed to apply for UAFRs to protect their tracks, along with other
facilities, and by extension the towns, cities, and public through and in which they operate.
Specifically, AAR proposes that in an application, a railroad would identify the
tracks, or segments thereof, that should be protected by the UAFR and justify that
protection with the requisite safety and security information. The railroad should be able to
propose a box around its tracks, including height above the track and width on either side
of the track, through which UAS operations would be prohibited or otherwise restricted.
AAR suggests that the prohibitions or restrictions need not be permanent, nor seasonal in
nature, but could be imposed on a temporary or part-time basis, such as when certain
14 See 49 CFR Part 1580 (TSA’s rail transportation security regulations which require, among other things,
routing reviews to avoid high-threat urban areas).
15 See, e.g., 49 CFR Parts 171-180 (PHMSA’s hazardous materials regulations); 49 CFR Parts 200-244 (FRA's
railroad safety regulations).
9

trains will be traversing those tracks.16 This would provide flexibility to railroads and clarity
to UAS operators regarding where and when they can operate around railroad tracks and
other facilities, while also protecting the railroad facilities and communities around them.
Doing so would serve the FAA’s intended goal of safely integrating UAS into the national
airspace.
Furthermore, over the last several years, freight railroads have experienced an
increase in cargo theft, costing the industry nearly $200 million per year. Sophisticated,
organized criminals are utilizing UAS to assist in their crimes by surveilling trains en route.
Congress has recognized this concern and required the federal government to focus more
on the issue.17 Railroads need to be able to protect their employees, equipment, and
customers’ property from these bad actors. Being able to apply to restrict the airspace
around moving trains would also help in these law-enforcement efforts.
III. Railroads Must Be Able to Utilize UAS Within Their UAFRs.
The operators and proprietors of FSFs, including railroads, must be able to utilize
UAS within their own UAFRs. Railroads were some of the early adopters of UAS which
serve a variety of purposes, including surveying damage to their facilities; enforcing
security in and around their facilities; conducting safety inspections of their facilities and
structures, like bridges; enforcing safety rules and policies; and managing the flow of goods
16 NPRM at 24663-64.
17 The U.S. House of Representatives recently passed on suspension of the rules H.R. 2853, Combating
Organized Retail Crime Act of 2025¸ which is a bipartisan piece of legislation to establish a unified federal response
to cargo theft. A companion bill exists in the Senate, S. 1404.
10

in and through their yards and other facilities. These uses are only scratching the surface of
the potential safety, security, and efficiency benefits of UAS. As structured, the proposed
rule, however, would not allow the operator or proprietor of an FSF to utilize UAS within
their UAFRs, except to transit the Standard UAFRs. AAR suggests that for both types of
UAFRs, Standard and Special, the final rule make clear that operators or proprietors of the
FSFs protected by the UAFR be allowed to operate UAS within those UAFRs without
restriction.
Specific to railroads, a number of railroad employees submitted comments
requesting railroads not be able to utilize UAS over railroad facilities. These suggestions
should be rejected. While AAR members appreciate the hard work and effort of their
employees, railroads have successfully used UAS to enforce rail safety rules and policies.
Railroads have done so without incident. If FAA does not allow railroads to utilize UAS
within their own UAFRs, that prohibition would limit railroads’ ability to maintain safe
working conditions for their employees and protect the communities in which railroads
operate.
IV. Standard UAFRs are Too Permissive to Provide Proper Protection.
A Standard UAFR is defined in proposed 49 CFR 74.5 as “airspace with clearly
defined horizontal and vertical limits within which unmanned aircraft would be restricted
from operating unless the operation fell within a few narrow exceptions (as described in
11

section V.H. of this preamble).”18 The exceptions consist of nearly all types of UAS
operations allowed under FAA regulations. This is much too lenient. It undermines
congressional intent and the purpose of protecting FSFs. The justification provided for the
“restrictions” is that “Congress directed the agency to create a process to ‘prohibit or
restrict’ (emphasis added) unmanned aircraft in close proximity to fixed site facilities. By
using the word ‘restrict,’ Congress recognized that some unmanned aircraft might be able
to access the designated airspace under certain circumstances.”19 This is a selective
misreading of the law. Any prohibition or restriction must be at the request of an applicant,
and on a case-by-case basis, not predetermined in a generally applicable rule.20
While FAA is correct that section 2209 says “prohibit or restrict,” FAA leaves out the
context of that statement. Specifically, section 2209(a) states that FAA “shall establish a
process to allow applicants to petition the Administrator of the Federal Aviation
Administration to prohibit or restrict, including temporarily, the operation” of UAS in close
proximity to an FSF.21 The applicant is the actor who Congress granted authority to petition
for a prohibition or a restriction of UAS operations. Railroads, and other FSF operators or
proprietors, must be able to apply, in the first instance, for a prohibition or restriction of
UAS operations. The proposed rule, instead, assumes that various UAS operations will be
allowed within the FSF’s Standard UAFR. Instead of assuming certain operations are
18 NPRM at 24651; see proposed 49 CFR 74.5.
19 NPRM at 24675.
20 See FESSA, section 2209(a).
21 Id.
12

always allowed, the final rule should recognize that the applicant may request a complete
prohibition on UAS operations in the clearly defined horizontal and vertical limits of the FSF
designation.
AAR also proposes that, FAA make clear that UAS operators may transit a UAFR only
with the permission of the FSF operator or proprietor. It should be noted, AAR’s proposal
would still allow lawful operations of UAS outside of the clearly defined horizontal and
vertical limits of the FSF designation or with permission. Conforming the final rule to these
changes would respect congressional intent, while balancing the need for UAS to be
integrated into the national airspace safely and securely.
V. Special UAFRs Must Be Revised to Meet Congressional Intent.
AAR is concerned about several aspects of Special UAFRs, which differ from
Standard UAFRs because they require federal involvement and are the only type of UAFR
that prohibit UAS operations. First, FAA explains “[u]nder proposed § 74.6, facilities owned
or operated by federal security or intelligence agencies or the Department of War, as well
as designated fixed site facilities endorsed by federal security or intelligence agencies, the
Department of War, or at the discretion of the Administrator may be eligible for a Special
UAFR when supported by a security assessment demonstrating credible risks.”22 But
nowhere in section 2209 did Congress require federal ownership or sponsorship for an FSF
designation. As FAA recognizes, the law was revised several times since its inception in
22 NPRM at 24651 (emphasis added).
13

2016, without ever adding such a requirement. Instead, revisions to the law were made to
incorporate more types of applicants that were not federal in nature. Therefore, no federal
involvement should be required for a Special UAFR.
Second, Congress intended any type of applicant to be allowed to request
prohibitions or restrictions of UAS operations near FSFs, not just FSFs that are federal or
federally sponsored. As stated in the text of section 2209 “[t]he procedures shall allow
operators or proprietors of fixed site facilities to apply for designation” and the attendant
prohibitions or restrictions.23 Any UAFR should be allowed to be requested by any entity
that operates or is the proprietor of an eligible FSF, as defined in section 2209.24 Therefore,
to comply with the statute, FAA should allow operators and proprietors of statutorily
defined FSFs to apply for Special UAFRs, or any UAFR that prohibits UAS operations,
without federal sponsorship.
VI. Requiring Notice and Comment for Every Application is Overly Burdensome.
FAA’s proposal requires that every application by an operator or proprietor of an FSF
go through a 30-day notice-and-comment process. The proposed process is quite
burdensome on the government, applicants, and other stakeholders. Nor does the statute
require a notice-and-comment rulemaking for every application. In the interest of time,
resources, and administrative efficiency, AAR suggests a different approach.
23 FESSA, section 2209(b)(1)(B).
24 FESSA, section 2209(b)(1)(B),(C).
14

Specifically, FAA would make a determination that an FSF should receive a
designation and identify the UAS prohibitions and/or restrictions for such FSF, among other
terms of the designation. FAA would then publish that UAFR designation and the operator
or proprietor’s application for public review and objection. FAA would allow for objections
to be made within a stated timeframe—AAR suggests 15 days. If no objections are
received, the designation would take effect on a date certain with no further action from
FAA. If an objection is received, the FAA can then rule on the objection within a certain
timeframe—AAR suggests a short timeframe as well, e.g., 10 or 15 days.25 The UAFR would
not go into place until the adjudication of the objection is completed. Such a process
would provide greater certainty for the applicant and stakeholders, while conserving FAA
resources.
VII. FAA Should Allow Applicants to Batch or Bundle Applications.
Section 2209, under the heading “Requirements,” mandates that “[t]he procedures
shall allow operators or proprietors of fixed site facilities to apply for designation
individually or collectively.”26 Railroads, like other critical infrastructure operators and
proprietors, own and operate numerous eligible FSFs across their nationwide network.
Many of the FSFs owned or operated by the same applicant may require a designation and
for similar reasons. As such, railroads, and other applicants, should be able to bundle or
25 A similar type of process is utilized by another government agency for a variety of purposes. See 49 CFR
Parts 1150, 1152, 1182 (establishing the Surface Transportation Board’s exemption process for a variety of
transactions, including construction, operating, abandonment, discontinuance, acquisition, merger, and change of
control transaction in the surface transportation industries).
26 FESSA, section 2209(b)(1)(B)(emphasis added).
15

batch their applications for different FSFs in one application. Revising the rule to allow for
bundling will meet the congressional intent to allow applications “collectively.”
Similarly, one operator or proprietor may have dozens of FSFs, and thereby dozens
of notices in the Federal Register. This would create an unnecessarily complex process.
The simple allowance of bundling or batching of applications will save time and resources
for the agency, as well, because it would only need to publish one notice for the whole
batch or bundle of applications. Other interested stakeholders also would not have to
monitor the Federal Register for multiple applications but could comment (or object if
AAR’s suggestion above is adopted) one time. FAA should revise the final rule to allow one
application to include multiple FSFs for designation.
VIII. Providing the Security-related Information Required Under this Proposal to FAA
Could Create a Cyber Target for Bad Actors.
Proposed section 74.64 requires applicants for a UAFR to provide to FAA the FSF’s
“unmanned aircraft system security and incident response plans” and “provide a
description of the security perimeter(s), as defined in § 74.1, if not included in the
unmanned aircraft system security and incident response plans.”27 It is not yet clear how
this provision will be implemented, since the “form and manner acceptable to the
Administrator” has yet to be determined.28 As such, AAR cautions that if this provision is
meant to require applicants to send this detailed security information to the FAA
27 NPRM at 24687 (proposed section 74.64.).
28 Id.
16

electronically, then the federal government is creating a target for bad actors to exploit.
Unfortunately, even some of the federal government’s most secure agencies have been
victims of a cybersecurity breach.29 Therefore, FAA should carefully consider how much
information it will require to be submitted to and stored by FAA electronically. FAA could
allow the most sensitive documents and information about an FSF to be maintained by the
applicant for FAA review at a physical location. The final rule should also establish clear
safeguards and cybersecurity standards governing the secure submission procedures,
encryption requirements, and other cybersecurity safeguards that would prevent
unauthorized access or disclosure of sensitive FSF information.
IX. The Transiting Notification Timeframe is Too Vague.
If FAA maintains its proposal to allow UAS to transit Standard UAFRs, it should be
more precise on the notification provided to the operator or proprietor of the FSFs. AAR
agrees that the FSF operators and proprietors must “have situational awareness of lawful
unmanned aircraft activity in the UAFR.”30 AAR believes the best way of doing so would be
29 See, e.g., DiMolfetta, David, “Hackers breached DHS information-sharing network, people familiar say”,
NextGov/FCW (June 30, 2026)(reporting that hackers targeted the Homeland Security Information Network servers
and a SharePoint system for collaborative efforts among federal, state, local, territorial, tribal, international and
private-sector partners); De Luce, Dan, et al., “FBI labels suspected China hack of law enforcement data 'a major
cyber incident'”, NBC News (Apr. 2, 2026)(acknowledging the FBI was breached by a suspected Chinese cyber
intrusion); Lyngaas, Sean, “US officials issue ‘emergency’ cybersecurity order after hackers breach at least one
government agency”, CNN (Sep. 26, 2025)(explaining that U.S. cyber officials issued an "emergency directive"
Thursday ordering federal agencies to defend their networks against an "advanced" group of hackers that have
breached at least one agency in an apparent espionage campaign.); Kapko, Matt, “Twins with hacking history
charged in insider data breach affecting multiple federal agencies“, Cyberscoop (Dec. 3, 2025)(noting individuals
who hacked the State Department in 2015 also were charged with compromising data from multiple federal
agencies including the Department of Homeland Security, Internal Revenue Service, and the Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission).
30 NPRM at 24678.
17

to require UAS operators to receive the FSF’s operator or proprietor’s permission prior to
transiting the UAFR.
In the alternative, if permission-only access is not incorporated into the final rule,
FAA should require a specific timeframe for notice prior to transiting the UAFR. Under
proposed section 74.255, the rule requires that notice to the FSF owner be made “as soon
as reasonably possible in advance of the operation” and if the operation is by or on behalf
of the government or law enforcement then notice “must be provided verbally as soon as
reasonably possible and written notification within seven calendar days.”31 AAR suggests
that written notice of any transiting of the UAFR should be made prior to the UAS transiting
the FSF. Specifically, notification should be made as soon as possible but not later than 7
days prior to transiting the UAFR, absent extraordinary circumstances. This would allow
FSF operators/proprietors to have awareness of when to expect UAS activity, and aid in
distinguishing between lawful and unauthorized UAS operations around the FSF. For
railroads in particular, this would help them identify those bad actors utilizing UAS to assist
in cargo theft.
X. There is No Need for a Full Reapplication Every 5 Years.
The proposal caps the term of a UAFR at five years.32 The proposed rules allow for
renewals for periods of an additional five years, and the draft advisory circular implies that
31 Id. at 24691.
32 See id. at 24690 (proposed section 74.200).
18

the renewal will require another rulemaking process to re-approve the UAFR.33 This is too
burdensome and will inundate the agency and stakeholders with multiple rulemakings
every five years—assuming the FAA maintains one rulemaking for every application as
proposed. AAR suggests that FAA should allow for a five-year renewal as a matter of right,
assuming there are no changes to the UAFR. FAA should adopt a process whereby once
the renewal is requested, FAA notifies the public of such request and that it will be
renewed.
XI. Enforcement Should Be Allowed Through Geofencing.
The NPRM proposes that violations of a UAFR may be enforced through criminal and
civil penalties, depending on the violation and type of UAFR. Technology exists, however,
that would allow for boundaries of approved UAFRs to be enforced through geofencing.
Having technology enforce the rules, rather than having FSFs operators and proprietors
record and report unauthorized UAS access, would reduce the number of unauthorized
incursions, while giving UAS operators confidence that they will not unwittingly incur fines
or penalties for unauthorized incursions into UAFRs.
CONCLUSION
AAR appreciates FAA’s efforts to move the section 2209 rulemaking forward.
Modification of the final rule in accordance with the comments above will ensure the final
33 FAA, Draft Advisory Circular, Restrict the Operations of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed
Site Facility, p. 23 (May 6, 2026) (explaining the process and noting that “[i]f approved, FAA will issue an NPRM and
a new effective date will be established with the Final Rule.”).
19

rule meets Congressional intent, while safely and securely integrating UAS into the national
airspace.
Respectfully submitted,
J. Frederick Miller Jr.
Theresa Romanosky
Counsel for the Association
of American Railroads
425 Third Street, SW
Washington D.C. 20024
(202) 639-2500

Docket No. FAA-2026-4558; RIN 2120-AL33

Dear Federal Aviation Administration Docket Operations:

The Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) appreciates the work the Federal Aviation
Administration (FAA) has put into this long-awaited rulemaking and the attention you’ve given
to the threat drones pose to critical infrastructure, including state prisons. It’s clear a great deal of
effort went into designing a process for flight-restricted airspace, and we value the opportunity to
offer feedback from a corrections perspective. Our goal is to help ensure the final rule works on
the ground, for the staff who must respond to drone activity in real time, and for the facilities that
face these threats every day.

The Drone Threat at TDCJ

At TDCJ, drone activity isn’t a hypothetical concern. It’s become a significant security issue that
directly affects our employees and the people in our custody. Drones are being used to move
cellphones, drugs, and other contraband over secure perimeters and into areas where they can do
real harm.

Our mission is to provide public safety, promote positive change in offender
behavior, reintegrate offenders into society, and assist victims of crime.

Huntsville, Texas 77342-0099

Page 2

Where the Proposed Rule Needs Adjustment for Prisons
Standard UAFRs Still Allow Overflight

Under the Standard UAFR, a drone can legally fly over a prison as long as it broadcasts Remote
ID, moves through quickly, and notifies the facility. Individuals using drones for contraband
won’t notify us, and fast overflight is still overflight. The secure perimeter is where drops occur,
and the proposed structure leaves that vulnerability in place.

Prisons need an airspace designation that actually blocks unauthorized operations overhead.
Prisons Should Be Eligible for Special UAFRs

The Special UAFR is the only tier that gives facilities control over who can fly into their
restricted airspace. As written, it’s largely limited to federal sites unless a facility has a federal
sponsor, which state corrections agencies do not currently have.

We ask FAA to allow state prisons to qualify for Special UAFRs and to designate Department of
Justice (DOJ) as the sponsoring agency. DOJ already partners with corrections under the SAFER
SKIES Act and aligning these federal frameworks would make sense for everyone involved.

Multi-Facility Applications Are Essential for a Statewide System

TDCI operates 104 facilities across a large state. Submitting one application per facility would
create a substantial administrative burden that doesn’t reflect how corrections systems actually
function.

Section 2209 allows operators to apply “individually or collectively.” A true multi-facility
application pathway would make this rule workable for statewide correctional agencies.

FAA Should Align This Rule With SAFER SKIES

Congress has already made clear that drones can pose credible threats to correctional facilities
under the SAFER SKIES Act. FAA’s rule should reflect this reality. Granting mitigation
authority while permitting routine overflight of correctional facilities is contrary to the intent of
the SAFER SKIES ACT and diminishes the effectiveness of that authority.

If Only a Standard UAFR Is Granted, Perimeter Approval Should Still Be Required

Even if a facility receives only a Standard UAFR, drones that want to pass directly over a secure
perimeter should need approval from the facility. That change alone would significantly reduce
contraband drops and improve staff safety.

Our mission is to provide public safety, promote positive change in offender
behavior, reintegrate offenders into society, and assist victims of crime.

Closing Thoughts

We appreciate FAA’s work on this rule and the recognition that state prisons are part of the
critical infrastructure landscape. Our requests are straightforward and aimed at making the rule
practical and effective:

* Allow correctional facilities to obtain Special UAFRs with DOJ as sponsor
e Provide a collective, multi-facility application option

e Require facility approval for perimeter overflight under Standard UAFRs

e Align the FAA rule with SAFER SKIES credible-threat realities

moves toward finalization.

RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558 — Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned
Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility (Section 2209 NPRM)

To Whom It May Concern:

The Clark County Water Reclamation District (CCWRD) appreciates the opportunity to
comment on the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM)
establishing a process for operators of critical infrastructure and fixed-site facilities to request
Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) pursuant to Section 2209 of the FAA Extension,
Safety, and Security Act of 2016. CCWRD strongly supports the proposed rule and encourages
the FAA to ensure that publicly owned wastewater treatment and collection system facilities are
clearly recognized as eligible critical infrastructure facilities under the final rule.

Importance of Wastewater Infrastructure

CCWRD operates wastewater treatment, conveyance, pumping, and reclaimed water facilities
that serve millions of residents and visitors throughout Southern Nevada. These facilities are
essential to public health, environmental protection, economic stability, and regional water
resource resilience. Disruption, damage, or unauthorized interference with wastewater operations
could have significant consequences, including impacts on public health, water quality, water
availability, critical services, and the local economy.

Wastewater utilities are widely recognized as critical infrastructure by the U.S. Department of
Homeland Security and are integral components of the nation's Water and Wastewater Systems
Sector. Given their importance, wastewater treatment plants, pump stations, lift stations, control
centers, and associated infrastructure should be eligible for consideration under the Section 2209
UAFR framework.

Documented Drone Activity Near Facilities

CCWRD has experienced numerous unauthorized unmanned aircraft incidents at its facilities. In
many documented instances, critical infrastructure and heavy equipment located near a radio-
controlled aircraft flying area have been struck by unmanned aircraft. Unauthorized personnel
have broken into facilities to retrieve unmanned aircraft that have crashed into the facilities’
structures or otherwise within the secure walls of the facilities, damaging infrastructure and
jeopardizing safety. Several of these incidents have nearly resulted in serious bodily harm to
District workers and contractors. These incidents clearly demonstrate that wastewater

infrastructure is not immune from drone incursions and the potential for accidental or intentional
impacts is real. Concerns remain over the use of drones or other unmanned aircraft by bad actors
for surveillance of critical facilities searching for vulnerabilities. Section 2209 NPRM would fill
that gap for enforcement assistance.

Support for Standard UAFRs for Wastewater Facilities

CCWRD supports the proposed Standard UAFR framework, which balances infrastructure
protection with legitimate aviation activities. We believe the proposed approach appropriately
allows certificated operators to conduct authorized operations under applicable FAA regulations
while restricting recreational and unauthorized drone activity in close proximity to sensitive
facilities.

Wastewater treatment plants and critical collection facilities frequently contain critical
operational assets necessary for the collection, conveyance, treatment, and discharge of
wastewater. Unauthorized drone operations over these facilities create safety, security, and
operational concerns that warrant access to the protections envisioned by the proposed rule.

Recommendation for Explicit Inclusion

CCWRD encourages the FAA to explicitly clarify in the final rule, guidance materials, or
application process that publicly owned wastewater utilities and related collection, conveyance,
pumping, and treatment facilities qualify as eligible critical infrastructure facilities under the
Water and Wastewater Systems Sector. Clear eligibility criteria will provide consistency
nationwide and avoid uncertainty for local governments and utility operators seeking to protect
critical public infrastructure.

Additional Recommendation

CCWRD recommends that the FAA recognize wastewater treatment plants, major pump stations,
collection infrastructure, control centers, and reclaimed water facilities as facilities
presumptively eligible for Standard UAFRs due to their designation within the Water and
Wastewater Systems Sector and their critical role in protecting public health and the
environment, and preserving essential water resources. This would reduce administrative burden
on both applicants and the FAA while advancing the security objectives of Section 2209.

Conclusion

CCWRD strongly supports implementation of Section 2209 and the establishment of a practical
process for critical infrastructure owners and operators to request UAFRs when justified by
documented risk and operational need. Wastewater facilities provide essential services that

directly affect public health, environmental protection, and community resilience. The FAA
should ensure these facilities are clearly eligible to seek protection under the final rule.

and security of the National Airspace System while protecting critical infrastructure.

BONNEVILLE POWER ADMINISTRATION FESSA 2209 Memorandum
MEMORANDUM FOR FAA
FROM: Bonneville Power Administration – Office of Security and Continuity of Operations
DATE: Aug 5, 2026
SUBJECT: Public Comments for FAA Proposed Rule on Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions
(FESSA 2209)
Comment #1: Clarify the Application of UAFRs to Linear Critical Infrastructure
• Subject: Application of "Fixed-Site Facility" Definition to Transmission Corridors.
• Reference: § 74.1, Definition of "Fixed site facility"; § 74.58 "Lateral boundary".
"The Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) supports the FAA's initiative to establish a process
for creating Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs). However, we urge the FAA to clarify
how this rule can be applied to protect linear critical infrastructure, which is a foundational
component of the nation's energy grid. The current definition of a 'fixed-site facility' and the
requirement that a UAFR's lateral boundary not exceed the applicant's property boundary (§
74.58) creates a significant security gap. Restricting UAS activity only at substations leaves
thousands of miles of critical transmission lines exposed to surveillance, attack, or interference.
We recommend that the FAA amend the rule to include a mechanism for designating
UAFRs for critical transmission corridors. This could be achieved by: 1) Defining 'corridor' as
a type of fixed-site facility for the purposes of this rule, and 2) Allowing the lateral boundary for
such corridors to be defined by the established right-of-way or a specified standoff distance,
rather than being strictly limited to a traditional property boundary. This is essential for securing
the bulk electric system."
Comment #2: Expand Energy Sector Eligibility Criteria to Include Functionally Critical
Assets
• Subject: Energy Sector Eligibility Criteria.
• Reference: § 74.88 "Energy sector."
BPA commends the FAA for including specific criteria for the Energy Sector but believes
that relying solely on physical metrics like voltage thresholds or generation capacity is
an incomplete method for assessing criticality. This approach overlooks assets whose
strategic importance is defined by their function in grid reliability and emergency
restoration.
For example, BPA operates and relies upon:
1. Facilities Housing Medium Impact Cyber Assets: A number of our 230 kV
substations are classified under NERC CIP-006 as housing Medium Impact Bulk
Electric System (BES) Cyber Systems. An incident at these sites could enable a
significant cyber-physical event.
2. Black Start and Grid Reconstitution Resources: We maintain designated
resources essential for ‘black start’ capabilities, which are indispensable for
restoring the grid following a wide-area outage and ensuring power to other
critical facilities, such as the Columbia Generating Station nuclear plant.
We strongly recommend the FAA expand the eligibility criteria in § 74.88 to include
facilities identified as critical based on their function. This should explicitly include: a)
Substations housing Medium Impact BES Cyber Systems as defined by NERC CIP
FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY Page 1

BONNEVILLE POWER ADMINISTRATION FESSA 2209 Memorandum
standards, and b) Facilities designated by a Balancing Authority as a critical black start
resource necessary for system-wide grid reconstitution."
Comment #3: Revise the "Demonstration of Need" to Account for Inherent Risk
• Subject: Requirements for Demonstrating Need (§ 74.66(a)).
• Reference: § 74.66(a) "Existing unmanned aircraft traffic patterns."
"BPA supports requiring applicants to demonstrate a need for a UAFR. However, we have
concerns regarding the emphasis on documenting 'existing unmanned aircraft traffic patterns.'
For an entity like BPA, which manages infrastructure across vast and remote territories,
comprehensively documenting all unauthorized UAS activity is not operationally feasible. The
absence of documented incursions should not be misinterpreted as an absence of risk.
We recommend the FAA revise the 'Demonstration of Need' criteria to give greater weight
to the inherent vulnerability and criticality of the asset. The rule should explicitly state that
for nationally critical infrastructure, a UAFR may be justified based on a credible security
vulnerability assessment alone, even without documented historical UAS activity. The potential
consequences of a single successful incident are severe enough to warrant proactive
protection."
Comment #4: Provide Flexibility for the Remote ID Sensing Requirement
• Subject: Mandated Protective Security Measure for Remote ID Sensing.
• Reference: § 74.56(d) "Protective security."
"BPA agrees that Remote ID is a vital tool for airspace awareness. However, the proposed
requirement in § 74.56(d) for each facility to have a dedicated RID sensing capability could
impose significant costs and logistical challenges for entities with numerous sites, potentially
creating a barrier to participation.
We recommend the FAA provide greater flexibility in how applicants can meet the RID
sensing requirement. The final rule should allow for alternative and scalable compliance
methods, such as: 1) A networked system of receivers providing regional coverage; 2) The use
of mobile or portable sensing systems; or 3) The use of data from FAA-qualified UAS Service
Suppliers (USS) to satisfy the monitoring requirement. This flexibility would achieve the FAA's
goal of airspace awareness while allowing infrastructure owners to implement the most efficient
and cost-effective solutions."

Re: Docket No. FAA-2026-4558— Designation—Restrict the Operation of Unmanned Aircraft in
Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility
The Data Center Coalition (DCC) submits these comments in response to the Federal Aviation
Administration’s (FAA) notice of proposed rulemaking published May 6, 2026, proposing to implement
section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA).
DCC is the membership association for the U.S. data center industry, representing leading data center
owners and operators, as well as companies that lease large amounts of data-center capacity. DCC’s
member companies provide the digital infrastructure that supports the applications, capabilities, and
essential services that enable the modern economy, including cloud computing and artificial intelligence
(AI). DCC member companies are making significant, multi-billion-dollar investments in U.S. data center
infrastructure, and they drive immense contributions to U.S. employment, labor income, gross domestic
product, and government tax revenues1.
DCC supports the FAA’s mission to ensure the safety and security of the national airspace and
appreciates the agency’s attention to the drone threat facing data center facilities. We write to raise
concerns about several aspects of the proposed rule that, if left unaddressed, would inadvertently create
security risks and significantly limit the rule’s effectiveness for the data center industry.
I. Risks to Data Centers from Unauthorized and Malicious Drone Activity
Data centers house the cloud platforms, financial transaction systems, healthcare databases,
communications networks, and AI infrastructure that underpin the American economy. Their physical
footprints, including cooling infrastructure, power systems, and networking equipment, present a
meaningful risk to drone surveillance and activity.
There are a number of legitimate uses of drones including by our own facilities in monitoring physical
security, inspections, and construction, as well as recognized, legitimate commercial delivery businesses.
However, unauthorized drones pose significant risks to data centers. An unauthorized drone operating
over a data center facility can conduct reconnaissance of physical security details, identify cooling and
power vulnerabilities, conduct surveillance on fiber entry points and network operations areas, and
potentially possess capabilities able to inflict physical damage to infrastructure. A deliberate attack on a
major data center or interconnected facility could disrupt financial systems, healthcare platforms,
communications networks, and government operations simultaneously.

A formal process for requesting flight restrictions over data center facilities is long overdue. DCC urges
the FAA to finalize a rule that is operationally effective and addresses the significant risks that malicious
drone use poses to the data center industry.
II. Definition of Covered Facilities
Under the proposed rule, data centers may qualify for a UAFR as covered facilities under either the
Communications Sector (for facilities that underpin other interconnected services, if certain conditions are
met, or contain peak traffic throughput of at least 1 terabit per second, see § 74.83); or (ii) the Information
Technology Sector at proposed § 74.93.
The Information Technology sector definition includes the following:
 Data center hosting cross-sectoral data or platform dependencies (e.g., software, cloud platforms,
federal systems, Infrastructure as a Service providers) where a loss, degradation, or compromise
of such services could have a debilitating impact on national security, defense, or continuity of
critical government operations;
 Data center underpinning interconnected services where disruption could result in regional or
national-level debilitating impact to multiple downstream sectors;
 Internet exchange point and collocated data centers that contain peak traffic throughput of at least
1 terabit per second (Tbps); or
 Exposed long-haul fiber-optic cables at data centers where a loss, degradation, or compromise of
such networking infrastructure could have a debilitating impact on national security, defense, or
continuity of critical government operations. § 74.93.
DCC appreciates that the FAA included data centers explicitly in both sectors. To ensure full coverage of
risks, DCC recommends that the FAA define “debilitating impact” in this section to include effects on
other critical infrastructure, including financial systems and healthcare. This would also better match the
criteria in the Communications sector, which covers a facility underpinning interconnected services
“where disruption could result in regional or national-level debilitating impact to multiple downstream
sectors ( e.g., financial systems, healthcare, energy grid supervisory control and data acquisition systems,
national security systems, network operations centers).”
More broadly, the DCC recommends a consistent definition of “debilitating impact” across the two
sectors that recognizes the risk of debilitating impact on financial systems, healthcare platforms, the
defense industry, and enterprise applications, which could in turn have significant downstream economic
or national security effects.
III. Process and Criteria Concerns
Owner/Proprietor Concurrence and Implications for Leaseholders
The Applicant and Facility Information section of the NPRM requires that all operators or proprietors
with a legal interest in the property, including lessors, and other third parties, reach consensus before a
UAFR application can be submitted. This requirement may be unworkable for parts of the commercial
data center industry.
A significant number of hyperscale and colocation data centers operate on leased land or leased facilities
and are granted authority to put in place security measures, without having to return for permission from

the lessor, let alone each and every property entity that may have a legal interest in the property, in order
to do so. This rule would effectively override carefully negotiated contractual agreements and require
leaseholders to get affirmative permission to engage in needed security measures, even if they are not
otherwise required to under the terms of their leases or other applicable contracts. Requiring unanimous
concurrence among all parties with a potential property interest before an application can proceed
imposes a significant burden.
DCC Recommendation:
 Clarify that a leaseholder with operational control of a facility can apply for a UAFR without
requiring sign-off from a non-operating property owner.
Vulnerability, Consequences of Exploitation, and Security Plan Details
The rule asks for detailed information about vulnerabilities, consequences if those vulnerabilities are
exploited, and details regarding facilities’ security plans. This is highly sensitive information that could
potentially give malicious actors a road map of key weaknesses and how to most effectively target
facilities.
DCC Recommendation:
 Create a self-certification and attestation requirement regarding vulnerabilities, consequences,
and sensitive details about security plans. Owners and operators could also be required to retain
specific information that FAA could inspect on demand.
 To the extent that any security-related information is shared with the FAA, it should be subject to
strong security protections, use and access limitations, and protections from public disclosure.
The DCC is concerned that the proposed rule does not include discussion of these critical
elements.
Historical Drone Traffic Data: Demonstration of Need
The proposed rule requires applicants to share detailed data on drone operations over their facility during
the previous 24 months, where available. Specifically, the proposed rule asks for information on the type
of unmanned aircraft operation, if known; identify whether the operator is known to the operators or
proprietors; and quantify the total number of operations not associated with the facility itself.
Most commercial data center operators do not have this kind of detailed information on historical drone
activity. To the extent that the FAA deems this information important, and a core element on which it
makes its approval decisions, new data centers and others that do not have this kind of granular historical
data would be effectively excluded from key protections.
Moreover, the drone industry is rapidly evolving, with drone use expanding and technology evolving at
an exponential rate. The rapid proliferation of low-observable, high-precision autonomous systems—
such as “dark drones” that bypass traditional radio frequency detection—means that historical localized
activity is no longer a reliable indicator of future safety. Thus, even if available, it is not evident that two-
year-old data is particularly telling or useful in making determinations about current flight requests. With
modern aerial threats defined by precision capabilities rather than static geographic track records, reliance
on historical logs fails to account for sudden changes in a facility's vulnerability profile.
DCC Recommendation:

 Limit the request for historical data to 12 months (at most), acknowledge that data may not be
able to be collected by commercial means, allow for more general descriptions of the kinds of
drone activity, and clarify that an absence of documented drone activity does not weigh against an
applicant, consistent with the proposed rule’s own statement that light traffic does not preclude a
finding of need.1
IV. Notice and Comment Process
The proposed rule would require each Standard UAFR to go through notice-and-comment rulemaking,
subsequent to conditional approval, and prior to final approval. DCC has two primary concerns about this
framework.
First, the Federal Register notice-and-comment process will publicly identify facilities that have been
conditionally approved for a UAFR, based on a finding of vulnerability and need. This will effectively
create a map of vulnerable facilities that are not yet protected, putting a target on the back of these
facilities. This is a significant security risk for the data center industry that could have national security
implications if the facility hosts defense entities or government agencies’ data and applications.
Second, the DCC is concerned that the notice-and-comment requirement will significantly delay the
issuance of UAFRs, given the multiple steps required to publish a notice in the Federal Register and then
gather, review, and adjudicate comments.
Moreover, there are alternative, more secure ways to achieve the intended goals of the notice and
comment process. The proposed process appears to be modeled after the notice and comment process
used to close airspace to commercial, manned aviation. But such notices do not create a mapping of
critical infrastructure vulnerabilities; closures of airspace to manned aviation also have a much more
significant impact on rights and interests than limits on the use of unmanned aircraft systems flying below
400 feet.
Rather than an advance notice and comment period, the FAA should create a post-UAFR issuance process
for those negatively affected to seek modification or rescission. This would protect against the significant
costs to public safety that would result from publishing what is effectively a map of yet-unprotected
critical infrastructure.
DCC Recommendations:
 Post-issuance publication only: Publish notice of the UAFR on a FAA website after the
restriction is in effect, so that UAS operators and software manufacturers can identify restricted
airspace.
 Post-issuance challenge process: Establish a petition-for-reconsideration mechanism allowing
affected third parties (commercial UAS operators, real estate interests, municipalities) to seek
1 See Federal Aviation Administratoin, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Designation-Restrict the Operation of
Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility at 260 (May 6, 2026),
https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-08943/p-260 (“Whether a facility has heavy or light unmanned aircraft
traffic would not be used to determine whether a fixed facility has vulnerabilities to UAS; rather, it is a factor FAA
would consider in the balance for ensuring use of airspace. For example, FAA understands that some facilities might
experience very light unmanned aircraft traffic; however, its unique vulnerabilities may lead FAA to conclude that a
UAFR is warranted. Similarly, a facility may report significant unmanned aircraft traffic, but without demonstrating
a vulnerability to those operations, FAA may conclude that the applicant has not demonstrated a need.”)

modification of issued UAFRs based on demonstrated impact. This preserves due process without
the security risks of pre-issuance publication.
 Withholding of Sensitive Identifying Information: Establish a formal mechanism in the final
rule allowing UAFR applicants to request that specific identifying details (such as precise
geographic coordinates, site names, and exact physical boundaries) be withheld from public
registers and the public-facing FAA website. Instead, the FAA should use generalized airspace
boundaries on aeronautical charts to prevent creating a curated target list of high-value sites for
malicious actors.
V. Protections for Standard UAFRs/Special UAFR Process
The two-tier framework between Standard and Special UAFRs creates a meaningful protection gap.
Special UAFRs operate similarly to the ways that most TFR’s currently operate. They require affirmative
approval for a UAS to operate in restricted airspace – thus enabling critical infrastructure owners to
manage and protect the airspace. Special UAFRs, however, will likely be difficult to obtain, even for data
centers that handle sensitive data or are otherwise strategically important. Special UAFRs are only
available if requested by a federal agency or otherwise authorized by the FAA Administrator. In practice,
this will require a strong relationship with a federal sponsor.
By contrast, standard UAFRs contain multiple exceptions, including for a wide range of commercial and
recreational drones, so long as they provide advance notice to the FAA, transit the area in the shortest
amount of time practicable, and broadcast a Remote ID. As a result, data center operators will have little
say in whether or when such drones fly over their facility. Additionally, they will have limited authority
to restrict commercial or recreational drones that might conflict with safety or security operations. And
they will have no remedy if a malicious actor abides by the relatively simple requirements of advance
notice, shortest transit route, and Remote ID broadcast, in order to do reconnaissance on a facility.
Conversely, the rules also appear to restrict data centers in the operation of their own drones for safety,
security, and inspection. Even the data centers own drones are, for example, subject to the requirement
that they transit the area in the shortest time practicable. This would make it challenging for data centers
to use drones for an array of critical safety and security purposes.
DCC Recommendation:
 Require commercial and recreational drones that seek transit airspace covered by a standard
UAFR to obtain advance, affirmative approval by the covered facility’s owner or manager.
 At a minimum, DCC recommends that the FAA limit standard UAFR transit to operators
transiting for public safety reasons or in case of emergency.
VI. Facility-Authorized Operations and Emergency Protections
The proposed rule does not create a process for critical infrastructure owners and operators to pre-approve
and thus deploy their own approved drones for the myriad safety, security, and inspection uses currently
being conducted by drones. To the contrary, even facility-owned and operated drones and state and local
public safety drones appear to be subject to the same requirements as other drones, including that they
transit the facility in the least time practicable.
DCC Recommendation:

 Establish a process for identifying facility-approved drones that can operate without being subject
to the “shortest transit” time requirement and without having to notify the FAA of each and every
operation. This list should also include federal, state, local, tribal and territorial UAS used for
public safety purposes that should similarly be exempted from otherwise-applicable requirements.
 The FAA should replace the manual “web-form” notification portal with automated, digital
notifications and the option to utilize network remote ID, which has the capability to automate
and eliminate the need for fixed site facilities to manually coordinate aircraft identification
information that would have been received through the UAFR Module. This allows for
streamlined notifications and the ability to detect network remote ID drones further away from
the facility than broadcast remote ID’s RF receiver capabilities.
 The final rule should exempt authorized facility-operated or third-party contracted flights (such as
security patrols and infrastructure inspections, as well as construction monitoring flights) from
standard UAFR transit restrictions. Specifically, an operator pre-authorized by the facility
owner—whose aircraft or Remote ID is registered on the facility's internal approved list—should
be permitted to operate within the UAFR airspace without being subject to "shortest transit" time
limitations or being required to file separate flight notifications with the FAA for each individual
flight.
VII. Timing
Lastly, although the underlying statute requires UAFR applications to be adjudicated within 90 days,
unless the applicant is provided with written notice describing the reason for the delay, the NPRM does
not establish timelines for FAA review. Clear timelines for each stage of the process would help operators
plan and integrate UAFR applications into their broader security planning.
Conclusion
DCC appreciates the FAA’s focus on protecting data centers as a key designated facility type under this
framework and is committed to working with the agency to ensure the rule is both operationally effective
and accessible to the full range of commercial data center operators. DCC looks forward to continued
engagement and is available to provide additional technical input as the agency finalizes the rule.
Respectfully,
The Data Center Coalition
Patrick Konrath
Senior Manager, Federal Affairs
Data Center Coalition
patrick@datacentercoalition.org

August 5, 2026 SUBMITTED ELECTRONICALLY
The Honorable Bryan K. Bedford

Dear Administrator Bedford,
Comments on the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) Designation-Restrict the Operation
of Unmanned Aircraft in Close Proximity to a Fixed Site Facility (Docket No. FAA-2026-4558)
The Metropolitan Water District of Southern California (Metropolitan) is pleased to provide
comments on the United States Department of Transportation (DOT) and the Federal Aviation
Administration (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) for the establishment of
Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFR), dated May 6, 2026 (hereinafter referred to as the
UAFR NPRM).
Metropolitan supports the UAFR NPRM as a starting framework to protect critical infrastructure,
ensure public safety, and enable law enforcement to efficiently distinguish lawful from unlawful
unmanned aircraft system(s) (UAS) operations around high-value facilities. As a large regional
water provider in southern California with extensive aerial operations and a network of critical
facilities, Metropolitan has direct interest in the safe and secure use of airspace near its assets.
To support Section 2209 of the FAA Extension Safety and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA), the
development of Part 74, and to assist in establishing FAA-approved criteria for operators or
owners of fixed-site facilities applying for a UAFR, Metropolitan submits the following
comments pertaining to specific sections within Part 74, with a focus on §74.96—water and
wastewater sector, one of the 16 critical infrastructure sectors identified by the FAA as eligible to
request a UAFR.
I. Background
Metropolitan is a regional water wholesaler that delivers about two million acre-feet of water
annually to 26-member public agencies, which in turn directly or through their retail agencies
provide water to approximately 19 million people in southern California. As the largest
distributor of treated drinking water in the United States, Metropolitan's service area covers
approximately 5,200 square miles across Los Angeles, Orange, San Diego, Riverside, San
Bernardino, and Ventura counties. In addition, Metropolitan operates a range of facilities,
700 N. Alameda Street, Los Angeles, California 90012 (cid:120) Mailing Address: Box 54153, Los Angeles, California 90054-0153 (cid:120) Telephone (213) 217-6000

Federal Aviation Administration
August 5, 2026
Page 2
including the Colorado River Aqueduct, 15 hydroelectric plants, nine reservoirs, over 830 miles
of large-scale pipes, and five water treatment plants. Under the Critical Infrastructure Protection
Act of 2001, Metropolitan’s 85 water and energy facilities qualify as critical infrastructure,
defined as systems and assets so vital to the nation that their incapacitation or destruction would
have a debilitating impact on security, national economic security, national public health or

II. Discussion of Proposed Rule (Section V)
The FAA proposes to establish a new Part 74 in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations,
creating a process for certain fixed-site facilities to request a UAFR. Section V of the UAFR
NPRM outlines the components of Part 74, including the types of facilities eligible to apply for a
UAFR, the information applicants must submit, and how the FAA will evaluate these requests. It
also addresses the terms and conditions that would apply once a UAFR is approved.
Metropolitan provides the following focused comments on specific aspects of Section V of the
UAFR NPRM.
(cid:120) Section V.B.1. General Provisions - Definitions (§74.1). Metropolitan supports
including natural features and procedural or system-based boundaries within the
definition of “security perimeter,” recognizing that large regional systems rely heavily on
nonphysical boundaries.
(cid:120) Section V.C.9. Demonstration of Need (§74.66) - Existing Unmanned Aircraft (UA)
Traffic Patterns. Metropolitan agrees that existing UA traffic patterns should not be
dispositive of the need for a UAFR. The unavailability of UA aircraft traffic data and
whether such data reveals heavy or light traffic, should not be determinative.
(cid:120) Section V.E.1. FAA Evaluation, Approvals, and Denials - Evaluation (§74.100). The
proposed evaluation procedures aim to streamline UAFR application processing but do
not expedite consideration of higher consequence facilities. Given the severe
consequences of disruption at major wholesale water systems, the FAA should prioritize
applications from such facilities with documented incidents and allow a staggered
application window that does not delay high risk applicants.
(cid:120) Section V.G.3. Term, Amendments, Renewal, Modification, and Cancelation of
UNFR- Renewal (§74.210). Metropolitan supports the renewal timeline but seeks
clarification on when new applications would be required if renewals are not processed
before expiration.
III. Water and Wastewater Systems Sector Requirements (§74.96).
The FAA, in collaboration with the Sector Risk Management Agencies (SRMAs), assessed
various facility types across sixteen sectors to identify those that may warrant a UAFR. To be
eligible to request a UAFR, facilities within these sectors must meet specific operational
criteria. Section V.D. of the UAFR NPRM outlines the eligibility requirements for each of the
identified sectors and includes additional questions FAA is requesting from each sector to refine
the determination criteria for limiting UAFRs.
To support the FAA in establishing criteria for the water and wastewater sector, Metropolitan
offers the following responses to the FAA's questions outlined in Section V.D.16 - Water and
Wastewater Sector (§74.96) of the UAFR NPRM.

Question 1: What types of drinking water and wastewater systems should be considered in
development of gating criteria?
The FAA should consider the full range of drinking water infrastructure components that, if
compromised, could produce cascading consequences for public health and regional stability.
These include:
(cid:120) Active surface water treatment plants and filtration facilities — where contamination or
operational disruption would have immediate downstream impacts.
(cid:120) Raw water intake structures and diversion points — exposed, difficult to harden, and highly
vulnerable to surveillance or physical interference.
(cid:120) Large-capacity pumping stations — critical for system pressure and flow management across
regional distribution networks.
(cid:120) Open reservoirs, storage facilities, and aquifer spreading grounds — inherently difficult to
enclose and directly accessible to airborne intrusion.
(cid:120) Aqueducts, canals, and conveyance infrastructure — which traverse large geographic areas
and present extended attack surfaces.
(cid:120) SCADA systems, electrical substations, high-voltage transformers, and solar generation
fields — supporting systems whose compromise could disable water delivery at scale.
(cid:120) Bulk chemical and hazardous waste storage areas, chemical unloading facilities, tank farms
and associated rail facilities — and other concentrated stores of treatment chemicals that, if
accessed, surveilled, or targeted, could enable contamination, theft, or catastrophic release.
(cid:120) Liquid oxygen (LOX) storage tanks — for ozone disinfection at many plants posing
significant hazard if subjected to airborne interference or hostile reconnaissance.
Gating criteria should not be limited to facilities that are enclosed or traditionally “secured.” The
open, distributed nature of water infrastructure requires a broader definitional scope than may
apply to other sectors.
In addition to physical and cyber threats, FAA should explicitly recognize the emerging risks
posed by drone-enabled psychological and disinformation operations. Unauthorized UAS
equipped with cameras or livestreaming tools can disseminate staged or misleading imagery
suggesting water contamination or system failure. Even when such imagery is fabricated or
manipulated, it can cause widespread public alarm, disrupt emergency operations, and erode
longstanding trust in drinking water safety. Such impacts may arise without the drone ever
making physical contact with infrastructure, making reputational and behavioral harm a discrete
threat vector warranting UAFR protection.
Metropolitan requests clarification that FAA’s statutory references to “public interest” and public
health include psychological impacts. Misperceptions about water quality can be difficult to
reverse and may persist long after the underlying threat is resolved. Recognizing psychological
harm as a cognizable public health consideration would strengthen the regulatory basis for
UAFR designation for facilities at heightened risk of such operations.
