Question 2: What are the characteristics of drinking water and wastewater systems that should
be considered in development of gating criteria?
The FAA should weigh the following facility characteristics in developing threshold criteria:
(cid:120) Population impact potential — recognizing that disruption to facilities serving large or dense
populations has amplified downstream consequences;
(cid:120) System interdependence and redundancy — facilities that serve as single points of failure
within a regional system carry elevated consequence profiles, as well as functional recovery
time to restore full service;
(cid:120) Operational exposure — prioritizing open-air infrastructure (reservoirs, canals, intake
structures) which is inherently more vulnerable to drone-enabled threats than enclosed
facilities and should receive equal or greater weighting than built footprint alone;
(cid:120) Presence of hazardous materials and impacts to public health and safety — treatment
chemicals, including chlorine and ammonia compounds, present dual-use concerns if
accessed or targeted by adversaries;
(cid:120) Critical customer dependencies — facilities that supply hospitals, military installations, or
other critical sectors multiply the consequence of any disruption; and
(cid:120) Prior threat history — documented unauthorized UAS activity or other security incidents
should factor into risk-tiering.
Question 3: Should population served by a drinking water or wastewater system be considered
in development of gating criteria, and if so, what are appropriate population thresholds?
No. While population served may be a useful metric for smaller, discrete water systems, it is not
an appropriate or practical primary gating criterion for large regional wholesalers that serve
entire metropolitan areas. Metropolitan’s 5,200 square mile service area is so extensive that
applying a population threshold would provide little meaningful differentiation and would
introduce administrative and operational complexity disproportionate to its value. For large
regional systems, the FAA should instead rely on facility level characteristics—such as the
criticality of a specific asset, its operational exposure, its function within the regional distribution
network, and the consequences of its disruption. These facility specific criteria, as discussed
throughout this letter, offer a far more accurate and workable basis for determining UAFR
eligibility.
The FAA should also avoid establishing population thresholds that inadvertently exclude
wholesalers or regional authorities whose service populations are dispersed across multiple
member agencies rather than served directly.
Question 4: Should critical customers served by a drinking water or wastewater system be
considered in development of gating criteria?
Yes. Critical customer dependencies materially elevate risk and should be weighted heavily.
Facilities serving critical infrastructure sectors present consequences that far exceed what
population numbers alone can capture. More specifically, the FAA should consider defining
“critical customers” broadly to include:
(cid:120) Hospitals, trauma centers, and dialysis facilities;
(cid:120) Military bases and defense installations;
(cid:120) Emergency services facilities (fire, law enforcement, emergency communications);
(cid:120) Other critical infrastructure operators (energy, transportation, communications); and

Question 5: Should a history of unauthorized drone flight over a drinking water or wastewater
system be considered in development of gating criteria?
Yes. Documented unauthorized UAS activity should be treated as an escalating factor. However,
the absence of observed incidents should not be interpreted as evidence of low risk; many
overflights go undetected due to limited monitoring capabilities.
Metropolitan supports developing a standardized, national mechanism—coordinated with DHS
and EPA—for reporting UAS incidents at water facilities. FAA should also allow applicants to
rely on regional or local law enforcement detection histories rather than requiring each utility to
maintain independent capabilities. This approach recognizes variations in resources while
ensuring high risk facilities are not undervalued.
Metropolitan also requests clarification regarding §74.20 obligations after a UAFR is granted—
including whether the FAA’s web-based portal will serve as a unified reporting mechanism,
whether incident reports will generate real-time alerts to law enforcement, and whether updates
will be required per incident or on a recurring schedule.
IV. UAFR NPRM General Comments.
Metropolitan provides the following focused comments pertaining to other sections of the UAFR
NPRM.
Section I. Executive Summary.
Section I.F. What Happens After the UAFR Goes Into Effect. The FAA seeks comments on
additional requirements for flyover operators after the UAFR goes into effect. Because Bluetooth
based Remote ID has limited range and is susceptible to circumvention, Metropolitan encourages
the FAA to require more robust broadcast technologies and stronger operator notification
requirements in proximity UAFR facilities.
Section II. Authority for this Rulemaking. Metropolitan acknowledges that the source of
FAA’s rulemaking authority includes matters of “public interest” including public health
impacts. Metropolitan requests explicit confirmation that FAA’s public health authority includes
psychological impacts, as previously noted in response to Question 1.
Section III. Background and Statement of the Problem.
Section III.B.4. FAA Capability Gap. Metropolitan agrees that existing tools available to the
FAA and law enforcement are not sufficient to address safety and security problems posed by
drone operators with malicious intent or willful disregard for the rules. The DOT and FAA
should strive to establish clear, uniform protocols for engaging law enforcement during active
unauthorized UAS incursions. Without actionable deconfliction procedures, perhaps through the
establishment of a UAS incursions task force, a UAFR designation provides limited operational
value.

V. Recommendation for a Mid-Tier UAFR Designation for Large Regional Water
Systems
Metropolitan encourages the FAA to establish a Mid-Tier UAFR designation tailored
specifically to large regional water systems. Large regional water systems operate expansive,
open air, and distributed facilities that face greater exposure than typical fixed site infrastructure.
A Mid-Tier UAFR would give the FAA a practical way to tailor protections for systems whose
risks exceed those addressed by the Standard designation. This tier could be structured to: :
(cid:120) Prioritize application processing for high consequence regional systems; and to reduce
asset vulnerabilities, eliminate the public notice and comment period;
(cid:120) Allow the submittal of coordinated, systemwide, or multifacility applications for closely
integrated infrastructure;
(cid:120) Provide more practicable and efficient methods for allowing buffer zones by defining
lateral boundaries where multiple adjacent properties or public rights of way are involved;
(cid:120) Streamline the Demonstration of Need to reflect sector specific risk characteristics rather
than requiring asset-by-asset vulnerability showings;
(cid:120) Designate these applications as categorically exempt under NEPA since the rule mainly
applies airspace procedures. (Section 5-6, FAA Order 1050.1F, July 16, 2015.);
(cid:120) Allow flexible compliance pathways for Remote ID sensing, including collaboration with
local and state law enforcement partners; and,
(cid:120) Provide simplified and streamlined renewal and amendment procedures appropriate for
large systems with evolving operational footprints.
These targeted refinements would provide a more proportionate and workable pathway for large
water systems while remaining consistent with Section 2209 and the overall structure of Part 74.

Metropolitan looks forward to continuing, constructive engagement with the DOT and the FAA

I oppose the FAA's proposed rule establishing Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions (UAFRs) for certain fixed-site facilities. While the FAA states that restrictions would be granted only when necessary for aviation safety, the protection of people and property, national security, or homeland security, the proposal would also make facilities within the food and agriculture sector eligible to seek these restrictions.

As drafted, the rule could provide some of the nation's largest industrial animal agriculture operations and slaughterhouses with a powerful tool to shield their activities from public scrutiny. The FAA has not demonstrated that drones pose a unique or widespread safety or security threat to factory farms or slaughterhouses that would justify restricting access to the airspace above them. Without such evidence, the proposal risks serving not legitimate aviation or security purposes but the suppression of documentation that is often critical to public accountability.

Drone photography and videography have become important tools for journalists, researchers, advocates, and community members seeking to document conditions that would otherwise remain hidden from public view. Aerial footage has exposed environmental and animal welfare problems at industrial agricultural facilities, including flooded manure lagoons following natural disasters, mass animal culling operations during disease outbreaks, and the true scale of concentrated animal feeding operations. It has also revealed misleading marketing claims. In one notable case, aerial footage helped document conditions at an egg producer whose facilities were marketed as providing "free-roaming" conditions, contributing to a class action settlement alleging consumers had been misled.

The public has a significant interest in understanding how food is produced, particularly when agricultural operations can affect nearby communities through water pollution, air pollution, disease outbreaks, waste management failures, and animal welfare concerns. Drone footage often provides information that cannot be obtained from public roadways and would be unavailable if facilities successfully obtained broad flight restrictions. Reducing transparency would make it more difficult for journalists, researchers, consumers, and affected residents to identify and report potential violations of environmental, consumer protection, and animal welfare laws.

The FAA should carefully consider the First Amendment and public accountability implications of this proposal. The rule should not be used to create no-observation zones around private facilities simply because operators wish to avoid criticism, negative publicity, or independent documentation of their operations. If the agency moves forward with the rule, it should explicitly exclude facilities whose primary justification relates to reputational concerns and should require a clear, evidence-based showing of genuine aviation safety, security, or public safety risks before granting any restriction. The FAA should also ensure a transparent application process, public notice of all requests, and meaningful opportunities for public challenge before restrictions are approved.

For these reasons, I urge the FAA to reject the proposed rule or, at minimum, substantially revise it to prevent its use as a mechanism for restricting lawful documentation and public oversight of industrial agricultural operations.

Thank you for considering these comments.
